LaTeX document setup, theorem-environment declarations, notation macros, typography and package configuration. These are authoring metadata, not independent mathematical obligations.

Title, purpose, reading policy and scope: all fifteen authored chapters are in scope, including the five bounded extensions (finite-regularity Morse normal form, regular moving domains, vector potentials, punctured-domain obstructions and curvilinear operators). The 158 editorial families are not a theorem or goal quota. Preserve stated mathematical hypotheses and conclusions; source-proof-only intermediate steps do not create extra deliverables. General measure theory, abstract manifolds, PDE, numerical analysis and Banach calculus are excluded beyond the expressly included Euclidean results.

Conventions throughout: vectors are columns; the total derivative Df(a) is represented by Jf(a)_{ij}=∂_j f_i(a); matrix composition is J(g∘f)(a)=Jg(f(a))Jf(a), as proved in the chain-rule obligation. The Euclidean metric represents df by the gradient. Coordinate wedge covectors satisfy (dx_{i₁}∧⋯∧dx_{i_k})(e_{i₁},…,e_{i_k})=1 for increasing indices. Boundaries use outward-normal-first orientation. The associated mathematical bridges and identities are included in the chapter obligations.

The general Stokes proof is independent of its earlier classical applications. Source-comparison and prior-library inspection notes do not certify new Lean declarations or automatically supply representation bridges.

Declared reusable foundation F1, not a new D04 theorem to reprove: classical sets/functions, finite sums/products, induction and countable choices; the least-upper-bound complete ordered field ℝ; ℂ=ℝ+iℝ as a real two-space. ℕ contains zero, empty products equal 1 and det of the 0×0 matrix is 1. Multivariable topological/analytic results are excluded from this declaration and must be covered by the chapters.

Declared reusable algebra foundation F2, not new D04 obligations: finite-dimensional real/complex linear algebra (bases, dimension, rank-nullity, quotients, duals, multilinear/alternating maps, matrices and basis changes), normalized determinant with product/cofactor/transpose identities and Cauchy–Binet, Cauchy–Schwarz and Gram–Schmidt, the real symmetric spectral theorem and Sylvester inertia, including positivity of positive-definite Gram determinants. Geometric volume transformation, inverse differentiability, surface area, moving frames and variable-coefficient differential-form calculus are expressly excluded; relevant chapter bridges remain required.

Declared reusable one-variable foundation F3: real/complex scalar sequences/completeness, compact real intervals, scalar continuity/uniform continuity/IVT, ordinary differentiation/product/chain rules, Rolle/MVT, finite-regularity scalar Taylor and FTC, interval Riemann Darboux/tagged integrals with algebra/order/norm properties and scalar monotone C1 substitution, uniform limits/tails, exponentials/trigonometry and ordinary derivatives. Finite-dimensional vector uses are componentwise and give no common exact vector MVT point. Multivariable compactness, differentiation/Taylor symmetry, Riemann Fubini/substitution and manifold integration are excluded.

Declared reusable measure-comparison foundation F4 only: standard complete Lebesgue measure on ℝⁿ with axis-box volumes, countable additivity/monotonicity, arbitrarily small countable open-box covers of null sets, measurable sets/functions, integral order/linearity, monotone/dominated convergence and integrability of bounded measurable functions supported in a bounded box. Riemann–Lebesgue agreement, multivariable Jacobian substitution, area/coarea, replacement of Riemann Fubini by measure Fubini, multivariable differentiation, partitions of unity, Poincare and Stokes are not assumed and remain chapter obligations where stated.

Version/evidence policy describes the inspected MathGenome v0.3.0, Lean 4.35.0 and fixed Mathlib release; these provenance statements are metadata, and reuse must check actual types and domain/integrability/coordinate bridges. No new formal acceptance follows from the prose.

For every integer n≥0, R^n is the real function space on {1,...,n}, represented by columns, with standard basis e_j, inner product <x,y>=Σ_j x_j y_j, Euclidean norm ||x||=sqrt(<x,x>), and sup norm ||x||∞=max_j |x_j|. R^0 has its unique vector 0; both its norms and the empty maximum in this definition are 0. Empty matrices represent the unique linear maps of the indicated dimensions. Complex coordinates mean pairs of real coordinates unless a complex-linear statement is expressly made.

For n≥1 and x∈R^n, ||x||∞≤||x||≤sqrt(n)||x||∞. The Euclidean norm obeys the triangle and reverse triangle inequalities, | ||x||−||y|| |≤||x−y||. A sequence in R^n converges iff each coordinate converges, and is Cauchy iff every coordinate sequence is Cauchy. R^n is complete and every bounded sequence has a norm-convergent subsequence. The sequential, completeness and compactness assertions include n=0; the norm comparisons have the stated n≥1 hypothesis.

In R^n, B(a,ρ)={x:||x−a||<ρ} for ρ>0. U is open iff every point has a ball contained in U; F is closed iff its complement is open. Int A consists of points admitting a ball contained in A; cl A consists of points whose every ball meets A; ∂A=cl A\Int A. A relative neighborhood of a∈A contains A∩B(a,ρ) for some ρ>0; a relatively open subset of A is A intersected with an ambient open set. An accumulation point of A has every punctured ball meeting A. This ambient boundary is distinct from manifold boundary.

For subsets of R^n, arbitrary unions and finite intersections of open sets are open. F is closed iff every convergent sequence in F has its limit in F. For every a, a∈cl A iff some sequence in A converges to a; a is an accumulation point of A iff such a sequence can be chosen in A\{a}. Consequently cl A is closed, Int A is open, and ∂A=cl A∩cl(R^n\A) is closed.

For f:A→R^m, A⊂R^n, and an accumulation point a of A, the relative limit lim_{x→a,x∈A} f(x)=b means: ∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 ∀x∈A, 0<||x−a||<δ ⇒ ||f(x)−b||<ε. Continuity at a∈A uses ||x−a||<δ and b=f(a), without puncturing. Uniform continuity on A means δ can be chosen independently of a∈A. Continuity at an isolated domain point is automatic; the accumulation hypothesis for punctured limits rules out vacuity.

For f:A→R^m and an accumulation point a of A, lim_{x→a,x∈A}f(x)=b iff f(x_k)→b for every sequence x_k∈A\{a} with x_k→a. For a∈A, f is continuous at a iff it sends every sequence in A converging to a to a sequence converging to f(a). Such relative limits are unique. A limit or continuity statement with finite-dimensional vector target holds iff it holds in each coordinate, including the zero-dimensional target.

Continuous maps compose. A map on a specified Euclidean domain is continuous iff every ambient open target set has relatively open preimage. Sums, constant scalar multiples, inner products and finite matrix products of continuous maps are continuous. Scalar quotients are continuous wherever the denominator is nonzero.

For f(x,y)=x²y/(x⁴+y²) on R²\{(0,0)}, every line y=mx approaching 0 has limit 0, and f is 0 on the vertical axis. On the punctured parabola y=x², f=1/2. Thus the two-dimensional limit at 0 does not exist despite every straight-line test giving 0. The relative limit on {(x,x²):x>0} is 1/2, whereas the relative limit on the punctured horizontal axis is 0.
K⊂R^n is compact iff every cover by ambient open sets has a finite subcover. It is sequentially compact iff every sequence in K has a subsequence converging to a point of K.
For every Euclidean subset K, compactness, sequential compactness, and closedness plus boundedness are equivalent. The equivalence includes K=∅ and the one-point space R^0.

For any compact K⊂R^n and cover (U_α) of K by relatively open sets, ∃δ>0 such that every nonempty S⊂K of diameter <δ lies in a single U_α. In particular all sufficiently small relative balls lie in cover members (one may take radius <δ/2). Empty K causes no exception.
If K⊂R^n is compact and f:K→R^m is continuous, then f(K) is compact, f is bounded, and f is uniformly continuous. If m=1 and K≠∅, f attains both its minimum and maximum.

For nonempty A⊂R^n define dist(x,A)=inf_{a∈A}||x−a||. For nonempty K,F the set distance dist(K,F) is the infimum of the pairwise distances, equivalently inf_{x∈K} dist(x,F). The source's point-to-set distance notation is restricted to nonempty target sets.

For every nonempty A⊂R^n, x↦dist(x,A) is 1-Lipschitz and its zero set is exactly cl A. If K is nonempty compact, F is nonempty closed and K∩F=∅, then dist(K,F)>0. For every nonempty compact K⊂U with U open there is ρ>0 such that K_ρ={x:dist(x,K)≤ρ}⊂U, and K_ρ is compact. This includes U=R^n, without taking distance to an empty complement. If desired an empty K has empty thickening by a separate convention.

For every norm N on R^n, n≥0, ∃c,C>0 ∀x, c||x||≤N(x)≤C||x||. Thus any two norms on a fixed finite-dimensional real space induce the same limits, topology, compact sets and differentiability remainder conditions. In dimension 0 one may take c=C=1. No infinite-dimensional assertion is included.

A space is connected if it admits no separation into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets. A path in A is a continuous map [0,1]→A; A is path connected iff every pair of points can be joined by one. A polygonal path is a finite concatenation of line segments. A is convex iff it contains every segment joining its points. A path connected space is simply connected iff every loop can be continuously contracted within the space while keeping its basepoint fixed.

Continuous images of connected spaces are connected. Real intervals are connected. Path connected spaces are connected. Every open connected U⊂R^n is polygonally connected, and every convex set is path connected. A continuous real-valued map on a connected space has the intermediate value property. Empty and zero-dimensional cases are allowed by the definitions.

For a∈U define C_a as the union of all connected subsets of U containing a. C_a is the unique maximal connected subset containing a, called its connected component. The components partition U. If U⊂R^n is open, every component is open and polygonally connected. Empty U has no components, and R^0 is included.
For a linear A:R^n→R^m define ||A||=sup_{||v||≤1}||Av||; this equals 0 if n=0. For a k-linear map T use sup ||T(v_1,...,v_k)|| over all ||v_i||≤1. For k=0 the norm is the norm of the value of T.

Every finite-dimensional real linear or multilinear map is continuous and has finite operator norm. Linear maps satisfy ||Av||≤||A||||v|| and ||BA||≤||B||||A||. If A=(a_ij) has m,n>0, max_{i,j}|a_ij|≤||A||≤sqrt(Σ_{i,j}a_ij²)≤sqrt(mn)max_{i,j}|a_ij|. Hence operator-norm convergence and continuity of linear-map-valued functions are equivalent to coordinate convergence and continuity. Analogous coordinate equivalences hold at each fixed multilinear order, including the zero-dimensional cases with empty coefficient arrays.

Bibliographic comparison and proof-origin notes for Chapter 1; the distinction between another source's closed-bounded compactness convention and this manuscript's open-cover convention is explanatory. No additional mathematical obligation is introduced.

Chapter 2 standing hypotheses: U⊂R^n is open, n,m≥0, and f:U→R^m. Openness provides sufficiently small increments in every direction. These are hypotheses of the chapter's mathematical entries, not an additional theorem.

Under U⊂R^n open and f:U→R^m, define ∂_v f(a)=lim_{t→0}(f(a+tv)−f(a))/t when it exists; ∂_j f=∂_{e_j}f. Total differentiability at a means there is a linear A:R^n→R^m with f(a+h)=f(a)+Ah+r(h), r(0)=0, and ||r(h)||/||h||→0 as h→0 through nonzero available increments. Write Df(a)=A and r(h)=o(||h||). For arbitrary subsets the relative remainder condition uses only available increments and is a separate condition which need not uniquely determine A.

For f:U→R^m, U⊂R^n open, the total derivative at a is unique; differentiability implies continuity and ∂_v f(a)=Df(a)v for all v. For f=(f_1,...,f_m), total differentiability is equivalent to that of every component. The standard-column matrix is Jf(a)_ij=∂_j f_i(a); a proposed matrix J is the matrix of the total derivative iff h↦Jh gives the small-remainder condition. For scalar f the gradient is the column ∇f(a) uniquely characterized by Df(a)h=<∇f(a),h>. All claims include n=0 and m=0.

On S={(x,0):x∈R}, the function f(x,0)=x satisfies the relative linear-approximation condition at zero with both A_1(h)=h_1 and A_2(h)=h_1+h_2. At an isolated domain point every linear map satisfies that relative condition. Thus the open-domain uniqueness conclusion does not hold for arbitrary relative domains.

For open U⊂R^n and V⊂R^m, f:U→V differentiable at a and g:V→R^p differentiable at f(a), g∘f is differentiable at a and D(g∘f)(a)=Dg(f(a))∘Df(a), equivalently J(g∘f)(a)=Jg(f(a))Jf(a) in standard column bases. No continuity of either derivative near its basepoint is assumed. Dimensions may be zero.
Bibliographic comparison note concerning the chain-rule proof and zero inner increments; it adds no obligation.

Linear maps between finite-dimensional real spaces have themselves as derivatives. Derivatives commute with finite sums and constant scalar multiplication. If B:E×F→G is fixed bilinear and u,v on a common open Euclidean domain are differentiable at a, then x↦B(u(x),v(x)) is differentiable at a and D(B(u,v))(a)h=B(Du(a)h,v(a))+B(u(a),Dv(a)h). This includes scalar and matrix multiplication, inner products, and the R³ cross product, with the written order retained.

If a scalar q on an open Euclidean domain is differentiable at a and q(a)≠0, then it is nonzero on a neighborhood of a, its scalar reciprocal is defined near a and differentiable at a, and D(q^(−1))(a)h=−Dq(a)h/q(a)². If u is a vector-valued map differentiable at a, D(u/q)(a)h=Du(a)h/q(a)−u(a)Dq(a)h/q(a)². The reciprocal is scalar, not entrywise matrix inversion.

Let [a,b]⊂U⊂R^n, f:U→R^m continuous on the segment and differentiable at every interior segment point in an ambient open neighborhood. If ||Df(x)||≤M at all those interior points, then ||f(b)−f(a)||≤M||b−a||. For scalar f and a≠b there is t∈(0,1) with f(b)−f(a)=Df(a+t(b−a))(b−a). The inequality includes zero-length segments and zero endpoint differences. A common exact intermediate point need not exist for vector targets.
For differentiable f on a convex open Euclidean set, ||Df||≤M makes f M-Lipschitz. On a connected open set, Df=0 everywhere implies f is constant. Every C¹ map is locally Lipschitz.

For f:U→R^m, U⊂R^n open, if each ∂_j f exists throughout a neighborhood of a and each such derivative map is continuous at a, then f is totally differentiable at a, with columns ∂_j f(a). If all first partials exist and are continuous on U, then the total derivative exists everywhere and x↦Df(x) is continuous. The assertions include n=0.

For maps on an open finite-dimensional real domain, C⁰ means continuous; recursively f∈C^{r+1} iff f is differentiable everywhere and x↦Df(x), with values in Hom(R^n,R^m), is C^r, for r a nonnegative integer. C^∞ means C^r for every finite r. Mere existence of derivatives omits the continuity requirement. Real analyticity means local representation by a convergent power series; C^∞ alone makes no analyticity assertion.

For every finite integer r≥1, f is C^r on an open Euclidean domain iff every iterated coordinate partial of each order ≤r exists and is continuous; the order of iteration is retained prior to a symmetry theorem. Finite sums, fixed multilinear operations, composition, and scalar quotients with nowhere-zero denominator preserve C^r, including r=0 and r=∞.

For f∈C¹(U,R^m), U⊂R^n open, and [a,a+h]⊂U, f(a+h)−f(a)=∫_0^1 Df(a+th)h dt. A continuous vector function on a compact interval is integrated by its finitely many scalar Riemann integrals, and its integral obeys ||∫v||≤∫||v||.
Define u(0,0)=0 and u(x,y)=xy/(x²+y²) away from the origin. Its two coordinate partial derivatives at 0 equal 0, but it is discontinuous there, since its restriction to y=x away from 0 is 1/2.

Define v(0,0)=0 and v(x,y)=x³/(x²+y²) elsewhere. It is continuous, with |v(x,y)|≤||(x,y)||. Every directional derivative at 0 exists; in nonzero direction (a,b) it equals a³/(a²+b²), which is not linear in (a,b), as seen from (1,0),(0,1),(1,1). Thus v is not totally differentiable at 0.

Define w(0,0)=0 and w(x,y)=x³y/(x⁴+y²) elsewhere. It is continuous, with |w(x,y)|≤|x|/2. Every directional derivative at 0 is 0, so these assemble to the zero linear map, yet w is not totally differentiable there. For b≠0, w(ta,tb)/t=t a³b/(t²a⁴+b²)→0; for b=0 the quotient is 0. Along (x,x²), w=x/2 and w(x,x²)/||(x,x²)|| does not tend to 0.

For z:R→R defined by z(0)=0 and z(x)=x² sin(1/x) for x≠0, z is differentiable at 0 with z'(0)=0, whereas for x≠0, z'(x)=2x sin(1/x)−cos(1/x), which does not tend to 0. Thus total differentiability does not imply continuity of the partial derivatives.
Chapter 2 proof-origin and bibliographic comparison notes; they introduce no additional result.

The space of k-linear maps (R^n)^k→R^m carries its operator norm. Put D⁰f=f. Identify the derivative of x↦D^k f(x) with a (k+1)-linear map by D^{k+1}f(a)[v_0,v_1,...,v_k]=(D(D^k f)(a)v_0)[v_1,...,v_k], using the actual finite-dimensional linear coordinate identification. A map is k times differentiable at a iff successive derivative maps through order k−1 are defined on a neighborhood and the last is differentiable at a, recursively at lower orders; no continuity of the top derivative on a neighborhood is required. Write T[h^k]=T[h,...,h], and T[h⁰]=T.

If all first coordinate partials of f exist in a neighborhood of a and each map ∂_i f is totally differentiable at a, then ∂_j∂_i f(a)=∂_i∂_j f(a) for all coordinate indices i,j. In particular every twice totally differentiable map at a has this crossed-partial symmetry. No neighborhood continuity of second derivatives is assumed; finite-dimensional vector targets are included.
Bibliographic note for the pointwise crossed-partial theorem; no additional obligation.

If f is k times totally differentiable at a, the k-linear differential D^k f(a) is symmetric, and its values on standard basis tuples are the corresponding ordered kth coordinate partials. Hence for C^k maps these partials do not depend on their order. For scalar f define H_f(a)_ij=∂_i∂_j f(a); then D²f(a)[u,v]=uᵀH_f(a)v and D²f(a)[h,h]=hᵀH_f(a)h. The quadratic Taylor term is (1/2)hᵀH_f(a)h. Orders 0 and 1 have vacuous permutation symmetry.

Whenever the indicated derivatives exist along a segment in an open Euclidean domain, the line restriction F(t)=f(a+th) has F^{(j)}(t)=D^j f(a+th)[h^j]. For every symmetric j-linear map T, j≥1, the polynomial p(x)=T[x^j]/j! is differentiable with Dp(x)v=T[v,x^{j−1}]/(j−1)!.

For integer k≥1, if f is k times totally differentiable at a in the recursive pointwise sense, then f(a+h)=Σ_{j=0}^k D^j f(a)[h^j]/j!+o(||h||^k). In particular C^k regularity on a neighborhood suffices, but neighborhood continuity of the top derivative is not assumed in the pointwise theorem. For k=0 the conclusion f(a+h)=f(a)+o(1) requires just continuity at a.

For integer k≥1, f∈C^k(U,R^m), U⊂R^n open, and [a,a+h]⊂U, f(a+h)=Σ_{j=0}^{k−1}D^j f(a)[h^j]/j!+(1/(k−1)!)∫_0^1(1−t)^{k−1}D^k f(a+th)[h^k]dt. Thus the remainder R_k after the degree-k Taylor polynomial equals (1/(k−1)!)∫_0^1(1−t)^{k−1}(D^k f(a+th)−D^k f(a))[h^k]dt. If f∈C^{k+1}, the alternative is R_k(a,h)=(1/k!)∫_0^1(1−t)^k D^{k+1}f(a+th)[h^{k+1}]dt. This last formula also holds for k=0 and is the segment FTC. Integrals are finite coordinatewise scalar Riemann integrals.
Bibliographic comparison of Taylor formulas, with explanatory remarks about vector targets and finite regularity; no additional mathematical obligation.

For k≥0, f∈C^{k+1}(U,R^m), [a,a+h]⊂U, and ||D^{k+1}f(x)||≤M on that segment, ||R_k(a,h)||≤M||h||^{k+1}/(k+1)!. For scalar f and h≠0 there is t∈(0,1) such that R_k(a,h)=D^{k+1}f(a+th)[h^{k+1}]/(k+1)!. Under the same scalar C^{k+1} hypotheses, if every order-(k+1) coordinate partial has absolute value ≤C on the segment, then |R_k(a,h)|≤C(Σ_i|h_i|)^{k+1}/(k+1)!≤C n^{(k+1)/2}||h||^{k+1}/(k+1)!. In dimension 0 there is no nonzero increment and the remainder is zero.

For compact K⊂U⊂R^n with U open, f∈C^k(U,R^m), k≥1, there exist ρ>0 and ω:[0,ρ]→[0,∞) with ω(s)→0 as s↓0 such that for every a∈K and ||h||≤ρ, the whole segment [a,a+h] lies in U and ||R_k(a,h)||≤ω(||h||)||h||^k/k!. If f∈C^{k+1}, there is also a uniform finite M with ||R_k(a,h)||≤M||h||^{k+1}/(k+1)! on all those segments. For k=0 the uniform assertion is uniform continuity (uniform vanishing of the order-zero remainder around compact K). Empty K is allowed and makes the assertions vacuous.

For n≥0 a multi-index is α∈N^n with 0∈N. Define |α|=Σ_i α_i, α!=Π_i α_i!, h^α=Π_i h_i^{α_i}; ∂^α denotes the coordinate partial of those multiplicities where symmetry applies. Define P^k_{f,a}(h)=Σ_{j=0}^k D^j f(a)[h^j]/j!. For n=0 there is exactly one empty multi-index, with degree 0, factorial 1 and monomial 1, giving the constant polynomial on the one-point domain.

For every symmetric order-j differential D^j f(a), including j=0, (1/j!)D^j f(a)[h^j]=Σ_{|α|=j}(∂^α f(a)/α!)h^α. Hence the multilinear and multi-index Taylor polynomials coincide. The identity includes empty tuples and n=0 under the prescribed conventions.

For maps k times totally differentiable at the basepoint (continuous when k=0), the Taylor polynomial of a sum is the sum of its Taylor polynomials. For a fixed bilinear operation it is that operation applied to the two Taylor polynomials with every term of total degree greater than k discarded. If f(a)=b, f and g are C^k near their respective basepoints, and k≥1, then P^k_{g∘f,a}(h)=[P^k_{g,b}(P^k_{f,a}(h)−b)]_{≤k}. For k=0 composition records its value. Under the same finite differentiability for a scalar denominator q with q(a)≠0, the reciprocal Taylor polynomial is computed by this truncated arithmetic with nonzero constant term. These identities include the zero-dimensional input space.

Set f(0,0)=0 and f(x,y)=xy(x²−y²)/(x²+y²) elsewhere. Then f is C¹, Df(0)=0, and |f(x,y)|≤|xy|≤||(x,y)||²/2. Its first derivatives away from 0 are homogeneous of degree 1 and bounded on the unit circle, hence continuous at 0. Along the axes ∂_x f(0,y)=−y and ∂_y f(x,0)=x. Therefore ∂_y∂_x f(0)=−1 while ∂_x∂_y f(0)=1: existence of these iterated partials does not supply twice total differentiability or the hypotheses of a second-order Taylor formula.

The scalar function f(0)=0, f(x)=exp(−1/x²) for x≠0 is C^∞, with every derivative at 0 equal to 0, and is positive elsewhere. Away from 0 each derivative is a polynomial in 1/x times exp(−1/x²); for every integer N, |x|^(−N)exp(−1/x²)→0 as x→0. Every finite Taylor polynomial at 0 vanishes, and the function does not agree locally with its Taylor series, so smoothness does not imply analyticity.

With n=m=1 the chapter's Taylor statements specialize to the one-variable Taylor formulas. The order-zero theorem is continuity. No exact vector Lagrange-remainder theorem holds in general: such a theorem already for degree 0 would imply the false common-point vector mean-value equality. The pointwise, segment-integral and compact-uniform results retain their separate regularity hypotheses.

Let A:R^n→R^n be invertible and let B be another linear map. If q=||A^(−1)(B−A)||<1, then B is invertible, B^(−1)=Σ_{j=0}^∞(−A^(−1)(B−A))^j A^(−1) (operator-norm convergent), ||B^(−1)||≤||A^(−1)||/(1−q), and ||B^(−1)−A^(−1)||≤||A^(−1)||²||B−A||/(1−q). Consequently GL(n,R) is open in the matrix space and matrix inversion is continuous. For n=0 the unique matrix is invertible with determinant 1, and all claims use the one-point matrix space and zero operator norms.
For every n≥0, inv:GL(n,R)→GL(n,R), A↦A^(−1), is C^∞, and its derivative at A applied to an arbitrary matrix H is D inv(A)H=−A^(−1)HA^(−1). The zero-dimensional case is included.

Let S be a nonempty complete subset of a Euclidean space with its induced metric. If T:S→S satisfies ||T(x)−T(y)||≤q||x−y|| for a fixed 0≤q<1 and every x,y∈S, then T has exactly one fixed point x_*. For every x_0∈S, iterates x_{j+1}=T(x_j) converge to x_*, and for every integer j≥0, ||x_j−x_*||≤q^j||x_1−x_0||/(1−q). For every x∈S, ||x−x_*||≤||x−T(x)||/(1−q). Closed subsets of R^n, in particular closed balls, are complete. The convention q⁰=1 includes q=0.

For U⊂R^n open, f∈C^r(U,R^n), r∈{1,2,...}∪{∞}, a∈U and Df(a) invertible, there exist open neighborhoods X⊂U of a and Y of f(a) such that f:X→Y is a bijection whose inverse g:Y→X is C^r. Every Df(x), x∈X, is invertible and Dg(y)=(Df(g(y)))^(−1). The inverse is locally unique among maps with values in X and can be chosen Lipschitz. Quantitatively, if ρ>0, closed B(a,ρ)⊂U, A=Df(a), and ||I−A^(−1)Df(x)||≤q<1 on this closed ball, then every y with ||A^(−1)(y−f(a))||<(1−q)ρ has exactly one preimage in that closed ball, and it lies in the open ball. For every two such y,z, ||g(y)−g(z)||≤||A^(−1)(y−z)||/(1−q). All claims include n=0.
Bibliographic and proof-route comparison for the inverse theorem; the comparison source's stronger quantitative derivative hypotheses are explicitly not assumed. No extra obligation.
If U⊂R^n is open, f∈C^r(U,R^n) for r≥1 finite or ∞, f is injective, and Df(x) is invertible for every x∈U, then f(U) is open and the bijection f:U→f(U) has a C^r inverse.

Let W⊂R^p×R^q be open, G:W→R^q be C^r for r≥1 finite or ∞, (a,b)∈W, G(a,b)=c and D_yG(a,b):R^q→R^q invertible. There exist open neighborhoods A of a and B of b with A×B⊂W and a unique C^r map φ:A→B such that ∀(x,y)∈A×B, G(x,y)=c iff y=φ(x). Moreover φ(a)=b, the solved-variable block D_yG(x,φ(x)) is invertible throughout A, and Dφ(x)=−(D_yG(x,φ(x)))^(−1)D_xG(x,φ(x)). These blocks belong to the same total derivative. The statement includes q=0 (unique map to R^0) and p=0 (local uniqueness of the solution point).
Bibliographic comparison and explanatory notes about product neighborhoods and finite C^r regularity; no new obligation.

Let f:U⊂R^n→R^m be C^r on an open domain, r≥1, and suppose rank Df(x)=k on a neighborhood of a∈U. Then 0≤k≤min(n,m), and there are local C^r coordinate diffeomorphisms Φ in the source and Ψ in the target with Φ(a)=0, Ψ(f(a))=0, such that (Ψ∘f∘Φ^(−1))(u_1,...,u_n)=(u_1,...,u_k,0,...,0) wherever this local composition is defined. Rank is assumed constant on a neighborhood, not just at a. The cases k=0, k=n, k=m and zero source or target dimensions use the corresponding empty blocks.

Let U⊂R^n be open, g:U→R^q be C^r, r≥1, M=g^(−1)(c), and a∈M with Dg(a) surjective. Then q≤n and after a coordinate permutation a relative neighborhood of a in M is the graph {(u,φ(u)):u∈A}, with A⊂R^{n−q} open and φ C^r. The graph map θ(u)=(u,φ(u)) is an injective regular parametrization and a homeomorphism onto this relative neighborhood; at each graph point Dθ(u)(R^{n−q})=ker Dg(θ(u)). This space is exactly the set of velocities at that point of C¹ curves in M defined on an open interval about 0. If all points of M are regular, the graph charts give M an embedded C^r manifold structure of dimension n−q, with C^r chart transitions. For q=0 the level is U; for q=n it is locally a point with zero tangent space; empty levels make the pointwise assertions vacuous.

For a C^r map on an open Euclidean domain, r≥1, a submersion at a means Df(a) is surjective, equivalently its scalar component differentials are linearly independent. Near a it has local C^r projection normal form (u,v)↦u. An everywhere submersion is an open map, without any claim of surjectivity onto the whole target. An immersion at a means Df(a) is injective. Near a it has local C^r inclusion normal form u↦(u,0) and is an embedding on a neighborhood (a homeomorphism onto its image with relative topology). An immersion need not be globally injective or a global embedding.

The map f:R²→R², f(x,y)=(e^x cos y,e^x sin y), has Jacobian determinant e^{2x}>0 everywhere and local inverses, but is 2π-periodic in y, hence has no global inverse on R²; its image omits 0. The scalar map x↦e^x is an everywhere submersion with proper open image (0,∞). The immersion t↦(cos t,sin t) is locally an embedding but periodic, so is not globally injective or an embedding.
The function x↦x³ is bijective R→R despite its derivative vanishing at 0. Its inverse is not differentiable at 0, since differentiability of both inverses there would make the chain rule give 1=0.

The function x↦x² has derivative rank 0 at 0 but is not constant on any neighborhood of 0, and therefore does not admit the rank-0 constant-rank normal form near 0. A rank hypothesis only at one point does not suffice.

For f:R→R given by f(0)=0 and f(x)=x/2+x²sin(1/x) for x≠0, f is differentiable at 0 with f'(0)=1/2 but is not one-to-one on any neighborhood of 0. Away from 0, f'(x)=1/2+2x sin(1/x)−cos(1/x), taking value −1/2 at arbitrarily small positive points with 1/x an even multiple of π and 3/2 at those with 1/x an odd multiple. Thus derivative continuity cannot simply be dropped from the stated inverse function theorem.
Bibliographic comparison notes for examples and the provided constant-rank and regular-level proofs; no additional mathematical obligation.

For f:S→R and a∈S, a relative local minimum means ∃ρ>0 ∀x∈S∩B(a,ρ), f(x)≥f(a); it is strict if the inequality is strict for x≠a. A global minimum uses every x∈S; maxima reverse inequalities. A stationary or critical point of a differentiable function on an open domain has Df(a)=0. A saddle point means that every neighborhood of a contains feasible points with both value >f(a) and value <f(a). Every notion retains its indicated feasible set; a boundary extremum need not be ambient stationary.

Every continuous real function on a nonempty compact feasible set attains its global minimum and maximum. If f is differentiable on an open neighborhood of a and has an unconstrained local extremum at a, then Df(a)=0. At a relative local extremum, Df(a) vanishes on the velocity of every two-sided differentiable feasible curve through a. For a feasible curve γ defined only for t≥0, at a minimum Df(a)γ'(0)≥0; at a maximum Df(a)γ'(0)≤0.

If f is twice totally differentiable at an interior point a, then a local minimum implies Df(a)=0 and D²f(a)[v,v]≥0 for every v; a local maximum implies Df(a)=0 and nonpositive Hessian quadratic form. Conversely if Df(a)=0 and the Hessian is positive definite, then a is a strict local minimum, and in positive dimension ∃c,ρ>0 ∀||h||<ρ, f(a+h)≥f(a)+c||h||². Negative definiteness at a stationary point gives a strict local maximum with the corresponding quadratic upper bound. An indefinite Hessian implies a is a saddle point, even without a stationary-point assumption (a nonzero first derivative already supplies both signs). Semidefiniteness alone is insufficient for a strict-extremum or saddle classification. In dimension 0 the sole point is both a strict relative minimum and maximum, vacuously, and there is no nonzero increment for growth tests.
Bibliographic comparison and note that the second-order tests use twice total differentiability, not an unstated smoothness assumption. No extra obligation.

Let U⊂R^n be open, f:U→R and g:U→R^q be C¹, and a∈M=g^(−1)(c) a relative local extremum of f. If Dg(a) is surjective, there is a unique covector λ∈(R^q)*, represented by λ_1,...,λ_q, such that Df(a)=λ∘Dg(a), equivalently ∇f(a)=Σ_{i=1}^q λ_i∇g_i(a). With the fixed convention L_λ(x)=f(x)−Σ_i λ_i g_i(x), DL_λ(a)=0. These are necessary, not sufficient or existence, conditions. For q=0 this reduces to Fermat; for q=n the feasible point is locally isolated and the unique multiplier still exists.

Let f:U→R and g:U→R^q be C² on open U⊂R^n, a∈M=g^(−1)(c), Dg(a) surjective, and Df(a)=λDg(a). Hold λ fixed and put L_λ=f−λg. At a constrained local minimum D²L_λ(a)[v,v]≥0 for every v∈ker Dg(a); a maximum reverses this inequality. If the restriction is positive definite, a is a strict constrained local minimum with quadratic growth in ambient distance: ∃c,ρ>0 ∀x∈M∩B(a,ρ), f(x)≥f(a)+c||x−a||². Negative definiteness gives the corresponding strict maximum and upper growth bound. If the restricted form takes both signs, every neighborhood contains feasible points with both greater and smaller value than f(a). When n−q=0, M is locally a single point and both strict relative extrema hold vacuously.

In the constrained second variation λ is its value at a and is held constant while differentiating x. The relevant quadratic form is the restriction of H_f(a)−Σ_i λ_i H_{g_i}(a) to ker Dg(a). This specifies the Lagrangian-Hessian interface; using H_f alone or requiring definiteness on the whole ambient space is not the stated test.

Let U⊂R^n be open and f:U→R, g:U→R^q, h:U→R^s be C¹. Set S={x∈U:g(x)=c and h_i(x)≥0 for 1≤i≤s}. For a∈S set I={i:h_i(a)=0}. Assume all covectors Dg_j(a), together with Dh_i(a) for i∈I, are linearly independent. If a is a relative local minimum on S, there are unique equality multipliers λ_j and active multipliers μ_i such that Df(a)=λDg(a)+Σ_{i∈I}μ_iDh_i(a), with each μ_i≥0. Extend by μ_i=0 for inactive indices; then μ_i h_i(a)=0 for every i. The Lagrangian convention is L=f−λg−Σ_i μ_i h_i. For a maximum apply the assertion to −f. The case I=∅ is the equality-constraint rule.

Under the active-constraint independence hypotheses, feasible set S, active set I and first-order multiplier equations above (including μ_i≥0 and zero inactive multipliers), assume f,g,h are C². Define the critical cone C={v:Dg(a)v=0, Dh_i(a)v≥0 for all i∈I, and Df(a)v=0}, and L=f−λg−Σ_i μ_i h_i with fixed multipliers. At a constrained minimum, D²L(a)[v,v]≥0 for every v∈C. Conversely if D²L(a)[v,v]>0 for every nonzero v∈C, then a is a strict local minimum on S and ∃c_0,ρ>0 ∀x∈S∩B(a,ρ), f(x)≥f(a)+c_0||x−a||². Sufficiency includes C={0}.

For n≥1 and v∈R^n\{0}, the unit sphere is nonempty compact, and f(x)=<v,x> on it has unique global minimum −||v|| at x=−v/||v|| and unique global maximum ||v|| at x=v/||v||. For g(x)=||x||², Dg(x)=2<x,·> is surjective on the sphere; the multiplier equations v=2λx give λ=−||v||/2 at the minimum and λ=||v||/2 at the maximum. On the tangent space x^⊥ the Lagrangian Hessian is −2λI, giving these classifications and quadratic growth when tangent directions exist. For n=1 the two sphere points are isolated and strict local extrema are relative and immediate; for v=0 every sphere point is both a global minimum and maximum.

For g(x,y)=x²+y², the level g=0 is {(0,0)}, so every real function restricted to it has both relative extrema at 0. For f(x,y)=x the multiplier equation fails, since (1,0) cannot equal λ(0,0). Regularity is necessary for the stated multiplier theorem.

The level set of g(x,y)=y² at value 0 is the horizontal axis. The function f(x,y)=y is constant on that feasible set and thus has relative extrema everywhere there, but Dg=0 on the axis whereas ∇f≠0, so no multiplier equation Df=λDg can hold. A smooth-looking feasible set may have a singular defining equation.

For f(x,y)=x on the closed unit disk, the unique minimum is at (−1,0), the unique maximum at (1,0), and neither is an ambient stationary point. With the inequality h=1−x²−y²≥0, the minimum obeys Df=μDh with μ=1/2≥0; the maximum satisfies the corresponding rule for −f.

For f(x,y)=x+y on [0,1]², (0,0) is the minimum; its active constraints h_1=x,h_2=y have μ_1=μ_2=1. The critical cone is {0}, and there is local quadratic growth at the corner, consistent with x+y≥sqrt(x²+y²) there. The disk, corner and singular-level examples show that interior stationary equations alone cannot find all compact-region extrema; regular boundary strata and singular feasible points must be included.

Let U⊂R^n be open and convex. A differentiable scalar f is convex iff ∀x,y∈U, f(y)≥f(x)+Df(x)(y−x). For f∈C²(U), this is equivalent to H_f(x) being positive semidefinite at every x. An everywhere positive definite Hessian implies strict convexity. A stationary point of differentiable convex f is a global minimum; for strictly convex f it is the unique minimum. For any convex feasible subset S⊂U and a∈S, a minimizes differentiable convex f on S iff ∀x∈S, Df(a)(x−a)≥0. This last characterization assumes neither closedness of S nor existence of a minimizer in advance.

Scope remark: the optimization results are those with the differentiability and finite regularity stated in each test, regular equalities or independent active inequalities, compact existence and the stated convex criteria. No unqualified multiplier rule, general convex duality, nonsmooth subgradients, other constraint qualifications or numerical optimization is asserted. Singular constraints require direct feasible-set reasoning, as already illustrated. This remark adds no independent theorem.

For a finite integer r≥1, let f be C^{r+2} on an open neighborhood of a∈R^n, with Df(a)=0 and D²f(a) nondegenerate. If the Hessian inertia is p positive and q negative eigenvalues, p+q=n, then there is a local C^r coordinate diffeomorphism χ with χ(a)=0 such that f(χ^(−1)(y))=f(a)+Σ_{i=1}^p y_i²−Σ_{i=p+1}^n y_i². If f is C^∞, χ and χ^(−1) can be C^∞. This is precisely the C^{r+2}-data/C^r-coordinates version; no specified positive coordinate regularity for arbitrary C² data or optimal derivative loss is claimed. For n=0 the empty Hessian is nondegenerate and the unique coordinate map suffices.

For a C² function f at a nondegenerate critical point a, every local C¹ coordinate change which gives a signed-square normal form has exactly as many negative squares as the negative index of H_f(a). The coordinate change and its inverse need only be C¹; no second derivative of the coordinate change is assumed.
Bibliographic note distinguishing a reference's mention of Morse's lemma from the finite-regularity theorem actually proved here; no stronger external regularity claim or extra obligation.

Bibliographic source-comparison and proof-provenance note. It supplies navigation and editorial context, not an additional comparison-book theorem, a required proof route, or evidence of formal acceptance. The ensuing original chapter statements are inventoried separately.

Chapter convention: dimensions in Chapter 6 are positive integers unless explicitly stated otherwise. All integrals constructed in the chapter are Riemann integrals. The null-set definition is by arbitrarily small countable box covers and does not presuppose measure integration. This fixes scope and interpretation rather than adding a separate theorem.

For Q=∏ᵢ₌₁ⁿ[aᵢ,bᵢ] with aᵢ≤bᵢ, its content is |Q|=∏ᵢ(bᵢ−aᵢ). A grid is a finite partition of every coordinate interval; its cells are the resulting closed boxes, and its mesh is the largest cell diameter. For bounded f:Q→ℝ and tags ξ_C∈C, define S(f,P,ξ)=Σ_C f(ξ_C)|C|, m_C=inf_C f, M_C=sup_C f, L(f,P)=Σ_C m_C|C| and U(f,P)=Σ_C M_C|C|. The lower integral is sup_P L(f,P), the upper integral is inf_P U(f,P); equality defines Riemann integrability and their common value ∫_Q f. On a degenerate box all sums and integrals of bounded functions are zero. In dimension zero the sole box is ℝ⁰, its content is the empty product 1, and integration is evaluation; the subsequent positive-dimensional null-set assertions do not apply to this point.

For every bounded real f on a nondegenerate compact box Q, the following are equivalent: equality of the Darboux lower and upper integrals; for every ε>0 there exists a grid P with U(f,P)−L(f,P)<ε; and there exists I∈ℝ such that for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 for which every grid of mesh<δ and every choice of tags has |S(f,P,ξ)−I|<ε. In the last condition I=∫_Q f.

For every fixed grid of Q, a bounded f:Q→ℝ is Riemann integrable if and only if its restriction to every grid cell is integrable; in that case its integral equals the sum of the cell integrals. Every uniform limit of integrable functions on Q is integrable and its integral is the limit of their integrals.

On a box Q the real Riemann-integrable functions form a real algebra (in particular products and absolute values are integrable). The integral is linear and order preserving, and |∫_Q f|≤∫_Q|f|≤|Q| sup_Q|f|.

For bounded f:Q→ℝᵏ, coordinatewise Riemann integration is equivalent to convergence, as grid mesh tends to zero uniformly over tags, of the vector tagged sums. For an integrable f the scalar function ‖f‖ is integrable and ‖∫_Q f‖≤∫_Q‖f‖.

A subset of ℝⁿ is null if, for every ε>0, it has a countable box cover whose sum of contents is <ε. It has content zero if a finite cover suffices for each ε. Open or closed boxes give the same two notions. For bounded f:Q→ℝ and x∈Q, its relative oscillation is ω_f(x)=inf_{r>0} sup{|f(y)−f(z)|: y,z∈Q∩B(x,r)}.

In positive dimension, countable unions of null sets are null; compact null sets have content zero; finite unions of coordinate faces in a bounded box have content zero; a nondegenerate box is not null; and the closure of a content-zero set has content zero. Bounded null sets need not have content zero.
A bounded real function f on a compact box Q is Riemann integrable if and only if its set of relative discontinuity points in Q is null.

Continuous functions on a compact box are Riemann integrable. If two bounded Riemann-integrable functions on a box agree outside a null set, their integrals agree. A bounded function vanishing off a content-zero set is integrable with integral zero. Changing values on an arbitrary null set alone need not preserve integrability: changing the zero function to 1 on ℚ∩[0,1] gives its nonintegrable indicator, whose oscillation is 1 everywhere.

A bounded E⊂ℝⁿ is Jordan measurable if its indicator, zero extended to a box whose interior contains closure(E), is Riemann integrable; its volume is vol(E)=∫1_E. For bounded f:E→ℝ, ∫_E f is defined as the integral of its zero extension when that extension is integrable. The same definition applies to a function on an open set with bounded support if its zero extension is integrable; the open set itself need not be Jordan measurable.

A bounded E⊂ℝⁿ is Jordan measurable if and only if its boundary has content zero. Integrals defined by zero extension are independent of the enclosing box. Finite unions, intersections, and differences of Jordan sets are Jordan; integrals are finitely additive on disjoint such sets whenever their zero extensions are integrable. If E is Jordan and bounded f:E→ℝ is relatively continuous except on a null subset of E, its zero extension is integrable. In particular every continuous function on closure(E) is integrable over E.

Let A⊂ℝᵖ and B⊂ℝᑫ be compact boxes, and let f:A×B→ℝ be Riemann integrable. For every x∈A define ℓ(x) as the lower Darboux integral over B of f(x,·), and u(x) as its upper Darboux integral. Both ℓ and u are Riemann integrable on A and ∫_Aℓ=∫_{A×B}f=∫_Au. The same assertions hold with the coordinate blocks interchanged. If every inner slice is integrable, its ordinary slice integral is an integrable outer function giving the product integral.

On [0,1]², f(x,y)=1_{ {0} }(x)1_ℚ(y) is Riemann integrable with product integral 0, since its support lies in a content-zero line, but its x=0 slice is not Riemann integrable. Its lower slice integral ℓ is identically 0 and its upper slice integral is u=1_{ {0} }; both outer integrals equal 0. Thus product integrability does not require integrability of every slice.

Under the Darboux Fubini hypotheses, the set of parameters with nonintegrable slices is null (in either coordinate-block order). This does not permit arbitrary changes of the outer integrand on that null set while retaining Riemann integrability.

Let A⊂ℝⁿ⁻¹ be Jordan measurable and let a,b:closure(A)→ℝ be continuous with a≤b. Then E={(x,t):x∈A, a(x)≤t≤b(x)} is bounded Jordan measurable. For every continuous f on closure(E), ∫_E f(x,t)d(x,t)=∫_A(∫_{a(x)}^{b(x)}f(x,t)dt)dx. Choices of including or excluding the endpoint graphs have no effect. In particular vol(E)=∫_A(b−a).

For nonnegative Riemann-integrable density ρ on bounded Jordan E, define mass m=∫_Eρ and first moments m_i=∫_E x_iρ(x)dx. If m>0 define the center of mass by c_i=m_i/m. The moment of inertia about a fixed affine axis L is ∫_E dist(x,L)²ρ(x)dx. These displayed integrands are integrable.

For open Ω⊂ℝⁿ, f is locally Riemann integrable if its restriction to each compact box contained in Ω is integrable. Such f restricts to an integrable function on every compact Jordan K⊂Ω. Let 𝒦 be these compact Jordan subsets and define ∫_Ω|f|=sup_{K∈𝒦}∫_K|f|∈[0,∞]; finiteness defines absolute convergence. A regular exhaustion is a nested sequence K_j∈𝒦 with K_j⊂Int(K_{j+1}) and ⋃_j Int(K_j)=Ω. Conditional convergence along a specified exhaustion means convergence of ∫_{K_j}f without absolute convergence, and includes that exhaustion as part of the assertion.

Every open Ω has a regular exhaustion. For nonnegative locally Riemann-integrable f, the integrals along every regular exhaustion increase to sup_{K∈𝒦}∫_K f, possibly +∞. If locally Riemann-integrable f is absolutely convergent, ∫_{K_j}f converges to the same finite value along every regular exhaustion; denote it ∫_Ωf. For every compact Jordan K⊂Ω, |∫_Ωf−∫_Kf|≤∫_Ω|f|−∫_K|f|.

On Ω=(0,1)² let f(x,y)=(x²−y²)/(x²+y²)². Its inner improper integral in y is 1/(1+x²), giving iterated integral π/4; its inner improper integral in x is −1/(1+y²), giving the reversed iterated integral −π/4. Every square truncation [δ,1−δ]², 0<δ<1/2, has integral 0 by antisymmetry, and any strictly decreasing δ_j→0 gives a regular exhaustion. Absolute convergence fails. Thus proper Fubini alone does not justify improper interchange.

Using the admitted basic complete Lebesgue measure and dominated/monotone integration foundation, every bounded Riemann-integrable real function on a compact box is Lebesgue measurable and Lebesgue integrable, and the Riemann and Lebesgue integrals agree. Consequently Jordan volume agrees with Lebesgue measure. The two integrals also agree for absolutely convergent locally Riemann-integrable functions on open sets. No multivariable change-of-variables result is assumed in this comparison.

Explanatory convention and proof order: ordinary volume integration uses the positive density |det Dφ| regardless of coordinate orientation; nonlinear image-volume formulas are not premises of the substitution proof. The mathematical determinant/sign and substitution conclusions are inventoried below.

Let K be a compact subset of open V, and let open sets V_α cover K. If continuous f:V→ℝ has support contained in K, there are finitely many continuous f_i with compact support in individual V_{α_i} such that f=Σ_i f_i; if K is empty the empty sum suffices. Consequently, a substitution identity for continuous compact-supported functions for a diffeomorphism follows globally if it holds locally over an open cover of its target.

Suppose T:U→V is a C¹ diffeomorphism of open subsets of ℝⁿ, changing only coordinate j: T(x₁,…,xₙ)=(x₁,…,x_{j−1},ψ(x),x_{j+1},…,xₙ). For every continuous f compactly supported in V, ∫_V f(y)dy=∫_U f(T(x))|∂_jψ(x)|dx. Coordinate permutations satisfy substitution as well, with absolute determinant 1.

If continuous compact-supported substitution holds for two composable diffeomorphisms, it holds for their composition. Every invertible affine map x↦Ax+b satisfies this substitution identity, with factor |det A|.

Let U,V⊂ℝⁿ be open and φ:U→V a bijective C¹ map with det Dφ(x)≠0 for every x. Then φ⁻¹ is C¹ and for every continuous compact-supported f:V→ℝ, ∫_V f(y)dy=∫_U f(φ(x))|det Dφ(x)|dx. Both are Riemann integrals of continuous compactly supported zero extensions. The same conclusion holds coordinatewise for finite-dimensional vector-valued f.

If F:U→ℝⁿ is C¹ on open U⊂ℝⁿ, it maps every null subset of U to a null set, and every compact content-zero subset of U to a content-zero set. If φ:U→V is a diffeomorphism and E is Jordan measurable with compact closure contained in U, then φ(E) is Jordan measurable and ∂φ(E)=φ(∂E).
Let bounded f:ℝⁿ→ℝ be Riemann integrable with compact support K contained in open V. For every ε>0 there are continuous compact-supported g₋,g₊ in V such that g₋≤f≤g₊ everywhere and ∫(g₊−g₋)<ε.

Let φ:U→V be a C¹ diffeomorphism and bounded f:V→ℝ have compact support in V. Its zero extension is Riemann integrable if and only if the zero extension of g(x)=f(φ(x))J(x), J(x)=|det Dφ(x)|, is Riemann integrable. If either is integrable, ∫_V f=∫_U(f∘φ)J.

Let E⊂U be bounded Jordan measurable with compact closure in U, and let φ:U→V be a C¹ diffeomorphism. Then φ(E) is Jordan measurable. For bounded f:φ(E)→ℝ, existence of either Riemann integral ∫_{φ(E)}f(y)dy or ∫_E f(φ(x))|det Dφ(x)|dx implies existence of the other, and they are equal. In particular vol(φ(E))=∫_E|det Dφ|.

For every bounded Jordan E⊂ℝⁿ and every linear map A:ℝⁿ→ℝⁿ, including singular A, A(E) is Jordan and vol(A(E))=|det A|vol(E). For nonsingular A this gives substitution in any nonorthogonal linear coordinate system. No inverse substitution is asserted for singular A.

For a C¹ diffeomorphism φ, det Dφ has constant sign on each connected component of its domain. For a normalized top form, φ*(f(y)dy₁∧⋯∧dyₙ)=f(φ(x))det Dφ(x)dx₁∧⋯∧dxₙ. Orientation-preserving changes give the ordinary integral formula; orientation reversal changes the sign of the oriented integral.

For every real α, polar P(r,θ)=(r cosθ,r sinθ) on r>0, α<θ<α+2π; cylindrical C(r,θ,z)=(r cosθ,r sinθ,z) on the same r,θ range with every z∈ℝ; and spherical S(r,φ,θ)=(r sinφ cosθ,r sinφ sinθ,r cosφ) on r>0, 0<φ<π, α<θ<α+2π are C¹ diffeomorphisms onto their images. In the displayed input coordinate orders their determinants are positive and equal respectively r, r, and r² sinφ. On compact Jordan subregions of these coordinate ranges substitution multiplies the integrand by the displayed factor.

The geometric coordinate formulas extend by regular compact truncations to bounded Cartesian Riemann integrals including the polar/cylindrical axis and angular seam, and to balls including the spherical axis, poles, and seam. For a bounded Riemann integrand on the full disk of radius R, the transformed integrand on the full closed polar coordinate rectangle is Riemann integrable and the full disk substitution identity holds by removing r<δ and the angular end strips and passing to the limit. The analogous cylindrical and spherical identities hold on bounded cylindrical regions and balls. The same limiting argument applies to subregions when the original zero extension is integrable and the truncated regions are Jordan. Bounded values on the content-zero parameter faces may be chosen arbitrarily without altering integrability or the integral; arbitrary Cartesian seam values are allowed whenever the stipulated Cartesian integrability holds.

Polar and spherical integration give disk area πR² and ball volume 4πR³/3. In ℝ³, the ellipsoid {Ax:‖x‖<R} for nonsingular A has volume |det A|4πR³/3. More generally, coordinates x=Σ_i u_i v_i in any basis (v₁,…,vₙ) contribute the volume factor |det(v₁,…,vₙ)|; orthogonality is unnecessary.

Suppose a parametrization has a finite decomposition into disjoint Jordan pieces E_i up to a content-zero set, and on a neighborhood of every E_i it agrees with a diffeomorphism φ_i. For bounded f with all relevant zero extensions integrable, Σ_i∫_{E_i} f(φ_i(x))|det Dφ_i(x)|dx=∫_{ℝⁿ} f(y)Σ_i1_{φ_i(E_i)}(y)dy. Thus the integral counts finite overlap multiplicity of the images; the discarded content-zero parameter boundaries contribute zero for bounded integrands.

For 1<r<2 and 0<θ<4π the polar map covers the annulus twice away from the positive radial seam, on which θ=2π gives one preimage. The parameter integral is 6π and the annulus area is 3π. The linked Lean multiplicity theorem counts the four open split charts off the radial seams.

Let φ:U→V be a C¹ diffeomorphism and f locally Riemann integrable on V. Then g=(f∘φ)|det Dφ| is locally Riemann integrable, and f is absolutely integrable if and only if g is; in that case ∫_Vf=∫_Ug (also the absolute integrals agree). A specified regular exhaustion and its image give equal conditional limits whenever these limits exist; no conclusion is asserted for an unrelated exhaustion without separate justification. In dimension zero substitution is evaluation and the empty determinant equals 1.

Chapter 8 explanatory scope: parameter spaces are finite dimensional. The chapter emphasizes uniform control on parameter neighborhoods; separate derivative formulas by themselves do not establish total differentiation or passage to improper limits. The mathematical hypotheses and failures are inventoried in the corresponding results and examples.

Let E⊂ℝⁿ be bounded Jordan, P⊂ℝᵐ any parameter set, and f:E×P→ℝᵏ have an integrable x-slice for every p. If sup_{x∈E}‖f(x,p)−f(x,p₀)‖→0 as p→p₀ relatively in P, then F(p)=∫_E f(x,p)dx is continuous at p₀. In particular joint continuity on closure(E)×P yields continuity of F when P is open, and relatively on any compact parameter set on which that joint continuity is given. Uniform convergence of integrands on E×P gives uniform convergence of their parameter integrals. When vol(E)=0, F is the zero function.

Let P⊂ℝᵐ be open and E⊂ℝⁿ bounded Jordan. Suppose f:E×P→ℝᵏ is Riemann integrable in x for each p, differentiable in p for each x, and x↦D_pf(x,p) is integrable with values in Hom(ℝᵐ,ℝᵏ) for each p. If at p₀, sup_{x∈E}‖D_pf(x,p)−D_pf(x,p₀)‖→0 as p→p₀, then F(p)=∫_Ef(x,p)dx is totally differentiable at p₀ and DF(p₀)h=∫_E D_pf(x,p₀)h dx for every h∈ℝᵐ. If f and D_pf are jointly continuous on closure(E)×P, F is C¹ on P with the formula at every point. No x-differentiability is assumed.

Under the proper-integral setting with bounded Jordan E and open P, if the finite parameter derivatives D_pʲf exist and are continuous on closure(E)×P for 0≤j≤r, then F(p)=∫_Ef(x,p)dx is Cʳ and DʲF(p)[h₁,…,h_j]=∫_E D_pʲf(x,p)[h₁,…,h_j]dx for 0≤j≤r. Equivalently ∂_p^αF=∫_E∂_p^αf for every multi-index |α|≤r.

For any nonnegative Riemann-integrable density ρ on bounded Jordan E⊂ℝⁿ, Z(p)=∫_E e^{p·x}ρ(x)dx (p∈ℝⁿ) is Cʳ for every finite r, although ρ need not be continuous. DZ(p)h=∫_E(h·x)e^{p·x}ρ(x)dx and D²Z(p)[h,k]=∫_E(h·x)(k·x)e^{p·x}ρ(x)dx. If ∫_Eρ>0, then Z(p)>0 and the derivative D log Z corresponds to the center of mass of the reweighted density e^{p·x}ρ. Its Hessian is nonnegative: D²log Z(p)[h,h]=∫_E(h·x−c_h)²e^{p·x}ρ(x)dx/Z(p)≥0, where c_h=∫_E(h·x)e^{p·x}ρ(x)dx/Z(p).

Let I⊂ℝ be an open interval, P⊂ℝᵐ open, f:I×P→ℝᵏ and D_pf continuous, and a,b:P→I be C¹. With oriented scalar integration also when b(p)<a(p), F(p)=∫_{a(p)}^{b(p)}f(t,p)dt is C¹ and for every h, DF(p)h=∫_{a(p)}^{b(p)}D_pf(t,p)h dt+f(b(p),p)Db(p)h−f(a(p),p)Da(p)h. This holds also at parameters where a(p)=b(p).
For a differentiable family of invertible square matrices A(p), J(p)=|det A(p)| is differentiable and DJ(p)h=J(p)tr(A(p)⁻¹ DA(p)h).

Let E⊂ℝⁿ be bounded Jordan with compact closure in open W, P⊂ℝᵐ open, and Φ:P×W→ℝⁿ jointly C¹. Suppose every Φ_p=Φ(p,·) is a diffeomorphism onto its open image, D_xΦ is differentiable in p, and D_pD_xΦ is continuous (joint C² is sufficient). Let scalar f(p,y) be C¹ on an open neighborhood of {(p,Φ(p,x)):p∈P,x∈closure(E)}. Put E_p=Φ_p(E), A(p,x)=D_xΦ(p,x), J=|det A| and F(p)=∫_{E_p}f(p,y)dy. Then each E_p is Jordan, F is C¹ and DF(p)h=∫_E J(p,x)[D_pf(p,Φ(p,x))h+D_yf(p,Φ(p,x))D_pΦ(p,x)h+f(p,Φ(p,x))tr(A(p,x)⁻¹ D_pA(p,x)h)]dx. If additionally D_xD_pΦ=D_pD_xΦ (in particular if Φ is jointly C²), fix p and define v_h(y)=D_pΦ(p,Φ_p⁻¹(y))h; then DF(p)h=∫_{E_p}[D_pf(p,y)h+D_yf(p,y)v_h(y)+f(p,y)div v_h(y)]dy, with divergence the trace of the spatial derivative. These assertions concern the stated bounded regular chart family.

For bounded Jordan E and t>0 set E_t=tE, and let f be C¹ near the relevant closures. With Φ(t,x)=tx the velocity is v(y)=y/t and div v=n/t, and d/dt ∫_{tE}f(y)dy=(1/t)∫_{tE}[Df(y)y+n f(y)]dy. In particular d/dt vol(tE)=n t^{n−1}vol(E); the volume term is present even for f=1.

Fix a regular exhaustion K_j of open Ω. For locally Riemann-integrable f(·,p), let F_j(p)=∫_{K_j}f(x,p)dx. Uniform convergence of the improper family on B⊂P means uniform convergence of F_j there; equivalently, for every ε>0 there is j₀ such that sup_{p∈B}‖∫_{K_k∖K_j}f(x,p)dx‖<ε whenever k≥j≥j₀. For scalar f the norm is absolute value. Uniform absolute tails are the stronger property with ∫_{K_k∖K_j}‖f(x,p)‖dx in place of the norm of the integral. With several singular endpoints each endpoint tail is controlled separately.

For the fixed exhaustion, if every F_j is continuous on a parameter neighborhood B and F_j converges uniformly on B, its limit F is continuous on B. More generally, if f(·,p)→g uniformly on every K_j as p→p₀ and the improper family has uniform Cauchy tails near p₀, then g has an improper integral along this exhaustion and lim_{p→p₀}∫_Ωf(x,p)dx=∫_Ωg(x)dx. A parameter-independent nonnegative absolutely integrable locally Riemann-integrable M with ‖f(x,p)‖≤M(x) on the parameter set implies uniform absolute tails there.

Let B be the closed Euclidean ball centered at p_* of radius r in ℝᵐ, and let F_j be ℝᵏ-valued C¹ maps on a neighborhood of B. If F_j(p_*) converges and DF_j converges uniformly on B to G, then F_j converges uniformly on B to a limit F, and F is C¹ on Int(B) with DF=G there.

On a compact parameter ball B=closed B(p_*,r)⊂P, suppose f satisfies the proper differentiation hypotheses on every exhaustion member K_j, so F_j is C¹ and DF_j(p)=∫_{K_j}D_pf(x,p)dx. If these derivative integrals converge uniformly on B and F_j(p_*) converges at one parameter, the improper integrals F_j converge uniformly on B to F, F is C¹ on Int(B), and DF(p)h=lim_j∫_{K_j}D_pf(x,p)h dx. A sufficient derivative-tail condition is ‖D_pf(x,p)‖≤M(x) on B for an absolutely integrable locally Riemann-integrable M. Uniform convergence of the signed derivative integrals suffices without absolute domination. Finite higher differentiation follows by repeating this result when the corresponding truncated derivatives and their uniform tails, including the base-point convergence required at each application, satisfy the same conditions at every order. Exhaustion independence follows only when absolute convergence is additionally present.

Let A be a compact box, K_j a regular exhaustion of open Ω, and f continuous on A×Ω. If H_j(x)=∫_{K_j}f(x,y)dy converges uniformly for x∈A, then both sides exist and ∫_A(lim_j∫_{K_j}f(x,y)dy)dx=lim_j∫_{K_j}(∫_A f(x,y)dx)dy. The right side is the specified exhaustion improper integral. The same result holds for finite-dimensional vector-valued f.

For x≥0 and a≥a₀>0, the j-th a-derivative of e^{−ax} is (−x)ʲe^{−ax}, dominated in absolute value by xʲe^{−a₀x}; this dominating function is absolutely integrable. Every finite derivative order consequently has uniform tails on compact subsets of a>0 (indeed for a≥a₀). For every integer j≥0 and a>0, ∫₀^∞xʲe^{−ax}dx=j!/a^{j+1}, obtained by differentiating ∫₀^∞e^{−ax}dx=1/a. No uniformity as a↓0 is asserted.

For 0<t<1 let f(x,t)=t⁻¹1_(0,t)(x) on [0,1], with f(x,0)=0. Each x-slice at fixed t is Riemann integrable; for every fixed x, f(x,t)→0 as t↓0, but ∫₀¹f(x,t)dx=1 for t>0. Thus pointwise convergence cannot replace the stated uniform proper-integral hypothesis.

Choose a nonnegative C¹ function ψ supported on [1,2] with integral 1, for instance a normalization of (u−1)²(2−u)² on [1,2] extended by zero. Set f(x,t)=tψ(tx) for t>0,x≥0 and f(x,0)=0. On every bounded x-interval it is identically zero for sufficiently small t, hence converges uniformly to zero there, while ∫₀^∞f(x,t)dx=1 for every t>0. Uniform improper tails fail. For every fixed x its one-sided parameter derivative at t=0 is zero as well, but the parameter integral is discontinuous at 0, so behavior on every fixed truncation alone does not justify improper differentiation.

For every p∈ℝ, ∫_ℝ(1+(x−p)²)⁻¹dx=π. On each compact parameter set this family has uniform tails by domination by C/(1+x²) for some C depending on that set. On the entire parameter set ℝ it has no uniform tails relative to [−R,R], since p can be taken so far beyond R that nearly all mass lies outside. These examples have no finite singularity; handling actual moving finite singularities requires a separately justified exhaustion or change of variables.

Contextual comparison with the admitted measure foundation: measurable dominated convergence is a distinct Lebesgue theorem and need not make a pointwise limit Riemann integrable. The established Riemann–Lebesgue bridge compares values only where its hypotheses hold. Banach-space parameter theory, weak transport, rough boundaries, and flow dependence are outside this finite-dimensional chapter and are not additional obligations.

A path is continuous γ:[a,b]→ℝⁿ; its trace is its image, forgetting visit order and multiplicity. It is piecewise C¹ if a finite a=t₀<⋯<t_m=b makes each restriction C¹ up to its endpoints, with one-sided derivatives at joins; it is piecewise regular if the derivative is nonzero on each closed piece. A simple arc is injective, and a simple closed path is injective except for equality of its endpoints. Constant paths are permitted and are not piecewise regular on a nondegenerate interval a<b. For a=b the zero-piece partition makes piecewise C1 and piecewise regular conditions vacuously true; all lengths and integrals remain zero. Arc-length parametrization conclusions requiring a nondegenerate interval explicitly assume a<b. For a partition P set ℓ_P(γ)=Σ_j|γ(t_j)−γ(t_{j−1})|; L(γ)=sup_Pℓ_P(γ), possibly infinite. Refinement increases polygonal length.

Every piecewise C¹ path γ:[a,b]→ℝⁿ has finite length L(γ)=Σ_{j=1}^m∫_{t_{j−1}}^{t_j}|γ′(t)|dt. Polygonal lengths for partitions containing all joins converge to this value as their mesh tends to zero.

For a regular C¹ path γ:[a,b]→ℝⁿ set s(t)=∫_a^t|γ′(u)|du and L=s(b). If a<b, s is a strictly increasing C¹ bijection [a,b]→[0,L] with C¹ inverse, and γ̃=γ∘s⁻¹ has |γ̃′|=1. A piecewise regular path has the corresponding piecewise unit-speed parametrization, allowing tangent jumps at joins. Regularity is essential for the inverse assertion: a stationary interval would make s constant.

For a continuous covector field α_x and piecewise C¹ path γ define ∫_γα=Σ_j∫_{t_{j−1}}^{t_j}α_{γ(t)}(γ′(t))dt, independently of the chosen join partition. In Euclidean coordinates α=Σ_iF_i dx_i corresponds to the vector field F through α_x(v)=F(x)·v, and this integral is denoted ∫_γF·dx; it uses directed displacement.

For a piecewise C¹ path γ and scalar f on its trace, define ∫_γ f ds=Σ_j∫_{t_{j−1}}^{t_j}f(γ(t))|γ′(t)|dt when the displayed bounded Riemann integrands are integrable; in particular continuous f on the trace qualifies. The value is independent of the chosen join partition. This is integration against positive length.

Let γ be piecewise C¹, and h:[c,d]→[a,b] a piecewise C¹ bijection with piecewise C¹ inverse and nonzero derivative on its regular pieces. Then h is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing. For continuous data, L(γ∘h)=L(γ) and ∫_{γ∘h}f ds=∫_γf ds; ∫_{γ∘h}α=∫_γα in the increasing case and =−∫_γα in the decreasing case. The same formulas hold for bounded Riemann data whenever substitution hypotheses ensure the indicated integrability on both parameter intervals.

For reversal γ⁻(t)=γ(a+b−t), scalar line integrals are unchanged and one-form integrals are negated. For composable piecewise C¹ paths γ₁,γ₂, concatenate after affine rescaling to adjacent intervals; L(γ₁*γ₂)=L(γ₁)+L(γ₂), ∫_{γ₁*γ₂}f ds=∫_{γ₁}f ds+∫_{γ₂}f ds, and ∫_{γ₁*γ₂}α=∫_{γ₁}α+∫_{γ₂}α. For the data for which these line integrals are defined, |∫_γf ds|≤sup_trace|f| L(γ) and |∫_γα|≤sup_trace‖α‖ L(γ).
If f∈C¹(U) on open U⊂ℝⁿ and piecewise C¹ γ:[a,b]→U, then ∫_γdf=∫_γ∇f·dx=f(γ(b))−f(γ(a)). The Euclidean metric correspondence is df_x(v)=⟨∇f(x),v⟩.

For each nonzero integer m, γ_m(t)=(cos mt,sin mt), 0≤t≤2π, has unit-circle trace and length 2π|m|. For F(x,y)=(−y,x)/(x²+y²) on ℝ²∖{0}, F(γ_m)·γ_m′=m and ∫_{γ_m}F·dx=2πm. On punctured ℝ² one has ∂_xF₂=∂_yF₁, yet F has no global scalar potential. Thus the scalar integral of 1 records absolute traversal and the work integral records signed traversal; neither is determined solely by the trace without a single-traversal convention.

For γ(t)=(a cos t,a sin t,bt), 0≤t≤T, a>0 and T≥0 (with b real), speed is √(a²+b²), L=T√(a²+b²), and arc length is s=t√(a²+b²). For f(x,y,z)=z the work ∫_γ∇f·dx is bT, whereas ∫_γz ds=bT²√(a²+b²)/2; the formulas include T=0.

A regular C¹ surface parametrization is φ:U⊂ℝ²→ℝⁿ of rank two everywhere, with U an open chart domain. It is an embedded patch if it is a homeomorphism onto its image; full rank yields this after local restriction. At p=φ(u,v), the tangent plane is im Dφ(u,v), independent of the embedded chart. For n=3 the two unit normals are ±N_φ=±(φ_u×φ_v)/|φ_u×φ_v|; the cross product is nonzero exactly when the two tangent columns are independent.

For a regular C¹ surface parametrization set G_φ=(Dφ)ᵀDφ and J₂φ=√det G_φ. For compact Jordan D⊂U and continuous f on φ(D), define ∫_{φ|D}f dA=∫_D f(φ(u,v))J₂φ(u,v)du dv. Bounded noncontinuous data are admitted when the indicated Riemann integrand is integrable. At f=1 this is parametrized area; a noninjective parametrization counts traversal rather than automatically the image once. The definition uses the metric Gram density.

For a regular patch in ℝ³, J₂φ=√(|φ_u|²|φ_v|²−(φ_u·φ_v)²)=|φ_u×φ_v|. For an affine patch this is the area of the parallelogram spanned by its derivative columns. More generally the factor J_kφ=√det((Dφ)ᵀDφ) of a regular k-patch in ℝⁿ is the Euclidean k-dimensional parallelepiped volume factor. It agrees with speed for k=1 and with the absolute volume Jacobian for k=n.

Let h:V→U be a C¹ diffeomorphism, φ a regular patch, and ψ=φ∘h. For compact Jordan E⊂V, D=h(E) is Jordan and ∫_{ψ|E}f dA=∫_{φ|D}f dA. This includes the integrability equivalence for bounded Riemann data supplied by region substitution. In ℝ³, ψ_s×ψ_t=(det Dh)(φ_u×φ_v)∘h. Define oriented flux by ∫_{φ|D}F·N_φ dA=∫_D F(φ)·(φ_u×φ_v)du dv. With parameter orientations, positive reparametrization preserves flux and negative reparametrization negates it. If a fixed geometric normal is used, adjust each chart sign to that normal and flux is invariant. No multiplicity cancellation for a many-to-one parameter map is asserted.

A compact embedded C¹ surface, with or without boundary, has a well-defined scalar integral for every continuous function, obtained from Gram densities in finitely many charts and a subordinate partition of unity, independently of the weights and charts. If a continuous unit normal is chosen it also has a global oriented flux integral, with chart signs adjusted to that normal. Overlap weights may be discarded only when the patches instead decompose the surface with area-zero intersections; adding overlapping whole charts otherwise counts their overlap twice.

A finite union of compact C¹ curves and points on an embedded surface has area zero. Such a set may be omitted in computing the integral of a bounded continuous function using regular charts covering its complement, provided the limiting integrals are taken over regular compact truncations. These truncated integrals converge to the whole-surface integral. The assertion does not license arbitrary changes on dense null sets.

For R>a>0, φ(u,v)=((R+v cos(u/2))cos u,(R+v cos(u/2))sin u,v sin(u/2)), 0≤u≤2π, |v|≤a, with (0,v) identified with (2π,−v), defines an embedded strip covered by regular local patches, including seam patches. Since R+v cos(u/2)>0, the only parameter ambiguity is that seam identification. One has |φ_v|=1, φ_v·φ_u=0 and |φ_u|²=(R+v cos(u/2))²+v²/4>0, hence rank two. Along v=0 the cross-product normal at u=2π is the negative of its value at u=0, so no continuous global unit normal exists and the strip is nonorientable. Its positive Gram area density and scalar area integral nevertheless exist by surface assembly; no global normal-oriented flux is defined for this surface without replacing it by an oriented parametrized chain.

For a C¹ graph patch φ(u,v)=(u,v,g(u,v)), φ_u×φ_v=(−g_u,−g_v,1) and dA=√(1+g_u²+g_v²)du dv. Its upward flux of F is ∫_D[−F₁(φ)g_u−F₂(φ)g_v+F₃(φ)]du dv when the integrand is admissible. For the paraboloid g=u²+v² over u²+v²≤a² (radius a≥0), area is 2π∫₀ᵃr√(1+4r²)dr=(π/6)((1+4a²)^{3/2}−1). The polar origin/ray are omitted by regular truncations and contribute zero by the seam result.

For R>0, φ(θ,φ)=(R sinθ cosφ,R sinθ sinφ,R cosθ), 0<θ<π, 0<φ<2π, parametrizes the sphere off a meridian and its poles. In this parameter order, φ_θ×φ_φ=R²sinθ n with outward n=φ/R. Regular compact truncations and omission of the negligible meridian and poles give area 4πR² and outward flux ∫_{S_R}x·n dA=4πR³. This parametrization is not a regular global chart at the poles and is not injective across the closed seam.

For a C¹ ruled surface φ(s,t)=a(s)+t b(s) in ℝ³, the tangent columns are a′(s)+t b′(s) and b(s), and the regular area factor is |(a′(s)+t b′(s))×b(s)| wherever this is nonzero. A cylinder (R cos s,R sin s,t), with radius R>0 and height H≥0, for a full angular traversal and 0≤t≤H has factor R and lateral area 2πRH, with its seam omitted. The cone ((1−t)R cos s,(1−t)R sin s,tH), with R>0, real H, a full angular traversal and 0≤t≤1, has factor R(1−t)√(R²+H²) and lateral area πR√(R²+H²). The cone apex t=1 is handled as the limit of regular truncations t<1 and contributes zero area; no tangent plane at that apex is claimed.

For a C^1 scalar f on open U⊂R^n, ∇f(x) is the unique vector with Df(x)v=⟨∇f(x),v⟩ for every v, and its column coordinates are (∂_1f,…,∂_nf)^T. For C^1 F:U→R^n, div F=tr DF=Σ_i∂_iF_i. In standard oriented R^3, curl F=(∂_yF_3−∂_zF_2,∂_zF_1−∂_xF_3,∂_xF_2−∂_yF_1); equivalently curl F is the unique vector field for which dα_F=β_(curl F), with α and β as in the oriented Euclidean dictionary. Reversing orientation changes this vector identification. For C^2 f, Δf=div∇f=Σ_i∂_i^2f.

For C^1 scalar fields f,g and vector fields F,G of the indicated common Euclidean domain and dimensions, ∇(fg)=f∇g+g∇f and div(fF)=∇f·F+f div F. In R^3, curl(fF)=∇f×F+f curl F and div(F×G)=G·curl F−F·curl G.
For C^2 data on open domains in R^3, curl∇f=0, div curl F=0, and curl curl F=∇div F−ΔF, where ΔF is the componentwise Laplacian.

Let U⊂R^n be open and connected and F:U→R^n continuous. The following are equivalent: F=∇f for some f∈C^1(U); work integrals along piecewise C^1 paths in U depend only on their endpoints; every closed piecewise C^1 path in U has zero work integral. Such a potential is unique up to one additive constant. If F∈C^r, the potential is C^(r+1), for r≥0 with C^0 meaning continuous. For disconnected open U these statements apply on each connected component, with one independent additive constant per component.

For F∈C^1(U;R^n) on an open domain, the symmetry equations ∂_iF_j=∂_jF_i are necessary for existence of a scalar potential. They suffice locally on every ball contained in U and globally when U is star-shaped about a. In the latter case f(x)=∫_0^1 F(a+t(x−a))·(x−a)dt is a potential, up to an additive constant. In R^3 these symmetry equations are exactly curl F=0.

If U⊂R^n is open, connected and simply connected, every C^1 field F:U→R^n with symmetric Jacobian has a global scalar potential. Here simply connected can be expressed by every continuous loop admitting a continuous contraction to a constant loop in U with agreeing endpoint tracks at every homotopy stage. This free-loop convention is equivalent to the based-contraction convention: a free contraction gives a based contraction by adjoining the basepoint track and its reverse, then contracting the final retracing loop; conversely a based contraction is a free contraction. No differentiability of the homotopy is required.

On R^2∖{0}, F(x,y)=(−y,x)/(x^2+y^2) has symmetric Jacobian and unit-circle work integral 2π. It has local scalar potentials but no global scalar potential. On a slit plane it has an angular potential: any continuously chosen single-valued polar-angle branch on that slit differentiates to F. No globally single-valued angle on the punctured plane is asserted.

If U⊂R^3 is open and star-shaped about a, F∈C^1(U;R^3), and div F=0, there is A∈C^1(U;R^3) with curl A=F; explicitly A(x)=∫_0^1 t F(a+t(x−a))×(x−a)dt. For every C^2 vector potential A, div curl A=0. On arbitrary domains a global vector potential of either C^1 or C^2 regularity need not exist.

R^3∖{0} is simply connected, but the radial closed two-form β_(x/|x|^3) on it is not exact. Thus simply connectedness is insufficient for a global primitive in degree two, although it suffices in degree one. The elementary contraction argument in this example is a proof route, not a request for general de Rham or homology theory.
Scope limitation: the finite explicit topological obstructions in this chapter do not introduce a general de Rham or homology construction.

Let x=φ(u_1,u_2,u_3) be an orientation-preserving C^2 diffeomorphism on an open parameter domain whose three derivative columns are mutually orthogonal and nonzero. Set h_i=|∂_iφ|, e_i=∂_iφ/h_i, and J=h_1h_2h_3>0. For C^1 scalar f set f̃=f∘φ and for C^1 vector F use the physical components F_i(u)=F(φ(u))·e_i(u). Then (∇f)∘φ=Σ_i(∂_if̃/h_i)e_i, (div F)∘φ=(1/J)Σ_i∂_i((J/h_i)F_i), and ((curl F)∘φ)·e_i=[∂_j(h_ℓF_ℓ)−∂_ℓ(h_jF_j)]/(h_jh_ℓ) for (i,j,ℓ)=(1,2,3),(2,3,1),(3,1,2). For C^2 f, (Δf)∘φ=(1/J)Σ_i∂_i((J/h_i^2)∂_if̃).

For cylindrical coordinates (x,y,z)=(r cosθ,r sinθ,z) with r>0 and θ in a single interval of length less than 2π, the orthogonal scale factors are (1,r,1). Hence div F=(1/r)∂_r(rF_r)+(1/r)∂_θF_θ+∂_zF_z and Δf=(1/r)∂_r(r∂_rf)+(1/r^2)∂_θ^2f+∂_z^2f. In spherical parameters (r,θ,φ) with r>0, 0<θ<π and one azimuth branch, the factors are (1,r,r sinθ). Hence div F=(1/r^2)∂_r(r^2F_r)+(1/(r sinθ))∂_θ(sinθ F_θ)+(1/(r sinθ))∂_φF_φ, and Δf=(1/r^2)∂_r(r^2∂_rf)+(1/(r^2 sinθ))∂_θ(sinθ∂_θf)+(1/(r^2 sin^2θ))∂_φ^2f. Scalar fields have C^2 regularity for the Laplacian and vector fields C^1 for divergence as in the coordinate theorem. These formulas apply only on the stated regular coordinate domains; the axis, poles, origin and angle seams require another chart or a limit.
Scope limitation: the cylindrical and spherical formulas form a selected Euclidean coordinate bridge; full Riemannian operator theory is outside the manuscript's scope.

Chapter organization: generalized Stokes is proved in chapter 15; chapter 12 supplies the domain, metric, normal, tangent, integrand and sign identifications for its classical specializations. This introductory description adds no separate theorem beyond the ensuing statements.

For n≥1 a bounded C^1 domain D⊂R^n is a bounded open set such that every ambient boundary point has a local C^1 defining function ρ with D={ρ<0}, ∂D={ρ=0}, and Dρ≠0 on the zero level locally. D may be multiply connected or disconnected. Its closure K carries standard ambient orientation. The outward unit normal is ν=∇ρ/|∇ρ| and is independent of the local defining function. C^r on a closure means locally extendible as a C^r function to an open neighborhood. On the compact closures here, finitely many local extensions and Euclidean cutoffs combine to give a single C^r extension near the closure.

For every bounded C^1 domain D⊂R^n, n≥1, as defined above, K=cl D is a compact C^1 embedded n-manifold with intrinsic boundary ∂K=∂D. K is Jordan measurable. For continuous f, its oriented manifold integral ∫_K f dx_1∧⋯∧dx_n equals the bounded-region Riemann integrals ∫_D f dx and ∫_K f dx. The boundary normal agrees with the outward-first manifold convention.

Let D⊂R^2 be a bounded C^1 domain, K=cl D, and P,Q be C^1 on a neighborhood of K. Give ∂D its positive boundary orientation induced by dx∧dy. Then ∫_(∂D)(P dx+Q dy)=∫_D(∂_xQ−∂_yP)dxdy, and ∫_(∂D)(P,Q)·ν ds=∫_(∂D)(P dy−Q dx)=∫_D(∂_xP+∂_yQ)dxdy. The same circulation and flux formulas hold for finite piecewise regular regions satisfying the finite-piece decomposition, matching-orientation, seam-cancellation and multiplicity-one hypotheses of the piecewise Stokes theorem.

For the annulus a<√(x^2+y^2)<b with 0<a<b, the outer normal is radial outward on the outer circle and radial inward on the inner circle. The positive tangent τ=(−ν_y,ν_x) is counterclockwise on the outer circle and clockwise on the inner circle, with the annulus to its left. The angular field (−y,x)/(x^2+y^2) has zero curl near the closed annulus; its directed boundary circulations are respectively 2π and −2π, summing to zero. A disk containing the origin fails this field's domain hypothesis and is excluded from that Green-theorem application.

For a bounded C^1 domain D⊂R^n, n≥1, and a C^1 vector field F on a neighborhood of cl D, ∫_D div F dx=∫_(∂D)F·ν dA. Here dA is the positive (n−1)-dimensional Gram density. When n=1 the boundary integral is the sum of endpoint values multiplied by their outward-normal signs. The finite decomposable piecewise version holds under the decomposition, cancellation and multiplicity conditions of finite piecewise Stokes.

Let S⊂R^3 be a compact oriented embedded C^1 surface with boundary, and N its corresponding continuous unit normal, so v_1×v_2 points along N for every positive tangent basis. For F∈C^1 on a neighborhood of S, ∫_S(curl F)·N dA=∫_(∂S)F·τ ds. The induced boundary unit tangent is τ=N×ν, where ν is the outward unit conormal tangent to S and perpendicular to ∂S. The same conclusion holds for a finite oriented union of regular surface pieces with matching seams and all cancellation and geometric multiplicity conditions of finite piecewise Stokes; the remaining boundary is piecewise regular.

For a horizontal disk with N=(0,0,1), its radial outward conormal gives τ=N×ν counterclockwise from above. For an upper hemisphere with outward normal the equatorial outward conormal points downward within the sphere and gives the same counterclockwise traversal. A lower hemisphere with outward normal gives the opposite traversal, so the two equatorial seam integrals cancel for the closed sphere. On a standard oriented box, the upper and lower i-faces have respectively coefficients (−1)^(i−1) and −(−1)^(i−1) in the remaining coordinate order. Boxes use finite-cell Stokes at corners; there is no smooth boundary chart at a box corner.

For every bounded C^1 domain D, C^1 functions f,g near cl D, and coordinate i, ∫_D f∂_ig dx=∫_(∂D)fgν_i dA−∫_D g∂_if dx. For u,v∈C^2 near cl D and ∂_νv=∇v·ν, ∫_D(uΔv+∇u·∇v)dx=∫_(∂D)u∂_νv dA and ∫_D(uΔv−vΔu)dx=∫_(∂D)(u∂_νv−v∂_νu)dA. If the relevant product or function has compact support in D, its corresponding boundary term vanishes. In particular, for u∈C_c^2(D), ∫_D uΔu dx=−∫_D|∇u|^2dx.

For F(x)=x on a sphere of radius R>0, the outward flux is 4πR^3; div F=3 and the ball volume is 4πR^3/3. On [0,a]×[0,b]×[0,c], a,b,c>0, F=x has zero lower-face flux and flux abc on each upper face, total 3abc. For F=(−y/2,x/2,0), curl F=(0,0,1); the radius-R horizontal disk with upward normal has boundary circulation πR^2, with direct boundary parameterization (R cos t,R sin t,0) producing work integrand R^2/2 for 0≤t≤2π. Reversing the surface normal reverses its boundary traversal and both directed integral signs.

For a C^1 field F near x∈R^n, n≥1, and balls B_r(x) contained in its domain, div F(x)=lim_(r↓0)[1/vol(B_r(x))]∫_(∂B_r(x))F·ν dA. For a C^1 field in R^3 and any unit vector N, let D_r be the oriented planar disk centered at x of radius r and normal N, with induced boundary tangent τ. Then curl F(x)·N=lim_(r↓0)[1/(πr^2)]∫_(∂D_r)F·τ ds.
