All vector spaces in the differential-form algebra are finite dimensional. The degree-k covector space is Alt^k(V;R), naturally identified with the k-th exterior power of the dual V*, with the normalized basis and wedge product specified in the forms and wedge obligations. Variable coefficients retain their explicitly stated finite regularity.

An alternating k-covector on a finite-dimensional real V is a multilinear map V^k→R changing sign under interchanging two arguments; a zero-covector is a scalar. For a basis e_1,…,e_n with dual dx_i and increasing multi-index I=(i_1<⋯<i_k), dx_I(v_1,…,v_k)=det(((v_b)_(i_a))_(a,b=1)^k). A C^r differential k-form on open U⊂R^n is a field x↦ω_x∈Alt^k(R^n;R) whose coordinate coefficients are C^r. Degrees k>n contain only zero, degree zero consists of functions, and no negative degrees are introduced.

Every alternating k-covector has the unique expansion Σ_I a_I dx_I, where a_I=ω(e_(i_1),…,e_(i_k)). For α of degree p and β of degree q, define (α∧β)(v_1,…,v_(p+q)) as the sum over (p,q)-shuffles σ of sgn(σ) α(v_(σ1),…,v_(σp))β(v_(σ(p+1)),…,v_(σ(p+q))); each shuffle preserves the order in each block. This product is bilinear and associative and obeys α∧β=(−1)^(pq)β∧α. Degree-zero factors act by ordinary scalar multiplication. For increasing I, dx_(i_1)∧⋯∧dx_(i_k)=dx_I. If Alt denotes the average over all (p+q)! permutations, then α∧β=((p+q)!/(p!q!))Alt(α⊗β). All statements include zero-sized blocks, using empty determinant and empty product equal to one.

For C^1 f:U⊂R^m→V⊂R^n between open sets, define (f*ω)_x(v_1,…,v_k)=ω_(f(x))(Df(x)v_1,…,Df(x)v_k). In degree zero pullback is composition. A continuous form has continuous pullback. If f is C^(r+1) and ω is C^r, the pullback is C^r.

Whenever the maps and forms have the regularity for pullback and the indicated compositions are defined, pullback is linear, f*(aω)=(a∘f)f*ω, f*(α∧β)=f*α∧f*β, and (g∘f)*=f*g*. In coordinates f*dy_i=Σ_j∂_jf_i dx_j. When m=n, f*(a dy_1∧⋯∧dy_n)=(a∘f)det Df dx_1∧⋯∧dx_n.

For a C^1 k-form ω=Σ_I a_I dx_I on an open Euclidean domain, define dω=Σ_(I,j)∂_ja_I dx_j∧dx_I. It is continuous; for C^r coefficients with r≥1 it is C^(r−1). For k=n it is zero. For a zero-form f it is its total derivative represented as a one-form.
For C^1 forms α,β of degrees p,q, d(α∧β)=dα∧β+(−1)^pα∧dβ. For any C^2 form ω, d(dω)=0. If f is C^2 and ω is C^1, then f*ω is C^1 and d(f*ω)=f*(dω).

A C^1 map does not in general pull a C^1 form back to a C^1 form: there exist such maps and forms for which the pullback fails C^1 regularity because its coefficients contain first derivatives of the map. Thus pointwise exterior-derivative naturality above is asserted for C^2 maps. The C^1-parametrization Stokes assertion is a separate integrated result, not a pointwise naturality claim.

A C^1 form ω is closed when dω=0. A positive-degree form ω is exact when ω=dη for a C^1 form η of one lower degree. Exact C^1 forms are closed even when η is only C^1; the elementary pointwise d² calculation itself requires η∈C^2, while the C^1-primitive result is established separately in chapter 15.
For a C^1 zero-form on an open Euclidean set, being closed is equivalent to being locally constant, hence to being constant on each connected component. No degree-minus-one primitive is asserted.

Let U⊂R^n be open and star-shaped about a∈U. For every continuous k-form ω with k≥1, define the continuous (k−1)-form (Hω)_x(v_1,…,v_(k−1))=∫_0^1 t^(k−1)ω_(a+t(x−a))(x−a,v_1,…,v_(k−1))dt. If ω is C^1 then Hω is C^1 and dHω+Hdω=ω. Consequently every closed C^1 positive-degree form on U has this displayed C^1 primitive. If its coefficients are C^r, the primitive is C^r for 1≤r≤∞.
For ω=z dx∧dz on R^3 and homotopy center 0, Hω=(−z²dx+xz dz)/3; dω=0 and direct differentiation gives dHω=z dx∧dz.

In standard oriented R^3 define α_F=F_1dx+F_2dy+F_3dz, β_F=F_1dy∧dz+F_2dz∧dx+F_3dx∧dy, and Ω=dx∧dy∧dz. Whenever the corresponding first derivatives are continuous, df=α_(∇f), dα_F=β_(curl F), and dβ_F=(div F)Ω. For vectors v,w, β_F(v,w)=F·(v×w).

For k≥1, an inner product and orientation on a k-dimensional real vector space determine a unique top covector equal to one on every positive orthonormal basis. Its absolute value on v_1,…,v_k is √det((⟨v_i,v_j⟩)_(i,j)). Reversing the orientation changes this top covector's sign and leaves the positive Gram density unchanged.

On R^2∖{0}, θ=(−y dx+x dy)/(x²+y²) is closed: ∂_x(x/(x²+y²))=∂_y(−y/(x²+y²)), hence dθ=0. Its integral along (cos t,sin t), 0≤t≤2π, is 2π, and therefore θ is not exact despite being locally exact. The corresponding closed nonexact two-form in punctured R^3 is the separate radial-obstruction example.

Scope limitation: manifolds here are embedded subsets of Euclidean spaces. Abstract manifold topology, curvature and general cohomology are outside scope.

Let 1≤r≤∞ and 0≤k≤n. For k>0 let H^k={u∈R^k:u_k≥0}. An embedded C^r k-manifold with boundary M⊂R^n is locally parametrized by homeomorphisms φ:V→M∩O, with O ambient open, V open in R^k or relatively open in H^k, and rank Dφ=k. Being C^r on a half-space means having a C^r full-rank extension to an open Euclidean neighborhood near every point. A boundary chart is centered on u_k=0, and charts may be restricted. For k=0 the manifold is discrete with empty intrinsic boundary; a compact zero-manifold is finite.

For 1≤r≤∞ and 0≤k≤n, every full-rank C^r parametrization is, after shrinking around a parameter point, a graph over a k-coordinate plane with parameter domain a local C^r image of its original domain. Its inverse on its image is the restriction of a C^r ambient map. Two embedded charts have C^r transition maps with invertible derivatives on overlaps. Interior chart points cannot be boundary chart points. Boundary charts map their flat boundaries onto the same intrinsic subset ∂M. For positive k, ∂M is a C^r (k−1)-manifold without boundary; M∖∂M is a k-manifold without boundary. The separate zero-dimensional convention gives ∂M=∅.

For 1≤r≤∞ and 0≤k≤n, if g:O⊂R^n→R^(n−k) is C^r on open O and rank Dg=n−k on g^−1(0), then g^−1(0) is an embedded C^r k-manifold without boundary. Conversely, every embedded chart near an interior point has a local regular-level description. Graphs of C^r maps are embedded-manifold examples.

For x=φ(u) in an embedded manifold, define T_xM=im Dφ(u); this is chart independent. At an interior point it is exactly the set of velocities of two-sided C^1 curves in M through x; at a boundary point it is the linear span of one-sided velocities. For a regular level set g^−1(0), T_xM=ker Dg(x). At a boundary point, T_x∂M is the image of {v_k=0} under a boundary chart derivative.

A C^r immersion is a full-rank parametrization and is locally an embedded patch. An embedding is additionally a homeomorphism onto its image. Immersions need not be globally injective; a circle traversed twice has rank one and multiplicity two. An injective immersion from a noncompact domain need not be an embedding: t↦(cos t,sin t) on [0,2π) is injective and regular but its inverse is discontinuous at (1,0). Every injective continuous map from a compact domain into Euclidean space has continuous inverse onto its image.
A sphere has empty intrinsic manifold boundary although its ambient topological boundary is the entire sphere.

For k>0 an orientation on a k-dimensional real space is one of the two equivalence classes of ordered bases under positive change-of-basis determinant. A manifold orientation is a continuous choice: derivative columns of every chart φ agree or disagree by a locally constant sign σ_φ∈{+1,−1}. If ψ=φ∘h then σ_ψ=(σ_φ∘h)sgn(det Dh). A positive chart has sign +1. Interior charts can be made positive by reflection. Boundary charts retain the fixed half-space u_k≥0; in dimension one they may necessarily have sign −1, so an all-positive boundary atlas is not assumed. In dimension zero an orientation is an explicitly chosen sign ±1 at each point.

For an oriented embedded k-manifold M with k≥1 and x∈∂M, there is a unique unit outward vector ν∈T_xM perpendicular to T_x∂M. For k≥2 a basis (v_1,…,v_(k−1)) is positive on ∂M exactly when (ν,v_1,…,v_(k−1)) is positive on M; this boundary orientation is chart independent and continuous. For k=1 the boundary point has sign +1 if ν agrees with the tangent-line orientation and −1 otherwise; this is an explicit signed-point convention. For standard oriented H^k, its flat boundary has (−1)^k times the standard orientation of R^(k−1). An oriented interval has terminal endpoint sign +1 and initial endpoint sign −1.

An oriented Euclidean k-manifold with k≥1 has the metric top form dV_M. In a positive chart φ, φ*dV_M=√det(Dφ^T Dφ) du_1∧⋯∧du_k; in an arbitrary chart multiply this expression by σ_φ. The unsigned Gram density exists without orientability. Its factor is speed for k=1, cross-product magnitude for k=2 in R^3, and |det Dφ| for k=n in R^n. In degree zero the unsigned density is 1 and the signed metric zero-form equals the chosen orientation sign at that point.
For every compact K⊂O⊂R^n with O open, there exists χ∈C^∞(R^n;[0,1]) equal to 1 on a neighborhood of K and with compact support contained in O.

Let K⊂M be compact in an embedded manifold, and let relative open sets U_α cover K. There exist finitely many nonnegative functions λ_i on M, each the restriction of an ambient smooth function near M, with compact support in some U_(α_i), and Σ_iλ_i=1 on a neighborhood of K in M. Their sum can be chosen in [0,1] everywhere. Their supports may be placed in arbitrarily small chart neighborhoods, including at boundary points. No general locally finite partition on an abstract manifold is assumed.
If a Euclidean map f is C^1 on an open neighborhood of a compact Euclidean rectangle Q, there are C^∞ maps f_j on a neighborhood of Q such that f_j→f and Df_j→Df uniformly on Q.

Scope limitation: for noncompact embedded manifolds and compactly supported forms, only a finite partition near the support is required. A general locally finite partition of unity on an arbitrary abstract manifold is not an added assumption or deliverable.

A C^r parametrized k-cell in open O⊂R^n is a map c:[0,1]^k→O having a C^r extension to a neighborhood of the cube; neither full rank nor injectivity is required. For a continuous k-form, if c*ω=a(u)du_1∧⋯∧du_k define ∫_cω=∫_[0,1]^k a(u)du as a proper Riemann integral. A zero-cell is a point and ∫_c f=f(c). A finite k-chain is a finite formal integer linear combination of cells, with its integral defined linearly and no implicit quotient by reparametrizations or homology. If F_i^ε inserts ε∈{0,1} in coordinate i with the remaining coordinate order retained, define ∂c=Σ_(i=1)^k(−1)^(i−1)(c∘F_i^1−c∘F_i^0), extend linearly, and set the boundary of every zero-chain to zero.
For every finite chain, ∂²c=0. The boundary face signs in the definition are exactly the outward-first signs for the standard oriented cube (upper i-face (−1)^(i−1), lower i-face its negative).

For every C^2 k-cell c, k≥1, and every C^1 (k−1)-form ω on a neighborhood of the image of c, ∫_c dω=∫_(∂c)ω. The same identity holds for finite chains by linearity, including the signed zero-dimensional boundaries when k=1.
If a C^1 k-form ω on an open subset of R^n, k≥1, satisfies ω=dη for a C^1 (k−1)-form η, then dω=0. This includes k≥n, where the exterior derivative is zero by degree; η is not assumed C^2.

For every C^1 k-cell c, k≥1, and C^1 ambient (k−1)-form ω on a neighborhood of its image, ∫_c dω=∫_(∂c)ω, with the finite-chain extension by linearity. No second derivative of c and no pointwise derivative d(c*ω) are required.

If h:V→W is a C^1 diffeomorphism between connected open subsets of R^k and η is a continuous compactly supported top form on W, then ∫_Vh*η=sgn(det Dh)∫_Wη, where the determinant sign is constant on V. The same statement, including existence of the Riemann integrals, holds on relatively open half-space domains for chart transitions and compactly supported coefficients continuous up to the flat boundary. On disconnected overlaps signs are taken separately on components.

For an oriented C^1 embedded k-manifold M with boundary, k≥1, and a continuous compactly supported top-covector field ω on its tangent spaces, choose a finite partition λ_i equal to one near supp ω subordinate to charts φ_i:V_i→U_i with constant orientation signs σ_i and define ∫_Mω=Σ_iσ_i∫_(V_i)φ_i*(λ_iω). Coordinate coefficients have compact support relative to V_i and are extended by zero inside a containing rectangle, restricted to H^k when needed. Sign +1 means the ordered chart derivative basis is positive. On a compact zero-manifold define the integral as the finite sum of values multiplied by chosen point-orientation signs. For unsigned densities use density coefficients and absolute determinants instead.

The embedded-manifold integral is independent of all choices of charts and finite partitions. It is linear, additive under finite localization, changes sign upon reversing orientation, and equals the signed single-chart integral when the support lies in one chart. Unsigned density integration is orientation independent and is defined even on nonorientable manifolds. In dimension zero these assertions hold for the finite signed sums.

On a C^2 embedded manifold, a C^1 intrinsic p-form is a tangent covector field whose pullbacks in charts are C^1. There is a unique continuous intrinsic (p+1)-form d_Mω such that φ*d_Mω=d(φ*ω) in every chart. For a C^1 ambient form, taking its tangent restriction then d_M equals tangent restriction of its ambient exterior derivative.

Let M⊂R^n be an oriented C^2 embedded k-manifold with boundary, k≥1, and let ω be a compactly supported C^1 intrinsic (k−1)-form. Give ∂M the outward-first orientation. Then ∫_M d_Mω=∫_(∂M)ω. In particular this holds for every such intrinsic form on compact M.

For an oriented C^1 embedded k-manifold M⊂R^n with boundary, k≥1, and a C^1 ambient (k−1)-form ω on a neighborhood of M with M∩supp ω compact, the outward-first boundary satisfies ∫_M(dω)|_(TM)=∫_(∂M)ω|_(T∂M). In particular compact M suffices. The left integrand is tangent restriction of ambient dω; intrinsic C^1 exterior differentiation is not presumed on a merely C^1 manifold.

The generalized Stokes classical interfaces identify d(Pdx+Qdy)=(∂_xQ−∂_yP)dx∧dy in the plane; d[Σ_i(−1)^(i−1)F_i dx_1∧⋯∧widehat(dx_i)∧⋯∧dx_n]=(Σ_i∂_iF_i)dx_1∧⋯∧dx_n in R^n; and dα_F=β_(curl F) on two-dimensional surfaces in R^3. These use C^1 coefficient data and the induced orientations, together with the normal and tangent identifications of chapter 12, to give Green, Gauss and classical Stokes.

For k≥1, let C=Σ_(j=1)^N a_jc_j be a finite chain of C^1 k-cells, or a finite sum of oriented compact C^1 embedded k-manifolds with boundary. Assume the internal boundary pieces can be paired with identical parametrizations up to an orientation-reversing C^1 diffeomorphism, so their directed contributions cancel, and that the unpaired pieces give the prescribed outer boundary with matching orientations. For an ambient C^1 (k−1)-form ω, Σ_j a_j∫_(c_j)dω=∫_(outer boundary)ω. If the pieces are intended to represent one geometric region or surface, require pairwise disjoint interiors and all remaining overlaps to lie in the displayed faces or finitely many lower-dimensional C^1 pieces; under those conditions the sum has multiplicity one and agrees with its usual piecewise integral.

Applicability clarification for finite piecewise Stokes: boxes and explicitly assembled finite regular-cell collections, as well as finite regular surface pieces with cancelling seams, fall under that theorem when its stated decomposition and matching hypotheses hold. A box lacks a smooth manifold boundary chart at its corners. No assertion covers an arbitrary set merely called piecewise smooth or rough without those hypotheses. The box-corner mathematical fact is also recorded in the chapter-12 sign example.

An exact form integrates to zero over every finite cell cycle when its primitive has the regularity required by the applicable cell Stokes theorem. On every compact oriented boundaryless manifold, ∫_M dη=0 under either the C^2-manifold/C^1-intrinsic-primitive hypotheses or the C^1-manifold/C^1-ambient-primitive hypotheses of generalized Stokes.

On R^3∖{0}, let F(x)=x/|x|^3 and ω=β_F. Then div F=3|x|^−3−3|x|^−5Σ_i x_i²=0, so dω=0. On the outward unit sphere F·n=1 and ∫_(S²)ω=4π. There is no global C^2 one-form η on punctured space with dη=ω; even a global C^1 ambient primitive is excluded by ambient Stokes. Consequently this divergence-free field has no global C^1 vector potential, and therefore no global C^2 vector potential either. This is a closed-surface flux obstruction distinct from the planar circulation obstruction.

Editorial and future-formalization audit policy: theorem/family/page counts, PDF compilation, source inspection and mathematical editorial review are not Lean acceptance certificates. This section contains no new mathematical theorem.

Advisory navigation index of authored statement titles and local source labels. It is not an additional source of mathematical assertions, a Lean specification, a mandatory goal list, or evidence of coverage or acceptance. The mathematical inventory is derived from the complete original paper.tex.

Preamble, title, purpose and source-comparison information are editorial context. The agreed mathematical scope is the eighteen chapters of this unified manuscript, including definitions, independently stated results, constructions and adopted substantive examples. Fundamental groups, covering-space and surface classification and general dimension theory are out of scope; comparison with four textbooks does not adopt every exercise or every counterexample in them. Equivalent valid proofs are allowed; proof-route-only intermediate steps are not independent obligations.

Declared relative foundation F1: classical logic, sets, functions, equivalence relations and set quotients, finite and countable families, elementary cardinal arithmetic, well-ordering and Zorn's lemma; the axiom of choice is permitted. These are allowed background, not new results to prove. Uses of choice for ultrafilters, arbitrary products and well-ordering open covers are explicit.

Declared relative foundation F2: the ordered complete real field, complex field, elementary scalar sequences and series, interval limits, scalar continuous functions, elementary trigonometry and one-variable differentiation and integration. General-space compactness, Urysohn/Tietze extension, Ascoli, Baire and general Stone-Weierstrass are expressly not assumed foundations; chapter 16 constructs its needed polynomial approximation.

Declared relative foundation F3: finite-dimensional linear algebra, inner products, Cauchy-Schwarz, determinants, finite sums and elementary affine geometry. Metric and topological consequences used in scope must be proved or reduced to earlier results; Sperner counting and arbitrarily fine triangulations are included in chapter 17 rather than assumed.

Declared relative foundation F4 is confined to ordinal examples: the standard ordinal construction, first uncountable ordinal omega_1, transfinite induction and countability of the supremum of countably many countable ordinals (using countable unions of countable sets under choice). No set-theoretic topological conjecture is assumed.

Standing conventions: every topology is attached to its underlying set; subsets carry the subspace topology unless another is specified. Empty spaces and empty indexing families are allowed, and the empty product is a singleton. Compact means the finite-subcover property without Hausdorffness. Regular and normal do not include T1; T3=regular and T1, T4=normal and T1, and Tychonoff=completely regular and Hausdorff. These conventions apply to every obligation in this inventory and are elaborated by the chapter definitions.

Standing conventions: proper filters exclude the empty set; convergence to x means containing the neighborhood filter N(x). Moore-Smith subnet maps are order-preserving and cofinal. A uniformity on a nonempty set is a proper entourage filter, while on the empty set the unique degenerate entourage family is treated separately and is not a proper convergence filter. A proper map is a continuous map for which inverse images of compact sets are compact; its equivalence with being closed with compact fibers is restricted to the hypotheses of chapter 11.

Scope convention: distinguish Euclidean, subspace, product and box topologies and distinguish specified supremum metrics, uniformities and compact-open topologies until the appropriate bridge is proved. Every series or infinite partition of unity used must have the convergence or local-finiteness justification that makes it well-defined. These are fidelity requirements, not additional standalone theorems.

A topology on a set $X$ is a family $\tau\subseteq\powset(X)$ containing $\varnothing,X$, closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. A member is open; a set with open complement is closed. The empty union is $\varnothing$ and the empty intersection is $X$. A topology $\sigma$ on the same set is finer than $\tau$ if $\tau\subseteq\sigma$. The discrete topology is $\powset(X)$ and the indiscrete topology is $\{\varnothing,X\}$.

Closed sets contain $\varnothing,X$, are closed under arbitrary intersections and finite unions, and any family with these properties is the family of closed sets of a unique topology. Every family $\mathcal A\subseteq\powset(X)$ is contained in a smallest topology. Intersections of topologies on a fixed set are topologies; unions need not be.

On a linearly ordered set $L$, the order topology is generated by the open rays $\{x:x<a\}$ and $\{x:x>a\}$, $a\in L$. This definition also covers empty and singleton ordered sets. For a set with more than one point a basis consists of open intervals, together with intervals $[m,b)$ when a minimum $m$ exists and $(a,M]$ when a maximum $M$ exists.

Every linearly ordered space is Hausdorff. If $A\subseteq L$ is convex, meaning that it contains every point between any two of its points, its order topology for the restricted order equals its subspace topology from $L$, whose open sets are intersections of $A$ with open sets of $L$.

A family $\BB$ of subsets of $X$ is a basis for a topology precisely when it covers $X$ and, for $x\in B_1\cap B_2$ with $B_i\in\BB$, there is $B_3\in\BB$ with $x\in B_3\subseteq B_1\cap B_2$. The generated topology consists of all unions of basis members. If $\BB,\mathcal C$ are bases for $\tau,\sigma$, then $\tau\subseteq\sigma$ precisely when every $x\in B\in\BB$ admits $C\in\mathcal C$ with $x\in C\subseteq B$.

For any family $\mathcal S\subseteq\powset(X)$, the finite intersections of members of $\mathcal S$, including the empty intersection $X$, form a basis. Its topology is the smallest topology containing $\mathcal S$. In particular, no covering assumption on a subbasis is necessary with this convention.

A neighborhood of $x\in X$ is a set $N$ for which $x\in U\subseteq N$ for some open $U$. Write $\mathcal N(x)$ for all such $N$. A local base at $x$ is a subfamily $\mathcal B_x\subseteq\mathcal N(x)$ such that every $N\in\mathcal N(x)$ contains a member of $\mathcal B_x$.

Every neighborhood contains $x$; supersets and finite intersections of neighborhoods are neighborhoods. A subset $G\subseteq X$ is open exactly when it is a neighborhood of every one of its points. If $\BB$ is a basis, its members containing $x$ form a local base at $x$.

For $A\subseteq X$ put \[ \cl_X A=\bigcap\{F:A\subseteq F\subseteq X,\ F\text{ closed}\},\qquad \Int_X A=\bigcup\{U:U\subseteq A,\ U\text{ open}\}. \] The boundary is $\partial_X A=\cl_X A\cap\cl_X(X\setminus A)$; $A$ is dense in $X$ if $\cl_X A=X$. A point $x$ is an accumulation point of $A$ if every neighborhood of $x$ meets $A\setminus\{x\}$; write $A'$ for the set of these points.

For $A\subseteq X$, $x\in\cl_X A$ if and only if every neighborhood of $x$ meets $A$, and $x\in\Int_X A$ if and only if $A$ is a neighborhood of $x$. Either test may be made using a local base. Moreover \[ \cl_X A=A\cup A',\qquad A\text{ dense}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ A\cap U\ne\varnothing \text{ for every nonempty open }U. \]

Closure is extensive, monotone, idempotent, preserves finite unions, and sends $\varnothing$ to $\varnothing$. A set is closed if and only if it equals its closure. Also \[ \Int_X A=X\setminus\cl_X(X\setminus A),\quad \partial_X A=\cl_X A\setminus\Int_X A,\quad \Int_X(A\cap B)=\Int_X A\cap\Int_X B. \] The boundary is closed; $A$ is both open and closed if and only if $\partial_X A=\varnothing$.

Suppose $c:\powset(X)\to\powset(X)$ satisfies $A\subseteq c(A)$, $c(c(A))=c(A)$, $c(A\cup B)=c(A)\cup c(B)$, and $c(\varnothing)=\varnothing$. There is a unique topology whose closure operator is $c$.

On R, the open intervals (a,b) form a basis of the usual topology, and intervals [a,b) form a basis of a strictly finer lower-limit topology; [0,1) witnesses strictness. For every set X, the empty set and complements of finite sets form the cofinite topology, and the empty set and complements of countable sets form the cocountable topology. On an infinite cofinite space the closed sets are exactly finite sets and X, and every infinite subset is dense. On an uncountable cocountable space every countable subset is closed and every uncountable subset is dense.

In the usual real line, A_n={1/n}, n>=1, satisfy union_n cl(A_n)={1/n:n>=1}, whereas 0 belongs to cl(union_n A_n) and not to that union of closures. For A=(-1,0), B=(0,1), cl(A intersect B) is empty while 0 belongs to cl(A) intersect cl(B). In the indiscrete space {a,b}, a is an accumulation point of {b}, although its neighborhoods meet that set in only one point. In every T1 space and for every subset A, x is an accumulation point of A if and only if every neighborhood of x meets A in infinitely many points; the reverse implication holds without T1.

A map $f:X\to Y$ is continuous if $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in $X$ for every open $V\subseteq Y$. It is continuous at $x$ if $f^{-1}(N)\in\mathcal N(x)$ for every $N\in\mathcal N(f(x))$. It is open, respectively closed, if it sends every open, respectively closed, subset of $X$ to an open, respectively closed, subset of $Y$. A homeomorphism is a bijection continuous in both directions. An embedding is a map inducing a homeomorphism $X\to f(X)$, where the image has the subspace topology $\{f(X)\cap V:V\text{ open in }Y\}$.

For $f:X\to Y$ the following are equivalent: continuity; continuity at every point; inverse images of closed sets are closed; and \[ f(\cl_X A)\subseteq\cl_Y f(A)\quad(A\subseteq X). \] To test continuity it suffices to test inverse images of a subbasis, and hence of a basis, of $Y$.

Identity maps, constant maps, and composites of continuous maps are continuous. If $A\subseteq X$ and $f:X\to Y$ is continuous, $f|_A$ is continuous. If $f(X)\subseteq B\subseteq Y$, then $f:X\to B$ is continuous if and only if $f:X\to Y$ is continuous. If $A\subseteq B\subseteq X$, the subspace topology induced on $A$ through $B$ is the one induced directly through $X$.

A continuous bijection is a homeomorphism if and only if it is open, equivalently if and only if it is closed. A map $e:X\to Y$ is an embedding if and only if it is injective, continuous, and every open subset of $X$ has the form $e^{-1}(V)$ for an open $V\subseteq Y$. Equivalently, the topology on $X$ is exactly $\{e^{-1}(V):V\text{ open in }Y\}$ and $e$ is injective. Composites of embeddings are embeddings.

For topologies $\tau,\sigma$ on $X$, the identity $(X,\sigma)\to(X,\tau)$ is continuous precisely when $\tau\subseteq\sigma$. Let $S=\{0,1\}$ have topology $\{\varnothing,\{1\},S\}$. The characteristic function $\chi_A:X\to S$ is continuous precisely when $A$ is open. With discrete topology on $\{0,1\}$ it is continuous precisely when $A$ is both open and closed.

Suppose $X=\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i$ and continuous maps $f_i:A_i\to Y$ agree on overlaps. They determine a unique map $f:X\to Y$. This map is continuous if all $A_i$ are open, or if $I$ is finite and all $A_i$ are closed.

An indexed family (A_i)_(i in I) is locally finite if each point has an open neighborhood meeting only finitely many indexed members. For every such locally finite family of closed subsets of X, union_i A_i is closed. More generally, if each F_i is closed in X and F_i subset A_i for a locally finite family (A_i), then union_i F_i is closed.

For arbitrary index set I, let (A_i) be a locally finite cover of X by closed subsets: each point has an open neighborhood meeting only finitely many indexed A_i. If continuous maps f_i:A_i -> Y agree on every overlap, there is a unique map f:X -> Y restricting to all f_i, and it is continuous.

The identity from a discrete two-point space to the indiscrete topology on the same set is a continuous bijection whose inverse is not continuous. A constant map into a singleton sends any accumulation point of a subset of its domain to a point that is not an accumulation point of its singleton image, so continuous maps need not preserve derived sets. On X={0} union {1/n:n>=1} with its usual real subspace topology, the singleton pieces give a countable closed cover that is not locally finite at 0; f(0)=0 and f(1/n)=1 restrict continuously to all pieces but f is not continuous. The real function h(x,y)=xy/(x^2+y^2) away from (0,0), with h(0,0)=0, is separately continuous in both variables but is not continuous at (0,0), as h(t,t)=1/2 for t!=0.

The first-coordinate projection R^2 -> R is continuous and open but not closed: the closed set {(x,y):xy=1} has image R minus {0}. The inclusion [0,1] -> R is continuous and closed but not open. A bijection from an indiscrete two-point space to a discrete two-point space is open and closed but not continuous.

For $A\subseteq X$, the sets $A\cap U$, $U$ open in $X$, form a topology on $A$. Its closed sets are $A\cap F$ with $F$ closed in $X$; for $B\subseteq A$, \[ \cl_A B=A\cap\cl_X B. \] The inclusion $i:A\hookrightarrow X$ is an embedding, and $g:Z\to A$ is continuous if and only if $i\circ g$ is continuous. If $\BB$ is a basis of $X$, $\{A\cap B:B\in\BB\}$ is a basis of $A$.

For B subset A subset X, A intersect Int_X(B) is contained in Int_A(B), but equality need not hold. For A=B={0} subset R, these sets are empty and {0}, respectively. Likewise boundary_A(B) need not equal A intersect boundary_X(B): for this same example they are empty and {0}, respectively. All subspaces have their subspace topologies.

Given maps $f_i:X\to Y_i$ from a set to topological spaces, there is a coarsest topology on $X$ making them continuous. It is generated by the subbasis $f_i^{-1}(V)$, $V$ open in $Y_i$. In this topology $g:Z\to X$ is continuous if and only if every $f_i\circ g$ is continuous.

For a family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ the product set $P=\prod_{i\in I}X_i$ consists of functions $x$ with $x(i)\in X_i$; write $x_i=x(i)$ and $\pi_i(x)=x_i$. The product topology is the initial topology of all $\pi_i$. Its basis consists of finite intersections $\bigcap_{i\in F}\pi_i^{-1}(U_i)$, where $F\subseteq I$ is finite and each $U_i$ is open. The box topology instead has all rectangles $\prod_i U_i$ as a basis. The empty product is a singleton. If any factor is empty, a product with that factor is empty.

A map $g:Z\to\prod_i X_i$ is continuous if and only if every coordinate $\pi_i\circ g$ is continuous. The projections are continuous and open. If the product is nonempty, every projection is surjective. Products over a finite index set have the box topology as their product topology.

If $A_i\subseteq X_i$, the product topology of $\prod_i A_i$ equals its subspace topology in $\prod_i X_i$. If $e_i:A_i\to X_i$ are embeddings, their product is an embedding. Coordinate permutations and regroupings of products are homeomorphisms.

In classical set theory with choice, for $A_i\subseteq X_i$, \[ \cl_{\prod_iX_i}\!\left(\prod_i A_i\right)=\prod_i\cl_{X_i}A_i. \] In particular a product of dense subsets is dense. The product of closed subsets is closed, without needing choice for that assertion.

The diagonal d:R -> R^N, d(t)_n=t for n>=1, is continuous in the product topology but not the box topology: the box-open product_n(-1/n,1/n) pulls back to {0}. The product {0,1}^N of discrete two-point spaces is not discrete, since every basic neighborhood contains at least two points. Product projections need not be closed (the first projection R^2 -> R and the hyperbola xy=1 witness this, as in d10:02:open-closed-examples). Separate continuity of a function on a product need not imply joint continuity (the function in d10:02:cautions supplies the example).

Let $S=\coprod_{i\in I}X_i=\{(i,x):i\in I,\ x\in X_i\}$. Declare $U\subseteq S$ open if $\{x:(i,x)\in U\}$ is open in every $X_i$. This is a topology; each summand inclusion $j_i$ is an embedding with open and closed image. A map $f:S\to Y$ is continuous if and only if every $f\circ j_i$ is continuous. The sum over an empty family is empty.

For maps $q_i:X_i\to Y$ to a set $Y$, the family \[ \{V\subseteq Y:q_i^{-1}(V)\text{ is open in }X_i\text{ for every }i\} \] is the finest topology making every $q_i$ continuous. For this topology $h:Y\to Z$ is continuous if and only if every $h\circ q_i$ is continuous.

A quotient map is a surjection $q:X\to Y$ such that $V\subseteq Y$ is open exactly when $q^{-1}(V)$ is open in $X$. A subset $A\subseteq X$ is saturated if $A=q^{-1}(q(A))$, equivalently if it is a union of fibers. The quotient topology of a surjection is the final topology for that map. For an equivalence relation $\sim$ on $X$, the quotient $X/{\sim}$ is the set of equivalence classes with this topology for the class map.

If $q:X\to Y$ is quotient, $h:Y\to Z$ is continuous if and only if $h\circ q$ is continuous. In particular a continuous $f:X\to Z$ constant on fibers of $q$ descends uniquely to a continuous $\bar f:Y\to Z$. Conversely a continuous surjection with the stated mapping test for every target space is quotient. Any continuous open surjection or continuous closed surjection is quotient. Composites of quotient maps are quotient. A continuous surjection admitting a continuous section is quotient.

If $q:X\to Y$ is quotient and $A=q^{-1}(B)$ is an open or a closed saturated subspace, then $q|_A:A\to B$ is quotient. If $q$ is open (respectively closed), its restriction over any $B\subseteq Y$ is open (respectively closed), and hence quotient. A product of continuous open surjections is a continuous open surjection in the presence of choice, so is quotient.

Give X=[0,1] coproduct [2,3] its disjoint-sum topology, and [0,2] its usual topology. The map q(t)=t on the first summand and q(t)=t-1 on the second is a continuous closed surjection and hence quotient. Its restriction to A=[0,1) coproduct [2,3], mapping onto the same [0,2], is not quotient: [1,2] is not open in the target but its restricted inverse image is the open second summand. This A is not saturated, since one preimage of 1 is kept and another discarded.

Let q:R -> Y be the quotient that collapses the positive integers {1,2,...} to one point b and leaves all other points distinct. With Q carrying its usual subspace topology, id_Q is quotient but q times id_Q:R times Q -> Y times Q is not quotient. Explicitly, for a_n=sqrt(2)/n define U_n={(x,r) in R times Q: |x-n|<1/4 and |r-a_n|>|x-n|}, and U=union_(n>=1) U_n. Then U is open and saturated for q times id_Q, while its image V contains (b,0) and is not open. Thus the product of these two quotient maps fails the quotient open-set criterion.

A directed set is a nonempty set $D$ with a reflexive transitive relation $\le$ such that any two elements have a common upper bound. Antisymmetry is not required. A net in $X$ is a function $d\mapsto x_d$ on a directed set. It is eventually in $A$ if $x_d\in A$ for all $d\ge d_0$ for some $d_0$, and frequently in $A$ if for every $d_0$ some $d\ge d_0$ has $x_d\in A$. It converges to $x$ if eventually in every $N\in\mathcal N(x)$, and clusters at $x$ if frequently in every such $N$. A Moore--Smith subnet is $x_{\phi(e)}$ indexed by a directed set $E$, where $\phi:E\to D$ is order-preserving and has cofinal range: for every $d\in D$ some $e\in E$ has $d\le\phi(e)$.

An order-preserving cofinal $\phi$ is eventually above each $d\in D$. A subnet of a convergent net converges to the same point, and a subnet of a subnet is a subnet. If a subnet clusters at $x$, the original net clusters at $x$.
A net clusters at $x$ if and only if it has a Moore--Smith subnet converging to $x$.

Let x:D -> X be a net on a nonempty directed preorder D, and let E be a nonempty directed preorder and phi:E -> D satisfy: for every d in D there is e_0 such that e>=e_0 implies phi(e)>=d; phi need not be monotone. For y_e=x_(phi(e)), there exists one net that is simultaneously a Moore-Smith subnet of y and of x (the refinement maps are monotone and cofinal). Consequently if y converges to x_0, the original net x clusters at x_0.

For $A\subseteq X$, $x\in\cl_X A$ if and only if a net with all its terms in $A$ converges to $x$. A subset is closed if and only if it contains every limit in $X$ of every net with terms in that subset.
A map $f:X\to Y$ is continuous at $x$ if and only if $x_d\to x$ implies $f(x_d)\to f(x)$ for every net in $X$. Thus continuity is equivalent to preservation of all net limits.

A proper filter $\FF$ on $X$ is a nonempty family of subsets, closed under supersets and finite intersections, with $\varnothing\notin\FF$. A filter base is a nonempty family $\mathcal B$ of nonempty subsets such that for $B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B$ some $B_3\in\mathcal B$ is contained in $B_1\cap B_2$. Its generated filter consists of the supersets of its members. A filter $\mathcal G$ is finer than $\FF$ when $\FF\subseteq\mathcal G$. It converges to $x$ when $\mathcal N(x)\subseteq\FF$, and clusters at $x$ when every $F\in\FF$ meets every neighborhood of $x$.

A filter base generates a proper filter. A family of subsets generates a proper filter by taking finite intersections and supersets exactly when all its finite intersections, including the empty intersection $X$, are nonempty. In particular no proper filter exists on the empty set. Neighborhoods form a proper filter at each point. For a map $f:X\to Y$ its image filter is \[ f_*\FF=\{B\subseteq Y:f^{-1}(B)\in\FF\}; \] it is the proper filter generated by the sets $f(F)$, $F\in\FF$.

A proper filter $\FF$ clusters at $x$ exactly when $x\in\bigcap_{F\in\FF}\cl F$, and exactly when some finer proper filter converges to $x$. Also $x\in\cl A$ exactly when $A$ belongs to some proper filter converging to $x$.
A map is continuous at $x$ if and only if $f_*\FF\to f(x)$ for every proper filter $\FF\to x$. It suffices to test $\FF=\mathcal N(x)$.

For a net $(x_d)$, the tail sets $T_d=\{x_e:e\ge d\}$ generate a proper filter $\FF_x$. It has exactly the same limits and cluster points as the net. Conversely, for a proper filter $\FF$, the pairs $(F,a)$ with $a\in F\in\FF$, ordered by reverse inclusion of $F$, define a net with value $a$ whose tail filter is exactly $\FF$. A Moore--Smith subnet has a tail filter finer than the original tail filter.

If a proper filter $\mathcal G$ contains the tail filter of $(x_d)$, there is a Moore--Smith subnet whose tail filter contains $\mathcal G$. In particular, if $\mathcal G\to x$, that subnet converges to $x$.

A net in a product converges to $x$ if and only if every coordinate net converges to $x_i$. A proper filter $\FF$ on that product converges to $x$ if and only if $(\pi_i)_*\FF\to x_i$ for every $i$. A space is Hausdorff if and only if each net has at most one limit, equivalently if and only if each proper filter has at most one limit. Here Hausdorff means that distinct points have disjoint open neighborhoods.

If $X$ is first countable, meaning that every point has a countable local base, then $x\in\cl A$ if and only if some sequence in $A$ converges to $x$. In such a domain, preservation of sequence limits characterizes continuity into any target space. No countability hypothesis on the target is needed.

On an uncountable set X with the cocountable topology, a sequence converges to x if and only if it is eventually equal to x (eventual equality implies convergence in every topology). Consequently id:X_cocountable -> X_discrete preserves all convergent sequences but is not continuous. Every uncountable proper subset A of X is dense, but no sequence of points of A converges to a point outside A; nets do detect those closure points. In R^2, the sequence alternating (0,1) and (1,0) has 0 as a cluster point of each coordinate sequence, while (0,0) is not a cluster point of the paired sequence.

A space $X$ is compact if every cover of $X$ by open sets has a finite subcover; an empty finite subcover is permitted. A family $\mathcal A$ of subsets has the finite intersection property (FIP) if every finite subfamily has nonempty intersection, including the empty subfamily whose intersection is $X$. A subset is compact when it is compact in its subspace topology.

A space is compact if and only if every family of closed subsets with the FIP has nonempty total intersection. Equivalently, for every family $\mathcal A$ with the FIP, \[ \bigcap_{A\in\mathcal A}\cl_X A\ne\varnothing. \]

A subset $K\subseteq X$ is compact if and only if every cover of it by ambient open sets has a finite subcover. Closed subsets of compact spaces are compact. A finite union of compact subsets is compact.
If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous and $X$ is compact, its image $f(X)$ is compact. In particular a continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact space attains both its maximum and its minimum.

If $K$ is compact in a Hausdorff space $X$ and $x\notin K$, there are disjoint open sets containing $x$ and $K$. Hence $K$ is closed. Two disjoint compact subsets of a Hausdorff space have disjoint open neighborhoods.
A continuous map from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is closed. If it is bijective, it is a homeomorphism; if it is injective, it is an embedding; if it is surjective, it is quotient.

Let $K$ be compact, $x\in X$, and $W\subseteq X\times K$ open with $\{x\}\times K\subseteq W$. There is an open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that $U\times K\subseteq W$. Consequently the projection $X\times K\to X$ is a closed map for every space $X$.
A finite product of compact spaces is compact.

An ultrafilter is a proper filter maximal among proper filters on its underlying set. The principal ultrafilter at $x$ is $\{A\subseteq X:x\in A\}$. A filter is free if the intersection of all its members is empty. An ultranet is a net eventually in $A$ or eventually in $X\setminus A$ for every $A\subseteq X$.

A proper filter $\UU$ is an ultrafilter if and only if, for each $A\subseteq X$, exactly one of $A$ and $X\setminus A$ belongs to $\UU$. An ultrafilter converges to each of its cluster points. For any map $f$, $f_*\UU$ is an ultrafilter.
Every proper filter is contained in an ultrafilter. More generally any family with the FIP is contained in an ultrafilter. This proof uses Zorn's lemma.

On an infinite set the complements of finite subsets generate a proper filter, whose ultrafilter extensions are free. The tail filter of a net is an ultrafilter exactly when the net is an ultranet. Every net has a Moore--Smith subnet that is an ultranet, using ultrafilter extension.

For a space $X$ the following are equivalent, working with choice: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)] \item $X$ is compact; \item every proper filter on $X$ has a cluster point; \item every net in $X$ has a cluster point; \item every net in $X$ has a Moore--Smith convergent subnet; \item every ultrafilter on $X$ converges to at least one point; \item every ultranet in $X$ converges to at least one point. \end{enumerate} The common limit need not be unique. The ultrafilter-extension implication below is the choice-dependent step.

An arbitrary product of compact spaces is compact in the product topology. Conversely, if a product is nonempty and compact, every factor is compact. These statements do not require Hausdorffness. The forward proof uses choice.

In set theory without assuming choice, the assertion that every product of compact spaces is compact implies the axiom of choice. Thus full arbitrary-space Tychonoff is stronger than simply ignoring the nonuniqueness of coordinate limits.
Every closed bounded real interval is compact in its usual topology.

A space is countably compact if every countable open cover has a finite subcover; it is sequentially compact if every sequence has a convergent subsequence indexed by a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers. It is limit point compact if every infinite subset has an accumulation point meaning a point x whose every neighborhood meets that subset away from x.

For an arbitrary topological space X, countable compactness is equivalent both to the countable closed-family FIP criterion (every countable family of closed subsets with all finite intersections, including the empty one, nonempty has nonempty total intersection) and to every sequence in X having a cluster point. Sequential compactness implies countable compactness; in every first-countable space countable compactness and sequential compactness coincide, without a separation assumption. Compactness implies countable compactness and limit point compactness. For T1 spaces, countable compactness and limit point compactness are equivalent. Here limit point compactness means every infinite subset has a point whose every neighborhood meets that subset away from the point, and sequential compactness uses strictly increasing subsequence indices.

The product {0,1}^(P(N)) with each factor discrete is compact Hausdorff but not sequentially compact. Specifically x_n(A)=1 if n belongs to A and 0 otherwise has no convergent subsequence: for any increasing indices n_1<n_2<..., the coordinate A={n_2,n_4,...} alternates. On N times {0,1}, with N discrete and {0,1} indiscrete and the product topology, every nonempty subset has an accumulation point (the other point of the same two-point fiber suffices), hence the space is limit point compact; nevertheless the countable open cover by fibers {n} times {0,1} has no finite subcover, so it is not countably compact.

A subset of $\R^n$, with its usual topology, is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded. This includes $n=0$ and the empty subset. The usual Euclidean topology on finite-dimensional R^n equals its finite coordinate product topology (including n=0).

Every finite topological space and every indiscrete space is compact, including empty spaces. Every infinite discrete space is not compact. Every cofinite space and each of its subspaces is compact. On an infinite cofinite space, every infinite proper subset is compact but not closed, illustrating the need for Hausdorffness in the compact-closed conclusion. In a two-point indiscrete space every proper filter converges to both points, so compactness gives existence rather than uniqueness of limits. General compactness does not imply sequential compactness, as witnessed in d10:05:variant-counterexamples.

For any topological space X, a separation is X=U∪V with U,V disjoint nonempty open subsets. X is connected iff no separation exists; A⊆X is connected iff its subspace is connected. The empty space and every one-point space are connected. A,B⊆X are separated iff A∩cl_X(B)=B∩cl_X(A)=∅. No separation axiom on X is imposed.

For any space X, equivalent conditions are: X is connected; the only clopen subsets of X are ∅ and X; every continuous map X→{0,1}, with the codomain discrete, is constant. A map with empty domain counts as constant. For A,B⊆X and Y=A∪B, the decomposition into A and B is a separation of the subspace Y iff A and B are nonempty separated subsets of X.

A continuous image of a connected space is connected. If A⊆B⊆cl_X(A) and A is connected, then B is connected, including A=∅. For an arbitrary indexed family (A_i) of connected subsets of X and a nonempty connected subset C⊆X such that A_i∩C≠∅ for every i, C∪⋃_i A_i is connected. In particular any union of connected sets with a common point is connected; the empty union is connected as well.

An arbitrary product ∏_i X_i of connected topological spaces is connected, including the empty-index product and products with an empty factor. If the product set is nonempty, it is connected iff each factor is connected.

For A⊆ℝ with the usual topology, A is connected iff it is order convex: for every a,b∈A and t∈ℝ with a<t<b, t∈A. Empty sets and singletons are included. Consequently, for every continuous f:X→ℝ on a connected space X, whenever a,b∈f(X) and a<t<b, one has t∈f(X).

Let L be a linearly ordered set with at least two points, dense order, and the least-upper-bound property for each nonempty subset bounded above. Every convex subset of L, with the subspace topology inherited from the order topology of L, is connected, including empty and singleton convex subsets.

For x∈X, the component C(x) is the union of all connected subsets of X containing x. A path from x to y is a continuous p:[0,1]→X with p(0)=x and p(1)=y. X is path connected iff every pair x,y∈X is joined by a path; the empty space counts as path connected. P(x) is the set of y reachable by a path from x.

The components of any space X are exactly its maximal nonempty connected subsets; they partition X and are closed. Its path components partition X and are exactly its maximal nonempty path connected subsets. Each path component lies in a component. Path components are not necessarily closed (a counterexample exists).

In ℝ² let G={(t,sin(1/t)):0<t≤1} and S=G∪({0}×[-1,1]), with subspace topologies. Then cl_{ℝ²}(G)=S; S is connected and has exactly two path components, G and {0}×[-1,1]. Both these pieces are path connected, and G is a path component of S that is not closed in S.

X is locally connected at x iff every neighborhood of x contains a connected neighborhood of x, and locally path connected at x iff every neighborhood contains a path connected neighborhood of x. Neighborhoods in these definitions need not be open. X is locally connected, respectively locally path connected, iff the corresponding condition holds at every x∈X.

For any space X, local connectedness is equivalent to every component of every open subset being open in X, and equivalent to having a basis of connected open subsets. Replacing connected by path connected and components by path components gives the corresponding equivalences for local path connectedness. In a locally path connected space the components equal the path components. Local connectedness and local path connectedness each pass to open subspaces.

The image under a quotient surjection of a locally connected space is locally connected. A continuous image of a path connected space is path connected. An arbitrary product of path connected spaces is path connected, including the empty-index product and products with an empty factor.

For a nonempty product ∏_i X_i, local connectedness holds iff each X_i is locally connected and all but finitely many X_i are connected. For a nonempty product, local path connectedness holds iff each X_i is locally path connected and all but finitely many X_i are path connected. Any compact locally connected space has finitely many components, including the empty space with zero components; no Hausdorff assumption is made on this last assertion.

Local connectedness does not imply connectedness: a discrete two-point space is locally connected and disconnected. Connectedness does not imply local connectedness: the sine-curve space S from d10:06:sine-curve is connected and is not locally connected at (0,0). Local connectedness is not inherited by arbitrary subspaces: ℚ⊆ℝ has only singleton nonempty connected subsets and singleton components, is not discrete, and is not locally connected, whereas ℝ is locally connected.

For x∈X the quasi-component Q(x) is the intersection of all clopen subsets of X containing x. X is totally disconnected iff each component is a singleton. In this manuscript X is zero-dimensional iff its clopen subsets form a basis; this definition imposes no separation axiom and is not covering dimension.
For every compact Hausdorff space X and x∈X, the quasi-component Q(x) equals the component C(x). Moreover for every open O⊆X with C(x)⊆O, there is a clopen H⊆X satisfying C(x)⊆H⊆O.

A compact Hausdorff space is totally disconnected iff it has a clopen basis. More generally every T₁ space with a clopen basis is Hausdorff and totally disconnected. Without T₁ a clopen basis need not imply total disconnectedness (there exists a counterexample).

Let K be compact Hausdorff, let I be nonempty, and let (K_i)_{i∈I} be nonempty closed connected subsets of K, filtered downwards in the sense that for all i,j∈I there exists k∈I with K_k⊆K_i∩K_j. Then ⋂_{i∈I}K_i is nonempty and connected.

A continuum here means a nonempty compact connected Hausdorff space; nonmetrizability is allowed. If K is a continuum and ∅≠A⊆K, there exists a subcontinuum L⊆K containing A that is inclusion-minimal among all subcontinua of K containing A. In particular every pair of points of K lies in a subcontinuum irreducible between them, meaning no proper subcontinuum of that subcontinuum contains both. Uniqueness is not asserted.

Scope/navigation only: the preceding compact refinements are adopted; Cantor models/classification/surjections and square-filling are treated in Chapter 18. Cut-point classifications of arcs and circles, general inverse-limit representation, and the full Hahn–Mazurkiewicz characterization are outside the adopted scope. The continuum convention permits nonmetrizable compact Hausdorff spaces and excludes the empty space.

For any space X: T₀ means each two distinct points are distinguished by an open set; T₁ means every singleton is closed; Hausdorff/T₂ means each two distinct points have disjoint open neighborhoods. Regular means a point and a closed set omitting it have disjoint open neighborhoods; normal means two disjoint closed sets have disjoint open neighborhoods. Regular and normal do not include T₁. T₃ means regular and T₁, and T₄ means normal and T₁. Completely regular means that for every closed F⊆X and x∉F there is continuous f:X→[0,1] with f(x)=1 and f|_F=0. Tychonoff means completely regular and Hausdorff. Empty closed sets are allowed, and all these properties hold on the empty space.

A space X is regular iff for every open U⊆X and x∈U there exists an open V with x∈V⊆cl_X(V)⊆U. X is normal iff for every closed F⊆X and open U⊆X with F⊆U there exists an open V with F⊆V⊆cl_X(V)⊆U. The conventions do not assume T₁ and include empty closed sets.

For arbitrary spaces: Hausdorff implies T₁, and T₁ implies T₀; complete regularity implies regularity; regular plus T₀ implies T₃; T₃ implies Hausdorff; normal plus T₁ implies regularity, hence T₄ implies T₃. Normality alone does not imply regularity (a normal nonregular space exists).

Each of T₀, T₁, Hausdorffness, regularity, and complete regularity is inherited by every subspace and preserved by arbitrary products, including empty products or products whose underlying set is empty. Normality is inherited by closed subspaces and preserved under closed continuous surjections. Consequently T₃ and Tychonoff are inherited by arbitrary subspaces and preserved by arbitrary products, while T₄ is inherited by closed subspaces and preserved under closed continuous surjections.
Every compact Hausdorff space is normal and therefore T₄, including the empty space.

Every metric space is T₄. If A,B are disjoint nonempty closed subsets of a metric space (X,d), the function f(x)=dist(x,A)/(dist(x,A)+dist(x,B)), where dist(x,A)=inf_{a∈A}d(x,a), is well defined, continuous, and equal to 0 on A and 1 on B. Every closed subset of a metric space, including ∅, is a G_δ, meaning a countable intersection of open sets.
A space X is normal iff for every pair of disjoint closed A,B⊆X, including empty sets, there exists a continuous f:X→[0,1] satisfying f|_A=0 and f|_B=1. No T₁ assumption is made.

Every T₄ space is Tychonoff. For a normal space X, every closed F⊆X and open U⊆X with F⊆U admit a continuous f:X→[0,1] equal to 1 on F and 0 on X\U. The function assertion does not assume T₁ and includes empty F.

In a normal space X, a closed set A⊆X is the exact zero set g^{-1}({0}) of a continuous g:X→[0,1] iff A is a G_δ. Consequently, if X is normal and every closed subset is a G_δ, then for every disjoint closed A,B⊆X there exists continuous f:X→[0,1] with exact fibers f^{-1}({0})=A and f^{-1}({1})=B. Empty prescribed sets and the empty space are included; exact fibers are asserted under this additional hypothesis, not for unrestricted Urysohn separation.

Let X be normal, A⊆X closed, a>0, and h:A→[-a,a] continuous. There exists continuous g:X→[-a/3,a/3] such that |h(x)-g(x)|≤2a/3 for every x∈A. Empty A is permitted, and no separation axiom is added to normality.

If X is normal, A⊆X is closed, a,b∈ℝ satisfy a≤b, and f:A→[a,b] is continuous, then there exists a continuous extension F:X→[a,b] with F|_A=f. The cases a=b, A=∅, and X=∅ are included; no T₁ hypothesis is required.

A space X is normal iff for every closed subspace A⊆X and every continuous real-valued function f:A→ℝ, there exists a continuous F:X→ℝ with F|_A=f. The prescribed function is allowed to be unbounded, and empty closed subspaces are included; normality does not include T₁.

If A is closed in a normal space X, every continuous map A→ℝⁿ extends continuously to X→ℝⁿ for each finite n≥0. More generally every continuous A→∏_{i∈I}J_i extends continuously into the same product whenever each J_i is a nonempty closed real interval, allowing bounded [a_i,b_i], either closed ray, and ℝ itself. Arbitrary and empty index sets are included; nonempty interval factors are required even when A=∅.

Normality is not inherited by arbitrary subspaces and is not preserved by arbitrary products (counterexamples exist). The product failure is witnessed by the Sorgenfrey plane; its embedding into a cube together with compact Hausdorff normality gives subspace failure. The remaining statements of the remark are scope only: scalar real extension and coordinate consequences are adopted, whereas absolute retract theory, locally convex vector-valued extension, and complete-normality classification are not assumed.

First countability means every point has a countable neighborhood basis; second countability means the topology has a countable basis. D⊆X is dense iff cl_X(D)=X, and X is separable iff it has a countable dense subset. Lindelof means every open cover has a countable subcover. Countable includes finite and empty, so the empty space has all four properties. Any countable neighborhood basis can be replaced by a countable open neighborhood basis and further by a decreasing countable open neighborhood basis.

If X is first countable, then for every A⊆X and x∈X, x∈cl_X(A) iff a sequence with all terms in A converges to x. For any space Y and map f:X→Y from a first countable X, f is continuous iff for every sequence (x_n) and every x with x_n→x in X, f(x_n)→f(x) in Y. No separation hypothesis on X or Y is imposed.

Every second countable space is first countable, separable, and Lindelof. Every subspace of a second countable space is second countable and hence separable and Lindelof. Every discrete subspace of a second countable space is countable. For any separable space, every family of pairwise disjoint nonempty open subsets is countable. These statements include empty spaces and impose no separation hypothesis.

First countability passes to arbitrary subspaces. A closed subspace of a Lindelof space is Lindelof, and an open subspace of a separable space is separable. Continuous surjections preserve separability and the Lindelof property. Open continuous surjections preserve first and second countability. Countable products preserve first countability, second countability, and separability, including the empty-index and empty-factor cases. If X is Lindelof and K is compact, X×K is Lindelof; no Hausdorff assumption is imposed on K.
If X is second countable, every basis C of X contains a countable subfamily that is still a basis for X. In a first countable T₁ space, every singleton is a G_δ.

For a metrizable space, second countability, separability, and the Lindelof property are equivalent. Every metrizable space is first countable. Every compact metrizable space is second countable. Empty spaces are included.
Every regular Lindelof space is normal, with regularity and normality both understood without T₁. Consequently every regular second countable T₁ space is T₄.

For an uncountable set E, form X=E⊔{∞}. Declare every subset of E open and declare a set containing ∞ open iff its complement in E is finite. These declarations form a topology; X is compact Hausdorff, hence Lindelof. Its open subspace E is uncountable discrete and is not Lindelof, since its singleton cover has no countable subcover. Thus Lindelofness fails to pass to arbitrary, even open, subspaces.

For any uncountable set X equipped with the cocountable topology (∅ and all subsets with countable complement are open), X is T₁ and Lindelof, but not separable and not first countable. In this topology no singleton is a G_δ.

Let F={p}⊔(ℕ_{≥1}×ℕ_{≥1}); all pairs are isolated, and a set containing p is a neighborhood of p exactly when it contains a tail of every branch {n}×ℕ_{≥1}. This specifies the fan topology. F is countable and T₁, every singleton is a G_δ, but F is not first countable at p. Hence the singleton G_δ condition does not characterize first countability.
The Sorgenfrey line S is ℝ with basis {[a,b):a<b}. It is T₃, first countable, separable, Lindelof, and normal, but it is not second countable and therefore is not metrizable.

If X is a topological space with a dense subset D and a closed discrete subspace E such that |E|≥2^{|D|}, then X is not normal. No separation axiom is assumed beyond the stated closed-discrete condition.

For the Sorgenfrey line S, S×S is separable, first countable, and T₃, but is neither Lindelof nor normal. It has a closed nonseparable subspace. Thus separability need not pass even to closed subspaces; a product of two Lindelof normal spaces need be neither Lindelof nor normal.

The second-countable/separable/Lindelof equivalence need not hold without metrizability even among T₃ spaces, as witnessed by the Sorgenfrey line. An uncountable discrete metric space is first countable but neither separable, Lindelof, nor second countable. The remark's statements about larger cardinal invariants, hereditary Lindelof spaces, and general product cardinal bounds are scope exclusions only.

A metric on a set X is d:X×X→[0,∞) with symmetry, d(x,y)=0 iff x=y, and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z). Its open balls are B_d(x,r)={y:d(x,y)<r} for r>0, and its induced open sets are those containing a ball about each of their points. A topological space is metrizable iff some metric induces its topology. A pseudometric satisfies the same conditions except that distinct points may have distance zero.

Metric balls form a basis, and the restricted metric on any subset gives its subspace topology. Every metric space is Hausdorff and first countable. A map f:(X,d)→(Y,e) is continuous iff for every x∈X and ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that d(x,x')<δ implies e(f(x),f(x'))<ε for all x'∈X. For every A⊆X, x∈cl_X(A) iff B_d(x,r)∩A≠∅ for all r>0. A sequence x_n converges to x iff d(x_n,x)→0.

Metrics on the same set are topologically equivalent iff their open sets agree; uniformly equivalent iff both identity maps between the metric spaces are uniformly continuous. Uniform continuity of f:(X,d)→(Y,e) means ∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 ∀x,x'∈X, d(x,x')<δ ⇒ e(f(x),f(x'))<ε. A map is L-Lipschitz iff e(f(x),f(x'))≤L d(x,x') for every x,x'. An isometry preserves all distances; a surjective isometry is an isometric isomorphism. Metrics d,e are bilipschitz equivalent iff there exist real c,C>0 with c d(x,y)≤e(x,y)≤C d(x,y) for every x,y.

Metrics d,e on the same set have the same topology iff for every x and ε>0 some δ>0 satisfies B_d(x,δ)⊆B_e(x,ε), and the same condition holds with d and e interchanged. The function min(1,d) is a metric uniformly equivalent to d. Bilipschitz equivalence implies uniform equivalence, which implies topological equivalence. Neither converse holds in general: there exist uniformly equivalent metrics not bilipschitz equivalent, and topologically equivalent metrics not uniformly equivalent. The source witnesses for these existential nonconverses are respectively the usual metric |x-y| and min(1,|x-y|) on ℝ, and the usual metric on (0,1) versus e(x,y)=|h(x)-h(y)| for h(x)=tan(π(x-1/2)); these witness descriptions do not require the source’s particular proof route.

A sequence (x_n)_{n≥1} in (X,d) is Cauchy iff for every ε>0 some N satisfies d(x_m,x_n)<ε for all m,n≥N. The metric space is complete iff every Cauchy sequence converges in X. A topological space is completely metrizable iff some compatible metric is complete. Completeness concerns a specified metric; complete metrizability concerns the topology. The empty metric space is complete.

Every convergent sequence in a metric space is Cauchy. Any Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges to that subsequence's limit. Uniformly continuous maps between metric spaces send Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences. Closed subspaces of complete metric spaces are complete; complete subspaces of any metric space are closed. Uniformly equivalent metrics have the same completeness status.

Euclidean ℝⁿ is complete for every finite n≥0 (n=0 is a singleton). The usual metric on (0,1) is incomplete, but e(x,y)=|h(x)-h(y)| with h(x)=tan(π(x-1/2)) is a compatible complete metric on (0,1), because h is a homeomorphism and an isometry onto usual ℝ for e. Thus the topology does not determine completeness of an arbitrarily selected compatible metric.

A metric space is complete iff for every decreasing sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets with diam(F_n)→0, the intersection ⋂_n F_n is nonempty. Such an intersection has exactly one point. Here diam(A)=sup{d(a,b):a,b∈A} is allowed to be +∞, and diam(∅)=0. The equivalence includes the empty space, for which both conditions are vacuous.
Every metric space (X,d), including X=∅, admits a completion: a complete metric space (X̂,d̂) together with an isometric embedding j:X→X̂ whose image is dense in X̂.

For a completion j:X→X̂, a complete metric space Y, and a uniformly continuous map f:X→Y, there exists a unique uniformly continuous f̂:X̂→Y with f̂∘j=f. If f is L-Lipschitz, f̂ is L-Lipschitz as well. Any two completions of X are related by a unique surjective isometry commuting with their embeddings of X. Empty X and empty completions are included.

Uniform continuity in the metric-completion extension theorem cannot be replaced by mere continuity: f:(0,1)→ℝ defined by f(x)=1/x is continuous for the usual metrics but has no continuous extension to the metric completion [0,1] of (0,1). This is a separately asserted limitation/counterexample after the completion-uniqueness argument, not an intermediate step of that argument.

A metric space X is totally bounded iff for each ε>0 finitely many open ε-balls with centers in X cover X. Such a finite set of centers is an ε-net. The empty union covers the empty space, so the empty metric space is totally bounded; this use of 'net' is unrelated to a Moore–Smith net.

Total boundedness is inherited by arbitrary subspaces, passes from a subset to its closure in any metric ambient space, and is preserved by uniformly continuous images. A totally bounded space is bounded and separable. Boundedness does not imply total boundedness (a bounded metric counterexample exists). A metric space is totally bounded iff every sequence in it has a Cauchy subsequence. Empty and finite spaces are included.

For every metric space, including the empty space, compactness is equivalent to sequential compactness (every sequence has a convergent subsequence), and equivalent to completeness together with total boundedness.

A metric space is totally bounded iff its completion is compact. If A is a subset of a complete metric space, then its closure is compact iff A is totally bounded. Uniformly equivalent metrics have exactly the same totally bounded subsets. Empty spaces and subsets are included.

For every open cover of a compact metric space X, there exists λ>0 such that every nonempty subset A⊆X with diam(A)<λ is contained in one member of the cover. A continuous map from any compact metric space into any metric space is uniformly continuous. The empty domain is included.

The usual metric on (0,1) is totally bounded. The compatible complete pullback metric e(x,y)=|tan(π(x-1/2))-tan(π(y-1/2))| on (0,1) is not totally bounded. Thus total boundedness and completeness individually are not determined by the topology, unlike compactness, and being bounded for a compatible metric must not be confused with total boundedness. References to function-space completeness/Ascoli in Chapter 13 and pseudometric/uniform completions in Chapter 12 are navigation, not additional results here.

For arbitrary continuous maps (f_i:X→Y_i)_{i∈I}, their evaluation e:X→∏_iY_i, e(x)=(f_i(x)), is an embedding iff e is injective and the topology of X is generated by all f_i^{-1}(V), where V is open in Y_i. Sufficient conditions are point separation by the family and: for every open U⊆X and x∈U, some i∈I and open V⊆Y_i satisfy x∈f_i^{-1}(V)⊆U. For [0,1]-valued functions the neighborhood condition follows if for every x∈U open some f_i has f_i(x)>0 and vanishes on X\U. The point-separation/injectivity condition remains required. Arbitrary and empty index sets and empty X are permitted.
A space X is Tychonoff iff it embeds into [0,1]^I for some index set I. If X is Tychonoff, the evaluation map indexed by all continuous functions X→[0,1] is such an embedding. Empty X is included.

If X is compact and Y Hausdorff, every continuous injection X→Y is an embedding; Hausdorffness of X is not separately assumed. Consequently a point-separating family of continuous maps from a compact X into Hausdorff target spaces yields an evaluation embedding into their product. Without compactness the latter implication can fail (a continuous point-separating family with nonembedding evaluation exists).

For metric spaces (X_n,d_n), n≥1, D(x,y)=Σ_{n=1}^∞2^{-n}min{1,d_n(x_n,y_n)} is a metric on ∏_{n≥1}X_n inducing its product topology. If each d_n is complete, D is complete. These assertions include an empty underlying product caused by an empty factor. More generally, a nonempty product ∏_{i∈I}X_i of topological spaces is metrizable iff every factor is metrizable and all but countably many factors are singletons. Empty-index products are singletons; the nonempty-product qualification in this characterization is essential.

Every regular second countable T₁ space is metrizable and embeds into the countable cube [0,1]^{ℕ_{≥1}}. The separation assumption is equivalently regular plus T₀. 'Regular' by itself does not include a separation axiom, and empty spaces are included.

The two-point indiscrete space is regular (without T₁) and second countable but is not metrizable. Thus regularity and second countability alone do not imply metrizability; a point-separation qualification in Urysohn metrization is necessary.

For any space X, X embeds into the countable cube [0,1]^{ℕ_{≥1}} iff X is second countable and T₃, equivalently iff it is separable and metrizable. Every compact Hausdorff second countable space is metrizable. A metrizable space admits a compatible totally bounded metric iff it is separable. All assertions include empty spaces.

An embedding into a cube preserves the topology but need not preserve a specified metric or its Cauchy sequences. If an incomplete metric space embeds topologically in a compact cube [0,1]^I, its image is not closed. A compatible complete metric, a uniformly equivalent metric, a topologically equivalent metric, and an isometric embedding are different requirements, as witnessed by d10:09:metric-comparison and d10:09:complete-examples.

For any subspace A of a metric space (X,d): (a) if A is completely metrizable for its subspace topology, A is a G_δ subset of X; (b) if X is complete and A is G_δ in X, then A is completely metrizable. Consequently a metrizable space is completely metrizable iff its image in a metric completion (of a compatible metric) is G_δ, and in that case its image is G_δ in every metric space into which it embeds. Empty A and X are included; no completeness of the ambient X is assumed in (a).

Every open subspace and every countable intersection of open subspaces of a completely metrizable space is completely metrizable. The irrational real numbers with their usual subspace topology are completely metrizable. Every closed subspace of a completely metrizable space is also completely metrizable. Empty subspaces are included.

Scope/navigation only: this chapter proves Urysohn metrization, cube embeddings, countable-product metrization, and the metric G_δ characterization of complete metrizability. Nagata–Smirnov and paracompact local metrization are treated in Chapter 15; Cantor models/classification/universal compact-metric images in Chapter 18. Development/star-refinement criteria, general topological-group metrization, Lavrentieff extension, infinite-dimensional Hilbert-space classification, arc/circle cut-point classification, and the full Hahn–Mazurkiewicz theorem are not invoked or adopted here.

A topological space X is locally compact if for every x in X there are a compact K⊆X and an open O⊆X with x∈O⊆K. Compactness and local compactness include no separation axiom. LCH means locally compact and Hausdorff.

If X is LCH, U⊆X is open and x∈U, there exists open V⊆X with x∈V⊆cl_X(V)⊆U and cl_X(V) compact. More generally, for every compact C⊆U there exists open V with C⊆V⊆cl_X(V)⊆U and compact closure, including C=∅. In particular every LCH space is regular, with regularity not implicitly including T1.

Every closed subspace of a locally compact space is locally compact, without separation assumptions. Every open subspace of an LCH space is LCH. An LCH space X is σ-compact (a countable union of compact subsets) if and only if there exist compact K_n⊆X (n≥1) with K_n⊆Int_X(K_{n+1}) and X=⋃_{n≥1}K_n. For every such exhaustion and every compact C⊆X there is n≥1 with C⊆K_n. The equivalence includes X=∅ and empty compact sets.
With the subspace topology inherited from the usual real line, Q is not locally compact, although Q is metrizable and R is LCH. Thus a metrizable subspace of an LCH space need not be locally compact.

A map f:X→Y is proper in this manuscript if it is continuous and f⁻¹(K) is compact for every compact K⊆Y. A perfect map means a continuous closed map all of whose fibers f⁻¹({y}), y∈Y, are compact. No separation axioms are built into these definitions.

Every continuous closed map f:X→Y with compact fibers is proper, for arbitrary spaces X,Y. Conversely every continuous proper map f:X→Y with LCH target Y is closed and has compact fibers. Neither direction requires the source X to be Hausdorff; empty fibers are allowed.

If f:X→Y and g:Y→Z are proper, then g∘f is proper. The inclusion A↪X of any closed subspace A is proper. Every continuous map from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is proper. If f:X→Y is proper and Y is compact, then X is compact. Compactness throughout does not include Hausdorffness unless stated.

The identity map from the discrete two-point space {0,1} to the indiscrete two-point space is continuous and proper but is not closed. Thus properness need not imply closedness without target hypotheses. The map f:[0,1]→{0,1} with indiscrete target given by f(0)=0 and f(x)=1 for x>0 is continuous and has compact domain, but is not proper: the compact singleton {1} has noncompact inverse image (0,1].

For every LCH space X, form X⁺=X⊔{∞} and declare its open sets to be all open subsets of X and all X⁺\K with K⊆X compact. These sets form a compact Hausdorff topology, X is an open subspace with exactly its original topology, and this is the unique compact Hausdorff topology on the set X⊔{∞} inducing the given topology on X. X is dense in X⁺ if and only if X is noncompact. If X is compact, ∞ is isolated; if X=∅, X⁺ is a singleton. Conversely, if Z is compact Hausdorff and X=Z\{p} for one point p, then X is LCH and, identifying p with ∞, the topology on Z is the just described one-point topology.

A Hausdorff compactification of X is an embedding i:X→K into a compact Hausdorff space K whose image is dense. K=i(X) is permitted, including X=K=∅. For the one-point construction above, X→X⁺ is a compactification in this sense exactly for noncompact LCH X; the construction for compact LCH X is not a dense compactification.

For continuous f:X→Y between LCH spaces, define f⁺:X⁺→Y⁺ by f⁺|_X=f and f⁺(∞)=∞. Then f⁺ is continuous if and only if f is proper. Every homeomorphism X→Y between LCH spaces extends in this way to a homeomorphism X⁺→Y⁺, including compact and empty cases.

For a Tychonoff space X (completely regular and Hausdorff), set I_X=C(X,[0,1]) and define e_X:X→[0,1]^{I_X} by e_X(x)_u=u(x). This evaluation map is an embedding. Every compact Hausdorff space H is Tychonoff, and e_H(H) is compact and closed in its Hausdorff evaluation cube.

For every Tychonoff space X, let βX be the closure of e_X(X) in [0,1]^{C(X,[0,1])}. With e_X viewed as a map into βX, (βX,e_X) is a Hausdorff compactification. For every compact Hausdorff space H and every continuous f:X→H, there exists a unique continuous f̄:βX→H with f̄∘e_X=f. Among Hausdorff compactifications this universal property determines βX up to a unique homeomorphism fixing the embedded copy of X. A space admits a Hausdorff compactification if and only if it is Tychonoff. Empty spaces and empty targets are included whenever a map f exists.

For every Tychonoff X, every bounded continuous f:X→R extends uniquely to a continuous function on βX. For every Hausdorff compactification i:X→K, there exists a continuous surjection βX→K whose composite with e_X is i. Every continuous f:X→Y between Tychonoff spaces has a unique continuous βf:βX→βY satisfying βf∘e_X=e_Y∘f. These extensions satisfy β(id_X)=id_{βX} and β(g∘f)=βg∘βf for all composable continuous maps between Tychonoff spaces. If X is compact Hausdorff then e_X(X)=βX; if X=∅ then βX=∅.

Scope clarification: the Stone–Čech construction here concerns bounded continuous coordinates; extensions of arbitrary unbounded functions, remainders of βN, their cardinalities, and the lattice of compactifications are not adopted results.

For U,V⊆X×X define U⁻¹={(y,x):(x,y)∈U}, U∘V={(x,z):∃y,(x,y)∈V and (y,z)∈U}, and U[x]={y:(x,y)∈U}. For nonempty X, a uniformity is a proper filter 𝒰 of subsets of X×X such that every entourage U∈𝒰 contains Δ_X, U⁻¹∈𝒰 for U∈𝒰, and for every U∈𝒰 some V∈𝒰 has V∘V⊆U. It is separated if ⋂𝒰=Δ_X. For X=∅ separately allow the unique degenerate entourage family {∅}, which is not a proper filter. All convergence and Cauchy filters remain proper, so none exist on ∅ and its completeness assertions are vacuous.

In every uniform space each entourage contains a symmetric entourage. For every entourage U and every integer m≥1, there is a symmetric entourage V with V^m⊆U. A nonempty family ℬ⊆P(X×X) generates a uniformity by taking all supersets if every B∈ℬ contains Δ_X, every finite intersection of members of ℬ contains a member of ℬ, each B⁻¹ contains a member of ℬ, and each B∈ℬ contains C∘C for some C∈ℬ.
