When X≠∅ the generated filter is proper; the empty-set convention applies when X=∅.

For a uniform space (X,𝒰), declare O⊆X open iff for every x∈O some U∈𝒰 satisfies U[x]⊆O. This defines a topology and {U[x]:U∈𝒰} is a neighborhood base at every x. The induced topology is Hausdorff if and only if 𝒰 is separated. Every induced uniform topology is regular, with no implicit T1 assertion. All statements include the empty uniform space.

In a uniform space every entourage contains an entourage that is both symmetric and closed in the induced product topology on X×X. More precisely, for every symmetric entourage V, cl_{X×X}(V)⊆V³. In particular every entourage U contains a closed symmetric entourage C with C³⊆U. These assertions include the empty relation on the empty space.

A map f:(X,𝒰)→(Y,𝒱) is uniformly continuous iff (f×f)⁻¹(V)∈𝒰 for every V∈𝒱. A uniform isomorphism is a bijection whose forward and inverse maps are uniformly continuous. A uniform embedding is an injective map inducing a uniform isomorphism onto its image with the subspace uniformity. Maps with empty domain are uniformly continuous under the declared empty uniform-space convention.

Uniformly continuous maps are continuous for the induced topologies; identity maps and composites of uniformly continuous maps are uniformly continuous. Equal induced topologies do not determine uniform continuity or completeness. Concretely, on R the metrics d(x,y)=|x−y| and ρ(x,y)=|arctan x−arctan y| induce the same usual topology, but (R,d) is complete and (R,ρ) is incomplete: the sequence n is ρ-Cauchy with no ρ-limit in R. The identity from (R,ρ) to (R,d) is not uniformly continuous. Thus completeness of a specified uniformity is not a topological invariant.

If A⊆X is a uniform subspace, the relations U∩(A×A), U∈𝒰_X, form a base for its subspace uniformity. For P=∏_{i∈I}X_i, the finite intersections ⋂_{i∈F}(π_i×π_i)⁻¹(U_i), with F⊆I finite and U_i an entourage of X_i, form a base for the product uniformity. These induced topologies equal respectively the subspace and product topologies. A map into P is uniformly continuous iff every coordinate map is uniformly continuous. Subspaces and products of separated uniform spaces are separated. Empty subspaces and products with empty factor carry the degenerate uniformity, while the empty product is the singleton with its unique uniformity.

A pseudometric p:X×X→[0,∞) vanishes on the diagonal, is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality, without requiring zero distance to imply equality. Any family (p_i)_{i∈I} generates a uniformity with base the finite intersections of {(x,y):p_i(x,y)<ε}, for i∈I and ε>0. The empty family gives the indiscrete uniformity. On X=∅ this is interpreted by the declared degenerate convention.

For a sequence (p_n)_{n≥1} of pseudometrics on X, the sum p(x,y)=Σ_{n≥1}2^{−n}min{1,p_n(x,y)} is a pseudometric generating exactly the same uniformity as the family. It is a metric iff for every distinct x,y some n has p_n(x,y)>0. Finite or empty countable families may be extended by zero pseudometrics. For every one pseudometric q, the relation x∼y iff q(x,y)=0 is an equivalence relation; q₀([x],[y])=q(x,y) is a well-defined metric on X₀=X/∼, and the original q-uniformity on X is exactly the inverse-image uniformity of q₀ under the quotient map r:X→X₀.

Let X be a uniform space, V₀=X×X, and let V_n (n≥1) be symmetric entourages satisfying V_n³⊆V_{n−1}. There exists a bounded pseudometric p on X such that for every n≥0, V_n⊆{(x,y):p(x,y)≤2^{−n}} and {(x,y):p(x,y)<2^{−(n+1)}}⊆V_n. The real-valued function p:X×X→R is uniformly continuous for the original product uniformity.

A uniformity has a countable entourage base iff it is generated by one pseudometric. In this countable-base case it is generated by a metric iff it is separated. Every uniformity, including those without countable base, is generated by a family of bounded pseudometrics p:X×X→R each uniformly continuous for the product uniformity and hence continuous in the induced product topology. These assertions include the empty uniform space with its zero pseudometric and degenerate uniformity.

A topology is induced by some uniformity iff it is completely regular, where complete regularity does not implicitly include a separation axiom. Every separated uniform topology is Tychonoff (completely regular and Hausdorff). Empty spaces are included.

A proper filter ℱ on a uniform space X is Cauchy iff for every entourage U there is A∈ℱ with A×A⊆U. X is complete iff every such Cauchy filter converges. X is totally bounded iff for every entourage U finitely many sections U[x] cover X. The empty space is totally bounded using the empty cover and complete vacuously, since there are no proper filters on it.

Every convergent proper filter on a uniform space is Cauchy. A Cauchy proper filter with a cluster point x converges to x. If f:X→Y is uniformly continuous and ℱ is a Cauchy proper filter on X, its image filter under f is a Cauchy proper filter on Y.
A uniform space is compact in its induced topology iff it is complete and totally bounded. No separatedness or Hausdorffness is required. The equivalence includes the empty space.

Every closed uniform subspace of a complete uniform space is complete. Every complete subspace of a separated uniform space is closed. The product uniformity of any family of complete uniform spaces is complete. Conversely, if the product is nonempty and complete then every factor is complete. A product with an empty factor is empty and complete and gives no completeness conclusion for its other factors; empty products are included.
For the uniformity induced by a metric, completeness defined using all proper Cauchy filters is equivalent to convergence of every Cauchy sequence. Empty metric spaces are included.

Let X carry the uniformity of one pseudometric p, equivalently of a specified countable family represented by the sum pseudometric of d10:12:countable-pseudometrics. Form its zero-distance metric quotient (X₀,p₀) and the metric completion (X̂,p̂). The composite j:X→X₀→X̂ has dense image and its inverse-image uniformity is exactly the given one on X. It is an embedding (indeed a uniform embedding) iff p separates distinct points. X̂ is complete and separated. For every complete metric space Y and every uniformly continuous f:X→Y there is a unique uniformly continuous f̂:X̂→Y with f̂∘j=f. If X=∅ take X̂=∅.

Let A be dense in an arbitrary uniform space Z and carry the induced uniformity. If Y is complete and separated, every uniformly continuous f:A→Y has a unique uniformly continuous extension f̄:Z→Y with f̄|_A=f. Z itself need not be separated or complete. Empty spaces are included when such a map f exists.

Every separated uniform space X has a complete separated uniform space X̂ and a dense uniform embedding j:X→X̂. For every complete separated uniform space Y and every uniformly continuous f:X→Y there is a unique uniformly continuous f̂:X̂→Y satisfying f̂∘j=f. The pair (X̂,j) is unique up to a unique uniform isomorphism commuting with j (between any two complete separated spaces containing dense uniformly embedded copies of X). No countable-base hypothesis is imposed. For X=∅ take X̂=∅.

For every uniform space X define x∼y iff (x,y) belongs to every entourage. This is an equivalence relation. On X₀=X/∼, with q:X→X₀ the class map, the relations (q×q)(U) for entourages U form a base of a separated uniformity. Its inverse-image uniformity on X is exactly the given one. Every uniformly continuous map f from X into a separated uniform space factors uniquely as f₀∘q with f₀ uniformly continuous. Composing q with the completion embedding of X₀ yields a map j:X→X̂ into a complete separated space, with dense image, the same inverse-image uniformity and the extension property: every uniformly continuous map X→Y with Y complete separated extends uniquely uniformly continuously across j. This j is injective iff X is separated. Empty quotients and completions are taken empty.

Scope and recap: separated uniform completion applies without a countable-base restriction; the nonseparated completion map identifies exactly pairs lying in every entourage, so need not be injective. No uniqueness assertion for nonseparated completions by inclusions, covering-uniformity convention, proximity theory, or hyperspace completion is adopted.

For spaces X,Y write Y^X for all functions and C(X,Y) for continuous functions. The pointwise topology is the product topology (or its restriction), with subbasic conditions f(x)∈O for x∈X and O⊆Y open. The compact-open topology has subbasic [K,O]={f:f(K)⊆O}, for compact K⊆X and open O⊆Y. For metric (Y,d) let d_b=min{1,d}, D(f,g)=sup_{x∈X}d_b(f(x),g(x)), with sup∅=0. D is a finite metric and defines the uniform topology. Uniform convergence on compact sets has neighborhood base at f formed by finite intersections of B_K(f,ε)={g:sup_{x∈K}d_b(f(x),g(x))<ε}, ε>0, for compact K. Its uniformity is generated by pseudometrics D_K(f,g)=sup_K d_b(f,g). These constructions give the unique topology on an empty function set; for X=∅ the function set is a singleton.

For every topological X and metric Y, on all functions Y^X the pointwise topology is contained in compact convergence, which is contained in the uniform topology. On C(X,Y), compact convergence equals compact-open, with no separation hypothesis on X. If X is compact, compact convergence and compact-open on C(X,Y) both equal uniform convergence. Consequently on C(X,Y) for compact X the uniform topology depends only on the topology of the metrizable target Y; the associated uniformity for an unrestricted domain need not be determined by that topology.

On the usual [0,1], continuous f_n(x)=x^n converge pointwise to f with f(x)=0 for x<1 and f(1)=1; f is discontinuous and the convergence is not uniform. The continuous functions h_n(x)=max{0,1−|nx−1|}, n≥1, converge pointwise to the continuous zero function on [0,1], but h_n(1/n)=1, so they do not converge uniformly or in compact convergence. On R the continuous g_n(x)=x/n converge uniformly on every compact subset to zero, but not uniformly on R, since sup_x min{1,|x|/n}=1. Thus both topology containments can be strict even within spaces of continuous functions.

For every topological X and metric Y, uniform limits of continuous maps X→Y are continuous, for both sequences and nets. If Y is a complete metric space, then the uniform metric space (C(X,Y),D) is complete for every topological X, including when C(X,Y) is empty. If additionally X is LCH, C(X,Y) is also complete for the uniformity of uniform convergence on compact sets.

Equip spaces of continuous functions with compact-open topologies. For every x∈X, evaluation ev_x:C(X,Y)→Y is continuous. If Y is Hausdorff then C(X,Y) is Hausdorff. For any continuous maps a:W→X and b:Y→Z, the maps C(X,Y)→C(W,Y), f↦f∘a, and C(X,Y)→C(X,Z), f↦b∘f, are continuous. No local compactness hypothesis is imposed.

If X is LCH, then joint evaluation ev:C(X,Y)×X→Y, (f,x)↦f(x), is continuous for the compact-open topology and arbitrary target Y. For arbitrary topological X,Z,Y, every continuous h:Z×X→Y determines a continuous map h̃:Z→C(X,Y), h̃(z)(x)=h(z,x). Conversely, if X is LCH and h̃:Z→C(X,Y) is continuous, then its associated h(z,x)=h̃(z)(x) is continuous.
If the middle space Y is LCH and X,Z are arbitrary topological spaces, then (f,g)↦g∘f from C(X,Y)×C(Y,Z) to C(X,Z) is jointly continuous for the compact-open topologies.
For every quotient map q:A→B and every LCH space X, id_X×q:X×A→X×B is a quotient map.

For a metric space (Y,d), a family 𝒜⊆C(X,Y) is equicontinuous at x∈X iff for every ε>0 there is a neighborhood U of x such that d(f(y),f(x))<ε for every y∈U and f∈𝒜. It is equicontinuous iff this holds at every x. It is pointwise relatively compact iff cl_Y({f(x):f∈𝒜}) is compact for every x. Pointwise boundedness is in general weaker for a metric target.

Let Y be metric and 𝒜⊆C(X,Y) be equicontinuous, with arbitrary topological domain X. Its closure H in all functions Y^X for the pointwise topology consists of continuous maps and is itself equicontinuous. On every equicontinuous family ℰ⊆C(X,Y), the relative pointwise and compact convergence topologies agree.

If X is compact, Y is metric, and 𝒜⊆C(X,Y) is equicontinuous with {f(x):f∈𝒜} totally bounded in Y for every x∈X, then 𝒜 is totally bounded for the uniform metric D. No Hausdorffness of X or completeness of Y is required. Empty domains and families are included.

For arbitrary topological X, metric Y and 𝒜⊆C(X,Y), if 𝒜 is equicontinuous and pointwise relatively compact, then its closure in the compact-open topology is compact. If X is LCH, the converse also holds. In particular, if X is compact Hausdorff (and hence if compact metric), compactness of the uniform closure of 𝒜 is equivalent to equicontinuity together with pointwise relative compactness. There is no completeness assumption on Y. Empty families and empty domains are included.

For compact Hausdorff X and finite-dimensional Euclidean target R^m, a family 𝒜⊆C(X,R^m) has compact uniform closure iff it is equicontinuous and pointwise bounded. Under these conditions 𝒜 itself is compact iff it is uniformly closed; equivalently compactness is equicontinuity plus pointwise boundedness plus uniform closedness. In particular every uniformly bounded family of continuous maps [a,b]→R^m sharing a common Lipschitz constant has compact uniform closure.

An infinite bounded discrete metric target Y gives counterexamples to replacing relative compactness by boundedness: on a nonempty domain X, the family of constant functions with all values in Y is equicontinuous and pointwise bounded but has no compact closure. For f_n(x)=sin(nx) on [0,2π], the family is pointwise bounded but not equicontinuous at 0: x_n=π/(2n)→0 and f_n(x_n)=1 while f_n(0)=0. Consequently this family has no compact uniform closure.
The Hausdorff-uniform-target version of Ascoli on general compactly generated spaces and the topology of continuous convergence are explicitly outside the adopted formulation.

Let X=R with basis the sets O\C where O is usual-real open and C is countable. This is a Hausdorff space whose compact subsets are exactly finite sets. Every countable subset is closed and discrete. Hence the compact-open topology on C(X,R) equals the pointwise topology. The usual continuous triangular functions h_n(x)=max{0,1−|nx−1|} remain continuous on X and converge pointwise to zero; H={0,h_1,h_2,…} is therefore compact in C(X,R) with its compact-open topology. Nevertheless H is not equicontinuous at 0: every neighborhood U of 0 contains a point x and an n with h_n(x)>1/2 and h_n(0)=0. Every neighborhood in X is infinite, so X is not locally compact. This provides a Hausdorff non-LCH domain where compact-open relative compactness does not imply equicontinuity.

For A⊆X, A is nowhere dense in the specified ambient space X iff Int_X(cl_X A)=∅; A is meager in X (first category) iff it is a countable union of subsets nowhere dense in X; A is residual or comeager in X iff X\A is meager in X; A is of second category in X iff it is not meager there. A Baire space is a space in which every countable intersection of dense open subsets is dense. The empty space is Baire.

For every topological space X, the following are equivalent: X is Baire; no nonempty open subset of X is meager in X; every countable union of closed subsets of X with empty interior has empty interior; every residual subset of X is dense. Every residual R⊆X contains a G_delta subset that is an intersection of open dense subsets of X, and this contained G_delta is dense if X is Baire. Conversely, every subset of X containing a dense G_delta subset is residual, without requiring X Baire.

In the usual R, Q is dense and meager, and R\Q is residual, so density need not imply residuality even in a Baire space. In the usual subspace Q every singleton is closed with empty interior; Q is meager in itself, so ∅ is residual in Q yet not dense there. A singleton as a subset of R is nowhere dense in R but, as its own one-point ambient space, is not meager. The topological disjoint sum R⊔Q is of second category in itself but is not Baire; its open Q summand is meager in the sum. Thus second category of the whole space is weaker than the Baire condition.
In every complete metric space, if F_n (n≥1) are nonempty closed sets with F_1⊇F_2⊇… and diam(F_n)→0, then ⋂_{n≥1}F_n contains exactly one point.

Every complete metric space is Baire, including the empty space. Consequently every completely metrizable topological space is Baire, independently of whether a particular chosen compatible metric is complete.
Every locally compact Hausdorff space is Baire. In particular every compact Hausdorff space is Baire. Empty spaces are included.

Every open subspace of a Baire space is Baire. Every dense G_delta subspace of a Baire space is Baire. Every G_delta subspace of a complete metric space or an LCH space is Baire, without requiring that subspace to be dense in the original ambient space.
The subspace R\Q of irrationals is Baire. No countable dense subset D of the usual real line R is a G_delta subset of R.

Let X be a Baire space, Y a metric space, f_n:X→Y continuous for all n≥1, and f:X→Y satisfy f_n(x)→f(x) for every x∈X. The set {x∈X:f is continuous at x} is a dense G_delta subset of X and is residual in X. No completeness assumption on Y or metrizability assumption on X is imposed.

For a nonempty Baire space X and a pointwise bounded family 𝒜⊆C(X,R), there exist a nonempty open U⊆X and an integer M≥1 such that |f(x)|≤M for every f∈𝒜 and x∈U. The family itself may be empty. The common bound is required only on U.

Let (X,d) be a nonempty complete metric space, q a real number with 0≤q<1, and T:X→X satisfy d(Tx,Ty)≤q d(x,y) for all x,y. Then there is a unique p∈X with Tp=p. For every x₀∈X, define x_{n+1}=T x_n for n≥0; then x_n→p and, for every n≥0, d(x_n,p)≤q^n d(x₁,x₀)/(1−q) and d(x_n,p)≤d(x_{n+1},x_n)/(1−q). For every n≥1 also d(x_n,p)≤q d(x_n,x_{n−1})/(1−q). Here q⁰=1 even for q=0. More generally for every z∈X, d(z,p)≤d(z,Tz)/(1−q).

Let X be a nonempty complete metric space and T:X→X any map. If for some integer m≥1 its iterate T^m is a contraction (there exists 0≤q<1 with d(T^m x,T^m y)≤q d(x,y) for all x,y), then T has a unique fixed point. No independent continuity assumption on T is needed.

Let X be a nonempty complete metric space and S,T:X→X contractions whose constants are both at most q with 0≤q<1. If sup_{x∈X} d(Sx,Tx)≤δ, then their unique fixed points p_S,p_T satisfy d(p_S,p_T)≤δ/(1−q). The supremum condition is the uniform bound d(Sx,Tx)≤δ for every x, so it entails δ≥0.

On the incomplete usual metric space (0,1), T(x)=x/2 is a contraction with no fixed point. On the complete space R, T(x)=x+1 has Lipschitz constant 1 (is nonexpansive) and no fixed point. On the complete space [1,∞), T(x)=x+1/x has no fixed point but strictly decreases the distance of every distinct pair: for x>y≥1, T(x)−T(y)=(x−y)(1−1/(xy)) lies strictly between 0 and x−y. Thus strict distance decrease does not imply a uniform contraction constant below 1. The unique self-map of the empty complete metric space has no fixed point, showing why Banach requires nonemptiness.

For an indexed family (A_i) indexed by I in a topological space X, local finiteness means that every x∈X has a neighborhood meeting A_i for only finitely many indices i. Repeated nonempty members count repeatedly; empty members are allowed. A refinement of a cover is a family still covering X, each member being contained in a member of the original cover. A family is σ-locally finite if it is a countable union of locally finite families. X is paracompact if every open cover admits a locally finite open refinement; this definition does not include Hausdorffness.
A locally finite indexed family is point finite (each point belongs to only finitely many indexed members), whereas point finiteness alone does not imply local finiteness.

If (A_i) is a locally finite indexed family in any topological space, (cl A_i) is locally finite and cl(⋃_i A_i)=⋃_i cl A_i. Consequently, a locally finite union of closed sets is closed. If a family of continuous real functions has locally finite indexed supports, its pointwise sum, evaluated using the finitely many nonzero terms near each point, is a continuous real function.
Every paracompact Hausdorff space is T4, meaning normal and T1. Every closed subspace of every paracompact space is paracompact, without requiring Hausdorffness of that space.

Every open cover of every metric space, including the empty space, has an open refinement expressible as a countable union of locally discrete families. Here a family is locally discrete if each point has a neighborhood meeting at most one indexed member of that family.
If X is regular (regularity does not include T1) and every open cover of X has a σ-locally finite open refinement, then X is paracompact.
Every metric space is paracompact. Every regular Lindelöf space is paracompact, with no T1 hypothesis added to regularity. Every compact space is paracompact, without any separation hypothesis.

For every finite indexed open cover (U_i) of a normal space X there exists a subordinate finite partition of unity: continuous φ_i:X→[0,1], with support cl{x:φ_i(x)≠0} contained in U_i, locally finite indexed supports, and Σ_i φ_i(x)=1 for every x. Neither T1 nor paracompactness is required. The zero-member cover is included: it forces X=∅, and the empty family is a partition of unity.

For every indexed open cover (U_i) indexed by I of a paracompact Hausdorff space X, there is a locally finite indexed open cover (V_i) with the same index set I such that cl V_i⊆U_i for all i. Empty V_i are allowed; the statement includes the empty-space and empty-index cases permitted by the cover condition.

A partition of unity subordinate to an indexed open cover (U_i) of X is an indexed family of continuous functions φ_i:X→[0,1] such that supp φ_i⊆U_i for every i, the indexed supports are locally finite, and Σ_i φ_i(x)=1 at every point x. The support of φ_i is cl{x:φ_i(x)≠0}, rather than merely its nonzero set; local finiteness defines the pointwise sum.

Every indexed open cover of a paracompact Hausdorff space admits a subordinate partition of unity as defined in d10:15:partition-definition. Conversely, for any topological space, if every indexed open cover admits such a partition of unity, then the space is paracompact. The converse has no Hausdorff assumption. Empty spaces and empty covers are included.

Let (U_i) be an open cover with a subordinate partition of unity (φ_i). Suppose s_i:U_i→E are continuous local sections solving an affine equation, with E a real topological vector space, and suppose finite affine combinations of solutions at a point remain solutions at that point. Then s(x)=Σ_i φ_i(x)s_i(x), interpreting each summand as zero outside U_i, is a global continuous solution. Closed support subordination ensures the zero-extended products are continuous across the boundaries, and local finiteness makes this a locally finite sum.

If a compact Hausdorff space X has a finite indexed open cover U_1,…,U_k with homeomorphisms χ_i:U_i→O_i⊆R^n, then X admits a topological embedding into R^{k(n+1)}. In particular, every compact Hausdorff topological n-manifold embeds into some finite-dimensional Euclidean space. The empty-atlas case k=0 is included: its cover condition forces X=∅ and the unique map into R^0 is an embedding.
If X is regular and T1 and has a σ-locally finite open base, then X is normal, every closed subset of X is a Gδ, and every open subset O of X has the form O={x:f(x)≠0} for a continuous f:X→[0,1].
A topological space X is metrizable if and only if it is regular, is T1, and has a σ-locally finite open base. The regularity convention itself does not include T1.

For a Hausdorff space X, X is metrizable if and only if it is paracompact and locally metrizable. Locally metrizable means that each point has an open neighborhood whose subspace topology is metrizable.

Cross-reference to the Sorgenfrey-plane counterexample: arbitrary products of paracompact spaces need not be paracompact. The mathematical instance and its derived nonparacompactness are inventoried at d10:18:sorgenfrey-product-paracompactness, reusing the earlier Sorgenfrey results; no duplicate proof obligation is intended here.

For every compact space X and continuous f:X→R, the supremum defining ||f||∞ is finite (and is defined as zero for X=∅), because continuous images of compact spaces are compact. Hausdorffness of X is not assumed.

For compact X, C(X,R) denotes the continuous real-valued functions equipped with the uniform norm ||f||∞=sup_{x∈X}|f(x)|, with norm zero for the unique function when X=∅. A real subalgebra is closed under addition, multiplication, and real scalar multiplication. It is unital if it contains the constant function 1; for nonempty X this includes every constant function, while for empty X all functions coincide.

If X is compact, u_n:X→R are continuous and increase pointwise to a continuous u:X→R, then u_n converges uniformly to u. The same holds for a pointwise decreasing sequence with continuous limit. Hausdorffness and nonemptiness of X are not required.
There exists a sequence of real polynomials p_n such that p_n(t) converges uniformly to |t| on the closed interval [-1,1].

For compact X, if A⊆C(X,R) is a unital real subalgebra, then its closure in the uniform norm is a unital real subalgebra. This closure is a lattice: whenever f,g belong to it, |f| and the pointwise functions min(f,g), max(f,g) belong to it. Hausdorffness and nonemptiness of X are not required.

If X is compact Hausdorff and A⊆C(X,R) is a unital real subalgebra separating points (for every distinct x,y there is a∈A with a(x)≠a(y)), then A is uniformly dense in C(X,R): every continuous real f and every ε>0 admit a∈A with ||f-a||∞<ε. The empty space is included.

For every finite dimension n and every compact subset K⊆R^n, restrictions to K of real polynomials in the coordinate functions are uniformly dense in C(K,R). In particular, continuous real functions on every compact interval can be approximated uniformly by real polynomials. The dimension n=0 and empty K cases are included (constants suffice on the empty set or singleton).

If X is compact Hausdorff and A⊆C(X,C) is a unital complex subalgebra separating points and closed under pointwise complex conjugation, then A is uniformly dense in C(X,C). The uniform norm uses complex absolute value; empty X is included.

On the unit circle {z∈C:|z|=1}, the algebra of restrictions of ordinary complex polynomials in z alone contains all constants and separates points but is not uniformly dense in C(S^1,C). Specifically, the continuous conjugation function z↦conj(z) cannot be uniformly approximated by those polynomials, exhibiting the need for the conjugation-invariance condition in the complex Stone–Weierstrass theorem.

For a locally compact Hausdorff space X, C0(X,R) consists of continuous real functions f for which {x:|f(x)|≥ε} is compact for every ε>0. Define C0(X,C) by the identical condition with complex absolute value.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let X*=X∪{∞} have the one-point compactification topology of d10:11:one-point, allowing ∞ to be isolated when X is already compact (including X=∅). For a continuous real f on X, f∈C0(X,R) if and only if the extension f* with f*(∞)=0 is continuous on X*. Such functions are bounded, form a real algebra under pointwise operations, and are closed under uniform limits.

For every locally compact Hausdorff X, if A⊆C0(X,R) is a real subalgebra separating points and vanishing nowhere (for each x∈X some a∈A has a(x)≠0), then A is uniformly dense in C0(X,R). For a complex subalgebra A⊆C0(X,C), the same conclusion holds when A separates points, vanishes nowhere, and is closed under complex conjugation. No unital hypothesis is imposed. Compact and empty X are included.

Scope clarification: the approximation theorems concern the specified algebras and uniform topology with their stated hypotheses. They make no claim that every point-separating family is uniformly dense or that pointwise density is enough; this paragraph supplies no separate counterexample construction or new result.

Comparison with the earlier contraction theorem: Banach's quantitative contraction hypotheses yield uniqueness, whereas the Brouwer results below assume continuity on nonempty compact convex finite-dimensional sets and assert existence. This is orientation and proof-route commentary, not a new fixed-point obligation.

For every n≥0, the standard simplex Δ^n is {t∈R^{n+1}: each t_i≥0 and Σ_{i=0}^n t_i=1}. An affine simplex is the convex hull of affinely independent vertices. Its faces are the convex hulls of nonempty subsets of its vertices, with the empty face allowed when discussing intersections. A finite geometric triangulation of an n-simplex is a finite collection of affine simplexes that covers it, is closed under faces, and has any two cells disjoint or intersecting in a common face; its maximal cells have dimension n. Its mesh is the largest diameter of its cells.

Every affine n-simplex, for every finite n≥0, admits a sequence of finite geometric triangulations whose meshes tend to zero, with compatible induced triangulations on all faces. Compatibility means the restrictions agree on common faces. For n=0 the single point already has mesh zero.

In every finite geometric triangulation of Δ^n with n≥1, each (n-1)-dimensional face belongs to exactly two n-cells when it is internal and to exactly one n-cell when it lies on the boundary. The boundary faces induce finite geometric triangulations of the original facets.

For each n≥0, label every vertex of a finite geometric triangulation of Δ^n by an element of {0,…,n}. Suppose a vertex lying in any original face receives one of that face's vertex labels. Then the number of n-cells whose vertex labels are all of {0,…,n} is odd, and therefore is nonzero. The n=0 case is included.
For every n≥0, every continuous self-map f:Δ^n→Δ^n has a fixed point: there exists x∈Δ^n with f(x)=x.

For every nonempty compact convex K⊆R^m and every x∈R^m there exists a unique point P(x)∈K minimizing distance to x. The map P:R^m→K is a retraction (P(x)=x for x∈K) and is 1-Lipschitz: ||P(x)-P(y)||≤||x-y|| for all x,y∈R^m. In particular it is continuous. This includes m=0 and lower-dimensional K.

For every finite m≥0 and every nonempty compact convex subset K⊆R^m, every continuous self-map f:K→K has a fixed point. The same assertion holds for nonempty compact convex subsets of any finite-dimensional real normed vector space. There is no nonempty-interior or full-affine-dimension requirement on K; dimension zero is included.

For every integer n≥1, no continuous retraction exists from the closed Euclidean unit ball B^n⊆R^n onto its boundary sphere S^{n-1}: there is no continuous r:B^n→S^{n-1} with r(x)=x for every point x on that sphere.

The nonemptiness, convexity, and compactness conditions in Brouwer's theorem have substantive boundary examples. The self-map of ∅ has no fixed point. A nontrivial rotation of the unit circle in R^2 has no fixed point, despite compactness. The continuous function f:(0,1)→(0,1), f(x)=(x+1)/2, has no fixed point although (0,1) is bounded and convex. The identity on a nontrivial compact convex set fixes every point and hence has multiple fixed points, so Brouwer's assumptions do not imply uniqueness or a contraction estimate.

The product C={0,1}^{N_{≥1}}, with discrete binary factors and the product topology, is nonempty, compact, metrizable, has a clopen base, and has no isolated points. The map a↦Σ_{n≥1}(2a_n/3^n) is a homeomorphism from C onto the middle-thirds Cantor subset of [0,1]. Here the middle-thirds set is K=⋂_{r≥0} ⋃_{a∈{0,1}^r} [s_r(a),s_r(a)+3^{−r}], where s_r(a)=Σ_{n=1}^r 2a_n/3^n and the r=0 retained interval is [0,1]. This defines the middle-thirds Cantor set.

For every compact zero-dimensional metric space X and every ε>0, there is a finite partition into nonempty clopen parts each of diameter less than ε; for X=∅ the empty partition is allowed. Such an arbitrarily small-mesh partition can be chosen to refine any prescribed finite clopen partition. If X has no isolated points, every nonempty clopen subset of X can be partitioned into any prescribed positive finite number of nonempty clopen subsets.

Every nonempty compact metrizable zero-dimensional space with no isolated points is homeomorphic to C={0,1}^{N_{≥1}}. Under these same nonempty compact metrizable and no-isolated-point hypotheses, the zero-dimensional condition can equivalently be replaced by total disconnectedness.
For every nonempty compact metric space K, there exists a continuous surjection C={0,1}^{N_{≥1}}→K. Nonemptiness is retained: the nonempty space C cannot surject onto ∅.
There exists a continuous surjection [0,1]→[0,1]^2. More generally, for each finite integer m≥1 there exists a continuous surjection [0,1]→[0,1]^m.

Equip {0,1} with the topology {∅,{1},{0,1}}. This Sierpinski space is T0, compact, and connected, but is neither T1 nor Hausdorff. The constant sequence 1,1,… converges to both 0 and 1, since every neighborhood of either point contains 1.

For any infinite set D, the metric with d(x,x)=0 and d(x,y)=1 when x≠y is bounded and complete but is neither compact nor totally bounded. If D is uncountable, this metric space is also locally compact and first countable, while failing separability, second countability, and the Lindelöf property.

Let K={1/n:n≥1}⊆R. The ordinary open intervals and their differences with K form a basis for a topology on R. The resulting K-topology is Hausdorff and second countable but is not regular and therefore is not metrizable.

Take the disjoint sum of two copies of R and identify points in different copies exactly when they have equal nonzero coordinate, keeping the two origins distinct; equip the quotient with its quotient topology. This particular doubled-origin line is T1, second countable, locally metrizable, and paracompact, but is neither Hausdorff nor metrizable.

Let D be uncountable and p∉D. On X=D∪{p}, every subset of D is open, and a set containing p is open exactly when its complement is an at-most-countable subset of D. This Fortissimo topology is normal, Hausdorff, zero-dimensional, and Lindelöf, but is not compact, first countable, or separable.
For every ordinal β, including β=0, the ordinal interval [0,β] with its order topology is compact and Hausdorff.

Let ω1 be the first uncountable ordinal, with Y=[0,ω1) and Z=[0,ω1] in their order topologies. Y is first countable, locally compact, countably compact, and sequentially compact, but is neither compact nor Lindelöf nor σ-compact. Z is compact Hausdorff but not first countable (specifically at ω1). No sequence of points of Y converges in Z to ω1, although ω1 belongs to the closure of Y in Z.
The rational numbers Q with their usual metric are not complete.

The atlas explicitly reuses earlier constructions and complete proofs rather than creating duplicate mathematical obligations: the topologist's sine closure (connected, not path connected, d10:06:sine-curve); Sorgenfrey line (separable and first countable, not second countable, d10:08:sorgenfrey-line); Sorgenfrey plane (product failures, d10:08:sorgenfrey-plane and the derived nonparacompactness below); cocountable topology (closure and continuity not sequence-detected, d10:08:cocountable and d10:04:closure-net); compact binary cube (compact Hausdorff, not sequentially compact, d10:05:variant-counterexamples); Q (metric without local compactness or completeness, d10:11:rationals and d10:18:rational-incomplete); arctan uniformity (one topology with complete and incomplete compatible metrics, d10:12:continuity-calculus); non-LCH Ascoli domain (compact-open compactness need not imply equicontinuity, d10:13:ascoli-nonlch); quotient times Q (arbitrary products need not preserve quotient maps, d10:03:quotient-product-failure). These references require their actual previously inventoried results, not new repetitions or axioms.

The Sorgenfrey line is regular Lindelöf and hence paracompact. The Sorgenfrey plane, its product with itself, is Hausdorff but not normal, and therefore is not paracompact by the paracompact-Hausdorff normality theorem. Consequently products of paracompact spaces need not be paracompact. This is a derived additional assertion reusing the established Sorgenfrey-line/plane constructions and their normality properties; it does not demand duplicate proofs of those earlier results.

Give C(Q,R) the compact-open topology and Q its usual topology. The evaluation map C(Q,R)_co×Q→R, (f,x)↦f(x), is not continuous at the pair (0,0), where the first 0 is the zero function and the second is the rational number zero.
