Global interpretation of every mathematical entry: positive measures are [0,∞]-valued; empty spaces and zero measures are allowed unless expressly excluded. Measure completeness means all subsets of measurable null sets are measurable. Euclidean dimension is a positive integer unless stated otherwise; λ_d is completed Euclidean Lebesgue measure, λ_d^B its Borel restriction. Abstract products and completions are distinct. Scalar integrability includes measurability and ∫|f|<∞, and linear integrals are asserted only with integrability; totalized nonintegrable library values do not satisfy this convention. Lp uses ordinary a.e. classes; the local-null L∞ is separate and requires its bridge. Radon means Borel, compact-finite, outer regular on Borel sets, inner regular on open sets; full Borel compact-inner regularity is separate. Density uniqueness is a.e. Stieltjes uses right-continuous generators and (a,b]. Hausdorff diameter costs have coefficient one and H^0 is counting. Daniell–Stone uniqueness is on the generated sigma-ring. These conventions are implemented by the definitions/results below, not additional assumed theorems.

For a countable family of nonnegative extended real numbers the sum is the supremum of its finite partial sums (equivalently finite subsums); permutation of the family does not change the sum. Use 0·∞=0. Empty spaces and zero measures are admitted.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Algebras and measurable spaces] An algebra $\mathcal A$ on a set $X$ contains $X$ and is closed under complements
relative to $X$ and finite unions. A sigma-algebra $\Sigma$ is an algebra
closed under countable unions. The pair $(X,\Sigma)$ is a measurable space;
its measurable sets are the members of $\Sigma$.

An algebra on X is closed under finite intersections, contains ∅, and is closed under differences. A sigma-algebra is also closed under countable intersections; for a measurable sequence (E_n), limsup E_n=⋂_N ⋃_{n≥N}E_n and liminf E_n=⋃_N ⋂_{n≥N}E_n are measurable (these formulas define the two set limits).

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Generation] For every $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ there is a smallest sigma-algebra
$\sigma(\mathcal C)$ containing $\mathcal C$. It is the intersection of all
sigma-algebras containing $\mathcal C$. If $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal D$,
then $\sigma(\mathcal C)\subseteq\sigma(\mathcal D)$, and
$\sigma(\sigma(\mathcal C))=\sigma(\mathcal C)$.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Trace structure] If $E\in\Sigma$, then
$\Sigma|_E=\{E\cap A:A\in\Sigma\}$ is a sigma-algebra on $E$; its members
are exactly the $\Sigma$-measurable subsets of $E$.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Measure] A positive measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ is a function
$\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ such that $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ and
\[
 \mu\Bigl(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n\Bigr)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu(E_n)
\]
for every pairwise disjoint measurable sequence. A finitely additive measure
on an algebra satisfies the same requirement for finite disjoint families.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Elementary bounds] If $A\subseteq B$ are measurable, then $\mu(A)\leq\mu(B)$. If moreover
$\mu(A)<\infty$, then $\mu(B\setminus A)=\mu(B)-\mu(A)$. For every
measurable sequence,
$\mu(\bigcup_n E_n)\leq\sum_n\mu(E_n)$.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Continuity of a measure] If $E_n\uparrow E$, then $\mu(E_n)\uparrow\mu(E)$. If $E_n\downarrow E$
and $\mu(E_N)<\infty$ for some $N$, then $\mu(E_n)\downarrow\mu(E)$.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Continuity criteria] For a finitely additive $p:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$, countable additivity is
equivalent to continuity from below. Continuity at the empty set from above
is also sufficient, and is necessary if $p(X)<\infty$.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Size assumptions] A measure is finite if $\mu(X)<\infty$, sigma-finite if
$X=\bigcup_n A_n$ for measurable $A_n$ with $\mu(A_n)<\infty$, and a
probability measure if $\mu(X)=1$. A measurable subset is sigma-finite when
it has such a cover by measurable subsets of itself.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Finite-measure exhaustions] A sigma-finite space admits a disjoint measurable partition $X=\bigsqcup_nD_n$
with finite measures, and an increasing finite-measure exhaustion.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Elementary measures] Counting measure assigns a finite measurable set its cardinality and an infinite
measurable set infinity. For $x\in X$, $\delta_x(E)=\mathbf 1_E(x)$ is a measure.
For $x_n\in X$ and $a_n\in[0,\infty]$,
$\mu(E)=\sum_n a_n\mathbf 1_E(x_n)$ is a measure; locations may repeat.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Nullity and completeness] A measurable $N$ is null if $\mu(N)=0$. An arbitrary set is negligible if it
is contained in a measurable null set. The measure space is complete if every
negligible set is measurable, hence null by monotonicity. This is not metric
completeness.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Restriction] For $E\in\Sigma$, restriction defines a measure on $(E,\Sigma|_E)$ by
$\mu_E(A)=\mu(A)$ for measurable $A\subseteq E$. On $X$ the formula
$\mu^E(A)=\mu(A\cap E)$ also defines a measure. Its mass is $\mu(E)$;
finiteness and sigma-finiteness are inherited from $\mu$.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Sums and increasing limits] If $\mu_n$ are measures and $a_n\geq0$ are finite, then
$\sum_n a_n\mu_n$ is a measure. If $\mu_n(A)$ increases with $n$ for every
measurable $A$, then $\mu(A)=\lim_n\mu_n(A)$ is a measure.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [First Borel--Cantelli lemma] If $\sum_n\mu(E_n)<\infty$, then $\mu(\limsup E_n)=0$.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Pi--lambda] A pi-system is closed under finite intersections. A lambda-system contains
$X$ and is closed under complements and countable disjoint unions.
For every pi-system $\mathcal P$, the lambda-system it generates equals
$\sigma(\mathcal P)$.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Uniqueness on generators] Let $\sigma(\mathcal P)=\Sigma$, with $\mathcal P$ a pi-system. Finite
measures agreeing on $\mathcal P$ and on $X$ agree on $\Sigma$.
The same conclusion holds if they agree on $\mathcal P$ and there are
$P_n\in\mathcal P$ increasing to $X$ with common finite measures.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Set monotone classes] A monotone class is closed under increasing countable unions and decreasing
countable intersections. The smallest monotone class containing an algebra
$\mathcal A$ is $\sigma(\mathcal A)$.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Bounded functional monotone classes] Let $H$ be a real vector space of bounded real functions on $X$, containing
$1$ and $\mathbf 1_A$ for every member $A$ of a pi-system $\mathcal P$.
Suppose $H$ is closed under pointwise increasing limits of uniformly bounded
sequences whose limit is bounded. Then $H$ contains every bounded
$\sigma(\mathcal P)$-measurable real function.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [A union need not be a sigma-algebra] On $X=\{1,2,3\}$, the sigma-algebras
$\{\varnothing,X,\{1\},\{2,3\}\}$ and
$\{\varnothing,X,\{2\},\{1,3\}\}$ have a union that is not an algebra:
it contains $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ but not their union.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Finite additivity is insufficient] On the finite/cofinite algebra of $\mathbb N$, let $p(A)=0$ for finite $A$ and
$p(A)=1$ for cofinite $A$. It is finitely additive: in a finite disjoint family
at most one set is cofinite, and the union is cofinite exactly when such a
member occurs. But $p(\mathbb N)=1\ne\sum_n p(\{n\})=0$. Thus it admits no
countably additive extension to $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$.

On arbitrary measurable spaces, with positive [0,∞]-valued measures where measures occur (no finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness unless specified). [Decreasing continuity needs a finite term] With the Lebesgue measure constructed in Chapter~\ref{ch:d11-03},
$E_n=(n,\infty)$ decrease to $\varnothing$ but all have infinite measure.
The limit of their measures is therefore not the measure of their intersection.
This example is not used in the construction of Lebesgue measure.

On arbitrary sets/measurable spaces, with [0,∞]-valued outer measures, premeasures and positive measures as specified; no implicit sigma-finiteness or completeness. [Outer measure] An outer measure is a function $m^*:\mathcal P(X)\to[0,\infty]$ that is zero
on the empty set, monotone, and countably subadditive. Its domain is every
subset of $X$; countable additivity on that whole domain is not required.

On arbitrary sets/measurable spaces, with [0,∞]-valued outer measures, premeasures and positive measures as specified; no implicit sigma-finiteness or completeness. [Covering costs] Let $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ contain $\varnothing$ and $X$, and
let $\rho:\mathcal C\to[0,\infty]$ satisfy $\rho(\varnothing)=0$. Then
\[
 m^*(E)=\inf\left\{\sum_n\rho(C_n):C_n\in\mathcal C,
                  \ E\subseteq\bigcup_n C_n\right\}
\]
is an outer measure. The infimum of an empty class is interpreted as infinity.

On arbitrary sets/measurable spaces, with [0,∞]-valued outer measures, premeasures and positive measures as specified; no implicit sigma-finiteness or completeness. [Caratheodory measurability] A set $A\subseteq X$ is $m^*$-measurable if
\[
 m^*(E)=m^*(E\cap A)+m^*(E\setminus A)\qquad(E\subseteq X).
\]
The quantifier tests all subsets $E$. Subadditivity already gives the
$\leq$ direction. To prove the reverse direction it is enough to test
$m^*(E)<\infty$, since an infinite left side makes it automatic.

On arbitrary sets/measurable spaces, with [0,∞]-valued outer measures, premeasures and positive measures as specified; no implicit sigma-finiteness or completeness. [Caratheodory construction] The $m^*$-measurable sets form a sigma-algebra $\mathcal M(m^*)$.
The restriction of $m^*$ to it is a complete measure.

On arbitrary sets/measurable spaces, with [0,∞]-valued outer measures, premeasures and positive measures as specified; no implicit sigma-finiteness or completeness. [Premeasure] A premeasure on an algebra $\mathcal A$ is a function $p:\mathcal A\to[0,\infty]$ with
$p(\varnothing)=0$ such that
$p(\bigcup_n A_n)=\sum_n p(A_n)$ whenever the $A_n$ are disjoint members
of $\mathcal A$ and their union belongs to $\mathcal A$. It is sigma-finite when $X$
has a countable cover by members of $\mathcal A$ of finite $p$-value.

On arbitrary sets/measurable spaces, with [0,∞]-valued outer measures, premeasures and positive measures as specified; no implicit sigma-finiteness or completeness. [Agreement of the covering construction] For a premeasure $p$ define
\[
 p^*(E)=\inf\left\{\sum_n p(A_n): A_n\in\mathcal A,
                               \ E\subseteq\bigcup_nA_n\right\}.
\]
Then $p^*$ is an outer measure, $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal M(p^*)$, and
$p^*(A)=p(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal A$.

On arbitrary sets/measurable spaces, with [0,∞]-valued outer measures, premeasures and positive measures as specified; no implicit sigma-finiteness or completeness. [Existence and the precise uniqueness assertion] The measure $\mu=p^*|_{\sigma(\mathcal A)}$ extends $p$. If $\nu$ is another
extension on $\sigma(\mathcal A)$, then $\nu(E)\leq\mu(E)$ for every measurable
$E$, with equality whenever $\mu(E)<\infty$. If $p$ is sigma-finite, the
extension on $\sigma(\mathcal A)$ is unique.

On arbitrary sets/measurable spaces, with [0,∞]-valued outer measures, premeasures and positive measures as specified; no implicit sigma-finiteness or completeness. [Completion] For a measure $\mu$ on $\Sigma$, let
\[
 \overline\Sigma=\{E\subseteq X:\ A\subseteq E\subseteq B
       \text{ for some }A,B\in\Sigma,\ \mu(B\setminus A)=0\}.
\]
Then $\overline\mu(E)=\mu(A)=\mu(B)$ is well-defined and is a complete
measure extending $\mu$. Its sigma-algebra is generated by $\Sigma$ and all
subsets of measurable $\mu$-null sets. Every complete extension contains
this sigma-algebra and agrees with $\overline\mu$ there.

On arbitrary sets/measurable spaces, with [0,∞]-valued outer measures, premeasures and positive measures as specified; no implicit sigma-finiteness or completeness. [Induced outer measure and sigma-finite completion] For a sigma-finite measure $\mu$ on $\Sigma$, put
$\mu^*(E)=\inf\{\mu(A):E\subseteq A,\ A\in\Sigma\}$.
This is an outer measure, $\mathcal M(\mu^*)=\overline\Sigma$, and its
measure on that class is $\overline\mu$.

On arbitrary sets/measurable spaces, with [0,∞]-valued outer measures, premeasures and positive measures as specified; no implicit sigma-finiteness or completeness. [Nonunique extensions] Let $\mathcal A$ be the algebra of finite unions of intervals $(a,b]$, $(-\infty,b]$
and $(a,\infty)$, together with $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb R$; all displayed finite
endpoints are real and $a<b$. Every nonempty member contains a nondegenerate
interval. Set $p(\varnothing)=0$ and $p(A)=\infty$ otherwise.
It is a premeasure: a disjoint union in the algebra is nonempty exactly when
at least one of its members is nonempty, and both sides of the premeasure
identity are then infinity. Its generated sigma-algebra is $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$.
Counting measure and the measure that is infinity on every nonempty Borel
set both extend $p$, but have values $1$ and infinity at a singleton.
Thus extension existence does not imply uniqueness.

On arbitrary sets/measurable spaces, with [0,∞]-valued outer measures, premeasures and positive measures as specified; no implicit sigma-finiteness or completeness. [An outer measure that is not additive] On $X=\{a,b\}$ let $m^*(E)=1$ for nonempty $E$, and $m^*(\varnothing)=0$.
It is monotone; if a countable union is nonempty some member is nonempty,
so it is subadditive. But $m^*(X)=1\ne2=m^*(\{a\})+m^*(\{b\})$.
The empty set and $X$ pass the splitting test; each singleton fails it when
tested against $E=X$. Thus its Caratheodory sigma-algebra is precisely
$\{\varnothing,X\}$.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Euclidean Borel sets] The Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ is generated by the Euclidean open sets.
A Borel set means a member of this sigma-algebra, not an arbitrary set to
which a completed measure will eventually assign a value.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Generators] The Borel sigma-algebra is generated by rational open boxes, by bounded
half-open boxes, or by the coordinate half-spaces $\{x:x_j\leq q\}$ with
$q\in\mathbb Q$. On $\mathbb R$, each of the open, closed and half-open interval families,
and each of the open or closed ray families, also generates it.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Outer volume] For $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ define
\[
 \lambda_d^*(E)=\inf\left\{\sum_n\prod_{j=1}^d(b_{nj}-a_{nj}):
 E\subseteq\bigcup_n\prod_{j=1}^d(a_{nj},b_{nj})\right\},
\]
using bounded open boxes. This is an outer measure and the outer measure of
every bounded box, with any endpoint convention, is its product of side lengths.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [The Lebesgue measures] Every Borel set is Caratheodory measurable for $\lambda_d^*$. Let $\mathcal L_d$ be
the full Caratheodory sigma-algebra. The restrictions $\lambda_d^B$ to
$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ and $\lambda_d$ to $\mathcal L_d$ are sigma-finite measures assigning
box volume; $\lambda_d$ is complete.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Countable null sets] Singletons and countable subsets of $\mathbb R^d$ have outer measure zero. Every
subset of a Lebesgue-null set is Lebesgue measurable and null.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Euclidean regularity] For $E\in\mathcal L_d$,
\[
 \lambda_d(E)=\inf_{E\subseteq U,\ U\ \text{open}}\lambda_d(U)
            =\sup_{K\subseteq E,\ K\ \text{compact}}\lambda_d(K).
\]
If $\lambda_d(E)<\infty$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there are compact
$K\subseteq E\subseteq U$ with $U$ open and $\lambda_d(U\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Global small errors] For every $E\in\mathcal L_d$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there are a closed $F$ and an open $G$
with $F\subseteq E\subseteq G$ and
$\lambda_d(E\setminus F)<\varepsilon$, $\lambda_d(G\setminus E)<\varepsilon$.
There is no finite-measure assumption on $E$; $F$ need not be compact.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Borel and box approximation] Every $E\in\mathcal L_d$ lies between an $F_\sigma$ set $F$ and a $G_\delta$ set
$G$ with both $E\setminus F$ and $G\setminus E$ null. If $\lambda_d(E)$
is finite, it can be approximated in symmetric-difference measure by a finite
disjoint union of bounded boxes.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Identification of the completion] The space $(\mathbb R^d,\mathcal L_d,\lambda_d)$ is the completion of
$(\mathbb R^d,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d),\lambda_d^B)$. In particular, a Lebesgue set is a Borel
set modulo a subset of a Borel null set.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Translations and dilations] For $a\in\mathbb R^d$, $r\ne0$ and any $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,
$\lambda_d^*(a+rE)=|r|^d\lambda_d^*(E)$. This invertible affine map
preserves Borel and Lebesgue measurability in both directions, with the same
formula for measurable sets. For $r=0$ the image is empty or a singleton;
the numerical outer-measure formula still holds with $0\cdot\infty=0$,
but there is no reverse measurability implication.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Uniqueness of volume] A Borel measure assigning all bounded half-open boxes their volumes is
$\lambda_d^B$. Every nonzero translation-invariant Borel measure finite on
bounded Borel sets is $c\lambda_d^B$ for a unique $c>0$.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Cantor sets] The middle-thirds Cantor set $C$ is compact, perfect, nowhere dense,
of cardinality continuum, and null. For every $0<\alpha<1$ there is a
closed nowhere-dense subset of $[0,1]$ of measure $\alpha$.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Vitali's obstruction] Assume choice and select $V\subseteq[0,1]$ containing exactly one
representative of every equivalence class for $x\sim y$ when $x-y\in\mathbb Q$.
Then $V$ is not Lebesgue measurable.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [A nonmeasurable subset in every positive outer-measure set] Assuming choice, every $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ with $\lambda_1^*(B)>0$ contains
a non-Lebesgue-measurable subset.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [The Cantor-function bridge] The Cantor set supports a continuous nondecreasing map
$\Gamma:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with $\Gamma(0)=0$, $\Gamma(1)=1$, constant on
each component of $[0,1]\setminus C$. Its derivative, absolute-continuity
and Stieltjes consequences will be treated in
\cref{d11:12:singular-continuous-counterexample}.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [A Lebesgue set that is not Borel] There is a non-Borel subset $N$ of the Cantor set. It is Lebesgue measurable
and null, so Borel Lebesgue measure is not complete.

In Euclidean R^d with d≥1 (R means d=1), λ_d^* is the open-box outer volume, λ_d is its full Caratheodory Lebesgue measure and λ_d^B its Borel restriction as constructed in this chapter. [Steinhaus] If $E\in\mathcal L_1$ has positive measure, then $E-E$ contains an open interval
about zero.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [Measurable maps] A map $f:(X,\Sigma)\to(Y,\mathcal T)$ is measurable if
$f^{-1}(B)\in\Sigma$ for every $B\in\mathcal T$.
Scalar measurability uses the Borel sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$, or
$\overline\mathbb R=[-\infty,\infty]$. A function on a measurable subset $E$
uses the trace sigma-algebra on $E$.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [Generator tests] If $\mathcal T=\sigma(\mathcal C)$, then $f$ is measurable if and only if
$f^{-1}(C)\in\Sigma$ for every $C\in\mathcal C$.
Real or extended-real measurability is equivalent to measurability of its
strict lower level sets, or of its non-strict lower level sets; rational
thresholds suffice. Upper level tests are equivalent as well.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [Composition] If $f:(X,\Sigma)\to(Y,\mathcal T)$ and
$g:(Y,\mathcal T)\to(Z,\mathcal U)$ are measurable, then $g\circ f$ is
measurable. In particular continuous scalar maps may be composed after
measurable scalar maps, with the appropriate Borel structures.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [Coordinate tests] A map $f:X\to\mathbb R^d$ is Borel measurable exactly when each coordinate is
measurable. A map to $\mathbb C$ is measurable exactly when its real and imaginary
parts are measurable. Finite tuples of measurable scalar maps are measurable;
modulus and complex conjugation preserve measurability.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [Algebra and comparisons] For measurable finite scalar $f,g$, the functions $af+bg$ and $fg$ are
measurable, and $f/g$ is measurable on $\{g\ne0\}$.
For extended-real measurable $f,g$, the sets $\{f<g\},\{f\leq g\},\{f=g\}$
and the functions $\max(f,g),\min(f,g)$ are measurable. Nonnegative extended
functions are closed under addition, multiplication with $0\cdot\infty=0$,
and multiplication by finite nonnegative constants.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [Countable limits] For measurable $f_n:X\to\overline\mathbb R$, their pointwise supremum, infimum,
limsup and liminf are measurable. Their finite-limit set is measurable;
the limit there, extended by zero elsewhere, is measurable. Everywhere
finite real or complex pointwise limits of measurable maps are measurable.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [Simple functions] A simple scalar function has finite range. It is measurable if and only if
each nonzero level set is measurable, equivalently if it has a representation
$f=\sum_{j=1}^n c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$ with measurable disjoint $E_j$.
A nonnegative simple function has finite nonnegative real values. There is
no finite-measure-support condition in this definition.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [Simple approximation] Every measurable $f:X\to[0,\infty]$ is an increasing pointwise limit of finite
nonnegative measurable simple functions $s_n\leq f$.
For measurable $f:X\to\overline\mathbb R$ one can choose real simple $s_n\to f$
with $|s_n|\leq|s_{n+1}|\leq|f|$; bounded real $f$ has uniform such
approximations. Complex measurable functions have pointwise simple
approximations, uniform when bounded.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [Almost everywhere] A property holds $\mu$-almost everywhere if it holds outside some
$N\in\Sigma$ with $\mu(N)=0$. Equality almost everywhere is an equivalence
relation on scalar functions: reflexivity uses the empty exceptional set,
symmetry uses the same set, and transitivity uses the union of two null sets.
Its equivalence classes are not actual functions. On an incomplete space the
failure set itself need not be measurable, although it has a measurable null
envelope.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [A common exceptional set] Countably many a.e. assertions hold simultaneously outside one measurable
null set. A.e. equality is consequently preserved by finite scalar operations
and countable pointwise limits whenever the stated operations are defined.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [A.e. changes and measurability] If $\mu$ is complete, a function equal a.e. to a measurable extended-real
function is measurable. An a.e. limit of measurable extended-real functions
has a measurable version on any measure space, and the given limit itself
is measurable when the space is complete.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [Versions for a completion] An extended-real function $f$ is $\overline\Sigma$-measurable if and only if
there are $\Sigma$-measurable extended-real $f_0\leq f\leq f_1$ everywhere
with $f_0=f_1$ a.e. In particular it has a $\Sigma$-measurable version.
For finite real or complex $f$ this version can be chosen finite-valued.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [Essential bounds] For measurable finite scalar $f$ set
\[
 \operatorname{ess\,sup}|f|=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty): |f|\leq M\ \mu\text{-a.e.}\},
 \qquad \inf\varnothing=\infty.
\]
The function is essentially bounded if this number is finite. Changing $f$
on a measurable null envelope does not change the set of admissible bounds.
This is the ordinary a.e. convention, not the locally-null convention used
in a separate Cohn variant later.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [Attainment of the essential bound] If $M=\operatorname{ess\,sup}|f|<\infty$, then $|f|\leq M$ a.e.
Also $\operatorname{ess\,sup}|f|=0$ iff $f=0$ a.e., and $|f|\leq|g|$ a.e. implies
$\operatorname{ess\,sup}|f|\leq\operatorname{ess\,sup}|g|$.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [An incomplete-space modification] Let $N\subseteq C$ be the non-Borel Cantor subset from
\cref{d11:03:lebesgue-not-borel}. On the Borel Lebesgue space, $\mathbf 1_N$
equals zero outside the Borel null set $C$ but is not Borel measurable:
the inverse image of $(1/2,\infty)$ is $N$. Thus an arbitrary null modification
need not be measurable before completion.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. Here N⊆C is a non-Borel subset of the middle-thirds Cantor set and measurability is for the Borel Lebesgue space on R. [Uncountable suprema] Each $\mathbf 1_{\{x\}}$, $x\in N$, is Borel measurable, but their supremum
is $\mathbf 1_N$, which is not. Thus the countability in the limit theorem is
a real hypothesis, even for nonnegative functions bounded by one.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), and an arbitrary positive measure μ when null sets occur; scalar functions are finite real/complex valued unless an extended codomain is displayed. No completeness is implicit. [A measurable modulus is insufficient] Let $V\subseteq[0,1]$ be non-Lebesgue-measurable and put
$f=2\mathbf 1_V-1$ on $[0,1]$. Then $|f|=1$ is measurable and has finite
integral by the simple-integral definition of the next chapter. But $f$
is not measurable, since $\{f>0\}=V$. A comparison with an integrable
modulus never licenses dropping measurability of the scalar function itself.

Forward interface marker: the general composition statement is covered by d11:04:composition and the precise completed-Lebesgue criterion and counterexample are independently inventoried under d11:09:von-neumann-composition and d11:09:composition-measurability-failure. This is not a separate adopted theorem or assumed bridge. [The middle sigma-algebra is part of composition] Continuity of an inner map ensures measurable inverse images of Borel sets,
not automatically of every subset of a target null set. Testing a composition
with $g=\mathbf 1_A$ makes this precise: measurability of all such compositions
requires that every admitted target measurable $A$ have measurable inverse
image. For a continuous strictly increasing $h:[a,b]\to[c,d]$ the exact
additional criterion, proved in \cref{d11:09:von-neumann-composition}, is
absolute continuity of $h^{-1}$. That independent later theorem and
\cref{d11:09:composition-measurability-failure} supply the refined criterion
and counterexample; neither is being assumed to prove the general composition
theorem here. This is a forward interface marker, not a second copy of that proof.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Integral of a simple function] If $s=\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$, where the $E_j\in\Sigma$ are pairwise
disjoint and $0\leq a_j<\infty$, set
\[
 I_\mu(s)=\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\mu(E_j).
\]
One may include the complement of the union among the sets with coefficient
zero. Thus this definition applies to every nonnegative measurable simple
function, without any restriction on the measure of its support.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Independence and elementary algebra] The value $I_\mu(s)$ is independent of the disjoint representation.
For nonnegative measurable simple $s,t$ and finite $a\geq0$,
\[
 I_\mu(as)=aI_\mu(s),\qquad I_\mu(s+t)=I_\mu(s)+I_\mu(t).
\]
If $s\leq t$, then $I_\mu(s)\leq I_\mu(t)$.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Nonnegative integral and its approximation property] For a measurable $f:X\to[0,\infty]$ define
\[
 \int f\,d\mu=\sup\{I_\mu(s):s\text{ measurable simple},\ 0\leq s\leq f\}.
\]
This agrees with $I_\mu$ on simple functions. If $s_n$ are any nonnegative
measurable simple functions with $s_n\uparrow f$, then
\[
 \int f\,d\mu=\lim_n I_\mu(s_n).
\]

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Algebra and restriction] For measurable $f,g:X\to[0,\infty]$ and finite $a\geq0$,
\[
 \int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu,
 \qquad \int af\,d\mu=a\int f\,d\mu.
\]
Pointwise order implies order of integrals. For $E\in\Sigma$ write
$\int_E f\,d\mu=\int\mathbf 1_Ef\,d\mu$; this is also the integral of $f|_E$
on the trace space with the restricted measure.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Null sets and order almost everywhere] If measurable $f,g:X\to[0,\infty]$ agree $\mu$-almost everywhere, their
integrals agree. For every measurable null set $N$, $\int_N f\,d\mu=0$,
even if $f$ is infinite there. If $f\leq g$ almost everywhere, then
$\int f\,d\mu\leq\int g\,d\mu$.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Monotone convergence] Let $f_n,f:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable. If, outside one measurable null
set, $f_n\leq f_{n+1}$ for every $n$ and $f_n\to f$, then
\[
 \int f\,d\mu=\lim_n\int f_n\,d\mu=\sup_n\int f_n\,d\mu.
\]

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Nonnegative series] For any measurable $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$,
\[
 \int\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\,d\mu
   =\sum_{n=1}^\infty\int f_n\,d\mu.
\]
Consequently, if $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint measurable sets, then
$\int_{\bigcup_nE_n}f\,d\mu=\sum_n\int_{E_n}f\,d\mu$ for every
nonnegative measurable $f$.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Fatou's inequality] For every sequence of nonnegative measurable $f_n$,
\[
 \int\liminf_n f_n\,d\mu\leq\liminf_n\int f_n\,d\mu.
\]
If a measurable $f\geq0$ satisfies $f\leq\liminf_n f_n$ almost everywhere,
then $\int f\,d\mu\leq\liminf_n\int f_n\,d\mu$ as well.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Markov's inequality] If $f:X\to[0,\infty]$ is measurable and $t>0$, then
\[
 t\mu\{f\geq t\}\leq\int_{\{f\geq t\}}f\,d\mu
 \leq\int f\,d\mu.
\]
Thus $\mu\{f\geq t\}\leq t^{-1}\int f\,d\mu$, as an extended inequality.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [What zero and finite integrals imply] For measurable $f:X\to[0,\infty]$, $\int f\,d\mu=0$ if and only if $f=0$
almost everywhere. If $\int f\,d\mu<\infty$, then $f<\infty$ almost
everywhere and $\{f>0\}$ is a countable union of measurable sets of finite
measure.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [A measure with density] For measurable $h:X\to[0,\infty]$, the prescription
\[
 \nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\Sigma)
\]
defines a positive measure. It is finite when $\int h\,d\mu<\infty$ and
vanishes on every measurable $\mu$-null set. No integrability assumption
is needed to construct it.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Atomic integrals] For nonnegative measurable $f$, $\int f\,d\delta_x=f(x)$.
On a countable set with its full power-set sigma-algebra and counting
measure, $\int f=\sum_x f(x)$. More generally, if
$\mu=\sum_n a_n\delta_{x_n}$ with $a_n\in[0,\infty]$, then
\[
 \int f\,d\mu=\sum_n a_nf(x_n).
\]
Repeated points and infinite weights are allowed.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Continuity with respect to the domain] If $E_n\uparrow E$ are measurable and $f\geq0$ is measurable, then
$\int_{E_n}f\uparrow\int_Ef$. If $E_n\downarrow E$ and
$\int_{E_N}f<\infty$ for some $N$, then $\int_{E_n}f\downarrow\int_Ef$.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Strict Fatou inequality through escape of mass] On $\mathbb R$ let $f_n=\mathbf 1_{[n,n+1)}$. Every fixed point is eventually outside
these intervals, so $f_n\to0$ pointwise. Each integral is the interval
length $1$. Therefore
\[
 \int\liminf_n f_n\,d\lambda=0<1=\liminf_n\int f_n\,d\lambda.
\]
Nonnegativity and pointwise convergence by themselves do not justify
interchanging a limit and an integral.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Absolute integrability] A measurable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ is integrable if
$\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. For real $f$ write
$f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-=\max(-f,0)$, so that
$|f|=f^++f^-$ and $f=f^+-f^-$. For an extended-real measurable $f$ with
$\int|f|<\infty$, replace $f$ by zero on the measurable null set
$\{|f|=\infty\}$ before assigning it a scalar integral. The resulting
finite version is unique almost everywhere.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Real and complex integrals] For real integrable $f$ set
\[
 \int f\,d\mu=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.
\]
Real integrability is equivalent to finiteness of both terms on the right.
For complex integrable $f$ set
\[
 \int f\,d\mu=\int\operatorname{Re}f\,d\mu
             +i\int\operatorname{Im}f\,d\mu.
\]
Complex integrability is equivalent to integrability of both coordinates.
These definitions give the usual finite scalar sum for an integrable
measurable simple function.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Linearity, order and absolute-value bound] If scalar functions $f,g$ are integrable and $a,b$ are scalars in their
field, then $af+bg$ is integrable and
\[
 \int(af+bg)\,d\mu=a\int f\,d\mu+b\int g\,d\mu.
\]
For real $f\leq g$ almost everywhere, $\int f\leq\int g$. In both fields,
$\big|\int f\,d\mu\big|\leq\int|f|\,d\mu$.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Integrable domination] If $f$ is measurable and $|f|\leq g$ almost everywhere for an integrable
measurable $g\geq0$, then $f$ is integrable. In particular, if $f=0$ off
a measurable $E$ of finite measure and $|f|\leq M$ almost everywhere,
where $M<\infty$, then $\int|f|\leq M\mu(E)$.
If $f$ is integrable and measurable $h$ is essentially bounded, then
$hf$ is integrable and
\[
 \int|hf|\,d\mu\leq(\operatorname{ess\,sup}|h|)\int|f|\,d\mu.
\]

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Almost-everywhere invariance and restriction] If measurable scalar $f,g$ agree almost everywhere, one is integrable if
and only if the other is, and their integrals then agree. An integrable
function remains integrable on every measurable subset. Removing a
measurable null subset changes neither its integral nor its absolute integral.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Small sets and finite-measure tails of one integral] If $f$ is integrable, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such
that $E\in\Sigma$, $\mu(E)<\delta$ imply $\int_E|f|<\varepsilon$.
Also, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $A\in\Sigma$, $\mu(A)<\infty$, with
$\int_{X\setminus A}|f|<\varepsilon$. These assertions hold on every positive
measure space.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Dominated convergence] Let measurable $f_n,f:X\to\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ satisfy $f_n\to f$ almost
everywhere. Suppose $g\geq0$ is integrable and $|f_n|\leq g$ almost
everywhere for every $n$. Then $f_n,f$ are integrable and
\[
 \int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad \int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.
\]
No finiteness, completeness or sigma-finiteness assumption on $\mu$ is needed.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Bounded convergence on a fixed finite domain] If $\mu(X)<\infty$, scalar $f_n,f$ are measurable, $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere, and
$|f_n|\leq M$ almost everywhere for one finite $M$, then
$\int|f_n-f|\to0$ and $\int f_n\to\int f$. The same conclusion holds
when the $f_n$ are all supported in one fixed measurable finite-measure set,
with the same measurable limit and the same uniform almost-everywhere bound.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Absolutely summable series under the integral] If measurable scalar $f_n$ satisfy $\sum_n\int|f_n|\,d\mu<\infty$, then
$\sum_n|f_n(x)|<\infty$ almost everywhere. Define $f=\sum_nf_n$ where
the series is absolutely convergent and $f=0$ elsewhere. Then $f$ is
measurable and integrable, its partial sums converge to $f$ in absolute
integral, and
\[
 \int f\,d\mu=\sum_n\int f_n\,d\mu,
\]
where the scalar series on the right converges absolutely.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Additivity and continuity in the domain] For integrable $f$ and pairwise disjoint measurable $E_n$,
\[
 \int_{\bigcup_nE_n}f\,d\mu=\sum_n\int_{E_n}f\,d\mu,
\]
with an absolutely convergent scalar series. If measurable $E_n$ increase
or decrease to $E$, then $\int_{E_n}f\to\int_Ef$, without an additional
finite-measure hypothesis.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Detecting order and equality by integrals] If real integrable $f$ satisfies $\int_Ef\,d\mu\geq0$ for every
$E\in\Sigma$, then $f\geq0$ almost everywhere. Consequently, if scalar
integrable $f,g$ have $\int_Ef=\int_Eg$ for every measurable $E$, then
$f=g$ almost everywhere.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Differentiating a parameter integral] Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and $F:X\times I\to\mathbb R$.
Assume each $F(\cdot,t)$ is measurable and integrable, each
$F(x,\cdot)$ is differentiable on $I$, and there is integrable $g\geq0$
such that, for every $x\in X$ and all distinct $s,t\in I$,
\[
 \left|\frac{F(x,t)-F(x,s)}{t-s}\right|\leq g(x).
\]
Then $H(t)=\int F(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$ is differentiable on $I$,
$\partial_tF(\cdot,t)$ is measurable and integrable, and
\[
 H'(t)=\int\partial_tF(x,t)\,d\mu(x).
\]

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Continuity of a parameter integral] Let $I=[a,b]$, $a<b$, and let $F:X\times I\to\mathbb C$ have measurable
integrable sections $F(\cdot,t)$. Suppose $|F(x,t)|\leq g(x)$ for every
$x,t$, where $g\geq0$ is integrable. If $F(x,t)\to F(x,t_0)$ as
$t\to t_0$ within $I$ for every $x$, then
$\int F(\cdot,t)\to\int F(\cdot,t_0)$. In particular continuous
parameter sections yield a continuous parameter integral on $I$.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. [Two failures without an integrable dominator] On $\mathbb R$, $f_n=n^{-1}\mathbf 1_{(0,n)}$ satisfies $\sup_x|f_n(x)|=1/n$,
yet $\int f_n=1$ for every $n$. Uniform convergence on an infinite-measure
space need not give integral convergence. On $(0,1)$,
$g_n=n\mathbf 1_{(0,1/n)}$ tends to zero at every point and again has integral
$1$. Thus finiteness of the domain and pointwise convergence alone are
insufficient. Neither sequence has a common integrable nonnegative
dominator, since such a dominator would make dominated convergence
contradict its constant integrals.

On an arbitrary positive measure space (X,Σ,μ), with no implicit finiteness, sigma-finiteness or completeness; nonnegative integrals have values in [0,∞] and 0·∞=0. Scalar functions are real/complex valued, and scalar integrals are defined only under measurability and ∫|f|<∞. Here g is a nonnegative integrable measurable dominator, every f_n is measurable, E and A are measurable; both uniform controls below are required as consequences of one dominator. [The interface with uniform integrability] One integrable dominator supplies two uniform controls. If $|f_n|\leq g$
almost everywhere, then
\[
 \sup_n\int_E|f_n|\leq\int_Eg,
 \qquad
 \sup_n\int_{X\setminus A}|f_n|\leq\int_{X\setminus A}g.
\]
The small-set and finite-measure-tail assertions of
\cref{d11:06:absolute-continuity-integral} make the right sides arbitrarily
small with one choice of $\delta$ and one choice of $A$, respectively,
independent of $n$. Chapter~\ref{ch:d11-17} distinguishes the definitions
and proves the corresponding Vitali theorems. Those theorems are not
prerequisites for the dominated-convergence proof above.

Chapter 7 conventions: all scalar functions are finite-valued and measurable unless explicitly stated otherwise. Global convergence in measure is literal and must not be replaced on an infinite space by convergence on each finite-measure subset. These are scope conventions, not a separate theorem.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Pointwise, uniform and measure convergence: For $f_n,f:X\to\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, pointwise convergence means convergence at each $x$, and almost-everywhere convergence means convergence outside a measurable null set. Uniform convergence means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ such that $|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ for every $n\geq N$ and every $x\in X$. Almost-uniform convergence means that for every $\delta>0$ there is $E\in\Sigma$ with $\mu(E)<\delta$ such that convergence is uniform on $X\setminus E$. Convergence in measure means \[ \mu\{|f_n-f|>\varepsilon\}\longrightarrow0\quad(\varepsilon>0). \] The sequence is Cauchy in measure if, for every $\varepsilon,\delta>0$, some $N$ satisfies $\mu\{|f_n-f_m|>\varepsilon\}<\delta$ for all $m,n\geq N$.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. $L^p$ convergence on representatives: For $1\leq p<\infty$, $f_n\to f$ in $L^p$ means that all these functions have finite integrals of their $p$th absolute powers and $\int|f_n-f|^p\,d\mu\to0$. For $p=\infty$ they are essentially bounded and $\operatorname{ess\,sup}|f_n-f|\to0$. The quotient spaces and their norms will be constructed in Chapter~\ref{ch:d11-10}; the convergence assertions here can already be stated using representatives.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Norm convergence implies convergence in measure: For $1\leq p<\infty$, \[ \mu\{|f_n-f|>\varepsilon\}\leq\varepsilon^{-p}\int|f_n-f|^p\,d\mu \qquad(\varepsilon>0). \] Consequently $L^p$ convergence, including $p=\infty$, implies global convergence in measure on any positive measure space.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Almost-everywhere convergence on a finite space: If $\mu(X)<\infty$ and $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere, then $f_n\to f$ in measure. On an arbitrary space the conclusion holds after restriction to each measurable subset of finite measure.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Subsequences and uniqueness: On any positive measure space, convergence in measure to $f$ supplies a subsequence converging to $f$ almost everywhere. If the same sequence converges in measure to $f$ and $g$, then $f=g$ almost everywhere.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Subsequence characterization on a finite space: If $\mu(X)<\infty$, convergence in measure to $f$ is equivalent to the assertion that every subsequence has a further subsequence converging to $f$ almost everywhere. The forward implication holds without finiteness.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Summable integral errors: If $\sum_n\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu<\infty$, then $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere, without any finiteness or completeness assumption on $\mu$.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Completeness for convergence in measure: Every globally Cauchy-in-measure sequence has a finite measurable scalar limit in measure. A subsequence converges to this limit almost everywhere, and the limit is unique modulo ordinary almost-everywhere equality. The measure space may have arbitrary total mass.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Egorov: Suppose $\mu(X)<\infty$ and $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is measurable $E$ with $\mu(E)<\varepsilon$ such that convergence is uniform on $X\setminus E$. On a Lebesgue measurable $E_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ of finite measure, a retained subset can be chosen closed in $\mathbb R$: there is closed $F\subseteq E_0$ with $\lambda(E_0\setminus F)<\varepsilon$ and uniform convergence on $F$.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Consequences of almost-uniform convergence: On every positive measure space, almost-uniform convergence implies both almost-everywhere convergence and global convergence in measure.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Lusin on the real line, without a finite-domain assumption: Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ be Lebesgue measurable and $f:E\to\mathbb R$ finite and measurable for the trace sigma-algebra. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there are a closed $F\subseteq E$ and a continuous $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that \[ \lambda(E\setminus F)<\varepsilon,\qquad g|_F=f|_F. \] The same assertion holds for complex-valued $f$ and $g$.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Continuous functions converging almost everywhere: For measurable $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ and finite real measurable $f:E\to\mathbb R$ there are continuous $g_n:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $g_n(x)\to f(x)$ for almost every $x\in E$.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Dominated convergence in measure: Suppose $f_n\to f$ in measure and $|f_n|\leq g$ almost everywhere for one integrable $g\geq0$. Then $f$ is integrable, $\int|f_n-f|\to0$, and $\int f_n\to\int f$ on an arbitrary measure space.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Fatou for convergence in measure: If finite nonnegative measurable $f_n,f$ satisfy $f_n\to f$ globally in measure, then $\int f\leq\liminf_n\int f_n$, allowing infinite integrals.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Local convergence in measure: The sequence converges locally in measure to $f$ if, for every $A\in\Sigma$ with $\mu(A)<\infty$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, $\mu(A\cap\{|f_n-f|>\varepsilon\})\to0$. Global convergence implies this property by monotonicity. Almost-everywhere convergence implies it by applying the finite-space theorem on each $A$. The example below shows that local convergence need not be global.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Operations on limits in measure: If $f_n\to f$ and $g_n\to g$ in measure, then $af_n+bg_n\to af+bg$ in measure for fixed scalars $a,b$ on any measure space. If $\mu(X)<\infty$, also $f_ng_n\to fg$ in measure. For a uniformly continuous $\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ or $\phi:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ on the chosen scalar field, $\phi\circ f_n\to\phi\circ f$ in measure.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. The typewriter sequence: On $[0,1)$ enumerate \[ f_{2^k+j}=\mathbf 1_{[j2^{-k},(j+1)2^{-k})}, \qquad k\geq0,\quad0\leq j<2^k. \] For $1\leq p<\infty$, each function in block $k$ has $\int|f_n|^p=2^{-k}$; these tend to zero, proving $L^p$ and measure convergence to zero. Every point belongs to exactly one interval in every block, so it sees infinitely many ones. For every block with $k\geq1$ it also lies outside at least one of that block's intervals, so it sees infinitely many zeros. Thus pointwise convergence fails everywhere.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Failures on an infinite space: The sequence $f_n=\mathbf 1_{[n,n+1)}$ on $\mathbb R$ tends to zero everywhere. For any finite-measure measurable $A$, \[ \lambda(A\cap[n,n+1))\leq\lambda(A\cap[n,\infty))\longrightarrow0 \] by continuity from above; hence it converges locally in measure. The global $1/2$-deviation measure is always $1$, so global measure convergence fails. Almost-uniform convergence fails as well: if the convergence were uniform off a removed set $E$ of measure less than $\varepsilon<1$, eventually every interval $[n,n+1)$ would be contained in $E$, because a value $1$ outside $E$ would violate a uniform tolerance $1/2$. Even one such interval contradicts $\lambda(E)<1$.

On a positive measure space $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, scalar functions in this chapter are finite-valued measurable real or complex functions unless a different range is explicitly stated; convergence in measure is global unless qualified as local. Which modes descend to almost-everywhere classes: Suppose measurable scalar functions satisfy $f_n=g_n$ almost everywhere for every $n$ and $f=g$ almost everywhere. Almost-everywhere, global and local in-measure, almost-uniform, and $L^p$ convergence ($1\leq p\leq\infty$, when defined) are invariant under these replacements. Pointwise and uniform convergence on the whole space need not be invariant. For the asserted failure of invariance, on $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure the sequence $n\mathbf 1_{\{0\}}$ is a.e. equal termwise to zero, but diverges at zero and has uniform error $n$.

Chapter 8 distinguishes the ordinary product sigma-algebra, its product measure, and the measure completion. The introductory claims about section measurability at every parameter versus almost everywhere summarize the separately inventoried Sections and Completed Product theorems; this entry is context only.

Products in this chapter use the ordinary sigma-algebra $\Sigma\otimes\mathcal T$ unless completion is explicitly specified; measures mentioned are positive. Write $\mathbb E_+=[0,\infty]$, $\mathbb B$ for the Borel sigma-algebra, $\mathcal L_d$ for the Lebesgue sigma-algebra, and $\lambda_d^B,\lambda_d$ for Borel and completed Lebesgue measure. Product sigma-algebra: For measurable spaces $(X,\Sigma)$ and $(Y,\mathcal T)$ put \[ \Sigma\otimes\mathcal T =\sigma\{A\times B:A\in\Sigma,\ B\in\mathcal T\}. \] It is the smallest sigma-algebra on $X\times Y$ making both coordinate projections measurable. Indeed their inverse images are $A\times Y$ and $X\times B$, whose intersections are all generating rectangles; conversely these inverse images belong to the generated sigma-algebra. This is a sigma-algebra of subsets of the product, not a set of pairs of subsets, and no completion is included in the notation.

It lies inside the measurable product-null rectangle $\{0\}\times[0,1]$, hence in the completed product. But its section at $x=0$ is $V$, so the sections theorem rules out $E\in\mathcal L_1\otimes\mathcal L_1$. A non-sigma-finite failure of Tonelli interchange: On $[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra let $\lambda$ be Borel Lebesgue measure and $c$ counting measure. The diagonal is closed in the square, so $f(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x=y\}}$ is ordinary-product Borel measurable. Every $y$-section is a singleton of counting mass $1$, while every $x$-section is a singleton of Lebesgue mass zero. Therefore \[ \int\left(\int f(x,y)\,dc(y)\right)d\lambda(x)=1, \qquad \int\left(\int f(x,y)\,d\lambda(x)\right)dc(y)=0. \] The measure $c$ is not sigma-finite: every finite-mass set is finite, and a countable union of finite sets cannot cover the uncountable interval. This is a failure of the iterated equality without the product-theorem hypotheses, even for a nonnegative function.

A scalar interchange without absolute integrability: On $\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$, here $\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}$, use counting measures and set \[ f(m,n)=\begin{cases}1&m=n,\\-1&m=n+1,\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} \] Every section is finitely supported. Summing first in $n$, the row at $m=1$ has sum $1$ and all other rows have sum zero. The outer sum is $1$. Summing first in $m$, every column has one $1$ and one $-1$, so the outer sum is zero. The countable product sigma-algebra is the full power set (every singleton is a rectangle), and $\sum_{m,n}|f(m,n)|=\infty$. Thus no scalar product integral is licensed by absolute integrability, and Fubini's hypothesis is essential here.

For Lebesgue measurable $h$ on $[A,B]$, define $H=h(F)F'$ where $F'$ exists and is positive, and $H=0$ where it is zero or undefined. Then $H$ is measurable. For $h\geq0$ the identity $\int_a^bH=\int_A^Bh$ holds with extended values; for integrable scalar $h$ it holds absolutely and as a scalar identity. Use $0\cdot\infty=0$. Unweighted composition can fail: There is a strictly increasing continuous AC $F$ and a null measurable target set $E$ for which $F^{-1}E$ is not Lebesgue measurable.
