Chapter 12 arranges interval variation and Stieltjes measure constructions before the AC fundamental theorem and general BV differentiation theorem; those results may use independently established direct RN and measure differentiation, without circular use of the AC fundamental theorem.

For a scalar function F:[a,b]→𝕂 with a<b, define Var_[a,b] F as the supremum over all finite partitions a=x₀<⋯<x_k=b of ∑_{j=1}^k |F(x_j)−F(x_{j−1})|. Set Var_[a,a] F=0 and V_F(x)=Var_[a,x] F. F is of bounded variation (BV) iff its variation is finite. For every a≤c≤b, Var_[a,b] F=Var_[a,c] F+Var_[c,b] F, including infinite variation and degenerate subintervals.

A real F on a compact interval [a,b] is BV iff it is the difference of two bounded nondecreasing real functions. For BV F explicitly F(x)=F(a)+P(x)−N(x), with P(x)=(V_F(x)+F(x)−F(a))/2 and N(x)=(V_F(x)−F(x)+F(a))/2. Both P and N are nonnegative, nondecreasing, bounded, and zero at a.

Scalar BV functions on [a,b] have finite left and right limits at every interior point and the corresponding one-sided endpoint limits. Their discontinuity set is at most countable. Globally BV scalar functions on ℝ have finite limits at both infinities, and replacing F(x) by the right limit F(x+) changes at most countably many values.

Define NBV(ℝ,𝕂) to be the globally BV scalar functions that are right-continuous and tend to zero at −∞. There is a bijection between NBV(ℝ,𝕂) and finite scalar Borel measures ν on ℝ, characterized by F(x)=ν((−∞,x]) and ν((a,b])=F(b)−F(a). For every x, ν({x})=F(x)−F(x−), and the cumulative distribution of total variation is |ν|((−∞,x])=V_F(x)=Var_(-∞,x] F. The generator is the normalized pointwise right-continuous representative, not an arbitrary a.e. representative.

For finite a<b and a scalar F:[a,b]→𝕂, absolute continuity (AC) means: for every ε>0 there is δ>0 such that every finite family of open subintervals (a_j,b_j)⊂[a,b] with pairwise disjoint interiors satisfies ∑_j(b_j−a_j)<δ ⇒ ∑_j|F(b_j)−F(a_j)|<ε. Shared endpoints are permitted. On ℝ, AC denotes this same uniform condition for all finite families of bounded intervals, not merely local AC.

On compact intervals, scalar AC functions are uniformly continuous and BV, and their variation functions V_F are AC. Finite scalar linear combinations and products of AC functions are AC. Every Lipschitz function is AC. The converse fails: x↦√x on [0,1] is AC and is not Lipschitz.

For f∈L¹([a,b],𝕂) and c∈𝕂, define F(x)=c+∫_a^x f. Then F is absolutely continuous, F′=f almost everywhere, and Var_[a,b] F=∫_a^b|f|. Every value F(x) is independent of the measurable representative chosen for the a.e. class f.

For F∈NBV(ℝ,𝕂), F is uniformly absolutely continuous on ℝ iff its finite scalar Stieltjes measure ν_F is absolutely continuous relative to Lebesgue measure m. In this case F′ exists a.e., belongs to L¹(ℝ), and F(x)=∫_(-∞)^x F′(t)dt for every x. The corresponding compact-interval statement uses the normalized constant extension of F−F(a).

For a scalar F on a finite interval [a,b], a<b, these are equivalent: (i) F is AC; (ii) there is f∈L¹([a,b]) with F(x)=F(a)+∫_a^x f for every x∈[a,b]; (iii) F is differentiable a.e., its a.e. derivative belongs to L¹([a,b]), and F(x)=F(a)+∫_a^x F′ for every x∈[a,b]. Any representing density in (ii) equals F′ almost everywhere.

For every nondecreasing real F:[a,b]→ℝ, the finite derivative exists almost everywhere in (a,b). Extending its derivative by zero on the exceptional set yields a measurable nonnegative integrable function with ∫_a^b F′≤F(b)−F(a).

For scalar BV F on [a,b], the finite derivative F′ exists almost everywhere, its derivative representative is integrable, and ∫_a^b|F′|≤Var_[a,b] F. This is the sharp scalar bound, including complex functions.

For scalar AC F,G on [a,b], both F′G and FG′ are integrable and ∫_a^b F′G+∫_a^b FG′=F(b)G(b)−F(a)G(a). These products are bilinear. Replacing G by its complex conjugate gives the sesquilinear integration-by-parts identity.

For scalar F,G∈NBV(ℝ,𝕂), if at least one is continuous, then for every finite a<b the Stieltjes integrals exist and ∫_(a,b] F dG+∫_(a,b] G dF=F(b)G(b)−F(a)G(a). The half-open endpoint convention is part of the formula.

Every finite scalar Borel measure ν on ℝ has a unique pairwise mutually singular decomposition ν=ν_d+ν_ac+ν_sc. If D is its set of nonzero atoms, then D is at most countable, ν_d=∑_{x∈D}ν({x})δ_x with ∑_{x∈D}|ν({x})|<∞, ν_ac≪m, and ν_sc is atomless and singular to m. The associated normalized BV functions decompose in the same way: the discrete part is a convergent pure-jump function, the AC part is AC, and the singular continuous part is continuous and has derivative zero a.e. The pure-jump part likewise has derivative zero a.e.

There exists a continuous nondecreasing C:[0,1]→[0,1] with C(0)=0, C(1)=1, variation one and C′=0 a.e. It is not AC. Its normalized extension has a nonzero atomless singular continuous probability Stieltjes measure. The middle-thirds Cantor function supplies the example: it is locally constant on the complement of the null Cantor set and its Stieltjes measure is supported on that set. In particular the monotone derivative integral inequality can be strict.
The function on [0,1] defined by F(0)=0 and F(x)=x cos(π/(2x)) for 0<x≤1 is continuous and has infinite variation. Consequently it is not AC; continuity implies neither BV nor AC.

On [−1,1], let F(t)=∛t and G(0)=0, G(x)=x² cos(π/(2x)) for x≠0. Both F and G are AC, but F∘G is not BV. For the positive composition statement, whenever the outer function is Lipschitz and the inner function is AC with image in its domain, their composition is AC.

For every continuous nondecreasing F:[a,b]→ℝ with finite a<b, the following are equivalent: F is AC; F sends every Lebesgue-null subset of [a,b] to a Lebesgue-null subset of ℝ; F sends every Lebesgue measurable subset of [a,b] to a Lebesgue measurable subset of ℝ. Measurability is completed Lebesgue measurability, and constant functions are included.

For continuous γ:[a,b]→ℝ^d, define its length as the supremum of polygonal sums ∑_j|γ(t_j)−γ(t_{j−1})| over finite partitions. The length is finite iff every coordinate is BV. If every coordinate is AC, then length(γ)=∫_a^b|γ′(t)|dt. In that AC case, for continuous scalar h on γ([a,b]), the arc-length integral along this parametrized curve exists and equals ∫_a^b h(γ(t))|γ′(t)|dt. Arc-length integration uses the Stieltjes length function and counts traversal multiplicity.
Function differentiation is proved from finite covering without RN; measure differentiation may use the independently proved direct RN construction, whose proof does not use differentiation.

For locally integrable scalar f on Euclidean ℝ^n, define A_r f(x)=m(B(x,r))⁻¹∫_{B(x,r)}f(y)dy for r>0, and Mf(x)=sup_{r>0} A_r|f|(x). Local integrability means absolute integrability on every compact set. For a fixed finite-valued representative f, x is a Lebesgue point iff A_r(|f−f(x)|)(x)→0 as r↓0.

From every finite family of open Euclidean balls in ℝ^n one can select pairwise disjoint balls B_{j₁},…,B_{j_k} such that the union of the original family is contained in ⋃_{ℓ=1}^k 3B_{j_ℓ}. Consequently the Lebesgue measure of the original union is at most 3^n∑_{ℓ=1}^k m(B_{j_ℓ}); 3B denotes the concentric ball of triple radius.
For every f∈L¹(ℝ^n), the centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal function Mf is measurable and m({x:Mf(x)>α})≤3^n α⁻¹‖f‖₁ for every α>0. In particular Mf is finite almost everywhere.

For every f∈L¹_loc(ℝ^n), almost every point is a Lebesgue point of its fixed measurable representative. Hence A_r f(x)→f(x) a.e. as r↓0. On one common conull set the same absolute-average conclusion, and thus scalar-average convergence, holds for all balls containing x whose diameters tend to zero.

For every Lebesgue measurable E⊂ℝ^n, almost every x∈E has density one and almost every x∉E has density zero with respect to centered balls: m(E∩B(x,r))/m(B(x,r)) tends to 1 or 0, respectively, as r↓0. No finiteness assumption on m(E) is made.

At a Lebesgue point x of f, let measurable E_i⊂B_i, where the balls B_i contain x and their radii tend to zero. If some fixed c>0 satisfies m(E_i)≥c m(B_i)>0 for all i, then m(E_i)⁻¹∫_{E_i}|f−f(x)|→0 and consequently m(E_i)⁻¹∫_{E_i}f→f(x). Cubes containing x with side lengths tending to zero satisfy these regular-shrinking hypotheses.
For a finite positive Borel measure λ on ℝ^n, define Mλ(x)=sup_{r>0} λ(B(x,r))/m(B(x,r)). For every α>0 the level set is measurable and m({Mλ>α})≤3^n λ(ℝ^n)/α.

Let ν be a finite positive Borel measure on ℝ^n with Borel Lebesgue decomposition ν=g(m_n restricted to Borel sets)+ν_s. For Lebesgue almost every x, the ratios ν(Q)/m(Q), taken over all nondegenerate closed axis-parallel cubes Q containing x with diameters tending to zero, converge to g(x). On the same conull set the singular ratios ν_s(Q)/m(Q) converge to zero.

Let ν on Borel ℝ^n be a positive measure, an extended signed measure omitting one infinity, or a finite complex measure. Assume |ν| is finite on compact sets and outer regular. Write its Lebesgue decomposition ν=ν_s+f(m_n restricted to Borel sets), with f∈L¹_loc. There is one Lebesgue-null set N such that for every x∉N and every Borel family E_r⊂B(x,r) with m(E_r)≥c m(B(x,r))>0 for some fixed c>0, ν(E_r)/m(E_r)→f(x) and ν_s(E_r)/m(E_r)→0 as r↓0. The exceptional set is independent of the family; all small-set numerators are finite, so no undefined extended signed subtraction is used.

At a Lebesgue point x of f, for every ε>0, m({y∈B(x,r):|f(y)−f(x)|>ε})/m(B(x,r))→0 as r↓0. Hence every locally integrable measurable scalar function is approximately continuous in this density sense almost everywhere.
For f=1_[0,1] on ℝ and x≥2, Mf(x)≥1/(2x). Thus f∈L¹(ℝ), but its maximal function Mf is not integrable, because its lower logarithmic tail diverges.
Signed and complex measure variation is constructed by measurable partitions before Radon–Nikodym. Every scalar integral used in Chapter 14 is an absolutely integrable integral.

On a measurable space (X,Σ), a finite signed measure is a countably additive map ν:Σ→ℝ with ν(∅)=0, and a complex measure is such a map into ℂ. Countable additivity includes convergence of the scalar series for every disjoint measurable sequence. An extended signed measure takes values in [−∞,∞], omits at least one infinity, and satisfies countable additivity with defined extended sums.
For every finite signed measure ν and measurable E∈Σ, there is a measurable negative set N⊂E with ν(N)≤ν(E). A negative set means that every measurable subset A⊂N has ν(A)≤0.

Every finite signed measure ν has a measurable partition X=P⊔N into a positive set P and negative set N, meaning all measurable subsets of P have nonnegative ν-value and all measurable subsets of N have nonpositive ν-value. Any two such positive sets differ by a set on every measurable subset of which ν vanishes, equivalently a |ν|-null set.

For every finite signed measure ν, there exist unique mutually singular finite positive measures ν⁺ and ν⁻ such that ν=ν⁺−ν⁻. For a Hahn partition X=P⊔N, ν⁺(E)=ν(E∩P) and ν⁻(E)=−ν(E∩N). For every representation ν=α−β by finite positive measures, ν⁺≤α and ν⁻≤β. The partition total variation is |ν|=ν⁺+ν⁻.

For a finite signed or complex measure ν, define |ν|(E)=sup{∑_{j=1}^k|ν(E_j)|: E=⊔_{j=1}^k E_j, a finite measurable partition}. This partition variation is a finite positive measure. It dominates |ν(E)| and satisfies |ν|(E)=0 iff ν(A)=0 for every measurable A⊂E.

Every countably additive real-valued or complex-valued measure on a sigma-algebra has finite total variation. Every such complex measure can be written α₁−α₂+i(α₃−α₄), where each α_j is a finite positive measure.

For finite scalar measures ν,η, scalar c, and measurable A,E, |cν|=|c||ν|, |ν+η|(E)≤|ν|(E)+|η|(E), and |(ν restricted to A)|(E)=|ν|(E∩A), where (ν restricted to A)(E)=ν(E∩A). Consequently ‖ν‖_var=|ν|(X) defines a norm on finite scalar measures.

Define ν⊥η if there exists measurable A with |ν|(X∖A)=0 and |η|(A)=0, taking the variation of a positive measure to mean itself. This is equivalent to concentration of ν and η on disjoint measurable parts and is symmetric.

A measurable scalar f is ν-integrable iff ∫|f|d|ν|<∞. Define ∫f dν by Jordan differences, and for complex ν by real and imaginary differences. This scalar integral is linear, independent of the chosen positive decomposition, and satisfies ∫1_E dν=ν(E) for every measurable E.
If f is ν-integrable, then for every measurable E, |∫_E f dν|≤∫_E|f|d|ν|. If measurable f_k,f satisfy f_k→f |ν|-a.e. and |f_k|≤g for an integrable g∈L¹(|ν|), then f is ν-integrable and ∫f_k dν→∫f dν.

For every positive measure μ and h∈L¹(μ,𝕂), ν(E)=∫_E h dμ defines a finite scalar measure and its total variation is |ν|(E)=∫_E|h|dμ for every measurable E. For real h, ν⁺ and ν⁻ have densities h⁺ and h⁻, respectively.

For two distinct points a,b and ν=δ_a−δ_b on X={a,b}, ν(X)=0 but |ν|(X)=2 and ν({a})=1. Thus a set having scalar measure value zero need not be null for total variation and cannot by itself justify scalar-integral a.e. changes.

For every finite scalar Borel measure ν on ℝ, its cumulative function F_ν(x)=ν((−∞,x]) is right-continuous, globally BV, and tends to zero at −∞. Its differences recover ν((a,b]) and its variation function recovers |ν|((−∞,x]). Conversely every normalized right-continuous globally BV scalar function gives exactly one finite scalar Borel measure with these identities.

An extended signed measure ν omitting one infinity has a Hahn partition and unique Jordan positive measures ν⁺,ν⁻, with at least one total mass finite. Its partition variation is ν⁺+ν⁻ and may be infinite. Scalar integration is adopted on L¹(|ν|), where all Jordan-component integrals are finite. Sigma-finiteness of ν means sigma-finiteness of |ν|.
The direct RN proof uses Hahn decomposition and maximal integrals, independently of Hilbert representation and Lp duality, so later duality may depend on this chapter without a cycle.

For positive measures μ,ν on the same sigma-algebra, ν≪μ means μ(E)=0 ⇒ ν(E)=0 for all measurable E. For finite scalar ν, ν≪μ means |ν|≪μ. Equivalently, μ(E)=0 ⇒ ν(E)=0 for all measurable E; the equivalence uses the vanishing of ν on every measurable subset of a μ-null set.

For arbitrary positive μ and finite scalar ν on the same sigma-algebra, ν≪μ iff for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that μ(E)<δ ⇒ |ν|(E)<ε for every measurable E. The equivalent criterion obtained by replacing |ν|(E) with |ν(E)| holds with the same ε–δ quantifier structure.

For finite positive measures μ,ν with ν≪μ, there is a nonnegative measurable h∈L¹(μ) satisfying ν(E)=∫_E h dμ for every measurable E. Such a density is unique μ-a.e. and may be chosen finite everywhere, including the zero-reference/zero-target case.
For sigma-finite positive μ,ν with ν≪μ, there exists a nonnegative measurable h, finite μ-a.e., with ν(E)=∫_E h dμ for every measurable E. It is unique μ-a.e.; its total integral need not be finite.

If μ is a sigma-finite positive measure and finite signed or complex ν satisfies ν≪μ, there is a unique a.e. class h∈L¹(μ,𝕂) such that ν(E)=∫_E h dμ for every measurable E. Moreover |ν|(E)=∫_E|h|dμ for all measurable E.

A finite scalar measure that is both absolutely continuous and singular relative to a positive measure μ is zero. Consequently finite decompositions of a scalar measure into an absolutely continuous part and a singular part, whenever they exist, are unique.

For every arbitrary positive reference measure μ and finite scalar target measure ν, there exist unique finite scalar measures ν_a,ν_s with ν=ν_a+ν_s, ν_a≪μ, and ν_s⊥μ. If ν is positive, both parts are positive. No sigma-finiteness of μ and no representation of ν_a by an RN density are asserted.

For sigma-finite positive μ,ν, there exist unique positive sigma-finite ν_a,ν_s with ν=ν_a+ν_s, ν_a≪μ, and ν_s⊥μ. The absolutely continuous part satisfies ν_a=hμ for a nonnegative measurable density h unique μ-a.e. If instead ν is finite scalar and μ sigma-finite positive, the analogous scalar decomposition exists uniquely and its density belongs to L¹(μ).

For positive μ and nonnegative measurable h, define ν=hμ by ν(E)=∫_E h dμ. For every nonnegative measurable g, ∫g dν=∫gh dμ with 0·∞=0. If h is finite a.e., a scalar measurable g is ν-integrable iff ∫|g|h dμ<∞, and then ∫g dν=∫gh dμ. If ν=kμ is finite scalar, the same scalar identity holds whenever ∫|g||k|dμ<∞.

For sigma-finite positive measures ν≪μ≪λ, their nonnegative RN densities satisfy dν/dλ=(dν/dμ)(dμ/dλ) λ-a.e., with measurable zero conventions for the product. If also λ≪μ, the reciprocal densities dλ/dμ and dμ/dλ have product one both λ-a.e. and μ-a.e.

Every finite complex measure ν has a measurable density u relative to |ν| such that ν=u|ν| and |u|=1 |ν|-a.e. The density is unique |ν|-a.e. and can be chosen with |u|=1 everywhere. For real ν one may choose u(x)∈{−1,1} everywhere.

On Borel [0,1], counting measure μ and Lebesgue measure ν satisfy ν≪μ because only the empty set is μ-null, but no nonnegative measurable RN density h can represent ν relative to μ: singleton values would force h(x)=0 for every x although ν([0,1])=1. Likewise on a one-point space with μ({a})=∞ and ν({a})=1, ν≪μ but no nonnegative density exists, since its integral is either zero or infinity. No reference-sigma-finite set carries the target mass in these examples; arbitrary-reference finite-target Lebesgue decomposition still applies without asserting densities.

On a probability space (Ω,Σ,P), for every sub-sigma-algebra 𝒯⊂Σ and integrable real random variable X, there exists a 𝒯-measurable Y∈L¹(P) with ∫_B Y dP=∫_B X dP for every B∈𝒯. Such Y is unique P-a.e. This is the conditional expectation interface only; no kernel, disintegration or martingale result is asserted.

Let μ be positive sigma-finite, and let the extended signed measure ν omit one infinity and have sigma-finite |ν|. There exist unique extended signed parts ν_a,ν_s with sigma-finite variations, ν=ν_a+ν_s, ν_a≪μ, and ν_s⊥μ. There is a real measurable density f, finite μ-a.e. and unique μ-a.e., with ν_a(E)=∫_E f⁺dμ−∫_E f⁻dμ for every measurable E, where at least one of the two total integrals is finite. For every measurable E with |ν_a|(E)<∞, f1_E∈L¹(μ). If ν≪μ then ν_s=0.
Riemann integrability is a property of a particular bounded function at every point; Lebesgue integrals depend only on a.e. classes. The chapter compares these notions through oscillation.

For every bounded real f on a finite interval [a,b] with a<b, f is Riemann integrable iff its discontinuity set is Lebesgue-null. Every such Riemann-integrable function is Lebesgue measurable. Continuity and discontinuity at the endpoints are computed in the relative topology of [a,b].

Every bounded real Riemann-integrable function on finite [a,b] belongs to L¹ and has equal Riemann and Lebesgue integrals. The same conclusion holds for complex functions with Riemann-integrable real and imaginary parts, and for bounded Riemann-integrable scalar functions on a compact Euclidean rectangle using ordinary rectangular Riemann partitions.

Let f:[a,∞)→𝕂 be Riemann integrable on every compact interval [a,R]. Then ∫_[a,∞)|f|dm=lim_{R→∞}∫_a^R|f| as an extended nonnegative value. Absolute improper convergence is equivalent to f∈L¹([a,∞)), and in that case the improper scalar integral equals the Lebesgue integral. For finite singular endpoints and for two-sided intervals the corresponding separate one-sided absolute limits are required, and the same equivalence and integral equality hold.

On [0,∞), define f(x)=0 for x<1 and f(x)=(−1)^n/n for x∈[n,n+1), n≥1. Every compact restriction is Riemann integrable and its improper Riemann integral exists. However ∫|f|=∞ and both ∫f⁺ and ∫f⁻ are infinite, so it has no ordinary signed Lebesgue integral over the half-line.

On [0,1], f=1_ℚ is Borel and zero almost everywhere, so it is Lebesgue integrable with integral zero. It is discontinuous everywhere in the relative topology and is not Riemann integrable. Thus a.e. equality preserves the Lebesgue integral but does not preserve Riemann integrability of particular representatives.

Henstock–Kurzweil and McShane gauge integrals are mentioned only as scope boundaries. No general gauge-integral equivalence or existence theorem is adopted; any future assertion would need fixed interval, scalar field, gauge and tag conventions.

Throughout Chapter 17, (X,Σ,μ) is an arbitrary positive measure space and functions are measurable scalar representatives; the integral conditions descend to a.e. classes. Supremum over an empty family of nonnegative quantities is zero. Neither atomlessness nor finiteness of μ(X) is implicit.

For a family ℱ⊂L¹(μ), small-set uniform integrability UI_small means: for every ε>0 there is δ>0 such that every measurable A with μ(A)<δ satisfies sup_{f∈ℱ}∫_A|f|dμ<ε. Each f is individually integrable, but uniform boundedness of their L¹ norms is a separate property.

A family ℱ⊂L¹(μ) has finite-measure spatial tails iff for every ε>0 there exists measurable E with μ(E)<∞ such that sup_{f∈ℱ}∫_{X∖E}|f|dμ<ε. For an Lp family apply this property to {|f|^p}. The capturing set need not be compact.

For an integrable scalar family ℱ, UI_tail means lim_{R→∞}sup_{f∈ℱ}∫_{|f|>R}|f|dμ=0. Uniform L¹ boundedness means sup_{f∈ℱ}‖f‖₁<∞. Neither amplitude-tail control nor uniform norm boundedness is included in the definition of UI_small.

On any positive measure space, UI_tail implies UI_small. UI_small together with a uniform L¹ norm bound implies UI_tail. If μ(X)<∞, UI_tail also implies a uniform L¹ norm bound. These statements include the zero measure and empty family.

For a family of real or complex L¹ functions on any positive measure space, the condition that for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that μ(A)<δ implies sup_{f∈ℱ}|∫_A f dμ|<ε is equivalent to UI_small, which uses sup_{f∈ℱ}∫_A|f|dμ.

On the one-point probability space, the sequence f_n=n has UI_small, since every measurable set of measure less than one is empty. Its L¹ norms are n, hence unbounded, and it has no UI_tail: for every fixed R the supremum of amplitude-tail integrals is infinite.

Every finite subset of L¹(μ) has both UI_small and finite-measure spatial tails. Every family satisfying |f|≤g μ-a.e. for one nonnegative g∈L¹(μ) likewise has both controls; the a.e. domination condition suffices at the representative level.

If f_n→f in L¹(μ), then {f_n} has UI_small, finite-measure spatial tails, and uniformly bounded L¹ norms. More generally, if f_n→f in Lp(μ), 1≤p<∞, then {|f_n|^p} has UI_small, finite-measure spatial tails, and uniformly bounded L¹ norms.

For every 1≤p<∞ and sequence f_n∈Lp(μ), (f_n) is Cauchy in the Lp norm iff it is Cauchy globally in measure (for every ε>0, μ{|f_n−f_m|>ε}→0 as n,m→∞), {|f_n|^p} has UI_small, and this family has finite-measure spatial tails. No finiteness assumption on μ(X) is made.

For 1≤p<∞, measurable scalar f, and f_n∈Lp(μ), f_n converges to f in Lp iff f_n converges globally in measure to f and {|f_n|^p} has both UI_small and finite-measure spatial tails. In the reverse implication f is thereby in Lp. The spatial-tail condition is automatic if μ(X)<∞.

For a Lebesgue measurable E⊂ℝ of finite measure, every UI_small sequence of integrable scalar functions on E converging pointwise to a finite measurable f has f∈L¹(E) and ∫_E f_n→∫_E f. On arbitrary Lebesgue measurable E the same conclusion holds when finite-measure spatial tails are added. The corresponding general-positive-measure-space variant with UI_small, spatial tails and pointwise convergence retains the extra hypothesis f∈L¹; under those hypotheses the integrals converge.

On (0,1) with Lebesgue measure, f_n=n1_(0,1/n) is uniformly L¹ bounded (‖f_n‖₁=1), converges to zero almost everywhere and globally in measure, but does not have UI_small and does not converge to zero in L¹. Its full integral one is concentrated on supports of measures 1/n→0.

On ℝ, f_n=1_[n,n+1] has UI_small and tends pointwise to zero, but has neither uniform finite-measure spatial tails nor L¹ convergence nor global convergence in measure to zero. Each norm and each m{|f_n|>1/2} is one. It nevertheless converges locally in measure to zero.

All locally compact spaces in chapter 18 are Hausdorff. Compact means topologically compact; finite measure is distinct from compact support. Compact-neighborhood, shrinking and cutoff topology inputs come from the declared topology foundation; measure regularity is to be established.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Borel and Baire sigma-algebras on LCH spaces: For a topological space $X$, $\mathcal B(X)$ is the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets. On an LCH space put
\[\operatorname{Ba}(X)=\sigma\{f^{-1}(A):f\in C_c(X,\mathbb R),\ A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}.\]
Every continuous real function is Borel measurable, so this $C_c$-generated Baire sigma-algebra is contained in $\mathcal B(X)$. Equality needs an additional argument.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Outer, inner, compact-finite and local-finite predicates: A positive Borel measure is \emph{outer regular on $E$} if
$\mu(E)=\inf_{U\supset E,\ U\text{ open}}\mu(U)$, and \emph{compact-inner regular on $E$} if
$\mu(E)=\sup_{K\subset E,\ K\text{ compact}}\mu(K)$.
It is compact-finite if every compact set has finite measure, and locally finite if every point has an open neighborhood of finite measure. The collection of sets on which a regularity assertion holds is part of the assertion.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Fix Radon predicates and translate source terminology: A positive Radon measure on an LCH space X is a positive Borel measure which is compact-finite, outer regular on all Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on all open sets. Full regularity additionally means compact-inner regularity on every Borel set.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Local finiteness and compact finiteness on LCH spaces: For a positive Borel measure on an LCH space, compact finiteness and local finiteness are equivalent.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Selected compact-support cutoff interface: If $K\subset U\subset X$, $K$ is compact and $U$ open in an LCH space, there is $\phi\in C_c(X,\mathbb R)$ with $0\le\phi\le1$, $\phi=1$ on $K$, and $\supp\phi\subset U$.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Baire equals Borel under second countability: In a second-countable LCH space every compact set is a $G_\delta$, and $\operatorname{Ba}(X)=\mathcal B(X)$.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Radon measures are inner regular on sigma-finite Borel sets: If $\mu$ is Radon and a Borel $E$ is a countable union of finite-measure Borel sets, then $\mu(E)=\sup_{K\subset E,\ K\text{ compact}}\mu(K)$.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Sigma-finite and sigma-compact regularity specializations: A sigma-finite Radon measure is compact-inner and outer regular on every Borel set. A Radon measure on a sigma-compact LCH space is sigma-finite and has the same conclusion.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Compact-finite Borel measures on second-countable LCH spaces: Suppose every open set of LCH $X$ is sigma-compact. Every compact-finite positive Borel measure on $X$ is Radon and is compact-inner and outer regular on all Borel sets. In the second-countable case it is sigma-finite.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Metric Borel regularity with finite balls: Let $X$ be metric and let every finite-radius ball have finite Borel measure. For Borel $E$ and $\varepsilon>0$, there are open $U\supset E$ and closed $F\subset E$ with $\mu(U\setminus E)<\varepsilon$ and $\mu(E\setminus F)<\varepsilon$. The closed $F$ need not be compact.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Ulam regularity and tightness of finite Polish-space measures: For every ε>0, the following compact and open approximations exist. A finite Borel measure on a separable complete metric space is compactly tight. Moreover every Borel $E$ has compact $K\subset E$ and open $U\supset E$ with $\mu(E\setminus K)<\varepsilon$ and $\mu(U\setminus E)<\varepsilon$.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Finite Radon measures are compact tight: If $\mu$ is a finite Radon measure on LCH $X$, every $\varepsilon>0$ admits compact $K$ with $\mu(X\setminus K)<\varepsilon$. For a family $\mathcal P$ of finite measures, \emph{uniform compact tightness} requires one such $K$ for all its members. The family assertion is a definition, not a consequence of individual tightness: the probabilities δ_n on ℝ are individually Radon and compactly tight, but no compact K satisfies δ_n(ℝ∖K)<1 for all n.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Support from null open sets: Let $N$ be the union of all open $\mu$-null sets for Radon $\mu$. Then $N$ is open and null, and $\supp\mu=X\setminus N$ is closed. A point $x$ belongs to the support exactly when every $f\in C_c(X,[0,1])$ with $f(x)>0$ has positive integral.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Borel product versus product Borel sigma-algebras: For LCH $X,Y$, $\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y)\subset\mathcal B(X\times Y)$. If both spaces are second countable, equality holds. In that case the ordinary product of compact-finite Borel measures is Radon.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Finite separate-variable approximation of a compact-support product function: For $f\in C_c(X\times Y,\mathbb K)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, a finite sum $\sum_jg_j(x)h_j(y)$ with $g_j\in C_c(X,\mathbb K)$ and $h_j\in C_c(Y,\mathbb K)$ approximates $f$ uniformly within $\varepsilon$. All approximants can have support in one fixed precompact product neighborhood. In particular $f$ is product-Borel measurable.

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Radon product from compact-support iterated integrals: For arbitrary positive Radon $\mu,
u$ on LCH $X,Y$, every $f\in C_c(X	imes Y)$ is product measurable and supported in a finite-measure rectangle. Its iterated integrals agree. There is a unique Radon measure $\mu\otimes_R

\[\int f\,d(\mu\otimes_R
u)=\int_X\int_Y f(x,y)\,d
u(y)\,d\mu(x).\]

Locally compact spaces in this chapter are Hausdorff. Agreement of sigma-finite Radon and ordinary products: If the two Radon factors are sigma-finite, then for every $E\in\mathcal B(X	imes Y)$ the section masses are Borel measurable and
\[(\mu\otimes_R

All spaces in chapter 19 are LCH and scalar functionals are scalar-linear; complex integral pairings have no implicit conjugation. Measure representation is constructed and is not an assumed foundation.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Compact support and vanishing at infinity: The space $C_c(X,\mathbb K)$ consists of continuous functions whose support $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}$ is compact. The space $C_0(X,\mathbb K)$ consists of continuous functions for which $\{|f|\ge\varepsilon\}$ is compact for every $\varepsilon>0$. Such functions are bounded; the uniform norm makes $C_0$ a normed space. Moreover $C_c\subset C_0$ is uniformly dense.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Finite compact-support decomposition subordinate to an open cover: If compact $K$ is covered by finitely many opens $U_1,\ldots,U_m$, there are $\phi_i\in C_c(X,[0,1])$, supported in $U_i$, whose sum is one on $K$ and at most one everywhere. Consequently any $f\in C_c$ supported in their union splits as $f=\sum_i f_i$ with $\supp f_i\subset U_i$; if $f\ge0$ the pieces can be nonnegative.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Positivity gives compact-support norm bounds: If $I:C_c(X,\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R$ is positive linear, then for every compact $K$ there is finite $C_K$ with $|I(f)|\le C_K\|f\|_\infty$ whenever $\supp f\subset K$. A complex-linear functional taking nonnegative real functions to nonnegative real values has the analogous bound.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Open content of a positive Cc functional defines a Radon measure: For positive real $I$ put
\[c(U)=\sup\{I(f):f\in C_c,\ 0\le f\le1,\ \supp f\subset U\},\qquad
\mu^*(A)=\inf_{U\supset A,\ U\text{ open}}c(U).
\]
Then $\mu^*$ is an outer measure, all Borel sets are Caratheodory measurable, and its Borel restriction is Radon.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Identify the constructed measure integral with the functional: For the preceding constructed measure, $I(f)=\int f\,d\mu$ for all real $f\in C_c$. If $f\ge0$, $K=\supp f$, and $\eta>0$, the two quantities lie between the same level sums with difference at most $\eta\mu(K)$. Explicitly, for nonnegative f, η>0 and an integer N with Nη≥‖f‖∞, set K_0=supp(f) and K_j={f≥jη} for 1≤j≤N. Both I(f) and ∫f dμ lie between η∑_{j=1}^N μ(K_j) and η∑_{j=1}^N μ(K_{j−1}); the gap between these sums is at most η μ(K_0).

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Riesz-Markov representation for positive Cc functionals: Every positive linear $I:C_c(X,\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R$ has a unique positive Radon representing measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal B(X)$ with $I(f)=\int f\,d\mu$. Every positive Radon measure induces such a functional. The complex-linear positive version has the same positive measure.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Recover open and compact masses from a positive functional: For this representation,
\[\mu(U)=\sup_{0\le f\le1,\ \supp f\subset U}I(f),\qquad
\mu(K)=\inf_{g\in C_c,\ g\ge0,\ g|_K\ge1}I(g).
\]
The first formula is for open $U$, the second for compact $K$.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Finite mass characterizes bounded C0 extension: For the positive integration functional of a positive Radon measure μ: The positive integration functional on $C_c$ extends boundedly and positively to $C_0$ exactly when $\mu(X)<\infty$. The extension is unique, is ordinary integration on $C_0$, and has norm $\mu(X)$.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Positive decomposition of real C0 functionals: For a bounded real-linear $I:C_0(X,\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R$, define, for $f\ge0$,
\[I^+(f)=\sup_{0\le g\le f,\ g\in C_0}I(g).
\]
It extends to a bounded positive linear functional, and $I^-=I^+-I$ is bounded positive. Hence $I=I^+-I^-$.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Finite signed/complex Radon measures and variation: A finite signed Borel measure is signed Radon if its Jordan parts are positive Radon. A finite complex Borel measure is complex Radon if its real and imaginary parts are signed Radon. Equivalently its total variation is Radon. The norm is $\|\nu\|=|\nu|(X)$, zero only for the zero measure.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Continuous compact-support functions detect total variation: For finite signed or complex Radon $
u$ and $\varepsilon>0$, there is $f\in C_c(X,\mathbb K)$ with $\|f\|_\infty\le1$ and $|\int f\,d
u|\ge|
u|(X)-\varepsilon$.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Finite Radon measures represent the bounded dual of C0: The map $

u$, is a scalar-linear isometric bijection from finite signed Radon measures onto $C_0(X,\mathbb R)^*$, and from finite complex Radon measures onto $C_0(X,\mathbb C)^*$. Its norm is $|
u|(X)$.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Compact-space C(K) specialization: On compact Hausdorff $X$, $C_c=C_0=C(X)$. Positive real functionals have unique finite positive regular Borel measures; bounded scalar functionals have unique finite signed/complex Radon measures, with norm the variation mass.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Compact-interval positive-functional variant: For $a\le b$, a positive real-linear $I:C([a,b],\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R$ is integration against a unique finite positive Borel measure on $[a,b]$, and conversely. Its norm is $I(1)$; no extra sequential-continuity assumption is needed.

Let X be locally compact Hausdorff, and let the scalar field be \mathbb K=\mathbb R or \mathbb C unless the assertion specifies real scalars. Functionals are scalar-linear. Bounded-support C0 on arbitrary metrics is not the canonical C0 theorem: In the discrete metric $d(m,n)=1$ on $X=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, let $\mu\{n\}=2^{-n}$. All balls have finite measure and $X$ is itself a closed ball. The continuous function $f(n)=2^n$ is supported in that closed ball but has infinite integral. In fact μ is a finite Borel measure of total mass one, and ∫f dμ=∑_{n≥1}2^n2^(−n)=∞. Thus this general-metric continuous bounded-support class need not carry a finite-valued integration functional from every finite-on-balls Borel measure.

\[\|[g]\|_{\rm loc}=\inf\{C\ge0:\{|g|>C\}\text{ is locally null}\}.
\]

\]

No second countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness is assumed for locally compact groups. Existence and uniqueness, product measurability, and modular properties are mathematical targets, not background assumptions; references to compact-product/content and compact-rectangle kernel arguments describe one proof route.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Locally compact Hausdorff group and translations: A topological group has continuous multiplication and inversion. Here a locally compact group is Hausdorff and locally compact. Left and right translations $L_a(x)=ax$, $R_a(x)=xa$, and inversion are homeomorphisms, hence preserve Borel measurability and compactness.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Left and right Haar measures in a precise regularity class: A left Haar measure is a nonzero positive Radon Borel measure $\mu$ with $\mu(aE)=\mu(E)$ for every $a$ and Borel $E$. A right Haar measure satisfies $\mu(Ea)=\mu(E)$. The Radon predicates are exactly those of \cref{d11:18:radon-and-source-names}; invariant set functions without that regularity are not included.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Finite compact covering ratios with fixed normalization: Choose compact $K_0$ with nonempty interior. Let $N(K:U)$ be the least number of left translates of an identity neighborhood $U$ covering compact $K$, and set $h_U(K)=N(K:U)/N(K_0:U)$. Then $h_U(K_0)=1$, $0\le h_U(K)\le N(K:K_0)$, and $h_U$ is left invariant, monotone, and subadditive on unions. If $KU^{-1}\cap LU^{-1}=\varnothing$, then $h_U(K\cup L)=h_U(K)+h_U(L)$.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Obtain invariant additive compact content by a compact-product cluster point: There is a finite nonnegative function $h$ on compact subsets with $h(\varnothing)=0$, $h(K_0)=1$, left invariance, monotonicity, finite subadditivity, and additivity on disjoint compact sets.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Convert invariant compact content into a nonzero invariant Radon measure: Put $c(U)=\sup_{K\subset U,\ K\text{ compact}}h(K)$ and $\mu^*(A)=\inf_{U\supset A,\ U\text{ open}}c(U)$. Then $\mu^*$ is an outer measure, its Borel restriction is left invariant and Radon, and $\mu(K_0)\ge1$.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Existence of left Haar measure: Every LCH group has a left Haar measure, without any countability assumption.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Haar measure is positive on nonempty opens: A Haar measure assigns positive mass to every nonempty open set. Every nonzero nonnegative $f\in C_c(G)$ has positive integral, and the measure has full support.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Conversely this identity for all real $C_c$ tests, for every $a$, makes a nonzero Radon measure left Haar.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Uniqueness of Haar measure up to a positive scalar: Two left Haar measures $\mu,\nu$ have $\nu=c\mu$ on all Borel sets for a unique finite real $c>0$. The same holds for right Haar measures.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Inversion exchanges left and right Haar measures: For Radon $\mu$, $\check\mu(E)=\mu(E^{-1})$ is Radon and
$\int f\,d\check\mu=\int f(x^{-1})\,d\mu(x)$ for nonnegative Borel or integrable scalar $f$. Left Haar corresponds under inversion to right Haar.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Finite total Haar mass characterizes compact groups: A left Haar measure has finite total mass exactly when $G$ is compact. Thus a compact Hausdorff group has a unique left Haar probability measure.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Modular function with an explicit right-set convention: For left Haar $\mu$, define $\Delta(a)>0$ by $\mu(Ea)=\Delta(a)\mu(E)$ for every Borel $E$. This convention uses right translation of sets. The scalar exists, is finite and positive, and is independent of normalization of $\mu$.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Continuity and homomorphism property of the modular function: The map $\Delta:G\to(0,\infty)$ is a continuous homomorphism, $\Delta(e)=1$ and $\Delta(a^{-1})=\Delta(a)^{-1}$. Moreover
$\int f(xa^{-1})\,d\mu(x)=\Delta(a)\int f\,d\mu$
for nonnegative Borel or integrable scalar $f$.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Abelian and compact groups are unimodular: A group is unimodular when $\Delta\equiv1$, equivalently its left Haar measures are also right Haar. Abelian and compact Hausdorff groups are unimodular, and compact Haar probability is invariant on both sides.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. The inversion measure has a modular density: With this modular convention,
\[\check\mu(E)=\int_E\Delta(x^{-1})\,d\mu(x)\quad(E\text{ Borel}).\]
Thus left and right Haar measures have the same Borel null sets.

Let G be a locally compact Hausdorff topological group, without second-countability, metrizability or sigma-compactness assumptions. Radon means a positive Borel measure, finite on compacts, outer regular on Borel sets, and compact-inner regular on open sets. Standard invariant measures and a nonunimodular example: Lebesgue measure on additive $\mathbb R^d$, counting measure on any discrete group, and arc-length measure on the circle are two-sided Haar. On the affine group $(a,b)(c,d)=(ac,b+ad)$, $a,c>0$, left and right Haar measures are $da\,db/a^2$ and $da\,db/a$, respectively, and $\Delta(a,b)=1/a$.

Hausdorff covers use arbitrary subsets and coefficient-one diameter powers. Statements are about outer measures until measurability is established. Exact zero-dimensional and Cantor masses use this normalization, and Euclidean volume constants must use the Euclidean metric.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Diameter-cover content at scale delta: For metric $X$, $s\ge0$, $\delta>0$, and $E\subset X$, define
\[H^s_\delta(E)=\inf\left\{\sum_j(\diam U_j)^s:E\subset\bigcup_jU_j,\quad \varnothing\ne U_j\subset X,\quad\diam U_j\le\delta\right\}.
\]
Covers are at most countable; the empty cover gives zero for $E=\varnothing$, and an empty admissible class has infimum infinity. When $s=0$ each nonempty covering set costs one, even a singleton. When $s>0$, a singleton costs zero.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Hausdorff outer measure as the small-scale limit: The contents increase as $\delta$ decreases. Their supremum $H^s(E)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(E)$ is an outer measure. If $\dist(A,B)>0$, then $H^s(A\cup B)=H^s(A)+H^s(B)$.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Metric outer measures make Borel sets measurable: Every outer measure $m^*$ on a metric space which is additive on positively separated sets makes all Borel sets Caratheodory measurable. In particular $H^s|_{\mathcal B(X)}$ is a measure and its full Caratheodory extension is complete.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Zero-dimensional Hausdorff measure counts points: With the stated convention, $H^0(E)$ is the number of points when $E$ is finite and is infinity when $E$ is infinite.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Isometry invariance and similarity scaling: An isometry preserves every $H^s$. A similarity with distance multiplier $r>0$ satisfies $H^s(f(E))=r^sH^s(E)$, including $s=0$. The assertions apply also to isometric/similarity embeddings into a larger ambient metric space, without surjectivity onto the target.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. The s=0 and zero-Lipschitz cases: If $f:E\to Y$ is $L$-Lipschitz with $L>0$, then $H^s(f(A))\le L^sH^s(A)$ for every $A\subset E$ and $s\ge0$. If $L=0$, all nonempty images are singletons: they have zero $H^s$ for $s>0$ and $H^0$ equal to one; the empty image has all masses zero.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Holder maps bound Hausdorff measures and dimension: If $0<\alpha\le1$, $C>0$, and $d(f(x),f(y))\le C d(x,y)^\alpha$ on $E$, then, for $s>0$,
\[H^{s/\alpha}(f(E))\le C^{s/\alpha}H^s(E),\qquad
\dim_H f(E)\le\dim_H E/\alpha.
\]

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Hausdorff measure has a critical exponent: If $H^s(E)<\infty$ and $t>s\ge0$, then $H^t(E)=0$. Equivalently $H^t(E)>0$ forces $H^s(E)=\infty$ for $s<t$.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Hausdorff dimension and endpoint conventions: For nonempty $E$, define $\dim_HE=\inf\{s\ge0:H^s(E)=0\}$ with infimum infinity for the empty set of exponents, and define $\dim_H\varnothing=0$. Above this critical value all masses vanish; below it they are infinite. At dimension zero there is no lower nonnegative exponent.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Countable stability of Hausdorff dimension: For a countable family, $\dim_H(\bigcup_nE_n)=\sup_n\dim_HE_n$, with the empty-family supremum zero. Dimension is monotone, and every countable set has dimension zero.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Euclidean n-dimensional measure agrees up to a positive constant: For each integer $n\ge1$ there is $c_n>0$ with $m_n(E)=c_nH^n(E)$ for Borel $E\subset\mathbb R^n$ in the Euclidean metric. Here $c_1=1$. For $n>1$ no explicit constant is asserted.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Ambient Euclidean dimension bounds: Every $E\subset\mathbb R^n$ has dimension at most $n$. Every nonempty open set has dimension $n$ and infinite $H^s$ for $0\le s<n$. A nondegenerate isometrically embedded $k$-cube has dimension $k$ and positive finite $H^k$. Also $H^s(\mathbb R^n)=0$ for $s>n$.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Lower-dimensional Hausdorff measures need not be sigma-finite: For $0\le s<n$, the Borel measure $H^s$ on $\mathbb R^n$ is not sigma-finite.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. The Cantor digit map is onto and has exact Holder constant one: Let $C$ be the middle-thirds Cantor set and $\alpha=\log2/\log3$. Every $x\in C$ has a unique digit sequence $x=\sum_{n\ge1}2a_n3^{-n}$, $a_n\in\{0,1\}$. The map $F(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n2^{-n}$ maps $C$ onto $[0,1]$ and satisfies $|F(y)-F(x)|\le|y-x|^\alpha$.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Elementary middle-thirds Cantor dimension: For the middle-thirds set, $0<H^\alpha(C)\le1$, $\dim_HC=\alpha$, and $m_1(C)=0$.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Exact critical mass of the middle-thirds Cantor set: In this coefficient-one diameter normalization, $H^\alpha(C)=1$.

Hausdorff outer measure uses the coefficient-one diameter-power normalization on the stated metric spaces; a nonempty diameter-zero set costs one at exponent zero, and costs zero at positive exponent. Covering sets may be arbitrary subsets. Large-scale content is not Hausdorff measure: The unrestricted one-dimensional diameter content of $[0,1]^2$ is at most $\sqrt2$, whereas its $H^1$ mass is infinity.

The Daniell–Stone lattice contains finite real-valued functions on an arbitrary set X, including X empty. The selected construction may use already established one-dimensional measure theory. Uniqueness is on the sigma-ring generated by positive levels; adjoining a unit is an additional hypothesis.

X may be an arbitrary set, including the empty set; all lattice functions are finite real-valued. Real vector lattices and Stone's condition: A real vector lattice $V\subset\mathbb R^X$ is a vector subspace closed under pointwise minimum and maximum. It contains $f^+,f^-$ and $|f|$ for $f\in V$. Stone's condition is $f\wedge1\in V$ for every $f\in V$; this does not require $1\in V$.

X may be an arbitrary set, including the empty set; all lattice functions are finite real-valued. Let V be a real vector lattice on X. Positive order-continuous elementary integral: An elementary integral is a real-linear $L:V\to\mathbb R$ which is positive on nonnegative functions and satisfies $L(f_n)\to0$ whenever $f_n\in V$ decreases pointwise to zero at every point. No norm or a.e. qualification occurs before the measure is built.

X may be an arbitrary set, including the empty set; all lattice functions are finite real-valued. Let V be a real vector lattice and L:V→ℝ an elementary integral (positive linear and continuous from above at zero). Monotone and series properties inside the elementary lattice: For nonnegative $f,f_n\in V$: if $f_n\uparrow f$, then $L(f_n)\uparrow L(f)$; if $f=\sum_nf_n$, then $L(f)=\sum_nL(f_n)$; and if $f\le\sum_nf_n$, then $L(f)\le\sum_nL(f_n)$.

X may be an arbitrary set, including the empty set; all lattice functions are finite real-valued. Let V be a real vector lattice on X. Generated sigma-ring and generated measurable space: Let $\mathcal F=\{\{f>b\}:f\in V,\ b>0\}$, let $\mathcal R_V$ be the sigma-ring it generates, and let $\mathcal A_V=\sigma(\mathcal F)$. A sigma-ring contains the empty set and is closed under differences and countable unions; it need not contain $X$. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal A_V$ is the smallest making every member of $V$ measurable.

For an arbitrary set X, including X empty, Extend a sigma-ring measure to its generated sigma-algebra: For any sigma-ring $\mathcal R$ on $X$, $\sigma(\mathcal R)=\mathcal R\cup\{X\setminus A:A\in\mathcal R\}$. If $\mu_0$ is a measure on $\mathcal R$, one extension to this sigma-algebra is
\[\mu(A)=\begin{cases}\mu_0(A),&A\in\mathcal R,\\ \infty,&A\notin\mathcal R.\end{cases}\]
This is not a uniqueness statement outside $\mathcal R$.

X may be an arbitrary set, including the empty set; all lattice functions are finite real-valued. Let V be a real vector lattice and L:V→ℝ an elementary integral. Elementary integral induces content on under-graph intervals: For $f,g\in V$ let $[f,g)=\{(x,t):f(x)\le t<g(x)\}$. These sets form a semiring $\mathcal I$. For $f\le g$ define $J([f,g))=L(g-f)$. This is well defined and nonnegative; it is countably additive for disjoint unions which remain in $\mathcal I$, and satisfies $J(I)\le\sum_nJ(I_n)$ whenever $I\subset\bigcup_nI_n$.

X may be an arbitrary set, including the empty set; all lattice functions are finite real-valued. Use the interval semiring and its content J from the preceding undergraph-content lemma for a real vector lattice V and elementary integral L. Covering by under-graph intervals gives an exact measure on their sigma-algebra: For arbitrary $A\subset X	imes\mathbb R$ put
\[
u^*(A)=\inf\{\sum_nJ(I_n):A\subset igcup_nI_n,\ I_n\in\mathcal I\},\]
with value infinity if there is no countable cover. Then $
u^*$ is an outer measure, every $I\in\mathcal I$ is Caratheodory measurable, and $
u^*(I)=J(I)$. Its restriction to $\mathcal B=\sigma(\mathcal I)$ is a measure $
u$.

X may be an arbitrary set, including the empty set; all lattice functions are finite real-valued. Let V be a Stone vector lattice and L an elementary integral. Let ℛ_V and 𝒜_V be generated by {f>b}, f∈V, b>0, as a sigma-ring and sigma-algebra respectively, and ν the preceding undergraph measure on ℬ=σ(ℐ). Stone truncations produce the representing measure and identify its integrals: For $f\in V$, $b>0$, the functions $u_n=\min(1,n(f-f\wedge b))$ lie in $V$ and increase to $\mathbf 1_{\{f>b\}}$. For $c>0$, $\{f>b\}\times[0,c)\in\mathcal B$. The formula $\mu_0(A)=\nu(A\times[0,1))$ defines a measure on $\mathcal R_V$; its preceding sigma-ring extension to $\mathcal A_V$ integrates every $f\in V$ and has $\int f\,d\mu=L(f)$.

X may be an arbitrary set, including the empty set; all lattice functions are finite real-valued. Let V be a Stone vector lattice and L an elementary integral; let ℛ_V and 𝒜_V be its positive-level generated sigma-ring and sigma-algebra. A representing measure is required to make every f∈V integrable and satisfy ∫f=L(f). Positive level sets localize uniqueness to the generated sigma-ring: Any two measures on $\mathcal A_V$ representing $L$ agree on every set of $\mathcal R_V$.

X may be an arbitrary set, including the empty set; all lattice functions are finite real-valued. Let ℛ_V and 𝒜_V denote the positive-level generated sigma-ring and sigma-algebra. Daniell-Stone existence and sigma-ring uniqueness: For an elementary integral on a Stone vector lattice $V$ on any set $X$, there is a positive measure on $(X,\mathcal A_V)$ integrating all $f\in V$ with $L(f)=\int f\,d\mu$. Its restriction to $\mathcal R_V$ is unique among all representing measures; uniqueness on all of $\mathcal A_V$ requires a further hypothesis.

X may be an arbitrary set, including the empty set; all lattice functions are finite real-valued. Let V be a real vector lattice, μ a positive measure making all its functions measurable and integrable, and L:V→ℝ the displayed integration functional; positivity, linearity and order continuity are conclusions here. Measure representation forces order continuity on integrable elementary functions: If a measure makes all $f\in V$ integrable and $L(f)=\int f\,d\mu$, then $L$ is positive linear and order-continuous above at zero, hence an elementary integral.

X may be an arbitrary set, including the empty set; all lattice functions are finite real-valued. Let V be a Stone vector lattice and L an elementary integral, with representing measures as in the preceding Daniell–Stone theorem. Let ℛ_V and 𝒜_V be the positive-level generated sigma-ring and sigma-algebra. A constant unit yields finite total mass and full uniqueness: If $1\in V$, then $X=\{1>1/2\}\in\mathcal R_V$, so $\mathcal R_V=\mathcal A_V$. The representing measure is unique and finite, with $\mu(X)=L(1)$; when $L(1)=1$ it is a probability. More generally $X\in\mathcal R_V$ suffices for full uniqueness.

For the following assertions functionals are real-linear, and elementary means positive and continuous from above at zero on finite-valued functions. Compact and compact-support continuous-function examples: For interval assertions assume real endpoints a≤b, including the degenerate interval. On a compact Hausdorff space, nonnegative continuous $f_n\downarrow0$ converge uniformly to zero. Thus the classical Riemann integral on $C([a,b],\mathbb R)$ is elementary. On LCH $X$, $C_c(X,\mathbb R)$ is a Stone vector lattice and every positive linear functional on it is elementary.

Let ℛ_V and 𝒜_V refer to the sigma-ring and sigma-algebra generated by {f>b}, f∈V, b>0, for V=C([a,b],ℝ). An integral-first construction agrees with Lebesgue integration on its initial lattice: For interval assertions assume real endpoints a≤b, including the degenerate interval. Daniell--Stone for the Riemann functional on $C([a,b],\mathbb R)$ yields the usual finite Borel Lebesgue measure on the interval. Their ordinary completions, and hence all integrals on their common completed space, agree.

Here elementary means positive linear and continuous from above at zero. A positive functional need not be an elementary integral: Let $V$ consist of continuous real functions on $[0,\infty)$ with a finite limit at infinity and set $L(f)=\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)$. It is positive linear on a Stone vector lattice but not elementary and has no measure representation integrating all its functions.

Let ℛ_V and 𝒜_V denote the sigma-ring and sigma-algebra generated by {f>b}, f∈V, b>0, for the specific lattice in this example. Representing measures can differ outside the generated sigma-ring: For $X=\mathbb R$, let $V$ consist of $C_c$ functions whose supports lie in $(0,\infty)$ and let $L$ be their Riemann integral. The measures $\mu_0(E)=m(E\cap(0,\infty))$ and $\mu_1(E)=\mu_0(E)+\delta_0(E)$ on $\mathcal A_V$ both represent $L$ but differ on $(-\infty,0]$. More precisely, (0,∞) belongs to the generated sigma-ring, every set in that ring is contained in (0,∞), and (−∞,0] belongs to the generated sigma-algebra but not the sigma-ring. The two displayed measures assign it mass zero and one respectively.

For a in C and r>0, B(a,r)={z in C: |z-a|<r}. A domain is a nonempty, connected, open subset of C. Throughout, Omega is open unless a stronger domain hypothesis is stated.

Complex limits and derivatives: For a function defined near \(a\), the assertion \(f(z)\to L\) means:
for every \(\eps>0\), some \(\delta>0\) makes
\(0<|z-a|<\delta\) imply \(|f(z)-L|<\eps\).
Continuity includes the value \(f(a)\). Its complex derivative is
\[
f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0,\ h\ne0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}h .
\]
A function is holomorphic on an open set when this derivative exists at
each point; no continuity of the derivative is assumed.

Limits and differentiation rules: Complex convergence is equivalent to convergence of both real coordinates,
and, for a punctured limit at \(a\), to convergence along every sequence
\(z_n\ne a\) in the domain tending to \(a\). Differentiability implies
continuity. Sums, products,
quotients where the denominator is nonzero, and compositions have derivatives
\[
(af+bg)'=af'+bg',\quad (fg)'=f'g+fg',\quad
(f/g)'=(f'g-fg')/g^2,\quad (g\circ f)'=(g'\circ f)f'.
\]
Every assertion is local at a point where all displayed functions and
derivatives exist; the corresponding holomorphic closure laws hold on the
open sets where they are defined.

The real differential and CR equations: Identify \(\C\) with \(\R^2\). A function is complex differentiable at \(a\)
if and only if it is real Fr\'echet differentiable there and its real
differential is complex-linear. For \(f=u+\iu v\), assuming real
differentiability at \(a\), this is equivalent to
\[
u_x=v_y,\qquad u_y=-v_x \quad\hbox{at }a.
\]
In that case \(f'=u_x+\iu v_x=v_y-\iu u_y\), and the real Jacobian is
\(\det D_{\R}f=|f'|^2\).

Sufficient regularity and its boundary: If \(u,v\) have continuous first real partial derivatives on an open set,
then \(u+\iu v\) is holomorphic exactly when CR holds there.
Existence of the four partial derivatives and CR at one point, even together
with continuity of the function there, does not suffice. The failure is witnessed by F(0)=0 and F(z)=z^5/|z|^4 for z≠0: F is continuous at 0, u_x(0)=v_y(0)=1 and u_y(0)=v_x(0)=0, but F is not complex differentiable at 0 (the difference quotient is 1 on the positive real axis and -1 on arg z=π/4).

Three initially distinct notions: A function is \(C^1\)-holomorphic if it is complex differentiable and its
derivative is continuous. It is power-series analytic if near every point
it equals a convergent series \(\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(z-a)^n\).
These definitions initially impose different requirements.

The eventual equivalence: On every open set, holomorphic, \(C^1\)-holomorphic and power-series analytic
are equivalent; each implies real smoothness and holomorphic derivatives
of every order.

Locality and examples: Restrictions of holomorphic functions to open subsets are holomorphic.
Functions holomorphic on members of an open cover and equal on overlaps
glue uniquely to a holomorphic function. Real smoothness does not imply
holomorphy, and differentiability at one point does not imply holomorphy
on any neighborhood of that point. In particular, z↦conj(z) is real smooth but nowhere complex differentiable; z↦|z|^2 is complex differentiable exactly at 0, with derivative 0, and is holomorphic on no neighborhood of 0.

Radius and calculus of a power series: For \(\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(z-a)^n\), put
\[
L=\limsup_{n\to\infty}|a_n|^{1/n},\qquad R=L^{-1},
\quad 0^{-1}=\infty,\quad \infty^{-1}=0.
\]
The series converges absolutely for \(|z-a|<R\), diverges for
\(|z-a|>R\), and converges absolutely and uniformly on every closed disk
of radius \(r<R\). Its sum is holomorphic there, its derivatives are the
termwise differentiated series, and each derivative and the termwise
primitive have the same radius \(R\). Thus
\(a_n=f^{(n)}(a)/n!\). The conclusions include zero series and polynomials (R=∞); when R=0 the open convergence disk is empty and no holomorphy assertion is made.

Series algebra and composition: On a common open convergence disk, sums are coefficientwise and products
are Cauchy products. Power-series coefficients representing a function
near their center are unique. If \(F(a)=b\), \(F\) is represented by a
power series near \(a\), and \(G\) by a power series near \(b\), then
\(G\circ F\) has the convergent formally substituted series on a sufficiently
small disk about \(a\).

Exponential and trigonometric functions: The entire function \(E(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!\) satisfies
\(E'=E\), \(E(z+w)=E(z)E(w)\), \(E(0)=1\), and never vanishes.
It agrees with the real exponential on \(\R\), and
\[
E(x+\iu y)=e^x(\cos y+\iu\sin y),\qquad
E(z)=E(w)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ z-w\in2\pi\iu\Z .
\]
Define
\[
\cos z=\tfrac12(E(\iu z)+E(-\iu z)),\quad
\sin z=\tfrac1{2\iu}(E(\iu z)-E(-\iu z)),
\]
and \(\cosh z=(E(z)+E(-z))/2,\ \sinh z=(E(z)-E(-z))/2\).
Their derivatives are \(\sin'=\cos,\ \cos'=-\sin,\
\sinh'=\cosh,\ \cosh'=\sinh\). Sine and hyperbolic sine are odd;
cosine and hyperbolic cosine are even. Their addition identities and
\(\sin^2z+\cos^2z=1,\ \cosh^2z-\sinh^2z=1\) hold for complex
arguments. The period set of sine and cosine is \(2\pi\Z\);
their zeros are respectively \(\pi\Z\) and \(\pi/2+\pi\Z\), all simple.
The hyperbolic functions are obtained by imaginary substitution and
have period set \(2\pi\iu\Z\). On their nonzero-denominator domains,
define \(\tan=\sin/\cos,\ \cot=\cos/\sin,\
\tanh=\sinh/\cosh,\ \coth=\cosh/\sinh\); their derivatives are
\(1/\cos^2,-1/\sin^2,1/\cosh^2,-1/\sinh^2\), respectively. Here the addition identities are sin(z+w)=sin(z)cos(w)+cos(z)sin(w), cos(z+w)=cos(z)cos(w)-sin(z)sin(w), sinh(z+w)=sinh(z)cosh(w)+cosh(z)sinh(w), and cosh(z+w)=cosh(z)cosh(w)+sinh(z)sinh(w); imaginary substitution is sinh(z)=-i sin(iz), cosh(z)=cos(iz).

Principal logarithm: On \(S=\C\setminus(-\infty,0]\) put
\(\operatorname{Log}z=\log|z|+\iu\operatorname{Arg}z\), where
\(-\pi<\operatorname{Arg}z<\pi\).
It is holomorphic, \((\operatorname{Log})'=1/z\),
\(E(\operatorname{Log}z)=z\), and \(\operatorname{Log}1=0\).
It is the inverse of \(E\) from the strip \(|\Imm z|<\pi\) onto \(S\).
Any two continuous logarithms of the same nonzero function on a connected
set differ by a constant in \(2\pi\iu\Z\).
There is no continuous logarithm of \(z\) on \(\C\setminus\{0\}\).

Powers with a chosen logarithm: On the principal slit plane, for every \(\alpha\in\C\),
\(z^\alpha=\exp(\alpha\operatorname{Log}z)\) is holomorphic with
derivative \(\alpha z^{\alpha-1}\), and
\(z^\alpha z^\beta=z^{\alpha+\beta}\) for this one chosen logarithm.
Changing a logarithm by \(2\pi\iu k\) multiplies the power by
\(e^{2\pi\iu k\alpha}\).

Local branches: If \(f\) is holomorphic and \(f(a)\ne0\), every chosen logarithm \(c\) of
\(f(a)\) extends to a holomorphic logarithm \(L\) of \(f\) near \(a\), with
\(L'=f'/f\). For each positive integer \(n\), every chosen \(n\)-th root
of \(f(a)\) extends to a holomorphic \(n\)-th root near \(a\).
Exponential and nonzero power maps have the corresponding local inverse
branches.

The general local inverse branch: A holomorphic function with nonzero derivative at a point has a
holomorphic inverse branch on a neighborhood of its value.

Abel's radial limit: If \(\sum_{n\ge0}a_n\zeta^n=S\) converges for a nonzero \(\zeta\), then
\[
\lim_{t\uparrow1}\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(t\zeta)^n=S,\qquad 0\le t<1.
\]
The interior sums converge absolutely. No general boundary convergence
or boundary extension follows merely from interior holomorphy. The geometric series ∑_{n≥0}z^n on |z|<1 is an explicit example: at every |z|=1 its terms fail to tend to zero, while its sum 1/(1-z) has no finite radial limit at 1.

Paths and finite chains: A path is a continuous \(\gamma:[a,b]\to\C\), \(a\le b\); its trace is
\(|\gamma|=\gamma([a,b])\). It is piecewise \(C^1\) when a finite
partition makes each restricted path \(C^1\), including its one-sided
endpoint derivatives. For a continuous \(f\) on its trace set
\[
\int_\gamma f(z)\dd z=\int_a^b f(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)\dd t,
\]
summing over those pieces. A finite chain is a finite integral linear
combination of paths; its integral is the corresponding linear sum.
A cycle uses closed paths. A degenerate or constant path has integral zero.

Real coordinate interpretation: For a piecewise C^1 path and a continuous function on its trace, For \(f=u+\iu v,\ \gamma=x+\iu y\),
\[
\int_\gamma f\dd z
=\int_\gamma(u\dd x-v\dd y)+\iu\int_\gamma(v\dd x+u\dd y).
\]
Refining the partition in the definition changes no value.

Reversal, concatenation and parameter changes: For a continuous integrand on the path trace and piecewise C^1 paths (or rectifiable paths in the stated extension), Integrals add under subdivision and concatenation and change sign under
reversal. For an increasing piecewise \(C^1\) surjection \(\phi\) of
compact parameter intervals, when both paths are piecewise \(C^1\),
\(\int_{\gamma\circ\phi}f\dd z=\int_\gamma f\dd z\).
The same equality holds for every continuous nondecreasing surjection
when the rectifiable integral below is used, with no differentiability
or strict monotonicity of \(\phi\).

Length, estimates and integral limits: For a piecewise \(C^1\) path its polygonal length is
\[
\ell(\gamma)=\sup_{a=t_0<\cdots<t_m=b}
\sum_j|\gamma(t_j)-\gamma(t_{j-1})|
=\int_a^b|\gamma'(t)|\dd t.
\]
For continuous \(f\) on its trace,
\[
\left|\int_\gamma f\dd z\right|
\le\int_a^b|f(\gamma(t))|\,|\gamma'(t)|\dd t
\le\ell(\gamma)\sup_{|\gamma|}|f|.
\]
Uniform convergence of continuous \(f_n\) to \(f\) on that fixed trace
implies convergence of their integrals. These estimates and uniform
interchange extend to all rectifiable paths. For a rectifiable path of length L with its unit-speed arclength representative σ, the corresponding bound is |∫_γ f dz|≤∫_0^L|f(σ(v))|dv≤L sup_{|γ|}|f|. For L=0 the integral is zero. No derivative of an arbitrary rectifiable parameterization is assumed.
Polygonal connectivity: Every open connected subset of \(\C\) is polygonally connected.

Primitives and zero periods: For a continuous \(f\) on a domain \(\Omega\), the following are equivalent:
\(f\) has a holomorphic primitive \(F\) with \(F'=f\);
its integrals over piecewise \(C^1\) paths depend only on endpoints;
its integral over every closed piecewise \(C^1\) path is zero.
For any such primitive and any rectifiable path in \(\Omega\),
\(\int_\gamma f\dd z=F(\gamma(b))-F(\gamma(a))\).
Primitives on a domain are unique up to an additive constant.

Triangle criterion for a local primitive: Let Omega be open. Suppose \(\Omega\) is star-shaped about \(a\), \(f\) is continuous there,
and its integral around every triangle whose closed interior lies in
\(\Omega\) is zero. Then
\(F(z)=\int_{[a,z]}f\dd w\) is a primitive of \(f\).
In particular this holds on a convex open set.

The rectifiable/Stieltjes representation: A continuous path is rectifiable exactly when its total variation
\(V(\gamma)=\ell(\gamma)\) is finite. For such a rectifiable path and any
continuous \(u:[a,b]\to\C\), the tagged sums
\[
\sum_j u(\xi_j)\bigl(\gamma(t_j)-\gamma(t_{j-1})\bigr),
\qquad t_{j-1}\le\xi_j\le t_j,
\]
have a unique limit as the partition mesh tends to zero.
Call it \(\int_a^b u\dd\gamma\), and define
\(\int_\gamma f\dd z=\int_a^b(f\circ\gamma)\dd\gamma\).
It is linear, additive on subintervals, and bounded in modulus by
\(V(\gamma)\sup|u|\). If \(\gamma\) is AC, it agrees with
\(\int_a^b u(t)\gamma'(t)\dd t\), hence with the original
piecewise \(C^1\) integral.

All monotone parameter changes: For a continuous rectifiable path gamma:[a,b]→C and continuous f on its trace, Let \(\phi:[c,d]\to[a,b]\) be a continuous nondecreasing surjection.
Then \(V(\gamma\circ\phi)=V(\gamma)\) and
\(\int_{\gamma\circ\phi}f\dd z=\int_\gamma f\dd z\).
For a nonincreasing surjection the integral has the opposite sign.

Measure and arclength bridges: Let gamma:[a,b]→C be continuous of bounded variation and let f be continuous on its trace. For continuous BV \(\gamma\), its normalized constant extension
\(\widetilde\gamma\), zero to the left after subtraction of \(\gamma(a)\),
has a finite complex Stieltjes measure \(\nu_\gamma\) satisfying
\[
\nu_\gamma((s,t])=\gamma(t)-\gamma(s),\quad
|\nu_\gamma|([a,b])=V(\gamma),\quad \nu_\gamma(\{a\})=0.
\]
For continuous \(u\) on \([a,b]\),
\(\int u\dd\gamma=\int_{[a,b]}u\dd\nu_\gamma\).
If \(L=V(\gamma)>0\), there is a \(1\)-Lipschitz path
\(\sigma:[0,L]\to\C\) and a continuous nondecreasing surjection
\(s:[a,b]\to[0,L]\) such that
\[
\gamma=\sigma\circ s,\qquad
\int_\gamma f\dd z=\int_0^L f(\sigma(v))\sigma'(v)\dd v,\qquad
|\sigma'|=1\ \hbox{a.e.}
\]
For \(L=0\) the path is constant and every integral is zero.

A finite-length trace has empty interior: The trace of a rectifiable path has planar Lebesgue measure zero and hence
empty interior.

Weak Goursat theorem: If \(f\) is complex differentiable on a neighborhood of a closed triangle
\(T\), its positively oriented boundary integral is zero. The same holds
for a rectangle by division along a diagonal. Continuity of \(f'\) is
not a hypothesis.

A continuous exceptional point: If f is continuous on a neighborhood of a closed triangle T and holomorphic on that neighborhood except possibly at one point (which may lie in the interior, on an edge or at a vertex of T), then its integral around the positively oriented boundary of T is zero.

Disk Cauchy theorem, formula and all derivatives: A holomorphic function on a disk has a primitive and zero integral on every
closed rectifiable path there. If \(f\) is holomorphic on a neighborhood
of \(\overline{B(a,r)}\), and \(C\) is its positively oriented circle, then
for \(|z-a|<r\),
\[
f(z)=\frac1{2\pi\iu}\int_C\frac{f(w)}{w-z}\dd w,\qquad
f^{(n)}(z)=\frac{n!}{2\pi\iu}
\int_C\frac{f(w)}{(w-z)^{n+1}}\dd w .
\]
All derivatives exist and are holomorphic. At the center, if
\(M=\max_C|f|\), then \(|f^{(n)}(a)|\le n!M/r^n\).
A preliminary Liouville theorem: A bounded entire function is constant.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON IV.2, printed 68--76, PDF 82--90; IV.8, printed 100--102, PDF 114--116; AHL IV.1.4--2.3, printed 109--124, PDF 125--140.

Index of a cycle: For a cycle \(\Gamma=\sum_jm_j\gamma_j\), with
\(|\Gamma|=\bigcup_{m_j\ne0}|\gamma_j|\), and \(a\notin|\Gamma|\), set
\[
\ind(\Gamma,a)=\frac1{2\pi\iu}\int_\Gamma\frac{\dd z}{z-a}.
\]
A zero chain has empty trace and zero index.

Integer index and its support: For any finite cycle Gamma and every point a outside its trace, The index is integer-valued, continuous and locally constant off the
trace, and zero on its unbounded complementary component.

Index operations and homotopy: For finite cycles and their indices at points off the trace, Index adds under chain addition and concatenation and changes sign under
reversal. If two closed piecewise \(C^1\) paths are joined by a continuous
homotopy of closed paths avoiding \(a\), their indices about \(a\) agree.
The homotopy need not be differentiable and its intermediate paths need
not be rectifiable.

Practical index computations: A positively traversed circle has index one at each interior point and
zero at each exterior point. More generally, suppose a closed piecewise
\(C^1\) path avoids \(a\), starts off a ray \(a+[0,\infty)\eta\)
(\(|\eta|=1\)), and has finitely many transverse crossings of that ray,
none at a corner. Then its index is
\[
\sum_{\gamma(t)-a\in(0,\infty)\eta}
\operatorname{sign}\Imm\!\left(\gamma'(t)/\eta\right).
\]
