In particular positive rectangle and half-disk boundaries have index
one in their indicated interiors and zero in their exteriors.
These statements concern these explicit regions, not separation by an
arbitrary Jordan curve. All mentioned index values are for points off the boundary trace.

Index from a specified region and Green's theorem: Let \(D\) be an already specified bounded planar region whose finite
piecewise \(C^1\) oriented boundary cycle \(\Gamma\) satisfies the
hypotheses of the real Green theorem, also after removing a sufficiently
small closed interior disk. Then
\(\ind(\Gamma,a)=1\) for \(a\in D\) and \(0\) for
\(a\notin\overline D\), or for any other complementary component on
which the same Green calculation has no pole.
No existence or separation theorem for the interior of an arbitrary
Jordan trace is asserted here.

Full finite-cycle Cauchy theorem and formula: Let \(f\) be holomorphic on an open set \(\Omega\), and let a finite
cycle \(\Gamma\) have its trace in \(\Omega\). If
\(\ind(\Gamma,w)=0\) for every \(w\notin\Omega\), then
\[
\int_\Gamma f(z)\dd z=0,\qquad
\ind(\Gamma,a)f(a)=\frac1{2\pi\iu}
\int_\Gamma\frac{f(z)}{z-a}\dd z\quad(a\in\Omega\setminus|\Gamma|).
\]
The derivative formula is
\[
\ind(\Gamma,a)f^{(n)}(a)
=\frac{n!}{2\pi\iu}\int_\Gamma
\frac{f(z)}{(z-a)^{n+1}}\dd z.
\]
Neither simple connectedness nor a simple trace is required. The derivative identity holds for every integer n≥0 and a∈Omega outside the cycle trace; the zero cycle is included.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON IV.4--5, printed 80--87, PDF 94--101, especially the global gluing proof at printed 84--85; AHL IV.4, printed 137--148, PDF 153--164.

Homotopic Cauchy theorem and simple connectivity: Integrals of a holomorphic function agree along piecewise \(C^1\) paths
that are fixed-endpoint homotopic in its open domain. They also agree
for freely homotopic closed loops. A null-homotopic closed path has zero
integral. Consequently every holomorphic function on a simply connected
domain has a primitive, and every zero-free holomorphic function there
has a holomorphic logarithm and an \(n\)-th root for every \(n\ge1\). Here homotopies are continuous; their intermediate paths need not be differentiable or rectifiable. The paths whose contour integrals are compared are piecewise C^1.

Global logarithm and root criteria: Let \(f\) be zero-free and holomorphic on a domain \(\Omega\).
It has a holomorphic logarithm if and only if
\(\int_\gamma f'/f=0\) on every closed piecewise \(C^1\) path.
It has a holomorphic \(n\)-th root, \(n\ge1\), if and only if
\[
\frac1{2\pi\iu}\int_\gamma\frac{f'}f\dd z\in n\Z
\quad\hbox{for every such closed path}.
\]
All logarithms differ by a constant \(2\pi\iu k\); all \(n\)-th roots
differ by a constant \(n\)-th root of unity.

Morera and continuous gluing: A continuous function on an open set is holomorphic if its integral
around every triangle compactly contained there is zero.
A continuous function holomorphic off one point, or off a locally
finite union of compact rectifiable arcs, is holomorphic everywhere.
The latter assertion is local: in each relatively compact small disk
only finitely many of the arcs are required. The function is continuous on the entire open set. The compact rectifiable arcs form a locally finite family in that open set; in particular straight segments and regular analytic arcs are covered.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON IV.5--6, printed 86--97, PDF 100--111; AHL IV.6.5, printed 172--174, PDF 188--190. The finite-length gluing argument is the explicit subdivision proof above.

Chapter 5, Taylor series, zeros and local maps. Throughout these statements the ambient scalar field is C, a domain is a nonempty connected open subset of C, and holomorphic means complex differentiable at every point, without initially assuming continuous derivatives.

For every a∈C, 0<R≤∞ and f holomorphic on B(a,R), f(z)=Σ_{n≥0} f^(n)(a)(z−a)^n/n! for every |z−a|<R. This series and every series obtained by any number of termwise derivatives converge absolutely and uniformly on each compact subdisk. Every holomorphic function is real C∞, all its complex derivatives are holomorphic, ∂_x f=f′ and ∂_y f=i f′; more generally ∂_x^p ∂_y^q f=i^q f^(p+q) for all nonnegative integers p,q. As recalled by the source, on any open set holomorphy, C¹-holomorphy (complex differentiability with continuous derivative), and being locally represented by a convergent complex power series are equivalent (the equivalence is separately stated at d12:01-04-equivalence).

With f holomorphic on B(a,R), 0<R≤∞, Taylor coefficients a_n=f^(n)(a)/n!, and 0<r<R, let M_r=max_{|w−a|=r}|f(w)|. For every n≥0, |a_n|≤M_r r^(−n). For every integer N≥0 and |z−a|<r, |f(z)−Σ_{n=0}^N a_n(z−a)^n|≤M_r (|z−a|/r)^(N+1)/(1−|z−a|/r). For every integer k≥0, |f^(k)(a)|≤k! M_r/r^k.
Source attribution for the Taylor representation and estimates: Conway IV.2 and Ahlfors V.1.2.

For f holomorphic near a∈C, either f is identically zero on a neighborhood of a, or there exists a unique integer m≥0 for which f(z)=(z−a)^m g(z) on some neighborhood, with g holomorphic and g(a)≠0. In the latter case, if f(a)=0 then m≥1 and this m defines its zero multiplicity. A finite-order zero is isolated. For two holomorphic functions of finite orders m,n at a, their product has finite order m+n at a.

If Ω is a domain, f is holomorphic on Ω, and the set {z∈Ω:f(z)=0} has an accumulation point in Ω, then f≡0 on Ω. Consequently if f,g are holomorphic on Ω and agree on a subset with an accumulation point in Ω, then f=g throughout Ω.

For a holomorphic f on a domain Ω with f not identically zero, every zero is isolated, every compact K⊂Ω contains only finitely many zeros, and the entire zero set is at most countable. On a disconnected open set these conclusions hold separately on each connected component where f is not identically zero; no such zero-set conclusion is asserted on a component where f≡0.
Source attribution for local factorization, identity, and discreteness/countability: Conway IV.3 and Ahlfors IV.3.2.

If f is holomorphic near a∈C and f′(a)≠0, there exist open neighborhoods U of a and V of f(a) such that f|_U:U→V is a biholomorphism. Its holomorphic inverse h:V→U satisfies h′(w)=1/f′(h(w)) for every w∈V.

If f is holomorphic near a and is not constant on any neighborhood of a, there exist an integer m≥1, a real r>0, an open neighborhood U of a, and a biholomorphism φ:U→B(0,r) with φ(a)=0 and f(z)−f(a)=φ(z)^m for all z∈U. The image f(U) is exactly B(f(a),r^m). Every value w in that disk other than f(a) has exactly m distinct preimages in U.

Every nonconstant holomorphic function on a domain Ω is an open map. Every injective holomorphic f on Ω has f′(z)≠0 for all z∈Ω, is a homeomorphism onto the open set f(Ω), and has a holomorphic inverse on f(Ω). A nonzero derivative yields local invertibility and does not imply global injectivity; the exponential has E′(z)=E(z)≠0 while E(z+2πi)=E(z).
For every nonzero complex polynomial P and every root a∈C, the analytic zero multiplicity of z↦P(z) at a equals the largest integer m for which the polynomial (X−a)^m divides P algebraically.
Source attribution for local mapping and multiplicities: Conway IV.7 and Ahlfors IV.3.3.
Chapter 6, Maximum principles and growth barriers.

Let Ω be a domain and f holomorphic on Ω. If |f| has an interior local maximum, f is constant on Ω. If f has no zeros, an interior local minimum of |f| likewise forces f constant. If Ω is bounded and f extends continuously to its closure, then |f(z)|≤max_{ξ∈∂Ω}|f(ξ)| for every z∈Ω. More generally, for bounded Ω and M≥0, if limsup_{Ω∋z→ξ}|f(z)|≤M at each ξ∈∂Ω, then |f(z)|≤M throughout Ω; continuous extension to the boundary is not required for this last version.

Every bounded entire function C→C is constant. Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root. Every polynomial P of degree n≥1 factors as P(z)=c∏_{j=1}^n(z−a_j), where c is its nonzero leading coefficient, and roots repeat with their analytic, equivalently algebraic, multiplicities.
Source attribution for maximum principles, Liouville, and algebraic closure: Conway VI.1 and Ahlfors IV.2.3, IV.3.4.

Let D={z∈C:|z|<1}. If f:D→D is holomorphic and f(0)=0, then |f(z)|≤|z| for all z∈D and |f′(0)|≤1. Equality |f(z₀)|=|z₀| at any z₀≠0 in D, or equality |f′(0)|=1, implies there exists c∈C with |c|=1 and f(z)=cz for every z∈D. Conversely every such rotation is a holomorphic self-map fixing zero and attains these equalities.

For each a∈D, φ_a(z)=(z−a)/(1−conj(a)z) is a disk biholomorphism whose inverse is w↦(w+a)/(1+conj(a)w). Every holomorphic f:D→D satisfies, for every a,z∈D, |(f(z)−f(a))/(1−conj(f(a))f(z))|≤|(z−a)/(1−conj(a)z)| and |f′(a)|/(1−|f(a)|²)≤1/(1−|a|²). Equality in the first inequality for any pair z≠a, or in the derivative inequality at any point a, holds if and only if f is a disk automorphism. All disk automorphisms, and only those, have the form cφ_a for a∈D and |c|=1.
Source attribution for Schwarz and Schwarz–Pick: Conway VI.2 and Ahlfors IV.3.4.

Let 0≤r₀<r₃≤∞, let f be holomorphic on {r₀<|z|<r₃} and not identically zero, and let r₀<r₁<r<r₂<r₃. For every admissible t, M(t)=max_{|z|=t}|f(z)| is positive and log M(r)≤[log(r₂/r)/log(r₂/r₁)]log M(r₁)+[log(r/r₁)/log(r₂/r₁)]log M(r₂). Equivalently u↦log M(e^u) is convex. For the identically zero function the corresponding multiplicative inequality M(r)≤M(r₁)^[log(r₂/r)/log(r₂/r₁)] M(r₂)^[log(r/r₁)/log(r₂/r₁)] holds with all values zero.

For real α≥1/2 define S_α={re^(iθ):r>0, |θ|<π/(2α)}; at α=1/2 use −π<θ<π, excluding the negative ray. Suppose f is holomorphic on S_α, M≥0, and limsup_{S_α∋z→ξ}|f(z)|≤M for every finite boundary point ξ, including zero. If there exist A>0, B≥0, 0≤β<α, and R>0 such that |f(z)|≤A exp(B|z|^β) for every z∈S_α with |z|≥R, then |f(z)|≤M for all z∈S_α, including the case M=0. The strict threshold β<α cannot be replaced by β=α: using the sector branch, f(z)=exp(z^α) has boundary modulus one, tends to one at the vertex, obeys |f(z)|≤exp(|z|^α), and is unbounded on the positive axis.

The sector Phragmén–Lindelöf theorem also applies to rotated or translated sectors by the explicit affine coordinate change: for b∈C and θ∈R use ζ=e^(−iθ)(z−b), transport S_α, its finite-boundary limsup hypotheses and its growth bound in |ζ|, and obtain the same bound |f|≤M throughout b+e^(iθ)S_α. This is an explicitly adopted extension in prose, not a proof-route auxiliary estimate.
Source attribution for growth barriers: Conway VI.3–4, especially the sector barrier.
Chapter 7, Laurent series, singularities and the sphere.

For every a∈C, 0≤r₀<R₀≤∞, and f holomorphic on A={z:r₀<|z−a|<R₀}, there is a unique Laurent expansion f(z)=Σ_{n∈Z}c_n(z−a)^n on A. For each n∈Z and every r₀<ρ<R₀, c_n=(2πi)^(−1)∫_{|w−a|=ρ} f(w)/(w−a)^(n+1) dw, with the circle positively oriented; this integral is independent of ρ. The nonnegative-power and negative-power series each converge absolutely and uniformly on every closed subannulus r₀<s≤|z−a|≤t<R₀, and both can be differentiated termwise any number of times on A with the corresponding convergence on such subannuli.
Source attribution for Laurent expansions: Conway V.1 and Ahlfors V.1.3.

An isolated singularity of f at a means that f is holomorphic on a full punctured disk 0<|z−a|<R for some R>0. It is removable if f has a holomorphic extension across a; it is a pole of order m≥1 if f(z)=(z−a)^(−m)g(z), where g is holomorphic near a and g(a)≠0; it is essential if neither of these alternatives holds. A general boundary point without a punctured neighborhood does not fall under these definitions.

For a function holomorphic on 0<|z−a|<R with Laurent coefficients (c_n)_{n∈Z}: the singularity is removable iff c_n=0 for all n<0; it is a pole of exact order m≥1 iff c_(−m)≠0 and c_n=0 for all n<−m; it is essential iff infinitely many c_n with n<0 are nonzero. For every integer m≥0, f(z)=O(|z−a|^(−m)) as z→a iff the singularity is removable or a pole of order at most m. For m≥1, f(z)=o(|z−a|^(−m)) iff the singularity is removable or a pole of order at most m−1. A finite limit f(z)→L∈C at a is equivalent to removability (the extension takes the value L). The condition |f(z)|→∞ as z→a is equivalent to a pole.

For f holomorphic on a punctured disk about a, boundedness near a implies a removable singularity. The weaker condition (z−a)f(z)→0 as z→a also implies removability. If a is an essential isolated singularity, then for every 0<r<R the image {f(z):0<|z−a|<r} is dense in C.
Source attribution for isolated singularities: Conway V.1 and Ahlfors IV.3.1–3.2.

A scalar meromorphic function on an open set Ω⊂C is holomorphic except at a relatively closed discrete set of poles, taking the value ∞ at those poles, and is not identically ∞ on any connected component. At a point where it is not identically zero locally and is not a pole, its signed order is its holomorphic zero multiplicity (zero at a regular nonzero point); a pole of order m≥1 has signed order −m.

Scalar meromorphic functions on an open set are exactly functions locally expressible on disks as p/q with p,q holomorphic and q not identically zero on that disk, after filling cancellable singularities. They are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication. If f is not identically zero on any connected component, 1/f exists as a scalar meromorphic function. On a domain scalar meromorphic functions with these operations form a field. At points where the factors have finite signed orders, ord_a(fg)=ord_a f+ord_a g and ord_a(f/g)=ord_a f−ord_a g. These operations are defined by local quotient arithmetic, including at apparent pointwise expressions such as ∞−∞.

The Riemann sphere is Ĉ=C∪{∞}, with the usual finite-point topology and neighborhoods of ∞ containing {∞}∪{z:|z|>R} for some R>0. Its finite coordinate is z and its coordinate near infinity is w=1/z, with w(∞)=0. A scalar function is holomorphic or meromorphic at infinity precisely when w↦f(1/w) has that property at w=0. An isolated singularity at infinity requires holomorphy on some full exterior region |z|>R.

The sphere Ĉ is compact, Hausdorff and connected. Its two coordinate charts have holomorphic transition w=1/z on their overlap. An entire f has a removable singularity at ∞ iff it is constant; it has a pole of exact order m≥1 at ∞ iff it is a polynomial of exact degree m; every nonpolynomial entire function has an essential singularity at ∞. For a reduced rational function P/Q with nonzero numerator and denominator and degrees p,q, infinity is a pole of order p−q if p>q, a zero of order q−p if p<q, and a finite nonzero value if p=q.
Source attribution for sphere coordinates and classification at infinity: Conway I.6, V.1 and Ahlfors I.2.4.

Every scalar meromorphic function on the whole compact sphere Ĉ is rational. For every nonconstant reduced rational function F=P/Q, its degree d=max(deg P,deg Q) equals the number of zeros on Ĉ and also the number of poles on Ĉ, each counted with multiplicity. More generally for every w∈Ĉ, the sum of local multiplicities of F at all preimages of w is d. A nonzero constant has no zeros or poles; no finite zero-count claim is made for the identically zero function.

A continuous map F into Ĉ is holomorphic if, near every source point, its expression in a target coordinate is holomorphic; near a point mapped to ∞ this expression is 1/F, given value zero at that point. The source can be a plane open set, or a sphere open set equipped with the finite and infinity source coordinates. These notions are independent of the stated coordinate choice because transition z↦1/z is holomorphic on the overlap.

On a connected plane domain or connected sphere domain, holomorphic sphere-valued maps are precisely scalar meromorphic functions with their pole values ∞ together with the constant map ∞. Every finite-valued holomorphic function on the whole sphere is constant.
Source attribution for rationality and sphere-valued maps: Conway V.3, VII.3 and Ahlfors II.1.4; the coordinate and compactness bridges are proved in this manuscript.
Chapter 8, Residues and controlled integral applications.

If f is holomorphic on a punctured disk about a and has Laurent expansion f(z)=Σ_{n∈Z}c_n(z−a)^n, define Res_a(f(z)dz)=Res(f;a)=c_(−1). Equivalently this equals (2πi)^(−1)∫_C f(z)dz for every sufficiently small positively oriented circle C centered at a.

If f has a pole of order at most an integer m≥1 at a (also permitting a removable singularity), then Res(f;a)=((m−1)!)^(−1) [d^(m−1)/dz^(m−1)((z−a)^m f(z))]_{z=a}, using the holomorphic extension of the product. If f=p/q with p,q holomorphic near a, q(a)=0 and q′(a)≠0, then Res(f;a)=p(a)/q′(a), including the removable case p(a)=0. For any isolated singularity, including an essential one, and any local holomorphic coordinate z=φ(w) with φ(b)=a and φ′(b)≠0, Res_b(f(φ(w))φ′(w)dw)=Res_a(f(z)dz).

Let Ω⊂C be open, A⊂Ω relatively closed and discrete, and f holomorphic on Ω∖A. Let Γ be a finite integral linear combination of closed piecewise C¹ paths with trace |Γ|⊂Ω∖A, and assume ind(Γ,w)=0 for all w∉Ω. Then ∫_Γ f(z)dz=2πi Σ_{a∈A} ind(Γ,a)Res(f;a). Only finitely many summands can be nonzero; no finiteness of A, simple connectedness, or Jordan trace assumption is required.
Source attribution for the residue theorem: Conway V.2 and Ahlfors IV.5.1.

If f(z)dz is holomorphic on a large punctured neighborhood of infinity, define Res_∞(f(z)dz)=Res_{w=0}(−f(1/w)w^(−2)dw). This equals minus the coefficient of z^(−1) in the exterior Laurent expansion of f; the minus sign includes the differential Jacobian.

Every meromorphic differential on Ĉ, written f(z)dz in the finite coordinate and −f(1/w)w^(−2)dw in the infinity coordinate, has finitely many poles and the sum of its residues at all sphere points, including ∞, is zero.

Let R=P/Q be a reduced rational function with no real poles and deg Q≥deg P+2. Its ordinary improper real integral is absolutely convergent and ∫_{−∞}^∞R(x)dx=2πi Σ_{Im a>0}Res(R;a). If S is a rational expression in two variables such that S(cos t,sin t) has no poles for real t, set T(z)=(1/(iz))S((z+z^(−1))/2,(z−z^(−1))/(2i)) after meromorphic cancellation. Then ∫_0^{2π}S(cos t,sin t)dt=2πi Σ_{|a|<1}Res(T;a), including any pole at zero. In particular, for real a,b with a>|b|, ∫_0^{2π}dt/(a+b cos t)=2π/√(a²−b²), and ∫_{−∞}^∞dx/(1+x²)=π.
Source attribution for rational and trigonometric integrals: Ahlfors IV.5.3 and Conway V.2.

For every c>0, r>0 and q continuous on the upper semicircle C_r={re^(it):0≤t≤π}, |∫_{C_r}e^(icz)q(z)dz|≤(π/c)sup_{C_r}|q|. Hence the arc integral tends to zero as r→∞ whenever its supremum tends to zero. For a proper rational function R (deg numerator<deg denominator) without real poles and c>0, both one-sided ordinary improper tails of e^(icx)R(x) exist and ∫_{−∞}^∞e^(icx)R(x)dx=2πi Σ_{Im a>0}Res(e^(icz)R(z);a). For c<0 the formula is −2πi times the sum over Im a<0. If the degree gap is at least two these real integrals are also absolutely convergent. For every b>0 and c∈R, ∫_{−∞}^∞cos(cx)/(x²+b²)dx=(π/b)e^(−b|c|).

Let R be proper rational whose real poles, if any, are all simple, and let c>0. Define the real-line principal value by symmetric deleted intervals around each real pole, each radius tending independently to zero, while the two far tails are ordinary independent one-sided improper limits. This principal value exists and equals PV∫_{−∞}^∞e^(icx)R(x)dx=2πi Σ_{Im a>0}Res(e^(icz)R(z);a)+πi Σ_{a∈R}Res(e^(icz)R(z);a). In particular PV∫_R e^(icx)/x dx=πi and ∫_0^∞sin(cx)/x dx=π/2. The latter is an ordinary improper integral and is not absolutely convergent. The complex former integrand is not absolutely integrable (in particular its modulus is nonintegrable at zero).
Source attribution for Jordan estimates and principal values: Ahlfors IV.5.3 and Conway V.2.

For every real s with 0<s<1, the ordinary improper integral ∫_0^∞x^(s−1)/(1+x)dx is absolutely convergent and equals π/sin(πs). The endpoints are excluded: the source explicitly notes that the real integrals diverge at s=0 and s=1 (lines 2212–2214).

For every real a>0, the bilateral sum Σ_{n∈Z}1/(n²+a²) converges absolutely and equals (π/a)coth(πa). Thus this is an ordinary absolutely convergent bilateral sum, not only a symmetric limiting value.
Source attribution for branch-cut integration and residue summation: Ahlfors IV.5.3 and Conway V.2; keyhole bank limits and square-contour estimates are supplied in this manuscript.
Chapter 9, Argument principle, Rouché and stability of zeros.

Throughout Chapter 9, zero and pole orders are the signed Laurent orders defined in Chapter 7. A cycle is finite, avoids all zeros and poles being counted, and has index zero on the complement of the relevant open set. Its images retain path parametrizations and integer coefficients; the following results do not presume arbitrary Jordan traces bound interiors.

For a finite cycle Γ with trace in an open set Ω and ind(Γ,w)=0 for all w∉Ω, the union of its trace with the closure of {z∉|Γ|:ind(Γ,z)≠0} is a compact subset of Ω. Consequently sums of zero/pole orders weighted by this index have only finitely many nonzero terms when the zero/pole set is relatively closed and discrete in the relevant components.

If a nonzero meromorphic function f has signed order m∈Z at a, then Res(f′/f;a)=m. The only possible poles of f′/f are the zeros and poles of f; at each nonzero order m they are simple, while order zero gives no pole. The assertion includes negative orders and regular nonzero points.
Source attribution for logarithmic derivatives: Conway V.3 and Ahlfors IV.5.2.

Let Ω be open and f meromorphic on Ω, not identically zero on any component relevant to a finite cycle Γ. Assume |Γ|⊂Ω has no zero or pole of f and ind(Γ,w)=0 for w∉Ω. Then (2πi)^(−1)∫_Γ(f′/f)dz=Σ_a ind(Γ,a)ord_a f=ind(f∘Γ,0), with the image retaining each path parametrization and integer coefficient. For a specified bounded region D on which f is meromorphic on a neighborhood of its closure, with no boundary zero or pole, and whose full positive boundary satisfies the real Green theorem hypotheses (C¹ boundary or the stated finite piecewise regular decomposition), this integral equals the ordinary number of zeros minus poles inside D, counted with multiplicity. It applies to a given Jordan domain only when that domain and boundary meet these hypotheses and asserts no general interior theorem for an arbitrary Jordan trace.
Source attribution for the argument principle: Conway V.3 and Ahlfors IV.5.2.

Let Γ be a finite cycle, and let f,g be holomorphic on an open neighborhood Ω of |Γ| and all points with nonzero index (so the cycle has index zero outside Ω). If |g(z)−f(z)|<|f(z)| for every z∈|Γ|, their index-weighted zero counts are equal: Σ_a ind(Γ,a)ord_a f=Σ_a ind(Γ,a)ord_a g, with the finite sums taken over their zeros. In particular ordinary zero counts agree when Γ is a positive circle or the full positive boundary of a specified Green-regular region under the preceding hypotheses.
Source attribution for Rouché: Conway V.3 and Stein–Shakarchi 3.4.

If f is holomorphic on a neighborhood of a compact counting contour and all its nonzero-index points, and f has no zero on that contour, every holomorphic perturbation g satisfying sup_contour|g−f|<min_contour|f| has the same (index-weighted) zero count. A monic polynomial of degree n has exactly n roots in C counted with multiplicity. For finitely many simple polynomial roots, choose disjoint sufficiently small isolating disks; all sufficiently small changes of the coefficients leave exactly one root in each disk. More generally, a root of multiplicity m leaves exactly m perturbed roots, with multiplicity, in its chosen isolating disk for sufficiently small coefficient changes; the boundary-uniform perturbation statement also applies to holomorphic perturbations.
Source attribution for perturbation and polynomial roots: Conway V.3 and Ahlfors IV.5.2, with the manuscript polynomial/analytic multiplicity bridge.

Let Ω be a domain and f_n be holomorphic on Ω with f_n→f locally uniformly, where f is holomorphic and not identically zero. For every isolating circle with closed disk contained in Ω and f nonzero on the circle, the zero counts of f_n and f in that disk, counted with multiplicity, agree for all sufficiently large n. In the general locally uniform holomorphic limit setting, if every f_n is zero-free on Ω, then f is zero-free or identically zero.
Source attribution for Hurwitz: Conway VII.2 and Stein–Shakarchi 8.3.2–3.3.
On a domain Ω, if injective holomorphic functions f_n:Ω→C converge locally uniformly to a holomorphic f, then f is injective or constant.

The constant alternative in the locally uniform limit theorem for univalent functions occurs: on a disk, f_n(z)=z/n for positive integers n are injective holomorphic maps and converge locally uniformly to the constant zero function.
Source attribution for limits of univalent functions: Conway VII.2 Exercise 10, proved in the manuscript, and Stein–Shakarchi 8 Proposition 3.5.
Chapter 10, Möbius geometry and explicit conformal maps.

If f is holomorphic near a and f′(a)=c≠0, its real differential is h↦ch, namely rotation by arg(c) followed by dilation |c|, with real determinant |c|²>0. It preserves oriented angles between nonzero tangent vectors, and f is a conformal equivalence on suitable neighborhoods of a and f(a). Having nonzero derivative everywhere gives no global injectivity conclusion; the exponential is an explicit counterexample.

For every a,b,c,d∈C with ad−bc≠0, T(z)=(az+b)/(cz+d) extends to a biholomorphism of Ĉ. If c≠0 it sends −d/c to ∞ and ∞ to a/c; if c=0 it sends ∞ to ∞. These transformations form a group under composition. Two invertible 2×2 complex matrices represent the same transformation iff they differ by a nonzero complex scalar. For any two ordered triples of pairwise distinct sphere points, there exists exactly one Möbius transformation taking the first triple respectively to the second. All cross ratios are preserved, with their coordinate limits used when an entry is infinity.

For pairwise distinct finite p,q,r, define A(z)=(z−p)(q−r)/((z−r)(q−p)); A(p)=0, A(q)=1 and A(r)=∞. The cross ratio in the manuscript convention is [z,p;q,r]=A(z), extended by the indicated sphere-coordinate limits when an entry is ∞. Equivalently A is the unique Möbius map sending the ordered triple (p,q,r) to (0,1,∞), defining the same cross ratio for arbitrary pairwise distinct sphere p,q,r.
Source attribution for Möbius transformations: Conway III.3 and Ahlfors III.3.

A generalized circle is a Euclidean circle, or a Euclidean line together with ∞. Every Möbius transformation maps generalized circles to generalized circles. Reflection in a generalized circle K is defined as A^(−1)∘(z↦conj(z))∘A for any Möbius A taking K to the extended real line; this definition is independent of A. All disk automorphisms are exactly z↦e^(iθ)(z−a)/(1−conj(a)z), for θ∈R and |a|<1. All upper-half-plane automorphisms are exactly (az+b)/(cz+d) with real a,b,c,d and ad−bc>0, with matrices identified modulo nonzero real scalar.

The Cayley map C(z)=(z−i)/(z+i) is a biholomorphism from {Im z>0} onto D, with inverse i(1+w)/(1−w). For every 0<θ≤2π, the exponential is a biholomorphism from {0<Im z<θ} onto {r e^(it):r>0, 0<t<θ}, excluding the endpoint rays; its inverse is the holomorphic logarithm having argument in (0,θ). On any sector of opening 0<θ<2π, after rotation the corresponding selected logarithm defines the power map z↦exp((π/θ)Log z), a biholomorphism onto a half-plane. The Joukowski map J(z)=(z+z^(−1))/2 is a biholomorphism {|z|>1}→C∖[−1,1]; its inverse may be written w+√(w²−1), with the square-root branch asymptotic to w at infinity obtained from that inverse.
Source attribution for explicit conformal maps: Stein–Shakarchi 8.1 and Ahlfors III.4.

For every holomorphic f on an open plane set Ω and every absolutely continuous path γ:[a,b]→Ω with compact trace, L(f∘γ)=∫_a^b |f′(γ(t))| |γ′(t)|dt. If f:Ω→f(Ω) is injective and holomorphic and E⊂Ω is Lebesgue measurable, then f(E) is Lebesgue measurable and m₂(f(E))=∫_E|f′(z)|²dm₂(z). More generally, for every nonnegative measurable h on f(Ω), ∫_{f(E)}h(w)dm₂(w)=∫_E h(f(z))|f′(z)|²dm₂(z), allowing infinite integrals. The scalar real or complex identity also holds when the absolute integral is finite. For a merely rectifiable non-AC parametrization, the derivative formula is used only after passage to its proved arc-length/AC representation.
Source attribution for length and area: Stein–Shakarchi 8.4.3 and the stipulated D11 C¹ change-of-variables and AC chain/length foundations.

Every Euclidean disk and every half-plane is conformally equivalent to the unit disk D. Every horizontal strip of finite positive width, every sector of opening θ∈(0,2π), and every plane slit along one ray is conformally equivalent to D. The exterior of a disk and the complement in C of a closed nondegenerate segment are conformally equivalent to one another. The source does not assert that either of these last two domains is equivalent to D.

Here $\Omega$ is any open subset of $\mathbb C$, possibly empty or disconnected, $j$ ranges over positive integers, and functions are defined on $\Omega$. The compact-open metric: For an open $\Omega\subset\C$ choose
$K_j=\{z\in\Omega:|z|\le j,\ \dist(z,\C\setminus\Omega)\ge1/j\}$, with distance to the empty set interpreted as infinity. Empty suprema are zero. On continuous complex-valued functions put
\[
 d(f,g)=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j}\min(1,\sup_{K_j}|f-g|).
\]
Its convergence is exactly uniform convergence on compact subsets. The space $\Hol(\Omega)$ is complete for this metric. The displayed $d$ is a metric on $C(\Omega,\mathbb C)$; $\Omega=\varnothing$ has a one-element function space, which is included.

For every open $\Omega\subset\mathbb C$, sequence $f_n\in\operatorname{Hol}(\Omega)$ and $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ with $f_n\to f$ uniformly on each compact subset: Holomorphic limits and all derivatives: A locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, and every derivative converges locally uniformly to the corresponding derivative of the limit. The derivative assertion holds for every integer $k\ge0$.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON VII.2 pp.151--152 (PDF165--166); SS2.5.2 pp.53--55 (PDF72--74).

On any open $\Omega\subset\mathbb C$: The compactness mechanism: A locally bounded family of holomorphic functions is equicontinuous on compact sets and every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset. For continuous maps into a compact metric space, local equicontinuity alone gives such a subsequence.

For any open $\Omega\subset\mathbb C$, using the ordinary compact-open metric of d12:11-01: Finite-valued Montel: A family $\mathcal F\subset\Hol(\Omega)$ is locally bounded if and only if every sequence in it has a locally uniformly convergent subsequence with finite holomorphic limit. Equivalently its closure in $\Hol(\Omega)$ is compact.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON VII.2 pp.153--154 (PDF167--168); SS8.3.2 pp.225--227 (PDF244--246).

Vitali convergence: Let $\Omega$ be a domain and $(f_n)$ locally bounded in $\Hol(\Omega)$. If $f_n$ converges at every point of a set having an accumulation point in $\Omega$, it converges locally uniformly on $\Omega$ to a holomorphic function.

For meromorphic scalar functions on a domain $\Omega$ (which exclude the identically-infinity function), with infinity adjoined among permitted limits, and with $\chi(\infty,\infty)=0$ and symmetry for its other mixed values: Spherical limits: Use the chordal metric
\[
 \chi(z,w)=\frac{|z-w|}{\sqrt{1+|z|^2}\sqrt{1+|w|^2}},\qquad
 \chi(z,\infty)=\frac1{\sqrt{1+|z|^2}}
\]
on $\Chat$. It is a compact complete metric with the sphere topology. A locally uniform spherical limit of meromorphic maps on a domain is meromorphic or identically infinity. If the original functions are holomorphic and finite, the limit is finite holomorphic or identically infinity. The space of meromorphic maps together with the constant infinity is complete in the compact-open chordal metric. Spherical normality does not imply local ordinary boundedness.

On any plane domain the constant holomorphic functions $f_n(z)=n$ converge uniformly in the chordal metric to the constant infinity, hence form a spherically normal family, while their ordinary values are not locally bounded. This supplies the spherical/finite-normality distinction.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON VII.3 pp.155--157 (PDF169--171), including the constant-infinity convention.

Here spherical normality means that every sequence has a locally uniformly chordally convergent subsequence whose limit is meromorphic or identically infinity. Marty's criterion: For a meromorphic map put $f^\#=|f'|/(1+|f|^2)$ off its poles, and use $(1/f)^\#$ at a pole. This is continuous and well defined. A family of meromorphic maps on a domain is spherically normal if and only if its spherical derivatives are locally bounded.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON VII.3 pp.157--160 (PDF171--174); forward proof and exercise-converse checked and completed here.

The mapping proof obtains square roots from the homotopy-Cauchy logarithm theorem d12:04-06 and does not use the later connected-complement characterization. This is proof-routing context, not an extra result.

The inequality on the complex derivative means it is a positive real number. A bounded univalent class: If a proper domain $\Omega$ admits a holomorphic square root of every zero-free holomorphic function, then, for $z_0\in\Omega$, there exists an injective holomorphic $h:\Omega\to\D$ with $h(z_0)=0$ and $h'(z_0)>0$.

The extremal map fills the disk: Let $\Omega\subsetneqq\mathbb C$ be a domain such that every zero-free holomorphic function on $\Omega$ has a holomorphic square root. For every $z_0\in\Omega$ there is a biholomorphism $F:\Omega\to\mathbb D$ with $F(z_0)=0$ and $F'(z_0)$ positive real.

The inequality on the complex derivative means it is a positive real number; no boundary extension is part of this theorem. Normalized planar Riemann mapping: For a nonempty simply connected proper plane domain and $z_0$ in it, there is a unique biholomorphism $F:\Omega\to\D$ such that $F(z_0)=0$ and $F'(z_0)>0$.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON VII.4 pp.160--164 (PDF174--178); AHL VI.1 pp.229--232; SS8.3 pp.224--231 (PDF243--250).

Line and circle reflection: Let a disk centered on a real interval be split into upper and lower halves. If $f$ is holomorphic in the upper half, continuous on it together with the interval, and real on the interval, its extension $F(z)=\overline{f(\bar z)}$ in the lower half is holomorphic on the whole disk. The conjugated assertion holds for any source and target generalized circles, locally away from a chosen chart pole.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: SS2.5.4 pp.57--60 (PDF76--79); CON IX.1 pp.210--213 (PDF224--227).

Analytic free arcs: Suppose source and target boundary arcs have parametrizations extending to injective holomorphic maps on neighborhoods of real intervals, with nonzero derivative, and the adjacent domains lie locally on one side. A holomorphic map on the source side, continuous through the arc and mapping the arc into the target arc, extends holomorphically across every interior arc point. If it is a conformal equivalence, is one-to-one on the arc, and carries the given sides to one another, its extension has nonzero derivative there.

Conditional Schwarz--Christoffel formula: Let $P$ be a bounded simple polygonal domain with vertices $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ and interior angles $\pi\alpha_j$, $0<\alpha_j<2$. Suppose a biholomorphism $F:\{\Imm z>0\}\to P$ is already given with a homeomorphic extension of the compactified boundaries. If the vertices correspond to finite real points $a_1<\cdots<a_n$ and infinity corresponds to an interior side point, then
\[
 F'(z)=C\prod_{j=1}^n(z-a_j)^{\alpha_j-1},\qquad C\ne0,
\]
where each factor uses its upper-half-plane logarithm. Hence $F(z)=A+C\int_{z_*}^z\prod(\zeta-a_j)^{\alpha_j-1}\dd\zeta$ for $z_* $ in the half-plane. If infinity corresponds to the last vertex, the product has just the finite $n-1$ prevertices. The finite-vertex local behavior is $F(z)-v_j=(z-a_j)^{\alpha_j}u_j(z)$, with a nonvanishing holomorphic factor after selecting the indicated branch.

The Schwarz-Christoffel assertion assumes the biholomorphism and compactified-boundary homeomorphism already exist. Accessory-parameter existence, general Jordan boundary extension and Schwarz-Christoffel existence are deferred.

All domains of harmonic or holomorphic functions in this statement are open subsets of $\mathbb C$; a real $C^2$ function means twice continuously differentiable in the two real coordinates. The differential definition: A real harmonic function is initially a $C^2$ function $u$ with $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$. Real and imaginary parts of a holomorphic function are harmonic. If $F:V\to U$ is holomorphic and $u$ harmonic on $U$, then $u\circ F$ is harmonic on $V$, including at critical points of $F$.

Let $u:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ with $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$ on an open plane set. A conjugate $v$ means a real function for which $u+iv$ is holomorphic. Conjugates and periods: Every harmonic function has a harmonic conjugate locally. On a domain it has a global single-valued conjugate if and only if the real one-form $-u_y\,dx+u_x\,dy$ has zero integral around every closed piecewise $C^1$ path. The conjugate is unique up to a real constant. In particular it exists on simply connected domains. Harmonic functions are consequently $C^\infty$ and real analytic locally.

The real harmonic function $u(z)=\log|z|$ on $\mathbb C^*$ has conjugate one-form $-u_y\,dx+u_x\,dy=d\arg z$, with integral $2\pi$ around a positively oriented circle surrounding zero. It therefore has no global single-valued harmonic conjugate on $\mathbb C^*$.

For real harmonic functions on open plane sets, with the constancy assertion requiring a domain (nonempty, open and connected): Mean values and maximum principles: A harmonic function equals its average on every circle whose closed disk lies in its domain. On a domain an attained maximum or minimum forces constancy. On a bounded open set, $\limsup_{z\to\xi}u(z)\le M$ at every boundary point implies $u\le M$. Conversely a continuous real function with the circle mean-value property on every sufficiently small disk is harmonic.

For every $R>0$, with an interior circle understood to have its closed disk contained in the harmonic function's domain: Poisson and the disk Dirichlet problem: For continuous real $\phi$ on $|\zeta|=R$, $R>0$, put
\[
 P\phi(z)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
 \frac{R^2-|z|^2}{|Re^{\iu t}-z|^2}\phi(Re^{\iu t})\dd t,
 \qquad |z|<R.
\]
It is harmonic, extends continuously to the circle as $\phi$, and is the unique continuous closed-disk harmonic solution. Every harmonic $u$ satisfies this formula with its own values on each interior circle.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: FOR22.3--22.5 printed176--178 (PDF185--187); AHL VI.3 pp.241--244.

For $R>0$ and all $|z|<R$: Schwarz integral: If $f$ is holomorphic in $|z|<R$ and its real part extends continuously to the closed disk with boundary values $\phi$, then
\[
 f(z)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
 \frac{Re^{\iu t}+z}{Re^{\iu t}-z}\phi(Re^{\iu t})\dd t
 +\iu\Imm f(0).
\]

Here $R>0$, $0\le r<R$, all limits are for $n\to\infty$, and the increasing sequence need not be nonnegative (the first member can be subtracted). Harnack inequality and convergence: For $u\ge0$ harmonic on $B(a,R)$ and $|z-a|=r<R$,
\[
 \frac{R-r}{R+r}u(a)\le u(z)\le\frac{R+r}{R-r}u(a).
\]
An increasing sequence of real harmonic functions on a domain either converges locally uniformly to a finite harmonic function or tends to $+\infty$ uniformly on every compact subset.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: FOR22.6 printed178--179 (PDF187--188); AHL VI.3 pp.242--244.

Harmonic reflection and removable punctures: A harmonic function on a half-disk, continuous and zero on its diameter, extends harmonically by odd reflection. A bounded real harmonic function on a punctured disk extends harmonically across the puncture.

$\log|z|$ is real harmonic on every punctured disk centered at zero and has no finite harmonic extension across zero, demonstrating that the boundedness assumption for harmonic removability is essential.

Continuous subharmonic functions: A continuous real $u$ on an open set is subharmonic if on each closed interior disk it is bounded above by the harmonic Poisson extension of its boundary values. Equivalently it has the submean property on every interior circle; equivalently it obeys comparison with every harmonic function continuous on such a closed disk.

Operations and harmonic replacement: Nonnegative linear combinations and finite maxima of continuous subharmonic functions are subharmonic. Replacing $u$ on an interior disk $B$ by its harmonic Poisson extension $H$ gives a continuous subharmonic function $u^B\ge u$. The replacement is monotone in $u$. A local subharmonic function may also be pasted by taking its maximum with another subharmonic function, when its boundary limsup is at most the latter and the resulting function is continuous.

Perron's harmonic envelope: Let $\Omega$ be a bounded domain and $\phi:\partial\Omega\to\R$ continuous. Let $\mathcal P_\phi$ consist of continuous subharmonic $u$ on $\Omega$ with $\limsup_{z\to\xi}u(z)\le\phi(\xi)$ at every boundary point. Then
$H_\phi(z)=\sup_{u\in\mathcal P_\phi}u(z)$ is finite and harmonic on $\Omega$.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: FOR22.8--22.13 printed179--182 (PDF188--191); CON X.3--4 pp.263--270 (PDF277--284).

Let $\Omega$ be a bounded plane domain and $\phi:\partial\Omega\to\mathbb R$ continuous, with Perron class/envelope as in d12:14-03. Superharmonic means the negative is continuous subharmonic. Barrier squeeze: A positive local barrier at $\xi\in\partial\Omega$ is a continuous superharmonic function $b$ on $\Omega\cap B(\xi,r)$, extending continuously to its relative closure, with $b(\xi)=0$ and $b>0$ at all other points there. Its existence implies $H_\phi(z)\to\phi(\xi)$ for every continuous boundary datum. Such a boundary point is called regular.

Regularity and barriers refer to bounded plane domains and the continuous real Dirichlet data/Perron envelope defined above. Explicit regular points and a failure: Disk boundary points and boundary points with an exterior cone are regular. An exterior tangent disk also gives a barrier. The puncture of a punctured disk is not regular for arbitrary continuous data on that domain's boundary.

On $\Omega=\mathbb D\setminus\{0\}$ the boundary datum $\phi$ equal to zero on $|z|=1$ and equal to one at the isolated boundary point $0$ is continuous on $\partial\Omega$. There is no real harmonic function on $\Omega$ continuous on $\overline\Omega$ with boundary values $\phi$. Its continuous-subharmonic Perron envelope $H_\phi$ is identically zero, so the puncture is not a regular point.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: FOR22.14--22.18 printed182--184 (PDF191--193); CON X.4 pp.269--275 (PDF283--289).

The regular Dirichlet problem: On a bounded domain every boundary point of which has a barrier, every continuous real boundary datum has a unique harmonic solution continuous on the closure. The solution is $H_\phi$, lies between the minimum and maximum of its boundary data, and depends linearly and positively on those data.

Circular exhaustions and the Green identity: Every plane domain has an exhaustion $D_j$ by connected finite unions of open disks, with $\overline D_j\subset D_{j+1}\Subset\Omega$, such that circle boundaries have no tangencies or triple intersections. These are regular domains. Their boundaries consist of finitely many analytic arcs and corners of interior angle in $(0,2\pi)$. If a harmonic function on $D_j$ is continuous and zero on a boundary arc through a corner of angle $\theta$, then near that corner
$u=O(r^{\alpha})$, $\nabla u=O(r^{\alpha-1})$, $\alpha=\pi/\theta>0$.
Consequently the second Green identity applies to pairs of their Green functions after removing poles and corners, and its corner boundary terms tend to zero.

The prior Green identity applies with its actual $C^2$ near-closure hypotheses on a bounded $C^1$ or specified piecewise domain. The separately stated circular-exhaustion/corner lemma supplies the additional hypotheses here; no general boundary PDE regularity theorem is assumed.

For every bounded plane domain $\Omega$ and every pole $a\in\Omega$, with $g_\Omega(\cdot,a)>0$ on $\Omega\setminus\{a\}$, the normalized-pole correction is required to extend harmonically over $a$. Least means pointwise least among all positive functions harmonic off $a$ with that normalized logarithmic singularity. Symmetry means $g_\Omega(z,a)=g_\Omega(a,z)$ for distinct $z,a\in\Omega$; invariance means $g_{\Omega\prime}(F(z),F(a))=g_\Omega(z,a)$ for a biholomorphism $F:\Omega\to\Omega\prime$ of bounded domains. Regular means having the local barriers of d12:14-04. Green functions, symmetry and invariance: Every bounded domain has a canonical positive Green function $g_\Omega(z,a)$: it is harmonic for $z\ne a$, and $g_\Omega(z,a)+\log|z-a|$ is harmonic at $a$. It is the least positive function with these properties. It is symmetric in $z,a$ and invariant under biholomorphisms between bounded domains. At every regular boundary point it tends to zero. On a bounded regular domain it is the unique Green function continuous with value zero at all boundary points, and is obtained by solving the boundary correction $\log|\xi-a|$.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON X.5 pp.275--278 (PDF289--292) proves bounded regular existence and invariance; its Green identity exercise is expanded here with an actual exhaustion and corner control.

Here regular means every boundary point has a local barrier, $m\ge1$, $1\le j\le m$, and all component data $c_j$ are real. Harmonic measures of boundary components: Suppose a bounded regular domain has finitely many disjoint compact boundary components $C_1,\ldots,C_m$. There are unique continuous closed-domain harmonic functions $\omega_j$ equal to one on $C_j$ and zero on the others. They satisfy $0\le\omega_j\le1$, $\sum_j\omega_j=1$, and the solution with constant component data $c_j$ is $\sum_jc_j\omega_j$. If $m>1$, each $\omega_j$ lies strictly between zero and one in the domain.

Here $n$ ranges over positive integers and $K_n\subset\Omega$; exhaustion of compact subsets means every compact $L\subset\Omega$ is contained in some $K_n$. A compatible compact exhaustion: Every open $\Omega\subset\C$ has compact sets $K_n\subset\operatorname{int}K_{n+1}$ exhausting its compact subsets, such that every component of $\Chat\setminus K_n$ meets $\Chat\setminus\Omega$. They may be chosen as finite unions of closed grid cells with selected bounded holes filled. Empty open sets and empty compact stages are allowed.

A finite polygon representation: If $K$ is compact, $K\subset U$ open, and $f\in\Hol(U)$, there is a finite oriented polygonal cycle $\Gamma$ in $U\setminus K$ such that
\[
 f(z)=\frac1{2\pi\iu}\int_\Gamma\frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}\dd\zeta\qquad(z\in K).
\] For $K=\varnothing$ the zero cycle is permitted.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON VIII.1 pp.195--197 (PDF209--211); SS2.5.5 Lemma5.8 pp.61--62 (PDF80--81).

Rational Riemann sums: If $K\subset\mathbb C$ is compact, $U\supset K$ is open, $f\in\operatorname{Hol}(U)$ and the finite oriented polygonal cycle $\Gamma\subset U\setminus K$ represents $f$ on $K$ by $f(z)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma f(\zeta)/(\zeta-z)\,d\zeta$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a rational function with poles on the trace of $\Gamma$ whose uniform error from $f$ on $K$ is less than $\varepsilon$. In particular the poles lie outside $K$.

Runge with specified allowed poles: Let $K\subset\C$ be compact and let $A\subset\Chat\setminus K$ meet every component of that spherical complement. Every function holomorphic on a neighborhood of $K$ is uniformly approximable on $K$ by rational functions with all poles in $A$. A nonconstant polynomial part gives a pole at infinity, permitted only when infinity belongs to $A$.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON VIII.1 pp.195--200 (PDF209--214); SS2.5.5 pp.60--64 (PDF79--83).

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb C$ be any open set, including the empty or disconnected case. Approximation on an open set: If $A\subset\Chat\setminus\Omega$ meets each component of that complement, every $f\in\Hol(\Omega)$ is a locally uniform limit of rational functions with poles in $A$. If $\Chat\setminus\Omega$ is connected, polynomials suffice. No connectedness of $\Omega$ is needed.

For an annulus surrounding zero, $f(z)=1/z$ cannot be uniformly approximated by polynomials on any positively oriented circle in that annulus surrounding zero, and hence cannot be approximated locally uniformly on the annulus by polynomials: its circle integral is $2\pi i$, while every polynomial circle integral is zero.

The planar polynomial hull: The polynomial hull $\widehat K=\{a:|p(a)|\le\sup_K|p|\text{ for every polynomial }p\}$ of a nonempty compact plane set is $K$ together with all bounded components of $\C\setminus K$. For the empty compact set the hull is empty, with the convention that constants separate every point from the empty set.

A plane domain is nonempty, open and connected; the full plane is included. Zero closed-path periods quantify over all closed piecewise $C^1$ paths. Primitives, logarithms and roots are single-valued holomorphic functions; an $n$th root is required for every integer $n\ge1$. Planar equivalences, with no circular prerequisite: For a plane domain the following are equivalent: simple connectivity; connected spherical complement; zero closed-path periods for every holomorphic function; existence of primitives for every holomorphic function; existence of logarithms for every zero-free holomorphic function; existence of square roots for every such function; and existence of all positive-integer roots for every such function.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON VIII.2 pp.200--204 (PDF214--218); FB IV AppendixA pp.233--238 (PDF239--244).

The scalar product is the limit of ordered partial products. In the holomorphic assertion $K$ ranges over all compact subsets of the open set and factors may have zeros; the identically-zero and exact-order clauses are componentwise. Infinite products and logarithms: For nonzero complex factors $u_n$, convergence of their product to a nonzero value is equivalent to $u_n\to1$ and convergence of the series of principal logarithms of a sufficiently late tail. In particular $\sum|u_n-1|<\infty$ ensures nonzero product convergence. If $u_n$ are holomorphic on an open set and $\sum\sup_K|u_n-1|<\infty$ on every compact subset, their products converge locally uniformly to a holomorphic function. On a component where no factor is identically zero, the local zero order of the product is the sum of the zero orders of the factors; only finitely many terms of this sum are nonzero. If a factor is identically zero on a component, the product is identically zero there instead. A tail has no zeros on any fixed compact neighborhood once its factors are sufficiently close to one.

For every integer $p\ge0$ the indicated $E_p$ is entire. Canonical factors: Put $E_0(w)=1-w$ and $E_p(w)=(1-w)\exp(w+w^2/2+\cdots+w^p/p)$ for $p\ge1$. It has precisely one zero, a simple zero at one. For $|w|\le1/2$,
\[
 |\log E_p(w)|\le2|w|^{p+1},\qquad
 |E_p(w)-1|\le6|w|^{p+1},
\]
where the logarithm is the branch zero at zero.

An effective divisor assigns positive integer multiplicities to a discrete set and is locally finite on the plane; all specified multiplicities, including multiplicity $m\ge0$ at zero, must be exact and there must be no other zeros. Entire prescribed zeros: Every locally finite effective divisor in $\C$ is the exact zero divisor of an entire function. If its nonzero points, repeated by positive multiplicity, are $a_n$ with $|a_n|\to\infty$, one may use
$z^m\prod_n E_n(z/a_n)$, where $m$ is the prescribed multiplicity at zero. Empty and finite divisors use the corresponding finite products.

Entire factorization: Every entire $f\not\equiv0$ has a representation
$f(z)=z^m e^{g(z)}\prod_n E_{p_n}(z/a_n)$,
where $g$ is entire, the $a_n$ list its nonzero zeros with multiplicity, and suitable nonnegative integers $p_n$ can be chosen, for example $p_n=n$. This is not the stronger finite-order degree bound of Chapter~\ref{ch:d12-17}. Here $m\ge0$ is the zero multiplicity at zero; finite or empty zero divisors use finite or empty products, including nonzero constants.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON VII.5 pp.169--170 (PDF183--184); SS5.3--5.4 pp.140--147 (PDF159--166).

For any open $\Omega\subset\mathbb C$, possibly empty or disconnected, and any locally finite set of designated zeros carrying positive integer multiplicities: Prescribed zeros on a general open set: Every locally finite effective divisor on an open plane set is the exact zero divisor of a holomorphic function there, chosen nonzero on every component outside its designated zeros.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON VII.5 Theorem5.15 pp.170--173 (PDF184--187), nearest-complement factors and infinity normalization checked explicitly.

Scalar meromorphic excludes identically infinity; the quotient is interpreted meromorphically at zeros of $h$. Holomorphic quotients: Every scalar meromorphic function $f$ on an open plane set is $g/h$ with $g,h$ holomorphic and $h$ nonzero on each component away from its locally finite zero set.

Here $\Omega\subset\mathbb C$ is open, with no connectedness assumption, $m_a$ is finite, and the coefficients $c_{ak}\in\mathbb C$ may all vanish at a designated point. The difference statement means differences are holomorphic on all of $\Omega$ and adding any holomorphic function gives another solution. Mittag--Leffler on an open plane set: Let $A$ be a locally finite subset of an open $\Omega$, and prescribe at each $a\in A$ a finite principal part $P_a(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{m_a}c_{ak}(z-a)^{-k}$. There is a meromorphic $f$ with these principal parts and no other poles. A designated point is an actual pole exactly when its prescribed principal part is nonzero. All solutions differ by a holomorphic function.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON VIII.3 pp.204--208 (PDF218--222); FB IV.3 pp.219--222 (PDF225--228). The finite-polynomial principal parts here give meromorphic functions; FB's more general entire encodings may prescribe essential singularities and are not silently conflated with them.

The cotangent identity is on $\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Z$ and the sine identity on all of $\mathbb C$, with the product taken in the indicated increasing order $n=1,2,\ldots$. Cotangent and sine: Off the integer poles,
\[
 \pi\cot(\pi z)=\frac1z+\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{2z}{z^2-n^2},
 \qquad
 \sin(\pi z)=\pi z\prod_{n\ge1}\left(1-\frac{z^2}{n^2}\right).
\]
The paired series and product converge locally uniformly on their appropriate domains. Their pairing/order is part of the stated formulas.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: FB III.7 cotangent partial fractions and IV.3 pp.220--223 (PDF226--229); SS5.3.2 pp.142--145 (PDF161--164).
The identically-zero function is excluded from all zero-divisor and order statements in this chapter. Zeros and poles are repeated according to multiplicity.

Assume $R>0$ and $f$ is not identically zero, with all zeros and poles listed according to multiplicity. Poisson--Jensen and Jensen: Let $f$ be meromorphic on a neighborhood of $\{|z|\le R\}$, with no
zero or pole on its boundary, and let $a_j,b_j$ be its zeros and poles
inside. For $|z|<R$ away from those points,
\[
 \log|f(z)|=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
 \Ree\frac{Re^{\iu t}+z}{Re^{\iu t}-z}\log|f(Re^{\iu t})|\,dt
 -\sum_j G_R(z,a_j)+\sum_jG_R(z,b_j),
\]
where $G_R(z,a)=\log\left|\dfrac{R^2-\bar a z}{R(z-a)}\right|$.
If $f(0)$ is finite and nonzero, then
\[
 \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|f(Re^{\iu t})|\,dt
 =\log|f(0)|+\sum_j\log\frac R{|a_j|}-\sum_j\log\frac R{|b_j|}.
\]

Let $R>0$ and $f$ be a nonzero scalar meromorphic function on a neighborhood of $\{|z|\le R\}$. In this statement the full center formula is $\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|f(Re^{it})|dt=\log|g(0)|+m\log R+\sum_{0<|a_j|<R}\log(R/|a_j|)-\sum_{0<|b_j|<R}\log(R/|b_j|)$, with boundary terms allowed since they are zero. The center and boundary zeros: If $f(z)=z^m g(z)$ near zero, where $m\in\Z$ and $g(0)$ is finite and
nonzero, Jensen's formula instead has center term
$\log|g(0)|+m\log R$ and counts only nonzero interior zeros and poles.
For a function meromorphic on a neighborhood of the closed disk,
$\log|f(Re^{\iu t})|$ is integrable even when boundary zeros or poles
occur. Jensen's center formula remains valid, with boundary divisor
terms contributing zero. The displayed Poisson--Jensen theorem above
is used only on divisor-free boundary circles.

For every $r>0$ zeros are counted with multiplicity, including zeros on the counting circle. Counting zeros: If $f$ is entire and $f(0)=1$, let $n(r)$ count its zeros in $|z|\le r$.
Then $n(r)\log2\le\log M(2r)$, where
$M(r)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|$. For a general nonzero entire function first
factor its center zero and normalize the nonzero remaining value.

Here $M(r)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|$, all nonzero zeros $a_j$ are repeated with multiplicity, and the infimum/least-integer conventions are as stated. Order, exponent, rank and genus: For a nonzero entire function set
\[
 \rho=\limsup_{r\to\infty}
       \frac{\log\log\max(e,M(r))}{\log r}\in[0,\infty].
\]
Nonzero constants and polynomials have order zero. For its nonzero
zeros $a_j$, let
$\lambda=\inf\{s>0:\sum_j|a_j|^{-s}<\infty\}$, with infimum
$+\infty$ for an empty set of admissible exponents and with $\lambda=0$
for a finite divisor. The canonical rank is the least integer $q\ge0$
such that $\sum|a_j|^{-q-1}<\infty$, or is infinite if none exists.
Write $E_q(w)=(1-w)\exp(w+\cdots+w^q/q)$, with $E_0(w)=1-w$.
If $f=z^m\prod E_q(z/a_j)e^{Q(z)}$ with $Q$ polynomial, its genus is
$\max(q,\deg Q)$; constants have degree convention zero here.

Let $f$ be a nonzero entire function of finite order $\rho$, with nonzero zeros $a_j$ repeated with multiplicity, convergence exponent $\lambda$ and canonical rank $q$ as in d12:17-04; $n(r)$ in the infinite-sequence formula counts these nonzero zeros in $|z|\le r$. Growth of the divisor: For a finite-order entire function, $\lambda\le\rho$ and
$q\le\lfloor\rho\rfloor$. If the nonzero zero sequence is infinite,
its counting function satisfies
$\lambda=\limsup_{r\to\infty}\log\max(1,n(r))/\log r$.
Whenever $q$ is finite, $q\le\lambda\le q+1$.

Here $0≤ρ<∞$ and $(a_j)$ is a locally finite nonzero plane divisor with multiplicities, $n(r)$ counts its elements in $|z|\le r$, and the hypothesis means that for each $s>\rho$ there is a finite constant $C_s$ with the displayed counting bound. The canonical factors are those of d12:16-02. Circles avoiding a canonical divisor: Let $\rho<\infty$, $p=\lfloor\rho\rfloor$, and suppose
$n(r)\le C_s r^s$ for every $s>\rho$. For
$P(z)=\prod_jE_p(z/a_j)$ and each $\rho<t<p+1$, there are radii
$r_k\to\infty$ and a constant $C_t$ such that
\[
                   \log|P(z)|\ge-C_t r_k^t\quad (|z|=r_k).
\]
The empty or finite product is included.

Here $m\ge0$ is the multiplicity at zero and the $a_j$ enumerate exactly all nonzero zeros with multiplicity; empty and finite products are included. The product is locally uniformly convergent and the displayed equality holds for all $z\in\mathbb C$, with genus and minimal canonical rank as defined in d12:17-04. Hadamard factorization: Every nonzero entire function of finite order $\rho$ has the factorization
\[
 f(z)=z^m e^{Q(z)}\prod_jE_p(z/a_j),\qquad
 p=\lfloor\rho\rfloor,\qquad\deg Q\le p.
\]
It also has a factorization using its minimal canonical rank $q$, with
exponential polynomial of degree at most $p$; its genus is at most $\rho$.

All listed $a_j$ lie in $\mathbb D\setminus\{0\}$, with zeros repeated according to multiplicity; finite and empty lists are included. Normal convergence means local uniform convergence on $\mathbb D$. Blaschke zeros and products: The nonzero zeros $a_j$ of a bounded, nonzero holomorphic function on
$\D$ satisfy $\sum_j(1-|a_j|)<\infty$. Conversely, a disk sequence
without interior accumulation satisfying this condition is the exact
zero sequence, with its listed multiplicities, of the bounded product
\[
             B(z)=z^m\prod_j\frac{|a_j|}{a_j}
                                      \frac{a_j-z}{1-\bar a_jz}.
\]
Here $m\ge0$ prescribes the center multiplicity; the product converges
normally and $|B|\le1$.

Finite-order value consequences: A nonconstant finite-order entire function omitting $a$ is
$a+e^{Q}$ for a nonconstant polynomial $Q$; it omits no other finite
value. A nonconstant entire function of finite nonintegral order assumes
every finite value infinitely often.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON XI.1--3, printed pp.280--290 (PDF pp.294--304), including
the center, meromorphic and Blaschke variants listed as exercises there;
SS V.5, printed pp.147--152 (PDF pp.166--171), for the avoiding-circle
growth route. The proof here supplies its own lower-product estimates
and real-part coefficient argument; an order infimum is never assumed
to be an attained exact growth bound.
All base domains in Chapter 19 are plane domains; paths are continuous, with piecewise differentiability required only for the displayed period integrals.

Every nonempty open connected subset of $\mathbb C$ is polygonally connected: for any two of its points there is a finite polygonal path in the set joining them. This repeats the earlier adopted polygonal-connectivity lemma d12:03:polygonal-connectivity and may be covered by that same result.

The base $\Omega$ is a plane domain and paths are continuous. A representative defining a germ at $a$ is defined on a neighborhood of $a$. Elements, germs and continuation: A function element is a holomorphic function on a connected open set. Two
elements near $a$ have the same germ $[f]_a$ if they agree on a neighborhood
of $a$. Along $\gamma:[0,1]\to\Omega$, a continuation of $\varphi$ is a
family $\varphi_t$ of germs at $\gamma(t)$, with $\varphi_0=\varphi$, which
is locally represented by one holomorphic function: near each parameter $s$
there are an open set $U$, a holomorphic $f$ on $U$, and a parameter interval
$I$ containing $s$ such that $\gamma(I)\subset U$ and
$\varphi_t=[f]_{\gamma(t)}$ for $t\in I$.

Fix a continuous path in a plane domain and an initial holomorphic germ at its initial point; concatenation applies to compatible continuations with matching terminal/initial germs. Uniqueness along a fixed path: Continuation, if it exists, is unique after its initial germ is fixed.
It can be reversed or concatenated, and is unchanged by an increasing
homeomorphic reparametrization of the parameter interval.

Fix a continuous $\gamma:[0,1]\to\Omega$ in a plane domain and initial germ at $\gamma(0)$; the finite-chain criterion requires its first germ to be that prescribed initial germ. The germ-space projection sends $[f]_z$ to $z$. Finite chains and continuous germ families: Continuation is equivalent to the existence of a partition
$0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=1$, connected open sets $U_j$ containing
$\gamma([t_{j-1},t_j])$, and holomorphic functions $f_j$ on $U_j$, such
that $f_j$ and $f_{j+1}$ agree on the component of $U_j\cap U_{j+1}$
containing $\gamma(t_j)$. The initial and final germs are those of $f_1$
and $f_N$. It is also equivalent to a continuous lift into the germ space
whose basic open sets are $\{[f]_z:z\in U\}$.

Along any continuous path in a plane domain, starting with germs which possess the indicated continuations and a relation valid for their initial representatives: Permanence of relations: Derivatives, sums and products continue by differentiating, adding and
multiplying the local representatives. A holomorphic identity between
finitely many simultaneously continued functions and their derivatives,
with single-valued holomorphic coefficients on the base, persists along
the path. Quotients are included wherever the denominator is nonzero.
Permanence of relations propagates a relation among functions whose simultaneous continuations already exist. It is not an existence theorem for a differential equation or an absent continuation.

All paths have parameter interval $[0,1]$ and lie in the same plane domain. In the varying-terminal-point clause the initial endpoint and initial germ remain fixed. Stability of a continuation chain: If $\varphi$ continues along $\gamma$, there is $\delta>0$ such that every
path $\eta$ with the same endpoints and
$\sup_t|\eta(t)-\gamma(t)|<\delta$ has a continuation with the same
terminal germ. With a varying terminal point, the terminal germ is that
of the same final representative at the new point.

Here $\Omega$ is a plane domain and $\varphi$ is a holomorphic germ at $a\in\Omega$; the hypothesis is actual continuation along every intermediate path of this given homotopy, including endpoints. Homotopy invariance: Let $H:[0,1]^2\to\Omega$ be continuous, with $H(0,s)=a$ and $H(1,s)=b$.
Suppose the germ $\varphi$ at $a$ admits continuation along every path
$t\mapsto H(t,s)$. All the resulting terminal germs at $b$ agree.

Here $\Omega$ is a plane domain and the resulting unique function has the given germ at $a$; the continuation assumption is along every continuous path in $\Omega$ starting at $a$. Monodromy: Suppose $\Omega$ is simply connected and a holomorphic germ at $a\in\Omega$
admits continuation along every path starting at $a$. It is the germ of a
unique holomorphic function on $\Omega$.

For roots the degree $n$ is any positive integer. The change of a logarithm is additive and that of the root is multiplicative after continuation around the loop with fixed initial germ; natural boundary means no holomorphic extension across any point of $|z|=1$. Monodromy and obstructions: A logarithm germ at a point of $\C^*$ continues along every path in
$\C^*$. Around a piecewise $C^1$ loop $\gamma$ its change is
$2\pi\iu\ind(\gamma,0)$. An $n$th-root germ changes by the factor
$\exp(2\pi\iu\ind(\gamma,0)/n)$. Simple connectivity alone does not
guarantee continuation. Moreover
\[
                         F(z)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty z^{n!}
\]
is holomorphic on $\D$ and has the unit circle as a natural boundary. The root germ continues along every path in $\mathbb C^*$ and returns after a closed loop precisely when its index is divisible by $n$.

The holomorphic germ of $(1-z)^{-1}$ at zero cannot be continued holomorphically through $1$, for example along the straight path from $0$ to $1$, even though the proposed larger base $\mathbb C$ is simply connected. Thus simple connectivity without the every-path continuation hypothesis does not ensure continuation.

Source-comparison attribution and proof-provenance commentary only; it creates no independent obligation and imports no unproved textbook result. Source text: CON IX.1--3, printed pp.210--221 (PDF pp.224--235),
especially printed pp.217--220 (PDF pp.231--234);
FOR \S7.1--7.8, printed pp.44--48 (PDF pp.53--57).
The all-intermediate-path hypothesis is retained explicitly; no surface
uniformization or future covering theorem is used.
The all-intermediate-path continuation hypothesis of homotopy invariance is retained; no surface uniformization or later covering theorem is assumed.

A Riemann surface is a nonempty connected Hausdorff second-countable topological space equipped with an atlas of homeomorphisms onto plane domains such that every transition map is holomorphic and has holomorphic inverse. Compatible atlases determine the same complex structure. Every plane domain, with its identity chart, is a Riemann surface; under this connected convention a disconnected open subset of C is a union of such surfaces, rather than one Riemann surface.
The union of compatible Riemann-surface atlases is again a compatible atlas. Consequently adjoining all compatible charts gives a uniquely determined maximal atlas for the complex structure.
Every connected Riemann surface is path connected.

The projective quotient CP^1=(C^2\{0})/C* by nonzero scalar multiplication, with its quotient topology, is a compact Riemann surface. The charts [1:z]↦z and [w:1]↦w identify it with the Riemann sphere Ĉ; the infinity coordinate is w=1/z.

For a continuous map f:X→Y between Riemann surfaces, holomorphicity means holomorphicity of its coordinate expressions, and this condition is independent of the charts. If f is nonconstant, each a∈X has a chart-independent positive integer multiplicity m_a and source/target holomorphic coordinates centered at a and f(a) in which f is exactly t↦t^{m_a}. The map is locally biholomorphic at a if and only if m_a=1.

Given one holomorphic plane germ with base in the plane domain Ω, the germs obtainable from it by analytic continuation form a Riemann surface S. The basepoint projection p:S→Ω is locally biholomorphic, and evaluation [f]_z↦f(z) is holomorphic. The full space of all holomorphic germs need not be second countable: the surface assertion is specifically about the single continuation component.
A covering map p:E→B is a map such that each point of B has a neighborhood U whose inverse image is a disjoint union of open subsets, each mapped homeomorphically onto U by p.

For a covering map p:E→B, each continuous path in B has a unique lift after choosing an initial point of E above its initial point. A fixed-endpoint path homotopy has a continuous lift with prescribed constant initial lift edge, and the terminal endpoints of the lifted paths agree.
The maps exp:C→C* and z↦z^n:C*→C* (for every positive integer n) are holomorphic coverings; the power covering has exactly n sheets.

The restricted exponential exp:C\{0}→C* is surjective and locally biholomorphic but is not a covering. For ε>0 the base path t↦e^t on −ε≤t≤0, with initial lift −ε, has no lift on the entire interval in C\{0}, since the unique lift in the full exponential covering ends at the excluded point 0.
Every scalar-valued holomorphic function f:X→C on a compact Riemann surface X is constant. The target here is C, rather than a sphere-valued meromorphic map.

Let X be a compact Riemann surface and Y a connected Riemann surface. Every nonconstant holomorphic map f:X→Y is surjective, has finite fibres and finitely many ramification points. There is a positive integer d, independent of b∈Y, such that ∑_{a∈f^{-1}(b)}m_a=d for every b∈Y. Away from its finitely many branch values f is a finite covering (of degree d).

For r>0, every connected finite holomorphic covering of the punctured disk {z:0<|z|<r} with m sheets, m a positive integer, is biholomorphically equivalent as a covering to t↦t^m from {t:0<|t|<r^{1/m}}. It admits a completion by exactly one added point with local coordinate t, ramification multiplicity m, and extended projection z=t^m.
A possibly disconnected finite holomorphic covering of a punctured disk completes by applying the connected cyclic-cover completion to each monodromy cycle, adding one point for each cycle.

Source comparison references to Conway IX.6, selected Forster §§1–2,7–8, and Ahlfors VIII.1.2–1.7, together with editorial descriptions of supplied proofs. These are citation/provenance context and do not add mathematical obligations beyond the chapter statements.
Polynomial coefficients are complex. An analytic branch is an actual holomorphic function on a specified open set satisfying the equation, rather than a pointwise selection of roots.

Let P(z,w) be a polynomial in w with coefficients holomorphic in z near a. If P(a,b)=0 and P_w(a,b)≠0, there are neighborhoods of a and b on which the zero set of P is exactly the graph w=f(z), where f is holomorphic and f(a)=b. If the polynomial has fixed positive w-degree, its leading coefficient is nonzero at a, and all roots at a are distinct, then on one disk about a all its roots are exhausted by finitely many pairwise disjoint such holomorphic branches.

Let P∈C[z,w] be irreducible of positive w-degree d, with leading coefficient a_d(z). There is a nonzero polynomial Δ(z), the resultant of P and P_w, such that for every z outside E={z∈C:a_d(z)Δ(z)=0}, P(z,·) has exactly d distinct finite roots. The exceptional set E is finite. This includes d=1; infinity is treated separately rather than included in the finite-point conclusion.

For the irreducible polynomial P of d12:21-02 and its finite exceptional set E, put Ω=C\E and S={(z,w)∈Ω×C:P(z,w)=0}. With its natural topology and holomorphic charts S→Ω is a d-sheeted holomorphic covering. Each branch continues along every path in Ω. Every based loop permutes the d root germs; homotopic based loops induce the same permutation. Concatenation induces successive application of permutations, with the first traversed loop acting first.

For the algebraic covering of d12:21-03, choose a punctured disk about c∈E containing no other exceptional point. A local monodromy cycle of length h has a single-valued cyclic parameter t with z=c+t^h, and its root is w=W(t), holomorphic for t≠0 on the corresponding punctured parameter disk. At infinity the corresponding cyclic parameter satisfies z=t^{-h}. This claim alone does not assert removability of W at t=0.

In every finite-point or infinity cyclic parameter from d12:21-04, the algebraic branch W(t) is meromorphic at t=0 and has a convergent Laurent expansion with only finitely many negative powers. At a finite exceptional point c with a_d(c)≠0 the branches are bounded and W extends holomorphically to t=0.

Suppose a finite collection of d analytic branches over the complement of a finite subset of the sphere Ĉ is invariant under analytic continuation. Suppose near every missing point each branch has at most power growth in a finite cyclic parameter (using the coordinate 1/z at infinity). Then there is one nonzero polynomial Q∈C[z,w] satisfied by all the branches.

For the irreducible polynomial P of d12:21-02, the monodromy action on its d roots is transitive and the covering S of d12:21-03 is connected. Completing its finitely many cyclic branches over E and over infinity yields a compact Riemann surface on which both coordinate functions z and w extend meromorphically. This constructs the specific algebraic finite-branch completion, not normalization or algebraization of arbitrary analytic spaces.

For every positive integer n the curve w^n=z has the smooth global parameter t=w, z=t^n. Its compact completion is CP^1, with projection multiplicity n at zero and infinity (unramified there when n=1). If P(z)∈C[z] is square-free of degree d≥1, the affine curve w²=P(z) is smooth. Its compact Riemann-surface completion has two unramified points over infinity for even d and one point of multiplicity two over infinity for odd d. A smooth surface model is not a claim that a singular affine curve is already a smooth embedded curve.

The cusp y²=x³ has the parameterization (x,y)=(t²,t³), but its affine subset is not a complex submanifold at the origin. In any nonconstant local parameterization through the origin, 2 ord(y)=3 ord(x) forces both coordinate derivatives to vanish, excluding an embedded manifold chart with nonzero differential.

The node y²=x²(x+1) has two different local branches y=±x√(1+x) at the origin. Removing the origin disconnects a sufficiently small neighborhood in the node, unlike a punctured disk, so the singular affine subset is not itself a Riemann surface there. Separating the branch parameters gives a smooth surface model without changing that singularity assertion.

Ahlfors VIII.2.1–2.3 and selected Forster §8 are source comparison references. The prose records the comparison scope and distinguishes leading-coefficient zeros, infinity and singular affine examples; it is citation/editorial context rather than extra mathematical assertions.

Let Λ=Zω₁+Zω₂, with ω₁≠0 and Im(ω₂/ω₁)>0. Then Λ is discrete, the series ∑_{λ∈Λ\{0}}|λ|^{-s} converges for every real s>2, and the quotient T=C/Λ is a compact Riemann surface. Its holomorphic charts come from sufficiently small plane disks and have lattice-translation transition maps. This lattice and orientation convention is used for the subsequent elliptic statements.

For the lattice Λ of d12:22-01, every Λ-periodic entire function is constant. Every meromorphic Λ-periodic scalar function has residue sum zero over a complete set of pole classes modulo Λ; in particular it cannot have exactly one pole class that is a simple pole.

For the lattice Λ and torus T of d12:22-01, a nonconstant elliptic (Λ-periodic meromorphic) function has the same finite number N of zeros and poles on T, counted with multiplicity. For any choices of representatives a₁,…,a_N of its zeros and b₁,…,b_N of its poles, with repetitions for multiplicities, ∑a_j−∑b_j∈Λ. Every finite value has exactly N preimages on T, counted with multiplicity.
