For Λ as in d12:22-01, the regularized Weierstrass series ℘(z)=z^{-2}+∑_{λ∈Λ\{0}}((z−λ)^{-2}−λ^{-2}) converges normally on C\Λ and defines a meromorphic function whose poles are precisely all lattice points, each a double pole with exact principal part (z−λ)^{-2}. Its derivative is ℘′(z)=−2∑_{λ∈Λ}(z−λ)^{-3}; this derivative series converges normally and absolutely away from Λ. The subtracted inverse-square terms are part of the definition; no separate convergence of the two inverse-square sums is asserted.
The Weierstrass function ℘ of d12:22-04 is even, its derivative ℘′ is odd, and both are Λ-periodic. The full set of periods of ℘ is exactly Λ.

For Λ as in d12:22-01, define g₂=60∑_{λ∈Λ\{0}}λ^{-4} and g₃=140∑_{λ∈Λ\{0}}λ^{-6}. The associated Weierstrass function satisfies ℘′²=4℘³−g₂℘−g₃ and ℘″=6℘²−g₂/2. Modulo Λ, the three nonzero half-period classes h₁=ω₁/2, h₂=ω₂/2, h₃=(ω₁+ω₂)/2 are precisely the zeros of ℘′, and each zero is simple. The three values e_j=℘(h_j) are distinct and 4X³−g₂X−g₃=4∏_{j=1}^3(X−e_j). In particular g₂³−27g₃²≠0.

The meromorphic map ℘:T→Ĉ for the lattice Λ of d12:22-01 has degree two and exactly the branch values e₁,e₂,e₃,∞ from d12:22-06. The projective curve E={ [Z:X:Y]∈CP² : Y²Z=4X³−g₂XZ²−g₃Z³ } is nonsingular. The map Φ:T→E given by Φ([z])=[1:℘(z):℘′(z)] for z∉Λ and Φ([0])=O=[0:0:1] is a biholomorphism, including the infinity charts and a holomorphic inverse there. The claim concerns the lattice-associated cubic, not converse uniformization of an arbitrary cubic. Here CP²=(C³\{0})/C* has its projective quotient topology, and E has the induced topology and the complex charts of the nonsingular cubic; the biholomorphism concerns these actual structures.

For Λ as in d12:22-01, the normally convergent regularized expressions ζ(z)=1/z+∑_{λ∈Λ\{0}}(1/(z−λ)+1/λ+z/λ²) and σ(z)=z∏_{λ∈Λ\{0}}E₂(z/λ), with E₂(u)=(1−u)exp(u+u²/2), satisfy ζ′=−℘ and σ′/σ=ζ away from their poles/zeros. Both functions are odd. The function σ is entire and its zeros are exactly Λ, each simple. Constants η₁,η₂ exist such that, for j=1,2, ζ(z+ω_j)=ζ(z)+η_j and σ(z+ω_j)=−exp(η_j(z+ω_j/2))σ(z). With the stated positive orientation they satisfy Legendre's relation η₁ω₂−η₂ω₁=2πi. Normal convergence for the ζ series is on compact subsets of C\Λ; the σ product converges locally uniformly on C.

For every m,n∈Z, let λ=mω₁+nω₂ and η_λ=mη₁+nη₂, with the constants from d12:22-08. The arbitrary lattice-shift formula is σ(z+λ)=(−1)^{m+n+mn} exp(η_λ(z+λ/2))σ(z). This includes positive, zero and negative integer coefficients.

Transport of addition on T=C/Λ through the biholomorphism Φ gives exactly the chord–tangent group law on E, with identity O=[0:0:1] and inverse [Z:X:Y]↦[Z:X:−Y]. For points where the displayed quotient is defined (and hence as a meromorphic identity), ℘(z+w)=−℘(z)−℘(w)+(1/4)((℘′(z)−℘′(w))/(℘(z)−℘(w)))². The comparison includes diagonal/tangent cases, vertical/opposite-point cases, half-periods and infinity, so it establishes the full abelian group law, including associativity. In particular finite distinct points of different x-coordinate add by reflecting their third line intersection; equal finite points use the tangent; opposites sum to O; a point with y=0 doubles to O; O+P=P and O+O=O.

Source comparisons to Ahlfors VII.2.4–3.3 and Freitag–Busam V.3 Appendix A.6–A.7, including editorial explanation that infinity charts, analytic inverse and group-law bridge are supplied. Citation/provenance information is not an additional obligation.

Editorial introduction distinguishing the omitted-values normality theorem proved in this chapter from locally bounded Montel and describing its quantitative constant as deliberately nonsharp. No additional mathematical assertion beyond the following results is introduced.

If f is holomorphic on the unit disk D and f′(0)=1, there exists an open disk S⊂D on which f is injective such that f(S) contains a disk of radius 1/64. More generally, if R>0, f is holomorphic on B(a,R) and f′(a)≠0, its image contains a disk of radius R|f′(a)|/64, with a single-valued holomorphic inverse on that target disk arising from a univalence disk in B(a,R). No boundary extension of f is assumed.

Let Ω be a simply connected plane domain and f:Ω→C be holomorphic with f(z)≠0,1 for all z∈Ω. There is a holomorphic g:Ω→C such that f(z)=−exp(πi cosh(2g(z))) for all z∈Ω. The image g(Ω) contains no open disk of radius 2.
Every nonconstant entire function C→C omits at most one finite complex value.

For every A>0 and 0≤r<1 there is an explicit finite C(A,r) such that each holomorphic f:D→C\{0,1} with |f(0)|≤A satisfies |f(z)|≤C(A,r) for all |z|≤r. A permitted value is A_*=max(2,A), C₀=1+log(A_*)/(2π), K=√C₀+√(C₀+1), and C(A,r)=1+exp(π exp(2(log K+π+128r/(1−r)))). By scaling, if f is holomorphic and omits 0,1 on B(a,R), R>0, with |f(a)|≤A, the same bound holds on |z−a|≤rR. The range r=0 is included; r=1 is excluded.

On every plane domain Ω, the family of all holomorphic f:Ω→C omitting 0 and 1 is spherically normal: every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset in the spherical metric either to a holomorphic finite-valued function or to the constant ∞. The finite limit is allowed to be the constant 0 or 1.

If a holomorphic function on a punctured neighborhood of a has an isolated essential singularity at a, then every finite complex value, with at most one exception, is taken infinitely many times in every punctured neighborhood of a within that domain. Precisely, the set of finite values b for which some punctured neighborhood of a contains only finitely many preimages of b has cardinality at most one. The possible exceptional value is common to all sufficiently small neighborhoods, not newly chosen for each radius.

For any domain Ω and any three fixed distinct values α,β,γ∈Ĉ, the family of meromorphic functions on Ω omitting α,β,γ is spherically normal: every sequence has a subsequence converging compactly in the spherical metric to a meromorphic map or a sphere constant (including ∞). Every meromorphic function on C omitting three sphere values is constant. If a meromorphic map to Ĉ has an isolated essential singularity at a, then every sphere value, with at most two exceptions, is taken infinitely often in every punctured neighborhood of a. Equivalently at most two sphere values have finite preimage in some punctured neighborhood; poles count as preimages of ∞.

Throughout the real theory, an ODE includes an open domain U⊂ℝ×ℝⁿ and a continuous field f:U→ℝⁿ, with coordinates (t,x). Fix a norm on ℝⁿ and its induced operator norms. Unless otherwise specified vector-field state spaces are finite-dimensional and real. A solution includes its interval, regularity, equation and initial data. Autonomous flows are partial and their group law is asserted only where both sides exist. C^k refers to the explicitly specified variables; continuity, differentiability, smoothness, real analyticity and holomorphy on an actual open complex domain are distinct regularity assertions.

Context only: all adopted independent theorem/lemma/proposition/corollary statements, required definitions, substantive examples, and necessary representation bridges are in scope, preserving hypotheses, domains, quantifiers and quantitative conclusions. Equivalent valid proofs and exact library applications are allowed; proof-route-only intermediate steps do not become extra deliverables. Full singular-endpoint spectral theory, general coupled center-manifold existence, high-codimension global bifurcation classification, KAM, general multiplicative ergodic theory and unrestricted dimension formulae are explicitly outside the adopted scope.

Context only: the previously established reusable prerequisites F1–F7, with their actual hypotheses, rather than new D13 assertions. F1: finite-dimensional real/complex linear algebra, Jordan reduction over a splitting field, self-adjoint finite-dimensional spectral decomposition and equivalent norms; no infinite-dimensional compact spectral theorem is inferred from it. F2: one-variable completeness, uniform convergence, continuous scalar/vector integration on compact intervals, FTC, controlled differentiation under integrals, Taylor remainders and convergent power series. F3: finite-dimensional Fréchet calculus, inverse/implicit functions, C^k cutoffs, change of variables on actual C^1 diffeomorphism domains, Green formula on actual bounded regular oriented planar domains; regular-curve separation is proved in Chapter 21. F4: metric compactness, finite-dimensional Heine–Borel, uniform continuity on compact sets, completeness of bounded continuous sup-norm spaces, the complete-metric contraction principle, Arzelà–Ascoli and continuity of uniform limits; new weighted-space identifications remain required where stated. F5: finite/probability measure convergence and integration theorems with their hypotheses, L^p completeness for 1≤p≤∞, finite-p bounded density, summable-measure Borel–Cantelli, premeasure extension and finite-measure uniqueness, Lebesgue regularity, and circle-continuous-function L² density; L^p identities are initially almost everywhere. F6: locally uniform holomorphic limits, Cauchy formula/estimates, Taylor/Laurent expansions on their domains, homotopy invariance of winding index avoiding the evaluation point, and Fourier–Fejér approximation; arc and boundary hypotheses remain binding. F7: the positive Riesz–Markov representation and converse for positive real linear functionals on C_c(X,R), X locally compact Hausdorff, by unique positive Radon Borel measures; on compact X, C_c=C and mass equals I(1). This is a measure representation prerequisite, not finite-dimensional Riesz representation or an assumption replacing the new dynamics results.
For finite-dimensional ℝⁿ, changing the fixed norm to an equivalent norm does not change existence, continuity, or differentiability assertions.

For the continuous field f:U→ℝⁿ on open U ⊂ ℝ×ℝⁿ, a classical solution on a nonempty open interval I is x:I→ℝⁿ of class C¹, whose graph lies in U, satisfying x′(t)=f(t,x(t)) for every t∈I. It solves the IVP at (s,ξ)∈U when s∈I and x(s)=ξ. On a compact interval require continuity everywhere and the appropriate one-sided derivative at included endpoints, equivalently the integral formulation. A maximal solution admits no extension to a strictly larger open interval; a global solution is defined for every t∈ℝ.

Let f:U→ℝⁿ be continuous on open U, let I be an interval containing s, and x:I→ℝⁿ continuous with graph in U. Then x solves x′=f(t,x), x(s)=ξ (with the endpoint convention for included endpoints) iff for all t∈I, x(t)=ξ+∫ₛᵗ f(r,x(r)) dr. The integral is oriented, and the equivalence applies also when t<s.

For a continuous ODE field on its open domain, restricting a solution to a subinterval gives a solution. Two solutions on intervals I₁,I₂ which agree on their nonempty intersection paste to a solution on I₁∪I₂. A left solution and a right solution that are continuous up to a common time s, have the same value ξ there, and satisfy the equation up to their respective sides also paste to a solution; equality on overlap is a hypothesis, without a uniqueness assumption.

An autonomous equation is x′=F(x) on an open Ω⊂ℝⁿ. A parameter-dependent equation is x′=f(t,x,p), with p in an open subset of ℝᵐ and constant along each solution. Once uniqueness is established, Φ(t,s,ξ,p) denotes the unique solution value for initial time s, state ξ and parameter p, whenever defined.

For every integer m≥1 and continuous G on an open subset of ℝ×(ℝᵈ)ᵐ, solutions y of y⁽ᵐ⁾=G(t,y,y′,…,y⁽ᵐ⁻¹⁾) are in bijection, on exactly the same time intervals and preserving all domain and initial-value conditions, with solutions of Y′=(Y₂,…,Yₘ,G(t,Y₁,…,Yₘ)), by Y=(y,y′,…,y⁽ᵐ⁻¹⁾) and inverse y=Y₁. The first-order equations imply Y₁∈Cᵐ and Yⱼ=Y₁⁽ʲ⁻¹⁾. Prescribing the m initial derivatives y(s),…,y⁽ᵐ⁻¹⁾(s) is equivalent to prescribing Y(s).

The nonautonomous parameter equation x′=f(t,x,p) is equivalent to the autonomous system (τ,x,p)′=(1,f(τ,x,p),0) on the open set of allowed (τ,x,p). A solution starting at (s,ξ,p) at elapsed time 0 has τ(h)=s+h and constant parameter p, and its x component corresponds to the original solution at t=s+h; when unique it is Φ(s+h,s,ξ,p). The correspondence is reversible with exactly translated solution intervals and holds whenever either side is defined.

For x′=f(t,x) on its prescribed domain, if H:Ω→Ω̃ is a C¹ diffeomorphism of state domains, z=H(x) gives a reversible correspondence with z′=DH(H⁻¹(z))f(t,H⁻¹(z)), preserving transformed domains and initial data. If θ:J→I is a C¹ diffeomorphism of intervals with nonzero derivative, y(r)=x(θ(r)) gives a reversible correspondence with y′(r)=θ′(r)f(θ(r),y(r)), including the transformed domain and initial data. In particular reversing time, with chosen time origin, transforms f(t,x) into −f(−t,x).

Every solution of y″+y=0 is y(t)=A cos t+B sin t. The boundary values y(0)=y(π)=0 leave B arbitrary (with A=0), whereas y(0)=0,y(π)=1 admit no solution. Thus IVP existence and uniqueness do not imply the corresponding statements for two-point boundary data.

Chapter 1 identifies its textbook sources and notes that singular implicit equations F(t,x,x′)=0 are not assumed to possess a global normal form; conversion to normal form is restricted to where the relevant implicit-function hypothesis holds. This is a scope limitation rather than an additional global theorem.
For 𝕂=ℝ or ℂ, continuous a,b:I→𝕂 on a real interval I and s∈I, put A(t)=∫ₛᵗa(r)dr. The unique solution on I of x′=a(t)x+b(t), x(s)=ξ, is x(t)=exp(A(t))(ξ+∫ₛᵗexp(−A(r))b(r)dr).

For open intervals I,J⊂ℝ, continuous a:I→ℝ and g:J→ℝ nowhere zero on J, s∈I,ξ∈J, define H(u)=∫ξᵘ1/g(v)dv. Then H is strictly monotone and has a C¹ inverse on H(J). The unique solution x′=a(t)g(x), x(s)=ξ taking values in J is x(t)=H⁻¹(∫ₛᵗa(r)dr), on the connected component containing s of {t∈I:∫ₛᵗa(r)dr∈H(J)}; every solution in J has this form. At any other allowed point c where the original g is defined and g(c)=0, the equilibrium x≡c is a separate solution excluded by division on the branch.

For r,K>0 and initial value ξ∈ℝ at time s, x′=rx(1−x/K) has solution x(t)=Kξe^{r(t−s)}/(K+ξ(e^{r(t−s)}−1)). Values ξ=0 and ξ=K give the equilibria. For 0<ξ<K the denominator stays positive for all real t, the solution is global and increasing, and x(t)→0 as t→−∞ and x(t)→K as t→+∞. For ξ>K the maximal interval is (s+r⁻¹log(1−K/ξ),∞); for ξ<0 it is (−∞,s+r⁻¹log(1−K/ξ)). The denominator has a simple zero at the finite endpoint, preventing continuation in ℝ; the C¹ field gives local uniqueness. The equation x′=rx instead has global solution ξe^{r(t−s)} and no finite-time pole.

On an open rectangle R=I×J, let P,Q∈C¹(R) satisfy Pₓ=Qₜ, and fix (s,ξ)∈R. The function F(t,x)=∫ₛᵗP(r,ξ)dr+∫ξˣQ(t,v)dv satisfies Fₜ=P and Fₓ=Q. A C¹ graph x(t) in R satisfies P(t,x(t))+Q(t,x(t))x′(t)=0 iff F(t,x(t)) is constant on its time interval. On the nonzero set of Q this equation is equivalently x′=−P/Q. The result is on a rectangle and asserts no arbitrary-domain global exactness.

For P,Q∈C¹ on a rectangle, any nowhere-zero C¹ function μ satisfying (μP)ₓ=(μQ)ₜ converts P+Qx′=0 into an exact equation with exactly the same solutions. If Q≠0 and (Pₓ−Qₜ)/Q=h(t) depends only on t, μ(t)=exp(∫ₛᵗh(r)dr) is such an integrating factor. If P≠0 and (Qₜ−Pₓ)/P=k(x) depends only on x, μ(x)=exp(∫ξˣk(v)dv) is such a factor.

For continuous real a,b, real p≠1, and positive unknown x, u=x^{1−p} is a bijection between positive solutions of x′=a(t)x+b(t)xᵖ and positive solutions of u′=(1−p)a(t)u+(1−p)b(t). The inverse is x=u^{1/(1−p)} on intervals where u>0. Positivity is part of both domains; no extension across u=0 or to u<0 for arbitrary real p is asserted.

For continuous a,b,c on I and a solution v′=av²+bv+c, on any interval where x−v never vanishes, x solves the same Riccati equation iff u=1/(x−v) is nowhere zero and solves u′=−(2av+b)u−a. The inverse correspondence is x=v+1/u. The known solution x=v is retained separately.

For ω>0 the unique solution of y″+ω²y=0 with y(s)=a,y′(s)=b is y(t)=a cos(ω(t−s))+(b/ω)sin(ω(t−s)). It is global, and ((y′)²+ω²y²)/2 is constant. In the boundary case ω=0 the unique solution is the global affine function a+b(t−s).

If V∈C¹(J) for an interval J and a classical solution y of y″=−V′(y) takes values in J, then E(t)=(y′(t))²/2+V(y(t)) is constant. On a branch with E−V(y)>0 and fixed sign of y′, y′=±√(2(E−V(y))) with the chosen sign, and the trajectory is recovered by the separable formula on that branch. No divided-square-root converse at a turning point is asserted; such points must satisfy the original second-order equation.
Chapter 2 identifies sources for the adopted elementary methods and emphasizes equilibrium, sign, denominator, and maximal-interval checks for methods which divide by an unknown.

A continuous f:U→ℝⁿ is locally Lipschitz in the state uniformly in time when every (s,ξ)∈U has a product neighborhood with a constant L satisfying ‖f(t,x)−f(t,y)‖≤L‖x−y‖ for every allowed t,x,y therein. For a parameter-dependent field, the same constant is also uniform for parameters in a sufficiently small parameter neighborhood. A single constant throughout U is not required.

On a convex state ball B, if Dₓf exists, is continuous in every variable, and has operator norm ≤L, then ‖f(t,x)−f(t,y)‖≤L‖x−y‖ for x,y∈B at every permitted choice of the other variables. In particular a jointly C¹ field on its open domain is locally Lipschitz in the state, uniformly in all its other variables.

Let X be a nonempty closed subset of a Banach space and K:X→X satisfy ‖Ku−Kv‖≤q‖u−v‖ for 0≤q<1. Then K has exactly one fixed point u*. For every u₀∈X and iteration uⱼ₊₁=Kuⱼ, one has ‖uⱼ−u*‖≤qʲ‖u₁−u₀‖/(1−q), so the iterates converge to u*.

Let f be continuous on Q=[s−a,s+a]×closedBall(ξ,b)⊂U, satisfy ‖f‖≤M there, and be state-Lipschitz there with constant L. If h>0, h≤a, Mh≤b and Lh<1, there is a solution with value ξ at s on [s−h,s+h] staying in the closed state ball. It is the uniform limit of Picard iterates u₀(t)=ξ and uⱼ₊₁(t)=ξ+∫ₛᵗf(r,uⱼ(r))dr, and is the only solution with those initial data whose whole graph remains in the controlled box on this interval. If additionally f is locally state-Lipschitz uniformly in time throughout U, any two local solutions with these initial data agree on their whole common interval.

If f is continuous and locally state-Lipschitz uniformly in time on open U⊂ℝ×ℝⁿ, every (s,ξ)∈U admits a local solution, unique on overlaps for that initial datum. Two solution trajectories which meet at a common time cannot subsequently separate while both are defined, to either side of that time.

For continuous f(t,x,p), suppose ‖f‖≤M and its state-Lipschitz constant is ≤L uniformly on [s₀−a,s₀+a]×closedBall(ξ₀,b)×closedBall(p₀,c) inside its open domain. Choose h>0 with h≤a, Mh≤b/2 and Lh<1. For every s∈(s₀−h/2,s₀+h/2), ξ∈B(ξ₀,b/2),p∈B(p₀,c), a solution with x(s)=ξ exists on the same J=[s₀−h/2,s₀+h/2] and stays in closedBall(ξ₀,b). The choices M,L,h are independent of the nearby datum.
Every uniformly bounded equicontinuous sequence of maps from a compact real interval to finite-dimensional ℝⁿ has a uniformly convergent subsequence (with continuous limit).

If f is continuous on [s,s+a]×closedBall(ξ,b), ‖f‖≤M there, 0<h≤a, and Mh≤b, there exists at least one classical solution on [s,s+h] with x(s)=ξ and values in closedBall(ξ,b). The time-reversed assertion gives a left solution when the analogous left box is available. Uniqueness is not claimed.

The continuous scalar field f(x)=2√|x| has for each a≥0 the global classical solution xₐ(t)=0 for t≤a and xₐ(t)=(t−a)² for t≥a, all with xₐ(0)=0; the identically zero solution is another one. At the joining time the derivative exists and equals zero. For x>0, |f(x)−f(0)|/|x|=2/√x is unbounded near 0, so the state-Lipschitz hypothesis fails there, and continuity alone does not give uniqueness.

For a continuous field in a compact local box, suppose ‖f(t,x)−f(t,y)‖≤ω(‖x−y‖), where ω:[0,∞)→[0,∞) is continuous, nondecreasing, ω(0)=0, ω(r)>0 for r>0, and the improper integral ∫₀δdr/ω(r)=∞ for every δ>0. Two solutions with the same initial value agree while remaining in a sufficiently small common box. If each coincidence point admits such a box with a possibly different Osgood modulus, local applications give uniqueness on that whole common interval, to both sides of the initial time.

Chapter 3 gives textbook references for fixed-point, Euler polygonal and modulus-based uniqueness methods. Only finite-dimensional Peano compactness is adopted; arbitrary infinite-dimensional state-space Peano existence is expressly outside the assertion.

Except where explicitly stated otherwise, Chapter 4 assumes f:U→ℝⁿ continuous on open U⊂ℝ×ℝⁿ and locally Lipschitz in the state uniformly in time. Its solution-map constructions retain this uniqueness hypothesis.

For continuous locally state-Lipschitz f:U→ℝⁿ uniformly in time on open U, every (s,ξ)∈U has exactly one maximal solution. Its domain is the open interval I(s,ξ)=(T₋(s,ξ),T₊(s,ξ)) with T₋<s<T₊, allowing infinite endpoints. Every other solution through (s,ξ) is its restriction on that solution’s own domain.

Under Chapter 4’s continuous local state-Lipschitz hypotheses, if r∈I(s,ξ) and η=Φ(r,s,ξ), then I(r,η)=I(s,ξ) and Φ(t,r,η)=Φ(t,s,ξ) for all t in that common maximal interval. This is a nonautonomous identity and does not require time-translation invariance of f.

For continuous locally state-Lipschitz f on open U, let x solve the equation on (a,b) with finite b. It extends to a solution on (a,b+ε) for some ε>0 iff there exists tⱼ↑b with (tⱼ,x(tⱼ))→(b,η)∈U. In that case the full limit x(t)→η as t↑b exists and the extended value x(b)=η. The analogous statement holds at every finite left endpoint after time reversal.

Under Chapter 4’s hypotheses, if a maximal solution has finite right endpoint T₊, then as t↑T₊ its graph eventually leaves every compact K⊂U. If U=ℝ×ℝⁿ, the stronger conclusion ‖Φ(t,s,ξ)‖→∞ holds. The corresponding graph-escape and full-space norm-divergence statements hold at finite left endpoints.

Under Chapter 4’s hypotheses, suppose a forward solution with initial time s has, for every finite B>s, a compact K_B⊂ℝⁿ such that every value at a defined t∈[s,B) lies in K_B and [s,B]×K_B⊂U. Then its maximal right endpoint is +∞.

Let continuous f:ℝ×ℝⁿ→ℝⁿ be locally state-Lipschitz uniformly in time. Assume that for every finite B>0 there are a_B,b_B≥0 with ‖f(t,x)‖≤a_B+b_B‖x‖ for all |t|≤B,x∈ℝⁿ. Every maximal solution is global. For any available interval between s and t contained in [−B,B], ‖x(t)‖≤‖x(s)‖exp(b_B|t−s|)+a_B(exp(b_B|t−s|)−1)/b_B if b_B>0; when b_B=0 the bound is ‖x(s)‖+a_B|t−s|.

The unique solution of x′=x²,x(s)=ξ is x(t)=ξ/(1−ξ(t−s)) on its pole-free maximal interval. If ξ>0, that interval is (−∞,s+1/ξ) and x(t)→+∞ at the right endpoint. If ξ<0, it is (s+1/ξ,∞), with a pole at the left endpoint. If ξ=0, the solution is globally zero. Smoothness gives uniqueness and the pole prevents extension through the finite endpoint.

On U=ℝ×(−1,1), x′=1,x(0)=0 has maximal solution x(t)=t on (−1,1). The state remains bounded but the solution is not global in this prescribed domain; its graph escapes each compact subset of U by approaching x=±1. Extending the formula to every real time changes the state domain.

The scalar field x↦x² is locally Lipschitz everywhere but has finite-time forward blow-up for positive initial values. Conversely f(x)=sin(x²) is bounded and smooth, so all its solutions are global, but f′(x)=2x cos(x²) is unbounded and f is not globally Lipschitz. Thus local Lipschitz control does not imply linear growth, and a globally bounded derivative is sufficient but unnecessary for global existence.
Chapter 4 identifies continuation references and emphasizes the distinction between escape from the ODE domain and divergence in norm. No uniqueness-free maximal-solution selection is used later.

For continuous nonnegative u,b,c on [s,T] and A≥0, if u(t)≤A+∫ₛᵗ(b(r)u(r)+c(r))dr, then u(t)≤A exp(∫ₛᵗb)+∫ₛᵗc(r)exp(∫ᵣᵗb)dr. For b≡L≥0,c≡δ≥0 this is A exp(L(t−s))+δE_L(t−s), with E_L(v)=(exp(Lv)−1)/L for L>0 and E₀(v)=v. After time reversal the analogous bound holds for an oriented interval to the left of s.
For continuous nonnegative u,b,a on [s,T] with u(t)≤a(t)+∫ₛᵗb(r)u(r)dr, one has u(t)≤a(t)+∫ₛᵗa(r)b(r)exp(∫ᵣᵗb)dr. If a is nondecreasing, this is at most a(t)exp(∫ₛᵗb).

On a compact interval containing s, let x solve x′=f(t,x) and y be C¹, with all their required graph points in the domain of f. Suppose L,δ≥0 and ‖f(t,x(t))−f(t,y(t))‖≤L‖x(t)−y(t)‖, ‖y′(t)−f(t,y(t))‖≤δ. Then for every t in the interval, ‖x(t)−y(t)‖≤exp(L|t−s|)‖x(s)−y(s)‖+δE_L(|t−s|), where E_L(v)=(exp(Lv)−1)/L if L>0 and E₀(v)=v. In particular it applies if y′=g(t,y) and ‖f(t,z)−g(t,z)‖≤δ on a set containing y’s graph. Only f requires the displayed Lipschitz control.

Two solutions of the same state-Lipschitz field with constant L≥0, on a common interval and in the set where that bound is valid, satisfy ‖Φ(t,s,ξ)−Φ(t,s,η)‖≤exp(L|t−s|)‖ξ−η‖. The factor cannot generally be replaced by a time-uniform constant: in dimension one x′=Lx gives equality for t≥s (and for L>0 produces unbounded amplification).

For an open interval J⊂ℝ and continuous f:[a,b]×J→ℝ locally Lipschitz in its second variable uniformly in time, let u,v∈C¹([a,b],J) satisfy u′(t)≤f(t,u(t)), v′(t)≥f(t,v(t)), and u(a)≤v(a). Then u(t)≤v(t) for every t∈[a,b].

Let x̄ solve a continuous locally state-Lipschitz field f:U→ℝⁿ, U open, and let [a,b] be a compact subinterval of its open solution interval. There exist ρ>0,L≥0 such that Qρ={(t,z):a≤t≤b,‖z−x̄(t)‖≤ρ} is a compact subset of U and each tube slice has state-Lipschitz constant L for f. Let g:U→ℝⁿ be continuous locally state-Lipschitz with sup_Qρ‖g−f‖≤δ, δ≥0. For s′∈[a,b] and ξ′ define d=‖ξ′−x̄(s′)‖ and T=b−a. If exp(LT)(d+δT)<ρ/2, the solution y′=g(t,y),y(s′)=ξ′ exists throughout [a,b], and ‖y(t)−x̄(t)‖≤d exp(L|t−s′|)+δE_L(|t−s′|)<ρ/2. E_L(v)=(exp(Lv)−1)/L for L>0 and E₀(v)=v.

Let continuous locally state-Lipschitz fⱼ,f:U→ℝⁿ satisfy fⱼ→f uniformly on every compact subset of U. If (sⱼ,ξⱼ)→(s,ξ) and [a,b] is a compact subinterval of the f-maximal interval I_f(s,ξ), with s in its interior, then for every sufficiently large j the fⱼ-solution starting at (sⱼ,ξⱼ) exists throughout [a,b] and converges uniformly there to the f-solution. No uniform bound on the Lipschitz constants of fⱼ is assumed.

Let U⊂ℝ×ℝⁿ×ℝᵐ be open and f(t,x,p) continuous and locally state-Lipschitz uniformly in time and parameters. For the unique maximal intervals I(s,ξ,p), the set D={(t,s,ξ,p):(s,ξ,p)∈U,t∈I(s,ξ,p)} is open, and its solution map Φ:D→ℝⁿ is jointly continuous in terminal time, initial time, initial state, and parameter.

For continuous f on open U⊂ℝ×ℝⁿ×ℝᵐ locally state-Lipschitz uniformly in time and parameters, T₊(s,ξ,p) is lower semicontinuous and T₋(s,ξ,p) is upper semicontinuous on the initial-data domain U, using extended real values for infinite endpoints.

For x′=x with initial time 0 and initial states 0 and ε, solution difference is εeᵗ. As ε→0 it converges to 0 uniformly on every fixed compact time interval but not uniformly on [0,∞). For x′=x², for every arbitrarily long fixed finite time interval around the global zero solution, all sufficiently small initial values give solutions on that interval; every fixed positive nonzero initial value nevertheless has finite forward lifespan. These examples delimit the compact-time continuous-dependence assertion.

Chapter 5 gives comparison/dependence sources. Parameter continuity by itself only supplies continuous parameter dependence, without an asserted parameter derivative or infinite-time uniform stability conclusion.

Chapter 6 distinguishes continuous, Cᵏ, smooth and analytic dependence. Its real solution maps use the open maximal domain D; differentiability is local on that domain and asserts no common infinite time interval.

Let A:[a,b]→ℝⁿˣⁿ and B:[a,b]→ℝⁿˣʳ be continuous, s∈[a,b], and Y_s∈ℝⁿˣʳ. There is exactly one solution on [a,b] of Y(t)=Y_s+∫ₛᵗ(A(u)Y(u)+B(u))du. If ‖A‖≤L and ‖B‖≤M on the interval, then ‖Y(t)‖≤‖Y_s‖exp(L|t−s|)+ME_L(|t−s|), with E_L(v)=(exp(Lv)−1)/L if L>0 and E₀(v)=v. Uniform continuous variation of A,B,Y_s on this fixed interval gives uniform-in-time continuous variation of Y; a jointly continuous coefficient/initial-value family has solutions jointly continuous in time and parameters locally in its parameters.

For f∈C¹(U,ℝⁿ), U⊂ℝ×ℝⁿ×ℝᵐ open, the unique solution map Φ(t,s,ξ,p) is jointly C¹ on its open maximal domain D. For fixed (s,ξ,p), define A(t)=Dₓf(t,Φ(t,s,ξ,p),p), Y(t)=DξΦ(t,s,ξ,p), Z(t)=D_pΦ(t,s,ξ,p). These derivatives are the uniquely determined solutions on the original maximal interval of Y′=AY,Y(s)=I_n and Z′=AZ+D_pf(t,Φ(t,s,ξ,p),p),Z(s)=0. Also ∂ₜΦ=f(t,Φ,p).

For f∈C¹ on open U⊂ℝ×ℝⁿ×ℝᵐ, at every point of the maximal domain, ∂ₛΦ(t,s,ξ,p)=−DξΦ(t,s,ξ,p)f(s,ξ,p). This is not generally −f(t,Φ(t,s,ξ,p),p) for a nonautonomous field: x′=t has Φ(t,s,ξ)=ξ+(t²−s²)/2, with initial-time derivative −s instead of −t.

If f∈Cᵏ(U,ℝⁿ), with U⊂ℝ×ℝⁿ×ℝᵐ open and integer k≥1, its solution map Φ is jointly Cᵏ on the open maximal domain D, and ∂ₜΦ=f(t,Φ,p) is itself jointly Cᵏ. If f is C∞, then Φ is jointly C∞ on D. The assertion includes all time, initial-state and parameter variables.

For F∈Cᵏ(Ω,ℝⁿ), Ω open, let ψ(t,ξ) be its autonomous flow with initial time 0 and Hⱼ(t,ξ)=Dξʲψ(t,ξ),1≤j≤k. For every v₁,…,vⱼ, H₁(0)=I_n and Hⱼ(0)=0 when j≥2, and d/dt Hⱼ(t)[v₁,…,vⱼ]=Σ_π D^{|π|}F(ψ(t))[H_{|B|}(t)[vᵢ:i∈B]:B∈π], summed over all set partitions π of {1,…,j}. The one-block term is DF(ψ)Hⱼ and all other terms involve only lower-order variations. In particular (H₂[v,w])′=DF(ψ)H₂[v,w]+D²F(ψ)[H₁v,H₁w] with H₂(0)[v,w]=0. Thus each new order solves a linear inhomogeneous equation once lower orders are known, on the original allowed solution domain.

Let f(t,x,ε) be C¹ near the graph (t,x₀(t),0) of a reference solution on a compact interval J containing s. Let ξ(ε) be C¹ near 0, ξ(0)=ξ₀=x₀(s), and solve xε′=f(t,xε,ε),xε(s)=ξ(ε). For every sufficiently small ε the solution exists on the same J and xε(t)=x₀(t)+εz(t)+o(ε) uniformly for t∈J, where z′=Dₓf(t,x₀,0)z+∂εf(t,x₀,0),z(s)=ξ′(0). If f and ξ are C², the remainder is uniformly O(ε²) on J.

For fixed s,t,p, define Ω_{s,t,p}={ξ:(t,s,ξ,p)∈D}. If f is Cᵏ with k≥1 on its open domain, ξ↦Φ(t,s,ξ,p) is a Cᵏ diffeomorphism from the open set Ω_{s,t,p} onto Ω_{t,s,p}, with inverse η↦Φ(s,t,η,p). Its state derivative is invertible at every allowed datum. These domains need not equal all ℝⁿ.
For maps on an open subset of ℂᵈ, holomorphic means locally represented by an absolutely convergent power series in all d complex variables; for ℂⁿ-valued maps this applies componentwise.

A locally uniform limit of holomorphic maps on an open subset of ℂᵈ is holomorphic in the several-variable absolutely-convergent-power-series sense. The result applies componentwise to maps valued in ℂⁿ.

If f(z,w,λ) is holomorphic on an open neighborhood of (z₀,w₀,λ₀)∈ℂ×ℂⁿ×ℂᵐ, the complex IVP ∂_z w=f(z,w,λ),w(z₀)=ξ has a solution jointly holomorphic in (z,ξ,λ) on sufficiently small product neighborhoods of (z₀,w₀,λ₀), unique as a local solution germ. The initial complex time η may also vary near z₀, with joint holomorphic dependence on η, the terminal complex time z, the initial state ξ and parameter λ.

If a real field f(t,x,p) is real analytic on its open domain U⊂ℝ×ℝⁿ×ℝᵐ, then its real maximal solution map Φ is jointly real analytic on the whole open maximal domain D. The assertion is local about every allowed (t,s,ξ,p), including arbitrarily long allowed real elapsed times; it makes no claim of single-valued complex continuation around singularities.

Define g(t)=exp(−1/t²) for t>0 and g(t)=0 for t≤0. Each positive-side derivative is a polynomial in 1/t times exp(−1/t²) and tends to 0 at t=0; g is C∞ and every derivative at 0 vanishes. The equation x′=g(t),x(0)=0 has smooth solution x(t)=∫₀ᵗg(r)dr, whose derivatives at 0 all vanish, but which is strictly positive for every t>0. Its zero Taylor series fails to represent it on any neighborhood of 0, so the solution is not real analytic there.
Chapter 6 identifies sources for variational, holomorphic Picard and parameter arguments, and explicitly does not infer analyticity from smoothness alone.
Chapter 7 works over 𝕂=ℝ or ℂ, in arbitrary finite dimension, with a real time interval I and compatible matrix/vector norms. Complex unknowns still have real time.

For every finite matrix A over 𝕂=ℝ or ℂ, the series exp(tA)=Σ_{j≥0}tʲAʲ/j! converges locally uniformly for real t, is C∞, and obeys d/dt exp(tA)=A exp(tA)=exp(tA)A, exp(0A)=I, and ‖exp(tA)‖≤exp(|t|‖A‖) for compatible norms. For all real s,t, exp((s+t)A)=exp(sA)exp(tA), so exp(tA)⁻¹=exp(−tA). For any commuting square matrices A,B of the same dimension, exp(A+B)=exp(A)exp(B); no such assertion is made without commutation.

Let 𝕂=ℝ or ℂ, I a real interval, A:I→𝕂ⁿˣⁿ continuous and s∈I. There exists a unique evolution matrix U(t,s) for all t∈I satisfying ∂ₜU(t,s)=A(t)U(t,s),U(s,s)=I. It is invertible. For any t,r,s∈I one has U(t,r)U(r,s)=U(t,s), U(t,s)⁻¹=U(s,t), and ∂ₛU(t,s)=−U(t,s)A(s). With compatible norms, ‖U(t,s)‖≤exp(∫_{min(s,t)}^{max(s,t)}‖A(r)‖dr). Every fundamental matrix is X(t)=U(t,s)C for a fixed invertible C.
For A∈𝕂ⁿˣⁿ with 𝕂=ℝ or ℂ and real t, define exp(tA)=Σ_{j=0}∞ tʲAʲ/j!.

Over ℂ, if J=λI+N with Nᵐ=0, then exp(tJ)=exp(λt)Σ_{j=0}^{m−1}tʲNʲ/j!. Hence every component of a constant-coefficient solution is a finite sum of polynomials times exponentials. For real A, a conjugate pair α±iβ yields real linear combinations of tʲexp(αt)cos(βt) and tʲexp(αt)sin(βt). If every eigenvalue of A has real part strictly less than −a<0, then for each 0<b<a there is a finite constant C_b with ‖exp(tA)‖≤C_bexp(−bt) for all t≥0.

Over 𝕂=ℝ or ℂ on a real interval I, let A:I→𝕂ⁿˣⁿ and b:I→𝕂ⁿ be continuous, s∈I and x₀∈𝕂ⁿ. For evolution matrix U and any fundamental matrix X of x′=A(t)x, the unique solution on I of x′=A(t)x+b(t),x(s)=x₀ is x(t)=U(t,s)x₀+∫ₛᵗU(t,r)b(r)dr=X(t)(X(s)⁻¹x₀+∫ₛᵗX(r)⁻¹b(r)dr).
For continuous A:I→𝕂ⁿˣⁿ, 𝕂=ℝ or ℂ and real interval I, every fundamental matrix X satisfies det X(t)=det X(s)exp(∫ₛᵗtr A(r)dr) for every s,t∈I. For a real system det X never changes sign.

For A=((0,1),(0,0)), exp(tA)=((1,t),(0,1)). Its only eigenvalue is 0, but the equilibrium at the origin for x′=Ax is not Lyapunov stable: initial data (0,ε),ε>0, reach first component 1 at t=1/ε. Thus nonpositive real parts of eigenvalues alone do not imply bounded solutions.
Chapter 7 gives its linear-system references, uses Jordan decomposition from the existing linear-algebra foundation and explicitly retains arbitrary finite dimension rather than only planar systems.

Let A:ℝ→𝕂^{n×n}, 𝕂=ℝ or ℂ, be continuous and T-periodic, T>0, and X the principal fundamental matrix with X(0)=I. The monodromy is M=X(T); the complex eigenvalues of M counted with algebraic multiplicity are the Floquet multipliers. Monodromy from initial time s is U(s+T,s)=X(s)MX(s)^{-1}; these matrices are similar for every real s, so the multipliers are independent of s.

For a continuous T-periodic matrix A:ℝ→𝕂^{n×n}, T>0, and its principal fundamental matrix X(0)=I with M=X(T), X(t+T)=X(t)M for all real t. Consequently X(kT+r)=X(r)M^k for every integer k, including negative integers, and every real r.

For continuous T-periodic A:ℝ→𝕂^{n×n}, 𝕂=ℝ or ℂ, T>0, and X(0)=I, after complexifying even when A is real there are a constant complex matrix B and a C¹ complex matrix function P:ℝ→GL(n,ℂ), T-periodic, with P(0)=I and X(t)=P(t)exp(tB) for every t∈ℝ. The substitution x=P(t)y converts x′=A(t)x to y′=By.

For continuous T-periodic A:ℝ→𝕂^{n×n}, T>0, with principal matrix X and monodromy M=X(T), the zero solution of x′=A(t)x is exponentially asymptotically stable iff every Floquet multiplier μ has |μ|<1. It is Lyapunov stable iff all |μ|≤1 and every Jordan block for a unit-modulus multiplier has size one. If some |μ|>1 or a unit-modulus multiplier has a nontrivial Jordan block, the zero solution is unstable. The conclusions apply to real as well as complex A.

For the same continuous T-periodic A, principal fundamental matrix X(0)=I, and M=X(T), the homogeneous system has a nonzero T-periodic solution iff 1 is an eigenvalue of M. For continuous T-periodic b:ℝ→𝕂^n, x′=A(t)x+b(t) has a T-periodic solution iff (I−M)x₀=M∫₀ᵀ X(r)^{-1}b(r)dr is solvable for x₀. In particular, if 1 is not a multiplier, the T-periodic inhomogeneous solution exists and is unique.
Every invertible complex finite square matrix M is exp(L) for some complex matrix L. No real logarithm or global scalar logarithm branch is asserted.

With T=1, R(t) rotation by πt, X(t)=R(t)diag(1,2^t), and A(t)=π[[0,−1],[1,0]]+R(t)diag(0,log 2)R(t)^{-1}, A is real and 1-periodic, X′=AX, X(0)=I, and M=X(1)=diag(−1,−2). There is no real matrix B with exp(B)=M (commutation with M forces B diagonal, whose real exponential has positive diagonal). Therefore no real period-one Floquet factorization X(t)=P(t)exp(tB) with real B and real invertible 1-periodic P exists for this example.
Bibliographic comparison and scope: adopts the complex Floquet representation and the explicit real same-period counterexample; no unstated real logarithm or doubled-period convention is adopted.

On a real interval let p,q be continuous and let y₁ be a nowhere-zero solution of y″+py′+qy=0. For a base point t₀ the function y₂(t)=y₁(t)∫_{t₀}^t exp(−∫_{t₀}^s p(r)dr)/y₁(s)^2 ds is a second solution linearly independent of y₁. The same formula holds locally on a simply connected complex domain where p,q,y₁ are holomorphic and y₁ is nowhere zero, with holomorphic primitives in place of the real integrals.

Let p(z)=∑_{k≥0}p_kz^k and q(z)=∑_{k≥0}q_kz^k be holomorphic on |z|<R. For each prescribed y(0),y′(0), the solution of y″+py′+qy=0 is holomorphic throughout that disc. Writing y(z)=∑_{n≥0}a_nz^n, its coefficients satisfy (n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}=−∑_{k=0}^n((n−k+1)p_ka_{n−k+1}+q_ka_{n−k}) for all integers n≥0. Conversely the coefficients determined by this recurrence and a₀=y(0), a₁=y′(0) converge on the disc and determine that solution.

For z²y″+zp(z)y′+q(z)y=0 with p,q holomorphic on |z|<R, p₀=p(0),q₀=q(0), the indicial polynomial is I(r)=r(r−1)+p₀r+q₀. Choose a branch of log z on a slit punctured disc and define z^r=exp(r log z); all solution claims involving these powers use that chosen domain.

For z²y″+zp(z)y′+q(z)y=0 with p(z)=∑p_kz^k,q(z)=∑q_kz^k holomorphic on |z|<R and I(r)=r(r−1)+p₀r+q₀, if I(r)=0 and I(r+n)≠0 for every integer n≥1, there is a solution y(z)=z^r∑_{n=0}^∞a_nz^n on the chosen slit punctured disc, with a₀=1, power series convergent on |z|<R, and I(r+n)a_n=−∑_{k=1}^n((r+n−k)p_k+q_k)a_{n−k} for every n≥1. If the two indicial roots differ by a noninteger, the constructions at those roots give two linearly independent solutions.

For the same regular singular equation with holomorphic p,q on |z|<R and a chosen log branch on a slit punctured disc, suppose the indicial roots are ordered so that r₁−r₂=m is a nonnegative integer. There is a solution y₁=z^{r₁}a(z), with a holomorphic and a(0)=1. On a sufficiently small slit disc there is a linearly independent second solution: if m≥1, y₂=z^{r₂}b(z)+c y₁(z)log z with b holomorphic, b(0)=1 and a constant c which may be zero; if m=0, y₂=y₁(z)log z+z^{r₁}b(z) with b holomorphic. Analytic coefficients away from the singularity do not justify deleting the logarithmic term in the resonant case.

For the Euler equation z²y″+azy′+by=0 with constant coefficients, distinct roots r₁,r₂ of r(r−1)+ar+b=0 give the independent solutions z^{r₁},z^{r₂}. A repeated root r gives independent solutions z^r,z^r log z, on the chosen slit punctured domain.

For Bessel’s equation z²y″+zy′+(z²−ν²)y=0, ν≥0, a larger-indicial-root solution is y(z)=z^ν∑_{j=0}^∞(−1)^jz^{2j}/(4^j j!∏_{k=1}^j(ν+k)), with the empty product equal to one and z^ν interpreted on the chosen branch. The power series converges for every complex z and its substitution gives the differential equation. This is the stated normalization without the optional gamma factor in customary J_ν notation.

For every integer m≥0, ((1−x²)y′)′+m(m+1)y=0 has a polynomial solution P_m of degree m, unique up to multiplication by a nonzero scalar. Polynomial solutions of different degrees are orthogonal in L²(−1,1): for distinct m,l their inner product, equivalently ∫_{−1}¹P_m(x)P_l(x)dx for real choices, is zero.
Bibliographic comparison for ordinary and regular singular equations; convergence and resonance are part of the adopted conclusions, not merely formal series manipulations.

Fix real a<b. In the regular Sturm–Liouville chapter, p∈C¹[a,b], q,w∈C[a,b] are real and p(x)>0,w(x)>0 everywhere. Define Ly=−(py′)′+qy, H=L²([a,b],w(x)dx), and ⟨u,v⟩_w=∫_a^b u(x)overline(v(x))w(x)dx. The classical eigen-equation is Ly=λwy. H uses weighted L² equivalence classes.

Under the regular Sturm–Liouville hypotheses a<b, real p∈C¹, real continuous q,w with p,w>0, separated real boundary conditions are α_a y(a)+β_a p(a)y′(a)=0 and α_b y(b)+β_b p(b)y′(b)=0, where each real coefficient pair (α_a,β_a),(α_b,β_b) is nonzero. Dirichlet means y(a)=y(b)=0. General separated conditions are adopted for boundary-form and orthogonality results; the complete eigenfunction basis theorem is specifically adopted for Dirichlet conditions.

Under the regular Sturm–Liouville hypotheses, for C² complex-valued u,v, ∫_a^b((Lu)overline(v)−u overline(Lv))dx=[p(u overline(v′)−u′ overline(v))]_a^b. The boundary term is zero when u,v satisfy the same separated real boundary conditions (nonzero real coefficient pair at each endpoint). Every eigenvalue for those conditions is real, and eigenfunctions for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal in H=L²([a,b],w dx).

For the real regular Sturm–Liouville equation Ly=λwy, a nonzero real solution never has y=py′=0 simultaneously; all its zeros are simple and isolated. Between any two consecutive zeros of one solution, every independent solution at the same λ has exactly one zero. If μ>λ, between consecutive zeros of a solution at λ every nonzero real solution at μ has a zero.

For a<b, real p∈C¹[a,b], q,w∈C[a,b] with p,w>0, choose c>0 with Q=q+cw≥1 on [a,b]. There exists a real continuous symmetric kernel G:[a,b]²→ℝ, strictly positive when a<x,t<b, such that Kf(x)=∫_a^b G(x,t)f(t)w(t)dt gives the inverse Dirichlet solution of −(pu′)′+Qu=wf. For f∈H this inverse is understood as u∈C¹, pu′ absolutely continuous and the equation holding almost everywhere (the regularity specified in its proof); for continuous f it gives the classical solution. As an operator H→H, K is compact, self-adjoint, injective and strictly positive: ⟨Kf,f⟩_w>0 for every nonzero L² class f. The Dirichlet inverse is unique.

For a<b, real p∈C¹[a,b], q,w∈C[a,b] with p,w>0, the Dirichlet problem −(pφ′)′+qφ=λwφ, φ(a)=φ(b)=0, has a sequence of simple real eigenvalues λ₁<λ₂<⋯ with λ_j→+∞ and real classical eigenfunctions φ_j forming an orthonormal basis of H=L²([a,b],w dx). Every f∈H has f=∑_{j=1}^∞⟨f,φ_j⟩_w φ_j with convergence in H, and ‖f‖_H²=∑_{j=1}^∞|⟨f,φ_j⟩_w|². The stated expansion is in L²; no unqualified pointwise or uniform convergence is asserted.

Under the regular Dirichlet Sturm–Liouville hypotheses and with the simple eigenvalues λ_j and H-orthonormal classical eigenfunctions φ_j above, for f∈H and λ∉{λ_j}, (L−λw)y=wf, y(a)=y(b)=0, has a unique solution y∈C¹[a,b] with py′ absolutely continuous and the equation almost everywhere. In H it is y=∑_j (⟨f,φ_j⟩_w/(λ_j−λ))φ_j. At λ=λ_k, the same Dirichlet equation is solvable iff ⟨f,φ_k⟩_w=0; when solvable all solutions differ by multiples of φ_k.

For the regular Dirichlet Sturm–Liouville problem on [a,b] with real p∈C¹, real continuous q,w, p,w>0, index the simple eigenvalues increasingly as λ₁<λ₂<⋯. The classical eigenfunction φ_j has exactly j−1 zeros in the open interval (a,b).

Let K be a compact self-adjoint positive operator on a real or complex Hilbert space; positive here permits a nontrivial kernel. The closed linear span of its positive-eigenvalue eigenspaces equals (ker K)^⊥. Every nonzero eigenvalue has finite multiplicity. There are at most countably many nonzero eigenvalues; if infinitely many are listed with multiplicity, they tend to zero.

For ℓ>0, p=w=1, q=0 on [0,ℓ] with Dirichlet endpoints, the eigenvalues and real orthonormal eigenfunctions are λ_j=(jπ/ℓ)² and φ_j(x)=sqrt(2/ℓ)sin(jπx/ℓ), j≥1. They satisfy the equation and endpoints, form the complete L²(0,ℓ) orthonormal eigenbasis, and have exactly j−1 interior zeros. By contrast the initial-value problem y″+λy=0 has a unique solution for every λ and prescribed initial data, while the homogeneous Dirichlet boundary problem has nonzero solutions precisely at these discrete eigenvalues.

Bibliographic and adopted-scope information: all endpoints in this chapter are regular; singular-endpoint domain classification is deferred. The complete basis result is for the general regular Dirichlet problem; general separated conditions are retained in the boundary-form and orthogonality statements.

Let Ω⊂ℝ^n be open and f∈C^k(Ω,ℝ^n), k≥1. For the maximal interval I_x through time zero and solution Φ(t,x) with initial point x, D={(t,x):x∈Ω,t∈I_x} is open and Φ:D→Ω is C^k. For s∈I_x and t+s∈I_x, Φ(0,x)=x, I_{Φ(s,x)}=I_x−s, and Φ(t,Φ(s,x))=Φ(t+s,x). For every fixed real t the time map x↦Φ(t,x) is a C^k diffeomorphism from its open domain {x:t∈I_x} onto {y:−t∈I_y}, with inverse the time −t map. For every (t,x)∈D, D_xΦ(t,x)f(x)=f(Φ(t,x)).

For f∈C^k(Ω,ℝ^n), Ω open, k≥1, p is an equilibrium iff f(p)=0, and its maximal solution is constant. Two maximal orbit traces are disjoint or identical as sets. Every nonconstant maximal orbit is either injectively parametrized by time or periodic. In the periodic case its solution is complete on ℝ, has a least positive period T, and its full additive group of periods is Tℤ.

For the maximal partial flow of a C^k field f:Ω→ℝ^n on an open Ω, k≥1, a subset S is positively invariant if every solution starting in S stays in S for all nonnegative times in its maximal interval; it is invariant if the analogous property holds for both signs of time. A compact positively invariant subset of Ω supports complete forward solutions. A compact invariant subset supports complete two-sided solutions.

For f∈C^k(Ω,ℝ^n), Ω⊂ℝ^n open, k≥1, a C¹ function H:Ω→ℝ is constant on each solution iff DH(x)f(x)=0 for every x∈Ω. More generally, if h:Ω→ℝ^m is C¹, has rank m at each point of S=h^{-1}(c), and Dh(x)f(x)=0 for every x∈S, then S is invariant for both time directions throughout maximal existence intervals. Tangency is required only on S and the rank hypothesis is retained.

Let Ω⊂ℝ^n be open, f∈C^k(Ω,ℝ^n), k≥1, and p∈Ω with f(p)≠0. A neighborhood of p has C¹ coordinates (s,z)∈(−ε,ε)×V, V⊂ℝ^{n−1} open, in which the vector field is ∂/∂s. For a C^k field the coordinate map (and corresponding diffeomorphic coordinate representation) is C^k.

For f∈C^k(Ω,ℝ^n), Ω open, k≥1, suppose the positive orbit of x has compact closure K⊂Ω. Its forward solution is complete, and define ω(x)=⋂_{s≥0} closure({Φ(t,x):t≥s}). Then ω(x) is nonempty, compact, connected and invariant; its points are exactly the limits Φ(t_j,x) for sequences t_j→+∞. Moreover dist(Φ(t,x),ω(x))→0 as t→+∞. Invariance gives complete two-sided orbits through points of ω(x).

For an open Ω⊂ℝ^{2m} and H∈C²(Ω), the Hamiltonian system q′=∂_pH, p′=−∂_qH preserves the value of H on every solution. Every local time map has Jacobian determinant one and preserves Lebesgue measure on its open domain and all measurable subsets thereof. The time map remains a partial map on its actual existence domain; no completeness assumption is added.

Bibliographic comparisons for local flows, orbits, transverse coordinates, invariant sets and first integrals; stresses that common existence domains and tangency conditions are retained for later interfaces.

Let f∈C¹(Ω,ℝ^n), Ω open, have an equilibrium translated to 0; local neighborhoods have closure in Ω. The origin is Lyapunov stable if ∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 such that ‖x₀‖<δ implies ‖Φ(t,x₀)‖<ε for every t≥0. It is locally asymptotically stable if it is stable and every sufficiently nearby solution tends to zero. It is locally exponentially stable if ∃C,α,δ>0 with ‖Φ(t,x₀)‖≤C exp(−αt)‖x₀‖ for every t≥0 and ‖x₀‖<δ. All three assertions include forward existence of the solutions being quantified.

Let f∈C¹(Ω,ℝ^n) have equilibrium 0. If V∈C¹ near 0, V(0)=0, V(x)>0 for x≠0 in that neighborhood and V̇(x)=DV(x)f(x)≤0, then 0 is Lyapunov stable. If V̇(x)<0 for every nonzero x near 0, the equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable. If, on a neighborhood, c₁‖x‖²≤V(x)≤c₂‖x‖² and V̇(x)≤−c₃‖x‖² with c₁,c₂,c₃>0, then it is locally exponentially stable and, for all sufficiently small x₀ and every t≥0, ‖Φ(t,x₀)‖≤sqrt(c₂/c₁) exp(−c₃t/(2c₂))‖x₀‖. These conclusions include forward existence.

For f∈C¹(Ω,ℝ^n) with equilibrium at 0, put A=Df(0). If every eigenvalue of A has negative real part, 0 is locally exponentially stable, including forward existence and a local exponential bound. If some eigenvalue of A has positive real part, 0 is unstable. Eigenvalues on the imaginary axis alone do not decide stability or instability; the nonhyperbolic examples below substantiate this limitation.

Let f∈C¹(Ω,ℝ^n), Ω open, K⊂Ω compact and positively invariant. Suppose V∈C¹ on a neighborhood of K and V̇=DV f≤0 on K. Define E={x∈K:V̇(x)=0}, and define M to be the largest invariant subset of E, namely the union of all complete orbits contained in E. For every x∈K, dist(Φ(t,x),M)→0 as t→+∞. If M is a singleton equilibrium, every such orbit converges to it. Positive invariance and compactness provide forward existence.

A real finite square matrix A has every eigenvalue in the open left half-plane iff, for any prescribed real symmetric positive definite matrix Q, there exists a real symmetric positive definite P with AᵀP+PA=−Q. When it exists, P is unique and P=∫₀^∞ exp(tAᵀ)Q exp(tA)dt; the improper matrix integral converges.

The scalar equations x′=−x³, x′=x³ and x′=0 all have derivative zero at equilibrium 0. For x′=−x³, x(t)=x₀(1+2tx₀²)^{−1/2} for t≥0 and 0 is locally asymptotically stable. For x′=x³ every positive nonzero initial value gives finite-time escape and 0 is unstable. For x′=0, 0 is stable but not attractive. Thus the zero linearization cannot classify these cases.

For x′=y, y′=−sin x−cy, c>0, the energy V(x,y)=y²/2+1−cos x satisfies V̇=−cy². In a sufficiently small compact energy sublevel around (0,0), the only complete orbit contained in {y=0} is (0,0), because remaining there requires sin x=0. The equilibrium (0,0) is therefore locally asymptotically stable. For the undamped system c=0, V is conserved, so nearby solutions with nonzero energy cannot converge to (0,0).

Bibliographic and scope discussion retaining compactness for invariance arguments and distinctions among stability, attraction and exponential decay. Hyperbolic invariant manifolds and topological linearization are developed separately in chapter 20, not assumed as prerequisites of these direct stability proofs.

Throughout planar dynamics Ω⊂ℝ² is open and f∈C¹(Ω,ℝ²); dimension and regularity apply to each limit-set theorem. A transverse segment is a sufficiently short straight segment on which the normal component of f never vanishes, with its points ordered by a fixed affine coordinate.

For the planar field x′=F(x,y), y′=G(x,y), coordinate nullclines are N_x={(x,y):F(x,y)=0} and N_y={(x,y):G(x,y)=0}. Equilibria are exactly N_x∩N_y. Away from both nullclines the signs of F,G give the quadrant of the tangent vector. On N_x\N_y the tangent is nonzero vertical; on N_y\N_x it is nonzero horizontal. A nullcline need not be invariant; these descriptions are coordinate dependent.

For a C¹ planar field on open Ω⊂ℝ² and a sufficiently short transverse straight segment ordered by a fixed affine coordinate, successive intersections of a forward orbit with the segment are either all the same point, in which case the orbit is periodic, or strictly monotone in the segment coordinate. In particular, an omega-limit set meets a sufficiently short transverse segment in at most one point.

Let Ω⊂ℝ² be open and f∈C¹(Ω,ℝ²). If a positive orbit has compact closure contained in Ω, and its omega-limit set contains no equilibrium, then that entire omega-limit set equals one nonconstant periodic orbit (not merely a set containing a periodic orbit).
For a C¹ field f on open Ω⊂ℝ², every nonempty compact positively invariant set K⊂Ω containing no equilibrium contains a nonconstant periodic orbit.

Let Ω⊂ℝ² be open, f∈C¹(Ω,ℝ²), D⊂Ω open and simply connected, and B∈C¹(D). If div(Bf) is everywhere strictly positive on D or everywhere strictly negative on D, no nonconstant periodic orbit is contained in D. The case B=1 is Bendixson’s criterion.

For x′=x(1−x−y), y′=y(x−a), 0<a<1, the first coordinate nullcline is {x=0}∪{y=1−x}, the second {y=0}∪{x=a}. In x,y>0, x′>0 exactly below y=1−x and y′>0 exactly to the right of x=a; the complementary signs give the complete four sign regions. In the closed positive quadrant equilibria are exactly (0,0),(1,0),(a,1−a). Along any solution, x(t)=x(0)exp(∫₀ᵗ(1−x(s)−y(s))ds) and y(t)=y(0)exp(∫₀ᵗ(x(s)−a)ds). Consequently positive coordinates remain positive throughout existence, and each coordinate axis is invariant. Most nullcline points are not equilibria.

The integer winding index of a closed piecewise C¹ curve about a point off its trace, and local constancy on the trace complement, are explicitly used as complex-analysis foundations. The following separately stated local index-jump lemma is adopted; a prior classification of every complementary component is not assumed.

If a closed piecewise C¹ planar curve meets a small disc in one oriented straight arc and has no other points in that disc, the winding index immediately to the left of that oriented arc is one greater than the winding index immediately to its right.

For x′=(1−x²−y²)x−y, y′=x+(1−x²−y²)y, polar coordinates on r>0 give r′=r(1−r²), θ′=1. The annulus 1/2≤r≤2 is positively invariant, contains no equilibria, and contains the periodic orbit r=1 of period 2π. Every nonzero solution approaches that circle as t→+∞, since its radial coordinate is monotone toward the unique positive radial equilibrium r=1.

For x′=y, y′=−sin x, E(x,y)=y²/2+1−cos x is conserved. For every integer k, equilibria (2kπ,0) have positive definite energy Hessian and are Lyapunov-stable centers; equilibria ((2k+1)π,0) have linearized eigenvalues 1,−1 and are unstable. For 0<E<2 each compact energy oval around a center is regular, invariant and is a periodic orbit. At E=2 a branch can instead approach a saddle, showing that the no-equilibrium hypothesis on the omega-limit set in Poincaré–Bendixson cannot be deleted.
Bibliographic and scope discussion: the regular compact Poincaré–Bendixson theorem does not assert a generalized classification of limit sets containing arbitrary equilibrium connections.

Let f∈C^k(Ω,ℝ^n), Ω open, k≥1, and p lie on a nonconstant periodic orbit Γ with least period T>0. Then f(p)≠0. Choose a linear functional ℓ with ℓ(f(p))≠0 and a sufficiently small local section Σ={z:ℓ(z−p)=0} around p.

For f∈C^k(Ω,ℝ^n), k≥1, p on a nonconstant periodic orbit Γ of least period T>0, and a small section Σ={z:ℓ(z−p)=0} with ℓ(f(p))≠0, an open neighborhood of p in Σ admits a unique C^k return-time function τ close to T with τ(p)=T and P(z)=Φ(τ(z),z)∈Σ. After shrinking, P is a C^k local diffeomorphism fixing p. The section can be chosen so this is the first positive return for the points under consideration. For M=D_xΦ(T,p) and every v∈ker ℓ, Dτ(p)v=−ℓ(Mv)/ℓ(f(p)) and DP(p)v=Mv−f(p)ℓ(Mv)/ℓ(f(p)). All maps and times remain in their actual common flow domains.

With the preceding C^k vector field, periodic orbit, local return map P and section at p, the variational equation along Γ has T-periodic coefficients A(t)=Df(Φ(t,p)). Its monodromy M=D_xΦ(T,p) satisfies Mf(p)=f(p). The operator on ℝ^n/span{f(p)} induced by M is conjugate to DP(p):ker ℓ→ker ℓ. Consequently det(λI−M)=(λ−1)det(λI−DP(p)), and det DP(p)=exp(∫₀ᵀ div f(Φ(t,p))dt). For n=2, the single transverse multiplier is strictly positive.

For a C^k vector field f on open Ω⊂ℝ^n, k≥1, and a nonconstant periodic orbit Γ with local return map P at p, if every eigenvalue of DP(p) has modulus less than one, Γ is locally exponentially orbitally stable. Precisely, there exist C,α,δ>0 such that every x∈Ω with dist(x,Γ)<δ has a forward-complete solution and dist(Φ(t,x),Γ)≤C exp(−αt)dist(x,Γ) for every t≥0. This estimate applies to all nearby initial points, not only points already on the section.

For the same C^k vector field, nonconstant periodic orbit Γ and local return map P at p, if DP(p) has an eigenvalue with modulus greater than one, Γ is orbitally unstable. For a planar orbit, the multiplier criteria give attraction (indeed the preceding local exponential orbital stability) when ∫₀ᵀ div f(Φ(t,p))dt<0, and orbital instability when that integral is positive. Equality alone leaves the nonlinear stability question undecided.

For a compact periodic orbit Γ, orbital stability means that for every neighborhood scale ε>0 there is δ>0 such that solutions with dist(x,Γ)<δ exist for all future time and stay within distance ε of Γ. Orbital asymptotic stability additionally requires distance to Γ to tend to zero for sufficiently close initial points. No convergence to a fixed equal-time phase point of the moving orbit is required.

For the oscillator x′=(1−x²−y²)x−y, y′=x+(1−x²−y²)y, the orbit Γ={x²+y²=1} has period 2π. Its radial variation satisfies ρ′=(1−3r²)ρ=−2ρ along Γ, so the transverse multiplier is exp(−4π)<1, whereas the tangential multiplier is 1. Thus Γ is attracting although its full monodromy has a multiplier on the unit circle.
Bibliographic and interface discussion retaining local sections, common existence domains, the neutral time direction and conversion from return-iteration count to actual elapsed time.

A discrete dynamical system is a map F:X→X. Its forward orbit at x is (F^n(x))_{n≥0}, where F^0=id and F^(n+1)=F∘F^n. A⊆X is positively invariant when F(A)⊆A and invariant when F(A)=A. A point has least period p≥1 when F^p(x)=x and no smaller positive integer fixes it. Negative iterates are used only if F is invertible.

For maps F:X→X and G:Y→Y on topological spaces, a topological conjugacy is a homeomorphism h:X→Y with h∘F=G∘h. A semiconjugacy is a continuous surjection satisfying that equation, without an injectivity requirement.

If h∘F=G∘h for maps F:X→X, G:Y→Y and h:X→Y, then h∘F^n=G^n∘h for every integer n≥0. If h is a topological conjugacy, it gives correspondences between periodic points preserving least period, between invariant sets by A↦h(A), and between dense forward orbits. At corresponding fixed points it preserves Lyapunov stability and asymptotic stability in both directions.

Every continuous map F:[a,b]→[a,b] of a nondegenerate real closed interval a<b has a fixed point. If F is Lipschitz with constant 0≤q<1, the fixed point p is unique, every forward orbit converges to p, and |F^n(x)−p|≤q^n|x−p| for every x∈[a,b] and every n≥0.

A fixed point p of a continuous map F on a metric space is Lyapunov stable if ∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 ∀x with dist(x,p)<δ ∀n≥0, dist(F^n(x),p)<ε. It is asymptotically stable if stable and attracts a neighborhood, meaning that each orbit starting there tends to p. In a normed setting it is locally exponentially stable if ∃C>0, 0<q<1 and a neighborhood of p on which ||F^n(x)−p||≤Cq^n||x−p|| for every n≥0.

Let A be a real or complex finite-dimensional linear operator. For every real a with spectral radius ρ(A)<a, there is an equivalent norm ||·||_* whose induced operator norm satisfies ||A||_*≤a. If A is invertible and all complex eigenvalues of A have modulus greater than a>0, there is an equivalent norm satisfying ||Av||_*≥a||v||_* for every v.

If F is C^1 near a fixed point p∈R^d and ρ(DF(p))<1, then p is locally exponentially stable: some C>0, 0<q<1 and neighborhood have all forward iterates defined and ||F^n(x)−p||≤Cq^n||x−p|| for n≥0 and x in that neighborhood.
If F is C^1 near a fixed point p∈R^d and DF(p) has a complex eigenvalue of modulus greater than 1, then p is Lyapunov unstable. There is no exclusion of eigenvalues of modulus 1 in other directions.

For a C^1 map, let p have least period m≥1. If ρ(D(F^m)(p))<1, its finite periodic orbit is locally exponentially attracting and Lyapunov stable. If D(F^m)(p) has an eigenvalue of modulus greater than 1, the periodic orbit is Lyapunov unstable.

The real maps F_−(x)=x−x^3 and F_+(x)=x+x^3 fix 0 and have derivative 1 there. For sufficiently small 0<|x|<1 the first strictly decreases |x| and its forward orbit tends to 0 (so 0 is locally attracting, and by the same decrease stable). The second strictly increases |x| until it leaves any fixed sufficiently small interval (so 0 is unstable). A unit-modulus multiplier therefore alone implies neither attraction nor instability.

The circle is T=R/Z with quotient distance dist([x],[y])=inf_{k∈Z}|x−y−k|. An increasing homeomorphism L:R→R satisfying L(x+1)=L(x)+1 induces the orientation-preserving circle homeomorphism F([x])=[L(x)] and is called its lift.

For every increasing circle lift L:R→R, ρ(L)=lim_{n→∞}(L^n(x)−x)/n exists and is independent of x∈R. For each integer k, ρ(L+k)=ρ(L)+k. The induced circle homeomorphism has a periodic point iff ρ(L) is rational. More precisely, for p∈Z and q≥1 an integer, ρ(L)=p/q iff ∃x∈R, L^q(x)=x+p; p/q need not be in lowest terms for this equivalence.

For the rigid circle rotation R_α([x])=[x+α], if α=p/q is in lowest terms with q≥1, every point has least period q. If α is irrational, every forward orbit is dense, no point is periodic, and the distance between any two points is preserved under all iterates.

For f_μ(x)=μx(1−x), [0,1] is positively invariant for 0≤μ≤4. On R its fixed points are 0 and, when μ≠0, 1−μ^(-1), with possible coincidence at μ=1; the latter lies in [0,1] for μ≥1. Zero is locally attracting for 0≤μ<1 and repelling for μ>1. The nonzero fixed point is locally attracting for 1<μ<3 and repelling for μ>3. No threshold stability assertion is made at μ=1 or μ=3.

The function h:[0,1]→[0,1], h(t)=sin²(πt/2), is an increasing homeomorphism. For the tent map τ(t)=2t on 0≤t≤1/2 and τ(t)=2−2t on 1/2≤t≤1, including the common endpoint, h∘τ=f_4∘h for f_4(x)=4x(1−x). Thus h is a topological conjugacy from τ to f_4.

Bibliographic coverage paragraph: references for map viewpoint, multipliers, interval iteration and conjugacy; symbolic coding and rigorous chaotic examples are assigned to Chapter 17. Logistic assertions here are exact algebraic statements, not numerical orbit-diagram claims.

A scalar flow family has equation x′=f(x,μ) with real parameter μ; a map family has x_(n+1)=F_μ(x_n). Local bifurcation statements study equilibria or periodic orbits in a fixed neighborhood of a distinguished state and parameter, with their number, stability and conjugacy type specified by the actual equations and nondegeneracy conditions.

If the scalar real function f is C^1 near (0,0), f(0,0)=0 and f_x(0,0)≠0, all nearby equilibria of x′=f(x,μ) form a unique C^1 graph x=x(μ). Their scalar linearized stability has constant type for sufficiently small μ. For a C^1 scalar map family fixing 0 at μ=0, the same unique C^1 nearby fixed-point graph exists if ∂_x F_0(0)≠1, by applying the assertion to F_μ(x)−x. The map assertion is persistence; no constant stability type is asserted at a multiplier such as −1.

For scalar real C^3 f near (0,0), assume f(0,0)=f_x(0,0)=0, f_μ(0,0)≠0 and f_xx(0,0)≠0. There exists a local C^1 state coordinate y=y(x), with y(0)=0 and y′(0)=1, in which the equilibrium set f(x,μ)=0 is exactly μ=a y², with a=−f_xx(0,0)/(2f_μ(0,0))≠0. Sufficiently locally there are exactly two equilibria when μ/a>0, none when μ/a<0, and one double equilibrium at μ=0. The two simple equilibria have opposite scalar stability (one attracting and one repelling). This is an exact zero-set description, without an assertion of an exact time-preserving vector-field normal form.

Let scalar f be C^3, with f(0,μ)=0 for every sufficiently small μ, f_x(0,0)=0, a=f_xμ(0,0)≠0 and b=f_xx(0,0)/2≠0. All nearby equilibria are x=0 and a unique branch x=χ(μ)=−aμ/b+o(μ). The branches meet only at μ=0 and exchange stability: for sufficiently small μ≠0, f_x at x=0 has sign sgn(aμ) and f_x at x=χ(μ) has sign −sgn(aμ).

Let scalar f be C^5 and odd in x, with f_x(0,0)=0, a=f_xμ(0,0)≠0 and b=f_xxx(0,0)/6≠0. Besides x=0, exactly two sufficiently small equilibria exist precisely on the parameter side −aμ/b>0. They are x=±sqrt(s(μ)) for a C^1 local function s with s(0)=0 and s′(0)=−a/b. For all sufficiently small μ≠0 the derivative f_x at 0 has sign sgn(aμ) and on each nonzero branch has sign −sgn(aμ), specifying their scalar stability.

The flow x′=μx−x³ has stable equilibrium branches x=±sqrt(μ) for μ>0. Adding a constant perturbation ε≠0, giving x′=μx−x³+ε, destroys the equilibrium branch x=0 and the odd symmetry; its equilibria instead solve μx−x³+ε=0. The symmetric pitchfork theorem therefore does not apply to the perturbed equation.

For the scalar map F_μ(x)=−(1+μ)x+x³, 0 is locally attracting for small negative μ and unstable for small positive μ. For every 0<μ<1, the distinct points ±sqrt(μ) form a stable orbit of least period 2, and its multiplier D(F_μ²)(sqrt(μ))=(−1+2μ)² has modulus <1. The cycle amplitude sqrt(μ) tends to 0 as μ↓0. This is the stated normal-form example, without a universal flip-family classification.

For a real C^5 planar family having an equilibrium at 0 for every sufficiently small μ, suppose its linearization has eigenvalues a(μ)±ib(μ), with a(0)=0 and b(0)=ω>0. There are parameter-smooth real local coordinates represented by w∈C in which w′=(a(μ)+ib(μ))w+c(μ)w² conjugate(w)+R(w,conjugate(w),μ), with R=O(|w|⁴) and D_w R=O(|w|³), uniformly for small μ and with the corresponding parameter-derivative estimates. The coefficient c(0) is specified by the finite homological normalization: choose a fixed real vector v≠0 and the parameter-smooth basis (v,(A(μ)−a(μ)I)v/b(μ)), identifying the linearization A(μ) with λ=a+ib; in these coordinates, eliminate each quadratic monomial via the near-identity change with coefficient (f_2)_(jk)/D_(jk), where D_(jk)=jλ+k conjugate(λ)−λ=(j+k−1)a+i(j−k−1)b; compute the resulting cubic polynomial g_3 including quadratic corrections; then eliminate the three nonresonant cubic monomials using (g_3)_(jk)/D_(jk), leaving the (j,k)=(2,1) coefficient c(μ)=(g_3)_(21). Set ℓ=Re c(0); ℓ≠0 is the cubic nondegeneracy condition. The coordinate maps are actual local changes, and the controlled remainder is retained rather than discarded.

For the finite-order normal form w′=(a(μ)+ib(μ))w+c(μ)w² conjugate(w)+R with a(0)=0, b(0)=ω>0, ℓ=Re c(0), and the uniform C^1 fourth-order remainder of the preceding lemma, the local first return to the positive real ray is defined for sufficiently small radii r≥0 and parameters. Its radial map is P(r,μ)=exp(2πa(μ)/b(μ))r+K(μ)r³+O(r⁴), where K(0)=2πℓ/ω. The remainder has radial derivative O(r³) and parameter derivative O(r⁴), uniformly locally. The section and return are local, without a global-section assertion.

For the real C^5 planar equilibrium family in the cubic normal-form lemma (eigenvalues a(μ)±ib(μ), a(0)=0, b(0)=ω>0, normalized cubic coefficient ℓ=Re c(0)), additionally assume a′(0)≠0 and ℓ≠0. For sufficiently small parameters a unique small nonconstant periodic orbit exists precisely when a(μ)ℓ<0; uniqueness is among periodic orbits contained in a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood. Its positive-real-ray radius in the normal coordinates satisfies μ=−ℓ r²/a′(0)+O(r³) and r²=−a′(0)μ/ℓ+o(|μ|). Its period tends to 2π/ω. It is asymptotically orbitally stable if ℓ<0 and unstable if ℓ>0. For nonzero sufficiently small μ the equilibrium is exponentially stable when a(μ)<0 and unstable when a(μ)>0; no strict linearization conclusion is imposed at μ=0.

For z′=(μ+iω)z−z|z|² with ω>0, no quadratic elimination is needed and the normalized cubic coefficient is c=−1. Its exact polar equations are r′=μr−r³, θ′=ω. For μ>0 it has the stable cycle r=sqrt(μ), with period 2π/ω. With the cubic term absent one has ℓ=0, so the nondegenerate Hopf theorem gives no conclusion.

For a C^1 system x′=f(x,y), y′=g(x,y), a C^1 graph y=h(x) is locally invariant iff Dh(x)f(x,h(x))=g(x,h(x)) on its domain. More precisely, this identity makes every reduced trajectory x′=f(x,h(x)), lifted as (x,h(x)), a full trajectory while it remains in the graph domain; uniqueness gives local invariance. Conversely local invariance implies this differential identity.

For x′=f(x), y′=−By+g(x) on R^m×R^k, assume f is C^1 and globally Lipschitz with constant L, f(0)=Df(0)=0; g is C^1, bounded, with bounded derivative and g(0)=Dg(0)=0; and ||exp(−Bt)||≤M exp(−βt) for every t≥0, with β>L. Let φ be the complete flow of x′=f(x). Then h(x)=∫_0^∞ exp(−Bs)g(φ_(−s)(x)) ds is well-defined and C^1, h(0)=Dh(0)=0, and its graph is invariant. Every full solution satisfies y(t)−h(x(t))=exp(−Bt)(y(0)−h(x(0))) for t≥0, hence ||y(t)−h(x(t))||≤M exp(−βt)||y(0)−h(x(0))||. The graph is tangent to the center subspace and attracts each vertical fiber exponentially. This assertion is limited to the triangular system.

Scope and references: the invariance equation does not itself construct a regular graph. The triangular theorem is the adopted center-graph construction. General coupled high-dimensional center-manifold existence, higher-codimension and global bifurcations are deferred; hyperbolic stable/unstable manifolds are treated separately in Chapter 20. The finite normal form and return estimates provide the generic planar Hopf bridge.

For a continuous self-map F of a metric space X, topological transitivity means ∀nonempty open U,V⊆X ∃n≥0, F^n(U)∩V≠∅. Sensitive dependence means ∃δ>0 ∀x∈X ∀neighborhoods U of x ∃y∈U ∃n≥0, dist(F^n(x),F^n(y))>δ. In this chapter chaos is the conjunction of topological transitivity, density of periodic points, and sensitive dependence.

The binary spaces are Σ^+={0,1}^{N_0} and Σ={0,1}^Z, with shift (σs)_j=s_(j+1). On Σ^+, d_+(s,t)=2^(−N) if N is the first differing index, and d_+(s,s)=0. On Σ, d_Z(s,t)=∑_{j∈Z}2^(−|j|−2)|s_j−t_j|. These are metrics inducing the respective product topologies. Cylinder sets specify finitely many coordinates; initial cylinders suffice on Σ^+. The one-sided shift is continuous and surjective but noninjective; the two-sided shift is a homeomorphism.
Both binary symbolic metric spaces Σ^+ and Σ are compact, have no isolated points, and are totally disconnected.

The one-sided and two-sided binary shifts are each topologically transitive, have dense periodic points, and have sensitive dependence, hence are chaotic under the chapter definition. For every integer n≥1, σ^n has exactly 2^n fixed points (without a claim that all have least period n). Each shift admits a dense forward orbit.

Let K be a nonempty compact metric space of finite diameter. Let b_0,b_1:K→K be injective contractions with common constant 0≤q<1 and disjoint images. Let F be continuous on a neighborhood containing these images and satisfy F∘b_i=id_K for i=0,1. For n≥1 put K_n=⋃_{s_0,…,s_(n−1)∈{0,1}} b_(s_0)∘⋯∘b_(s_(n−1))(K) and Λ=⋂_{n≥1}K_n. There exists a homeomorphism π:Σ^+→Λ with F∘π=π∘σ. In particular Λ is compact, invariant F(Λ)=Λ, has no isolated points, and is totally disconnected, and F restricted to Λ is chaotic.

For every real μ≥5, the quadratic polynomial f_μ(x)=μx(1−x) has a compact invariant Cantor set Λ_μ⊆[0,1] on which f_μ is topologically conjugate to the one-sided binary shift, hence chaotic. Here Cantor means nonempty compact, perfect (no isolated points), and totally disconnected. The conclusion concerns this set, not invariance of all [0,1].

The tent map τ:[0,1]→[0,1], τ(t)=2t for t≤1/2 and τ(t)=2−2t for t≥1/2, is chaotic. It is exact in the stated interval sense: for every nonempty relatively open interval I⊆[0,1], there is n≥0 with τ^n(I)=[0,1]. Consequently f_4(x)=4x(1−x) is chaotic on its entire invariant interval [0,1].

For the tent map the two inverse branches meet at the turning point, so injectivity of the disjoint-branch coding conclusion cannot be imposed there without justification. In particular [0,1] is connected and the full binary symbolic space is totally disconnected, so [0,1] is not homeomorphic to that symbolic space. Thus the full-interval tent/logistic dynamics cannot be topologically conjugate to the full binary shift by a homeomorphism.

Fix 0<r<1/2 and define C_r={(1−r)∑_{j=0}^∞s_j r^j:s_j∈{0,1}}⊆[0,1]. On the disjoint strips V_0=[0,r]×[0,1], V_1=[1−r,1]×[0,1], define H(x,y)=((x−(1−r)i)/r, ry+(1−r)i) when (x,y)∈V_i. Then H is a homeomorphism from V_0∪V_1 onto the two disjoint horizontal strips [0,1]×[0,r] and [0,1]×[1−r,1]. Its maximal set admitting a bi-infinite orbit in the unit square is Λ=C_r×C_r. H restricted to Λ is conjugate to the two-sided binary shift. On each strip its derivative is diag(r^(−1),r), with expanding factor r^(−1) and contracting factor r. Only the explicit local strip map is asserted; no smooth extension across the gap is assumed.

An irrational circle rotation has all forward orbits dense, is an isometry, and has no periodic points. It is not sensitive: for every proposed δ>0 one can take a neighborhood of radius less than δ, and all distances of its points from the reference orbit remain less than δ for all iterates. Thus dense orbits alone do not imply chaos. Its measure ergodicity is the separate Chapter 19 assertion.

Bibliographic and scope paragraph: the explicitly proved coding and affine strip horseshoe theorems are adopted. A transverse-homoclinic theorem and a numerically observed Lorenz attractor are not adopted as proved consequences.

For a C^1 map F:U→U with U⊆R^d open, x∈U and v≠0, define finite-time directional growth λ_n(x,v)=(1/n)log(||D(F^n)(x)v||/||v||), n≥1. The directional Lyapunov exponent is lim_{n→∞}λ_n when the limit exists, possibly −∞, using log 0=−∞. The operator-norm upper rate is limsup_n (1/n)log||D(F^n)(x)||. For a differentiable flow replace n by t→+∞; for a matrix cocycle A over T replace D(F^n)(x) by A(T^(n−1)x)⋯A(x). A limsup does not by definition assert an existing limit.

In a fixed finite-dimensional space, existence and value of every directional growth limit, operator-norm limit or corresponding limsup just defined are independent of the chosen equivalent norm, for map derivatives, flow derivatives, and matrix cocycles, including the value −∞.

Let A be a real or complex finite-dimensional matrix and v≠0. In its complex generalized-eigenspace decomposition (complexifying a real space), define α(v)=max{Re λ:the component of v in E_λ is nonzero}. Then lim_{t→∞}(1/t)log||exp(tA)v||=α(v). The operator-norm limit lim_{t→∞}(1/t)log||exp(tA)|| is the largest real part of an eigenvalue. Nontrivial Jordan blocks do not change these limits.

Let F be C^1 on an open subset of R^d, K a compact invariant set within that open set, and μ an invariant probability measure on K. Assume g(x)=log|det DF(x)| belongs to L^1(μ). Then (1/n)log|det D(F^n)(x)| converges for μ-almost every x to an invariant integrable function g^*, with ∫g^*dμ=∫g dμ. If μ is ergodic the limit equals the constant ∫g dμ almost everywhere. For d=1 this is the directional derivative exponent for every nonzero direction; for d>1 only volume growth, rather than existence of all directional exponents, is asserted.

Over the one-sided binary shift, the scalar cocycle A(s)=exp(s_0) is continuous, bounded and invertible. There exists a base point s made of alternating all-zero/all-one blocks of lengths L_j=2^(2^j), for which (L_1+⋯+L_(j−1))/L_j→0. The logarithmic growth averages of A along this point have subsequences converging to 0 and to 1, so no pointwise Lyapunov exponent exists there. This is a pointwise counterexample and does not assert that the point is typical for an invariant measure.

For a continuous self-map F of a metric space, a stable attractor is a nonempty compact invariant set A, F(A)=A, that is Lyapunov stable as a whole set and attracts a neighborhood: dist(F^n(x),A)→0 for every x in that neighborhood. Whole-set stability means every neighborhood V of A admits a neighborhood W of A with F^n(W)⊆V for all n≥0. Its basin is {x:dist(F^n(x),A)→0}. No transitivity or positive-exponent hypothesis is part of this definition.

Let F:X→X be continuous on a metric space and let nonempty compact K satisfy F(K)⊆int K. Then A=⋂_{n≥0}F^n(K) is a stable attractor: nonempty, compact, F(A)=A, Lyapunov stable, and attracting a neighborhood. Attraction from K is uniform in the neighborhood formulation: every neighborhood V of A contains F^n(K) for all sufficiently large n. The basin contains the open set ⋃_{n≥0}F^(−n)(int K), where F^(−n) denotes preimage under F^n and requires no inverse map.

For F(x)=x/2 on R, K=[−1,1] is trapping, ⋂_{n≥0}F^n(K)={0}, and {0} is a stable attractor. Its derivative Lyapunov exponent is −log 2. The dynamics is not sensitive; attraction alone does not imply chaos.

For a metric-space set E, s>0 and δ>0, H^s_δ(E)=inf{∑_i(diam U_i)^s:E⊆⋃_i U_i, diam U_i≤δ}, using countable covers. Define H^s(E)=lim_{δ↓0}H^s_δ(E) and dim_H E=inf{s>0:H^s(E)=0}. For compact E⊆R, N_ε(E) is the least number of intervals of length at most ε covering E; its box dimension is lim_{ε↓0}log N_ε(E)/log(1/ε), when that limit exists.

If a Borel probability measure ν supported on E⊆R satisfies ν(J)≤C|J|^s for every sufficiently short interval J, with C>0 and s>0, then H^s(E)≥C^(−1), for the unnormalized diameter-based Hausdorff measure defined above.

For every 0<r<1/2, C_r={(1−r)∑_{j=0}^∞s_j r^j:s_j∈{0,1}} satisfies dim_H C_r=dim_box C_r=d=log 2/log(1/r), with the box-dimension limit existing and 0<H^d(C_r)<∞. In particular the middle-thirds Cantor set C_(1/3) has dimension log 2/log 3.

Scope and bibliography: finite numerical rates, limsups and almost-everywhere existing exponents are distinct; box dimension alone does not imply a Hausdorff dimension formula. The general multiplicative ergodic theorem and general dimension formulas are explicitly deferred. Adopted results here are the stated linear, integrable scalar/volume and separated-Cantor results.

For a probability space (X,A,μ), a measurable map T:X→X is measure preserving if μ(T^(−1)(E))=μ(E) for every measurable E. E is invariant modulo null sets if μ(T^(−1)(E) Δ E)=0. T is ergodic if every such measurable set has measure 0 or 1. It is mixing if μ(A∩T^(−n)(B))→μ(A)μ(B) for all measurable A,B. Here T^(−n) always means preimage and no inverse transformation is required.

If T is a measurable measure-preserving map on a finite measure space (in particular a probability space), then for every measurable E, almost every x∈E satisfies T^n(x)∈E for infinitely many integers n≥1. Invertibility is not assumed.

For a measure-preserving map T on the probability space, ∫h∘T dμ=∫h dμ for every nonnegative measurable h and every integrable h. Composition Uh=h∘T therefore induces a well-defined linear isometry of L^p(μ) into itself for each 1≤p≤∞. For every n≥1 the averaging operator A_n h=(1/n)∑_{j=0}^{n−1}U^j h has operator norm at most 1 on each such L^p space.

Let X be a second-countable metric space, μ a Borel probability measure, and T a measurable μ-preserving self-map. Then for μ-almost every x∈X there is a sequence of positive integer times n_k→∞ for which T^(n_k)(x)→x.
