Front matter and global applicability conventions. All rings are associative and unital; ring homomorphisms preserve 1; the zero ring is permitted unless the passage specifies a field, domain, proper maximal ideal, or nonzero ring. Modules are unital left modules unless specified; right modules are left modules over the opposite ring. Balanced tensors over a noncommutative ring put a right module first and a left module second; commuting extra scalar actions must be tracked. Chapters 4–7 and 12 use commutative rings. Chapters 8–9 use a field unless another coefficient ring is specified, and complex character inner products are linear in their first variable. Homological differentials lower degree, cohomological ones raise degree; resolutions start in degree zero; the tensor total differential in bidegree (p,q) is d_C⊗1+(-1)^p 1⊗d_D. Choice, elementary algebra/linear algebra, category language, and the cited preliminary results are background, not additional newly asserted theorem obligations. The title, overview, references, and typesetting are contextual.

For every unital ring R and two-sided ideal I, the additive quotient R/I admits a unique ring structure making π:R→R/I a unital ring homomorphism. For every unital ring homomorphism f:R→S, there exists a unique unital ring homomorphism f̄:R/I→S satisfying f̄∘π=f if and only if I⊆ker f; its formula is f̄(r+I)=f(r). Include I=R: the quotient is the zero ring, and such a factorization then forces S to be the zero ring.

For any linear map f:M→N of unital left R-modules over any ring, the induced linear map M/ker f→im f is an isomorphism. Quotients by submodules use r(m+U)=rm+U. The inclusion ker f↪M has the kernel universal property: every linear map into M killed by f factors uniquely through it. The quotient map N→N/im f has the cokernel universal property: every linear map out of N vanishing on im f factors uniquely through it. All these assertions hold for right modules by passage to Rᵒᵖ.

A composable pair L --u→ M --v→ N is exact at M precisely when im u=ker v. For a sequence with a zero term immediately before a map, exactness at its domain is equivalent to injectivity of the map; a zero term immediately after a map tests surjectivity by exactness at its codomain. These conventions and equivalences apply to left or right modules over any ring.

For a commutative unital ring k, a unital k-algebra is a ring A equipped with a unital ring homomorphism k→Z(A); the k-action is multiplication by its image. A k-algebra homomorphism is a unital ring homomorphism compatible with the structure homomorphisms. For any unital ring homomorphism u:R→S, without a centrality hypothesis, a left S-module restricts to a left R-module by r·x=u(r)x; these formulas satisfy the module laws.

For a commutative ring k, the central structure homomorphism of a unital k-algebra makes multiplication k-bilinear. Conversely, an associative unital k-bilinear multiplication on a k-module A recovers a central unital structure homomorphism k→Z(A), a↦a·1_A. These constructions recover the same algebra structure and the same convention for algebra morphisms.

For an arbitrary set X and unital ring R, the free left R-module on X is R^(X), the finitely supported functions X→R, with its standard basis. Every function X→M into a left R-module has a unique R-linear extension R^(X)→M, given by the finite sum of coefficient multiples. There is no finiteness restriction on X.

For every short exact sequence 0→A --i→ B --p→ C→0 of R-modules, the following are equivalent: p has a linear section; i has a linear retraction; and the sequence is isomorphic, by maps inducing the identity on A and C, to 0→A→A⊕C→C→0. In particular the middle module splits as A⊕C compatibly with its specified inclusion and quotient.
A commuting map between two short exact sequences of modules whose maps on both end modules are isomorphisms has an isomorphism as its middle map. This applies over arbitrary rings on either side.

For a commutative diagram of module sequences A --i→ B --p→ C and A′ --i′→ B′ --p′→ C′, with exactness at B and B′, p surjective, and i′ injective, let a:A→A′, b:B→B′, c:C→C′ be the vertical maps. There is a natural linear connecting map δ:ker c→coker a and an exact sequence ker a→ker b→ker c --δ→ coker a→coker b→coker c. The arrows other than δ are induced by the horizontal maps. If i is injective the first arrow is injective, and if p′ is surjective the last arrow is surjective. Naturality is with respect to maps of such diagrams. No injectivity of i or surjectivity of p′ is required for the interior exact sequence. Valid for left and right modules over arbitrary rings.

In a commuting diagram of two five-term module sequences, each exact at its three interior terms, write h₁,…,h₅ for the vertical maps. If h₂ and h₄ are injective and h₁ is surjective, h₃ is injective. If h₂ and h₄ are surjective and h₅ is injective, h₃ is surjective. Consequently h₃ is an isomorphism whenever all four outer vertical maps are isomorphisms. These statements apply to either side of any ring.

For any right R-module A and left R-module B, construct an abelian group A⊗_R B with its biadditive universal pairing (a,b)↦a⊗b subject to (ar)⊗b=a⊗(rb). For every abelian group C, homomorphisms A⊗_R B→C correspond uniquely to biadditive R-balanced pairings A×B→C. If A has a commuting left scalar action and/or B a commuting right scalar action, the unused actions descend to the tensor, making the appropriate outer module or bimodule structure.

Balanced tensor has natural associativity, left and right unit, and arbitrary direct-sum isomorphisms, with all compatible outer actions. Explicitly, for compatible bimodules, (A⊗_R B)⊗_S C≅A⊗_R(B⊗_S C) by (a⊗b)⊗c↦a⊗(b⊗c); A⊗_R R≅A and R⊗_R B≅B by multiplication; tensoring an arbitrary direct sum in either variable gives the direct sum of the tensors. The isomorphisms are natural in all modules involved.

For a right R-module A, an R–S bimodule B, and a right S-module C, Hom_S(B,C) is a right R-module via (g·r)(b)=g(rb), and there is a natural isomorphism of abelian groups Hom_S(A⊗_R B,C)≅Hom_R(A,Hom_S(B,C)). The bijection sends f to a↦(b↦f(a⊗b)), with inverse evaluation on pure tensors, and is natural in all three variables.

For every unital ring map R→S, extension of left scalars S⊗_R− is left adjoint to restriction of left S-modules. The natural bijection identifies S-linear maps S⊗_R M→N with R-linear maps M→Res N via f↦(m↦f(1⊗m)), with inverse u↦(s⊗m↦s·u(m)). The unit is m↦1⊗m, the counit is multiplication S⊗_R Res N→N, and they satisfy the triangle identities.

Over an arbitrary ring, Hom_R(P,−) is left exact for every module P, and Hom_R(−,Q) is contravariantly left exact for every module Q. Thus a short exact 0→A→B→C→0 induces exact 0→Hom(P,A)→Hom(P,B)→Hom(P,C) and 0→Hom(C,Q)→Hom(B,Q)→Hom(A,Q). Balanced tensor is right exact separately in each variable, respecting the required right/left sides; if outer bimodule actions are present these exactness statements hold in the corresponding outer module categories.

For 0→ℤ --2→ ℤ→ℤ/2→0, tensoring over ℤ with ℤ/2 gives a zero first arrow with nonzero domain, so tensor need not preserve injections. With P=ℤ/2, the identity ℤ/2→ℤ/2 in the covariant Hom sequence does not lift to a homomorphism ℤ/2→ℤ, so Hom(P,−) need not preserve surjections. With Q=ℤ, restriction along multiplication by 2 is multiplication by 2 on Hom_ℤ(ℤ,ℤ), and is not surjective, so contravariant Hom need not turn the inclusion into a surjection.

For every left module P over an arbitrary unital ring, the following equivalent properties characterize projectivity: every map P→N lifts through every surjection M→N; every short exact sequence ending in P splits; P is a direct summand of some free module (arbitrary rank permitted); and Hom_R(P,−) is exact. The same equivalences hold for right modules.

A left R-module E is injective precisely when each linear map U→E extends along every inclusion U↪M of left modules. This is equivalent to the restricted extension test for inclusions I↪R of all left ideals I (Baer’s criterion), to exactness of contravariant Hom_R(−,E), and to splitting of every short exact sequence starting with E. For right modules the corresponding ideal test uses right ideals.

A module M is finitely presented precisely when it is the cokernel of a linear map between finite-rank free modules, equivalently when it admits a surjection from a finite-rank free module with finitely generated kernel. If M is finitely presented, every surjection from a finite-rank free module to M has finitely generated kernel.
For any two projective presentations 0→K_i→P_i→M→0, i=1,2, of the same module over any ring, with no finite generation hypothesis, there exists an isomorphism K₁⊕P₂≅K₂⊕P₁.

A left R-module P is projective if and only if there is a possibly infinite family of elements p_j∈P and R-linear maps φ_j:P→R such that, for every x∈P, only finitely many φ_j(x) are nonzero and x=∑_j φ_j(x)p_j. For a finitely generated projective module the family can be finite. The right-module version has x=∑_j p_j φ_j(x), with coefficients on the right and right-linear φ_j.

An extension M↪E is essential if every nonzero submodule of E has nonzero intersection with the copy of M. An injective envelope of M is an injective essential extension of M. Maximal essential extension means an essential extension of M admitting no proper essential enlargement over M; minimal injective extension means an injective extension containing no proper injective submodule that contains M.

Every module over any unital ring embeds in an injective module and possesses an injective envelope. For an extension M↪E, the following are equivalent: E is injective and M is essential in E; E is a maximal essential extension of M; E is an injective extension of M minimal among its injective submodules containing M. Any two injective envelopes are isomorphic by an isomorphism restricting to the identity on M. All assertions hold for left and right modules.

For a left R-module M, a finite system of relations consists of finitely many x_i∈M and finitely many rows ∑_i r_{ji}x_i=0. A factorization consists of finitely many y_ℓ∈M and coefficients s_{iℓ}∈R such that x_i=∑_ℓ s_{iℓ}y_ℓ and ∑_i r_{ji}s_{iℓ}=0 for every j,ℓ. The multiplication order is as displayed; this is over an arbitrary, possibly noncommutative ring.

For a left R-module M, the following are equivalent and characterize flatness: (i) the functor −⊗_R M on right modules preserves injections, equivalently is exact; (ii) I⊗_R M→R⊗_R M is injective for every finitely generated right ideal I; (iii) every finite system of relations in M has the finite factorization defined in lines 412–417; (iv) M is a filtered colimit of finite-rank free left modules. The transition maps in (iv) are unrestricted, not required to be injective. All assertions have right-module versions with sides reversed.

Every projective module over any unital ring is flat. Every finitely presented flat module is projective. Both assertions apply on the left and on the right; finite presentation, not merely finite generation, is the hypothesis in the second assertion.

Finite generation alone does not imply that a module has finitely many relations: in general a finitely generated module need not be finitely presented. This is the unnumbered limitation stated after the flatness theorem.

For a flat right R-module P the following are equivalent: P⊗_R− detects nonzero left modules (P⊗_R M=0 implies M=0); it reflects exactness of sequences; and P⊗_R(R/𝔪)≠0 for every maximal left ideal 𝔪. In this case the exact functor P⊗_R− is faithful on morphisms. The left-module version tests maximal right ideals and tensors on the opposite side. No commutativity or finite generation is assumed.

For a module over an arbitrary ring, the following equivalent conditions define Artinianity: every descending chain of submodules stabilizes; every nonempty family of submodules has a minimal member. Artinianity is inherited by submodules and quotients, and is preserved by extensions in short exact sequences. The statement applies on either side.

For a module over an arbitrary ring, the following equivalent conditions define Noetherianity: every ascending chain of submodules stabilizes; every nonempty family of submodules has a maximal member; every submodule is finitely generated. Noetherianity is inherited by submodules and quotients, and if 0→A→B→C→0 is short exact with A,C Noetherian, then B is Noetherian. The statement applies on either side.

A module has a finite composition series precisely when it is both Noetherian and Artinian. Here a composition series is a finite chain from 0 to M with all successive factors simple. For any two such series, the multisets of simple factors agree up to isomorphism and permutation. The length ℓ_R(M), the number of factors, is therefore well-defined; ℓ_R(0)=0 and ℓ_R(B)=ℓ_R(A)+ℓ_R(C) for every short exact sequence 0→A→B→C→0 of finite-length modules. Valid for either side of an arbitrary ring.

A simple module is a nonzero module whose only submodules are 0 and itself. Every nonzero linear map between simple modules is an isomorphism. The endomorphism ring of a simple module is a division ring. The nonzero condition on simple modules is essential and is part of the definition.

For a module M, including M=0 and with arbitrary possible index sets, the following are equivalent and define semisimplicity: M is a direct sum of simple modules; M is the sum of its simple submodules; every submodule of M is a direct summand. Submodules and quotients of semisimple modules are semisimple. No finite generation or finite length is assumed.

For every unital ring R, define J(R) as the intersection of all maximal left ideals. It equals the intersection of the annihilator ideals of all simple left modules, is a two-sided ideal, and equals the intersection of the maximal right ideals. For every x∈R, x∈J(R) if and only if 1−rx is a unit for every r∈R. These statements include the zero ring, using the unit ideal as the intersection of the empty family.

Let I be a two-sided ideal of any unital ring R satisfying I⊆J(R), and let M be a finitely generated left R-module. If IM=M, then M=0. Equivalently, for every submodule N⊆M, M=N+IM implies M=N; in particular any family in M whose images generate M/IM generates M. For finitely generated right modules the corresponding statements use MI. No commutativity is assumed.

If R is left Artinian, its Jacobson radical J(R) is nilpotent, R/J(R) is semisimple as a left module over itself, and the left regular module R has finite composition length; consequently R is left Noetherian. For a right Artinian ring the analogous right-sided statements hold via the opposite ring. The zero ring is included.

For a ring R with nilpotent Jacobson radical J and semisimple left regular module R/J, every Noetherian left R-module has finite length. There is no separate Artinian hypothesis on R or M. The side-reversed assertion applies via the opposite ring.
Every commutative Artinian ring is isomorphic to a finite product of local Artinian rings. The zero ring is covered by the empty product.

For a nonzero ring R, the following are equivalent: the left regular module is semisimple; R is left Artinian and J(R)=0; R is isomorphic to a finite product ∏_i M_{n_i}(D_i), with n_i positive integers and D_i division rings. The factors are unique up to permutation and ring isomorphism, and for an individual factor its matrix size n_i and division ring D_i are determined up to the indicated isomorphism. A simple Artinian ring has exactly one factor. The accompanying zero-ring boundary convention is the empty product.

Work with right modules over any unital ring R. A finitely generated projective generator P_R is a finitely generated projective right module such that every right R-module is a quotient of a direct sum of copies of P. Put S=End_R(P_R), with composition as multiplication, and Q=Hom_R(P,R). P has its S–R bimodule structure by s·p=s(p), and Q has its R–S bimodule structure (r·q·s)(x)=r q(s(x)).

For a right progenerator P_R, S=End_R(P), and Q=Hom_R(P,R) with the stated bimodule structures, the balanced maps P⊗_R Q→S, p⊗q↦(x↦p q(x)), and Q⊗_S P→R, q⊗p↦q(p), are respectively S–S and R–R bimodule isomorphisms.

For the same right progenerator, the functors Mod-R→Mod-S, N↦N⊗_R Q, and Mod-S→Mod-R, L↦L⊗_S P, are inverse equivalences, with natural isomorphisms of the composites to the identity induced by the two bimodule evaluations. Conversely any equivalence from right S-modules to right R-modules sends S_S to a finitely generated projective generator P_R and identifies End_R(P) with S; thus transporting a regular module recovers a progenerator. The converse concerns equivalences of the module categories, without an extra stipulated additive-equivalence hypothesis. Opposite rings give the left-handed form, where a left progenerator uses the opposite endomorphism ring.

For every unital ring R and every positive integer n, R and M_n(R) have equivalent right module categories, and correspondingly equivalent left module categories. The right progenerator is R^n_R with endomorphism ring M_n(R). The assertion includes the zero ring and requires n>0.

From Chapter 4 through Chapter 7, all rings are commutative and unital, maps preserve identity, the zero ring is allowed, and prime and maximal ideals are proper. In particular Spec(0) is empty. Localization is allowed to yield the zero ring even when the original ring is nonzero. References and chapter headings are contextual.

For a commutative unital ring R and any multiplicatively closed subset S containing 1, construct a commutative ring S⁻¹R with j:R→S⁻¹R sending every s∈S to a unit, universal among unital ring maps g:R→B sending S to units: such g factors uniquely through j. Elements are fractions a/s, and a/s=b/t exactly when some u∈S satisfies u(ta−sb)=0. The operations are a/s+b/t=(ta+sb)/(st) and (a/s)(b/t)=ab/(st); j(a)=a/1. If 0∈S the localization is the zero ring. Neither R nor its localization is assumed a domain or nonzero.

For every R-module M over a commutative ring and multiplicative S containing 1, construct S⁻¹M from fractions m/s, where m/s=n/t exactly when some u∈S satisfies u(tm−sn)=0. In particular m/s=0 exactly when some element of S kills m. There is a natural S⁻¹R-linear isomorphism S⁻¹R⊗_R M≅S⁻¹M, given by (a/s)⊗m↦am/s with inverse m/s↦(1/s)⊗m.

A homomorphism of arbitrary modules over a commutative unital ring R is injective, surjective, or bijective if and only if its localization at every maximal ideal of R has the corresponding property. A composable pair of module maps is exact at its middle term if and only if it is exact at every maximal localization; this also detects the zero-composite condition. Equivalently, M=0 if and only if M_𝔪=0 for every maximal ideal 𝔪. The zero ring is included: its spectrum of maximal ideals is empty and its unital modules are zero.

For any multiplicative subset S of a commutative ring R, localization of modules preserves exact sequences and finite intersections of submodules. In particular it preserves injections and surjections, and the localization R→S⁻¹R is flat. These statements hold for arbitrary modules and include localizations that are the zero ring.

For a finitely presented module M over a commutative ring R, any R-module N, and any flat commutative R-algebra B, the natural map B⊗_R Hom_R(M,N)→Hom_B(B⊗_R M,B⊗_R N) is an isomorphism. On a pure tensor b⊗f it maps b′⊗m to bb′⊗f(m). This applies in particular to B=S⁻¹R for every multiplicative subset S. N has no finiteness hypothesis.

For a commutative ring R, Spec R is its set of proper prime ideals. Define V(I)={𝔭∈Spec R | I⊆𝔭} for each ideal I, and D(f)={𝔭∈Spec R | f∉𝔭}. The sets V(I) are the closed sets of the Zariski topology: arbitrary intersections correspond to sums of ideals, and V(I)∪V(J)=V(IJ); V(0)=Spec R and V(R)=∅. These formulas include the zero ring.

The principal open subsets D(f) form a basis for Spec R, and D(fg)=D(f)∩D(g). For every f∈R, contraction along R→R_f identifies Spec(R_f) homeomorphically with D(f). This includes f nilpotent, when both spaces are empty.

For every ideal I of a commutative ring R, its radical √I={a∈R | a^n∈I for some integer n≥1} is exactly the intersection of all prime ideals containing I. The intersection of an empty such family is R. In particular the nilradical, the set of nilpotent elements, is √(0), equivalently the intersection of all prime ideals.

For every ideal I of a commutative ring R, contraction along the quotient map R→R/I identifies Spec(R/I) homeomorphically with the closed subspace V(I)⊆Spec R, with prime ideals corresponding to prime ideals of R containing I. The unit-ideal case I=R yields empty spectra.

Every unital homomorphism g:R→A of commutative rings induces by contraction a continuous map Spec A→Spec R, 𝔮↦g⁻¹(𝔮). This construction is contravariantly functorial in ring maps, and the inverse image of D(f) is D(g(f)).

For every multiplicative subset S of a commutative ring R, contraction along R→S⁻¹R is a homeomorphism from Spec(S⁻¹R) onto the subspace {𝔭∈Spec R | 𝔭∩S=∅}. The inverse sends such a prime 𝔭 to S⁻¹𝔭, and fraction membership is determined by the numerator. The topology is the subspace topology; the general image need not be open. When S consists of powers of f it is D(f), and if 0∈S it is empty.

For a commutative R-algebra A, an element a∈A is integral over R if it satisfies a monic polynomial whose coefficients lie in the image of R. The algebra is integral if all its elements are integral. A finite R-algebra is finite as an R-module; a finite-type R-algebra is finitely generated as an algebra. These notions do not assume an injective structure map R→A.

Let A be a commutative R-algebra, let S⊆R be multiplicatively closed with 1∈S, and let C be the integral closure of the image of R in A, that is, the subring of elements of A integral over R. The image of S⁻¹C in S⁻¹A is the integral closure of the image of S⁻¹R in S⁻¹A. The maps may be noninjective on the base and denominators may be zero divisors; no domain assumption or cancellation is allowed.

For every a in a commutative R-algebra A, a is integral over R if and only if the R-subalgebra R[a] is a finite R-module. A commutative R-algebra A is finite as an R-module if and only if it is both integral and of finite type. The zero algebra is included. No Noetherian hypothesis is imposed on R.

The elements of any commutative R-algebra A integral over R form an R-subalgebra. Integrality is transitive in towers: if B is integral over R and C is integral over B, then C is integral over R; equivalently, an element integral over an integral intermediate algebra is integral over the bottom ring. Structure maps need not be injective.

For every integral homomorphism g:R→A of commutative unital rings, the image of Spec A→Spec R is exactly V(ker g). Thus every prime of R containing ker g is the contraction of a prime of A, and for an integral inclusion the spectrum map is surjective. This includes the zero-ring and empty-spectrum cases.

For every integral map g:R→A of commutative rings and prime 𝔮⊆A, 𝔮 is maximal if and only if its contraction g⁻¹(𝔮) is maximal. If primes 𝔮⊆𝔮′ of A have the same contraction to R, then 𝔮=𝔮′ (incomparability). No injectivity or domain hypotheses are imposed.

For every integral homomorphism g:R→A of commutative rings, Krull dimension satisfies dim A=dim(R/ker g). The comparison uses suprema of all finite strict prime-chain lengths, permits infinite dimension, and includes the case of empty spectra with the common empty-spectrum dimension convention. In particular this is not restricted to finite-dimensional or Noetherian rings.

Every integral ring map has going up: if 𝔭⊆𝔭′ are prime ideals of R and 𝔮 is a prime of A contracting to 𝔭, there is a prime 𝔮′⊇𝔮 of A contracting to 𝔭′. This includes noninjective integral maps whenever the given prime over 𝔭 exists. The one-step result iterates to finite prime chains.

If R⊆A is an integral extension of commutative domains and R is integrally closed in Frac(R), then the extension has going down: for primes 𝔭⊆𝔭′ of R and a prime 𝔮′ of A contracting to 𝔭′, there exists a prime 𝔮⊆𝔮′ contracting to 𝔭. No finiteness, separability, or Noetherian assumption on the extension is imposed. The one-step result iterates to finite prime chains.

Every flat homomorphism R→A of commutative unital rings has going down: given primes 𝔭⊆𝔭′ in R and a prime 𝔮′ in A contracting to 𝔭′, there is a prime 𝔮⊆𝔮′ in A contracting to 𝔭. This assertion is independent of the integral-extension/domain/integrally-closed-base hypotheses of the preceding result; neither injectivity nor finite generation nor faithful flatness is an additional global assumption. The one-step result iterates to finite prime chains.
For a commutative ring R, R is Noetherian when its ideals satisfy the ascending chain condition; an R-module M is Noetherian when its submodules satisfy the ascending chain condition.
A commutative ring is Noetherian if and only if each ideal is finitely generated. An R-module is Noetherian if and only if each submodule is finitely generated.

Hilbert basis theorem and finite modules: if the commutative ring R is Noetherian, then R[X_1,...,X_n] is Noetherian for every finite n, including n=0, and every finite-type R-algebra is Noetherian. Every finitely generated R-module M and every submodule of M are Noetherian and finitely presented R-modules.

For ideals J,I_1,...,I_n of a commutative ring R, n>=1, if J is contained in the union of the I_i, and either at most two I_i are nonprime or R contains an infinite field, then J is contained in some I_i.
For a commutative ring R, R-module M and prime ideal p, p belongs to Ass_R(M) if and only if there is an R-linear embedding R/p into M.

For an R-module M, Ass_R(M) is the set of prime ideals of R that occur as annihilators Ann_R(x) of elements x of M; Supp_R(M) is the set of prime ideals p for which the localized module M_p is nonzero.

In every nonzero module M over a commutative Noetherian ring R, there exists an annihilator Ann_R(x) maximal among annihilators of nonzero elements x in M, and every such maximal annihilator is a prime ideal. In particular a nonzero module over a Noetherian ring has an associated prime; no finite-generation assumption on M is required for this observation.

Let R be commutative Noetherian and M a finitely generated R-module. For every multiplicatively closed subset S, Ass_{S^{-1}R}(S^{-1}M) = {S^{-1}p : p in Ass_R(M), p intersect S is empty}. The elements of R killing some nonzero element of M are exactly the union of its associated primes. For every short exact sequence 0 -> Mprime -> M -> Mdoubleprime -> 0 of finite R-modules, Ass(Mprime) is contained in Ass(M), which is contained in Ass(Mprime) union Ass(Mdoubleprime), and Supp(M)=Supp(Mprime) union Supp(Mdoubleprime). For two finite modules M_1,M_2, Ass(M_1 direct_sum M_2)=Ass(M_1) union Ass(M_2).

If R is commutative Noetherian and M is a finitely generated R-module, Ass_R(M) is finite, and is nonempty if M is nonzero. Supp_R(M)=V(Ann_R(M)), where V is the set of prime ideals containing the module annihilator, and every minimal prime in Supp_R(M) belongs to Ass_R(M). For M=0 both Ass and Supp are empty.

For a primary proper submodule N of an R-module M over a commutative ring R, p=sqrt(Ann_R(M/N)) is prime and is exactly the set of zero divisors on the nonzero module M/N (the scalars killing some nonzero class). If R is Noetherian, then Ass_R(M/N) is exactly the singleton {p}.

A proper submodule N of an R-module M is primary if, whenever r*m belongs to N and m does not belong to N, there is an integer n>=1 such that r^n*M is contained in N. Its associated radical is sqrt(Ann_R(M/N)); when this radical is p, N is called p-primary.

Lasker--Noether decomposition: for a commutative Noetherian ring R, a finite R-module M and a proper submodule N, there exist finitely many primary proper submodules N_1,...,N_h with h>=1 and pairwise distinct primes p_i=sqrt(Ann_R(M/N_i)) such that N is their intersection. They may be chosen irredundantly. In every irredundant primary decomposition with distinct radicals, Ass_R(M/N)={p_1,...,p_h}. For every multiplicatively closed S in R, {m in M : m/1 belongs to S^{-1}N} is the intersection of those N_i with p_i intersect S empty, with empty intersection interpreted as M. The primary component corresponding to each minimal associated prime is uniquely determined by N (it is the contraction of N_p from localization at that prime).

Every proper ideal I of a commutative Noetherian ring R is a finite irredundant intersection of primary ideals with pairwise distinct radicals, and these radicals are exactly Ass_R(R/I). The primary ideal condition is a*b in Q and b not in Q implies a in sqrt(Q). Each component belonging to a minimal associated prime is unique; embedded primary components need not be unique.

For any field k, in k[X,Y] the ideal I=(X^2,X*Y) has two distinct irredundant primary decompositions I=(X) intersect (X^2,Y)=(X) intersect (X^2,X*Y,Y^2). The two displayed latter components are distinct primary ideals with radical (X,Y), whereas (X) is prime, so the component at the embedded prime (X,Y) is not unique.

The length of a finite strictly increasing chain of prime ideals is its number of strict inclusions, and Krull dimension is the supremum of these lengths. Infinite dimension is allowed and the empty spectrum has formal dimension -infinity. The height of a prime p is the dimension of R_p. For a finite module M, dim(M)=dim(R/Ann_R(M)), equivalently the dimension of Supp_R(M).

If R is commutative Noetherian, r is a nonnegative finite integer and p is minimal among the prime ideals containing a proper ideal generated by r elements, then ht(p)<=r. This includes r=0 and implies that every prime minimal over a proper principal ideal has height at most one.

Let (R,m) be commutative Noetherian local, and M a nonzero finitely generated R-module of dimension d. Then d is finite. For every ideal Q contained in m, M/Q*M has finite length if and only if sqrt(Q+Ann_R(M))=m. The least number of elements of m generating an ideal with this property is exactly d (zero generators are allowed when d=0). Such a d-element collection is a system of parameters for M. For each x in m, dim(M/x*M)>=d-1. The quotient M/Q*M is nonzero for Q contained in m; for Q=R it is zero of length zero, outside the stated equivalence.

For every field k, every n>=1 and nonconstant f in k[X_1,...,X_n], an invertible triangular change of variables, followed by multiplication by a nonzero scalar of k, makes f monic of positive degree in the last variable. For n=1 only scalar rescaling is needed. No infinitude assumption on k is made.
For every field k and nonnegative finite n, dim(k[X_1,...,X_n])=n. For each nonzero prime ideal P of this polynomial ring, dim(k[X_1,...,X_n]/P)<=n-1.

For any field k and nonzero finite-type k-algebra A, there is a nonnegative integer d and algebraically independent elements y_1,...,y_d of A such that A is finitely generated as a module over the polynomial subalgebra k[y_1,...,y_d]. Necessarily d=dim(A), including d=0. No restriction on the cardinality or characteristic of k is imposed.

For every field k and finite nonnegative n, dim(k[X_1,...,X_n])=n. For each finite-type k-domain A, dim(A)=trdeg_k(Frac(A)). For each nonzero finite-type k-algebra A, dim(A) is the maximum of dim(A/p) over its minimal prime ideals p.

For every finite-type algebra A over an arbitrary field k, each maximal ideal has residue field finite over k, and every prime ideal of A equals the intersection of all maximal ideals containing it. If k is algebraically closed, the maximal ideals of k[X_1,...,X_n] are exactly the kernels of evaluations at points of k^n. For every ideal J of that polynomial ring, the ideal I(V(J)) of polynomials vanishing on the common zero set V(J) in k^n equals sqrt(J). Include J equal to the unit ideal (V(J) empty and I(V(J)) the unit ideal) and n=0 (k^0 a singleton).

For a field k of arbitrary characteristic, a finite-type k-domain A and a finite field extension L/Frac(A), the integral closure of A in L is finite as an A-module and is itself a finite-type k-domain. No separability or perfectness assumption is imposed.
A finitely generated graded module over a nonnegatively graded algebra is bounded below, since it admits finitely many homogeneous generators.

A nonnegatively graded algebra A=direct_sum_{j>=0} A_j is standard over A_0 if it is generated over A_0 by finitely many degree-one elements. Finite graded A-modules may be Z-graded; the shift M(-1) is defined by M(-1)_j=M_{j-1}.

Let B be a commutative Artinian ring, A a standard graded B-algebra with A_0=B, and M a finite Z-graded A-module. Every M_j has finite B-length. Its Hilbert series H_M(t)=sum_j length_B(M_j)*t^j is a rational function with a Laurent polynomial numerator and denominator a power of 1-t. The coefficients length_B(M_j) eventually agree with a polynomial in j. If the reduced denominator is (1-t)^e with e>0, the eventual polynomial has exact degree e-1; if e=0 the coefficients are eventually zero. This defines the length Hilbert series also for modules with nonzero negative-degree pieces.

Let k be any field, A a standard graded k-algebra with A_0=k, and M a nonzero finite Z-graded A-module. Put d=dim(M). If d>0, the reduced denominator of H_M(t)=sum_j dim_k(M_j)*t^j is (1-t)^d, and j -> dim_k(M_j) eventually agrees with a polynomial of exact degree d-1. If d=0, its graded pieces are eventually zero. For the zero module the series and eventual polynomial are both zero.
For a commutative ring R, Jac(R) is the intersection of its maximal ideals. A local ring (R,m) has unique maximal ideal m.

If a belongs to Jac(R) for a commutative ring R, then 1-a is a unit. In a local ring (R,m), the nonunits are exactly m. Conversely if the nonunits of a commutative ring form a proper ideal, that ideal is the unique maximal ideal, so the ring is local.

Let R be a commutative ring, M a finitely generated R-module, I an ideal contained in Jac(R), and N a submodule. If M=N+I*M then M=N. In particular I*M=M implies M=0. Any set of elements of M whose images generate M/I*M generates M.

For an ideal I of a commutative Noetherian ring R and a finite R-module M, construct the Rees algebra Rees_I(R)=direct_sum_{n>=0} I^n*t^n as a graded subalgebra of R[t], and the Rees module Rees_I(M)=direct_sum_{n>=0} I^n*M*t^n as its graded module inside M[t]. If a_i generate I, the Rees algebra is generated over R by the a_i*t and is Noetherian; the Rees module is finite over it, generated by any R-generators of M in degree zero. Quotienting by the ideal I in degree zero yields gr_I(R) with pieces I^n/I^(n+1) and gr_I(M) with pieces I^n*M/I^(n+1)*M. The former is standard graded over R/I and the latter a finite graded module over it.
For an ideal I of a commutative Noetherian ring R, a finite R-module M and submodule N of M, there exists an integer c>=0 such that I^n*M intersect N = I^(n-c)*(I^c*M intersect N) for every n>=c.

For an ideal I in a commutative Noetherian ring R and finite R-module M, put N=intersection_{n>=0} I^n*M. Then I*N=N, and there is a in I with (1-a)*N=0. If I is contained in Jac(R), then N=0. If R is a domain and I is proper, intersection_{n>=0} I^n is the zero ideal. The last domain assertion is for M=R, without an asserted general torsion-module analogue.

In the commutative Noetherian domain R=Z with proper ideal I=(2), the finite module M=Z/3 satisfies I^n*M=M for every n>=0. Thus its I-adic intersection is M rather than zero, showing why properness of I and the domain property alone do not force the intersection to vanish for arbitrary finite modules.

For a commutative ring R, ideal I and R-module M, its I-adic completion is Mhat=inverse_limit_{n>=1} M/I^n*M, the module of compatible residue classes. Rhat acts on Mhat by coordinatewise multiplication. The canonical map M -> Mhat sends m to its compatible residues; its kernel is intersection_{n>=0} I^n*M, so it need not be injective.

For a commutative Noetherian ring R and arbitrary ideal I, I-adic completion preserves short exact sequences of finitely generated R-modules. For each finite R-module M, the natural Rhat-linear map Rhat tensor_R M -> Mhat sending r tensor m to r*mhat is an isomorphism, natural in M.

Let R be commutative Noetherian, I any ideal, Rhat its I-adic completion, and J=I*Rhat. Then Rhat is Noetherian and flat over R. For each n>=1 there are compatible natural identifications Rhat/J^n isomorphic to R/I^n, and gr_J(Rhat) isomorphic as a graded ring to gr_I(R). Rhat is faithfully flat over R if and only if I is contained in Jac(R). If R is local and I its maximal ideal m, Rhat is local with maximal ideal J and residue field canonically R/m. These statements include I=0 and I=R.

Let (R,m) be commutative Noetherian local, M a nonzero finite R-module with dimension d, and Q an ideal contained in m such that M/Q*M has finite length. For all sufficiently large nonnegative integers n, L_Q(n)=length_R(M/Q^(n+1)*M) equals a polynomial of exact degree d. The layer length length_R(Q^n*M/Q^(n+1)*M) eventually equals a polynomial of exact degree d-1 if d>0, and is eventually zero if d=0.

For a commutative Noetherian local ring (R,m,k) of dimension d, its embedding dimension is dim_k(m/m^2); the ring is regular local when this number is d. A sequence x_1,...,x_d in R is regular here when each x_i acts injectively on R/(x_1,...,x_(i-1)) and its final generated ideal is proper.

Let (R,m,k) be a commutative Noetherian local ring of dimension d. The minimum size of a generating set of m equals dim_k(m/m^2), and is at least d. If R is regular local, then for any minimal generating set x_1,...,x_d of m, the map k[X_1,...,X_d] -> gr_m(R) taking X_i to the degree-one initial class of x_i is a graded k-algebra isomorphism. R is a domain and x_1,...,x_d is a regular sequence. If d=0, R is a field (and the sequence is empty).

Let R be a commutative ring separated and complete for the powers of an ideal I. For f in R[T], a in R and d=fprime(a), if f(a) belongs to d^2*I then there exists b in a+d*I with f(b)=0. This root b is unique in a+d*I if multiplication by d on R is injective. In particular every simple root of the reduction of f over the residue field of a complete local ring lifts uniquely to a root in its residue class. No invertibility of d is required for the general existence assertion; d=0 gives f(a)=0 and the singleton coset {a}.

Let a commutative ring R be separated and complete for powers of I, and let f in R[T] be monic. Suppose its reduction modulo I is gbar*hbar, where gbar,hbar are monic and generate the unit ideal of (R/I)[T]. There exist unique monic g,h in R[T] with f=g*h, with reductions gbar,hbar and degrees equal to their prescribed residual degrees. A factor equal to 1 is allowed.

Chapter 8 notation and field conventions: A_G=k[G], Hom_G(V,W) denotes k-linear intertwiners, representations are left representations and irreducibles are nonzero. Linear representation theory is over arbitrary fields unless specified; Hermitian products and ordinary character results use C. These are conventions fixing scope, not independent theorem obligations.

For any group G and field k, a representation on a k-vector space V is a homomorphism rho:G -> GL_k(V). Construct k[G] as finite formal sums sum_g a_g*g with multiplication obtained by bilinear extension of group multiplication. There is an equivalence between representations on V and left k[G]-module structures extending the given k-vector-space structure: (sum_g a_g*g)*v=sum_g a_g*rho(g)(v), with inverse given by the actions of basis elements g. Equivariant k-linear maps are exactly k[G]-module maps. Invariant subspaces, kernels and images of intertwiners, and quotient representations correspond to their module versions; for invariant U, g*(v+U)=g*v+U defines the quotient action.

Over any field k and any group G, every nonzero intertwiner between nonzero irreducible representations is an isomorphism, and the intertwining endomorphism ring of an irreducible representation is a division ring. If V is additionally finite-dimensional and k algebraically closed, each intertwining endomorphism of V is a unique scalar multiple of its identity.

Let G be finite, n=|G|, and k any field. If n*1_k is nonzero, every invariant subspace of every k-representation V, without a dimension restriction, has an invariant complement and every representation is semisimple; a finite-dimensional one has a finite decomposition into irreducibles. If n*1_k=0, the augmentation map k[G] -> k onto the trivial representation has no equivariant section.
For a finite-dimensional representation rho of any group G over a field k, define its character by chi_V(g)=trace(rho(g)). The character is constant on conjugacy classes.

For finite-dimensional representations V,W of any group G over any field k, the dual action is (g*lambda)(v)=lambda(g^(-1)*v) and chi_{Vdual}(g)=chi_V(g^(-1)); chi_{V direct_sum W}=chi_V+chi_W; and chi_{V tensor_k W}=chi_V*chi_W for the diagonal tensor action. If 2 is invertible in k, the +1 and -1 eigenspaces of the flip on V tensor_k V identify equivariantly with Sym^2(V) and wedge^2(V), respectively, and chi_{Sym^2 V}(g)=(chi_V(g)^2+chi_V(g^2))/2, chi_{wedge^2 V}(g)=(chi_V(g)^2-chi_V(g^2))/2.

For a finite group G and finite-dimensional complex representations V,W, each representation has a G-invariant positive-definite Hermitian inner product and chi_V(g^(-1))=conjugate(chi_V(g)). Define the Hermitian inner product on complex functions on G, linear in the first argument, by <f,h>_G=(1/|G|)*sum_g f(g)*conjugate(h(g)). Then <chi_V,chi_W>_G=dim_C Hom_G(W,V)=dim_C Hom_G(V,W).

For a finite group G, there are finitely many isomorphism classes V_i of irreducible complex representations, and all V_i are finite-dimensional. Write d_i=dim_C(V_i) and A=C[G]. As a left A-module, A is isomorphic to the direct sum of d_i copies of each V_i, and |G|=sum_i d_i^2. For any finite-dimensional complex representation V the multiplicity of V_i is <chi_V,chi_i>_G. Thus two such representations are isomorphic if and only if their ordinary characters are equal.

For a finite group G choose unitary representatives V_i of its irreducible complex representations and an orthonormal basis in each. With d_i=dim_C V_i and u^(i)_(ab)(g)=rho_i(g)_(ab), one has <u^(i)_(ab),u^(j)_(cd)>_G=(1/d_i)*delta_(ij)*delta_(ac)*delta_(bd). The functions sqrt(d_i)*u^(i)_(ab) form an orthonormal basis of C^G. The action map C[G] -> product_i End_C(V_i), a -> ahat=(rho_i(a))_i, is a C-algebra isomorphism. Its inverse is given by a_g=(1/|G|)*sum_i d_i*trace(rho_i(g^(-1))*ahat_i), where a=sum_g a_g*g. For a field k with |G| invertible and k[G] split (all division-ring blocks in its semisimple decomposition equal to k), the corresponding action map gives the analogous k-algebra isomorphism k[G] -> product_i End_k(V_i), or product_i Matrix_(d_i)(k). The normalized Hermitian orthogonality assertions are confined to C.

For a finite group G, its irreducible complex characters chi_i are an orthonormal basis of the complex class functions, so their number equals the number of conjugacy classes. For g,h in G, sum_i chi_i(g)*conjugate(chi_i(h)) equals |C_G(g)| if g and h are conjugate and equals 0 otherwise, with C_G(g)={x in G : x*g=g*x}.

For a finite group G and its irreducible complex types V_i of degrees d_i and characters chi_i, in any complex G-representation the sum of all submodules isomorphic to V_i is an intrinsic isotypic direct summand, independent of decomposition. Its projection is the action of e_i=(d_i/|G|)*sum_g chi_i(g^(-1))*g in C[G]. These e_i are exactly the primitive central idempotents, are pairwise orthogonal and sum to 1. The class sums sum_{g in D}g, indexed by conjugacy classes D, form a basis of the center of C[G]. The representation need not be finite-dimensional.

Every irreducible representation of a finite abelian group G over a splitting field k of characteristic prime to |G| is one-dimensional. This holds in particular when k contains all roots of X^m-1, where m is the exponent of G, and the characteristic is prime to |G|. For finite groups G,K with irreducible complex types V_i,W_j, the outer tensor representations V_i boxtimes W_j with action (g,k) -> rho_i(g) tensor sigma_j(k) are irreducible and give every irreducible complex representation of G times K, uniquely up to the pair of isomorphism types. When G=K, restricting this action to the diagonal gives the ordinary tensor product.

For S_3 over C, on the conjugacy classes represented by the identity, a transposition, and a three-cycle (sizes 1,3,2), the trivial and sign characters are (1,1,1) and (1,-1,1). The invariant subspace {(x_1,x_2,x_3) in C^3 : x_1+x_2+x_3=0} of the coordinate permutation representation has character (2,0,-1), of squared norm (4+3*0+2*1)/6=1, and is irreducible. These three representations exhaust the irreducible complex types because 1^2+1^2+2^2=6.

For a finite group G, every value of every ordinary complex character is an algebraic integer. For an irreducible complex representation V of degree d, each conjugacy-class sum z_D=sum_{g in D}g acts as an algebraic-integer scalar, namely omega_D=|D|*chi_V(g_D)/d for g_D in D. Moreover the positive integer d divides |G| and divides [G:Z(G)].

For a nonzero irreducible finite-dimensional complex representation V of a finite group G, define nu(V)=(1/|G|)*sum_g chi_V(g^2). It is 0 precisely for the non-self-dual case V not isomorphic to Vdual, +1 precisely when V admits a nonzero invariant symmetric complex bilinear form, and -1 precisely when V admits a nonzero invariant alternating complex bilinear form. In either nonzero case every such nonzero invariant form is nondegenerate. Indicator +1 is exactly the existence of a real form, i.e. a real G-representation whose complexification is isomorphic to V. The -1 case has a real-valued character and has no real form.

Let V be any finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G, with multiplicities m_i of its irreducible types V_i. Its character is real-valued if and only if m_i=m_j for every non-self-dual pair V_j isomorphic to V_i dual. It has a real form if and only if those equalities hold and every irreducible type of Frobenius--Schur indicator -1 has even multiplicity. Equivalently V has a real form if and only if it has a nondegenerate invariant symmetric complex bilinear form. This includes the zero representation and arbitrary multiplicities of indicator +1 types.

Chapter 9 conventions and scope: k is a field; representations are left representations; G/H always denotes left cosets gH, without requiring H normal; in KsH, K acts on the left and H on the right. Induction and coinduction are algebraic constructions for arbitrary groups. Finiteness is imposed only where stated, including comparison of products with sums and ordinary characters. The cited references are contextual.

For any group G, subgroup H≤G, field k, H-representation V, and G-representation W, restriction Res_H^G W is W with its action restricted to H, with intertwiners restricted in the same way. Construct the G-representation Ind_H^G V = k[G] ⊗_{k[H]} V, where k[G] is the (k[G],k[H])-bimodule from multiplication and G acts by left multiplication on its factor. The construction must respect tensor balancing and maps of V.

For any H≤G, H-representation V over a field k, and any set T of representatives of the left cosets G/H, the linear map ⨁_{t∈T} V → Ind_H^G V whose t-summand map is v↦t⊗v is an isomorphism of underlying vector spaces. If [G:H] and dim_k V are finite, dim_k Ind_H^G V=[G:H] dim_k V. There is a representative-independent G-equivariant isomorphism with the vector space of functions f:G→V satisfying f(xh)=h⁻¹f(x) and supported in only finitely many cosets xH, with action (gf)(x)=f(g⁻¹x).

For arbitrary groups H≤G, any H-representation V and G-representation W over k, establish the k-linear isomorphism Hom_G(Ind_H^G V,W) ≅ Hom_H(V,Res_H^G W), natural in both V and W, so induction is left adjoint to restriction.

For finite G, H≤G, and finite-dimensional complex representations V of H and W of G, the ordinary character inner products satisfy ⟨χ_{Ind_H^G V},χ_W⟩_G = ⟨χ_V,χ_{Res_H^G W}⟩_H. With induction of class functions given by the finite conjugacy sum, the same equality holds for arbitrary complex class functions on H and G by linearity and conjugate-linearity. If V and W are irreducible, the multiplicity of W in Ind_H^G V equals the multiplicity of V in Res_H^G W.

For arbitrary H≤G and H-representation V over k, define Coind_H^G V = Hom_{k[H]}({}_{k[H]}k[G],V), with action (gF)(a)=F(ag). This is a G-representation. Restricting F to group elements identifies it with all functions F:G→V satisfying F(hx)=hF(x), with G-action (gF)(x)=F(xg); no finite support condition is imposed.

For arbitrary H≤G, H-representation V and G-representation W over k, coinduction is right adjoint to restriction: there is a k-linear isomorphism Hom_G(W,Coind_H^G V) ≅ Hom_H(Res_H^G W,V), natural in V and W.

For arbitrary H≤G and H-representation V, Ind_H^G V identifies naturally with the subrepresentation of Coind_H^G V whose corresponding covariant functions F(hx)=hF(x) are supported in finitely many right cosets Hx. In particular, if [G:H] is finite, this comparison is a natural G-representation isomorphism Ind_H^G V≅Coind_H^G V. There is no assumption that G itself is finite.
For arbitrary groups H≤K≤G and H-representation V over k, there is a natural G-representation isomorphism Ind_K^G(Ind_H^K V) ≅ Ind_H^G V.

For arbitrary subgroups H,K≤G and H-representation V, choose one representative s for each double coset in K\G/H. Put L_s=K∩sHs⁻¹ and define the L_s-representation {}^sV on the underlying vector space of V by ℓ·v=ρ(s⁻¹ℓs)v. There is a natural K-representation isomorphism Res_K^G Ind_H^G V ≅ ⨁_{s∈K\G/H} Ind_{L_s}^K({}^sV). The summands and their identification with the induced representation are independent of the chosen double-coset representatives up to isomorphism. Naturality is with respect to H-intertwiners V→V′. No finiteness assumptions are imposed.

Let G be finite, H≤G, V a finite-dimensional complex H-representation, and g∈G. Then χ_{Ind_H^G V}(g)=(1/|H|)∑_{x∈G, x⁻¹gx∈H}χ_V(x⁻¹gx). In particular the value at 1 equals [G:H]dim_C V, and the character is zero on elements of G not conjugate to an element of H. The same finite-sum formula defines induction on arbitrary complex class functions on H; it is a class function on G and agrees with linear extension of induction from characters.

For any field k, arbitrary groups H≤G, H-representation V and G-representation W, there is a natural G-representation isomorphism Ind_H^G(V⊗_k Res_H^G W) ≅ (Ind_H^G V)⊗_k W, with the diagonal tensor actions. No finite-dimensionality or finite-index hypothesis is required.

Let G be finite, H≤G, and V≠0 a finite-dimensional complex H-representation. Ind_H^G V is irreducible if and only if V is irreducible and, for every nonidentity double coset HsH≠H, the representations Res_{H∩sHs⁻¹}^H V and {}^sV of H∩sHs⁻¹ have no common irreducible constituent, where {}^sV has action ℓ↦ρ(s⁻¹ℓs). If H is normal, this criterion becomes: V is irreducible and {}^sV is not isomorphic to V for every s∈G\H. The nonisomorphism simplification is stated under the retained irreducibility condition on V.

Let A◁G be a normal subgroup of a finite group and V an irreducible complex representation of G. The irreducible isomorphism types occurring in Res_A^G V form one G-conjugacy orbit and all have the same multiplicity. Conjugation transports an A-type ρ under g to the type a↦ρ(g⁻¹ag).

In the setting A◁G finite and V an irreducible complex G-representation, choose any A-isotypic component U of Res_A^G V. Define its inertia subgroup I={g∈G:gU=U}. Then I is a subgroup with A≤I, U is an irreducible I-representation under the inherited action, and the balanced map Ind_I^G U→V, g⊗u↦gu, is a G-representation isomorphism. If I=G, Res_A^G V is isotypic.

Let G=S₃ and H=A₃=⟨c⟩, and let V be a one-dimensional complex H-representation in which c acts by a primitive cube root of unity. A transposition conjugates c to c⁻¹, so V and its nontrivial conjugate are distinct. Ind_H^G V is irreducible, of dimension 2, and has character values (2,0,−1) on, respectively, the identity, transpositions, and three-cycles. The transposition value is zero because none is conjugate into H, and the three-cycle value is the sum of the two primitive cube roots.

For a finite group G, form the ring R(G) of virtual complex characters (the additive group completion of the direct-sum monoid of finite-dimensional complex representations/characters), with multiplication induced by tensor product. Its character realization is injective into complex class functions; additively it is the free abelian group on the irreducible complex characters, and its product is pointwise multiplication of characters. Induction and restriction, being additive on direct sums, extend to maps of these additive groups.

Let G be a finite group and ℋ any family of subgroups of G. The rational linear map ⨁_{H∈ℋ}(Q⊗_Z R(H)) → Q⊗_Z R(G), (x_H)↦∑_{H∈ℋ}Ind_H^G(x_H), is surjective if and only if the union of all conjugates gHg⁻¹, with H∈ℋ and g∈G, equals G. The direct sum means each input has finite support.

For any finite group G, every ordinary complex character of G is a finite rational linear combination of characters induced from its cyclic subgroups. Equivalently, for every virtual complex character χ∈R(G), there exists a positive integer N such that Nχ is a finite integer linear combination of characters induced from cyclic subgroups (or equivalently inductions of virtual characters from those cyclic subgroups). No universal choice of N is asserted.

Chapter 10 concerns modules over an arbitrary unital ring, on either one fixed side. Chain differentials lower degree and cochain differentials raise degree. Terms outside a specified degree range are zero. The shift and tensor-product sign conventions here are also used in Chapter 11. These are scope and notation conventions, not additional finiteness restrictions.

A chain complex C of modules has terms C_n and module maps d_n:C_n→C_{n−1} with d_{n−1}d_n=0. Define Z_n(C)=ker d_n, B_n(C)=im d_{n+1}, and H_n(C)=Z_n(C)/B_n(C), using d²=0 to view boundaries as a submodule of cycles. A cochain complex has d^n:C^n→C^{n+1}, with Z^n(C)=ker d^n, B^n(C)=im d^{n−1}, and H^n(C)=Z^n(C)/B^n(C). A complex is acyclic if all its homology (respectively cohomology) modules vanish.

A chain map f:C→D is a degreewise family of module maps f_n with d_D f_n=f_{n−1}d_C; a cochain map has the analogous equation with degree increasing. Such maps preserve cycles and boundaries and induce well-defined module maps H_n(f):H_n(C)→H_n(D), [z]↦[f_n(z)], respectively H^n(f)[z]=[f^n(z)]. These assignments preserve identities, composition, and addition, giving the additive homology and cohomology functors in every degree.
A chain or cochain map is a quasi-isomorphism if its induced map on homology or cohomology is an isomorphism in every degree. The references following the definition are contextual.

For chain maps f,g:C→D, a chain homotopy from g to f consists of module maps s_n:C_n→D_{n+1} satisfying f_n−g_n=d^D_{n+1}s_n+s_{n−1}d^C_n in every degree. Homotopic maps induce the same homology map. A chain homotopy equivalence (maps each way whose composites are homotopic to the respective identities) therefore induces isomorphisms in all homology degrees. The corresponding statements hold for cochain complexes, with homotopy s lowering degree and f^n−g^n=d_D^{n−1}s^n+s^{n+1}d_C^n.

A chain complex C is contractible, meaning 1_C is chain homotopic to zero, if and only if C is acyclic and every short exact sequence 0→Z_n(C)→C_n→^{d_n} Z_{n−1}(C)→0 splits. This applies in every degree and over the arbitrary unital ring and fixed module side of the chapter. Reindexing yields the cochain version: contractibility is equivalent to acyclicity and splitting of 0→Z^n(C)→C^n→^{d^n}Z^{n+1}(C)→0 for all n.

The chain complex given by 0→Z/2→Z/4→Z/2→0 in consecutive degrees, with first nonzero map [1]₂↦[2]₄ and the second the quotient map, is acyclic but is not contractible. The quotient Z/4→Z/2 has no section, since every lift of [1]₂ has order four. The following citations are contextual.

For any degreewise short exact sequence of chain complexes 0→A→^i B→^p C→0, construct a natural long exact homology sequence …→H_n(A)→^{H_n(i)}H_n(B)→^{H_n(p)}H_n(C)→^∂H_{n−1}(A)→H_{n−1}(B)→…, exact in every degree. The connecting module map has ∂[c]=[a], where c∈C_n is a cycle, b∈B_n is any lift with p(b)=c, and a∈A_{n−1} is the unique element satisfying i(a)=d_B(b). The map is independent of choices and representative, is linear, and is natural for commuting maps of short exact sequences of complexes. Dually a degreewise short exact sequence of cochain complexes gives the natural exact sequence …→H^n(A)→H^n(B)→H^n(C)→^∂H^{n+1}(A)→…, with the corresponding lift formula and the same stated sign convention.

For a chain complex C, construct the shift C[1] with C[1]_n=C_{n−1} and differential −d_C. For a chain map f:C→D, construct Cone(f)_n=D_n⊕C_{n−1} with differential (y,x)↦(d_Dy+f(x),−d_Cx); it squares to zero. The summand injection and projection give a short exact sequence of chain complexes 0→D→Cone(f)→C[1]→0. For a cochain map u:Y→X, construct Cone(u)^n=X^n⊕Y^{n+1} with differential (x,y)↦(d_Xx+u(y),−d_Yy), again a cochain complex, using the corresponding signed shift.

For any chain map f:C→D, in the short exact sequence 0→D→Cone(f)→C[1]→0, the connecting map H_n(C[1])→H_{n−1}(D) identifies under H_n(C[1])≅H_{n−1}(C) with H_{n−1}(f), with the positive sign indicated. Consequently f is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if Cone(f) is acyclic. The same criterion holds for a cochain map u:Y→X and its cochain cone Cone(u)^n=X^n⊕Y^{n+1} with differential (d_Xx+u(y),−d_Yy).
For any chain complex C, Cone(1_C) is contractible. With Cone(1_C)_n=C_n⊕C_{n−1}, a contracting homotopy is s_n(y,x)=(0,y)∈Cone(1_C)_{n+1}.

Let P be the chain complex Z→^2 Z in degrees 1 and 0 (zero elsewhere), and let (Z/2)[0] be concentrated in degree 0. The augmentation P→(Z/2)[0], quotient in degree 0 and zero in degree 1, is a quasi-isomorphism. Every chain map (Z/2)[0]→P is zero, so no map in the reverse direction can induce the inverse on degree-zero homology; this quasi-isomorphism is not a chain homotopy equivalence.

For a bicomplex E_{p,q} of modules with commuting horizontal and vertical chain differentials d_h,d_v, supported in a first quadrant or any fixed translate of it, construct the direct-sum total chain complex Tot(E)_n=⨁_{p+q=n}E_{p,q} with differential on E_{p,q} equal to d_h+(−1)^p d_v. For commuting first-quadrant cochain differentials, use the analogous cochain totalization Tot(E)^n=⨁_{p+q=n}E^{p,q} and d=d_h+(−1)^p d_v. If the two differentials anticommute, their ordinary sum d_h+d_v is instead the total differential. In each case this is a well-defined complex.

For a bicomplex of modules supported in the first quadrant, allowing a fixed translation, with commuting chain differentials and signed direct-sum total differential d_h+(−1)^p d_v, if every column is acyclic then Tot(E) is acyclic; the same conclusion holds if every row is acyclic. Both assertions also hold for commuting first-quadrant cochain differentials and their signed totalization. For anticommuting differentials, the assertions use the ordinary-sum total differential instead. There are no projectivity, finite-rank, or finite-dimensionality assumptions.

The first-quadrant assembly theorem has the following augmented form, for chain and cochain bicomplexes and also with rows and columns interchanged. Horizontally augment a first-quadrant chain bicomplex E to a column Y at p=−1, so each augmented row …→E_{1,q}→E_{0,q}→Y_q→0 is exact and the augmentation is compatible with vertical differentials. If X=Tot(E) is the unaugmented total, the induced augmentation map f:X→Y is a quasi-isomorphism. In the cochain case, if a horizontal augmentation from a column Y at p=−1 gives exact rows 0→Y^q→E^{0,q}→E^{1,q}→…, the induced map Y→Tot(E) is a quasi-isomorphism. The corresponding vertical augmentation conclusions hold by signed interchange of indices. The paragraph's cone identifications prove this consequence; their coordinate calculations are not separate required intermediate results.

For every module A over an arbitrary unital ring on either fixed side, construct a free resolution and therefore a projective resolution …→P₁→P₀→A→0, and construct an injective resolution 0→A→I⁰→I¹→…. A resolution is exact as an augmented sequence, and all its P_n are free (respectively projective) or all its I^n injective as appropriate. The resolution regarded as a chain or cochain complex for homology deletes the term A and its augmentation; terms beyond its indicated nonnegative degree range are zero.
Bibliographic references for the resolution existence theorem; no further mathematical assertion is stated in this passage.

For a module map u:A→B, any projective resolution P of A, and any resolution Q of B, there exists a chain map P→Q lifting u (commuting with the augmentations), and any two such lifts are chain homotopic. Dually, u extends to a cochain map from any augmented rightward cochain resolution 0→A→J⁰→J¹→… to any injective cochain resolution 0→B→I⁰→I¹→…, and any two such extensions are cochain homotopic. Consequently any two projective resolutions of one module are chain homotopy equivalent, and any two injective resolutions are cochain homotopy equivalent.

Applying an additive functor to the appropriate projective or injective resolutions and then taking homology/cohomology gives maps induced by module morphisms that are independent of the chosen lifts. These maps are functorial in the module (identity and composition), and the constructions using different projective resolutions, or different injective resolutions, are related by canonical natural isomorphisms. This includes covariant or contravariant additive functors on the appropriate side, with degree reversed for a contravariant functor, in a module/abelian target where the indicated homology is defined.
Bibliographic comparison-theorem references; this passage states no additional result.

Given a short exact sequence 0→A′→A→A″→0 and chosen projective resolutions P′ of A′ and P″ of A″, construct a projective resolution P of A, with P_n=P′_n⊕P″_n, and a short exact sequence of augmented resolutions 0→P′→P→P″→0 compatible with the given module sequence, split in every nonaugmented degree. Dually, from injective resolutions of A′ and A″ construct an injective resolution I of A with I^n=I′^n⊕I″^n and the corresponding degreewise split short exact sequence of augmented injective resolutions. For any commuting map between short exact module sequences, a map of the associated chosen horseshoe resolutions can be chosen so that the full diagram commutes; the analogous assertion holds for the injective construction. The comparison theorem makes the resulting maps on homology after an additive functor independent of choices.

Because the horseshoe short exact sequence of resolution complexes is split in every nonaugmented degree, an additive functor on the appropriate side preserves it as a short exact sequence of complexes even when that functor is not exact on all modules (for a contravariant functor, with the arrows reversed). The connecting maps in the resulting long exact homology/cohomology sequences are natural. The final bibliography is contextual.

Chapter 11 uses ordinary nonnegative resolutions, with augmentations deleted in the complexes used to compute derived groups. Ext has two left R-module variables (and the analogous right-module theory over Rᵒᵖ); Tor has a right R-module first and a left R-module second. Values are abelian groups generally, and natural R-modules for commutative R; in that case the coefficient sequences are R-linear. These are scope and type conventions, not assumed vanishing or balance results.

For every unital ring R, left R-modules A,B and integer n≥0, choose an ordinary projective resolution P→A and define Ext_R^n(A,B)=H^n(Hom_R(P_•,B)), with cochain differential d^n(φ)=φ∘d^P_{n+1}; delete the augmentation and the term A. The right-module version is obtained over Rᵒᵖ.

For a right R-module A, left R-module B and n≥0, choose an ordinary projective resolution P→A of right modules and define Tor_n^R(A,B)=H_n(P_•⊗_R B), with differential d_n^P⊗1 and with augmentation deleted.

Ext_R^n is an additive bifunctor contravariant in A and covariant in B: lift A′→A to projective resolutions and precompose, and postcompose for B→B′. Tor_n^R is additive and covariant in both variables, using the lifted resolution map in the first variable and the tensor of the given map in the second. These maps are independent of the chosen lifts, preserve identities and composition, and any two choices of resolutions give canonical natural comparison isomorphisms, inverse to one another.

For left R-modules A,B, any ordinary projective resolution P→A and injective resolution B→I give quasi-isomorphisms Hom_R(P_•,B) → Tot Hom_R(P_•,I^•) ← Hom_R(A,I^•). In bidegree (p,q) the commuting unsigned cochain differentials are precomposition by d_P and postcomposition by d_I, with total sign (-1)^p on the latter. The induced Ext identifications are natural in both variables.

For every right R-module A and left R-module B, and ordinary projective resolutions P→A and Q→B on the respective sides, both augmentation maps P_•⊗_R B ← Tot(P_•⊗_R Q_•) → A⊗_R Q_• are quasi-isomorphisms. Totalization uses direct sums and d_P⊗1+(-1)^p1⊗d_Q in bidegree (p,q). The induced identifications of Tor computed in either variable are natural in A,B.

For commutative R, interchange on the total tensor complex sends a_p⊗b_q to (-1)^(pq)b_q⊗a_p and is a chain isomorphism. Together with balance it yields the natural symmetry Tor_n^R(A,B)≅Tor_n^R(B,A) for R-modules A,B and all n≥0.

For every ordinary nonnegative flat resolution F→A of a right R-module, every left R-module B, and all n≥0, Tor_n^R(A,B)≅H_n(F⊗_R B). For every ordinary nonnegative flat resolution G→B of a left module, Tor_n^R(A,B)≅H_n(A⊗_R G). The comparisons are natural with respect to maps of augmented resolutions, and identify different flat-resolution models canonically via the derived-group comparison.

The flat-resolution calculation is stated for nonnegative augmented resolutions; the paragraph does not assert the same computation for arbitrary unbounded complexes of flats. Bibliographic and applicability commentary only.
For all appropriately sided R-modules A,B there are natural identifications Ext_R^0(A,B)≅Hom_R(A,B) and Tor_0^R(A,B)≅A⊗_R B.

A short exact sequence in either variable induces a natural long exact Ext sequence, including the degree-zero Hom terms. For 0→A′→A→A″→0 in the first variable the order reverses, with segments Ext_R^n(A″,B)→Ext_R^n(A,B)→Ext_R^n(A′,B)→Ext_R^(n+1)(A″,B). For 0→B′→B→B″→0 in the second variable the segments are Ext_R^n(A,B′)→Ext_R^n(A,B)→Ext_R^n(A,B″)→Ext_R^(n+1)(A,B′). Connecting maps and sequences are natural and independent of resolution and horseshoe choices.
A right R-module A is flat if and only if Tor_1^R(A,B)=0 for every left R-module B. A left R-module B is flat if and only if Tor_1^R(A,B)=0 for every right R-module A.
For every n>0, Ext_R^n(A,B)=0 if A is projective or B is injective (on the same module side). Tor_n^R(A,B)=0 if the right module A is flat or the left module B is flat.

For a short exact sequence 0→A′→A→A″→0 of right R-modules and any left B there is a natural long exact Tor sequence, with segments Tor_n^R(A′,B)→Tor_n^R(A,B)→Tor_n^R(A″,B)→Tor_(n-1)^R(A′,B) for n≥1 and right exact tensor tail in degree zero. For a short exact sequence 0→B′→B→B″→0 of left modules the corresponding sequence is Tor_n^R(A,B′)→Tor_n^R(A,B)→Tor_n^R(A,B″)→Tor_(n-1)^R(A,B′), again ending in the tensor tail. All maps including connecting maps are natural and choice independent.

Let R be commutative, r∈R a nonzerodivisor and B any R-module. The augmented complex 0→R --r→ R→R/(r)→0 is a free resolution. It gives Tor_1^R(R/(r),B)≅{b∈B:rb=0} and Ext_R^1(R/(r),B)≅B/rB; all Tor and Ext degrees ≥2 vanish. The degree-zero values are Tor_0≅B/rB and Ext^0≅{b:rb=0}. If r is a zero divisor the first arrow is not injective and this particular free resolution is unavailable; the formulas are asserted under the nonzerodivisor hypothesis.

For a short exact sequence 0→K→P→A→0 with P projective and n≥1, Ext_R^(n+1)(A,B)≅Ext_R^n(K,B) for every B on the same side. For 0→B→I→L→0 with I injective and n≥1, Ext_R^(n+1)(A,B)≅Ext_R^n(A,L). These are the identifications from the long exact sequences and include the right-module theory over Rᵒᵖ.

For a short exact sequence 0→K→F→A→0 of right R-modules with F flat (in particular projective), every left B and n≥1 satisfy Tor_(n+1)^R(A,B)≅Tor_n^R(K,B). For 0→L→G→B→0 of left modules with G flat, every right A satisfies Tor_(n+1)^R(A,B)≅Tor_n^R(A,L) for n≥1.

At the degree-zero edges, for 0→K→P→A→0 with P projective, Ext_R^1(A,B)≅coker(Hom_R(P,B)→Hom_R(K,B)); with P merely flat on the right, Tor_1^R(A,B)≅ker(K⊗_R B→P⊗_R B). For 0→B→I→L→0 with I injective, Ext_R^1(A,B)≅coker(Hom_R(A,I)→Hom_R(A,L)); the second-variable Tor edge for 0→L→G→B→0 with G flat is Tor_1^R(A,B)≅ker(A⊗_R L→A⊗_R G). These are the explicit degree-zero addenda; n=0 is not substituted into the positive-degree shifting formula.

For left R-modules A,B, equivalence classes of short exact sequences 0→B→E→A→0, where equivalence is an extension map fixing A and B, are naturally in bijection with Ext_R^1(A,B). The class of an extension is δ(1_A), where δ:Hom_R(A,A)→Ext_R^1(A,B) is its second-variable connecting homomorphism. The split extension represents zero. Under the bijection Baer addition agrees with addition in Ext; Baer addition takes the direct sum of two extensions, pulls back along A→A⊕A and pushes out along B⊕B→B. Naturality is contravariant by pullback in A and covariant by pushout in B.

For a principal ideal domain R, every submodule N of every free R-module F is free, with no restriction on the cardinality of a basis of F. This includes N=0 with the empty basis; no finite-rank hypothesis may replace the arbitrary-rank assertion.

Let C be a nonnegative chain complex of right R-modules such that each C_n and each boundary module B_n(C) is flat. For every left R-module M and n≥0 there is a natural short exact sequence 0→H_n(C)⊗_R M→H_n(C⊗_R M)→Tor_1^R(H_(n-1)(C),M)→0, where H_(-1)(C)=0. The left map sends [z]⊗m to [z⊗m]. The sequence splits if the boundary projections C_n→B_(n-1)(C) split, in particular if all boundary modules are projective. The splitting is not claimed canonical.

Let C be a nonnegative chain complex of left R-modules with every C_n and B_n(C) projective. For every left R-module M and n≥0 there is a natural short exact sequence 0→Ext_R^1(H_(n-1)(C),M)→H^n(Hom_R(C,M))→Hom_R(H_n(C),M)→0, where H_(-1)(C)=0. The right map is restriction of a cocycle to cycles, descended to homology. Choosing sections of the boundary projections splits the sequence, without a claim of a canonical splitting.
For every nonnegative complex of free modules over a PID, of arbitrary ranks, both universal coefficient sequences above apply and split noncanonically for every coefficient module and every n≥0.

Over a field k let R=k[ε]/(ε²), C_n=R for all n≥0, and d_n be multiplication by ε for n>0; let M=R/(ε)≅k. Then H_n(C)=0 for n>0 (and H_0(C)≅k), whereas every differential of C⊗_R M is zero and H_n(C⊗_R M)≅k for every n≥0. Thus for n≥2 both proposed outer homology coefficient terms vanish while the middle does not. Hom_R(C,M) likewise has zero cochain differential (and H^n≅k in every n≥0), so the corresponding unsupported cohomology sequence also fails in n≥2. This demonstrates that freeness of chain terms alone does not remove the boundary flatness/projectivity hypotheses over general rings.

Let C,D be nonnegative chain complexes of right and left R-modules, respectively, with each C_p and B_p(C) flat. Their tensor complex is the direct-sum totalization with d(c⊗x)=d_C(c)⊗x+(-1)^p c⊗d_D(x) for c∈C_p. For every n≥0 there is a natural short exact sequence 0→⊕_(p+q=n) H_p(C)⊗_R H_q(D)→H_n(C⊗_R D)→⊕_(p+q=n-1) Tor_1^R(H_p(C),H_q(D))→0. The last sum is zero for n=0, and the first arrow sends [c]⊗[x] to [c⊗x]. Over a PID the sequence splits noncanonically if at least one complex is degreewise free, in particular if both are; arbitrary ranks are allowed.

The Künneth sequence has the corresponding version with the flatness hypotheses on D_q and B_q(D), instead of on C_p and B_p(C), with the same module sides and signed tensor differential. This is the explicit second-factor variant of the theorem, obtained by the signed interchange (over a general ring reversing sides uses the opposite-ring interpretation). Over a PID the noncanonical splitting still holds when either factor is free.

The Künneth theorem here concerns algebraic tensor complexes. Application to topological products would require a separate chain comparison; this paragraph supplies no topological product theorem as an additional deliverable.
Chapter 12 assumes commutative unital rings. Its Tor base-change comparisons have no local finiteness hypothesis; the later local criterion has the stated Noetherian and finite S-module hypotheses.

For a flat map R→S of commutative rings, with R Noetherian and A a finitely generated R-module, any R-module B and n≥0, there is a natural S-linear isomorphism S⊗_R Ext_R^n(A,B)≅Ext_S^n(S⊗_R A,S⊗_R B). In particular for a multiplicative subset T⊆R this gives T⁻¹Ext_R^n(A,B)≅Ext_(T⁻¹R)^n(T⁻¹A,T⁻¹B); the same Noetherian and finite-A hypotheses apply.

For a flat map R→S of commutative rings, arbitrary R-modules A,B and n≥0, there is a natural S-linear isomorphism S⊗_R Tor_n^R(A,B)≅Tor_n^S(S⊗_R A,S⊗_R B). In particular it applies to every localization S=T⁻¹R, with scalar extension identified with localization.

Let R→S be a flat map of commutative rings, A any R-module, C any S-module and n≥0. There is a natural S-linear isomorphism Tor_n^S(S⊗_R A,C)≅Tor_n^R(A,Res_R C), where the right-hand S-action is through C. No finite-generation or Noetherian hypothesis is imposed.

For all R-modules A,B and n≥0, Tor_n^R(A,B)=0 if and only if Tor_n^(R_p)(A_p,B_p)=0 for every prime p, equivalently for every maximal ideal. The analogous equivalence holds for Ext_R^n(A,B) and Ext_(R_p)^n(A_p,B_p) when R is Noetherian and A is finitely generated, with B arbitrary. These are the localization vanishing tests for the derived groups and use the comparison hypotheses just stated.

For a free module P with an infinite basis J, the Hom expression is a product: Hom_R(P,B) is naturally the product of J copies of B, rather than a finite power. This is the unnumbered observation explaining the finite-generation condition in the Ext comparison; it is already covered by the arbitrary-basis free-module universal property and does not assert that flat scalar extension commutes with arbitrary products.

Let (R,m)→(S,n) be a local homomorphism of commutative Noetherian local rings, and let M be a finitely generated S-module. Then M, restricted to R, is flat over R if and only if Tor_1^R(R/m,M)=0. M is not required to be finitely generated as an R-module.
