Preserve the main statements including boundary, corner, and zero-dimensional cases and the distinctions between embedded and intrinsic calculus, Stokes and its comparison interface, and locally proved results versus statements whose full proofs belong to later topics. The source-map counts and suggested dependency interfaces guide reading and reuse; they do not add mathematical deliverables.

The source map records 74 writing items, their source positions, dependencies, textbook references, and proof-routing notes. It is advisory metadata, not an independent source of mathematical assertions or a prescription of goal count.
Typesetting declarations, title and publication information, and the overview of the twelve-chapter development are contextual material, not additional mathematical obligations.

Throughout, manifolds are finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable real manifolds of a fixed dimension unless indicated otherwise, and smooth means C^∞. For n≥1 the boundary model is H^n={x∈R^n:x_n≥0}, with relatively open chart images and smoothness at faces by local extension to Euclidean open sets. The zero-dimensional model is a point with empty boundary. Intrinsic boundary, ambient frontier, and corner faces are distinct. The support of a section is the closure, in its base, of its nonzero locus.

Use df_p=T_pf for the differential, [X,Y] for the commutator on smooth functions, and φ_t for the local flow of X on its actual domain. Lie differentiation is the derivative at zero of φ_t^*. Contraction ι_X inserts X into the first slot. A wedge of one-forms evaluates by the determinant on the ordered vectors. Boundary orientation is outward-normal first. Cochain differentials raise degree; oriented simplex boundaries use alternating face signs. Differential forms and de Rham cohomology have real coefficients. These conventions are implemented by the corresponding chapter constructions.

Finite-dimensional linear and multilinear algebra, elementary topology, Euclidean calculus, Lebesgue integration and Fubini, and local Euclidean ODE existence, uniqueness and smooth dependence are prerequisites. Euclidean inverse/implicit/constant-rank and change-of-variables theorems and regular Lindelöf paracompactness are used in their usual stated settings; citations and the table of contents are contextual rather than new theorem assertions.

An n-dimensional topological manifold is a Hausdorff, second-countable space locally homeomorphic by charts with open domain to relatively open subsets of the half-space H^n for n>0; R^n may be used when all points are interior. Dimension zero uses the one-point model. A chart is a homeomorphism onto its image. Unless an ambient frontier is explicitly specified, boundary means intrinsic boundary.

Every topological manifold is locally compact and locally path connected, admits a countable chart cover, is paracompact, and admits compact sets K_j (j>=1) with K_j contained in int(K_{j+1}) and M equal to the union of int(K_j). Its connected components are open and path connected and form an at most countable family. The statement includes the empty manifold, with all K_j empty.

For a relatively open subset of a Euclidean half-space, a map into Euclidean space is smooth if near each point it agrees on the relative domain with a smooth map on a Euclidean open neighborhood. Maps with values in a half-space use this convention componentwise; the ambient extension may take values outside the target half-space. The analogous convention applies to finite C^r regularity.

In positive dimension a relatively open half-space domain is locally the closure of its Euclidean interior. Consequently two smooth ambient extensions agreeing on that domain have equal derivatives of every available order there, including at the boundary; the same independence holds for C^r extensions through every order available for finite r.

An atlas is a chart cover. It is smooth when every chart transition on an overlap and its inverse are smooth on the model domains. A smooth structure is a maximal smooth atlas; a smooth manifold is a topological manifold equipped with such a structure.

Every smooth atlas extends uniquely to a maximal smooth atlas, obtained by adjoining all charts smoothly compatible with every chart in the original atlas. Any smooth atlas containing the original atlas is contained in this maximal extension.

Given a covering family of parametrizations of a set whose coordinate overlap domains are relatively open and whose transition maps are homeomorphisms, declare a subset open precisely when its intersection with every chart domain has relatively open coordinates. This defines a topology in which all chart domains are open and all charts are homeomorphisms. Hausdorffness must additionally be checked, and a countable chart subcover, when it exists, gives second countability. Smooth compatibility then equips the resulting topological manifold with a smooth structure.

Open subsets of a smooth manifold carry the restricted smooth structure. Products of two manifolds without boundary carry the product smooth structure. A product with exactly one factor having boundary carries the half-space product structure, placing its boundary coordinate last. Product charts for two boundary factors instead have corner models at pairs of boundary points; these charts are used later for manifolds with corners.

The sphere S^n in R^(n+1) has its natural smooth structure: on each positive or negative coordinate hemisphere, omit that coordinate; the inverse reinserts plus or minus sqrt(1-||x||^2) on the open unit ball. These charts are smoothly compatible. The construction includes S^0.

The torus (S^1)^k carries the product atlas. Periodic angle coordinates induce a homeomorphism R^k/Z^k -> (S^1)^k; on sufficiently small coordinate boxes the angle map has a smooth inverse, yielding the corresponding quotient charts and smooth structure.

Real projective space RP^n is the antipodal quotient of S^n, with its Hausdorff, second-countable quotient topology and natural smooth atlas. On the chart where x_i is nonzero use the ratios x_j/x_i, j!=i; the inverse inserts 1 in position i and takes the line of the resulting vector. The chart transitions are smooth rational expressions with nonzero denominators. The description includes RP^0.

For a smooth n-manifold with n>=1, the condition that a point have last coordinate zero in a half-space chart is independent of the smooth chart. The intrinsic boundary defined by this condition is closed and naturally a smooth (n-1)-manifold without boundary, with charts restricted to the face; its inclusion into M is smooth. Its complement is the manifold interior. For n=0 the boundary is defined to be empty.

The boundary argument uses smooth compatibility and proves smooth boundary invariance directly, without presupposing topological invariance of boundary. References to Lee and Tu supply comparison and background, rather than an additional theorem obligation.

A continuous f:M->N is smooth if each source point has a source chart whose f-image lies in a target chart and whose coordinate representative is smooth. This local criterion is independent of the chosen charts, respects restriction and gluing on open subsets, and is closed under composition. All these assertions also hold for C^r maps between C^r atlases.
A diffeomorphism is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse.
The function R->R, x |-> x^3, is a smooth bijection whose inverse is not differentiable at 0; a smooth bijection need not be a diffeomorphism.
A diffeomorphism transports the smooth atlas and preserves the intrinsic boundary.

For any subset A of a smooth manifold M, a map A->R^k is smooth on A when, near each point of A, it agrees on the intersection with A with a smooth map defined on a neighborhood in M. The analogous local extension convention applies to a boundaryless manifold target. The global extension theorem below is asserted for vector-valued targets, not for arbitrary manifold targets.

Define theta(t)=exp(-1/t) for t>0 and theta(t)=0 for t<=0. This is smooth. The smooth quotient eta(t)=theta(1-t)/(theta(1-t)+theta(t)) is 1 for t<=0 and 0 for t>=1. For 0<a<b, eta((||x-x0||^2-a^2)/(b^2-a^2)) is nonnegative smooth, is 1 on the closed radius-a ball and has support in the closed radius-b ball. Restricting to a half-space gives the same relative construction at boundary points. If the larger closed relative ball lies in a chart domain, its transported bump extends smoothly by zero outside that chart domain.

Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a subordinate smooth partition of unity: a locally finite family of nonnegative smooth functions summing to 1 whose closed supports are contained in the assigned cover members. The functions may be grouped according to the original cover index, still with closed support contained in its assigned member. For an empty manifold the empty partition is allowed.

If A is a closed subset of a smooth manifold M and A is contained in an open U, there exists a smooth chi:M->R with 0<=chi<=1, equal to 1 on a neighborhood of A, and supp(chi) contained in U. If A is compact, chi can additionally be chosen compactly supported.

The localization construction uses closed support containment, a condition enabling smooth extension by zero and common refinements for integration. The following Lee and Tu references are contextual.

Let M be a smooth manifold, A a closed subset, and U an open subset containing A. Every smooth f:A->R^k in the local extension sense admits a global smooth extension M->R^k with support contained in U.
Every smooth manifold M admits a smooth nonnegative real-valued function rho whose sublevel set {x:rho(x)<=c} is compact for every real c. This includes noncompact and empty manifolds.

For every closed subset A of a smooth manifold M, there exists a smooth nonnegative real-valued function g on M with zero set exactly A. No compactness assumption on A or M is imposed; boundary and zero-dimensional cases are included.
The preceding extension, exhaustion and zero-set constructions apply to arbitrary closed subsets and noncompact manifolds; the cited Lee results are background references.

C_p^infinity(M) is the real algebra of germs at p of smooth real-valued functions, with two representatives equivalent when they agree near p. A derivation at p is an R-linear map D:C_p^infinity(M)->R satisfying D(fg)=f(p)Dg+g(p)Df. Let m_p be the ideal of germs vanishing at p.

A derivation at p kills constants. Restriction to m_p identifies derivations naturally with the R-linear dual of m_p/(m_p)^2: a derivation vanishes on products of vanishing germs, and a functional on this quotient acts on a general germ f through the class of f-f(p).

For every p in a smooth n-manifold, the derivations at p form the n-dimensional vector space T_pM. In coordinates x=(x^1,...,x^n), the coordinate partial derivations at p form a basis and the coordinates of D are D(x^i). A smooth curve c with c(0)=p gives the derivation f |-> (f composed with c)'(0). Every derivation is represented by such a curve, allowing 0 as either endpoint of the parameter interval at a boundary point. Equality of curve velocities is independent of chart. In dimension zero T_pM is the zero space.
References to Lee, Tu and the Lee errata explain the boundary curve convention. These references are not additional obligations.

Derivations at p defined on all global smooth real-valued functions are equivalent to derivations of germs. A global derivation kills every function vanishing near p and hence depends only on its germ; every germ has a global smooth representative after multiplication by a cutoff, giving the converse correspondence.

For p in the boundary of a smooth n-manifold, the differential of the boundary inclusion identifies T_p(boundary M) with the hyperplane v_n=0 in a half-space chart. Velocities of forward curves remaining in M are exactly v_n>=0; backward velocities are exactly v_n<=0; velocities of two-sided curves are exactly T_p(boundary M). These cones and hyperplane are chart independent. The full tangent space still has dimension n, and its quotient by the boundary tangent hyperplane has a well-defined inward and outward half.
Restricting the tangent model to two-sided curves at a boundary point would discard its normal direction. References compare this convention with Lee and Tu.

For smooth f:M->N, define df_p(v) by (df_p(v))(h)=v(h composed with f) on target germs h. This is an R-linear map T_pM->T_(f(p))N, represented in coordinates by the Jacobian. Differentials respect identity maps and obey d(g composed with f)_p=dg_(f(p)) composed with df_p. For products allowed in M01.03, the tangent space at (p,q) is canonically T_pM direct-sum T_qN, and the differential of a pair is the pair of differentials. A diffeomorphism induces fiberwise linear isomorphisms. The coordinate differential and chain rule hold also for C^r maps of C^r manifolds, r>=1.

For a C^r manifold with r>=1, tangent spaces can be constructed from coordinate vector representatives identified by derivatives of coordinate transitions, independently of ambient extensions at boundary points. The resulting tangent-space transitions and induced tangent map of a C^r map have regularity C^(r-1). This finite-regularity construction uses coordinate derivatives and does not require the smooth-germ algebra model.
The cited Lee and Tu sections are background for differentials and the chain rule.

The disjoint union TM of T_pM over p in M has a canonical smooth manifold structure, locally trivialized by v in T_pM |-> (x(p),dx_p(v)). Its projection pi_M:TM->M is locally a product with R^n, and fiber-coordinate transitions are linear isomorphisms depending smoothly on the base point. The zero section, fiberwise addition on equal-base pairs, and scalar multiplication are smooth. A smooth f:M->N induces a smooth Tf:TM->TN covering f by v |-> df_p(v), with T(id_M)=id_(TM) and T(g composed with f)=Tg composed with Tf. For manifolds with boundary, boundary(TM)=pi_M^(-1)(boundary M). In dimension zero the fibers are singletons and this reduces to the discrete base.
The tangent bundle is a smooth vector bundle in the sense defined later in M05.01. Lee and Tu references supply background, without adding independent deliverables here.

Suppose a smooth n-manifold M is identified with a subset of R^N, its local parametrizations into R^N are smooth of rank n, and j is its inclusion. For every local parametrization psi sending u to p, dj_p(T_pM)=dpsi_u(R^n), independently of the parametrization, and dj_p is a linear isomorphism from T_pM onto this image. At a boundary point, dj_p(T_p(boundary M)) is the image under dpsi_u of the parametrizing half-space's tangent hyperplane.

In the setting of the embedded tangent comparison, let gamma be a smooth two-sided ambient curve with gamma(0)=j(p) and a continuous local lift through p to M. Then this lift is smooth. The continuous local lift is automatic if M has the subspace topology and gamma remains in j(M). If p is a boundary point, gamma'(0) belongs to dj_p(T_p(boundary M)). This is the additional ambient-curve comparison stated at the end of the proof, rather than a required reproduction of its inverse-function-theorem proof route.

The tangent comparison is intended for the embedded calculus in D04; comparing intrinsic and embedded integration also requires agreement of boundary and tangent data, not only equality of underlying sets.

The rank of a C^1 map at a point is the rank of its differential. It is an immersion where that differential is injective and a submersion where it is surjective. These properties are invariant under change of charts. Subsequent normal-form statements distinguish interior models from the boundary cases admitting suitable ambient extensions.
Let f:M^m->N^n be C^r with r>=1. If p and f(p) are interior points and df_p is invertible, f is a local C^r diffeomorphism near p.

Let f:M^m->N^n be C^r, r>=1. If p and f(p) have interior charts and the rank of f is constantly k near p, local C^r coordinates put f in the form (u,v) |-> (u,0) with u in R^k. Consequently immersions and submersions between these interior models have the local inclusion and projection normal forms. The rank cases k=0, k=m and k=n are included.

Let f:M^m->N^n be C^r, r>=1. If f is an immersion at a boundary point p of M and f(p) is interior in N, source and target C^r coordinates put f into the inclusion form u |-> (u,0), with the source restricted to its original half-space.

Let f:M^n->N^n be C^r, r>=1, with p and f(p) boundary points. If f maps nearby boundary points into the target boundary and df_p is invertible, then f is a local C^r diffeomorphism of half-space models.
Lee, Tu and D04 are referenced for Euclidean inverse and constant-rank normal forms.

For n>=1, inclusion H^n->R^n has invertible differential everywhere but is not a local diffeomorphism at a boundary point into R^n, demonstrating the need for explicit boundary hypotheses in the local inverse theorem.
An embedding is an injective immersion which is a homeomorphism onto its image equipped with the subspace topology. A map between manifolds is proper when inverse images of compact sets are compact.

Every immersion is locally an embedding, including when either source or target has boundary. Every proper injective immersion is an embedding. In particular, every injective immersion from a compact manifold is an embedding.

For irrational real alpha, the map R->(R/Z)^2, t |-> ([t],[alpha*t]), is an injective immersion with local derivative (1,alpha), but is not an embedding. There exist positive integers q_j tending to infinity for which alpha*q_j tends to 0 modulo Z, so the image of q_j tends to the image of 0 while q_j does not tend to 0. Thus its inverse onto its image is not continuous. The quoted pigeonhole approximation is the proof of this recurrence, rather than an extra standalone deliverable.
A smooth submersion between boundaryless manifolds has a smooth local section through every source point and is an open map.

A surjective smooth map q:M->N with smooth local sections around every point of N is a quotient map. For every smooth h:M->P constant on each fiber of q, there exists a unique smooth hbar:N->P with h=hbar composed with q. Consequently, two surjective smooth maps from the same source, both having smooth local sections and with exactly the same fibers, have canonically diffeomorphic target manifolds, with the diffeomorphism intertwining the two quotient maps.

Surjectivity of a differential at a boundary point does not by itself imply smooth local sections or local surjectivity onto an open target neighborhood. Inclusion H^n->R^n for n>=1 has surjective differential at a boundary point but is not locally onto any open target neighborhood there.

An immersed submanifold S of M is a smooth manifold structure on the underlying subset S for which inclusion into M is an injective immersion. Its topology may be strictly finer than the subspace topology, as for the irrational line. It is embedded when inclusion is an embedding. Intrinsic boundary of S and ambient frontier of its image in M are distinct notions.

In a boundaryless n-manifold, every embedded k-dimensional submanifold is locally a coordinate k-slice, with a k-dimensional half-slice at each point of the submanifold's own boundary. Conversely any subset admitting these local slice or half-slice charts carries a unique embedded smooth structure.

A smooth map restricts smoothly to an immersed submanifold of its source. If a smooth map has image contained in an immersed submanifold of its target and is continuous for that submanifold's topology, the induced map into the submanifold is smooth. For an embedded submanifold this continuity condition is automatic. These restriction assertions allow boundary points under the manuscript's local extension conventions.

Every smooth real-valued function on an embedded submanifold extends smoothly to some open neighborhood of it in the ambient manifold. If the embedded submanifold is closed, it extends smoothly to the entire ambient manifold. The same conclusion holds componentwise for R^k-valued functions, as expressly noted in the proof. Both submanifold boundary points and ambient boundary charts are covered by the local extension convention.
Lee and Tu are cited for slice, restriction and embedded-function extension results.
A point y in the target of a smooth map F is a regular value if dF_p is surjective for every p in F^(-1)(y); an empty fiber satisfies this condition vacuously.

Let F:M^m->N^n be smooth between boundaryless manifolds and let y be a regular value. Its fiber F^(-1)(y) is closed and, if nonempty, is an embedded submanifold of codimension n. At each p in the fiber, the differential of its inclusion identifies its tangent space with ker(dF_p). The empty fiber is allowed. In particular a regular fiber with m<n is empty, and when n=0 a fiber is open as well as closed.
Every embedded boundaryless submanifold of a boundaryless manifold is locally the regular zero set of a submersion to a Euclidean space whose dimension is its codimension.
The regular-level tangent identification agrees with the Euclidean regular-level construction in D04. Lee and Tu are referenced for background.

Let F:M->N be smooth, with M possibly having boundary and N boundaryless. If y is a regular value of both F and its restriction to boundary M, then S=F^(-1)(y) has an embedded manifold structure with boundary S=S intersection boundary M. At a boundary point p its full tangent space is identified by inclusion with ker(dF_p), and its boundary tangent space with ker(dF_p) intersection T_p(boundary M). The nonempty fiber has dimension dim(M)-dim(N); the empty fiber is allowed. A nonempty boundary fiber necessarily has dim(N)<=dim(M)-1, and for zero-dimensional N the fiber is an open and closed portion of M.
In a boundaryless manifold M, a regular domain is a closed codimension-zero embedded submanifold D with boundary.

Let M be boundaryless and D a closed codimension-zero embedded submanifold with boundary. Its intrinsic interior equals its ambient interior and its intrinsic boundary equals its ambient frontier. There exists smooth f:M->R with D={f<=0}, boundary D=f^(-1)(0), and 0 a regular value. If D is compact, f can additionally be chosen to have compact sublevel sets for every real level. Conversely, if f:M->R is smooth and 0 is a regular value, its closed sublevel set {f<=0} has this codimension-zero embedded manifold-with-boundary structure and these boundary and interior descriptions. Empty sets, full components and zero-dimensional cases are not excluded.

For F:H^2->R defined by F(x,s)=s+x^2, the value 0 is regular for F but not for its restriction to the boundary. Its zero fiber is the singleton (0,0), which has no codimension-one half-slice near that point. Thus boundary regularity in the boundary regular-level theorem is necessary.
The circle S^1 has empty intrinsic boundary, but its frontier as a subset of R^2 is the entire circle.

Let p:E->M be a topological covering of a smooth manifold, with countable fibers. Then E has a unique smooth manifold structure for which p is a smooth covering: each sheet over a sufficiently small connected evenly covered neighborhood maps diffeomorphically onto that neighborhood. The same conclusion holds if E is connected, because its fibers are then countable. In either case boundary E=p^(-1)(boundary M). If a continuous map ftilde:X->E lifts a smooth map f:X->M from a smooth manifold X, then ftilde is smooth. Empty coverings and boundary charts are included.

The path- and homotopy-lifting theorems for topological coverings provide smooth lifts whenever their base maps are smooth, under the covering smooth structure, including in boundary charts. A simply connected topological covering, whenever supplied by the usual covering existence theorem, has a canonical smooth structure.
The periodic angle map R^k->(S^1)^k and the antipodal quotient S^n->RP^n with the previously constructed smooth structures are smooth coverings, as witnessed by their lifted coordinate neighborhoods.
Lee pages 91–95 are cited for covering-space background.

The stated chartwise nullity convention is independent of smooth charts: a smooth coordinate change is Lipschitz on sufficiently small compact Euclidean neighborhoods to which it extends, and a same-dimensional Lipschitz map sends Lebesgue-null sets to null sets; a countable cover by such neighborhoods suffices.

Nullity of a subset of a manifold means Lebesgue nullity in every chart, measured in the ambient Euclidean dimension of the chart even at boundary points; in dimension zero the measure convention is counting measure.

Smooth Sard theorem (M04.01): for every smooth map f:M^m→N^n of smooth manifolds, either or both allowed to have boundary, the set of critical values is null in N, where p is critical exactly when df_p:T_pM→T_{f(p)}N is not surjective and a critical value is an image of a critical point. If m<n, the whole image f(M) is null. If n>0, the regular values are dense in N. The dimension-zero nullity convention is counting measure.

Good projection directions: let e:M^n→R^q be an injective immersion (M may have boundary). If q>2n+1, a dense set of lines L in R^q has the property that projection along L, restricted to e(M), gives an injective immersion of M into a complementary (q−1)-plane. For e merely an immersion, the corresponding immersion conclusion holds for a dense set of lines when q>2n. In either conclusion the good lines may also be required to avoid any prescribed proper projective linear subspace of RP^{q−1}.
Proper weak Whitney embedding (M04.02): every smooth n-manifold, possibly with boundary, has a proper smooth embedding into R^{2n+1}.

Compact approximation part of M04.03: if M^n is a compact smooth manifold (boundary allowed), q≥2n+1, f:M→R^q is smooth, and ε>0, there is a smooth embedding g:M→R^q such that ||g(p)−f(p)||<ε for every p∈M.
Weak immersion part of M04.03: every smooth n-manifold, with or without boundary, admits a smooth immersion into R^{2n}, including n=0.

entries.coverage_note: The two Prop declarations record the strong bounds. Their proofs belong to the later differential topology unit.
entries.title: The cited stronger Whitney bounds for boundaryless smooth n-manifolds are: if n>0, there is a smooth embedding into R^{2n}; if n>1, there is a smooth immersion into R^{2n−1}. These mathematical assertions are stated here with their stronger proofs assigned to differential topology, rather than claimed to follow from the local proofs in this chapter.

Shrinking around an embedded image: let F:U→N be continuous, N a manifold, and S⊆U a subspace such that F|_S is a homeomorphism onto a locally closed subset of N. If each point of S has an open neighborhood in U on which F is injective, then there is an open neighborhood V of all of S in U on which F is injective.

Euclidean tubular neighborhood (M04.04): if S is a boundaryless embedded submanifold of R^q, with normal bundle NS consisting of the orthogonal complements (T_pS)^⊥, there is an open neighborhood V of its zero section such that (p,v)↦p+v is a diffeomorphism V→W onto an open neighborhood W of S in R^q. V can be chosen fiberwise star-shaped. The bundle projection transported to W gives a smooth retraction W→S, and radial contraction (p,v)↦(p,(1−t)v), 0≤t≤1, gives a deformation of W to S fixed on S.

Relative Whitney approximation into Euclidean space (M04.05): let M be a smooth manifold, boundary allowed, F:M→R^q continuous, and A⊆M closed. Suppose each point of A has a neighborhood on which F|_A admits a smooth extension. For every positive continuous ε:M→R there is a smooth G:M→R^q with G|_A=F|_A and ||G(p)−F(p)||<ε(p) for all p. There is a homotopy from F to G fixed on A.

Manifold-target part of relative Whitney approximation (M04.05): let the source M be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, and let N be a boundaryless smooth manifold. If F:M→N is continuous, A⊆M is closed, and F|_A has smooth local extensions at every point of A, then F is homotopic relative to A to a smooth G:M→N. Given any open neighborhood O of the graph of F in M×N, the homotopy H can be chosen with (p,H(t,p))∈O for every p and 0≤t≤1. If F is smooth on a neighborhood of A, the constructed homotopy is smooth on a neighborhood of A×[0,1].

Transverse inverse image (M04.06): let N be boundaryless, S⊆N a boundaryless embedded submanifold, and f:M→N smooth. Assume df_p(T_pM)+T_{f(p)}S=T_{f(p)}N at every p with f(p)∈S. If M has boundary, also assume df_p(T_p∂M)+T_{f(p)}S=T_{f(p)}N at each p∈∂M with f(p)∈S. Then f^{-1}(S) is an embedded submanifold wherever nonempty, of codimension codim_N S, with boundary f^{-1}(S)∩∂M and tangent space T_p(f^{-1}(S))=(df_p)^{-1}(T_{f(p)}S).

Parametric transversality (M04.07): let P be a boundaryless parameter manifold, N a boundaryless manifold, S⊆N a boundaryless embedded submanifold, and F:P×M→N a smooth map transverse to S. If M has boundary, also require F|_{P×∂M} to be transverse to S. Except for parameters a in a null subset of P, the slice F_a:M→N, p↦F(a,p), is transverse to S; when ∂M is present, its boundary restriction F_a|_{∂M} is also transverse to S.

Let M be boundaryless, S⊆R^n a boundaryless embedded submanifold, and H:[0,1]×M→R^n a smooth homotopy with transverse endpoint maps. The family H(t,p)+t(1−t)a yields, for arbitrarily small suitable a∈R^n, a transverse smooth homotopy with the same endpoint maps. Its inverse image of S is an embedded submanifold whose boundary is exactly the two endpoint inverse images. The parameter derivative is surjective for 0<t<1; the restrictions at t=0,1 already satisfy transversality.

For a smooth f:M→R^n and a boundaryless embedded submanifold S⊆R^n, the translation family F(a,p)=f(p)+a has surjective parameter derivative, including on its restriction to parameters times ∂M. Consequently arbitrarily small translations a make f+a transverse to S, and also transverse on ∂M when present; such perturbations are homotopic to f.

A smooth real vector bundle of rank r over M is a smooth map π:E→M whose fibers are real vector spaces and which has smooth local trivializations E|_U≅U×R^r linear on fibers. If the change from i-coordinates to j-coordinates is (p,v)↦(p,g_{ji}(p)v), then g_{ji}:U_i∩U_j→GL_r(R) is smooth and g_{ki}=g_{kj}g_{ji} on triple overlaps. A rank-zero bundle has zero fibers.

Gluing from transition functions (M05.01): given an open cover (U_i) of a smooth manifold M and smooth maps g_{ji}:U_i∩U_j→GL_r(R) with g_{ii}=I and the cocycle identities g_{ki}=g_{kj}g_{ji}, there is a smooth real rank-r vector bundle with these specified transitions. Any two realizations are uniquely isomorphic by the bundle map preserving the specified local trivializations. This includes rank zero and bases with boundary.
A frame for a vector bundle on a domain is an ordered list of sections whose values form a basis of each fiber on that domain.

For the tangent bundle the transition matrices are derivatives of the base coordinate changes; their cocycle condition is the chain rule and their smoothness supplies the smooth vector-bundle structure.

Sections, frames, and extension (M05.02): in any smooth local frame, a section is smooth if and only if all its coefficient functions are smooth. A smooth rank-r bundle is trivial if and only if it has a global smooth frame. If a section is prescribed on a closed A⊆M and has smooth local extensions near each point of A, it has a global smooth extension. Given an open U⊇A with local extensions taken inside U, the global extension can be chosen with support contained in U. In particular, a smooth section of the bundle restricted to a closed embedded submanifold has such smooth local extensions at every point, including boundary points, so the global extension and support-control conclusions apply to it.

Kernels, images, and quotients (M05.03): a smooth vector-bundle morphism A:E→F over id_M with constant fiber rank has smooth kernel and image subbundles. For a smooth subbundle K⊆E, the fiber quotients E_p/K_p form a smooth quotient vector bundle over M. These assertions apply componentwise when the relevant ranks vary between components.

For an embedded submanifold S⊆M the normal bundle is the smooth quotient TM|_S/TS (with TS included through the derivative of the embedding, including at boundary points). The dual bundle of TM is the cotangent bundle T^*M.

Pullback-bundle part of M05.04: for a smooth f:P→M and a smooth bundle E→M, the fibers E_{f(p)} assemble into a smooth bundle f^*E over P. For a further smooth g:Q→P, (f∘g)^*E is canonically isomorphic to g^*(f^*E).

Algebraic-bundle part of M05.04: dual bundles, direct sums, tensor products, and exterior powers of smooth real vector bundles are smooth bundles. Their local transitions are respectively inverse-transposes, block sums, tensor-product matrices, and minors of the original transition matrices. The conventions are Λ^0E=M×R and Λ^kE the zero bundle when k exceeds the fiber rank.

Metrics and splitting (M05.05): every smooth real vector bundle E admits a smooth positive-definite fiber metric. For each smooth subbundle K⊆E, the metric orthogonal complement K^⊥ is a smooth subbundle and E=K⊕K^⊥ as smooth bundles. Every short exact sequence of smooth vector bundles therefore splits. A fiber metric gives a smooth bundle isomorphism E≅E^* by v↦⟨v,·⟩. For tangent bases changed by B, the Gram matrix transforms by G↦BᵀGB, so √det(BᵀGB)=|det B|√det G, the transformation law used for volume densities.

Differentials and covector pullback (M05.06): a one-form on M is a smooth section of T^*M. In coordinates x=(x^1,…,x^n), the covectors dx^i are dual to the coordinate vector fields. For every smooth function u, du is a smooth one-form with coefficients ∂_iu. For a smooth map f:P→M, the pullback is the smooth one-form (f^*α)_p(v)=α_{f(p)}(df_pv), and d(u∘f)=f^*(du). Pullback respects composition and restriction to a submanifold, where restriction uses the tangent inclusion.

Tensor fields and transformations (M05.07): for nonnegative integers r,s define T^r_sM=(TM)^{⊗r}⊗(T^*M)^{⊗s}. Symmetrization and alternation on like slots, tensor products, and contraction of paired tangent/cotangent slots are smooth bundle operations. Any smooth map has pullback of covariant tensors. A local diffeomorphism has pullback of tensors of arbitrary mixed variance, and this pullback commutes with tensor products and every permitted contraction.

Abstract tubular neighborhood (M05.08): if S is a boundaryless embedded submanifold of a boundaryless smooth manifold M, there is an open neighborhood V of the zero section in the quotient normal bundle TM|_S/TS and a diffeomorphism V→W onto an open neighborhood W of S in M which restricts to the inclusion S→M on the zero section. The domain V can be chosen fiberwise star-shaped.

Vector fields as derivations (M06.01): smooth sections X of TM correspond bijectively to real-linear derivations C^∞(M)→C^∞(M), acting by (Xf)(p)=df_p(X(p)). Locally the coordinate coefficients of X are Xx^i. If f:M→N is smooth, fields X on M and Y on N are f-related, meaning df_p(X(p))=Y(f(p)) for all p, if and only if X(u∘f)=(Yu)∘f for every u∈C^∞(N).

For a diffeomorphism f:M→N, every smooth field X on M pushes forward to a smooth field on N by (f_*X)(q)=df_{f^{-1}(q)}X(f^{-1}(q)); the construction is local for a local diffeomorphism. For a general smooth map, different points of a fiber can give different candidate vectors, so no unconditional global pushforward is asserted and related fields must be specified.

Lie bracket (M06.02): the commutator [X,Y]f=X(Yf)−Y(Xf) of smooth fields is a smooth vector field, with coordinate coefficients [X,Y]^j=Σ_i(X^i∂_iY^j−Y^i∂_iX^j). It is real-bilinear and antisymmetric, satisfies the Jacobi identity and, for every smooth function h, [X,hY]=h[X,Y]+(Xh)Y, and preserves related fields under smooth maps. For integer r≥1 the same coordinate formula for C^r fields defines a C^{r−1} vector field.

On a Lie group G, every v∈T_eG determines a smooth left-invariant vector field X_v(g)=d(L_g)_e(v), and every left-invariant field is of this form. Brackets of left-invariant fields are left-invariant, giving the bracket [v,w]=[X_v,X_w](e) on T_eG. For the open matrix group GL_n(R), X_v(g)=gv and [X_v,X_w](g)=g(vw−wv), so the induced bracket is the matrix commutator.

Maximal integral curves and flow (M06.03): for a smooth field X on a boundaryless manifold M and every p∈M, there is a unique maximal integral curve γ_p:I_p→M, with I_p an open interval containing 0, γ_p(0)=p, and γ_p′(t)=X(γ_p(t)). The flow domain D={(t,p):t∈I_p} is open in R×M and φ(t,p)=γ_p(t) is smooth on D. For s∈I_p, I_{φ_s(p)}=I_p−s and φ_t(φ_s(p))=φ_{s+t}(p) whenever s+t∈I_p. Each time map φ_s is a diffeomorphism from its open domain onto the domain of φ_{−s}, with inverse φ_{−s}.

Escape and completeness (M06.04): at either finite endpoint of the maximal interval of an integral curve of a smooth vector field on a boundaryless manifold, the curve eventually leaves each compact subset of the manifold. Every compactly supported smooth field on a boundaryless manifold is complete, meaning every maximal interval is R. Consequently every smooth field on a compact boundaryless manifold is complete.

Collar part of M06.05: every smooth manifold M with boundary has a smooth collar c:∂M×[0,1)→M which is a diffeomorphism onto an open neighborhood of ∂M and satisfies c(q,0)=q. The construction uses the one-sided flow of a smooth strictly inward-pointing field; an empty boundary gives the empty collar.

Flow-box and flowout parts of M06.05: near a point where a smooth vector field X on a boundaryless manifold is nonzero, there are local flow coordinates in which X is the first coordinate field. More generally, if a boundaryless smooth embedded hypersurface S is transverse to X, the flow map (t,q)↦φ_t(q) is a diffeomorphism from a neighborhood of {0}×S in its flow domain onto its open image, restricts to the inclusion at t=0, and carries ∂_t to X. No uniform time width is asserted for noncompact S.

Boundary-tangent-flow part of M06.06: a smooth field X on M tangent to ∂M has a maximal flow for two-sided local times, on a relatively open domain in R×M. The flow is smooth, preserves ∂M and Int M, and has the maximal-curve, domain, translated-lifespan, composition, and inverse-time-map properties of M06.03.
Interior homotopy-equivalence part of M06.06: for every smooth manifold M with boundary, the smooth inclusion Int M→M is a smooth homotopy equivalence.

Smoothing part of M06.06: every continuous map from a smooth manifold (source boundary allowed) into a smooth manifold with boundary is homotopic to a smooth map. Every continuous homotopy between smooth maps into such a target can be replaced by a smooth homotopy with the same two endpoint maps.

Brackets from the flow (M06.07): let X,Y be smooth fields on a boundaryless manifold and φ the local flow of X. Define (φ_t^*Y)(p)=d(φ_{−t})_{φ_t(p)}Y(φ_t(p)). Then (d/dt)|_{t=0} φ_t^*Y=[X,Y], and at every other time in the local domain (d/dt)φ_t^*Y=φ_t^*[X,Y]. The same derivative formulas hold when M has boundary and X is tangent to ∂M.

Commuting-flow and coordinate parts of M06.07: on a boundaryless manifold, smooth fields X,Y with [X,Y]=0 have locally commuting flows; if both fields are complete their flows commute for all times. Conversely, local commutation of their flows forces [X,Y]=0. A finite family X_1,…,X_k of commuting smooth fields on a boundaryless manifold which is linearly independent at a point can simultaneously be made the first k coordinate vector fields in coordinates near that point.

Evolution maps (M06.08): let J⊆R be an open interval, M a boundaryless manifold, and X_t a smooth time-dependent vector field defined on an open subset of J×M. For every initial pair (s,p) in the field domain there is a unique maximal solution interval containing s, remaining in the field domain. These solutions assemble into a unique maximal evolution Ψ(t,s,p), smooth on its open domain, with Ψ(s,s,p)=p and ∂_tΨ(t,s,p)=X_t(Ψ(t,s,p)). It obeys Ψ(t,u,Ψ(u,s,p))=Ψ(t,s,p) on the corresponding translated maximal intervals. For fixed s,t the two time maps in opposite directions are inverse diffeomorphisms between their open domains. This is an evolution, not an assertion of a one-parameter action on M.
Every smooth left-invariant vector field on a Lie group is complete. If γ_e:R→G is its integral curve through the identity, then γ_e(s+t)=γ_e(s)γ_e(t) for all s,t, so γ_e is a one-parameter subgroup.

The chapter develops exterior differentiation without choosing a metric or a connection; the coordinate construction is to commute with changes of variables, including at boundary points, and all local formulas are understood only where their indicated charts and flow maps are defined.

For a real n-dimensional vector space V, Λ^kV^* is the space of alternating k-linear covariant tensors. The wedge has determinant normalization (products of one-forms evaluate as determinants, equivalently the unnormalized signed shuffle sum over argument splits). Λ^0V^*=R and Λ^kV^*=0 for k>n. On an n-manifold M, a differential k-form is a smooth section of Λ^kT^*M.

Exterior algebra and smooth sections (M07.01): for a basis e^1,…,e^n of V^*, the increasing wedges e^{i_1}∧⋯∧e^{i_k}, i_1<⋯<i_k, form a basis of Λ^kV^*. The determinant-normalized wedge is associative and α∧β=(−1)^{kℓ}β∧α for degrees k,ℓ, including degree zero and degrees beyond n. The coefficients of a differential form in the increasing coordinate wedges uniquely determine the form and detect its smoothness; pointwise wedge sends smooth forms to smooth forms.

Form pullback (M07.02): for a smooth F:M→N and a k-form ω, define (F^*ω)_p(v_1,…,v_k)=ω_{F(p)}(dF_pv_1,…,dF_pv_k), with degree-zero pullback composition with F. Pullback produces a smooth form, is contravariantly functorial, and satisfies F^*(α∧β)=F^*α∧F^*β. Restriction to a submanifold is pullback by inclusion. For source and target of equal dimension the top-form coefficient changes by the signed coordinate Jacobian determinant.

Tautological one-form part of M07.02: on the cotangent bundle T^*M with projection π, the rule θ_ξ(V)=ξ(dπ_ξV) defines a canonical smooth one-form. In induced coordinates (x^i,p_i), where ξ=Σ_i p_i dx^i, it is θ=Σ_i p_i dx^i.

Exterior differentiation (M07.03): there exists a unique family of real-linear operators d:Ω^k(M)→Ω^{k+1}(M) agreeing with the differential on functions, satisfying d²=0, and satisfying d(α∧β)=dα∧β+(−1)^kα∧dβ for α of degree k. It is local, natural under every smooth map F (F^*dω=dF^*ω), and supp(dω)⊆supp(ω). In coordinates d(Σ_I a_I dx^{i_1}∧⋯∧dx^{i_k})=Σ_{I,j}(∂_ja_I)dx^j∧dx^{i_1}∧⋯∧dx^{i_k}. This formula is independent of local coefficient extensions and agrees in smoothly compatible Euclidean, half-space, and orthant charts, including boundary and corner points; on a zero-dimensional model d is zero.

C^1 part of M07.03 and its stated face consequence: the same coordinate formula defines a continuous exterior derivative for C^1 forms, is local and natural under smooth maps, and is independent of local extensions in smoothly compatible Euclidean, half-space, and orthant charts. In particular a C^1 form restricts to a C^1 form on a smooth face, and differentiation commutes with this restriction.

For a continuous differential form ω and a smooth map F, supp(F^*ω)⊆F^{-1}(supp ω). If F is proper and ω has compact support, F^*ω has compact support. In particular the inclusion of a closed embedded face is proper, so this compact-support conclusion applies to restriction to such a face.
For the tautological cotangent one-form θ, its exterior derivative is dθ=Σ_i dp_i∧dx^i in induced cotangent coordinates; these expressions therefore define a global smooth two-form on T^*M.

For a smooth k-form ω and smooth vector fields X_0,…,X_k, the exterior derivative has the invariant evaluation formula (dω)(X_0,…,X_k)=Σ_i(−1)^i X_i(ω(X_0,…,X̂_i,…,X_k))+Σ_{i<j}(−1)^{i+j}ω([X_i,X_j],X_0,…,X̂_i,…,X̂_j,…,X_k), where omitted fields retain their original order after the bracket placed first. The equality is an identity of forms/functions in the indicated local domains and includes the boundary coordinate extension.

Cartan identities (M07.04): let X,Y be smooth vector fields on a boundaryless manifold, or boundary-tangent smooth fields when the manifold has boundary. First-slot contraction ι_X has degree −1, with (ι_Xω)(v_1,…,v_{k−1})=ω(X,v_1,…,v_{k−1}), and vanishes on functions. Lie differentiation L_X is defined by differentiating pullback by the local flow. On forms L_X=dι_X+ι_Xd, [L_X,d]=0, [L_X,ι_Y]=ι_[X,Y], [L_X,L_Y]=L_[X,Y], and ι_Xι_Y+ι_Yι_X=0. The displayed commutators involving degree-zero operators are ordinary commutators. For fields not tangent at a boundary the identities hold on the ordinary interior and extend as coordinate identities to the boundary, without asserting a boundary-preserving flow.

For a smooth k-form ω and smooth fields X,Y_1,…,Y_k in the local-flow setting, (L_Xω)(Y_1,…,Y_k)=X(ω(Y_1,…,Y_k))−Σ_iω(Y_1,…,[X,Y_i],…,Y_k). At a boundary this agrees with the actual two-sided flow for boundary-tangent X and has the coordinate extension for a general X described in M07.04.

Path integration part of M07.05: for a smooth one-form α and a piecewise smooth path γ:[a,b]→M, define ∫_γα as the sum over smooth pieces of ∫_a^b α_{γ(t)}(γ′(t))dt. It is additive under concatenation, changes sign under reversal, and is invariant under piecewise smooth nondecreasing reparametrizations onto the original interval. For every smooth function u, ∫_γdu=u(γ(b))−u(γ(a)).

Exactness part of M07.05: on any smooth manifold M (boundary and the empty manifold allowed), a smooth one-form α is exact, meaning α=du for a smooth function u on M, if and only if its integral over every piecewise smooth closed path is zero; equivalently, its path integrals depend only on their fixed endpoints. A primitive is unique up to addition of a locally constant function, equivalently a constant on each connected component.

On the unit circle S^1⊆R^2, the restriction of α=x dy−y dx is a closed one-form (all two-forms on the one-dimensional circle vanish). Its integral on one positively oriented turn is 2π, so it has no primitive. Thus a closed form can have a nonzero period.

Integrals of a smooth closed one-form along piecewise smooth paths are invariant under continuous homotopy with fixed endpoints, including when the manifold has boundary. This conclusion is announced at this location, with its proof assigned to Stokes and stated precisely later as M10.07.

Tensor Lie derivatives (M07.06): differentiating pullback along the local diffeomorphisms of a smooth field X’s flow defines Lie differentiation of smooth tensors of every variance wherever the flow is defined. It agrees with Xf on functions and [X,Y] on vector fields, is a derivation for tensor products, and commutes with contraction and permutations of slots. For every covariant tensor A, (L_XA)(Y_1,…,Y_s)=X(A(Y_1,…,Y_s))−Σ_{i=1}^s A(Y_1,…,[X,Y_i],…,Y_s). These formulas do not depend on a connection and extend smoothly to boundary charts: for boundary-tangent X they agree with the flow, and for a general X they are the unique smooth coordinate extension of the interior formulas.

A smooth rank-k distribution on a boundaryless manifold M is a smooth rank-k vector subbundle D of TM. It is involutive when the bracket of every pair of smooth local sections of D again takes values in D. An immersed integral submanifold is a k-dimensional immersed manifold whose tangent maps have image D at the corresponding points. D is integrable when every point of M lies on an integral submanifold.

For a smooth distribution D on a boundaryless manifold, integrability implies involutivity. Involutivity is equivalent to requiring the brackets of the members of each local frame of D to take values in D. The annihilator D° is the subbundle of T*M whose fiber consists of covectors vanishing on D. D is involutive if and only if dθ(v,w)=0 for every smooth local section θ of D° and all vectors v,w of D at a common point; equivalently, the graded ideal of smooth differential forms whose restrictions to D vanish is stable under exterior differentiation.

Bibliographic pointer for the bracket, annihilator and integrability tests: Lee, Proposition 19.3, Lemma 19.4, Theorem 19.7 and Proposition 19.11; no additional mathematical obligation is asserted here.

For a smooth rank-k distribution D on a boundaryless n-manifold M, D is involutive if and only if every point has local coordinates (u¹,…,uᵏ,z¹,…,zⁿ⁻ᵏ) in which D is spanned by the u-coordinate fields. The slices with z constant are integral submanifolds. This includes k=0, with point slices, and k=n, with the whole chart as the integral slice.
Bibliographic pointer for the local Frobenius construction: Lee, Theorem 19.12 and Corollary 19.13; no separate mathematical obligation.

An involutive smooth constant-rank distribution D on a boundaryless manifold M partitions M into unique maximal connected immersed integral submanifolds (leaves). Each leaf has compatible local plaque charts inherited from adapted coordinates and a Hausdorff, second-countable manifold topology, for which its inclusion in M is a smooth injective integral immersion. Maximality concerns connected integral submanifolds: the image of any connected integral immersion lies in a unique leaf, with its smooth local factorization through that leaf. The leaf topology can be strictly finer than the subspace topology.

For irrational real α, the rank-one distribution on the smooth torus R²/Z² spanned by the constant field (1,α) has origin leaf given by the injective map t ↦ (t,αt) mod Z². This map is a diffeomorphism from R to the leaf with its manifold topology. Its image is dense in the torus, and the leaf topology is strictly finer than its subspace topology: ambient convergence to the origin along the leaf need not imply convergence of the real parameter to zero.

Let a finite-dimensional Lie group G act smoothly, freely and properly on a nonempty boundaryless n-manifold M, where properness means that (g,p) ↦ (p,gp) from G×M to M×M is proper. The orbit space M/G, with its quotient topology, has a unique smooth manifold structure of dimension n−dim G making the quotient projection q:M→M/G a smooth submersion. For every map f from M/G to a smooth manifold, f is smooth if and only if f∘q is smooth. If G is discrete, q is a smooth covering.

For n≥1, the antipodal action on Sⁿ satisfies the free proper smooth action theorem and yields the smooth real projective-space quotient. Its quotient charts agree with the projective charts, by the local-section characterization of the quotient smooth structure.
The free translation action of Zⁿ on Rⁿ is smooth and proper, and its smooth orbit manifold is the smooth n-torus.

An orientation of a manifold is a continuously varying choice, at each point p, of one of the two positive rays in the determinant line ΛⁿT_pM. This determinant-line convention applies also in dimension zero and in boundary charts.

For every smooth n-manifold M, including manifolds with boundary and n=0, the following descriptions of an orientation are equivalent: a continuous choice of positive ray in ΛⁿT_pM; smooth local determinant-line generators with positive transition factors; compatible signs for coordinate frames (related on overlaps by the sign of the transition Jacobian); and a nowhere-vanishing smooth top form modulo multiplication by an everywhere-positive smooth function. In dimension zero an orientation is a sign at each point. A connected nonempty orientable M has exactly two orientations. The empty manifold has its unique empty choice under this convention.
The orientation description follows Lee, Chapter 15, and Tu, Section 21. In the signed-coordinate convention the sign belongs to the chart convention while the resulting orientation is intrinsic.

A local diffeomorphism between oriented manifolds has a locally constant orientation sign. For composable local diffeomorphisms the signs multiply (pointwise, with the first sign evaluated at the image where necessary).

The product of oriented manifolds has the product orientation obtained by concatenating positive determinant vectors, with the first factor before the second. Equivalently use the determinant-line tensor identification for the ordered tangent direct sum. The convention includes factors of dimension zero.

Every manifold M has a canonical smooth two-sheeted orientation covering π:M̃→M. Its fiber over p consists of the two orientations o_p of T_pM, so its points are pairs (p,o_p); local frame trivializations identify the sheets with the two signs and change labels by the transition determinant sign. M̃ is orientable, canonically by pulling o_p back along dπ at (p,o_p). For connected nonempty M, M̃ has exactly two connected components if M is orientable, and is connected if M is not orientable. The canonical deck involution exchanges the two orientations in each fiber and reverses this canonical orientation of the cover.
The standard S² orientation induced by the boundary of the unit ball in R³ is reversed by the antipodal map. The real projective plane RP² is nonorientable.

For an oriented smooth n-manifold M with boundary and n≥1, ∂M has the canonical outward-first orientation: a determinant vector η of T_p∂M is positive exactly when v∧η is positive in T_pM for any outward-pointing vector v. This criterion is independent of the outward representative. In a half-space chart x_n≥0 of bulk orientation sign ε_U, the ordered first n−1 coordinate directions have boundary sign ε_U(−1)ⁿ. Thus a positively oriented interval has zero-dimensional boundary sign −1 at its left endpoint and +1 at its right endpoint.

For oriented manifolds M,N of dimensions m,n, orient their product with M first. On the codimension-one face ∂M×Int N the induced outward-first boundary orientation equals the product orientation. On Int M×∂N it equals (−1)^m times the product orientation. These assertions concern codimension-one faces; higher-codimension corner intersections are not extra boundary terms.

A smooth positive-definite metric g on an oriented n-manifold M determines a unique smooth top form vol_g taking value one on the positive unit determinant vector in each ΛⁿT_pM, using the norm induced by g. In signed coordinates with G=(g(∂_i,∂_j)), vol_g=ε_U√det(G) dx¹∧⋯∧dxⁿ. On any manifold with g, without requiring orientability, √det(G)|dx¹⋯dxⁿ| is a positive smooth density. In dimension zero the determinant is one: vol_g has the assigned point sign and the metric density has value one.
Reversing the manifold orientation negates vol_g and leaves its metric density unchanged. The pointwise density associated to a positive-definite metric is nowhere zero.

Coordinate integration concerns continuous top forms with compact support. A form supported in a chart is required to have support compact in that coordinate domain when its coefficient is extended by zero outside the coordinate image. In a half-space chart the support may meet the true boundary, but the zero extension is zero on an open neighborhood of every artificial chart edge.

For an oriented n-dimensional chart with n≥1, a compactly supported continuous top form a(x) dx¹∧⋯∧dxⁿ has integral ε_U times its ordinary Euclidean coefficient integral, where ε_U is the chart orientation sign. This local integral is the same in any two charts containing the support, including half-space charts. In dimension zero local integration is signed evaluation; for a compactly supported zero-form globally this is the finite sum of point signs times values.

On every oriented manifold M with or without boundary there is a unique linear integral on compactly supported continuous top forms compatible with local signed coordinate integration and finite localization. It is independent of the subordinate coordinate partition used in its construction. Reversing orientation negates the integral. For a diffeomorphism F:M→N and a compactly supported continuous top form η on N, ∫_M F*η=∫_Nη when F preserves orientation, and ∫_M F*η=−∫_Nη when F reverses orientation; if its orientation sign varies between components, use the corresponding sign on each component.

entries.coverage_note: The declarations prove the support inclusion and the positive preservation cases. The negative caveat is context.
entries.title: General smooth pullback and restriction to a general open submanifold do not universally preserve compact support. Restriction of a compactly supported form to a closed embedded submanifold S⊂M does preserve compact support, since the restricted support is contained in S intersected with the original compact support. In particular restriction to the boundary preserves compact support.
The integration construction is referenced to Lee, Chapter 16, and Tu, §§23.1–23.4. The cited Tu errata require retaining the determinant sign in signed-coordinate change of variables.

For every n≥1 and every compactly supported C¹ (n−1)-form ω on Rⁿ, ∫_{Rⁿ}dω=0. For every such form on Hⁿ={x_n≥0}, with the standard bulk orientation and induced outward-first boundary orientation, ∫_{Hⁿ}dω=∫_{x_n=0}j*ω. This includes n=1, where the boundary integral is signed endpoint evaluation.

Let M be an oriented smooth n-manifold with boundary, n≥1, and equip ∂M with the outward-first orientation. For every C¹ (n−1)-form ω compactly supported in M, ∫_M dω=∫_{∂M}j*ω, where j:∂M→M is the inclusion. If M is compact the support condition is automatic. If ∂M is empty, the right side is zero.

For a compact smooth planar domain D oriented by dx∧dy, applying Stokes to a C¹ one-form P dx+Q dy gives ∫_{∂D}(P dx+Q dy)=∫_D(∂_x Q−∂_y P) dx∧dy. The outward-first induced orientation is counterclockwise on the outer boundary and opposite on inner boundary components.

In an oriented Euclidean domain of positive dimension n, the (n−1)-form ω=ι_X(dx₁∧⋯∧dx_n) associated to a C¹ vector field X satisfies dω=(div X) dx₁∧⋯∧dx_n. Its restriction to the boundary is the outward flux form, using the outward-first convention. Under the compact-support or compact-domain conditions of Stokes this yields the divergence/flux integral identity.

On an oriented surface in R³, the pullback of the exterior derivative of the Euclidean one-form associated to a C¹ vector field is its curl normal component times oriented area. With the outward-first boundary convention and the support conditions of Stokes, this identifies the surface Stokes formula with the circulation/curl formula.

Continuous compactly supported densities on any manifold have a linear integral, independent of any orientation and invariant under diffeomorphisms. For an equal-dimensional smooth map F, pullback of a continuous density is continuous, including at rank drops. If the density is smooth and F is a local diffeomorphism, its pullback is smooth. Locally pullback changes the coefficient b to b(F(x))|det DF(x)|. In dimension zero integration is the finite unsigned sum of the coefficients at support points.

A density on an n-manifold is a section of its real density line: frame evaluations transform by the absolute determinant (μ(Av)=|det A|μ(v) for a change of basis), rather than the signed determinant. Evaluation on linearly dependent n-tuples is zero. In local coordinates a density is written b(x)|dx₁⋯dx_n|.

A smooth Riemannian metric gives the positive density √det(g_ij)|dx₁⋯dx_n|. Intrinsically this evaluates a frame as the volume of its parallelepiped, which has the required absolute-determinant frame transformation law. This repeats the metric-density construction of Chapter 9.

The smooth map x↦x² pulls the smooth density |dy| back to 2|x||dx|, which is not smooth at zero. Thus smoothness of density pullback cannot be asserted for arbitrary smooth maps. Likewise the pointwise absolute value density of a smooth top form need not be smooth at a zero of the form.

The corner models are relatively open subsets of R_+^k×R^{n−k}, with coordinate transitions and inverse transitions smoothly extendible to ambient Euclidean open sets. At a point p, I(p) denotes the subset of the k constrained coordinates that vanish there (the active faces).

At a point p of an orthant model, the velocity cone of curves defined for t≥0 is exactly {v:v_j≥0 for j∈I(p)}. The derivative of every corner coordinate transition sends this cone isomorphically to the corresponding cone in the new coordinates. Its maximal linear subspace has codimension |I(p)|, so the number of active faces is invariant. A transition derivative permutes the facets (codimension-one cone faces); each facet germ corresponds locally to a boundary hypersurface through p.
At a corner of a square where two active faces meet, there are two distinct local face germs, even though they lie over the same base point.

Let M be an oriented smooth n-manifold with corners, n>0, using the stated smoothly extendible orthant coordinate convention. For every compactly supported C¹ (n−1)-form ω, Stokes holds: ∫_M dω equals the sum of the integrals of the restrictions of ω over codimension-one local faces, each counted once and given its outward-first orientation. The boundary integral is understood with multiplicity of local face germs, including distinct germs at a multiple corner; their higher-codimension intersections add no extra boundary terms. The result includes oriented simplices, boxes and products such as an interval times a manifold with boundary.

For an interval times a manifold with boundary, the corner charts are products of the corresponding half-space charts. The standard simplex has corner charts because its active affine face functions are independent on their common intersection and can be completed to affine coordinates.

The pair-of-face-germs description specifies the boundary integral in the corner theorem, without requiring a more general category of corner maps. References are Lee, Chapter 16 (with errata at pages 418–419), and Joyce for other corner conventions.

For a smooth closed one-form α on a manifold, line integrals along piecewise smooth paths are invariant under continuous homotopies with fixed endpoints: two such paths joined by such a homotopy have equal α integrals. This applies to manifolds with boundary as well as boundaryless manifolds. On a simply connected manifold, every smooth closed one-form is exact, with a smooth global primitive.

Let M be a smooth embedded Euclidean submanifold, possibly with boundary, with the abstract smooth structure induced by its embedded charts. For an orientation and differential form in the common domain of the abstract and D04 constructions, the induced boundary orientations, restrictions and intrinsic exterior derivatives agree under the canonical tangent identification. Their compactly supported top-form integrals and density integrals also have equal values. Consequently abstract Stokes specializes to the intrinsic D04 Stokes formula on this common domain. The statement includes signed zero-dimensional boundary integration and zero-dimensional point sums; for a D04 scalar density coefficient ρ, the corresponding abstract density is ρ times the induced Euclidean metric density.

The comparison uses the embedded chart/tangent and intrinsic derivative/integration interfaces of D04 Chapters 14–15. The separately stated intrinsic D04 Stokes interface admits C² embedded charts with an intrinsic C¹ form, while its ambient C¹ formulation restricts the ambient exterior derivative. The manuscript comparison concerns their shared smooth embedded setting and does not assert that an intrinsic derivative can be obtained from merely C¹ charts.

For every smooth manifold M, let Ω^k(M) be smooth real k-forms, with Ω^k(M)=0 for k<0. A closed k-form is in ker(d:Ω^k→Ω^{k+1}), an exact k-form is in im(d:Ω^{k−1}→Ω^k), and H_dR^k(M)=ker d/im d. The relation d²=0 makes this quotient defined.

Wedge product descends to a well-defined real graded-commutative algebra structure on H_dR^*(M). Every smooth map f:M→N induces a pullback homomorphism of graded algebras f^*:H_dR^*(N)→H_dR^*(M), with identity and contravariant composition laws.

For any smooth manifold M, df=0 precisely when f is locally constant; H_dR^0(M) is the vector space of independently chosen real constants on the connected components of M. In particular H_dR^0(M)≅R if M is nonempty and connected and H_dR^0(∅)=0. For dim M=n, H_dR^k(M)=0 for k>n (and for k<0 by the complex convention).

If smooth maps f_0,f_1:M→N are continuously homotopic, then f_0^*=f_1^*:H_dR^k(N)→H_dR^k(M) for every degree k. Source and target are smooth manifolds under the global conventions and may have boundary; the homotopy is only required to be continuous.

For every star-shaped open set U⊆R^n and every positive degree k, every closed smooth k-form on U has a smooth (k−1)-form primitive. More generally, every nonempty contractible smooth manifold, including the allowed boundary case, has H_dR^k(M)=0 for every k>0; no exactness claim is made for nonzero constants in degree zero.

The preceding ordinary open-cover sequence induces the natural long exact sequence …→H_dR^k(M)→H_dR^k(U)⊕H_dR^k(V)→H_dR^k(U∩V)→δ H_dR^{k+1}(M)→…, with q the second-minus-first restriction and δ raising degree by one. Naturality is for smooth maps respecting the two cover members.

For an open cover M=U∪V of a smooth manifold, there is a short exact sequence of real de Rham cochain complexes 0→Ω^•(M)→Ω^•(U)⊕Ω^•(V)→Ω^•(U∩V)→0. The first nonzero map is r(ω)=(ω|_U,ω|_V); the second is q(a,b)=b|_{U∩V}−a|_{U∩V}. All maps commute with exterior differentiation.

For each integer n≥1, the only nonzero real de Rham groups of S^n are H_dR^0(S^n)≅R and H_dR^n(S^n)≅R; every other degree is zero. The initial zero-sphere case has H_dR^0(S^0)≅R², consistent with the general component calculation (explicitly recalled at lines 2339–2340).

For every nonnegative integer r, the real graded de Rham algebra of the smooth torus (S^1)^r is the exterior algebra on the r degree-one classes of its coordinate circle one-forms. In the model S^1=R/Z, the circle one-form descends from dt (lines 2342–2343); in particular all ordered wedge products give the exterior-algebra relations and span the graded groups. The r=0 torus is a point.

The oriented genus-two smooth surface obtained as the connected sum of two tori has real de Rham cohomology dimensions 1,4,1 in degrees 0,1,2 respectively, with all other degrees zero. The specified surface is formed by deleting a disk from each torus and gluing boundary circles by an angular reflection; signed radial collars provide its smooth seam charts and compatible orientation (construction detailed at lines 2386–2396).

For each smooth manifold M, Ω_c^k(M) is the real vector space of compactly supported smooth k-forms, with zero spaces in negative degree. Exterior differentiation preserves these spaces, so they form a subcomplex of Ω^•(M); its cohomology is H_c^k(M)=ker(d:Ω_c^k→Ω_c^{k+1})/im(d:Ω_c^{k−1}→Ω_c^k).

For any open cover M=U∪V, extension by zero gives a short exact sequence of cochain complexes 0→Ω_c^•(U∩V)→Ω_c^•(U)⊕Ω_c^•(V)→Ω_c^•(M)→0, with arrows γ↦(ext_0 γ,−ext_0 γ) and (a,b)↦ext_0 a+ext_0 b. It induces the long exact sequence …→H_c^k(U∩V)→H_c^k(U)⊕H_c^k(V)→H_c^k(M)→H_c^{k+1}(U∩V)→…. Both displayed nontrivial arrows use extension by zero.

Every smooth proper map f:M→N pulls compactly supported smooth forms on N back to compactly supported smooth forms on M and induces pullback f^*:H_c^k(N)→H_c^k(M). This uses properness, not an unrestricted compact-support assertion for arbitrary smooth maps.

For every integer n≥0, H_c^k(R^n)=0 for k≠n, and integration in the standard orientation induces a real-linear isomorphism H_c^n(R^n)≅R. Equivalently, a compactly supported smooth top-degree form on R^n has a compactly supported primitive exactly when its total integral is zero. At n=0 exactness is interpreted using Ω_c^{−1}=0, so the condition is that the zero-form is zero.

The ordinary positive-degree homotopy operator obtained from radial contraction does not in general preserve compact support of forms. Thus ordinary radial Poincaré homotopy alone does not establish the compact-support Poincaré result; the support-corrected conclusion above is a distinct assertion.
For every nonempty connected noncompact smooth n-manifold without boundary, H_dR^n(M)=0, whether or not M is orientable.

For every nonempty connected nonorientable smooth n-manifold without boundary, H_c^n(M)=0. In the compact case the ordinary and compact-support complexes coincide, so H_dR^n(M)=0 there as well; combined with the noncompact assertion this gives ordinary top-degree vanishing in either case.

Let M be a nonempty connected smooth n-manifold without boundary, n≥0. If M is oriented, integration descends to an isomorphism of real vector spaces H_c^n(M)→R. Consequently, if M is also compact and oriented, H_dR^n(M)≅R. The zero-dimensional case is a single oriented point with signed evaluation.

A closed manifold means compact and without boundary. For a nonempty closed connected oriented n-manifold, the top-degree de Rham class of integral one is the distinguished generator; a smooth map between two such n-manifolds acts by a real scalar on the integral generators. The degree theorem constructs this scalar as an integer.

For every smooth map F:M→N between nonempty closed connected oriented n-manifolds of the same dimension, n≥0, there is an integer deg(F) such that ∫_M F^*η=deg(F)∫_N η for every smooth n-form η on N. The orientations on both manifolds are part of the data.

Under the hypotheses of the degree theorem, for every regular value y∈N the fiber F^{-1}(y) is finite and deg(F)=Σ_{x∈F^{-1}(y)} sign(dF_x). The sign uses the tangent isomorphism relative to the specified source and target orientations. The empty fiber contributes zero. In dimension zero connected manifolds are oriented points, and the same orientation-sign formula applies.

For a smooth map between the nonempty closed connected oriented equal-dimensional manifolds above, the signed regular-fiber count is independent of the regular value even when the fiber cardinality varies. If deg(F)≠0, then F is surjective; a point omitted from the image is a regular value with empty fiber and hence degree zero.

Let N be a nonempty closed connected oriented n-manifold and W a compact oriented smooth (n+1)-manifold with boundary. For every smooth G:W→N, the sum Σ_C deg(G|_C) over the connected components C of ∂W, oriented by the induced outward-first boundary orientation, is zero. The sum is finite, and an empty boundary has sum zero. No connectedness of W or its boundary is assumed.

For smooth maps between nonempty closed connected oriented n-manifolds, degree is invariant under continuous homotopies with smooth endpoints, deg(id_M)=1, and deg(G∘F)=deg(G)deg(F) whenever F:M→N and G:N→P satisfy these hypotheses.

For every integer n≥0, the identity map on S^n does not extend to a continuous map from the closed (n+1)-ball to S^n; in particular it has no smooth extension. For n≥1 the smooth obstruction uses the induced boundary sphere orientation and degree, and continuous extension is also excluded; n=0 is excluded by connectedness of the interval. Equivalently there is no continuous retraction of the closed ball to its boundary sphere.

The text identifies sphere nonextension as the usual no-retraction input to Brouwer and refers to equivalent fixed-point statements in D10. It does not separately state a new Brouwer fixed-point theorem in this manuscript; the explicit nonextension example is inventoried above.

For each q≥0, Δ^q={(t_1,…,t_q)∈R^q:t_i≥0 and Σ_i t_i≤1}, with vertices v_0=0,v_i=e_i and the standard dt_1∧…∧dt_q orientation (point convention at q=0). It carries its smooth corner structure, including higher face intersections. A smooth singular q-simplex σ:Δ^q→M is smooth up to all faces, by local Euclidean extensions in manifold charts. C_q^sm(M;R) is the real vector space freely generated by these maps.

For q≥1 define the smooth singular boundary on a generator σ by ∂σ=Σ_{j=0}^q (−1)^j σ∘ε_j, where ε_j:Δ^{q−1}→Δ^q is the affine face map omitting vertex j and preserving the order of the other vertices. In degree zero ∂=0. These maps satisfy ∂²=0. The real cochain complex is C_sm^q(M;R)=Hom_R(C_q^sm(M;R),R) with (δc)(σ)=c(∂σ), δ²=0; its cohomology is H_sm^q(M;R). Smooth maps act on chains by postcomposition and hence on cochains by pullback.

For every smooth manifold M and q≥0, I_M(ω)(σ)=∫_{Δ^q} σ^*ω for ω∈Ω^q(M) and smooth singular q-simplex σ defines a real-linear cochain map Ω^•(M)→C_sm^•(M;R): I_M(dω)=δ I_M(ω). For every smooth F:M→N, I_M(F^*ω)(σ)=I_N(ω)(F∘σ). Thus it induces a natural real-linear map I_M^*:H_dR^q(M)→H_sm^q(M;R). The q=0 integral uses the oriented point convention.

The continuous singular chain complex C_•(M;R) is defined using all continuous maps Δ^q→M as generators, with the same alternating affine-face boundary, and dual real cochains define H_sing^q(M;R). Restricting continuous-singular cochains to the smooth simplex generators is a cochain map r:C_sing^•(M;R)→C_sm^•(M;R).

The full de Rham comparison theorem is stated at the comparison interface with proof assigned to the algebraic-topology comparison unit; the proven integration cochain map alone does not prove this isomorphism.

The source-map groups and reuse/interface suggestions are advisory; they do not prescribe a goal count or add mathematical assertions. Required statements retain their source hypotheses, conclusions, measurability, regularity and degenerate cases; Polish and standard Borel spaces, original and completed sigma-algebras, pairwise and mutual independence, and arbitrary and countable index sets must remain distinct.

Advisory bibliography, source locations, provenance, scope routing and result-group metadata for 54 groups. This registry is not a substitute for the statements of paper.tex, is not a separate mathematical source of deliverables, and its numbered-result list does not enumerate all definitions, examples or unnumbered assertions.
TeX setup, title, contents and introductory description of the nine-chapter project; no separate mathematical deliverables.

The listed measure theory, analysis, topology and finite-dimensional spectral results are prerequisites available for reuse, not additional standalone deliverables imposed by this paragraph. Statements separately made in the mathematical chapters remain in scope, including integral convergence and determining classes.

Throughout the manuscript a probability space need not be complete; all random elements use the specified sigma-algebra (metric spaces use Borel sets unless otherwise specified). Family independence means independence of every finite subfamily, and weak convergence of probability laws means convergence of integrals against all bounded continuous real functions. Euclidean statements use d≥1, with d=0 the one-point case, and characteristic functions use φ_μ(t)=∫exp(i⟨t,x⟩) μ(dx). Brownian path properties beyond the stated Wiener-law construction, functional limit theorems, general stable laws, stochastic integration and large-deviation theory are outside scope.
Bibliographic orientation and the advisory source map; the map is not an independent goal list.

Throughout, a probability space is part of the data; a specified measurable space retains its specified sigma-algebra, while a metric space carries its Borel sigma-algebra unless otherwise specified. The usual Lebesgue integral and Tonelli theorem for sigma-finite factors are background; citations and the chapter roadmap impose no additional separate mathematical results.

A probability space is (Ω,F,P), with F a sigma-algebra on Ω and P a nonnegative countably additive measure satisfying P(Ω)=1; an event is an element of F. A random element of (S,Sigma) is an F/Sigma-measurable map; a real random variable has target (R,Borel R). For integrable real or complex X, EX=∫X dP; nonnegative measurable variables may have expectation +∞. For every event A, E[1_A]=P(A). A property holds almost surely when it holds on a measurable event of probability one.

For any countable event family (A_n), P(⋃_n A_n)≤∑_n P(A_n). If A_n increases to A, then P(A_n) increases to P(A). If A_n decreases to A, then P(A_n) decreases to P(A). For a general measure the decreasing conclusion holds whenever some member of the decreasing measurable sequence has finite measure. For a general measure, continuity from below for increasing measurable sequences holds without any finiteness condition.

On N with counting measure, the measurable tails A_n={n,n+1,…} form a decreasing sequence with empty intersection, while every A_n has infinite measure. Thus the finite-measure hypothesis in continuity from above cannot be omitted.

For measurable X:Ω→(S,Sigma), its law is the pushforward probability X_#P given by (X_#P)(B)=P(X^{-1}(B)) for B∈Sigma. For random elements X_i:Ω→S_i indexed by any set I, their joint law is the law of ω↦(X_i(ω))_i into the product equipped with its product sigma-algebra. The law of any coordinate subfamily is the corresponding marginal.

For any index set I and random elements X_i, the joint map into the product sigma-algebra is measurable, and its marginal on every coordinate subfamily is the pushforward of the joint law under the coordinate restriction. For measurable X:Ω→S and g:S→T, (g∘X)_#P=g_#(X_#P). For nonnegative extended measurable f:S→[0,+∞], ∫_S f d(X_#P)=∫_Ω f∘X dP. For real or complex measurable f, integrability under X_#P is equivalent to integrability of f∘X under P, and in the integrable case the same integral equality holds.

Let C be a collection of subsets of S closed under intersections of nonempty finite subfamilies. Two finite measures of equal total mass on σ(C) that agree on C agree on all of σ(C). Consequently their integrals agree for every nonnegative measurable function and every integrable function.

For every Borel probability μ on R, F(x)=μ((-∞,x]) is nondecreasing and right-continuous, with limits 0 at −∞ and 1 at +∞. Conversely every real function with these properties is the distribution function of a unique Borel probability law on R. For real a≤b this law satisfies μ((a,b])=F(b)−F(a), and for every real a it satisfies μ({a})=F(a)−F(a−), where F(a−)=lim_{t↑a}F(t). In every finite dimension d, the masses of all lower orthants ∏_{j=1}^d(-∞,x_j] determine a Borel probability law on R^d uniquely.

For a nonnegative measurable Y (including extended value +∞), p>0, and a>0, E[Y^p]=p∫_0^∞ t^(p−1)P(Y>t)dt; E[Y^p 1_{Y≤a}]=p∫_0^a t^(p−1)P(Y>t)dt−a^p P(Y>a); and E[Y^p 1_{Y>a}]=a^p P(Y>a)+p∫_a^∞ t^(p−1)P(Y>t)dt. Each integral on the right is unchanged on replacing > by ≥ in its tail-probability integrand. Changing the endpoint convention on a truncated expectation changes its value by the boundary term a^p P(Y=a): specifically, E[Y^p1_{Y≤a}]=E[Y^p1_{Y<a}]+a^pP(Y=a) and E[Y^p1_{Y≥a}]=E[Y^p1_{Y>a}]+a^pP(Y=a).

For a>0 and nonnegative measurable Y, P(Y≥a)≤E[Y]/a, allowing infinite expectation. In particular, for p>0 and a random variable X, P(|X|≥a)≤a^(−p)E|X|^p. For real X with finite second moment, Var(X)=E[(X−EX)^2] and P(|X−EX|≥a)≤Var(X)/a^2. For real X, real x and θ>0, P(X≥x)≤exp(−θx)E exp(θX), allowing an infinite exponential moment. Each inequality also holds with the strict corresponding upper-tail event.

On a finite measure space (S,Sigma,μ), write ||f||_1=∫|f|dμ. A family H⊆L¹(μ) is uniformly integrable exactly when lim_{R→∞}sup_{f∈H}∫_{|f|>R}|f|dμ=0.
