A sequence f_n converges in measure to f exactly when μ({|f_n−f|>ε})→0 for every ε>0. On a probability space this is called convergence in probability.

On a finite measure space and for a family H⊆L¹(μ), the following are equivalent: (1) H is uniformly integrable; (2) sup_{f∈H}||f||_1<∞ and for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that every measurable A with μ(A)<δ satisfies sup_{f∈H}∫_A|f|dμ<ε; (3) there exists an increasing convex Φ:[0,∞)→[0,∞) with Φ(0)=0 and Φ(t)/t→∞ as t→∞ such that sup_{f∈H}∫Φ(|f|)dμ<∞. The family may be real or complex, as in the surrounding L¹ discussion.

On a finite measure space, let f_n∈L¹(μ) and let f be a finite-valued real or complex measurable function, not initially assumed integrable. Then f_n→f in L¹ if and only if f_n→f in measure and {f_n:n≥1} is uniformly integrable; the latter two conditions also imply f∈L¹(μ).
The citation introduces the collected convergence and completion facts; it adds no separate mathematical assertion beyond the following propositions.

On an arbitrary measure space, for nonnegative measurable f_n and f, increasing almost-everywhere convergence f_n↑f implies ∫f_n↑∫f. For arbitrary nonnegative measurable f_n, ∫liminf_n f_n≤liminf_n∫f_n. If measurable real or complex f_n converge almost everywhere to a measurable f and |f_n|≤g almost everywhere for a single measurable integrable g≥0, then f is integrable and ∫|f_n−f|→0. In particular the conclusion holds when the variables have one common finite bound on a measurable set of finite measure and vanish almost everywhere outside that set.

Let Fbar be the P-completion of the original sigma-algebra F. Every Fbar-measurable real or extended-real variable has an F-measurable version equal to it outside an F-measurable P-null set. The same is true for Fbar-measurable random elements in every nonempty separable metric space (with its Borel sigma-algebra). Passing between these versions and between P and its completion leaves the law and all nonnegative or integrable expectations unchanged.
The chapter distinguishes mutual independence of every finite subfamily from pairwise independence; the cited sources and introductory prose add no separate result.

For a probability space (Ω,F,P), a family (F_i)_{i∈I} of sub-sigma-algebras of F is mutually independent when for every finite list of distinct indices i_1,…,i_m and A_j∈F_{i_j}, P(⋂_{j=1}^m A_j)=∏_{j=1}^m P(A_j). Random elements X_i are mutually independent when (σ(X_i)) is mutually independent; an event family is mutually independent when the sigma-algebras generated by the individual events are mutually independent. Pairwise independence imposes this condition only on two distinct indices.

For any index set I, if each C_i is a pi-system generating the sub-sigma-algebra F_i, then (F_i) is mutually independent if and only if the finite-distinct-indices independence equality holds whenever each event is chosen from its corresponding C_i. For a finite family of random elements this is equivalent to equality of the joint law with the product of all marginal probability laws. For an arbitrary family, mutual independence is equivalent to this product-law identity for every finite joint law.

Let U and V be independent uniform random signs in {−1,1}, and set W=UV. Each of the three pairs (U,V), (U,W), (V,W) is uniform on {−1,1}², so U,V,W are pairwise independent. But UVW=1 almost surely; three mutually independent uniform signs have a uniform random-sign product. In particular E[UVW]=1 while EU·EV·EW=0, so pairwise independence does not imply the three-factor expectation identity or mutual independence.

Any finite family of specified probability laws on arbitrary measurable spaces is realized by the mutually independent coordinate maps on the product probability space, with each coordinate having its specified law. Measurable coordinatewise transformations of any mutually independent family of random elements preserve mutual independence. If (F_i)_{i∈I} is mutually independent and (J_α)_α is a family of pairwise disjoint subsets of I (with no countability restriction), then G_α=σ(⋃_{i∈J_α}F_i) form a mutually independent family of sigma-algebras.

For a finite mutually independent family X_1,…,X_m with laws μ_i, every nonnegative measurable f on the product satisfies E f(X_1,…,X_m)=∫f d(μ_1⊗⋯⊗μ_m); the same identity holds for integrable real or complex f. These product integrals admit iterated evaluation by Tonelli in the nonnegative case and Fubini in the integrable case. In particular, for nonnegative extended measurable factors f_i:S_i→[0,+∞], E∏_i f_i(X_i)=∏_i∫f_i dμ_i, with any product having a zero factor interpreted as zero even when another factor is +∞. For real or complex measurable f_i with ∫|f_i|dμ_i<∞, their product is integrable and the same factorization holds.
For a sequence of events A_n, define A_∞=⋂_{m≥1}⋃_{n≥m}A_n, the event that infinitely many A_n occur.

For events A_n, if ∑_n P(A_n)<∞ then P(A_∞)=0. If the events are pairwise independent and ∑_nP(A_n)=∞, then P(A_∞)=1. More precisely, in the latter case define N_n=∑_{k≤n}1_{A_k} and a_n=∑_{k≤n}P(A_k); eventually a_n>0 and N_n/a_n→1 almost surely.

For real random variables X_n,X on a common probability space, almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability, and L^p convergence implies convergence in probability for every 0<p<∞. Convergence in probability to X is equivalent to every subsequence admitting a further subsequence converging almost surely to X. If one sequence converges in probability to both X and Y, then X=Y almost surely. Convergence in probability together with uniform integrability of {X_n} implies X∈L¹ and X_n→X in L¹.

For real random variables X_n,X on one probability space and 0<p<∞, convergence in L^p means X_n,X∈L^p and E|X_n−X|^p→0. Almost sure convergence and convergence in probability have their previously specified meanings.

On [0,1) with Lebesgue probability, enumerate all dyadic half-open intervals [j2^(−m),(j+1)2^(−m)) level by level, 0≤j<2^m. Their indicators converge to zero in every L^p, p>0, because each level-m indicator has p-th moment 2^(−m), but the indicator sequence fails to converge at every point: each point is contained in exactly one interval of each level and omitted by the others. Conversely, for each fixed p>0, on (0,1) with Lebesgue probability the random variables n^(1/p)1_(0,1/n) converge pointwise to zero and satisfy E|X_n|^p=1 for every n. Thus almost sure/probability convergence need not imply L^p convergence, and L^p convergence need not imply almost sure convergence.
For a mutually independent sequence (F_n)_{n≥1} of sigma-algebras, define its tail sigma-algebra T=⋂_{m≥1}σ(⋃_{n>m}F_n). Every A∈T satisfies P(A)=0 or P(A)=1.

Let μ be the law of an i.i.d. sequence of random elements in an arbitrary measurable space S, regarded as a probability law on S^N with its product sigma-algebra. If a product-measurable event A is invariant modulo μ-null sets under every finite permutation of coordinates (μ(A△π^{-1}A)=0 for every such π), then μ(A)∈{0,1}.

Throughout chapter 3, G⊆F is an arbitrary sub-sigma-algebra of the probability space (Ω,F,P); neither G nor F is assumed complete. Versions are characterized by test-integral identities on original measurable events. Finite-positive-measure Radon–Nikodym is background, and the citations add no further separate results.

For an integrable real X, a version U of E[X|G] is a G-measurable integrable real random variable such that ∫_A U dP=∫_A X dP for every A∈G. For a nonnegative measurable X (allowed +∞), a version U is G-measurable with values in [0,+∞] and satisfies the same test identities, whose integrals may be infinite. For B∈F, its conditional probability given G is E[1_B|G].

For every integrable real X and every nonnegative extended measurable X, a conditional-expectation version as defined exists and is unique almost surely, with no completion assumption on F or G. For nonnegative integrable X, the integrable-real and nonnegative-extended definitions give the same almost-everywhere equivalence class.

For real integrable inputs and arbitrary sub-sigma-algebra G⊆F, conditional expectation is real-linear, preserves almost-sure order and positivity, and fixes G-measurable integrable variables almost surely. For any H⊆G, E[E[X|G]|H]=E[X|H] almost surely, E E[X|G]=EX, and the reversed-order identity E[E[X|H]|G]=E[X|H] holds almost surely. Monotonicity, nonnegative addition, the fixed-point property and both orders of the tower identity also hold for nonnegative extended inputs, with the extended nonnegative integral conventions.

For nonnegative G-measurable H and nonnegative F-measurable X, E[HX|G]=H E[X|G] almost surely, allowing extended values and using 0·∞=0. If H is real and G-measurable, X is real integrable, and HX is integrable, then H E[X|G] is integrable and the same formula holds for integrable conditional expectations. In particular the corresponding formulas apply to bounded factors under their respective hypotheses.

For real integrable X and a finite convex function φ:R→R, the negative part φ(X)^− is integrable. Define E[φ(X)|G] as E[φ(X)^+|G]−E[φ(X)^−|G], allowing +∞ (the second term is finite almost surely). Then φ(E[X|G])≤E[φ(X)|G] almost surely. If φ(X) is integrable, this extended definition agrees with its usual integrable conditional-expectation version.

For real X∈L¹, |E[X|G]|≤E[|X||G] almost surely. For every 1≤p≤∞ and every real X∈L^p, E[X|G]∈L^p and ||E[X|G]||_p≤||X||_p. Consequently, for real integrable X,Y that both lie in L^p, ||E[X|G]−E[Y|G]||_p≤||X−Y||_p, including p=∞.

All variables are measurable for the original F. If 0≤X_n↑X almost surely, then versions of E[X_n|G] increase almost surely to a version of E[X|G], allowing +∞. If real X_n→X almost surely and |X_n|≤Y almost surely for one integrable Y≥0, with X F-measurable, then X is integrable and E[X_n|G]→E[X|G] almost surely and in L¹. These statements require no completion of F or G.
For a real X∈L², set M=E[X|G] and define the conditional variance V=E[(X−M)²|G]. Then V=E[X²|G]−M² almost surely, and Var(X)=EV+Var(M).
For each fixed real X∈L¹(P), the family of all conditional expectations {E[X|G]: G⊆F any sub-sigma-algebra} is uniformly integrable, including arbitrary incomplete sub-sigma-algebras.

A measurable space is standard Borel iff it is measurably isomorphic to a Borel subset of some complete separable metric space. A measurable isomorphism is a bijection measurable in both directions; B(T) denotes the specified sigma-algebra of a standard Borel space T.
Every standard Borel space, including the empty space, is measurably isomorphic to a Borel subset of R.
The sigma-algebra of every standard Borel space admits a countable generating pi-system containing the entire space.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, equipped with the product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

For a map X from a set Omega into any measurable space (S,Sigma) and a map Y into a nonempty standard Borel space T, if Y is sigma(X)-measurable, there exists a measurable g:S->T with Y=g composed with X everywhere.

If Omega carries a probability and Y takes values in a nonempty standard Borel T and is measurable for the probability completion of sigma(X), where X:Omega->S and S is any measurable space, there is a measurable g:S->T with Y=g(X) almost surely.

For measurable spaces S,T, a probability kernel K:S rightsquigarrow T assigns a probability measure K(s,.) on T to every s, with s->K(s,B) measurable for every measurable B in T. The identity kernel at S is I_S(s,.)=Dirac_s.
For any probability kernel K:S rightsquigarrow T and product-measurable C subset S x T, each section C_s={y:(s,y) in C} is measurable and s->K(s,C_s) is measurable.

Given a probability mu on S and probability kernel K:S rightsquigarrow T, (mu tensor K)(C)=integral K(s,C_s) mu(ds), on product-measurable C subset S x T, defines a probability measure on S x T with first marginal mu.

For a probability mu on S, probability kernel K:S rightsquigarrow T and nonnegative product-measurable f:S x T->[0,infinity], the inner integral s->integral f(s,y) K(s,dy) is measurable and integral f d(mu tensor K)=integral [integral f(s,y) K(s,dy)] mu(ds). For integrable real product-measurable f, the absolute fiber integral is finite for mu-almost every s, and the same formula holds with any measurable choice of the signed inner integral on the exceptional set.

For probability kernels K:S rightsquigarrow T and L:T rightsquigarrow U, (KL)(s,C)=integral L(y,C) K(s,dy) defines a probability kernel. For every nonnegative measurable h:U->[0,infinity], integral h(z)(KL)(s,dz)=integral [integral h(z)L(y,dz)] K(s,dy). For each fixed s the formula also holds if h is integrable against (KL)(s,.), with the inner signed integral wherever it exists. Composition is associative and the kernels I_S are two-sided identities.
For probability kernels K:S rightsquigarrow T and L:S rightsquigarrow U, the map s->K(s,.) tensor L(s,.) is a probability kernel from S into T x U with its product sigma-algebra.
Bibliographic attribution for kernel integration, composition and parameter measurability; no additional mathematical assertion.

Let S be any measurable space, T a nonempty standard Borel space and M a probability on the product measurable space S x T with first marginal mu. There exists a probability kernel K:S rightsquigarrow T such that M=mu tensor K.
Attribution and explanation of the rational-cut disintegration proof and its exceptional-set normalization; proof-route commentary rather than an additional deliverable.

If Y is a measurable random element in a nonempty standard Borel T on (Omega,F,P), then for every sub-sigma-algebra G subset F there is a probability kernel K:(Omega,G) rightsquigarrow T satisfying integral_A K(omega,B) P(domega)=P(A intersect {Y in B}) for all A in G and B in B(T).

For measurable X:Omega->S into any measurable S and measurable Y:Omega->T into nonempty standard Borel T on a probability space, there is a probability kernel K_X:S rightsquigarrow T such that Law(X,Y)=Law(X) tensor K_X.

Let T be nonempty standard Borel and let (Ω,F,P) be a probability space. Existence of a conditional probability kernel for a T-valued Y given any sub-sigma-algebra G⊆F, and disintegration of Law(X,Y) over Law(X) for X valued in an arbitrary measurable S, remain valid for inputs admitting F-measurable versions equal almost everywhere. In this case laws and event probabilities may be taken on the completion of F; replacing inputs by their versions preserves the joint laws and conditional-law identities.

For S any measurable space, nonempty standard Borel T, and probability M on S x T with first marginal mu, any two probability-kernel disintegrations K,L of M agree as probability measures K(s,.)=L(s,.) for every s outside one measurable mu-null set.

Let S be any measurable space, T nonempty standard Borel, μ a probability on S and K:S↝T a probability kernel. If measurable (X,Y) has joint law μ⊗K, then for every nonnegative product-measurable f:S×T→[0,∞], the map ω↦∫f(X(ω),y)K(X(ω),dy) is a version of E[f(X,Y)|σ(X)]. If f is real and integrable under μ⊗K, the same holds, with arbitrary measurable values on the exceptional set where the absolute fiber integral is infinite.

For a regular conditional law K:(Omega,G) rightsquigarrow T of Y given G and any nonnegative G tensor B(T)-measurable f(omega,y), omega->integral f(omega,y)K(omega,dy) is a version of E[f(omega,Y)|G]. The corresponding statement holds for integrable real f, with arbitrary measurable values where the absolute fiber integral is infinite.

Random elements Y,Z are conditionally independent given G iff for every pair of measurable target sets B,C, E[1_{Y in B,Z in C}|G]=E[1_{Y in B}|G] E[1_{Z in C}|G] almost surely. Each identity is equality of conditional-expectation versions, with its own allowable null set.
If Y,Z are conditionally independent given G in the indicator sense, then for all bounded measurable real functions u,v, E[u(Y)v(Z)|G]=E[u(Y)|G]E[v(Z)|G] almost surely.

For random elements Y,Z with standard Borel values, conditional independence given G is equivalent to their regular conditional joint law given G equaling the product of their regular conditional marginal laws outside one G-measurable null set.

Let M be a probability on S x T and N a probability on S x U with the same S-marginal mu, where S is any measurable space and T,U are standard Borel. There exists a probability on S x T x U projecting to M on S x T and N on S x U, whose last two coordinates are conditionally independent given the first. It is unique among joint laws with those projections and that conditional independence.
Bibliographic attribution for conditional integration and gluing; no additional mathematical assertion.

For a probability kernel K:S rightsquigarrow T with T nonempty standard Borel, there is a jointly measurable g:S x [0,1]->T such that for every s the map u->g(s,u) pushes Lebesgue probability on [0,1] to K(s,.).

Let K:S↝T be a probability kernel with nonempty standard Borel T, and let jointly measurable g:S×[0,1]→T push Lebesgue probability to K(s,·) in every fiber s. If X has law μ on S and V is an independent uniform [0,1] variable, then (X,g(X,V)) has law μ⊗K.

Given a joint probability M on S x T with T nonempty standard Borel, on every probability space carrying X with the first marginal of M and an independent uniform V there is a measurable sampling function of (X,V) whose output, jointly with X, has law M. Given two such conditional laws with the same first marginal and uniforms V_1,V_2 mutually independent and with their pair independent of X, applying the respective sampling functions to (X,V_1),(X,V_2) realizes the unique conditional gluing. These independent uniforms can always be supplied on a product enlargement of the original probability space.
Bibliographic attribution for randomization and transfer interfaces; no additional mathematical assertion.

For measurable spaces S_1,S_2,..., the sequence space S=product_{j>=1} S_j carries the sigma-algebra generated by prefix cylinders pi_n^{-1}(B), with B measurable in S_{<=n}=product_{j=1}^n S_j; S_{<=0} is a singleton. A finite law is consistent with a shorter prefix law iff prefix restriction pushes the former to the latter.

For arbitrary measurable coordinate spaces S_n, an initial probability μ_1 on S_1 and probability kernels K_{n+1}:S_{≤n}↝S_{n+1} for n≥1 determine a unique probability μ on the sequence space with its prefix-generated product sigma-algebra. Its first prefix law is μ_1 and its subsequent prefix laws satisfy μ_{n+1}=μ_n⊗K_{n+1} for every n≥1.
Bibliographic attribution and proof-route explanation of extension via recursive continuity; no additional deliverable.

For any index set I and measurable spaces S_i, write S_F=product_{i in F}S_i for every finite F subset I, with singleton empty product, and pi_{F,E}:S_F->S_E for restriction when E subset F. A family of probability laws (mu_F) is consistent iff (pi_{F,E})#mu_F=mu_E for all E subset F subset I with F finite. S_I carries the product/cylinder sigma-algebra generated by all finite-coordinate projections.

Suppose a consistent family (mu_F) of finite-dimensional probabilities has nonempty coordinate spaces S_i. If each countable coordinate subfamily has a probability extension with its specified finite-dimensional laws, then there is a unique probability extension of the whole family to the cylinder sigma-algebra on S_I, for arbitrary I.

For any index set I and standard Borel coordinate spaces S_i, every consistent family (mu_F) of finite-dimensional probability laws, including the singleton empty-product law, extends uniquely to a probability on the cylinder sigma-algebra of S_I. Nonemptiness of factors follows from their one-coordinate probability laws.
Bibliographic comparisons for arbitrary-index and countable-coordinate probability extension; no additional assertion.

For an arbitrary index set I and probabilities lambda_i on arbitrary measurable spaces S_i, there is a unique probability on the cylinder sigma-algebra of S_I whose coordinate maps have laws lambda_i and are mutually independent.

For any index set and arbitrary measurable coordinate spaces, a probability law of a product-valued process on the product/cylinder sigma-algebra is uniquely determined by all its finite-dimensional laws.
Bibliographic attribution for independent products; no additional assertion.

If I is uncountable and S_i={0,1} with the discrete topology, every cylinder-measurable subset of {0,1}^I has membership determined by at most countably many coordinates. The singleton all-zero point is product-topologically closed but is not determined by any countable coordinate set and hence is not cylinder measurable. Consequently the product-topological Borel sigma-algebra is strictly larger than the cylinder sigma-algebra.

Processes X,Y on the same probability space are modifications of one another iff P(X_t=Y_t)=1 at each fixed t. They are indistinguishable iff there is one measurable event of probability one on which X_t=Y_t simultaneously for every t.

For random elements taking values in a separable metric state space, the event {X_t=Y_t} is measurable at each fixed t: the diagonal is closed and the Borel sigma-algebra on the product equals the product sigma-algebra.

Let T>0 and let (X_t)_{0<=t<=T} be a process in a complete separable metric space (S,d). If p>0, beta>0 and finite C satisfy E[d(X_t,X_s)^p]<=C |t-s|^(1+beta) for every s,t in [0,T], then X has a modification Y on the same probability space with continuous paths. There is one measurable full-probability event on which each Y path is Holder continuous for every exponent 0<gamma<beta/p, with a finite Holder constant depending on the path and gamma. Any two modifications with almost surely continuous paths are indistinguishable.
At T=0 a process has a single time coordinate and the continuity conclusion holds with no increment-moment assumption.

If S is a nonempty separable metric space and T>0, the continuous-path space C([0,T],S), with the uniform metric, is separable; it is complete if S is complete. For every countable dense D_0 subset [0,T], its Borel sigma-algebra is exactly that generated by the evaluations e_t(f)=f(t) for t in D_0.

For nonempty separable metric S, T>0 and countable dense D_0 subset [0,T], every process with measurable coordinates and continuous paths defines a measurable map into C([0,T],S), and its path law is uniquely determined by its finite-dimensional laws at times in D_0. For a process with almost surely continuous paths the same holds after assigning a fixed constant path off a measurable full-probability continuity event.
Bibliographic explanation of path laws and transfer of regularity; no additional assertion.

On ([0,1],Borel,Lebesgue probability), define X_t(omega)=1_{omega=t}, Y_t(omega)=0 for t in [0,1]. Every X coordinate is measurable and every finite-dimensional joint law of X equals that of Y, because outside the finite set of sampled times their coordinates agree. Every path of X is discontinuous at t=omega, including endpoints under relative topology; Y is a continuous modification of X, but X,Y are not indistinguishable.

For a metric space S with its Borel sigma-algebra, P(S) is the space of Borel probability laws and is equipped with the initial/weak topology of the maps mu->integral f dmu for all bounded continuous real f on S. Write mu_n weakto mu for convergence in this topology and X_n => X when Law(X_n) weakto Law(X). Any space carrying a probability law is nonempty.

Scope clarification and bibliographic attribution: open/closed approximation is for any metric space, whereas compact approximation needs additional hypotheses. Its mathematical assertions are supplied by the following regularity proposition and later tightness theorems.
For every finite Borel measure mu on any metric space S, every Borel A subset S and every epsilon>0, there exist closed F and open G with F subset A subset G and mu(G minus F)<epsilon.
Two Borel probability measures on any metric space S that have equal integrals against every bounded continuous real function are equal.
A Borel set A is a mu-continuity set iff mu(boundary A)=0.

For any finite Borel measure mu on a metric space and any fixed center x, the open balls B(x,r), r>0, are mu-continuity sets for all but countably many radii. More generally, a finite measure gives positive mass to at most countably many members of any disjoint family of measurable sets.
Bibliographic attribution for Portmanteau and determining classes; no additional assertion.

For Borel probability laws mu_n,mu on any metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) weak convergence mu_n->mu; (ii) limsup mu_n(F)<=mu(F) for every closed F; (iii) liminf mu_n(G)>=mu(G) for every open G; (iv) mu_n(A)->mu(A) for every Borel A with mu(boundary A)=0; (v) liminf integral f dmu_n>=integral f dmu for every lower semicontinuous f:S->(-infinity,infinity] bounded below. Equivalently, every upper semicontinuous f:S->[-infinity,infinity) bounded above satisfies limsup integral f dmu_n<=integral f dmu, allowing the value -infinity.

Suppose a Borel probability mu on metric S gives mass one to a separable Borel subset M. For every r>0 and epsilon>0 there is a finite Borel partition (A_0,A_1,...,A_k) of S consisting of mu-continuity sets, with mu(A_0)<epsilon and diameter(A_i)<r for i>0. Empty cells may be discarded except that the remainder A_0 is allowed to remain empty.

On a separable metric S, for every Borel probability mu there exists a countable base of open mu-continuity balls. If probabilities mu_n have masses converging to mu on every finite intersection of those balls, then mu_n converges weakly to mu.
For probability laws mu_n,mu on R, with F_n(t)=mu_n((-infinity,t]) and F(t)=mu((-infinity,t]), weak convergence mu_n->mu holds iff F_n(t)->F(t) at every continuity point t of F.

Let E,F be arbitrary topological spaces with Borel sigma-algebras, and let probability laws mu_n,mu on E converge against all bounded continuous real tests. For every continuous g:E->F, the pushforwards g#mu_n converge weakly to g#mu. In particular X_n=>X implies g(X_n)=>g(X).

Let S,T be metric spaces, mu_n->mu weakly on S, and g_n,g:S->T Borel. If there is a Borel C subset S with mu(C)=1 such that for every x in C and every sequence x_n->x in S one has g_n(x_n)->g(x), then (g_n)#mu_n converges weakly to g#mu.
For metric spaces S,T, weak convergence mu_n->mu on S is preserved under a fixed Borel g:S->T that is continuous at mu-almost every point of the entire domain S; namely g#mu_n->g#mu weakly.

Let eta_n->eta weakly on metric S, and let K_n,K be probability kernels from S to the Borel space of a metric T. Suppose there is a Borel eta-full C such that for every x in C and x_n->x, the laws K_n(x_n,.) converge weakly to K(x,.). Then the mixed laws eta_n K_n converge weakly to eta K.
Bibliographic attribution for fixed/varying maps and mixtures; no additional assertion.

For every m,n, let X_n and X_n^(m) be S-valued random elements on a common probability space for that pair, with measurable distance d(X_n,X_n^(m)). Suppose for every fixed m, Law(X_n^(m))->mu_m weakly as n->infinity; mu_m->mu weakly as m->infinity; and for every epsilon>0, limit_{m->infinity} limsup_{n->infinity} P(d(X_n,X_n^(m))>epsilon)=0. Then Law(X_n)->mu weakly. In particular a measurable-distance perturbation tending to zero in probability preserves a given weak limit.

Let random vectors X_n,Y_n be on the same space for each n, with X_n=>X and Y_n->c in probability for a constant vector c. Then (X_n,Y_n)=>(X,c), and every continuous function of that pair converges in distribution to the corresponding function of (X,c). For scalars this gives X_n+Y_n=>X+c and X_n Y_n=>c X; if c is nonzero, X_n/Y_n=>X/c, with any Borel convention at zero denominators.
For real random variables X_n=>X and every p>0, E|X|^p<=liminf_n E|X_n|^p, allowing infinite moments.
For real random variables X_n=>X and p>0, if the family (|X_n|^p) is uniformly integrable, then E|X_n|^p->E|X|^p<infinity.

Let X_n=>X be S-valued for metric S and let h:S->R be Borel and continuous at Law(X)-almost every point. If (h(X_n)) is uniformly integrable, then h(X) is integrable and E h(X_n)->E h(X). In particular, if X_n=>X are real and (|X_n|^p) is uniformly integrable for p>0, this conclusion holds for every continuous h:R->R with |h(x)|<=C(1+|x|^p).

An L1 bound alone does not imply expectation convergence under convergence in distribution: if X_n takes n with probability 1/n and 0 otherwise (n>=1), then X_n converges in law to 0 but E X_n=1 for every n, despite the uniform L1 bound.

A family A subset P(S) is uniformly tight iff for every epsilon>0 there is a compact K subset S with sup_{mu in A} mu(S minus K)<epsilon; a single probability law is tight iff its singleton family is uniformly tight.
The laws Dirac_n, n>=1, on R are each tight, but the family {Dirac_n:n>=1} is not uniformly tight, because each compact subset of R is bounded.
If H is any compact metric space, including the empty space, then the space P(H) of Borel probability laws is compact and metrizable for its weak topology.
For every metric space S, a uniformly tight family A subset P(S) has compact closure in the weak topology. Every sequence in A has a subsequence converging weakly to a Borel probability law on S.
Bibliographic comparison and proof-route description using compact representation of positive functionals rather than representations of random elements; no further deliverable.

If S is complete and separable metric and A subset P(S), then either of the following implies uniform tightness of A: every sequence from A has a weakly convergent subsequence with limit in P(S); the weak closure of A is compact. Together with forward Prokhorov these two compactness conditions and uniform tightness are equivalent.
Every Borel probability law on a complete separable metric space is tight.

Let mu_n->mu weakly on a metric space S, with mu concentrated on a separable Borel subset of S. There is one probability space carrying random elements X,X_n with Law(X)=mu, Law(X_n)=mu_n and X_n->X almost surely. The mu_n need not be concentrated on that same separable subset. In particular this applies to every separable metric S without a completeness assumption.
Bibliographic attribution and scope explanation: the representation realizes probability laws, with no promise to preserve the original joint relationships of any given random sequence.

For separable metric S_1,...,S_k, probability laws lambda_n,lambda on their finite product satisfy lambda_n->lambda weakly iff lambda_n(A_1 x ... x A_k)->lambda(A_1 x ... x A_k) whenever each A_i is a Borel continuity set of the i-th marginal of lambda.
For probability laws mu_{n,i},mu_i on separable metric S_i (1<=i<=k), product_i mu_{n,i}->product_i mu_i weakly iff mu_{n,i}->mu_i weakly for every i.

For separable metric spaces S_i, i>=1, probability laws lambda_n,lambda on S=product_i S_i with its product topology converge weakly iff all their finite-dimensional marginals converge weakly to the corresponding marginals of lambda. In particular coordinatewise weak convergence mu_{n,i}->mu_i implies weak convergence of the countable product laws product_i mu_{n,i}->product_i mu_i.
Bibliographic attribution for weak convergence and products; no additional assertion.

For a Borel A in metric S and a>0 let A^a={x:d(x,A)<a}, with empty^a=empty. For probabilities mu,nu define pi(mu,nu)=inf{a>0: for every Borel A, mu(A)<=nu(A^a)+a and nu(A)<=mu(A^a)+a}. Define d_BL(mu,nu)=sup{|integral f dmu-integral f dnu|: f:S->R, sup norm(f)<=1 and Lipschitz constant(f)<=1}.

For every metric S the Prokhorov function pi and bounded Lipschitz function d_BL are metrics on P(S). If S is separable, each induces exactly the weak topology. For arbitrary metric S, convergence in either metric implies weak convergence; as clarified in the proof at lines 2100–2112, these are continuity assertions for the topologies, including convergent nets, rather than only sequential assertions.
Bibliographic attribution and explanation of the finite-partition proof for the two weak metrics; no further deliverable.
For probabilities mu,nu on separable metric S, a coupling is a probability law on S x S whose respective marginals are mu,nu.
For separable metric S, the Borel sigma-algebra of S x S with its product topology equals B(S) tensor B(S).

Let (p_i),(q_j) be finite vectors of nonnegative reals each summing to one, R a set of allowed left-right edges, and R(I) the right neighbors of a subset I of left indices. If sum_{i in I}p_i<=sum_{j in R(I)}q_j+delta for every I, then there is a nonnegative matrix with row sums p_i and column sums q_j whose total mass on edges outside R is at most delta. The empty-subset hypothesis forces delta>=0.

Let S be separable metric, mu,nu Borel probabilities and a>0. If pi(mu,nu)<a, there exists a coupling gamma of mu,nu with gamma{(x,y):d(x,y)>a}<a. Conversely, every such coupling with gamma{d(x,y)>a}<=a implies pi(mu,nu)<=a.

If S is separable metric, (P(S),pi) is separable. If S is also complete, the Prokhorov metric pi is complete. Thus the probability-law space of a complete separable metric S is itself complete separable for pi.
Bibliographic comparison and clarification that the completeness assertion is for the Prokhorov metric; it does not assert completeness of the displayed bounded Lipschitz metric.

Fix T>0 and C=C([0,T],R^d) with the supremum norm. For x in C define its modulus w_x(delta)=sup{norm(x(s)-x(t)):s,t in [0,T], |s-t|<=delta}, for nonnegative scale delta (only positive delta are used in the tightness criterion).

For T>0 and finite dimension d, C([0,T],R^d) with the supremum norm is complete and separable. Polygonal interpolants on the grids jT/m, with m≥1 integer and rational vector values at the nodes, form a countable dense family. Thus its Borel probability laws are laws on a complete separable metric space.

For T>0 and C=C([0,T],R^d) in the supremum topology, a family A subset P(C) is uniformly tight iff its time-zero marginal family is uniformly tight and for every eta>0, limit_{delta downarrow 0} sup_{mu in A} mu{x:w_x(delta)>eta}=0.

For T>0 and C=C([0,T],R^d), if a sequence (mu_n) in P(C) is uniformly tight and its finite-dimensional marginals at every finite set of times from a fixed dense countable subset D of [0,T] converge weakly, then mu_n converges weakly on C to a unique probability law with those limiting marginals. If a candidate law mu in P(C) is already given, mu_n->mu weakly iff (mu_n) is uniformly tight and its finite-dimensional marginals on such a D converge weakly to the corresponding marginals of mu.

In C([0,1],R), for n>=1 define x_n to be zero outside [2^(-n),2^(1-n)], linear on each half of that interval, zero at its endpoints and one at its midpoint. At every fixed t one has x_n(t)->0, so Dirac_{x_n} has the finite-dimensional limits of the zero path. Nevertheless norm(x_n)_infinity=1, and the bounded continuous test x->min(1,norm(x)_infinity) rules out weak convergence to the point mass at zero. Any possible weak limit would have to be that point mass by marginal uniqueness, so the sequence has no weak limit. The family fails the modulus condition: for every delta>0, all sufficiently large n satisfy w_{x_n}(delta)=1.
Bibliographic attribution and clarification that these path criteria use the uniform topology of continuous paths; no additional assertion.

For every probability law μ on R^d, define its characteristic function φ_μ(t)=∫ exp(i⟨t,x⟩) μ(dx), t∈R^d. The convention has a positive exponent and no 2π; relative to the Fourier convention exp(−2πi⟨ξ,x⟩), use ξ=−t/(2π). For a random vector X, φ_X is the characteristic function of its law.

For any probability law μ on R^d, φ_μ is uniformly continuous, φ_μ(0)=1, φ_μ(−t)=conj(φ_μ(t)) for every t, and |φ_μ(t)|≤1. It is positive definite: for every finite family c_j∈C and t_j∈R^d, the complex sum ∑_{j,k} c_j conj(c_k) φ_μ(t_j−t_k) is real and nonnegative.
For all probability laws μ,ν on R^d, the convolution (the pushforward of μ⊗ν by addition) satisfies φ_{μ*ν}(t)=φ_μ(t)φ_ν(t) for every t∈R^d.

For an R^d-valued random vector X and any integer m≥1, if E||X||^m<∞, then φ_X has continuous partial derivatives through order m; for every multi-index α with |α|≤m and every t∈R^d, ∂^α φ_X(t)=E[(iX)^α exp(i⟨t,X⟩)].
For every R^d-valued random vector X with E||X||²<∞, as t→0 in R^d, φ_X(t)=1+i⟨t,EX⟩−(1/2)E[⟨t,X⟩²]+o(||t||²).

Construct a symmetric real random variable X by taking a nonnegative variable with tail P(|X|>r)=1/(r log r) for r≥e and 1/e for 0≤r<e, and giving it an independent fair sign. This is a probability law with an atom of mass 1−1/e at zero. It satisfies E|X|=∞, but its characteristic function is differentiable at zero with φ_X′(0)=0. Thus a finite first absolute moment is sufficient but unnecessary for differentiability at zero.
For σ>0 and x∈R^d define g_σ(x)=(2πσ²)^(−d/2) exp(−||x||²/(2σ²)), the centered Gaussian density of scalar covariance σ²I.
For every σ>0 and t,x∈R^d, ∫_{R^d} exp(i⟨t,y⟩)g_σ(y)dy=exp(−σ²||t||²/2), and g_σ(x)=(2π)^(−d)∫_{R^d} exp(−i⟨t,x⟩)exp(−σ²||t||²/2)dt. In particular g_σ has total integral one.
For probability laws μ,ν on R^d, equality φ_μ(t)=φ_ν(t) for all t∈R^d implies μ=ν: a characteristic function determines its probability law.

If μ is a probability on R^d and φ_μ is Lebesgue integrable on R^d, then μ has a bounded continuous density f with respect to Lebesgue measure, given for every x by f(x)=(2π)^(−d)∫_{R^d} exp(−i⟨t,x⟩)φ_μ(t)dt. The inverse integral is real, nonnegative, and has total integral one.

For any probability law μ on R and every a<b, lim_{T→∞}(1/(2π))∫_{−T}^{T} ((exp(−ita)−exp(−itb))/(it))φ_μ(t)dt = μ((a,b))+(1/2)μ({a})+(1/2)μ({b}). At t=0 the quotient has its continuous extension b−a. Atoms at either endpoint are allowed.

Let μ_n be probability laws on R^d and φ:R^d→C. If φ_{μ_n}(t)→φ(t) for every t and φ is continuous at zero, there exists a unique probability law μ on R^d with φ_μ=φ, and μ_n converges weakly to μ. Conversely, if μ_n converges weakly to a probability law μ on R^d, then φ_{μ_n}(t)→φ_μ(t) for every t.
For a probability law μ on [0,∞)^d define L_μ(t)=∫ exp(−⟨t,x⟩)dμ(x) for t∈[0,∞)^d.

For probability laws μ_n on [0,∞)^d, if L_{μ_n}(t)→L(t) for every t∈[0,∞)^d and L is continuous at zero within the orthant, then there is a unique probability law μ on [0,∞)^d with Laplace transform L, and μ_n converges weakly to μ. Conversely, weak convergence to μ implies pointwise convergence of the Laplace transforms to L_μ. In particular the Laplace transform determines a probability law on the positive orthant.
Two probability laws μ,ν on R^d coincide if their pushforwards by every real linear functional x↦⟨t,x⟩, t∈R^d, agree.
For probability laws μ_n,μ on R^d, μ_n converges weakly to μ if and only if, for every real linear functional x↦⟨t,x⟩, its pushforward of μ_n converges weakly to its pushforward of μ.

For each m∈R^d and each real symmetric positive semidefinite d×d matrix Σ, construct the unique Gaussian probability law N(m,Σ), whose characteristic function is exp(i⟨t,m⟩−(1/2)tᵀΣt). Its mean is m and covariance is Σ. Positive semidefinite singular matrices and zero covariance are allowed; univariate zero variance is a point mass.
An R^d-valued random vector is Gaussian if and only if every real linear projection is a univariate Gaussian. Univariate Gaussians include zero-variance point masses.
For X∼N(m,Σ), every real matrix A of compatible dimensions and vector b give AX+b∼N(Am+b,AΣAᵀ), including singular and degenerate cases.
For two coordinate blocks of a jointly Gaussian vector, the blocks are independent if and only if their cross-covariance matrix is zero; the conclusion allows singular covariance matrices.

Every continuous positive definite φ:R^d→C with φ(0)=1 is the characteristic function of a unique probability law on R^d. Positive definiteness means that every finite quadratic sum ∑_{j,k}c_j conj(c_k)φ(t_j−t_k) is real and nonnegative.

For every T>0 construct the unique Borel probability on C([0,T],R) for which the coordinate process B starts at zero almost surely, is centered Gaussian with covariance E[B_sB_t]=min(s,t), and has independent normal increments, each increment B_t−B_s over 0≤s≤t≤T having variance t−s. Independence applies to increments over disjoint time intervals; zero-length increments are identically zero.
For a sequence of real random variables X_k indexed by positive integers, set S_n=∑_{k=1}^n X_k.

Organizational and bibliographic framing: the chapter explicitly distinguishes pairwise independence in the first-moment strong law from mutual independence in the maximal inequality and three-series theorem; this directs interpretation of their hypotheses and is not an additional theorem.
Let (X_k) be pairwise uncorrelated square-integrable real random variables. If n^(−2)∑_{k=1}^n Var(X_k)→0, then (S_n−ES_n)/n→0 in L² and in probability.

Let (X_k) be identically distributed pairwise independent real random variables. If nP(|X_1|>n)→0, then S_n/n−m_n→0 in probability, where m_n=E[X_1 1_{|X_1|≤n}]. No finite first absolute moment is assumed for this truncated-center assertion.
For identically distributed pairwise independent real random variables (X_k) with E|X_1|<∞, S_n/n converges to EX_1 both in probability and in L¹.

For every 1<p<2, the tail condition r^pP(|X_1|>r)→0 as r→∞ does not by itself imply n^(−1/p)S_n→0. The deterministic identically distributed sequence X_k=1 satisfies the tail condition, whereas n^(−1/p)S_n=n^(1−1/p)→+∞. Thus the zero-mean condition in the cited uncentered version must be retained; the referenced theorem itself is not incorporated as another assertion.
For identically distributed pairwise independent real random variables (X_k) with E|X_1|<∞, S_n/n→EX_1 almost surely.

For an identically distributed pairwise independent sequence of real random variables, if S_n/n converges almost surely to a finite random variable, then E|X_1|<∞, and the almost sure limit equals the constant EX_1.
For mutually independent centered square-integrable real random variables X_1,…,X_n and every λ>0, P(max_{1≤k≤n}|S_k|≥λ)≤λ^(−2)∑_{k=1}^n Var(X_k).
If (X_k) is a mutually independent sequence of centered square-integrable real random variables and ∑_k Var(X_k)<∞, then ∑_k X_k converges almost surely and in L² (to the same random variable).
For real sequences (a_k),(b_k), if 0<b_1≤b_2≤… and b_n→+∞ and the real series ∑_k a_k/b_k converges in its given order, then b_n^(−1)∑_{k=1}^n a_k→0. Non-strict monotonicity of b_k is sufficient.

For mutually independent square-integrable real random variables X_k and a deterministic real sequence 0<b_1≤b_2≤… with b_n→+∞, if ∑_k Var(X_k)/b_k²<∞ then b_n^(−1)∑_{k=1}^n(X_k−EX_k)→0 almost surely. In particular, if ∑_k Var(X_k)/k²<∞, then n^(−1)∑_{k=1}^n(X_k−EX_k)→0 almost surely.

For mutually independent real random variables X_k and every fixed threshold a>0, put Y_k=X_k 1_{|X_k|≤a}. Then ∑_kX_k converges almost surely if and only if all of ∑_kP(|X_k|>a), ∑_kEY_k, and ∑_kVar(Y_k) converge. The middle series requires ordinary convergence in its specified order, not absolute convergence. The same equivalence holds for every choice of positive threshold a.

Let (X_k) be i.i.d. real random variables, 0<p<2, and E|X_1|^p<∞. Almost surely, S_n/n^(1/p)→0 when 0<p<1, and (S_n−nEX_1)/n^(1/p)→0 when 1≤p<2. The second case includes p=1, when the moment assumption guarantees EX_1 exists.

Let (X_k) be i.i.d. real random variables and 0<p<2. If for some real constant c the sequence (S_n−nc)/n^(1/p) has a finite almost sure limit, then E|X_1|^p<∞. When 1<p<2 this finite-limit hypothesis also forces c=EX_1. No equality of c and EX_1 is asserted when p≤1.
For i.i.d. real random variables (X_k) with common distribution function F, define the empirical distribution function F_n(x)=n^(−1)∑_{k=1}^n 1_{X_k≤x}, for n≥1 and x∈R.

For i.i.d. real random variables (X_k) with any common distribution function F and empirical functions F_n(x)=n^(−1)∑_{k=1}^n1_{X_k≤x}, sup_{x∈R}|F_n(x)−F(x)|→0 almost surely. No continuity of F is assumed; arbitrary atoms are allowed.

Let (X_k) be i.i.d. random vectors in R^d with finite second moment, mean m, and covariance matrix Σ. The laws of n^(−1/2)∑_{k=1}^n(X_k−m) converge weakly to N(0,Σ). Singular covariance matrices are allowed. In dimension one Σ is the scalar variance; when that variance is zero, every centered sum is zero almost surely and the limit is the point mass at zero.

Let (U_j)_{j≥1} be independent fair {0,1} bits. Enumerate all nonzero finite binary coefficient vectors v by increasing largest occupied coordinate, and put X_k=(−1)^(∑_jv_jU_j) for the kth vector. These are identically distributed pairwise independent fair signs (hence mean zero and variance one). For n_m=2^m−1, S_{n_m}=2^m−1 if the first m bits vanish and S_{n_m}=−1 otherwise. Consequently S_{n_m}/sqrt(n_m)→0 in probability, so pairwise independence alone cannot replace mutual independence in the central limit theorem.

The nth triangular-array row is a finite family of mutually independent centered real variables X_{nj} with finite variances and positive total variance s_n²=∑_jE[X_{nj}²]>0. Define s_n to be its positive square root, Y_{nj}=X_{nj}/s_n, v_{nj}=E[Y_{nj}²], T_n=∑_jY_{nj}, and L_n(ε)=∑_jE[Y_{nj}²1_{|Y_{nj}|>ε}], so ∑_jv_{nj}=1. No independence between different rows is required.

For each n let (X_{nj})_{j∈J_n} be a finite family of mutually independent centered real random variables with finite variances, with s_n²=∑_{j∈J_n}E[X_{nj}²]>0 and s_n the positive square root. Set Y_{nj}=X_{nj}/s_n and T_n=∑_jY_{nj}. No independence across rows is required. If for every ε>0, L_n(ε)=∑_jE[Y_{nj}²1_{|Y_{nj}|>ε}]→0, then Law(T_n) converges weakly to N(0,1).

For each n let (X_{nj})_{j∈J_n} be a finite family of mutually independent centered real random variables with finite variances, with s_n²=∑_{j∈J_n}E[X_{nj}²]>0 and s_n the positive square root. Set Y_{nj}=X_{nj}/s_n and T_n=∑_jY_{nj}. No independence across rows is required. Define v_{nj}=E[Y_{nj}²] and L_n(ε)=∑_jE[Y_{nj}²1_{|Y_{nj}|>ε}]. If Law(T_n) converges weakly to N(0,1) and max_j v_{nj}→0, then L_n(ε)→0 for every ε>0.

For each n let (X_{nj})_{j∈J_n} be a finite family of mutually independent centered real random variables with finite variances, with s_n²=∑_{j∈J_n}E[X_{nj}²]>0 and s_n the positive square root. Set Y_{nj}=X_{nj}/s_n and T_n=∑_jY_{nj}. No independence across rows is required. If for some δ>0 all E|X_{nj}|^(2+δ) are finite and s_n^(−(2+δ))∑_jE|X_{nj}|^(2+δ)→0, then Law(T_n) converges weakly to N(0,1).

For each n let (B_{nj}) be a finite row of mutually independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities p_{nj}. If max_j p_{nj}→0 and ∑_jp_{nj}→λ for a finite λ∈[0,∞), then ∑_jB_{nj} converges in law to Poisson(λ). Rows may be empty: their sums and maximal parameters are defined to be zero. The case λ=0 yields the point mass at zero. No independence between rows is assumed.

Expository and bibliographic explanation of why the smoothing argument retains finite first absolute moments and integrability of the characteristic-function difference quotient; it discusses a correction to the cited edition and introduces no additional theorem beyond the following stated smoothing inequality.

There exists a universal finite numerical constant C such that for any probability distribution functions F,G on R with finite first absolute moments, their characteristic functions φ_F,φ_G, and any M≥0 for which G is M-Lipschitz, for every T>0 one has sup_{x∈R}|F(x)−G(x)|≤C(∫_{−T}^{T}|φ_F(t)−φ_G(t)|/|t| dt+M/T). The value of the integrand at t=0 is irrelevant to its Lebesgue integral; the finite first moments ensure integrability near zero. The same constant works for all laws, M, and T.

There exists a universal finite constant C such that for every i.i.d. sequence of real random variables X_k with mean m, variance σ²>0, and E|X_1−m|³<∞, and every integer n≥1, sup_{x∈R}|P((∑_{k=1}^n(X_k−m))/(σsqrt(n))≤x)−Φ(x)|≤(C/sqrt(n))E|X_1−m|³/σ³, where Φ is the standard normal distribution function and σ>0 is the standard deviation.
Bibliography and document closing material; no mathematical obligations.
Document formatting, title, date, contents, chapter overview and source-map counts are context, not additional mathematical deliverables.

Global conventions: locally convex spaces are real and Hausdorff unless stated otherwise; X′ is the continuous dual with ⟨x′,x⟩=x′(x). A proper extended-real convex function has no −∞ value and is finite somewhere. Cones contain 0. For closed convex K, K*={y:⟨y,x⟩≥0 for all x∈K}. For smooth minimization with g_i≤0 and h_j=0, L=f+∑λ_i g_i+∑ν_j h_j, λ_i≥0. In the complex Hilbert variational problem, a is conjugate-linear in its unknown (first slot), linear in its test (second slot), and ℓ is linear in the test.

The listed Hahn–Banach, Alaoglu, Riesz, contraction, linear algebra, Taylor, implicit-function, linear ODE, integration, Hölder, Lp duality/reflexivity, density, mollification, Arzelà–Ascoli, Lipschitz extension/trace and regular-domain Green results are analytic prerequisites used at their stated hypotheses. Bibliographic guidance and interfaces to relaxation, elliptic regularity and numerical algorithms are context, not separate additional theorems.

An affine set is closed under finite affine combinations (coefficients sum to 1); a convex set under convex combinations (also nonnegative coefficients); a convex cone contains 0 and is closed under addition and nonnegative scalar multiplication. Affine, convex and conic hulls are the smallest such sets containing the generators. A face F of convex C is a convex subset such that x,y∈C and (1−t)x+ty∈F with 0<t<1 imply x,y∈F. An extreme point x has {x} a face. For nonempty finite-dimensional convex C, ri C is the interior of C in aff C.

Affine, convex and conic hulls consist of finite combinations of the respective types (the conic empty combination is 0). Intersections, affine images, affine inverse images, Cartesian products and Minkowski sums preserve convexity; linear images of convex cones are convex cones.
Every nonempty finite-dimensional convex set C has nonempty ri C, including affine dimension 0. If a∈ri C, b∈closure C and 0≤t<1, then (1−t)a+tb∈ri C.
For nonempty convex C in finite dimension and x∈C, x∈ri C iff for every y∈C there is s>0 such that x+s(x−y)∈C.
For nonempty finite-dimensional convex C, closure(ri C)=closure C and ri(closure C)=ri C.
For a finite family of finite-dimensional convex sets C_i having a common relative-interior point, ri(⋂_i C_i)=⋂_i ri C_i and closure(⋂_i C_i)=⋂_i closure C_i.

For affine A:E→F between finite-dimensional real spaces and nonempty convex C⊆E, ri(A C)=A(ri C). For convex D⊆F, if A(E) meets ri D then ri(A⁻¹D)=A⁻¹(ri D). For nonempty convex C,D in the same finite-dimensional space, ri(C+D)=ri C+ri D.
If S has affine dimension at most d, every point of convexHull S is a convex combination of at most d+1 points of S.

For nonempty closed convex C in finite dimension and x∈C∖ri C, a nonzero linear functional on the direction space of aff C supports C at x (l(u−x)≤0 for all u∈C) and is strictly smaller than its value at x at some point of C.
Every nonempty compact convex set in finite dimension is the convex hull of its extreme points, including a singleton.
Every indexed collection of d+2 points of ℝ^d, with repetitions allowed, admits a partition of its indices into two nonempty blocks whose point sets have intersecting convex hulls.
For convex subsets C₁,…,C_m of ℝ^d with m≥d+1, if every d+1-member subfamily has nonempty intersection, then ⋂_{i=1}^m C_i is nonempty.

Let A,B be disjoint nonempty convex subsets of a real Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space. If A is open, there exist a nonzero continuous linear l and α∈ℝ with l(a)<α≤l(b) for all a∈A,b∈B. If A is compact and B closed, there exists a nonzero continuous linear l with sup_A l<inf_B l (a uniform gap).

Every boundary point of a nonempty closed convex set in a positive-dimensional Euclidean space admits a supporting hyperplane; a relative boundary point admits one within its affine hull. Two nonempty finite-dimensional convex sets C,D have disjoint relative interiors iff there is a linear l with l(c)≤l(d) for every c∈C,d∈D and strict inequality for at least one pair.

For S⊆X, σ_S(l)=sup_{x∈S}⟨l,x⟩ on X′ and its negative polar is S°={l:σ_S(l)≤0}. A cone K has positive dual K*=−K°. For subsets of X′, the polar in X uses the same nonpositive pairing inequality. Suprema use the extended-real convention, including empty S.

In a real Hausdorff locally convex space every closed convex set, including the empty set, equals the intersection of the closed continuous-linear halfspaces containing it. For every subset S, S°° is its closed convex conic hull. Consequently a closed convex cone is recovered by taking its positive dual twice in the given dual pairing.
For a nonempty closed convex set C, rec C={d: x+td∈C for every x∈C and t≥0}; its lineality space is rec C∩(−rec C).
For nonempty closed convex C, rec C is a closed convex cone. A ray x₀+[0,∞)d⊆C from any one x₀∈C suffices for d∈rec C. In finite dimension, C is unbounded iff rec C contains a nonzero vector.

Let f:E→(−∞,+∞] be proper, convex and lower semicontinuous in finite dimension. For every x with f(x)<∞ and every direction d, define f∞(d)=inf{r∈ℝ:(d,r)∈rec(epi f)}, with empty-fiber infimum +∞. Then f∞(d)=sup_{t>0}(f(x+td)−f(x))/t; these quotients are nondecreasing in t and the supremum is independent of the finite point x. Every nonempty real sublevel C_α={f≤α} satisfies rec C_α={d:f∞(d)≤0}.
Under the hypotheses for recession of a function, a nonempty real sublevel of f is unbounded iff some nonzero direction d satisfies f∞(d)≤0.
For nonempty closed convex C⊆E and linear A:E→F between finite-dimensional spaces, if rec C∩ker A is contained in the lineality space of rec C, then A C is closed.

The cone of real symmetric positive semidefinite 2×2 matrices is closed. The linear projection [[a,b],[b,c]]↦(a,b) has image {(a,b):a>0}∪{(0,0)}; (0,1) lies in its closure but not its image. In particular a linear image of a closed convex cone need not be closed.
A polyhedron in a finite-dimensional real space is an intersection of finitely many affine closed halfspaces; an affine equality can be represented by two inequalities.

Every coordinate projection of a polyhedron is a polyhedron (Fourier–Motzkin elimination). Thus every affine image of a polyhedron is a polyhedron and is closed; empty and degenerate systems are included.
The convex cone generated by finitely many vectors in finite dimension is closed, including the zero cone generated by the empty list.

For every real matrix A and compatible real b, exactly one of (i) ∃x≥0, Ax=b and (ii) ∃y, Aᵀy≥0 and bᵀy<0 holds. Vector inequalities are componentwise, with no rank or nonemptiness hypothesis on matrix dimensions.
For every real matrix B, exactly one of (i) ∃d, Bd<0 componentwise and (ii) ∃μ≥0 with μ≠0 and Bᵀμ=0 holds. The zero-row case is included: the first system is vacuous and the second impossible.
Farkas and Gordan alternatives also apply to a subspace of directions, by writing the associated linear map in coordinates on that subspace.
For x∈C in Euclidean space, the contingent tangent cone T_C(x) is the set of limits (x_k−x)/t_k with x_k∈C and t_k>0 tending to 0. For convex C, N_C(x)={l:⟨l,y−x⟩≤0 for all y∈C}.

Let P={x:a_i·x≤b_i, e_j·x=d_j} be a finite polyhedron and x∈P, with I(x)={i:a_i·x=b_i}. Then T_P(x)={v:a_i·v≤0 for i∈I(x), e_j·v=0 for every j}, and N_P(x)={∑_{i∈I(x)}λ_i a_i+∑_jν_j e_j:λ_i≥0,ν_j∈ℝ}. No strict feasibility condition is required; empty active/equality lists are allowed.

For f:X→(−∞,+∞], proper means finite somewhere; dom f={x:f(x)<+∞}, epi f={(x,t)∈X×ℝ:f(x)≤t}, and the real sublevel at a is {f≤a}. Convexity means epi f is convex, and lower semicontinuity means {f>a} is open for every a∈ℝ.

Epigraph convexity is equivalent to f((1−t)x+ty)≤(1−t)f(x)+tf(y) for finite endpoints and 0≤t≤1; it implies all finite Jensen inequalities with nonnegative weights summing to 1, discarding zero weights (a positive infinite term makes the bound trivial). Lower semicontinuity is equivalent both to closedness of all real sublevels and to closedness of epi f.

Positive finite weighted sums, pointwise suprema and affine pullback preserve convexity. The perspective (x,t)↦t f(x/t) for t>0, extended by +∞ for t≤0, is convex. If F is convex on X×Y and v(x)=inf_y F(x,y) is proper, then v is convex. Positive finite sums, suprema and continuous affine pullback preserve lower semicontinuity for proper lower-semicontinuous inputs. The open perspective and inf-projection need not preserve lower semicontinuity (the nonpreservation conclusions are part of this proposition; its particular proof witnesses are not extra goals).

A proper convex function on a real normed space that is bounded above on a neighborhood of a is finite and Lipschitz on some smaller neighborhood of a. Every proper convex function in finite dimension is locally Lipschitz on ri(dom f), with the relative topology of aff(dom f), including affine dimension 0.

In a real normed space, every norm-closed convex set is weakly closed and every norm-lower-semicontinuous convex function is weakly lower semicontinuous. If x_n converges weakly to x, there exist finite convex combinations z_n of {x_k:k≥n} such that z_n→x in norm.
For proper f on a real locally convex space X, f*(y)=sup_{x∈dom f}(⟨y,x⟩−f(x)) for y∈X′. The extended-real indicator δ_C equals 0 on C and +∞ outside C.

For proper f, f* is convex and lower semicontinuous in σ(X′,X), and f(x)+f*(y)≥⟨y,x⟩ for every x,y. For nonempty C, δ_C*=σ_C; if C is also closed convex, σ_C*=δ_C in the same pairing. For a real normed space, the conjugate of x↦‖x‖ is the indicator of the closed dual unit ball.

For real symmetric positive semidefinite Q, the conjugate of q(x)=xᵀQx/2 is q*(y)=yᵀQ†y/2 for y∈ran Q and +∞ otherwise, where Q† is the inverse on (ker Q)⊥ and zero on ker Q. Singular Q, including Q=0, is included.
In the continuous-dual pairing, f**(x)=sup_{y∈X′}(⟨y,x⟩−f*(y)); a term with f*(y)=+∞ is −∞.

If X is real Hausdorff locally convex and f is proper, lower semicontinuous and convex, then f=f**. Equivalently f is the pointwise supremum of its continuous affine minorants, and at least one such minorant exists. There is no reflexivity hypothesis.
A proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a real Hausdorff locally convex space has proper conjugate in the pairing X,X′, without a reflexivity assumption.

For x∈dom f, ∂f(x) consists of y∈X′ such that f(z)≥f(x)+⟨y,z−x⟩ for every z∈X; it is empty off dom f. For a function on X′, the subdifferential in the pairing is tested by x∈X acting on X′ by evaluation.

For proper convex f and x∈dom f, x is a global minimizer iff 0∈∂f(x), and y∈∂f(x) iff f(x)+f*(y)=⟨y,x⟩. For nonempty convex C and x∈C, ∂δ_C(x)=N_C(x)={y∈X′:⟨y,z−x⟩≤0 for all z∈C}. If f is also lower semicontinuous on real Hausdorff locally convex X, the Fenchel-equality conditions are further equivalent to x∈∂f*(y) in the pairing.

For proper convex f and x∈dom f, the extended-real directional derivative f′(x;d)=lim_{t↓0}(f(x+td)−f(x))/t exists and equals inf_{t>0}(f(x+td)−f(x))/t. If f is finite and continuous in a neighborhood of x in a real normed space, d↦f′(x;d) is finite, continuous and sublinear, ∂f(x)={y∈X′:⟨y,d⟩≤f′(x;d) for all d}, and f′(x;d)=max_{y∈∂f(x)}⟨y,d⟩ for every d, including d=0. In finite dimension, ∂f(x) is nonempty at every x∈ri(dom f).

At an interior point where a convex function is Fréchet differentiable, its derivative is its unique subgradient. Conversely, in finite dimension, proper convex f with singleton ∂f(x) at an interior point of dom f is Fréchet differentiable there. Convex subdifferentials are monotone: y_i∈∂f(x_i) implies ⟨y₁−y₂,x₁−x₂⟩≥0. A differentiable real-valued function on an open convex set is convex iff f(z)≥f(x)+Df(x)(z−x) holds throughout that set.
The convex function f(t)=−√t on [0,∞), extended by +∞ to negative t, has f′(0;1)=−∞ and ∂f(0)=∅, illustrating possible infinite directional derivatives and absent boundary subgradients.

For real Hilbert H (identified with its continuous dual), proper lower-semicontinuous convex f and λ>0, e_λ f(x)=inf_{u∈H}(f(u)+‖u−x‖²/(2λ)); P^f_λ(x) denotes its unique minimizing point, whose existence/uniqueness is the following result.

For the preceding f,λ and every x∈H, e_λ f(x) is finite and the infimum is attained uniquely at p=P^f_λ(x). For p∈dom f, p=P^f_λ(x) iff (x−p)/λ∈∂f(p). The map P=P^f_λ is firmly nonexpansive: ‖Px−Py‖²≤⟨Px−Py,x−y⟩ for all x,y, and both P and I−P are nonexpansive.

For real Hilbert H, proper lower-semicontinuous convex f and λ>0, e_λ f is convex and Fréchet differentiable with gradient (x−P^f_λ(x))/λ, which is 1/λ-Lipschitz. For every x, x=P^f_λ(x)+λP^{f*}_{1/λ}(x/λ), and e_λ f(x)+e_{1/λ}f*(x/λ)=‖x‖²/(2λ).
For the indicator of a nonempty closed convex set in real Hilbert space, its proximal map (for every λ>0) is the nearest-point projection.
The canonical map J_X of a real normed space is isometric. For reflexive X, the weak and weak-star topologies on X′ agree.

For real normed X, its weak topology is generated by all elements of X′; the weak-star topology on X′ is generated by evaluation at X. The canonical map J_X:X→X″ is given by J_X(x)(f)=f(x). Reflexivity means J_X is onto.
Every bounded sequence in a real reflexive Banach space has a weakly convergent subsequence; every closed norm ball (any center) is weakly compact.

An extended-real objective is proper if it never takes −∞ and is finite somewhere. Coercivity on C means each real sublevel in C is bounded. Weak sequential closedness means containment of all weak sequential limits. Weak sequential lower semicontinuity on C means J(x)≤liminf J(x_n) for every weakly convergent sequence in C with limit x∈C.

Let J be proper on nonempty C. If C is compact and J lower semicontinuous, J has a finite attained infimum. More generally, it suffices that for some finite-energy x₀∈C, {x∈C:J(x)≤J(x₀)} is compact and J is lower semicontinuous on that sublevel.
Let J be proper on nonempty closed C in finite dimension. If J is lower semicontinuous on C and coercive on C, it attains its infimum.

In a real reflexive Banach space, if C is nonempty and weakly sequentially closed and J is proper on C, bounded below, coercive and weakly sequentially lower semicontinuous on C, then J attains its infimum.

For proper J on nonempty C, if for some real α the sublevel {x∈C:J(x)≤α} is nonempty and weakly compact and J is weakly lower semicontinuous on it, then J attains its infimum. Nonemptiness of the sublevel is required; this is the compact direct method in the weak topology.

On the closed unit ball of ℓ²(ℕ;ℝ), J(x)=1−‖x‖²+∑_{j≥1}x_j²/j is norm continuous and positive at every point, yet J(e_n)=1/n, so inf J=0 is not attained. Moreover e_n⇀0 and J(0)=1, so J is not weakly lower semicontinuous.

For convex C and proper convex J:C→(−∞,+∞], every finite local minimizer is global. If J is strictly convex between distinct finite points it has at most one minimizer. If J extends to a differentiable convex function on an open convex Euclidean neighborhood of C, then x*∈C minimizes J iff ⟨∇J(x*),y−x*⟩≥0 for all y∈C.
Let differentiable J:ℝ^d→ℝ be μ-strongly convex for μ>0, meaning J−μ‖·‖²/2 is convex. If x* minimizes J, then for every x∈ℝ^d, (μ/2)‖x−x*‖²≤J(x)−J(x*)≤‖∇J(x)‖²/(2μ).

Let (M,d) be complete and f:M→(−∞,+∞] proper, lower semicontinuous and bounded below. For ε,λ>0 and x₀ with f(x₀)≤inf_M f+ε, there is x*∈M with f(x*)≤f(x₀), d(x₀,x*)≤λ, and f(y)>f(x*)−(ε/λ)d(y,x*) for every y≠x*.
Under Ekeland’s hypotheses/conclusion with M a Banach space X carrying its norm metric, if f is Fréchet differentiable at the supplied x*, then ‖Df(x*)‖≤ε/λ.

For a nonempty closed convex C in real Hilbert H, every x∈H has a unique nearest point P_Cx∈C, characterized by p=P_Cx iff p∈C and ⟨x−p,y−p⟩≤0 for all y∈C. For every x,z, ‖P_Cx−P_Cz‖²≤⟨P_Cx−P_Cz,x−z⟩. The complex Hilbert version uses the real part of the inner product and convexity with real parameters.

Let H be real Hilbert, C⊆H nonempty closed convex, and a:H×H→ℝ bilinear with |a(u,v)|≤M‖u‖‖v‖ and a(v,v)≥α‖v‖² for all u,v, α>0. For ℓ∈H′ there is a unique u∈C satisfying a(u,v−u)≥ℓ(v−u) for every v∈C. If a is symmetric, this inequality is equivalent to minimizing v↦a(v,v)/2−ℓ(v) on C. The zero-dimensional case is included.

Let H be real or complex Hilbert, a bounded bilinear real form or bounded complex sesquilinear form conjugate-linear in its first (unknown) slot and linear in its second (test) slot, and ℓ a continuous linear functional in the test variable. If Re a(v,v)≥α‖v‖² for all v, α>0, then there is exactly one u with a(u,v)=ℓ(v) for all v and ‖u‖≤‖ℓ‖/α. When a is real symmetric or complex Hermitian, u is the unique minimizer of E(v)=a(v,v)/2−Re ℓ(v) (the diagonal is then real).

The concluding discussion explains that coercivity suffices for the full variational equation and estimate, while energy minimization requires symmetry/Hermitian symmetry; the more explicit symmetric/Hermitian-part characterizations are inventoried at chapter 9. Citations and this explanation add no stronger nonsymmetric energy assertion.

For real locally convex Hausdorff spaces X,Y and a proper convex extended-real function Φ on X×Y, define the perturbation marginal v(u)=inf_{x∈X} Φ(x,u), with inf ∅=+∞. X′,Y′ are continuous duals and ⟨y,u⟩=y(u). The marginal may take −∞ before properness is established.

The marginal v of a proper convex Φ satisfies the convexity inequality at finite endpoint values. If one marginal endpoint has value −∞ and the other admits a finite candidate, every interior convex combination of those perturbations has marginal value −∞. In particular the extended-real marginal is convex with these conventions; properness is a separate condition.

For the perturbation construction on real locally convex Hausdorff X,Y, assume v is proper and p=v(0)∈ℝ. For every y∈Y′, v*(y)=Φ*(0,y). The dual value d=sup_{y∈Y′}[−Φ*(0,y)] equals v**(0) and satisfies d≤p. Equality d=p holds if and only if v is lower semicontinuous at 0. A given continuous functional y attains the dual value with d=p if and only if y∈∂v(0). Neither primal attainment nor global lower semicontinuity is assumed.

Let v be a convex marginal value on a real normed space. If v(0)∈ℝ and there exist M<∞ and r>0 with v(u)≤M whenever ‖u‖<r, then v is proper, is Lipschitz on some neighborhood of 0, and has a continuous subgradient at 0.

Explanation of the already stated perturbation theorem: lower semicontinuity at one point controls equality of values, whereas a continuous affine minorant through the graph point controls attainment. References provide context, not extra deliverables.

Let X,Y be finite-dimensional real spaces, A:X→Y linear, and f:X→ℝ∪{+∞}, g:Y→ℝ∪{+∞} proper convex. If A(ri dom f)∩ri dom g≠∅ and p=inf_x[f(x)+g(Ax)]∈ℝ, then p=max_{y∈Y′}{−f*(−A*y)−g*(y)}. The maximum is attained. No closedness of f or g, no primal attainment, and no full-dimensionality of the perturbation domain are required.

Applicability explanation for finite-dimensional Fenchel duality: the qualification admits lower-dimensional perturbation spaces, including S={0}; proper closed convex functions are included, but closedness is not required. The mathematical scope is included in v04_finite_fenchel.

Let X,Y be real Banach spaces, A:X→Y bounded linear, and f,g proper convex on X,Y. Suppose some x₀∈dom f has g finite and continuous at Ax₀ in the ambient norm topology of Y. If p=inf_x[f(x)+g(Ax)]∈ℝ, then p=max_{y∈Y′}{−f*(−A*y)−g*(y)}, with attainment in the continuous dual Y′. Primal attainment and closedness of f,g are not hypotheses.

Explanation distinguishing ambient norm continuity in the Banach theorem from the finite-dimensional relative-interior qualification. The pointer to coercivity, weak sequential lower semicontinuity and reflexivity recalls the earlier direct method for primal attainment; this paragraph does not impose primal attainment on the duality theorem.

For proper convex f,g on a real Banach space, if g is finite and norm-continuous at some point of dom f, then ∂(f+g)(x)=∂f(x)+∂g(x) at every x where both f,g are finite. In finite dimension the norm-continuity qualification may instead be ri dom f∩ri dom g≠∅.

Let B(x)=Ax+b, where A is bounded linear between real Banach spaces and g is proper convex on the target. If g is finite and norm-continuous at some Bx₀, then at every x with g(Bx)<∞, ∂(g∘B)(x)=A*∂g(Bx). In finite dimension the qualification may instead be B(X)∩ri dom g≠∅. The translation b is retained.

Let f be proper convex on a finite-dimensional real space X and P={x:a_i(x)≤b_i (1≤i≤m), e_j(x)=d_j (1≤j≤k)} with linear a_i,e_j. If ri dom f∩P≠∅ and p=inf_P f∈ℝ, then there exist λ_i≥0 and ν_j∈ℝ such that f(x)+Σ_i λ_i(a_i(x)−b_i)+Σ_j ν_j(e_j(x)−d_j)≥p for every x∈dom f. With n=Σ_i λ_i a_i+Σ_j ν_j e_j, the same bound is f(x)+n(x)−max_P n≥p; the indicated maximum on P exists. Empty constraint families are allowed.
A proper convex extended-real function g on a finite-dimensional real space is polyhedral when epi g is a polyhedron.

Let f,g be proper convex functions on a finite-dimensional real space, with g polyhedral (epi g a polyhedron). If ri dom f∩dom g≠∅, then ∂(f+g)(x)=∂f(x)+∂g(x) at every common finite point. The condition uses dom g, not ri dom g.

For convex sets C,D and x∈C∩D, N_{C∩D}(x)=N_C(x)+N_D(x) under the corresponding exact indicator-sum qualification: in a real Banach space, I_D is finite and norm-continuous at some point of C (or with C,D interchanged); in finite dimension ri C∩ri D≠∅ suffices. In finite dimension, if D is a polyhedron it suffices that D∩ri C≠∅. Normal cones use n(z−x)≤0 for z in the set.

For proper closed convex f,g and bounded linear A between the primal and target spaces, define the Fenchel saddle function ℒ(z,w)=f(z)+⟨w,Az⟩−g*(w) for z∈dom f and w∈dom g*. The source does not restate stronger ambient-space assumptions in this theorem.

For proper closed convex f,g and bounded linear A, take x with finite primal objective f(x)+g(Ax) and y with f*(−A*y),g*(y) finite. The primal–dual gap f(x)+g(Ax)+f*(−A*y)+g*(y) vanishes if and only if −A*y∈∂f(x) and y∈∂g(Ax). These conditions are equivalent to ℒ(x,w)≤ℒ(x,y)≤ℒ(z,y) for every z∈dom f,w∈dom g*, where ℒ(z,w)=f(z)+⟨w,Az⟩−g*(w).

Under the perturbation-duality assumptions (proper convex marginal v on a real locally convex Hausdorff space with p=v(0)∈ℝ), every dual maximizer y of value p gives v(u)≥p+⟨y,u⟩ for every u. If the perturbation space is normed and v is finite and Fréchet differentiable at 0, the unique continuous supporting functional at 0 is Dv(0).

In a finite-dimensional real space minimize a convex f subject to convex g_i(x)≤0 and affine a_i(x)≤b_i,e_j(x)=d_j. Put D=dom f∩⋂_i dom g_i and let P be the polyhedron of affine constraints. If the primal value p is finite and some x₀∈ri D∩P has g_i(x₀)<0 for every inequality in the convex first group, then the Lagrange dual, whose defining infimum is over D, attains value p with nonnegative multipliers for all inequalities and free multipliers for equalities. The witness may have equality in affine inequalities. The first group may be empty; strict feasibility is then vacuous.

Proof interpretation and references: strict nonlinear inequalities give an open perturbation neighborhood; affine constraints are treated through the polyhedron and supporting normals. This is explanation of the refined Slater proof, not an additional statement to formalize.

For the finite-dimensional convex problem of v04_refined_slater, a feasible finite x* is a global minimizer if admissible multipliers (nonnegative on inequalities and unrestricted on equalities) make x* minimize the Lagrangian on D and each inequality multiplier times its residual at x* vanishes. This sufficiency needs no Slater qualification. Conversely, if the refined Slater hypotheses hold and x* attains the optimum, such multipliers exist. Complementarity applies to both convex inequalities and affine inequalities.

For the convex KKT problem, global minimization of the Lagrangian over D is equivalent to 0∈∂(ℒ+I_D)(x*), extending the function by +∞ outside D. For differentiable convex data on an open convex domain containing x*, this is equivalent to the usual gradient stationarity equation. The four KKT requirements are primal feasibility, nonnegative inequality multipliers, stationarity and complementarity.

For min_{x∈ℝ} x subject to x²≤0, the primal value 0 is attained at x=0. The Lagrange dual function is −1/(4λ) for λ>0 and −∞ for λ=0. Hence the dual supremum is 0, equal to the primal value, but no admissible finite multiplier λ≥0 attains it.

For minimizing e^(−x) on {(x,y):y>0} subject to x²/y≤0, the constraint function is convex (the perspective of the square). Every feasible point has x=0, so p=1. For every λ≥0, inf_{x∈ℝ,y>0}[e^(−x)+λx²/y]=0: the expression is nonnegative and tends to 0 as x→+∞ with y=x³. Thus the attained dual value is 0 and the duality gap is 1.
The two examples illustrate distinct failures when the qualification is absent; bibliographic cross-reference only.

For a real matrix A and compatible real vectors b,c, the standard primal linear program is inf{cᵀx:Ax=b,x≥0}; its dual is sup{bᵀy:Aᵀy≤c}, where inequalities are coordinatewise and y is unrestricted in sign.

For the standard primal–dual linear programs, if the primal is feasible and its value is finite, both primal and dual optima are attained and have equal values. For every feasible pair (x,y), cᵀx−bᵀy=Σ_i x_i(c−Aᵀy)_i; every summand is nonnegative and the gap is zero exactly when every summand is zero.

For the standard primal–dual linear programs: if both are feasible, both have finite attained optima; if exactly one is feasible, that side is unbounded in its optimizing direction (primal infimum −∞ or dual supremum +∞). It is also possible that both sides are infeasible.

A free real variable can be replaced by the difference of two nonnegative variables, and an affine inequality can be replaced by an equality with a nonnegative slack variable. These substitutions preserve feasibility and objective values, extending standard-form linear-program duality to general finite polyhedral linear programs.

Let Q be a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix and P a nonempty polyhedron. If p=inf_{x∈P}[½xᵀQx+cᵀx] is finite, the infimum is attained. At every x*∈P, global optimality is equivalent to −(Qx*+c)∈N_P(x*). For any affine inequality/equality description of P, this is equivalent to existence of KKT multipliers, with free equality multipliers, nonnegative inequality multipliers and complementarity for the inequalities.

Let A have full row rank and Q be real symmetric. Assume uᵀQu>0 for every nonzero u∈ker A; positivity is only required on feasible differences. For every b,c, the block system [Q Aᵀ; A 0][x;ν]=[−c;b] has a unique solution, and its x is the unique global minimizer of ½xᵀQx+cᵀx over Ax=b. The kernel may be {0}, making its positivity condition vacuous; Q need not be positive semidefinite on the whole space.

Positive semidefiniteness of Q on the ambient space alone does not ensure feasibility of a quadratic-program constraint system or boundedness of its objective: the constraints may be infeasible, and a linear objective can be unbounded along ker Q. Reduced-Hessian positivity refers only to feasible differences.

Let X,Y be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, K⊆X a closed convex cone containing 0, A:X→Y linear, b∈Y,c∈X. Its positive dual is K*={s∈X:⟨s,x⟩≥0 for all x∈K}. The conic primal and dual are inf_{x∈K,Ax=b}⟨c,x⟩ and sup_{y∈Y,c−A*y∈K*}⟨b,y⟩.
For any feasible pair of the conic programs, ⟨c,x⟩−⟨b,y⟩=⟨c−A*y,x⟩≥0. Zero primal–dual gap is equivalent to the complementary pairing ⟨c−A*y,x⟩=0.

For the finite-dimensional conic primal–dual pair with K closed convex, if the primal value is finite and there exists x₀∈ri K with Ax₀=b, then the dual maximum is attained and equals the primal value. Relative interior, rather than ambient interior, suffices, and primal attainment is not claimed.

For the same conic pair, if the dual value is finite and there exists y₀ with c−A*y₀∈ri K*, then the primal minimum is attained and equals the dual value. This uses strict feasibility on the dual side and does not assume primal feasibility in advance.
Explanation of the two conic Slater statements: a relative-interior witness on one side supplies attainment on the opposite side under a finite-value assumption. Reference only beyond those results.
The nonnegative orthant in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space is self-dual under its Euclidean inner product, using the positive-dual convention.
The Lorentz cone ℚ={(t,u):t≥‖u‖₂} in ℝ×ℝⁿ is self-dual under the product Euclidean pairing.
The cone Sⁿ_+ of real symmetric positive semidefinite n×n matrices is self-dual in the real vector space of symmetric matrices under ⟨S,T⟩=tr(ST).

For a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix R, define R† to act as the inverse of R on ran R and as 0 on ker R, using the orthogonal decomposition into range and kernel. Singular and zero R are included.

For every real symmetric positive semidefinite R, real scalar t and compatible vector w, the symmetric block matrix [t wᵀ;w R] is positive semidefinite if and only if w∈ran R and t≥wᵀR†w. No invertibility of R is assumed; the range condition is essential.
The constraint ‖Bx+d‖₂≤aᵀx+β is exactly the affine Lorentz-cone constraint (aᵀx+β,Bx+d)∈ℚ. In particular it includes the nonnegativity of the scalar right-hand side.
The squared-norm epigraph t≥‖Bx+d‖₂² is exactly the semidefinite constraint [t (Bx+d)ᵀ; Bx+d I]⪰0, obtained from the Schur complement with R=I.

An affine cone constraint can be put in standard conic form by introducing a cone-valued variable and an equality identifying it with the affine expression. Free variables can be incorporated by taking a product cone with a full linear space. These substitutions give the standard second-order-cone and semidefinite representations and preserve the represented constraints.

The projection of S²_+ to the (a,b) coordinates of [a b;b c] has image {(a,b):a>0}∪{(0,0)}, which is not closed. The target (0,1) is infeasible but lies in the closure of that image (weak infeasibility). There is no strict separating conic Farkas certificate: no continuous linear functional nonnegative on the image can take a negative value at (0,1).

The semidefinite program inf{a:[a 1;1 c]⪰0} is strictly feasible (for example a=c=2 is positive definite). Its finite primal infimum is 0 and is not attained; its conic dual has attained maximum 0. Thus primal strict feasibility does not ensure primal attainment.

Let M be a real m×n matrix with m,n≥1 and Δ_m={p∈ℝᵐ:p≥0,Σ_i p_i=1}, Δ_n={q∈ℝⁿ:q≥0,Σ_j q_j=1}. Then max_{p∈Δ_m}min_{q∈Δ_n}pᵀMq=min_{q∈Δ_n}max_{p∈Δ_m}pᵀMq. Both outer optima are attained, and there exist p*,q* forming a saddle at the common value v: for every p∈Δ_m,q∈Δ_n, pᵀMq*≤p*ᵀMq*=v≤p*ᵀMq.
This chapter proves finite polyhedral minimax; the general topological minimax problem has distinct compactness and continuity assumptions and is referenced only as context.

Let f be real-valued on an open subset U of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and x*∈U. If f is differentiable at a local minimizer x*, then Df(x*)=0. If f is twice Fréchet differentiable there, its Hessian at the local minimizer is positive semidefinite.
