Conversely, twice Fréchet differentiability at x*, Df(x*)=0 and positive definiteness of D²f(x*) imply existence of c,ρ>0 with f(x)≥f(x*)+c‖x−x*‖² whenever ‖x−x*‖<ρ (shrinking ρ inside U). The result includes dimension 0; no C²-neighborhood hypothesis is added to the stated pointwise twice Fréchet differentiability.
At 0, the real functions x↦x⁴ and x↦−x⁴ have identical zero gradient and zero Hessian, but 0 is a strict minimum of the first and a strict maximum of the second.

On the real Hilbert space ℓ², F(x)=½Σ_{j=1}^∞2^(−j)x_j²−‖x‖⁴ is smooth, DF(0)=0, and D²F(0)[h,h]=Σ_j2^(−j)h_j²>0 for every h≠0. Nevertheless F(2^(−j/2)e_j)=−2^(−2j)/2 and 2^(−j/2)e_j→0, so 0 is not a local minimum. Strict positivity of the Hessian on each nonzero vector in infinite dimension does not give a uniform positive quadratic lower bound; such a bound must be checked separately for the finite-dimensional growth argument to extend.

Let h:U→Y be Cʳ, r≥1, on an open subset U of a real Banach space X, where Y is a real Banach space. If h(x*)=0 and B=Dh(x*) has a bounded linear right inverse R:Y→X, then near x* the feasible set h=0 is a Cʳ graph over K=ker B (using the complement R(Y)). Every d∈K is the derivative at parameter 0 of a Cʳ curve through x* lying in h=0, defined for both positive and negative sufficiently small parameters.

Under the Banach equality-chart assumptions, if x* locally minimizes f on h=0 and f is differentiable at x*, there is a unique ν∈Y′ with Df(x*)+Dh(x*)*ν=0. In finite dimensions, surjectivity of Dh(x*) alone suffices for both the graph and multiplier conclusions, since a bounded linear right inverse then exists.

For finitely many equality constraints on a real Banach space (finite-dimensional target Y), a surjective derivative has a bounded linear right inverse, obtained by choosing preimages of a basis. Thus the equality-chart and equality-multiplier conclusions apply under surjectivity in this setting as well; the integral-constraint pointer is an application context.

For C¹ objective/constraint data on an open subset of a finite-dimensional real space, the smooth feasible set is S={x:g_i(x)≤0 (1≤i≤m), h_j(x)=0 (1≤j≤k)}. At a feasible x*, the active inequality index set is I={i:g_i(x*)=0}. The equality vector is h=(h_j)_j, and empty constraint families are allowed.
At x*∈S, the Bouligand tangent cone T_S(x*) consists of all limits d=lim_n (x_n−x*)/t_n for sequences x_n∈S and real t_n>0 with t_n→0. No monotonicity of t_n beyond convergence to 0 is required.
At a feasible x*, define C_lin={d:Dh(x*)d=0 and Dg_i(x*)d≤0 for every active i∈I}. Only active inequalities occur in this cone.
LICQ at a feasible point means linear independence of the equality differentials Dh_j(x*) together with the active inequality differentials Dg_i(x*) for i∈I.
MFCQ at a feasible point means Dh(x*) is surjective and there exists w∈ker Dh(x*) with Dg_i(x*)w<0 for every active i∈I. When I is empty the strict inequality requirement is vacuous.
For the finite-dimensional C¹ smooth feasible set, always T_S(x*)⊆C_lin. Under MFCQ, T_S(x*)=C_lin. LICQ implies MFCQ, including the cases of empty active or equality families.

For the minimization convention g_i≤0,h_j=0, the KKT system at x* consists of primal feasibility, λ_i≥0, λ_i g_i(x*)=0 for every i, and Df(x*)+Σ_i λ_iDg_i(x*)+Σ_j ν_jDh_j(x*)=0, with equality multipliers ν_j unrestricted in sign.

At a constrained local minimum x* of finite-dimensional C¹ data, there exist λ₀,λ_i≥0 and ν_j∈ℝ, jointly nonzero, such that λ₀Df(x*)+Σ_i λ_iDg_i(x*)+Σ_j ν_jDh_j(x*)=0 and λ_i g_i(x*)=0 for every i. Under MFCQ the objective coefficient λ₀ is positive, so division by λ₀ gives the KKT system. LICQ in particular suffices. Without qualification λ₀=0 (the abnormal case) is allowed.

An explicitly introduced alternative qualified proof of KKT uses the necessary tangent-direction inequality Df(x*)d≥0, equality of tangent and linearized cones under MFCQ, and the polyhedral polar formula. These are proof-route explanations for the already required KKT conclusion, not an additional deliverable requiring this particular argument. Bibliographic references are contextual.

At a constrained local minimizer of finite-dimensional C¹ data satisfying LICQ, the KKT multiplier pair is unique. At a constrained local minimizer satisfying MFCQ, the KKT multiplier set is nonempty and compact. Compactness does not imply uniqueness.
For minimizing −x subject to two copies of x≤0, 0 is a constrained minimizer and MFCQ holds there with w=−1. Its KKT multiplier set is exactly {(λ₁,λ₂):λ₁,λ₂≥0, λ₁+λ₂=1}, a compact non-singleton set.
Complementarity requires only λ_i g_i(x*)=0. Strict complementarity additionally requires λ_i>0 for every active inequality.
For minimizing x² subject to x≤0, LICQ holds at the minimizer 0 and the unique KKT multiplier is λ=0. Thus LICQ need not imply strict complementarity.

For minimizing x subject to x²≤0, 0 is the only feasible point. KKT stationarity with objective coefficient 1 is impossible because Dg(0)=0 and Df(0)=1. An abnormal Fritz John tuple exists with objective coefficient λ₀=0 and inequality multiplier λ=1.
At a feasible KKT point x* with a chosen KKT pair (λ,ν), define the critical cone C_crit={d∈C_lin:Df(x*)d≤0} and L=f+Σ_i λ_i g_i+Σ_j ν_j h_j. L uses the same fixed multipliers as the KKT system.

At a feasible KKT point, every d∈C_lin satisfies Df(x*)d=−Σ_{i∈I}λ_iDg_i(x*)d≥0. Consequently d∈C_crit exactly when Df(x*)d=0, and equivalently exactly when Dg_i(x*)d=0 for every i with λ_i>0. In particular each critical direction has these zero derivatives; these characterizations are among linearized directions and include the case of no positive multipliers.
Assume f,g_i,h_j are C² near a constrained local minimum x* in a finite-dimensional real space and LICQ holds there. Form L using its KKT multipliers. Then D²L(x*)[d,d]≥0 for every d∈C_crit.

Explanation of why LICQ is used in the preceding proof: it realizes each critical direction with the needed active equalities. Reference only; it does not introduce another constraint qualification or conclusion.

Let f,g_i,h_j be C² near a feasible point x* of the finite-dimensional smooth problem. Suppose one fixed multiplier pair (λ,ν) satisfies KKT at x*. If D²L(x*)[d,d]>0 for every nonzero d∈C_crit, then there exist c,ρ>0 such that f(x)≥f(x*)+c‖x−x*‖² for every feasible x with ‖x−x*‖<ρ. In particular x* is a strict local minimizer relative to the feasible set. No constraint qualification is assumed, and C_crit={0} is allowed, making the Hessian condition vacuous.

Explanation of the scope of the fixed-multiplier sufficiency theorem: it starts with a KKT pair and uses feasible secants and finite-dimensional compactness, so it applies without any constraint qualification. This applicability is already retained in v06_constrained_quadratic_growth.

For a<b and u:[a,b]→ℝ^m, the action is J(u)=∫_a^b L(t,u(t),u′(t))dt. The state variable is z, the velocity variable is v, and the momentum and state derivative along u are p(t)=L_v(t,u(t),u′(t)) and q(t)=L_z(t,u(t),u′(t)), with Euclidean derivative pairings.

For C¹ curves with fixed endpoint values, a weak local minimum is a minimum in a C¹ neighborhood within the admissible class, whereas a strong local minimum uses the uniform distance between curves. This chapter’s weak-local-minimum terminology refers to this topology, rather than weak Banach-space convergence; the competitor class permits piecewise C¹ curves only where later specified.
Fundamental lemma: if h∈L¹_loc(a,b) and ∫_a^b hφ=0 for every φ∈C_c^∞(a,b), then h=0 almost everywhere. If h is also continuous, then h vanishes everywhere on (a,b).

If p,q∈L¹_loc((a,b);ℝ^m) satisfy ∫_a^b(p·φ′+q·φ)=0 for every φ∈C_c^∞((a,b);ℝ^m), then the L¹_loc class p has a locally absolutely continuous representative whose derivative equals q almost everywhere.

First variation at fixed endpoints: let u∈C¹([a,b];ℝ^m) be a weak or strong local minimum with fixed endpoints, and let L be C¹ on an open neighborhood of the complete path (t,u(t),u′(t)). For every η∈C¹([a,b];ℝ^m) with η(a)=η(b)=0, DJ(u)[η]=∫_a^b(q·η+p·η′)dt=0. Consequently p′=q in distributions; under these continuity assumptions p is C¹ and p′(t)=q(t) pointwise on (a,b).

The same interior first-variation identity ∫_a^b(q·η+p·η′)dt=0 holds for every compactly supported smooth variation η if the unperturbed energy is finite and, for each such η, s=0 is a two-sided local minimum of J(u+sη), the integrand along this line is differentiable in s near zero for almost every t, and its s-derivative for small s is bounded in absolute value by one integrable function of t (which may depend on η).

Inner time variation: for u∈C¹([a,b];ℝ^m) stationary under compactly supported changes of time and a C¹ Lagrangian L, H(t)=L(t,u(t),u′(t))−p(t)·u′(t) is C¹ and H′(t)=L_t(t,u(t),u′(t)). In particular a C¹ local minimum is stationary under those changes of time.

Moving-endpoint boundary formula: let u be a C¹ extremal with p′=q, stationary under compactly supported changes of time, and let L be C¹ on an open neighborhood of its state–velocity graph including both endpoints. Consider u_s on [a_s,b_s], u_0=u, where a_s,b_s are differentiable at zero and, for the increasing affine map t_s:[a,b]→[a_s,b_s], z_s(t)=u_s(t_s(t)) is differentiable at zero as a C¹([a,b];ℝ^m)-valued map. If δt is the endpoint time variation and δz is the total endpoint state variation, the action’s first variation is [p·δz+(L−p·u′)δt]_a^b, with the right endpoint contribution minus the left.

Under the moving-endpoint setup, at a C¹ local minimum whose independent endpoint constraints are smooth submanifolds of time–state space, the endpoint covector (δt,δz)↦p·δz+(L−p·u′)δt annihilates each endpoint submanifold’s tangent space. At a fixed time with free state this gives p=0; at a fixed time with state constrained to a submanifold, p annihilates its state tangent space.
In the transversality setup, a free terminal time with terminal state held fixed gives the terminal condition L−p·u′=0.

Du Bois–Reymond identity: let L be C¹ near u, let p=L_v(t,u,u′) be C¹ with p′=L_z(t,u,u′), and suppose either u∈C² or u∈C¹ is stationary under compactly supported time changes. Then d/dt[L(t,u,u′)−p(t)·u′(t)]=L_t(t,u,u′).

Under the first-integrals proposition’s hypotheses (L C¹ near u, p=L_v C¹, p′=L_z, and either u C² or u C¹ stationary under compactly supported time changes), an autonomous L gives a constant L−p·u′, and a state coordinate absent from L gives a constant corresponding component of p.

Isoperimetric multiplier rule: J and G=(G₁,…,G_k) are integrals of C¹ integrands near a C¹ curve u with fixed endpoints, and u is a constrained local minimum under G=G(u). For the vector space V of C¹ endpoint-zero variations, there exist multipliers (λ₀,λ)≠0 with λ₀≥0 such that λ₀DJ(u)[η]+λ·DG(u)[η]=0 for every η∈V.
Under the isoperimetric multiplier rule’s hypotheses, if DG(u):V→ℝ^k is surjective, one may normalize λ₀=1 and the resulting λ∈ℝ^k is unique.
An isoperimetric multiplier (λ₀,λ) is abnormal when λ₀=0.

For the stationary augmented integrand supplied by the isoperimetric multiplier rule, the fundamental lemma gives its Euler–Lagrange equation: writing J=∫L and G_i=∫K_i, the integrand λ₀L+∑_i λ_iK_i has d/dt[λ₀L_v+∑_i λ_i(K_i)_v]=λ₀L_z+∑_i λ_i(K_i)_z along u (at least distributionally, and with the C¹ regularity obtained from the continuous coefficients).

At a classical C¹ weak local minimum with fixed endpoints and C² integrand, the second variation is Q(η)=∫_a^b[L_zz[η,η]+2L_zv[η,η′]+L_vv[η′,η′]]dt and is nonnegative for every C¹ endpoint-zero variation η; all second derivatives are evaluated at (t,u(t),u′(t)).
Legendre necessity in one dimension: at a classical C¹ weak local minimum with fixed endpoints and C² integrand, L_vv(t,u(t),u′(t)) is positive semidefinite for every interior t∈(a,b).

Legendre–Hadamard necessity: let Ω⊆ℝ^d be open, u:Ω→ℝ^m be C¹, L(x,z,F) be C² near the graph (x,u,∇u), and u be a weak local minimum under compactly supported smooth variations of the finite energy ∫_ΩL(x,u,∇u)dx. Then for every x∈Ω, e∈ℝ^m and b∈ℝ^d, L_FF(x,u(x),∇u(x))[e⊗b,e⊗b]≥0.
The quadratic form F↦det F on 2×2 real matrices vanishes on rank-one matrices but takes both signs on general matrices, illustrating that the Legendre–Hadamard condition is only a rank-one test.

Coercive scalar second variation and sufficient condition: let a scalar C² stationary curve u have fixed endpoints and C³ integrand near its graph. Along u set P=L_vv, B=L_zv, C₀=L_zz and V=C₀−B′, and suppose P>0 throughout [a,b]. Let v₀ solve (Pv₀′)′=Vv₀ with v₀(a)=0 and v₀′(a)=1. If v₀ has no zero in (a,b], then ∃κ>0 such that Q(η)≥κ‖η‖²_H¹ for all η∈H¹₀(a,b). Moreover u is a strict weak local minimum: in a sufficiently small C¹ neighborhood among the fixed-endpoint curves, J(u+η)−J(u)≥c‖η‖²_H¹ for some c>0 and every endpoint-zero perturbation η.

The explanatory sentence identifies the positive lower bound for the quadratic form as the reason Taylor’s remainder can be absorbed; it introduces no additional result beyond the preceding coercive sufficient condition.

Weierstrass excess inequality: suppose u∈C¹ is a strong local minimum among continuous piecewise C¹ curves with fixed endpoints. Fix t₀∈(a,b) and a tested velocity w∈ℝ^m. Assume L is C¹ on an open neighborhood of the reference graph and the graph obtained by inserting velocity w near t₀, including all velocity segments joining the two graphs. Then L(t₀,u(t₀),w)−L(t₀,u(t₀),u′(t₀))−p(t₀)·(w−u′(t₀))≥0.

Weierstrass–Erdmann corner conditions: let u be a continuous piecewise C² curve with a single interior corner c, stationary on both pieces, and a strong local minimum in a class allowing piecewise C¹ perturbations at c. Assume L is C¹ on an open neighborhood of both closed one-sided state–velocity graphs, including both limiting velocities at c. If the joined state is free, p(c⁻)=p(c⁺). If the corner time is also free, (L−p·u′)(c⁻)=(L−p·u′)(c⁺).

Periodic Wirtinger inequality with equality cases: for a scalar C¹ function f of period T>0 with ∫₀ᵀf=0, ∫₀ᵀ|f|²≤(T/(2π))²∫₀ᵀ|f′|². Equality holds exactly when f(t)=A cos(2πt/T)+B sin(2πt/T) for real A,B, including A=B=0.

Planar isoperimetric inequality: a regular C¹ simple closed plane curve parametrized by a C¹ embedding of the circle, enclosing area A and having length T, satisfies 4πA≤T². Equality holds exactly for circles.
For a bounded open Ω⊆ℝ^d and scalar u∈W^{1,1}(Ω), the graph-area functional is A(u)=∫_Ω√(1+|∇u|²)dx.

For bounded open Ω⊆ℝ^d and scalar u∈W^{1,1}(Ω), graph area has directional first variation along every φ∈C_c^∞(Ω) given by ∫_Ω(∇u·∇φ)/√(1+|∇u|²)dx. Hence a local minimum under these two-sided tests satisfies the weak minimal-surface equation ∫_Ω(∇u·∇φ)/√(1+|∇u|²)dx=0 for all such φ.
Throughout Chapter 8, Ω⊆ℝ^d is bounded and open with d≥1, the maps take values in ℝ^m with m≥1, Du is the m×d matrix of weak first derivatives, and matrix pairings are Frobenius pairings.

A Carathéodory integrand is measurable in the base point and continuous in its finite-dimensional arguments for almost every base point. One may choose a common exceptional null set and define the integrand harmlessly there.
Composition of a Carathéodory integrand with measurable fields in its finite-dimensional arguments is measurable.
The exposition distinguishes the lower bound used for existence from the upper derivative bound used for stationarity; these assumptions have different roles and are not interchangeable.
For 1≤p<∞, W^{1,p}(Ω;ℝ^m) is the space of L^p equivalence classes whose distributional first derivatives belong to L^p, with norm (‖u‖_p^p+‖Du‖_p^p)^{1/p}.
W^{1,p}_0(Ω;ℝ^m) is the closure of C_c^∞(Ω;ℝ^m) in the stated Sobolev norm. For prescribed u₀∈W^{1,p}(Ω;ℝ^m), the admissible affine class is u₀+W^{1,p}_0(Ω;ℝ^m), for 1≤p<∞.

On a bounded Lipschitz open set, for 1≤p<∞ the ordinary trace map into L^p(∂Ω) has kernel W^{1,p}_0(Ω); the identification of zero boundary values with zero trace is asserted only in this Lipschitz setting.
For 1≤p<∞, W^{1,p}(Ω;ℝ^m) is Banach; for 1<p<∞ it is also reflexive.
For 1≤p<∞ and u₀∈W^{1,p}(Ω;ℝ^m), the prescribed affine class u₀+W^{1,p}_0(Ω;ℝ^m) is norm closed and weakly closed.

For 1≤p<∞, extending u∈W^{1,p}_0(Ω;ℝ^m) by zero to ℝ^d yields an element of W^{1,p}(ℝ^d;ℝ^m) with exactly the same Sobolev norm, and its weak first derivatives are the zero extensions of the weak derivatives of u.

Exact strip Poincaré estimate: if the bounded open Ω is contained in the strip a<x₁<b, then ‖u‖_{L^p(Ω;ℝ^m)}≤(b−a)‖∂₁u‖_{L^p(Ω;ℝ^m)} for every u∈W^{1,p}_0(Ω;ℝ^m), including p=1. The norms of the vector values are Euclidean; no boundary regularity or connectedness assumption is imposed.
For 1≤p<∞ and bounded Lipschitz Ω, every bounded subset of W^{1,p}(Ω;ℝ^m) is relatively compact in L^p(Ω;ℝ^m).
For 1≤p<∞ and arbitrary bounded open Ω, every bounded subset of a fixed affine class u₀+W^{1,p}_0(Ω;ℝ^m) is relatively compact in L^p(Ω;ℝ^m).

The section explains that convexity is required only in the gradient/fiber variables for the following lower-semicontinuity result, and that its different fiber exponents will later apply to minors; the citations and motivation add no separate obligation.

Strong–weak lower semicontinuity: let (S,μ) have finite measure, 1≤q<∞ and 1<r_i<∞ for i=1,…,k. Suppose s_n→s strongly in L^q(S;ℝ^m) and z_{i,n}⇀z_i weakly in L^{r_i}(S;ℝ^{d_i}). Write z=(z₁,…,z_k). Let F(x,s,z) be finite Carathéodory and convex in the entire z-vector for each s at almost every x. Assume uniformly in s,z that F(x,s,z)≥−a(x)−C|s|^q, where a∈L¹(S) and C≥0. Then ∫_S F(x,s(x),z(x))dμ≤liminf_n∫_S F(x,s_n(x),z_n(x))dμ. The energy may equal +∞.

Convex-gradient direct method: let Ω be bounded open, p>q≥1, u₀∈W^{1,p}(Ω;ℝ^m), and F(x,s,Z) be finite Carathéodory and convex in Z. Suppose F(x,s,Z)≥α|Z|^p−C|s|^q−a(x) with α>0, C≥0, a∈L¹(Ω). If J(u)=∫_ΩF(x,u,Du)dx is finite at some u in u₀+W^{1,p}_0, then J attains a finite minimum in that affine class.

Scalar Dirichlet model: for bounded open Ω, u₀∈H¹(Ω) and b∈L²(Ω), J(u)=½∫_Ω|Du|²dx−∫_Ωbu dx has a unique minimizer on u₀+H¹₀(Ω). An admissible u is that minimizer exactly when ∫_ΩDu·Dφ dx=∫_Ωbφ dx for every φ∈H¹₀(Ω).

Joint strict convexity uniqueness: on a bounded open Ω, for 1≤p<∞ consider u₀+W^{1,p}_0 and an integral energy whose negative part is integrable at every admissible map. If F(x,·,·) is strictly convex jointly in (s,Z) for almost every x, then any finite minimizer is unique.

Gradient-only strict convexity uniqueness: under the same bounded-open-domain, fixed affine class, 1≤p<∞ and integrable-negative-part hypotheses, any finite minimizer is unique if F is independent of s and is strictly convex in Z for almost every x.

Linear-growth nonattainment: among W^{1,1}(0,1) functions with endpoint values 0 and 1, the convex-gradient functional ∫₀¹(1+x)|u′(x)|dx has infimum 1 and no minimizer. Every competitor has ∫|u′|≥1 and ∫x|u′|>0; u_n(x)=min(nx,1), n≥1, has energy 1+1/(2n). The gradient growth is linear and the energy is coercive on this W^{1,1} affine class.

Lack-of-coercivity nonattainment: on H¹₀(0,1), the finite continuous-valued convex integral J(u)=∫₀¹e^{−u(x)}dx is positive for every competitor but has infimum 0, approached by u_n(x)=nx(1−x). It does not bound the norms of minimizing sequences.

Nonconvex-gradient failure of weak lower semicontinuity: let u_n be the continuous tent map, zero at the endpoints of each of the n subintervals of length 1/n in (0,1), with slopes +1 then −1 on the two halves. Then u_n→0 uniformly and u_n′⇀0 in L⁴(0,1), but ∫₀¹(((u_n′)²−1)²)dx=0 for every n whereas the limiting map 0 has energy 1.

For ordered distinct row and column indices α=(a₁,…,a_j), I=(i₁,…,i_j), listed increasingly, M_{α,I}(Z) is the corresponding j×j determinant minor of an m×d matrix Z. The vector M_j(Z) lists all j-minors; M₁(Z) is the list of matrix entries.
For 1≤j≤min(m,d) and a chosen minor M_{α,I}(Du), C_l(Du) denotes its cofactor in the first row and l-th column; at j=1 the convention is C₁=1.

For each 1≤j≤min(m,d) and each smooth u, the first-row cofactors obey ∑_{l=1}^j ∂_{i_l}C_l(Du)=0, and the minor has divergence form M_{α,I}(Du)=∑_{l=1}^j ∂_{i_l}(u^{a₁}C_l(Du)). These include the convention C₁=1 for j=1.
For 1≤j≤min(m,d), p≥j and u∈W^{1,p}(Ω;ℝ^m), the divergence-form minor identity M_{α,I}(Du)=∑_{l=1}^j ∂_{i_l}(u^{a₁}C_l(Du)) holds distributionally, with C₁=1 at j=1.

Fixed-boundary integrals of minors: for 1≤j≤min(m,d), p≥j, u,v∈W^{1,p}(Ω;ℝ^m), and u−v∈W^{1,p}_0(Ω;ℝ^m), one has ∫_ΩM_j(Du)dx=∫_ΩM_j(Dv)dx, as equality of the complete j-minor vectors. Ω is the chapter’s bounded open set, with no boundary regularity hypothesis.
Weak continuity of minors: for 1≤p<∞, suppose u_n⇀u in W^{1,p}(Ω;ℝ^m) and u_n→u strongly in L^p. For every integer 1≤j

In the weak-minors theorem, for 1≤p<∞ the strong L^p convergence premise is automatic for the full weakly W^{1,p}-convergent sequence when Ω is bounded Lipschitz, or when all sequence members belong to one fixed affine zero-boundary class u₀+W^{1,p}_0 on an arbitrary bounded open Ω.
With r=min(m,d), a polyconvex representation has the form F(x,s,Z)=G(x,s,M₁(Z),…,M_r(Z)), where G is convex in the full vector of independent minor coordinates.
Convex dependence of F on the matrix Z provides a polyconvex representation by letting G ignore all higher-order minor coordinates.

Polyconvex existence: let Ω be bounded Lipschitz, r=min(m,d), p>max(r,q) with q≥1, and let G be a finite Carathéodory polyconvex representation F(x,s,Z)=G(x,s,M₁(Z),…,M_r(Z)), convex in the full vector of independent minor coordinates. Suppose uniformly in independent z₁,…,z_r that G(x,s,z₁,…,z_r)≥α|z₁|^p−C|s|^q−a(x), with α>0, C≥0 and a∈L¹(Ω). For u₀∈W^{1,p}(Ω;ℝ^m), if the energy has a finite competitor in u₀+W^{1,p}_0, then it has a finite minimizer there. This includes 2×2 matrix-and-determinant representations with p>max(2,q).

Polyconvexity implies the quasiconvex test inequality: freeze a base point and value argument, and suppose F has a finite convex representation in the full minor vector. Then for every cube Q, every matrix Z and every φ∈C_c^∞(Q;ℝ^m), F(Z)≤|Q|^{-1}∫_QF(Z+Dφ)dx.

For 2×2 matrices, F(Z)=|Z|^p+(det Z−γ)², with p>2 and γ>0, is polyconvex but not convex. On the line Z=tI, F(tI)−F(0)=2^{p/2}|t|^p−2γt²+t⁴<0 for all sufficiently small nonzero t; evenness along this line excludes convexity.

For the example F(Z)=|Z|^p+(det Z−γ)² on a bounded domain with zero boundary values, the zero map is a finite competitor. When 2<p<4 the energy need not be finite at every W^{1,p} competitor, so the attained energy is allowed to be extended-valued away from its finite minimum.

The full characterization of lower semicontinuity by quasiconvexity and the critical minor exponent p=r are explicitly placed outside the present theorem’s hypotheses and scope; no such general characterization or critical-exponent result is asserted here.

For an integrand differentiable in its state and gradient variables, F_s and F_Z denote those derivatives. The weak Euler–Lagrange identity for an admissible test φ is ∫_Ω[F_s(x,u,Du)·φ+F_Z(x,u,Du):Dφ]dx=0.

Dominated-direction weak Euler–Lagrange theorem: suppose J(u) is finite and, for every φ∈C_c^∞(Ω;ℝ^m), t=0 is a local minimum of J(u+tφ) for both signs of small t. Suppose F is Carathéodory with continuous first derivatives in (s,Z) almost everywhere. For each such direction assume, for all sufficiently small |t|, |F_s(x,u+tφ,Du+tDφ)·φ+F_Z(x,u+tφ,Du+tDφ):Dφ| is bounded by an integrable function of x. Then ∫_Ω[F_s(x,u,Du)·φ+F_Z(x,u,Du):Dφ]dx=0 for every such test.

In the dominated-direction Euler–Lagrange theorem, if the composed F_s and F_Z are locally integrable, the weak identity is F_s−div F_Z=0 distributionally, row by row. If the composed F_s and the divergence are continuous, this equation holds pointwise.

All-Sobolev-tests stationarity and finiteness: let 1≤p<∞ and let F and its first derivatives have the Carathéodory/C¹-in-(s,Z)-almost-everywhere regularity of the dominated-direction theorem. Assume a finite reference energy exists in u₀+W^{1,p}_0. If p>1, suppose |F_s(x,s,Z)|+|F_Z(x,s,Z)|≤b(x)+C(|s|^{p−1}+|Z|^{p−1}) with b∈L^{p′}(Ω), p′=p/(p−1). If p=1, instead assume a common L∞ bound on these derivatives. Then the energy is finite on the entire affine class, and every local minimizer in its W^{1,p} topology satisfies the weak Euler–Lagrange identity for every φ∈W^{1,p}_0(Ω;ℝ^m).

With the preceding Sobolev Euler–Lagrange regularity and 1≤p<∞, if only an upper p-growth bound for both first derivatives is available, of the form b(x)+C(|s|^p+|Z|^p) with b∈L¹(Ω), then a finite local minimizer still satisfies the weak Euler–Lagrange identity for all compactly supported smooth tests φ∈C_c^∞(Ω;ℝ^m). This conclusion does not assert the identity for all W^{1,p}_0 tests under the p-growth assumption.

Convex sufficiency: in the all-tests setting of the Sobolev Euler–Lagrange theorem (including its p−1 growth or p=1 bounded-derivative assumption and finite reference energy), suppose F(x,·,·) is jointly convex for almost every x. Every weak stationary point, satisfying the identity for all W^{1,p}_0 tests, is a global minimizer in the fixed affine class.

Natural boundary equivalence: let the bounded open Ω have C¹ boundary, let the composed flux P=F_Z(x,u,Du) be C¹ up to the boundary, and let the composed F_s be continuous. The weak stationarity identity ∫_Ω[F_s·φ+P:Dφ]dx=0 for every restriction to Ω of a smooth test defined on a neighborhood of Ω̄ is equivalent to the pair F_s−div P=0 in Ω and Pν=0 on ∂Ω, where divergence is row by row and ν is the outward normal.

Chapter overview: Banach-space perturbation duality is to be applied to function spaces, with dual vector fields representing the load through weak divergence; the actual constraint, equality of values and attainment are stated in the subsequent results.

Let Ω have finite Lebesgue measure, let 1<p<∞ and p′=p/(p−1), and use real Euclidean vector values ℝᵈ. The continuous dual of Lᵖ(Ω;ℝᵈ) is represented by Lᵖ′(Ω;ℝᵈ) under the pairing (σ,v)↦∫Ω σ(x)·v(x) dx: every continuous linear functional has such a representative, unique as an Lᵖ′ equivalence class.

Let Ω have finite Lebesgue measure, 1<p<∞, and let F:Ω×ℝᵈ→ℝ be finite Carathéodory and convex in z for almost every x. Suppose a₀>0, a₁≥0 and a∈L¹(Ω), a≥0, satisfy a₀|z|ᵖ−a(x)≤F(x,z)≤a(x)+a₁|z|ᵖ for almost every x and all z∈ℝᵈ. Then G(v)=∫Ω F(x,v(x)) dx is finite-valued, convex and norm-continuous on Lᵖ(Ω;ℝᵈ).

On a finite-Lebesgue-measure domain Ω, let 1<p<∞, p′=p/(p−1), and F:Ω×ℝᵈ→ℝ be finite Carathéodory, convex in z for almost every x, with a₀|z|ᵖ−a(x)≤F(x,z)≤a(x)+a₁|z|ᵖ for all z almost everywhere, where a₀>0, a₁≥0 and 0≤a∈L¹(Ω). Define G(v)=∫Ω F(x,v(x)) dx on Lᵖ(Ω;ℝᵈ), and F*(x,w)=sup_{z∈ℝᵈ}(w·z−F(x,z)). The functional conjugate G* uses the integral Lᵖ′–Lᵖ pairing.

Under the following hypotheses: Ω has finite Lebesgue measure; 1<p<∞ and p′=p/(p−1); F:Ω×ℝᵈ→ℝ is finite Carathéodory, convex in z almost everywhere; and a₀|z|ᵖ−a(x)≤F(x,z)≤a(x)+a₁|z|ᵖ almost everywhere for all z, where a₀>0, a₁≥0 and 0≤a∈L¹(Ω). For every σ∈Lᵖ′(Ω;ℝᵈ), the conjugate of G(v)=∫Ω F(x,v(x)) dx satisfies G*(σ)=∫Ω F*(x,σ(x)) dx, where F*(x,w)=sup_{z∈ℝᵈ}(w·z−F(x,z)); this right-hand integral is finite.

Let Ω⊂ℝᵈ be bounded and open, X=W₀¹,ᵖ(Ω), 1<p<∞, p′=p/(p−1), and ℓ∈X′. Let F:Ω×ℝᵈ→ℝ be finite Carathéodory, convex in z for almost every x, with a₀|z|ᵖ−a(x)≤F(x,z)≤a(x)+a₁|z|ᵖ for almost every x and all z, where a₀>0, a₁≥0 and 0≤a∈L¹(Ω). Then min_{u∈X}[∫Ω F(x,Du) dx−ℓ(u)] equals max_{σ∈Lᵖ′(Ω;ℝᵈ), ∀v∈X, ∫Ωσ·Dv dx=ℓ(v)}[−∫ΩF*(x,σ) dx]. Both extrema are finite and attained. No nonemptiness or boundary regularity assumption on Ω beyond bounded openness is imposed.

For bounded open Ω⊂ℝᵈ, 1<p<∞, p′=p/(p−1), X=W₀¹,ᵖ(Ω) and ℓ∈X′, let F:Ω×ℝᵈ→ℝ be finite Carathéodory, convex in z for almost every x, and suppose a₀|z|ᵖ−a(x)≤F(x,z)≤a(x)+a₁|z|ᵖ for almost every x and all z, with a₀>0, a₁≥0 and 0≤a∈L¹(Ω). The Dirichlet–flux pair consists of minimizing J(u)=∫Ω F(x,Du) dx−ℓ(u) over u∈X and maximizing −∫Ω F*(x,σ) dx over σ∈Lᵖ′(Ω;ℝᵈ) subject to ∫Ω σ·Dv dx=ℓ(v) for every v∈X.

In the Dirichlet–flux setting (Ω⊂ℝᵈ bounded open, 1<p<∞, X=W₀¹,ᵖ(Ω), ℓ∈X′), for σ∈Lᵖ′(Ω;ℝᵈ) the identity ∫Ω σ·Dv dx=ℓ(v) for every v∈X is equivalent to −div σ=ℓ distributionally, meaning ∫Ω σ·Dφ dx=ℓ(φ) for every smooth compactly supported test φ∈C_c^∞(Ω). This equivalence requires no smooth boundary.

In the Dirichlet–flux theorem with bounded open Ω⊂ℝᵈ, X=W₀¹,ᵖ(Ω), 1<p<∞, ℓ∈X′ and p′=p/(p−1), specialize to F(z)=|z|ᵖ/p. Its flux dual objective is −∫Ω |σ|ᵖ′/p′ dx on the same feasible fluxes ∫Ωσ·Dv=ℓ(v) for all v∈X, and the primal minimizer of ∫Ω|Du|ᵖ/p−ℓ(u) is unique.

Under the Dirichlet–flux hypotheses (Ω⊂ℝᵈ bounded open; X=W₀¹,ᵖ(Ω), 1<p<∞; ℓ∈X′; finite Carathéodory F, convex in z almost everywhere, with a₀|z|ᵖ−a≤F≤a+a₁|z|ᵖ for a₀>0, a₁≥0, 0≤a∈L¹), a primal-admissible u∈X and dual-feasible σ∈Lᵖ′(Ω;ℝᵈ), ∫Ωσ·Dv=ℓ(v) for all v∈X, are both optimal if and only if σ(x)∈∂_z F(x,Du(x)) almost everywhere.

In the Dirichlet–flux problem for F(z)=|z|ᵖ/p, bounded open Ω⊂ℝᵈ, 1<p<∞, X=W₀¹,ᵖ(Ω) and ℓ∈X′, the optimality constitutive condition is σ=|Du|^(p−2)Du almost everywhere, with the vector field defined to be zero where Du=0. Together with flux feasibility it gives ∫Ω |Du|^(p−2)Du·Dv dx=ℓ(v) for every v∈X. Equivalently, a primal u satisfying this weak p-Laplace equation with that constitutive flux gives an optimal primal–dual pair; for a feasible pair simultaneous optimality is equivalent to the stated constitutive relation.

For p=2 on bounded open Ω⊂ℝᵈ, H₀¹(Ω) equipped with the gradient inner product (u,v)↦∫Ω Du·Dv dx is a Hilbert space, by Poincaré. For ℓ∈(H₀¹)′, the weak equation ∫Ω Du·Dv dx=ℓ(v) for every v∈H₀¹ is the Riesz representation problem in this Hilbert space.

On H₀¹(Ω) with its gradient Hilbert norm, for bounded open Ω, let a be a bounded symmetric coercive real bilinear form and ℓ∈(H₀¹)′. The quadratic energy E(u)=½a(u,u)−ℓ(u) has the same weak characterization: its unique minimizer is the unique u satisfying a(u,v)=ℓ(v) for all v∈H₀¹. Boundedness means |a(u,v)|≤M‖u‖‖v‖ for some M, and coercivity means a(v,v)≥α‖v‖² for some α>0, in accordance with the cited §V03.07.

In the real Hilbert setting, including H₀¹(Ω) on bounded open Ω, a bounded coercive real bilinear form a, without a symmetry assumption, still gives a unique Lax–Milgram solution of a(u,v)=ℓ(v) for every test v, for each continuous linear ℓ. For E(u)=½a(u,u)−ℓ(u), the directional derivative in direction v is ½(a(u,v)+a(v,u))−ℓ(v), so energy stationarity characterizes the symmetric-part weak equation rather than the full nonsymmetric form. Coercivity is a(v,v)≥α‖v‖² with α>0.

In the complex Hilbert convention of §V03.07, a is a bounded sesquilinear form conjugate linear in its first (unknown) slot and linear in its second (test) slot. Define its Hermitian part by h(u,v)=½(a(u,v)+overline(a(v,u))). The test functional ℓ is continuous and complex linear.

Let H be a complex Hilbert space as in §V03.07, let a be bounded sesquilinear, conjugate linear in the first slot and linear in the second, let ℓ be continuous complex-linear, and put h(u,v)=½(a(u,v)+overline(a(v,u))). The real directional derivative of E(u)=½Re a(u,u)−Re ℓ(u) in direction v is Re(h(u,v)−ℓ(v)). Vanishing for all directions, equivalently testing both v and iv, is equivalent to h(u,v)=ℓ(v) for every v. Under real coercivity Re a(v,v)≥α‖v‖² with α>0, Lax–Milgram gives a unique solution of the full equation a(u,v)=ℓ(v), whereas this energy characterizes the solution for the Hermitian part h (and its unique minimizer).

Let Ω⊂ℝᵈ be bounded open, ℓ∈(H₀¹(Ω))′ and ψ be measurable. The obstacle admissible set is K={v∈H₀¹(Ω):v≥ψ almost everywhere}; the theorem assumes this set is nonempty. No Sobolev regularity or boundary trace for ψ is imposed.

Let Ω⊂ℝᵈ be bounded open, ℓ∈(H₀¹(Ω))′ and ψ measurable, and assume K={v∈H₀¹(Ω):v≥ψ almost everywhere} is nonempty. The Dirichlet energy E(u)=½∫Ω|Du|² dx−ℓ(u) has a unique minimizer on K. This minimizer is characterized, among u∈K, by ∫Ω Du·D(v−u) dx≥ℓ(v−u) for every v∈K.

Under the obstacle theorem hypotheses (Ω⊂ℝᵈ bounded open, ℓ∈(H₀¹)′, ψ measurable and K={v∈H₀¹:v≥ψ almost everywhere} nonempty), its unique constrained minimizer u satisfies −Δu−ℓ≥0 as a distribution: ∫Ω Du·Dφ dx−ℓ(φ)≥0 for every nonnegative φ∈C_c^∞(Ω).

Under the obstacle theorem hypotheses (Ω⊂ℝᵈ bounded open, ℓ∈(H₀¹)′, ψ measurable and K={v∈H₀¹:v≥ψ almost everywhere} nonempty), let u be the unique constrained minimizer. If u and ψ have continuous representatives in Ω, then U={x∈Ω:u(x)>ψ(x)} is open and −Δu−ℓ=0 on U in distributions, i.e. ∫Ω Du·Dφ dx=ℓ(φ) for every φ∈C_c^∞(U).
For each dimension d≥0, the standard simplex is Δᵈ={x∈ℝ^(d+1):x_i≥0 for i=0,…,d and ∑_{i=0}^d x_i=1}. Its ith vertex is identified with the coordinate index i.

A Sperner labeling of a finite geometric triangulation of Δᵈ assigns to each triangulation vertex x an index i∈{0,…,d} for which x_i>0. Equivalently, a vertex lying in a face receives one of that face’s vertex indices.

For every dimension d≥0 and every finite geometric triangulation of Δᵈ with a Sperner labeling (each vertex x is assigned an index i with x_i>0), the number of d-simplices whose vertices carry all d+1 distinct labels is odd. In particular the statement includes the dimension-zero singleton case.

For every dimension d≥0, Δᵈ admits a sequence of finite geometric triangulations whose mesh tends to zero and whose restrictions are compatible with faces. Mesh is the maximum simplex diameter; the claim includes the dimension-zero simplex.

Brouwer: if K is a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed space and F:K→K is continuous, there exists x∈K with F(x)=x. The statement includes ambient dimension zero, lower-dimensional convex subsets and singleton subsets.

Schauder: let C be nonempty, closed and convex in a real Banach space, and let F:C→C be continuous. If F(C) is relatively compact, equivalently its ambient closure is compact, then F has a fixed point in C. The hypothesis is relative compactness of the image; no boundedness or compactness of the whole domain C is assumed.

Schaefer: let X be a real Banach space and T:X→X continuous, mapping each bounded subset of X to a relatively compact subset. If {x∈X:there exists t∈[0,1] with x=tT(x)} is bounded, then T has a fixed point. The continuation parameter includes both endpoints t=0 and t=1.

The antipodal rotation x↦−x on the unit circle in ℝ² is a continuous self-map without a fixed point; its domain is compact and nonconvex. This exhibits the need for a convexity hypothesis in the compact fixed-point theorem.

The function T(x)=(1+x)/2 is a continuous self-map of the bounded convex open interval (0,1) and has no fixed point there: its only possible fixed point as a real-valued affine map is the omitted endpoint 1.

On the closed unit ball B of real ℓ², define T(x)=(sqrt(1−‖x‖²),x₁,x₂,…). This is a continuous self-map, its image lies in the unit sphere, and it has no fixed point. A hypothetical fixed point would have every coordinate equal to the first, hence all zero by square summability, while T(0)≠0. Moreover T(e_n)=e_{n+1}, so T(B) is not relatively compact. Thus closedness, boundedness and convexity alone in infinite dimension do not guarantee a fixed point.

Banach contraction principle: let M be a nonempty complete metric space, and let T:M→M be Lipschitz with Lipschitz constant q<1 (including q=0 in the standard nonnegative-constant convention). There is a unique fixed point x*. For every starting point x₀∈M, the recursively defined iterates x_{n+1}=T(x_n) converge to x*, and for every integer n≥0 satisfy d(x_n,x*)≤qⁿ d(x₀,x₁)/(1−q).

For gradient-only power energies with p>1, strict convexity in Du and the fixed affine zero-boundary class imply uniqueness of a finite attained minimizer.
