Throughout, spatial domains are open subsets of R^n with n≥1, trace-theorem time intervals have positive length, −ΔΦ=δ₀, outer boundary normals are outward, and the Fourier transform is f̂(ξ)=∫ exp(−2πi x·ξ)f(x) dx. H⁻¹(Ω) is the continuous dual of H₀¹(Ω) using the L² pivot, and H⁻¹ᐟ² boundary functionals pair with the H¹ᐟ² trace space. Real forms are used for weak PDE; spectral complexification uses conjugation in the second test factor. Maximum assertions concern real solutions.

Standard measure and Bochner integration, functional analysis, ODE, Lp duality, density/mollification, Fourier/Riesz tools, and the cited trace, lifting, embedding, form, compact-operator, generator and flow theorems are permitted prerequisites. Bibliographic guidance is context, not an additional list of results to formalize.

For a multi-index α∈N^n define |α|=Σαj and ∂^α=∏∂j^αj. A scalar linear differential operator of order m is Lu=Σ|α|≤m aα(x)∂^αu with at least one order-m coefficient nonzero somewhere. Define σm(L)(x,ξ)=Σ|α|=m aα(x)(iξ)^α. Scalar ellipticity means σm(L)(x,ξ)≠0 for every x and ξ≠0. On exp(ix·ξ), exp(−ix·ξ)L exp(ix·ξ)=Σaα(x)(iξ)^α; hence with the stated Fourier convention the constant-coefficient principal multiplier is σm(L)(2πξ).

Define linear Lu=f with prescribed source; semilinear equations have linear top-order terms whose coefficients depend only on independent variables and may have nonlinear lower-jet terms; quasilinear equations are linear in highest derivatives with coefficients depending on lower jets; fully nonlinear equations may depend nonlinearly on highest derivatives.
The equations Δu+u³=0, (1+u²)Δu=0, and det D²u=1 (n≥2 in the last case) exemplify, respectively, semilinear, quasilinear and fully nonlinear dependence as defined in C01.
For a real symmetric second-order principal matrix a, scalar ellipticity (its second-order symbol has no nonzero real zero) is equivalent to positive or negative definiteness of q(ξ)=ξᵀaξ.

For a real quadratic principal form q having one positive direction and all remaining directions negative, every covector e with q(e)>0 is a time direction: for every η not proportional to e, the equation q(η+τe)=0 has two distinct real roots τ.

Uniform ellipticity in the positive convention means qx(ξ)≥θ|ξ|² for a single θ>0 throughout the region; uniformly negative definite matrices enter this convention by changing the overall sign. The speed-c wave model has q(τ,ξ)=τ²−c²|ξ|². The heat model has a first-order time derivative and an elliptic spatial second-order part with the diffusion sign; degeneracy of the total spacetime quadratic part alone does not define parabolic evolution.
For locally integrable vector fields F, define the distribution −div F by ⟨−div F,φ⟩=∫Ω F·∇φ for φ∈C_c^∞(Ω), using real duality here.

On any bounded Lipschitz open Ω, the Sobolev trace Tr:H¹(Ω)→H¹ᐟ²(∂Ω) is bounded, onto, has a bounded linear right inverse, and has kernel H₀¹(Ω). In dimension one the boundary is a finite set of endpoints, H¹ᐟ²(∂Ω)=ℓ²(∂Ω) with counting measure; endpoint trace has the same kernel and intervalwise affine interpolation is a bounded linear right inverse. These are the explicitly reused trace/lifting interfaces, including the separate one-dimensional case.
For A∈C¹(Ω;R^{n×n}), u∈C²(Ω), and f∈C(Ω), the pointwise equation −div(A∇u)=f holds if and only if ∫Ω A∇u·∇φ=∫Ω fφ for every φ∈C_c^∞(Ω).
If F∈L²(Ω;R^n), f∈H⁻¹(Ω), and −div F=f distributionally, then ∫Ω F·∇v=⟨f,v⟩ for every v∈H₀¹(Ω). No boundary regularity is imposed.
Interior testing does not impose a boundary value: on a ball both u=0 and every constant u satisfy the homogeneous Laplace equation against all compactly supported interior tests.

On bounded Lipschitz Ω, for v∈H¹(Ω) with Δv∈L²(Ω), Green’s first identity is ∫Ω(∇v·∇u+uΔv)=⟨γν∇v,Tr u⟩ for every u∈H¹. If also Δu∈L², then ∫Ω(uΔv−vΔu)=⟨γν∇v,Tr u⟩−⟨γν∇u,Tr v⟩. The first identity is the normal-trace formula with F=∇v.

For bounded Lipschitz Ω, F∈L²(Ω;R^n) with div F∈L²(Ω), there exists a unique γνF∈H⁻¹ᐟ²(∂Ω) such that ⟨γνF,Tr v⟩=∫Ω(F·∇v+(div F)v) for all v∈H¹(Ω). Its norm is ≤CΩ(‖F‖₂+‖div F‖₂), and for fields smooth up to the boundary it is the outward flux, including endpoint flux in dimension one. It is a functional on the trace space, without a required pointwise representative.

A Cauchy problem prescribes values on an initial hypersurface, including required initial time derivatives; a boundary-value problem prescribes spatial boundary data; an initial-boundary problem specifies both. Classical equations and boundary conditions require the continuity/differentiability where evaluated. Energy solutions impose boundary data by Sobolev trace and initial data by a continuous time representative; mild solutions are defined by C07.

For fixed topological data and solution spaces, Hadamard well-posedness is existence for the stated data, uniqueness in the stated solution class, and continuity of the solution map for those topologies.

Suppose the difference of two solutions u,v has nonnegative energy E(t) controlling ‖u(t)−v(t)‖² in the chosen solution norm and E(t)≤C E(0) throughout the time interval. If identical data imply E(0)=0, identical-data solutions agree. If E(0) is exactly the squared norm of the data difference and E(t)=‖u(t)−v(t)‖², the solution map has stability constant √C.

For every T>0 on the unit circle with periodic coordinate x, u_j(t,x)=exp(−4π²j²(T−t))cos(2πjx) are smooth solutions of u_t+Δu=0. Their initial data tend to zero in every fixed Sobolev norm, while ‖u_j(T)‖₂=1/√2. Thus on a class containing these solutions there is no L²-valued extension of the time-T solution map to the initial-data set with zero adjoined that is continuous at zero in any fixed Sobolev data topology; when the class also contains the zero solution the map is discontinuous at zero.
For every distribution u∈D′(Ω) and χ∈C^∞(Ω), Δ(χu)=χΔu+2∇χ·∇u+(Δχ)u in D′(Ω). If χ is compactly supported in Ω then χu has compact support in Ω.
For a coordinate vector e_j and h≠0 define D_h w(x)=(w(x+he_j)−w(x))/h, evaluating this on a domain only where all arguments lie in that domain.
If U⋐U′⋐Ω, w∈W^{1,p}(U′), 1≤p<∞, and for every x∈U the segment from x to x+he_j stays in U′, then ‖D_h w‖_{Lp(U)}≤‖∂j w‖_{Lp(U′)}.

Conversely for 1<p<∞, if w∈Lp(U′) and the coordinate difference quotients are uniformly bounded by M in Lp(U) for all sufficiently small nonzero h (with the above interior-domain convention), then the distributional derivative ∂j w is in Lp(U) with norm ≤M.

For the coordinate difference quotient D_h on the whole space, or with translated tests supported away from the domain boundary, discrete integration by parts gives ∫(D_h w)ψ=−∫w D_{−h}ψ (whenever the displayed pairings are defined).

Let V be a real Hilbert space, a a bilinear form satisfying |a(u,v)|≤M‖u‖‖v‖ and a(v,v)≥α‖v‖² with α>0, and ℓ∈V′. For any nested finite-dimensional V_m⊂V of dense union, there is a unique u_m∈V_m with a(u_m,v)=ℓ(v) for v∈V_m, and a unique full weak solution u∈V. The error satisfies ‖u−u_m‖≤(M/α)inf_{v∈V_m}‖u−v‖, and u_m→u strongly.

Let V be a real reflexive Banach space, V_m nested finite-dimensional subspaces with dense union, a a bounded bilinear form and ℓ∈V′. If (u_m) is bounded in V and a(u_m,v)=ℓ(v) for every v∈V_m, then a subsequence converges weakly to u satisfying a(u,v)=ℓ(v) for every v∈V. If a is coercive, this solution is unique and the only possible weak cluster point. Membership u_m∈V_m is not an additional assumption in this proposition.

Given a dense continuous embedding of real Hilbert spaces V↪H, the pivot map h↦(v↦(h,v)_H) is continuous and injective, identifying H⊂V′ and giving V↪H↪V′. A V′-valued distributional time derivative is defined using Bochner integration against smooth scalar time tests.

Under the same real Hilbert triple and T>0, if u,v∈L²(0,T;V) and u′,v′∈L²(0,T;V′), then for their continuous H representatives (u,v)_H is absolutely continuous in time and has derivative ⟨u′,v⟩+⟨v′,u⟩ almost everywhere.

For a dense continuous real Hilbert triple V↪H↪V′, T>0, u∈L²(0,T;V) with distributional u′∈L²(0,T;V′), there is a unique C([0,T];H) representative. For it, ‖u(t)‖_H²−‖u(s)‖_H²=2∫_s^t⟨u′(r),u(r)⟩dr for every 0≤s≤t≤T. The trace into C([0,T];H) is continuous with respect to ‖u‖_{L²(V)}+‖u′‖_{L²(V′)}.

For a strongly continuous semigroup S(t) on a real or complex Banach space X with generator A, give D(A) its complete graph norm ‖x‖+‖Ax‖. For h≥0 set J(h)x=∫₀ʰS(r)x dr. Then J(h)x∈D(A), AJ(h)x=S(h)x−x, h↦J(h)x is graph-norm continuous, and J(h):X→D(A) are uniformly bounded on compact h intervals. Local semigroup norm bounds, dense D(A) and closedness of A are the stated standard generator interfaces.

In the same semigroup setting, if x₀∈D(A) and f∈C¹([0,T];X), the mild formula yields u∈C¹([0,T];X)∩C([0,T];D(A)) for the graph norm, with u′=Au+f and u(0)=x₀. Conversely every classical solution in this class satisfies that formula.

For a strongly continuous semigroup S(t) on a real or complex Banach X with generator A, x₀∈X and f∈L¹(0,T;X), there is a unique continuous u:[0,T]→X such that ∫₀ᵗu(s)ds∈D(A) and u(t)=x₀+A∫₀ᵗu(s)ds+∫₀ᵗf(s)ds for every t. It is exactly u(t)=S(t)x₀+∫₀ᵗS(t−s)f(s)ds; this equivalence defines the mild solution.
For n≥1 and r>0, the Euclidean ball has volume |B(0,r)|=ω_{n−1}r^n/n; use endpoint counting measure for the one-dimensional sphere.

For spatial dimension n≥1, ω_{n−1}=|S^{n−1}| is surface measure of the Euclidean unit sphere; in dimension one S^0 consists of two endpoints, each with weight one. The notation dashint denotes the integral divided by the measure of its integration set.

Define the Laplacian fundamental-solution function on R^n by Φ(x)=−|x|/2 for n=1, Φ(x)=−(1/(2π))log|x| for n=2, and Φ(x)=|x|^{2−n}/((n−2)ω_{n−1}) for n≥3, interpreted as a locally integrable function and thus as a distribution; the values assigned at the singular point in n≥2 do not affect its distribution.

For every integer n≥1 the function Φ with the dimension-dependent formulas in P003 is locally integrable and satisfies −ΔΦ=δ_0 in distributions on R^n, with the stated negative-Laplacian sign and exact normalization in all three cases.
For f∈C_c^∞(R^n), n≥1, the Newtonian potential u=Φ*f is smooth on all R^n and satisfies −Δu=f pointwise (and distributionally).
For every compactly supported distribution F on R^n, n≥1, the distributional convolution Φ*F is defined and satisfies −Δ(Φ*F)=F.

The two-dimensional normalization Φ(x)=−(1/(2π))log|x| has logarithmic growth in magnitude at infinity; its fundamental-solution identity is understood locally in the sense of distributions, with no imposed decay at infinity.
A function is harmonic on an open set Ω⊂R^n if it is C^2 on Ω and Δu=0 there. The chapter’s local harmonic statements apply componentwise and do not presume Ω connected unless expressly stated.
If u is harmonic on a neighborhood of the closed ball B̄(a,r), with r>0 and n≥1, then u(a)=dashint_{∂B(a,r)}u dS=dashint_{B(a,r)}u dx. In n=1 the sphere average uses weight one at each endpoint.
If u is continuous on an open Ω⊂R^n and satisfies either the sphere mean-value identity or the ball mean-value identity at every center a and radius r>0 with B̄(a,r)⊂Ω, then u is harmonic on Ω.
Weyl’s lemma: for any distribution U on an open Ω⊂R^n with ΔU=0 distributionally, there exists a smooth harmonic function on Ω representing U.

For every n≥1 and multi-index α there is a constant C_{n,α}, depending only on n and α, such that every u harmonic on a neighborhood of B̄(a,r), r>0, satisfies |∂^αu(a)|≤C_{n,α}r^{−n−|α|}∫_{B(a,r)}|u(y)|dy.
A real harmonic function u on all of R^n, n≥1, which is bounded above or bounded below is constant.
Every harmonic function on an open subset of R^n, n≥1, is real analytic locally.
If two harmonic functions on a connected open Ω⊂R^n agree on a nonempty open subset of Ω, then they agree everywhere on Ω.

For n≥2 and open Ω⊂R^n, a subharmonic function is an upper semicontinuous u:Ω→[−∞,∞), not identically −∞ on any connected component, satisfying u(a)≤dashint_{∂B(a,r)}u dS for every r>0 with B̄(a,r)⊂Ω. The surface integral is an extended integral; it is defined because u is bounded above on each compact sphere, but may equal −∞.

For n≥2, under the upper semicontinuity, range [−∞,∞), and non-identically-−∞-on-components hypotheses of P016, the sphere submean condition is equivalent to the ball submean condition u(a)≤dashint_{B(a,r)}u dx on every B̄(a,r)⊂Ω, using extended integrals.

Under the hypotheses of P016 the sphere (equivalently ball) submean condition is equivalent to harmonic comparison: for every ball D compactly contained in Ω and every h harmonic in D and continuous on D̄, if limsup_{x→ζ, x∈D}u(x)≤h(ζ) for every ζ∈∂D, then u≤h throughout D.

If a subharmonic function attains a finite maximum over a connected component of its open domain at an interior point of that component, it is constant on that component. The hypothesis concerns a componentwise maximum, not merely an arbitrary local maximum.

If Ω⊂R^n is bounded and open, n≥2, u is subharmonic in the extended-real sense of P016, and limsup_{x→ζ, x∈Ω}u(x)≤M at every ζ∈∂Ω for a finite real M, then u≤M throughout Ω. No boundary smoothness or connectedness is assumed.
For a real C^2 function u on an open Ω⊂R^n, n≥2, the submean condition (sphere or equivalently ball) is equivalent to Δu≥0 pointwise on Ω.
For n≥2, B=B(a,r), r>0, define the ball Poisson kernel P_B(x,ζ)=(r^2−|x−a|^2)/(rω_{n−1}|x−ζ|^n), for x∈B and ζ∈∂B.

For every n≥2, ball B=B(a,r) with r>0, and continuous boundary function g∈C(∂B), the Poisson integral Pg(x)=∫_{∂B}P_B(x,ζ)g(ζ)dS_ζ is harmonic in B and extends continuously to B̄ with boundary value g; it is the unique function having those properties. Real and complex data are allowed, as made explicit by the uniqueness argument at lines 895–900.
For every ball B=B(a,r) in R^n, n≥2 and r>0, the kernel P_B is positive, is harmonic as a function of x∈B for each ζ∈∂B, and satisfies ∫_{∂B}P_B(x,ζ)dS_ζ=1 for every x∈B.
Every function harmonic on a neighborhood of B̄, where B is a ball in R^n and n≥2, equals the Poisson integral in B of its boundary trace; the formula gives its continuous extension to the boundary.

Let u≥0 be harmonic on an open connected Ω⊂R^n. For B̄(a,r)⊂Ω, r>0, 0≤ρ<1, and |x−a|≤ρr, the Harnack bounds are ((1−ρ)/(1+ρ)^{n−1})u(a)≤u(x)≤((1+ρ)/(1−ρ)^{n−1})u(a). In the section n≥2, and the affine one-dimensional counterpart is also stated at lines 948–949. Include the boundary parameter ρ=0 and allow u to vanish identically.

For u≥0 harmonic on an open connected Ω⊂R^n, any compact K⊂Ω, and any fixed a_0∈Ω, there are positive constants c,C, depending on Ω,K,a_0 (and dimension) but not on u, with c u(a_0)≤u(x)≤C u(a_0) for every x∈K. The one-dimensional interval counterpart is included by lines 948–949.

An increasing sequence of real harmonic functions on an open connected Ω⊂R^n either tends to +∞ at every point or converges uniformly on every compact subset to a harmonic function. The harmonic-limit alternative holds if the sequence is bounded above at one point. The one-dimensional interval counterpart is included by lines 948–949; no nonnegativity assumption is imposed on the individual sequence members.

The statements of the Poisson-kernel/Harnack section have their one-dimensional counterparts for affine harmonic functions on intervals, where needed. Boundary spheres in one dimension are two endpoints with weight one; in particular continuous data at the two endpoints have their unique affine harmonic interpolation, and the Harnack estimates and monotone convergence statements apply on connected intervals.

Let n≥2, B⊂R^n be a ball of positive radius, f∈C_c^∞(B), and g∈C(∂B). There exists a unique u∈C^2(B)∩C(B̄) satisfying −Δu=f in B and u=g on ∂B. It is u(x)=∫_B G_B(x,y)f(y)dy+∫_{∂B}P_B(x,ζ)g(ζ)dS_ζ, where G_B is the Dirichlet Green kernel of −Δ. In the second variable −∂_{ν_y}G_B(x,ζ)=P_B(x,ζ) on ∂B with ν the outward normal.

The Dirichlet Green kernel G_B used in the ball Poisson–Dirichlet representation is normalized by −Δ_y G_B(x,·)=δ_x distributionally and has continuous zero boundary values, with harmonicity away from the pole. The dimensions n≥3 and n=2 use the corresponding fundamental solution Φ, including the logarithmic case.

If Ω⊂R^n is a bounded C^2 open set with n≥2, every g∈C(∂Ω) has a unique harmonic extension h∈C(Ω̄), with h=g on ∂Ω. The domain need not be connected, and real or complex data are allowed (the proof treats real and imaginary parts at line 1100).

Under the bounded C^2-open-set assumptions and n≥2 of P032, if g is the trace of a smooth function G_0 on Ω̄, its continuous harmonic extension agrees with the weak harmonic solution in G_0+H_0^1(Ω) and belongs to H^2(Ω). Smoothness of G_0 is the source hypothesis; no arbitrary continuous boundary datum is asserted to give H^2 regularity.

For a bounded C^2 open Ω⊂R^n and each x∈Ω, there exists a unique Dirichlet Green function G(x,·) of −Δ, satisfying −Δ_yG(x,y)=δ_x distributionally and continuous zero boundary values away from the pole. The statement covers every n≥1, with n=1 verified separately at lines 1194–1206.

On every bounded C^2 open Ω⊂R^n, n≥1, its Dirichlet Green function is symmetric off the diagonal: G(x,y)=G(y,x) for x≠y. It is strictly positive for distinct x,y in the same connected component, and equals zero for x,y in different components. In dimension one the kernel is in fact continuous at the pole, while the stated positivity away from the diagonal remains required.

For a bounded C^2 open Ω⊂R^n, n≥1, every u∈C^2(Ω̄), and x∈Ω, Green representation is u(x)=∫_Ω G(x,y)(−Δu(y))dy−∫_{∂Ω}u(y)∂_{ν_y}G(x,y)dS_y. The normal ν_y is outward, and the derivative may be interpreted as the weak normal trace on a collar of the boundary. For n=1, the boundary integral is endpoint counting measure, with outward derivative −∂_y at a left endpoint and +∂_y at a right endpoint as specified at lines 1203–1205.
Bibliographical comparisons finishing the preceding potential-theory chapter; these lines are not part of the elliptic chapter despite the stale INPUT_LOCK offset.

Except in the spectral sections all functions and coefficients in the elliptic chapter are real. A matrix field A on an open subset of R^n is elliptic with constant lambda>0 when xi^T A(x) xi >= lambda |xi|^2 for every xi in R^n, almost everywhere x for measurable coefficients and every x for continuous coefficients. The antisymmetric part does not enter this inequality. The positive divergence-form convention is -div(A grad); the classical nondivergence maximum principle uses positive second-order coefficients and the opposite sign convention.
H^{-1}(Omega) is the continuous dual (H_0^1(Omega))', with duality <f,v>. Unless otherwise specified H_0^1 carries the full H^1 norm.

Coercive homogeneous weak Dirichlet problem: For every bounded open Omega subset R^n, n>=1, every A in L^infinity(Omega; R^{n x n}) elliptic with lambda>0, and every f in H^{-1}(Omega), there exists exactly one u in H_0^1(Omega) such that a(u,v):=integral_Omega A grad u dot grad v = <f,v> for all v in H_0^1(Omega). No symmetry, Lipschitz boundary or connectedness is assumed. The solution obeys ||u||_{H^1} <= C_Omega lambda^{-1} ||f||_{H^{-1}}.

Nonhomogeneous weak Dirichlet problem: Under the preceding bounded-open-domain, n>=1, bounded-real-elliptic-coefficient and f in H^{-1} hypotheses, if additionally Omega is Lipschitz and g in H^{1/2}(boundary Omega), there exists exactly one u in H^1(Omega) with trace g and a(u,v)=<f,v> for every v in H_0^1(Omega). It satisfies ||u||_{H^1} <= C_Omega (lambda^{-1}||f||_{H^{-1}} + (1+lambda^{-1}||A||_infinity)||g||_{H^{1/2}(boundary Omega)}). The Lipschitz trace spaces include the separate one-dimensional boundary convention of the common framework.

References for trace/lifting, the nonsymmetric Hilbert solvability theorem, zero-boundary compactness, and comparisons. These identify reusable background, not extra assumptions or additional separately required intermediate lemmas.

Symmetric weak Dirichlet minimization: Under the weak Dirichlet hypotheses with A symmetric, fix an H^1 lift w of the prescribed trace (w=0 in the homogeneous case). On its affine trace class define J(w+z)=(1/2)a(w+z,w+z)-<f,z>, z in H_0^1. This definition is valid for f acting only on H_0^1; replacing the lift changes J by an additive constant. The weak solution is its unique minimizer: for every v in H_0^1 its J increment is (1/2)a(v,v). For nonsymmetric A the derivative of the quadratic expression uses the symmetric part of A, so that expression is not asserted to represent the general nonsymmetric weak equation.

Weak Neumann solution: On a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz open Omega subset R^n, for f in L^2(Omega) and g in H^{-1/2}(boundary Omega), a solution of -Delta u=f, partial_nu u=g means u in H^1(Omega) satisfying integral_Omega grad u dot grad v = integral_Omega f v + <g,gamma v> for every v in H^1(Omega), where gamma is the trace.

Neumann compatibility and quotient estimate: For the preceding nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz Omega, f in L^2 and g in H^{-1/2}, a weak Neumann solution exists if and only if integral_Omega f + <g,1>=0. It is unique modulo constants. The unique mean-zero representative satisfies ||u||_{H^1} <= C_Omega (||f||_2+||g||_{H^{-1/2}(boundary Omega)}), and the same bound holds for the quotient norm on H^1(Omega)/R.

Disconnected Neumann variant: On a finite disjoint union of components with componentwise Lipschitz closures and separate traces, the preceding Neumann existence, uniqueness and estimate argument applies on each component: there is one compatibility condition integral_component f + <g_component,1>=0 and one freely chosen additive constant per component (and one mean-zero representative per component).

Classical strong maximum principle: For the same bounded connected open Omega and continuous-coefficient, symmetric uniformly positive nondivergence L with c<=0, if u in C^2(Omega) intersect C(closure Omega), Lu>=0, and u attains its global maximum over Omega at an interior point with nonnegative maximum, then u is constant. If c=0, no sign condition on the attained maximum is needed.

Classical weak maximum principle: Let Omega be bounded, connected and open, L u=sum_{i,j} a^{ij}u_{ij}+sum_i b^i u_i+c u, with a^{ij}=a^{ji}, all coefficients continuous in Omega, principal matrix uniformly positive definite, and c<=0. For u in C^2(Omega) intersect C(closure Omega) with Lu>=0, sup_Omega u <= max{0,sup_boundaryOmega u}. For c=0 this improves to sup_Omega u <= sup_boundaryOmega u. Only continuity inside Omega is assumed; no global coefficient boundedness or boundary smoothness is required.

Classical comparison: Under the same domain and operator hypotheses as the maximum principle, for u,v in C^2(Omega) intersect C(closure Omega), Lu>=Lv in Omega and u<=v on boundary Omega imply u<=v throughout Omega.

Hopf boundary inequality: Suppose Lu>=0 for the preceding nondivergence-type operator, u in C^2(Omega) intersect C(closure Omega), z in boundary Omega has an interior tangent ball, the coefficients are bounded near z in that ball with uniform ellipticity, and c<=0. If u(z)>u(x) for all x in that ball and u(z)>=0, then liminf_{h downarrow 0}(u(z)-u(z-h nu))/h>0, where nu is the outward radial unit direction of the tangent ball at z. For c=0 there is no restriction on the sign of u(z). If the outward directional derivative exists it is positive. At a differentiable boundary point having a tangent ball this direction equals the outward unit normal. The tangent-ball condition is an additional geometric assumption.
Bibliographical comparisons and clarification that the C^1-domain maximum principle is a special case while the Hopf tangent-ball condition is an additional geometric assumption.

For a real v in H^1(Omega), its positive part v^+=max{v,0} belongs to H^1(Omega), with weak gradient grad(v^+)=1_{v>0} grad v almost everywhere. The weak gradient of v vanishes almost everywhere on its zero set {v=0}.
Positive part is a continuous map H^1(Omega) to H^1(Omega): if v_k converges strongly to v in H^1 then v_k^+ converges strongly to v^+ in H^1.
On a Lipschitz domain the trace commutes with positive part: gamma(v^+)=(gamma v)^+ for v in H^1(Omega), using the corresponding Sobolev and boundary trace spaces.

Weak divergence-form comparison: Let Omega be bounded and open, A bounded and elliptic, and 0<=c in L^infinity. If u in H^1(Omega), u^+ in H_0^1(Omega), and integral_Omega (A grad u dot grad phi + c u phi)<=0 for every nonnegative phi in C_c^infinity(Omega), then u<=0 almost everywhere. Consequently weak subsolutions and supersolutions for -div(A grad)+c compare whenever the positive part of their difference is in H_0^1. Ordered traces imply this condition on a Lipschitz domain. No symmetry of A or boundary regularity in the primary assertion is assumed.

Caccioppoli inequality: If u in H^1_loc(Omega) solves -div(A grad u)=f weakly, f in L^2_loc(Omega), and A is bounded and elliptic with constant lambda>0 on a neighborhood of the support of eta in C_c^infinity(Omega), then integral_Omega eta^2 |grad u|^2 <= C integral_Omega |grad eta|^2 |u|^2 + (2/lambda) integral_Omega |eta^2 f u|. The constant C depends only on the local bound for A and lambda.

Interior H^2 regularity and estimate: If A is locally Lipschitz and locally uniformly elliptic in Omega, u in H^1_loc(Omega) solves -div(A grad u)=f weakly, and f in L^2_loc(Omega), then u in H^2_loc(Omega). For open Omega' compactly contained in Omega'' compactly contained in Omega, ||u||_{H^2(Omega')} <= C(||u||_{H^1(Omega'')}+||f||_{L^2(Omega'')}). C depends on the nested sets and corresponding coefficient and ellipticity bounds. A need not be symmetric; no derivative of f is required.

Global zero-Dirichlet H^2 estimate: Let Omega be bounded with C^{1,1} boundary and let A be real symmetric, bounded, Lipschitz and uniformly elliptic on Omega. If f in L^2(Omega), u in H_0^1(Omega), and -div(A grad u)=f weakly, then u in H^2(Omega) and ||u||_{H^2} <= C(||f||_{L^2}+||u||_{H^1}). C depends on the domain and coefficient bounds including ellipticity. This includes n=1.

Lifted global Dirichlet H^2 regularity: Under the global H^2 theorem's C^{1,1} domain and bounded Lipschitz real-symmetric uniformly elliptic A hypotheses, let w in H^2(Omega) be a prescribed lift and let u-w in H_0^1(Omega). Any weak solution -div(A grad u)=f in L^2 belongs to H^2, with ||u||_{H^2} <= C(||f||_{L^2}+||u||_{H^1}+||w||_{H^2}). In particular its weak first derivatives have H^{1/2}(boundary Omega) traces.

Comparisons with Grisvard, Evans, RR and GT for the global C^{1,1} H^2 theorem; remarks explaining the role of transformed-coefficient Lipschitz control. No extra theorem beyond the stated regularity estimates.

For 0<alpha<1 define [g]_{alpha;U}=sup_{x!=y in U}|g(x)-g(y)|/|x-y|^alpha. The ordinary Holder norms add the relevant supremum norms to the indicated Holder seminorms. All Holder exponents used below lie strictly between zero and one.

Cancellation on Holder data: In R^m let K be smooth off zero, homogeneous of degree -m, and have zero spherical mean. For g in C_c^{0,alpha}(R^m), 0<alpha<1, the principal value Tg(x)=pv integral K(x-y)g(y)dy exists and is C^{0,alpha}. If supp g lies in a fixed ball, ||Tg||_{C^{0,alpha}} <= C||g||_{C^{0,alpha}}, where C depends on alpha, that ball, and the bounds of K and grad K on the unit sphere.

Newtonian Hessian identity: For n>=2, let Phi be the normalized fundamental solution of -Delta from L01, sigma=|S^{n-1}|, and K_ij(x)=(1/sigma)(n x_i x_j/|x|^{n+2}-delta_ij/|x|^n). In distributions D_i D_j Phi = pv K_ij - (delta_ij/n)delta_0. In particular the negative contact term and the -Delta sign convention are part of the assertion; n=2 uses the logarithmic Phi.

Holder Newtonian potential: In the n>=2 setting of the Newtonian Hessian lemma, if F in C_c^{0,alpha}(R^n), then Phi*F is C^{2,alpha}_loc. On every fixed bounded set its C^{2,alpha} norm is bounded in terms of that set, a bound for supp F, and ||F||_{C^{0,alpha}}.

Interior Poisson Schauder regularity: For 0<alpha<1, if u in C^2(Omega), f in C^{0,alpha}_loc(Omega), and -Delta u=f, then u in C^{2,alpha}_loc(Omega). For bounded open Omega' compactly contained in Omega'' subset Omega, ||u||_{C^{2,alpha}(Omega')} <= C(||u||_{C^0(Omega'')}+||f||_{C^{0,alpha}(Omega'')}) whenever the right-hand side is finite. The norms on Omega itself can in particular be used when finite. All dimensions n>=1 are included.

Scaled interior Poisson Schauder estimate: For the preceding Poisson equation on concentric balls B_r and B_{2r}, r>0, the estimate rescales to ||u||_{infinity;B_r}+r||Du||_{infinity;B_r}+r^2||D^2u||_{infinity;B_r}+r^{2+alpha}[D^2u]_{alpha;B_r} <= C(||u||_{infinity;B_{2r}}+r^2||f||_{infinity;B_{2r}}+r^{2+alpha}[f]_{alpha;B_{2r}}). The dimension-two estimate requires no additive logarithmic constant.

The Riesz operators used in the W^{2,p} section have Fourier multiplier -i xi_j/|xi|; these multipliers are unchanged by the Fourier normalization. Their L^p boundedness holds for 1<p<infinity, as proved in the referenced Unit U3.
Whole-space Poisson W^{2,p} estimate: For every 1<p<infinity and u in C_c^infinity(R^n), ||D^2 u||_{L^p(R^n)} <= C_{n,p}||Delta u||_{L^p(R^n)}. This includes n=1.

Distributional local Poisson W^{2,p} regularity: For 1<p<infinity, if u,f in L^p_loc(Omega) satisfy -Delta u=f as distributions, then u in W^{2,p}_loc(Omega). For Omega' compactly contained in Omega'' compactly contained in Omega, ||u||_{W^{2,p}(Omega')} <= C(||f||_{L^p(Omega'')}+||u||_{L^p(Omega'')}). No initial W^{1,p} representative is required.
Bibliographical comparison and clarification already reflected in the distributional W^{2,p} statement: its initial distributional solution need not have a W^{1,p} representative.

In variable-coefficient Schauder theory L=a^{ij}D_iD_j+b^iD_i+c has a symmetric uniformly positive principal matrix; this convention is shared by the flat-boundary, local/global Schauder and classical Dirichlet results. Except where expressly imposed for solvability, no sign condition on c belongs to the a priori Schauder estimates.

Flat-boundary constant-coefficient Schauder estimate: For r>0 let B_{2r}^+=B_{2r}(0) intersect {x_n>0}. If u in C^2(B_{2r}^+) is continuous up to the flat face, vanishes on that face, satisfies Delta u=f, and f is C^{0,alpha} up to that face, then u has the up-to-flat-face C^{2,alpha} regularity and scaled Schauder estimate on B_r^+ (including its flat face): ||u||_infinity+r||Du||_infinity+r^2||D^2u||_infinity+r^{2+alpha}[D^2u]_alpha on the smaller half-ball is bounded by C times ||u||_infinity+r^2||f||_infinity+r^{2+alpha}[f]_alpha on the larger half-ball, when these norms are finite. Both this flat estimate and the interior-ball estimate hold with any constant symmetric positive definite matrix in place of the identity, constants controlled by its ellipticity and upper bounds. This includes n=1. The source need not vanish on the plane.

Variable-coefficient interior Schauder a priori estimate: Let L have the preceding symmetric uniformly positive principal matrix, locally C^{0,alpha} coefficients, and f locally C^{0,alpha}, and let a C^{2,alpha}_loc solution satisfy Lu=f. On Omega' compactly contained in Omega'', ||u||_{C^{2,alpha}(Omega')} <= C(||u||_{C^0(Omega'')}+||f||_{C^{0,alpha}(Omega'')}) if the indicated data and coefficient norms are finite. Constants depend on domains, exponent, ellipticity and coefficient norms; no sign condition on c is imposed.

Variable-coefficient global and local-boundary Schauder a priori estimates: On a bounded C^{2,alpha} domain with coefficients of the symmetric uniformly elliptic L Holder continuous on closure Omega, if Lu=f and u in C^{2,alpha}(closure Omega) has boundary values of G in C^{2,alpha}(closure Omega), then ||u||_{C^{2,alpha}(closure Omega)} <= C(||u||_{C^0(closure Omega)}+||f||_{C^{0,alpha}(closure Omega)}+||G||_{C^{2,alpha}(closure Omega)}). C depends on domains, alpha, ellipticity and coefficient norms, without a sign restriction on c. A corresponding local estimate holds up to any C^{2,alpha} boundary portion away from its ends.

Classical Dirichlet solvability and estimate: Let Omega be bounded with C^{2,alpha} boundary, 0<alpha<1, and a,b,c,f in C^{0,alpha}(closure Omega), with the section's symmetric uniformly positive principal matrix and c<=0. For every G in C^{2,alpha}(closure Omega) there exists a unique u in C^{2,alpha}(closure Omega) with Lu=f and boundary values G. The global Schauder bound in this setting improves to ||u||_{C^{2,alpha}} <= C(||f||_{C^{0,alpha}}+||G||_{C^{2,alpha}}), omitting the ||u||_{C^0} term. This includes the one-dimensional interval/domain case.

Initially C^2 local solutions gain Schauder regularity: For a C^2 solution Lu=f with locally C^{0,alpha} coefficients and source, symmetric uniformly positive principal matrix, and no sign restriction on c, the local interior C^{2,alpha} conclusion and the preceding nested-domain interior Schauder estimate hold.

References and distinction between the nondivergence C^{2,alpha} theorem with Holder coefficients/data and the C^{1,1} divergence-form H^2 theorem. The even-source potential and Poisson lift describe the proof route, not extra mandatory deliverables.

Spectral form-associated operator: The Hilbert inner product (u,v) is linear in u. The symmetric problem may be posed in real Hilbert spaces or their complexifications. For a dense form domain V subset H and a form a, define D(A_H)={u in V: there exists f in H such that a(u,v)=(f,v) for every v in V}, and A_H u=f. Density of V makes this f unique.

Closed forms representation and compact resolvent: Let a be a densely defined nonnegative symmetric form in H, with domain V complete for ||u||_V^2=a(u,u)+||u||_H^2. Its associated operator A_H is nonnegative and self-adjoint. (I+A_H)^{-1} is the shifted-form solution map, meaning for f in H its value u in V is the unique solution of a(u,v)+(u,v)=(f,v) for every v in V. If inclusion V -> H is compact then this inverse is compact.

Friedrichs extension: Every densely defined symmetric operator T bounded below by m I on a Hilbert space has a self-adjoint extension with the same lower bound m I, obtained by closing its shifted quadratic form and then undoing the shift.

Dirichlet spectrum: Let Omega subset R^n, n>=1, be nonempty bounded Lipschitz, and A bounded real symmetric uniformly elliptic. In H=L^2(Omega), V=H_0^1(Omega), with a(u,v)=integral_Omega A grad u dot conjugate(grad v), the associated operator L has a compact positive self-adjoint inverse on H. There is an orthonormal basis (e_j)_{j>=1} of H with L e_j=lambda_j e_j, 0<lambda_1<=lambda_2<=..., and lambda_j tending to infinity; eigenvalues are repeated according to finite multiplicity. Real Hilbert spaces or their complexifications are allowed.

Dirichlet min-max principle: Under the nonempty bounded Lipschitz Omega and bounded real symmetric uniformly elliptic A hypotheses of the Dirichlet spectrum theorem, lambda_j = min over j-dimensional linear subspaces W subset H_0^1(Omega) of max over nonzero u in W of a(u,u)/||u||_2^2, for every integer j>=1.

References for Friedrichs/compact spectral theory and reminder that form and operator domains differ: energy membership is in V, while D(L) requires form representation by an L^2 source, as specified by the associated-operator definition.

General elliptic form for spectral parameters: For bounded Lipschitz Omega, H=L^2(Omega), V=H_0^1(Omega), bounded uniformly elliptic A (possibly nonsymmetric), and bounded b,d,c, use a(u,v)=integral_Omega (A grad u dot conjugate(grad v)+(b dot grad u) conjugate(v)+u d dot conjugate(grad v)+c u conjugate(v)). For complex coefficients the principal form must have real part at least lambda_0 |xi|^2 on every complex xi, for lambda_0>0. The associated operator is defined by the form-association construction, with inner product linear in the first variable.

Shifted elliptic Fredholm alternative: For the preceding bounded Lipschitz domain and bounded general elliptic form, its associated L is densely defined and closed on H=L^2. For sufficiently large real mu, (L+mu I)^{-1} exists and is compact. For every lambda in C and every f in H, (L-lambda I)u=f is solvable if and only if f is orthogonal to ker(L^*-conjugate(lambda) I). Both ker(L-lambda I) and this adjoint kernel are finite dimensional. Solutions are unique modulo ker(L-lambda I); if lambda is not an eigenvalue there is a unique solution for every f. This allows nonsymmetric A and complex coefficients satisfying the stated real-part ellipticity; no sign condition on c or unshifted coercivity is assumed.

Symmetric spectral compatibility: For a coercive symmetric Dirichlet realization on a bounded Lipschitz domain with compact L^2 resolvent, and every real lambda, the equation (L-lambda I)u=f is uniquely solvable for every f in L^2 if lambda is not an eigenvalue. At an eigenvalue it is solvable exactly for f orthogonal to its eigenspace, and its solutions are unique modulo that eigenspace.

References for the Riesz-Schauder/Atkinson compact alternative and the observation that the shifted operator carries coercivity while compactness and the adjoint kernel govern spectral-parameter solvability.

Throughout the heat chapter n≥1, Δ=Σ_{j=1}^n ∂²_{x_j}, P=∂_t−Δ, and a function satisfying Pu=0 is caloric. For a nonnegative elliptic realization B the evolution equation is u′+Bu=f and its semigroup generator is −B. Banach-valued integrals are Bochner integrals.
For every n≥1 and t>0 define the whole-space Gaussian heat kernel K_t(x)=(4πt)^(−n/2) exp(−|x|²/(4t)), x∈R^n.
For the Gaussian K_t(x)=(4πt)^(−n/2) exp(−|x|²/(4t)) in every dimension n≥1, K_t≥0, ∫_{R^n}K_t(x)dx=1, ∂_t K_t=ΔK_t for t>0, and K_t*K_s=K_{t+s} for all s,t>0.
The causal kernel Γ(x,t), equal to K_t(x) for t>0 and zero for t≤0, is locally integrable on R^n×R and satisfies (∂_t−Δ)Γ=δ_(0,0) in distributions.

For S(t)g=K_t*g when t>0 and S(0)g=g, (S(t))_{t≥0} is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on L^p(R^n) for every 1≤p<∞. The same convolution operators are contractions on L^∞(R^n); strong continuity on all of L^∞ is not asserted.
For every bounded continuous g on R^n, K_t*g→g locally uniformly as t↓0. If g is bounded and uniformly continuous, this convergence is uniform on R^n.

Let T>0, g∈C_b(R^n), and f∈C([0,T];C_b²(R^n)), with the C_b² norm given by the supremum norms of the function and spatial derivatives through order two. Then u(t,x)=S(t)g(x)+∫_0^t S(t−s)f(s)(x)ds, 0<t≤T, extends continuously to t=0 with u(0,x)=g(x), satisfies (∂_t−Δ)u=f classically for 0<t≤T (using a left time derivative at T), and is the unique such solution bounded on R^n×[0,T].

For all 1≤p≤q≤∞, every g∈L^p(R^n), every spatial multi-index α, and every integer j≥0, S(t)g has a smooth representative for t>0 and ‖∂_t^j D_x^α S(t)g‖_{L^q}≤C(n,α,j,p,q)t^(−j−|α|/2−(n/2)(1/p−1/q))‖g‖_{L^p}. Here 1/∞=0 and the time derivatives agree with the corresponding powers of Δ.

If u is a distribution on an open O⊂R^n×R and (∂_t−Δ)u=0 on O, then u is represented on O by a smooth caloric function. For every r>0 and (x_0,t_0) with closure(B_r(x_0))×[t_0−r²,t_0]⊂O, every spatial multi-index α, and every integer j≥0, |∂_t^j D_x^α u(x_0,t_0)|≤C(n,α,j)r^(−n−2−|α|−2j)∫_{t_0−r²}^{t_0}∫_{B_r(x_0)}|u(y,s)|dy ds. In a smaller cylinder contained in a larger cylinder compactly contained in O, a common admissible radius gives the corresponding estimate at every point of the smaller cylinder.
For a bounded nonempty open Ω⊂R^n and T>0, the parabolic boundary of Q_T=Ω×(0,T] is ∂_pQ_T=(closure(Ω)×{0})∪(∂Ω×[0,T]). Interior spatial points at the top t=T remain in the comparison region.

Let Ω⊂R^n be bounded, nonempty and open, T>0, and let a^{ij}, b^i, c be continuous real coefficients on Ω×(0,T], with a symmetric uniformly positive definite and c≤0. For u∈C^{2,1}(Ω×(0,T])∩C(closure(Ω)×[0,T]), define Lu=u_t−Σ_{i,j}a^{ij}u_{ij}−Σ_i b^i u_i−cu. If Lu≤0 at interior spatial points, then max_{closure(Ω)×[0,T]}u≤max(0,max_{∂_pQ_T}u). When c=0 the outer maximum with zero is omitted. The derivative at the terminal time is one-sided; coefficient continuity up to the lateral boundary is not required.

Under the bounded-cylinder coefficient hypotheses of the classical maximum theorem (continuous real a^{ij},b^i,c on Ω×(0,T], a symmetric uniformly positive definite, c≤0), if u,v∈C^{2,1}(Ω×(0,T])∩C(closure(Ω)×[0,T]), Lu≤Lv, and u≤v on ∂_pQ_T, then u≤v throughout closure(Ω)×[0,T]. Consequently classical solutions with the same source, initial values, and lateral values are unique, including the terminal time with its one-sided derivative.
For r>0 and z_0=(x_0,t_0)∈R^n×R define E_r(z_0)={(y,s):s<t_0 and K_{t_0−s}(x_0−y)>r^(−n)}. Its space-time closure includes its top point z_0.

For r>0, suppose u is caloric on a space-time neighborhood of closure(E_r(x_0,t_0)); alternatively u is classically caloric at points of this closure at times s<t_0 and continuous up to the top point. Then u(x_0,t_0)=(1/(4r^n))∫∫_{E_r(x_0,t_0)}u(y,s)|x_0−y|²/(t_0−s)² dy ds. In particular the nonnegative weight (1/(4r^n))|x_0−y|²/(t_0−s)² on E_r has total mass one.

Let Ω⊂R^n be connected and open, T>0, and let u be caloric on Ω×(0,T], continuous there with the one-sided convention at T. If u≤M throughout this cylinder and u(x_0,t_0)=M for x_0∈Ω and 0<t_0≤T, then u=M on Ω×(0,t_0]. The analogous minimum statement holds with u≥m and attainment of m.

Let u≥0 be caloric on Ω×(0,T), and let V⊂Ω be nonempty and connected with compact closure contained in Ω. For every pair 0<t_1<t_2<T, sup_{x∈V}u(x,t_1)≤C inf_{y∈V}u(y,t_2), where C depends on n,Ω,V,t_1,t_2 and is independent of u. No openness hypothesis on V is stated; its connectedness and compact containment are the source assumptions. The earlier supremum is compared with the later infimum.

Let V↪H be a dense continuous injection of real Hilbert spaces. Embed H in V′ by ⟨h,v⟩=(h,v)_H. The energy space on (0,T) is {u∈L²(0,T;V): distributional u′∈L²(0,T;V′)}, used with its unique continuous H-valued representative supplied by the earlier Hilbert-triple time-trace result.

For a dense continuous injection V↪H of real Hilbert spaces, let a_t:V×V→R be bilinear for 0<t<T and define ⟨A(t)v,w⟩=a_t(v,w). Assume t↦A(t)v is strongly measurable in V′ for every v∈V. Assume there are M,α,c_0 with α>0,c_0≥0 and one exceptional time-null set independent of v,w such that |a_t(v,w)|≤M‖v‖_V‖w‖_V and a_t(v,v)≥α‖v‖_V²−c_0‖v‖_H² for all v,w outside that set. For every u_0∈H and f∈L²(0,T;V′), there is a unique energy solution u∈L²(0,T;V), u′∈L²(0,T;V′), with continuous H representative, u′+A(t)u=f in V′ almost everywhere, and u(0)=u_0. For every 0≤t≤T it satisfies (1/2)‖u(t)‖_H²+∫_0^t a_s(u(s),u(s))ds=(1/2)‖u_0‖_H²+∫_0^t⟨f(s),u(s)⟩ds. Moreover sup_{0≤t≤T}‖u(t)‖_H²+‖u‖_{L²(V)}²+‖u′‖_{L²(V′)}²≤C(‖u_0‖_H²+‖f‖_{L²(V′)}²), with C depending only on the form bounds and T. This applies to general Hilbert triples without a separability assumption, and includes the autonomous bounded coercive case a_t=a,c_0=0.

In a separable Hilbert triple with the uniformly bounded bilinear forms a_t of the parabolic-form theorem, scalar measurability of t↦a_t(v,w) for every v,w implies that t↦A(t)v is strongly measurable as a V′-valued function for each v.

Let Ω⊂R^n be bounded Lipschitz, T>0, u_0∈L²(Ω), and f∈L²(0,T;H^(−1)(Ω)), where H^(−1)(Ω)=(H_0¹(Ω))′. There exists a unique u∈L²(0,T;H_0¹(Ω))∩C([0,T];L²(Ω)) with u′∈L²(0,T;H^(−1)(Ω)), u(0)=u_0, and ⟨u′(t),v⟩+∫_Ω∇u(t)·∇v=⟨f(t),v⟩ for every v∈H_0¹(Ω), as an H^(−1) identity almost everywhere in time. For every t∈[0,T], (1/2)‖u(t)‖_2²+∫_0^t‖∇u(s)‖_2²ds=(1/2)‖u_0‖_2²+∫_0^t⟨f(s),u(s)⟩ds. The supremum L², integrated H_0¹, and L²(H^(−1)) derivative energy norms are bounded by the corresponding data norms as in the parabolic-form theorem. The lateral condition is zero Sobolev trace for almost every time, and the initial condition is an L² value.

Let Ω be bounded Lipschitz and w∈L²(0,T;H¹(Ω))∩C([0,T];L²(Ω)) with distributional w′∈L²(0,T;H^(−1)(Ω)), where H^(−1)=(H_0¹)′. If the Sobolev trace of w is nonpositive almost everywhere in time and boundary measure, then w_+=max(w,0) belongs to L²(0,T;H_0¹(Ω))∩C([0,T];L²(Ω)), and for all 0≤s≤t≤T, (1/2)‖w_+(t)‖_2²−(1/2)‖w_+(s)‖_2²=∫_s^t⟨w′(r),w_+(r)⟩dr.

Let Ω be bounded Lipschitz, T>0, and A(t,x) a bounded measurable real matrix field with ξ·A(t,x)ξ≥ν|ξ|² almost everywhere for all ξ, ν>0; symmetry is not assumed. Suppose u,v∈L²(0,T;H¹(Ω))∩C([0,T];L²(Ω)), with distributional derivatives in L²(0,T;H^(−1)(Ω)), and w=u−v satisfies ⟨w′(t),η⟩+∫_Ω A(t,x)∇w(t)·∇η dx≤0 for every nonnegative η∈H_0¹(Ω), almost everywhere in t. If u(0)≤v(0) almost everywhere and their lateral Sobolev traces are ordered u≤v almost everywhere, then u(t)≤v(t) almost everywhere for every t∈[0,T]. The inequality on w holds in particular for solutions whose sources are ordered in the positive dual cone; neither solution is required individually to have zero boundary trace.

For a dense continuous injection V↪H of real Hilbert spaces and a symmetric bounded coercive bilinear form a on V, define the associated operator B=A_H by D(B)={v∈V: there exists h∈H with a(v,w)=(h,w)_H for every w∈V}, and Bv=h; density of V makes this h unique.

For V↪H a dense continuous injection of real Hilbert spaces and a symmetric bounded coercive form a on V, the associated operator B with a(v,w)=(Bv,w)_H on D(B) is densely defined, nonnegative and self-adjoint on H. Its square-root form domain is D(B^(1/2))=V and a(v,v)=‖B^(1/2)v‖_H² for every v∈V. If V↪H is compact, B has compact resolvent.

In the Dirichlet setting of E10, take Ω nonempty bounded Lipschitz, H=L²(Ω), V=H_0¹(Ω), and a(v,w)=∫_Ω A∇v·∇w with bounded real symmetric uniformly elliptic A. Poincaré gives coercivity and Rellich gives the compact injection V↪H, so this is a concrete instance of the symmetric coercive form operator and its compact resolvent.

Let B be the operator of a symmetric bounded coercive form on a densely continuously embedded real Hilbert space V↪H. Then S_B(t)=exp(−tB), t≥0, is a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup on H with generator exactly −B. For every integer m≥1 and every t>0, S_B(t)H⊂D(B^m) and ‖B^mS_B(t)‖_{L(H)}≤(m/(et))^m.

For the operator B of a symmetric bounded coercive form on a dense continuous injection V↪H of real Hilbert spaces, if its resolvent is compact there exists an orthonormal eigenbasis (φ_j) of H with eigenvalues λ_j, and S_B(t)g=Σ_j exp(−tλ_j)(g,φ_j)_H φ_j, converging in H norm for every g∈H and t≥0. If H is finite-dimensional the sum is finite.

For B associated with a symmetric bounded coercive form a on a dense continuous real Hilbert triple V↪H↪V′, u_0∈H and f∈L¹(0,T;H), the H-valued mild solution is U(t)=S_B(t)u_0+∫_0^t S_B(t−s)f(s)ds, using the H-valued Bochner integral.

Let B,a,V,H be as in the symmetric coercive form theorem, u_0∈H, and f∈L¹(0,T;H). Whenever an energy solution of u′+Au=f in V′ with u(0)=u_0 exists, it agrees at every time with U(t)=S_B(t)u_0+∫_0^t S_B(t−s)f(s)ds. In particular this agreement holds for f∈L²(0,T;H), for which energy existence follows by the inclusion H↪V′. For arbitrary f∈L²(0,T;V′), energy existence and uniqueness are those of the parabolic-form theorem in V,V′; an H-valued mild convolution is not asserted for such general data.

For a symmetric time-independent bounded coercive form a on a dense continuous injection V↪H of real Hilbert spaces, with associated operator B, assume u_0∈V and f∈L²(0,T;H). The energy solution satisfies u′∈L²(0,T;H), Bu∈L²(0,T;H), u∈L^∞(0,T;V), u(t)∈D(B) for almost every t, and u′+Bu=f in H almost everywhere. Quantitatively, ‖u′‖_{L²(H)}²+‖Bu‖_{L²(H)}²+sup_{0≤t≤T}‖u(t)‖_V²≤C(‖u_0‖_V²+‖f‖_{L²(H)}²), with C depending on the form bounds. The displayed genuine supremum concerns the continuous H representative, which takes values in V at every t.

Under the additional-energy-derivative hypotheses u_0∈V and f∈L²(0,T;H), if B is the homogeneous Dirichlet operator −div(A∇·) on a bounded C^{1,1} domain Ω with bounded real symmetric uniformly elliptic Lipschitz coefficients A, then the energy solution also lies in L²(0,T;H²(Ω)). Its spatial bound is obtained from the elliptic estimate ‖u(t)‖_{H²(Ω)}≤C(‖Bu(t)‖_2+‖u(t)‖_{H¹(Ω)}) for almost every t, and hence ‖u‖_{L²(H²)}≤C(‖Bu‖_{L²(L²)}+‖u‖_{L²(H¹)}), with the domain/coefficient constant of E06 and the preceding energy bounds.
Throughout the hyperbolic chapter n≥1, wave speed c>0, all endpoint time derivatives are one-sided, and complex-valued energy identities use the real part of the Hilbert pairing.

Let b∈C¹([0,T]×R^n;R^n) be bounded with bounded spatial derivative. Its flow X(t,s,y), defined by ∂_tX(t,s,y)=b(t,X(t,s,y)) and X(s,s,y)=y, exists on the whole time slab; for every s,t∈[0,T], X(t,s,·) is a C¹ diffeomorphism of R^n with inverse X(s,t,·).
If b∈C¹([0,T]×R^n;R^n) is bounded with bounded spatial derivative and g∈C¹(R^n), the unique classical solution of u_t+b·∇u=0 with u(0)=g is u(t,x)=g(X(0,t,x)). No boundedness of g is assumed.

If b∈C¹([0,T]×R^n;R^n) is bounded with bounded spatial derivative, g∈C¹(R^n), and q,f are continuous with continuous first spatial derivatives, the classical transport solution with u(0)=g to u_t+b·∇u+qu=f is u(t,x)=exp(−∫_0^t q(r,X(r,t,x))dr)g(X(0,t,x))+∫_0^t exp(−∫_s^t q(r,X(r,t,x))dr)f(s,X(s,t,x))ds. It is unique among classical solutions, as follows by restriction to each characteristic. For a local C¹ vector field, both the homogeneous and forced formulas apply on the actual flow domain where the entire characteristic reaches the initial data; global reachability is not assumed in that local version.
Under b∈C¹([0,T]×R^n;R^n) bounded with bounded spatial derivative, set J(t,y)=det D_yX(t,0,y). Then J(t,y)=exp(∫_0^t div b(r,X(r,0,y))dr), in particular J(t,y)>0.

Under the preceding global C¹ bounded-flow hypotheses, every locally integrable initial density g∈L¹_loc(R^n) gives the transported density ρ(t,X(t,0,y))=g(y)/J(t,y). This density satisfies ρ_t+div(bρ)=0 with initial density g in the distributional sense. Equivalently, for smooth compactly supported tests φ on [0,T)×R^n, ∫_0^T∫ρ(φ_t+b·∇φ)dxdt=−∫g(y)φ(0,y)dy. No spatial differentiability of g or stronger-than-C¹ regularity of b is required.

Locally for a C¹ vector field b, prescribed C¹ data on a C¹ hypersurface transverse to the space-time vector (1,b) determine a unique C¹ transport solution near the initial point. The same assertion holds for u_t+b·∇u+qu=f with q,f continuous and having continuous first spatial derivatives, as in the characteristic formula theorem.
For n≥2 define M_nh(x,r)=∫_{S^{n−1}}h(x+rω)dμ(ω), using probability surface measure on the unit sphere. It extends evenly to negative r and satisfies M_nh(x,0)=h(x). Define D_r=r^(−1)∂_r for r>0.

For smooth h on R^n and positive wave speed c, define the wave velocity operators for t>0 by S_1(t)h(x)=(1/(2c))∫_{x−ct}^{x+ct}h(y)dy; for odd n≥3, S_n(t)h(x)=[D_r^((n−3)/2){r^(n−2)M_nh(x,r)}/(c(n−2)!!)]_{r=ct}; for even n≥2, S_n(t)h(x)=[D_r^((n−2)/2){r^(n−1)M̃_nh(x,r)}/(c(n−1)!!)]_{r=ct}. Here M̃_n is the normalized spherical mean in dimension n+1 of the lift of h independent of the last coordinate, explicitly M̃_nh(x,r)=(2/|S^n|)∫_{|z|<1}h(x+rz)/sqrt(1−|z|²)dz. These formulas have the smooth zero-time extensions used for the Cauchy initial values.

For smooth g,h and smooth forcing f(t,x), the solution to u_tt−c²Δu=f with u(0)=g, u_t(0)=h is u(t)=∂_tS_n(t)g+S_n(t)h+∫_0^t S_n(t−s)f(s)ds, in every dimension n≥1 and with the same normalized S_n. The source convolution has zero initial displacement and velocity.

For all n≥1, c>0, and smooth whole-space data g,h, the classical solution of u_tt−c²Δu=0 with u(0)=g and u_t(0)=h is u(t)=∂_tS_n(t)g+S_n(t)h, with S_n given by the stated one-dimensional, odd-dimensional spherical-mean, and even-dimensional descent formulas. The solution is unique among smooth classical solutions; global finite-energy hypotheses are not imposed on these smooth data (the source proves uniqueness by the local cone estimate). Endpoint derivatives and the zero-time extensions are one-sided as prescribed for the chapter.
The normalized wave formulas specialize to S_3(t)h(x)=tM_3h(x,ct), and in dimension two to S_2(t)h(x)=(1/(2πc))∫_{|y−x|<ct}h(y)/sqrt(c²t²−|y−x|²)dy, for smooth h and t>0.

For the homogeneous classical whole-space wave equation in odd dimensions n≥3, the value at (x,t), t>0, depends only on the initial data and their relevant derivatives on the sphere |y−x|=ct, as prescribed by the spherical-mean formula. This sphere-only Huygens conclusion is separate from finite-speed dependence on the entire ball; it is not asserted for n=1 or even n.

For n≥1, c>0, g∈H¹(R^n), h∈L²(R^n), and f∈L¹_loc([0,∞);L²(R^n)), there is a unique distributional solution of u_tt−c²Δu=f in C([0,∞);H¹(R^n))∩C¹([0,∞);L²(R^n)) with u(0)=g and u_t(0)=h. The assertion allows real or complex scalar data, with real parts in energy identities.

For the unique energy wave with g∈H¹(R^n), h∈L²(R^n), f∈L¹_loc([0,∞);L²), set G(t)=(‖u_t(t)‖_2²+c²‖∇u(t)‖_2²)^(1/2) and E(t)=G(t)²/2. For every 0≤r≤t, E(t)−E(r)=∫_r^t Re(f(s),u_t(s))_{L²}ds, G(t)≤G(r)+∫_r^t‖f(s)‖_2ds, and ‖u(t)‖_2≤‖u(r)‖_2+∫_r^tG(s)ds. Homogeneous energy is conserved. On every bounded time interval, the solution depends continuously on (g,h,f) in H¹×L²×L¹(L²), with solution topology C(H¹)∩C¹(L²).

For an energy solution u∈C([0,∞);H¹(R^n))∩C¹([0,∞);L²(R^n)) of u_tt−c²Δu=f with f∈L¹_loc([0,∞);L²), fix x_*∈R^n and R>0. For 0≤s<R/c set B_s=B(x_*,R−cs) and E_{B_s}(s)=(1/2)∫_{B_s}(|u_t(s)|²+c²|∇u(s)|²)dx. Then for every 0≤t<R/c, sqrt(2E_{B_t}(t))≤sqrt(2E_{B_0}(0))+∫_0^t‖1_{B_s}f(s)‖_2ds. No moving-sphere trace hypothesis on the weak gradients is imposed.

For the same whole-space energy solution and shrinking balls B_s=B(x_*,R−cs), if both initial data g and h vanish almost everywhere on B_0 and f vanishes almost everywhere in the backward cone {(x,s):0<s<R/c, x∈B_s}, then u(t) vanishes almost everywhere on B_t for every 0≤t<R/c. Applied to differences, equality of both data on B_0 and of sources in the cone forces equality of the two solutions on every B_t. The hypothesis includes the initial displacement itself, rather than only its gradient.
For a homogeneous energy wave f=0 with both initial data supported in closure(B(x_0,R_0)), its essential support at every t≥0 is contained in closure(B(x_0,R_0+ct)).

Let Ω⊂R^n be nonempty bounded Lipschitz, H=L²(Ω), V=H_0¹(Ω), and a a bounded symmetric coercive form on V (Hermitian over C). Given g∈V, h∈H and f∈L¹(0,T;H), there is a unique u∈C([0,T];V)∩C¹([0,T];H) with u(0)=g, u_t(0)=h, and ⟨u_tt,v⟩+a(u,v)=(f,v)_H for each v∈V as a distribution in time. In particular u_tt∈L¹(0,T;V′). For E_a(t)=(1/2)(‖u_t(t)‖_H²+a(u(t),u(t))), every 0≤r≤t≤T satisfies E_a(t)−E_a(r)=∫_r^t Re(f(s),u_t(s))_Hds. For the Dirichlet elliptic realization with bounded real symmetric uniformly elliptic matrix A and a(u,v)=∫_Ω A∇u·overline(∇v), this is the weak wave equation with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary trace.

For Ω nonempty bounded Lipschitz, H=L²(Ω), V=H_0¹(Ω), and bounded symmetric coercive a (Hermitian in the complex case), let A_H be its associated self-adjoint operator. For g∈V, h∈H, f∈L¹(0,T;H), the Dirichlet energy wave has the spectral formula u(t)=cos(t sqrt(A_H))g+[sin(t sqrt(A_H))/sqrt(A_H)]h+∫_0^t[sin((t−s)sqrt(A_H))/sqrt(A_H)]f(s)ds. The displacement datum is in the form domain V; it is not required to be in D(A_H).

Let A^j=A^{j*} be C¹ matrix fields on [0,T]×R^n with bounded first derivatives, and let B be bounded. For every smooth solution of u_t+Σ_{j=1}^n A^j(t,x)∂_j u+B(t,x)u=f(t,x), with u(0)∈L² and f∈L¹(0,T;L²), one has ‖u(t)‖_2≤e^(Ct)(‖u(0)‖_2+∫_0^t‖f(s)‖_2ds), 0≤t≤T, where C=(1/2)Σ_j‖∂_jA^j‖_∞+‖(B+B*)/2‖_∞ and the matrix norms are operator norms. The principal coefficients A^j themselves need not be bounded and may grow linearly in x. The estimate proves the solution is L² at later times and applies to differences, yielding uniqueness and stability.

Let s be an integer with s>n/2+1. For u_t+Σ_{j=1}^nA^j(t,x)∂_ju+B(t,x)u=f, assume A^j=A^{j*} and B are smooth matrix fields whose spatial derivatives of every order through s, including order zero, are bounded uniformly on [0,T]×R^n. For every g∈H^s(R^n) and f∈C([0,T];H^s(R^n)), there is a unique u∈C([0,T];H^s)∩C¹([0,T];H^{s−1}) with u(0)=g solving this system. For 0≤t≤T, ‖u(t)‖_{H^s}≤exp(C_s t)(‖g‖_{H^s}+∫_0^t‖f(r)‖_{H^s}dr), where C_s depends on the stated coefficient bounds, s and n. The squared H^s norm is the sum of squared L² norms of all spatial derivatives of orders at most s. The estimate applies to differences and gives continuous dependence on the data.

For every compact Hausdorff space K, finite positive Borel measure μ of full support, and k∈C(K×K;C), define T:C(K;C)→C(K;C) by Tf(x)=∫K k(x,y)f(y)dμ(y). It is a well-defined compact bounded complex-linear operator in the supremum norm and ‖T‖≤μ(K)‖k‖∞. The range includes arbitrary compact Hausdorff K and general finite Borel measures as stated, including the empty compact space; no Euclidean, metrizable or measure-regularity hypothesis is added.

For the continuous-kernel operator T with exactly the preceding compact Hausdorff/full-support finite positive Borel hypotheses, for every complex λ≠0 set Fλ=λI−T and let Fλ′ be its complex-linear Banach transpose. Ran Fλ is closed and dim ker Fλ=codim Ran Fλ=dim ker Fλ′<∞. For every g∈C(K;C), Fλ f=g is solvable iff ℓ(g)=0 for every ℓ∈ker Fλ′, and when solvable its solution set is one solution plus ker Fλ. Either Fλ is boundedly invertible or both its kernel and transpose kernel have positive dimension. The transpose convention is Fλ′=λI−T′, without conjugating λ.

With a≤b, k continuous on Δ and λ any real or complex scalar as in I02_VOLTERRA_OBJECTS, the series Rλ(t,s)=Σ_{m≥1}λ^{m−1}k_m(t,s) defines a continuous resolvent kernel on Δ and gives u(t)=g(t)+λ∫ₐᵗRλ(t,s)g(s)ds for the unique continuous solution. This includes λ=0 with the zeroth power equal to one and a=b.

For real a≤b, either scalar field R or C, a continuous kernel k on Δ={(t,s):a≤s≤t≤b}, and g∈C([a,b]), set M=‖k‖∞ and Vu(t)=∫ₐᵗk(t,s)u(s)ds on C([a,b]). Define k₁=k and k_{m+1}(t,s)=∫_s^t k(t,r)k_m(r,s)dr for m≥1. These constructions include the degenerate interval a=b.

Under those Volterra hypotheses, for every scalar λ (including zero) there is a unique continuous u satisfying u(t)=g(t)+λ∫ₐᵗk(t,s)u(s)ds. The two-sided solution operator has operator-norm convergent expansion (I−λV)⁻¹=Σ_{m=0}∞λ^mV^m and ‖(I−λV)⁻¹‖≤exp(|λ|M(b−a)). If a=b all integrals vanish and the conclusion specializes to u=g and the identity solution operator.

Under the Volterra hypotheses a≤b, scalar field R or C, k continuous on Δ={(t,s):a≤s≤t≤b}, and g∈C([a,b]), for every scalar λ and every starting value u₀∈C([a,b]), the successive approximations u_{j+1}=g+λVu_j converge uniformly on [a,b] to the unique solution of u=g+λVu. This includes a=b and λ=0.
