Ordinary topology conventions: a pair (X,A) is a space with a specified subspace; singular chains are finite sums and cochains are algebraic duals with the ring, abelian group or module specified at use. Compact supports are imposed only when stated; ordinary chains are not locally finite chains.

Throughout the geometry, manifolds are finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second countable, smooth and without boundary unless a boundary is specified; metrics are smooth and positive definite. Length distance is finite on each connected component. Set R(X,Y)Z=∇_X∇_Y Z−∇_Y∇_X Z−∇_[X,Y]Z and, for independent X,Y, K(X,Y)=⟨R(X,Y)Y,X⟩/(⟨X,X⟩⟨Y,Y⟩−⟨X,Y⟩²); use Δ_g=div_g grad_g and E(γ)=½∫⟨γ̇,γ̇⟩dt. Differential equations and flows have their actual maximal domains.
Bibliographic guidance and corrected reference editions; these references are prerequisites or proof resources, not an instruction to formalize their entire contents.

Paths in a topological space X have domain I=[0,1]; for a(1)=b(0), ab traverses a on [0,½] and b on [½,1], and ā(t)=a(1−t). A path homotopy is a continuous I×I→X with the specified initial/final paths and both endpoint sides constant. π₁(X,x) is the set of endpoint-fixed homotopy classes of loops at x, with concatenation product. All covering maps in this chapter are surjective.

Proposition prop:p202-path-classes (groupoid): endpoint-fixed path homotopy classes form a groupoid under concatenation, with constant paths as identities and reversal as inverses. In particular loops at every x∈X form the group π₁(X,x).

Proposition prop:p202-path-classes (basepoint change): a path d:x→y induces an isomorphism π₁(X,y)→π₁(X,x), [b]↦[d b d̄]. Replacing d by another path with the same endpoints changes this isomorphism by an inner automorphism.

Proposition prop:p202-path-classes (functoriality): a continuous pointed map f:(X,x)→(Y,y) induces a homomorphism π₁(X,x)→π₁(Y,y) by postcomposition, functorially. Pointed homotopic maps induce equal homomorphisms, and a pointed homotopy equivalence induces an isomorphism.

For an ordinary continuous homotopy F:X×I→Y from f to g, a loop a at x and d(t)=F(x,t), the endpoint-fixed path classes satisfy [f∘a]=[d (g∘a) d̄] in π₁(Y,f(x)). Thus ordinary homotopies induce the usual change-of-basepoint correction.

A covering map p:E→B is a continuous surjection such that each b∈B has an open neighborhood U whose preimage is a disjoint union of open sheets, each mapped homeomorphically to U by p. Such U is evenly covered.

Theorem thm:p202-cover-lifting (homotopies): for any covering p:E→B, arbitrary topological space Z, continuous F:Z×I→B and continuous h:Z→E with p∘h=F(·,0), there exists a unique continuous F̃:Z×I→E with p∘F̃=F and F̃(·,0)=h. No connectedness or local hypotheses on Z are required.
Theorem thm:p202-cover-lifting (paths): for any covering p:E→B, continuous path a:I→B and e∈E with p(e)=a(0), there exists a unique continuous lift ã:I→E satisfying p∘ã=a and ã(0)=e.

For a covering, a lift of a constant path is constant. For a homotopy of paths relative to both endpoints, fixing the initial lift fixes the lifted endpoint throughout the homotopy; this holds without connectedness of the total space.

Theorem thm:p202-van-kampen: if X=U∪V with U,V open and path connected and U∩V nonempty and path connected, then for every x∈U∩V the inclusion homomorphisms exhibit π₁(X,x) as the group pushout π₁(U,x) *_{π₁(U∩V,x)} π₁(V,x), including its universal property.
Theorem thm:p202-basic-pi1 (circle): winding number is a group isomorphism π₁(S¹,1)≅ℤ.

Theorem thm:p202-basic-pi1 (products): for a product of pointed topological spaces, the coordinate projections induce an isomorphism from its fundamental group to the product of the fundamental groups, with no path connectedness assumptions on the factors.
Theorem thm:p202-basic-pi1 (spheres): for each integer n≥2, Sⁿ is simply connected.

Theorem thm:p202-cover-criterion: if p:(E,e)→(B,b) is a covering and f:(Y,y)→(B,b) a continuous pointed map with Y path connected and locally path connected, then a continuous lift f̃:Y→E with f̃(y)=e exists if and only if f_*(π₁(Y,y))⊆p_*(π₁(E,e)); the lift is unique.

Theorem thm:p202-cover-criterion (injectivity): any pointed covering p:(E,e)→(B,b) induces an injective homomorphism p_*:π₁(E,e)→π₁(B,b). This assertion does not require E or B to be connected or Y to be present.

Corollary cor:p202-cover-action (connected case): if E and B are path connected and e∈p⁻¹(b), the right monodromy action is transitive and, for H=p_*π₁(E,e), Hg↦e·g identifies the right G-sets H\G={Hg:g∈G} and p⁻¹(b). The number of sheets is the subgroup index [G:H], also for infinite index.
Corollary cor:p202-cover-action: for any covering p:E→B and b∈B, lifting a loop at b from a point of p⁻¹(b) and taking its endpoint defines a well-defined right action of G=π₁(B,b) on p⁻¹(b).

A space B is semilocally simply connected if each b has an open neighborhood whose loops based at b are nullhomotopic in B. If B is locally path connected, these neighborhoods can be chosen path connected, with loops based at any of their points nullhomotopic in B.

Theorem thm:p202-cover-classification: let B be path connected, locally path connected and semilocally simply connected, fix b∈B, and put G=π₁(B,b). The association (p:E→B,e∈p⁻¹(b))↦p_*π₁(E,e) is a bijection between isomorphism classes of connected pointed coverings and all subgroups H≤G. Forgetting e gives a bijection between isomorphism classes of connected unpointed coverings and conjugacy classes of subgroups.

Theorem thm:p202-cover-classification (universal cover): under the same three hypotheses on B, the trivial subgroup of π₁(B,b) is realized by a simply connected pointed covering. It admits a unique pointed map over B to every connected pointed covering of B.

For a covering p:E→B, a deck transformation is a homeomorphism h:E→E with p∘h=p. A connected covering is regular when its deck group acts transitively on a fiber (equivalently, under the classification hypotheses, its subgroup is normal).

Theorem thm:p202-deck-group: let B be path connected, locally path connected and semilocally simply connected, G=π₁(B,b), and let p:E→B be connected with chosen e∈p⁻¹(b) and H=p_*π₁(E,e). Then Deck(E/B)≅N_G(H)/H. The deck action on the fiber is transitive if and only if H is normal in G.

For every integer m≥1, z↦zᵐ is an m-sheeted covering S¹→S¹, its subgroup under winding number is mℤ, and its deck transformations are precisely multiplications by mth roots of unity, giving deck group ℤ/mℤ.
For every n≥2, the antipodal quotient Sⁿ→ℝPⁿ is a two-sheeted covering. Its simply connected total space has trivial image subgroup, and π₁(ℝPⁿ)≅ℤ/2ℤ.

A CW complex is a Hausdorff space with skeleta obtained by successive disk attachments: Xⁿ is the pushout of Xⁿ⁻¹ and a disjoint union of closed n-disks along their boundary-sphere attaching maps. Characteristic maps restrict to homeomorphisms from disk interiors to disjoint open cells (which need not be open in X). Each cell closure lies in a finite union of cells, and X has the weak topology for its closed characteristic disks. A subcomplex consists of cells together with their closures.

An abstract simplicial complex is a collection of nonempty finite subsets of a vertex set closed under nonempty subsets. Its weak geometric realization consists of nonnegative barycentric coordinates summing to one and supported in a simplex, with faces identified by zero coordinates. A Δ-complex glues ordered geometric simplices by order-preserving face maps, allowing distinct faces to have the same image and distinct simplices with the same vertices.

Proposition prop:p202-cw-basics: every subcomplex of a CW complex is closed and its own weak topology equals the subspace topology. Every compact subset of a CW complex is contained in a finite subcomplex. The weak realization of any simplicial complex, and likewise of any Δ-complex, has the associated CW structure with one open cell per simplex interior.

For every quotient map q:P→Q, the product q×id_I:P×I→Q×I is a quotient map for the ordinary product topology, where I=[0,1]. Consequently continuity on X×I for a weak CW complex can be tested on the characteristic-disk products Dⁿ×I; the analogous claim is not asserted for arbitrary products of infinite CW complexes.

Theorem thm:p202-cw-hep: if A is a subcomplex of a CW complex X, f:X→Y is continuous and h:A×I→Y is continuous with h(a,0)=f(a), there exists a continuous H:X×I→Y extending h and with H(x,0)=f(x). No conditions on the target space Y are imposed.
Proposition prop:p202-cw-neighborhood (collapse): if A is a nonempty contractible subcomplex of a CW complex X, the quotient projection X→X/A is a homotopy equivalence.
Proposition prop:p202-cw-neighborhood (attachments): replacing attaching maps Sⁿ⁻¹→X by homotopic maps produces attached spaces homotopy equivalent relative to X.
Proposition prop:p202-cw-neighborhood (neighborhood): every subcomplex A of a CW complex X is a strong deformation retract of some open neighborhood in X.

Theorem thm:p202-graph-attach (attachments): attaching a 2-cell to a path connected space X changes π₁(X) to its quotient by the normal closure of the attaching-loop class, with a path to the basepoint if needed. Attaching a cell of dimension at least 3 induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups.

Theorem thm:p202-graph-attach (presentation): a connected finite CW complex has fundamental-group presentation with one generator for each oriented edge outside a maximal tree of its 1-skeleton and one relation for each 2-cell attaching loop.

Theorem thm:p202-graph-attach (graphs): for every connected graph, finite or infinite, and a maximal tree containing its vertices, its fundamental group is free on the edges outside the tree after choosing one orientation for each such edge.

For the standard polygon model of a closed orientable genus-g surface, g≥1, the cell structure has one vertex, 2g edges a₁,b₁,…,a_g,b_g and a disk attached by ∏ᵢ aᵢbᵢaᵢ⁻¹bᵢ⁻¹. Its fundamental group has these generators and this one relation. For g=1 the group is ℤ², agreeing with π₁(S¹×S¹).

Theorem thm:p202-simplicial-approx: for any continuous f:|K|→|L| with K finite and L any simplicial complex, there exists a sufficiently iterated barycentric subdivision K′ and a simplicial g:K′→L such that its realization |g|, identified on |K′|=|K|, is homotopic to f.

Lemma lem:p202-avoid-cell: if f:Dⁿ→Z is continuous, Z is Hausdorff, e is an open k-cell in Z with complement W, and k>n, then f is homotopic, fixing every point of f⁻¹(W) throughout, to a map missing some point of e. No full CW structure on Z is assumed.
For CW complexes X,Y, a map is cellular if it maps Xⁿ into Yⁿ for every skeleton n; being cellular on a subcomplex A means this condition holds on A with its induced skeleta.
Theorem thm:p202-cellular-approx: any continuous map f:X→Y of CW complexes that is cellular on a subcomplex A is homotopic relative to A to a cellular map.

As consequences of relative cellular approximation, a map from an n-dimensional CW complex into a CW complex Y is homotopic to a map into Yⁿ. A homotopy between maps already cellular on its two ends can be replaced relative to those ends by one in Yⁿ⁺¹ when the source cylinder has dimension n+1, using I with both endpoints as 0-cells. This includes the corresponding control for based homotopy classes.

For each n≥1 and path d:y₀→y₁, the inner-cube/outer-collar construction transports πₙ(Y,y₀) isomorphically to πₙ(Y,y₁), with reversed d giving the inverse. A homotopy moving its basepoint along d induces the usual change-of-basepoint identity, by making it based at y₁ using the remaining path on the collar.

For n≥1, πₙ(Y,y) is formed from maps (Iⁿ,∂Iⁿ)→(Y,y) modulo homotopies fixing the boundary, with the group law given by concatenation in one cube coordinate. Relative disk classes for (Y,X) allow the boundary to map into X; in dimension 1 these are paths from a specified basepoint to a variable endpoint in X, modulo homotopies allowing that endpoint to move in X, interpreted as a pointed set.

Lemma lem:p202-whitehead-disk: if an inclusion X⊆Y induces a bijection on path components and isomorphisms on πₙ for every n≥1 and every basepoint in X, then for each n≥0 every continuous f:Dⁿ→Y whose boundary maps into X is homotopic relative to its boundary to a map into X. No CW hypothesis is required for this lemma.

Theorem thm:p202-whitehead: a continuous map of CW complexes inducing a bijection on path components and isomorphisms on all positive-dimensional homotopy groups at all basepoints is a homotopy equivalence, including disconnected CW complexes.

In singular homology R is a commutative ring with identity unless an abelian group is specified, and chains are always finite sums; no local-finiteness assumption on X is made. For n≥0, Cₙ(X;R) is the free R-module on continuous singular simplices Δⁿ→X. With ordered vertices, δᵢ omits vertex i and ∂σ=Σᵢ₌₀ⁿ(−1)ⁱσδᵢ for n>0; ∂:C₀→0 is zero. The augmentation ε:C₀→R sends each point to 1. Ordinary Hₙ is homology of the unaugmented complex, and reduced H̃ₙ is homology with R in degree −1; in particular H̃₋₁(∅;R)=R.

Proposition prop:p202-singular-functor (degree zero): H₀(X;A) is naturally the direct sum of the coefficient group A over all path components of X; H̃₀(X;A) is the kernel of the sum map from that direct sum to A. This includes the empty space and does not require local path connectedness.

Proposition prop:p202-singular-functor: the singular boundary satisfies ∂²=0 and postcomposition makes C_*(−;R) a functor of topological spaces to chain complexes (and induces the corresponding homology functors). For an abelian group A the coefficient complex is C_*(X;ℤ)⊗_ℤ A with the same face formula; for an R-module M the equivalent construction is C_*(X;R)⊗_R M.

For a point, the singular complex has one simplex in every nonnegative degree, differential identity in positive even degrees and zero in odd degrees. Its ordinary homology is R in degree 0 and zero in positive degrees, and reduced homology is zero. For S⁰ the complex is the direct sum of the two point complexes, with H̃₀(S⁰;R)=R and zero positive homology.

Theorem thm:p202-prism: any continuous homotopy from f to g induces a chain homotopy between f_# and g_#; a homotopy of pairs gives the same chain-homotopy identity on relative chains. Hence based or unbased homotopic maps induce equal ordinary and reduced homology maps (and relative homology maps for homotopies of pairs), and every nonempty contractible space has zero reduced homology.

For every pair (X,A), C_*(X,A;R)=C_*(X;R)/C_*(A;R) with the induced boundary, and H_*(X,A;R) is its homology. Inclusion is injective on the singular-simplex bases; the quotient is free on simplices of X not contained in A.

Lemma lem:p202-chain-les: every degreewise short exact sequence of chain complexes 0→K —i→ L —p→ M→0 has a natural long exact homology sequence …→Hₙ(K)→Hₙ(L)→Hₙ(M) —δ→ Hₙ₋₁(K)→…. For a cycle z∈Mₙ and lift c∈Lₙ, δ[z]=[i⁻¹(∂c)]; it is well-defined independently of choices and natural for maps of short exact sequences.

Theorem thm:p202-relative-les: for every pair (X,A) there is a natural exact sequence …→Hₙ(A;R)→Hₙ(X;R)→Hₙ(X,A;R) —∂→ Hₙ₋₁(A;R)→…. The connecting map takes a relative cycle represented by c to the ordinary homology class of ∂c in A. The reduced variant uses the same augmentation R in degree −1 on A and X; the relative quotient is zero in degree −1 and unchanged in nonnegative degrees.

For an open cover 𝒰 of X, C_*^𝒰(X;R) is the subcomplex generated by singular simplices whose image lies in one member of 𝒰. For A⊆X use the restricted cover, dropping empty intersections,. A chain support is the union of images of its finitely many simplices with nonzero coefficients.

Lemma lem:p202-subdivision: barycentric subdivision gives a natural chain map S:C_*(X;R)→C_*(X;R) chain homotopic to the identity. S and its chain homotopy K do not enlarge a simplex support, with ∂K+K∂=S−id.

Theorem thm:p202-small-chains: for any open cover 𝒰 of any X, the inclusion C_*^𝒰(X;R)→C_*(X;R) induces homology isomorphisms and is a chain homotopy equivalence over R. For every subspace A⊆X the corresponding small-relative-chain inclusion into C_*(X,A;R) has both properties. No PID assumption is imposed.
Theorem thm:p202-excision: for subsets Z⊆A⊆X with cl_X(Z)⊆int_X(A), the inclusion (X∖Z,A∖Z)→(X,A) induces isomorphisms Hₙ(X∖Z,A∖Z;R)≅Hₙ(X,A;R) in every degree. Z and A need not be open or closed.

Corollary thm:p202-good-pair: if ∅≠A⊆X is closed and is a strong deformation retract of an open neighborhood W in X, the quotient projection induces Hₙ(X,A;R)≅H̃ₙ(X/A;R) for every n≥0, including degree 0. The nonempty hypothesis is essential to this ordinary/reduced formulation.

Theorem thm:p202-mv: for X=U∪V with U,V open, there is a natural exact sequence …→Hₙ(U∩V;R) —(i_*,-j_*)→ Hₙ(U;R)⊕Hₙ(V;R) —sum→ Hₙ(X;R)→Hₙ₋₁(U∩V;R)→…. For every A⊆X the relative version has terms for (U∩V,A∩U∩V), (U,A∩U), (V,A∩V), and (X,A). Naturality is with respect to maps respecting the cover members and the second terms; no connectedness assumptions are imposed.

Ordinary singular homology with the stated coefficients satisfies functoriality, homotopy invariance, the pair long exact sequence, excision and the dimension axiom, as established above. For an arbitrary disjoint union ⨿ᵢXᵢ, singular chains and homology split as direct sums: C_*(⨿ᵢXᵢ;R)≅⊕ᵢ C_*(Xᵢ;R) and Hₙ(⨿ᵢXᵢ;R)≅⊕ᵢ Hₙ(Xᵢ;R).

Chapter coefficient and grading conventions: chains are over a commutative unital ring R unless specified; integral chains use R=Z. For an R-module A, change coefficients by C_*(-;R) tensor_R A for chains and Hom_R(C_*(-;R),A) for cochains. Ordinary H_{-1}=0; reduced degree-zero formulas use the augmented complex. The oriented standard n-simplex has vertex order 0,...,n; its positive-dimensional boundary is the signed ordered-face sum, and a vertex has ordinary boundary zero.

For an abstract simplicial complex K, the oriented simplicial q-chain module is generated by oriented simplices [v_0,...,v_q], with permutations of vertices acting by their sign. Its differential is the alternating affine-face boundary, which is compatible with the orientation relation.

A Delta-complex has specified parametrizations of cells with faces identified by order-preserving affine maps. Its chain module is generated by its oriented parametrized cells, and the differential is the signed sum of all faces, counting multiplicities even when distinct faces represent the same cell.
For both the oriented simplicial chain construction and the Delta-complex chain construction, the face boundary satisfies boundary composed with boundary = 0.

[thm:p202-simplicial-comparison, simplicial case] For a simplicial complex K with weak realization topology, any coefficient R-module A, and every q>=0, the chain map taking each oriented simplex in a chosen increasing vertex order to its affine singular parametrization induces an isomorphism H_q^simp(K;A) ≅ H_q(|K|;A). The isomorphism is natural for arbitrary simplicial maps, including maps collapsing vertices, and applies also to subcomplex pairs.

[thm:p202-simplicial-comparison, Delta-complex case] For a Delta-complex and any coefficient module A, the map given by its specified oriented simplex parametrizations induces an isomorphism from Delta-complex homology to singular homology in every degree q>=0. This is natural for maps preserving the ordered simplex parametrizations and holds for subcomplex pairs.

[thm:p202-cellular-comparison, cellular complex] For a CW complex X, put X^{-1}=empty and C_n^cell(X;A)=H_n(X^n,X^{n-1};A). Put d_0=0; for n>0 let d_n be the connecting homomorphism into H_{n-1}(X^{n-1};A), followed by projection into H_{n-1}(X^{n-1},X^{n-2};A).

[thm:p202-cellular-comparison, homology comparison] For every CW complex X and coefficient module A, the constructed cellular differential squares to zero. C_n^cell(X;A) is the direct sum of one copy of A for each oriented n-cell, and its nth homology is naturally isomorphic to H_n(X;A), naturally for cellular maps.

[thm:p202-cellular-comparison, attaching coefficients] For an n-cell of a CW complex with n>1, its differential coefficient at a selected (n-1)-cell is the degree of the composite S^{n-1} -> X^{n-1} given by its attaching map and the collapse of X^{n-2} and all other (n-1)-cells to the basepoint of the selected sphere. For n=1 the coefficient is the signed incidence of the final and initial endpoints.
[prop:p202-homology-computations, spheres] For any coefficient module A, n>=0, and j>=0, reduced H_j(S^n;A) is isomorphic to A when j=n and is zero otherwise.
[prop:p202-homology-computations, contractible spaces] A point, and every nonempty contractible space, has zero reduced homology with any coefficient module A.

[prop:p202-homology-computations, finite wedges] For a finite wedge of based CW complexes joined at vertices, and more generally a finite wedge of good pointed pairs with the usual wedge topology, reduced homology with coefficient module A is the direct sum of the reduced homologies of its summands. Here goodness means the basepoint is closed and is a strong deformation retract of an open neighborhood, as in the good-pair hypothesis stated at paper.tex 1340–1344.
[prop:p202-homology-computations, tori] For m>=1 and j>=0, H_j(T^m;Z) ≅ Z^{binomial(m,j)}; in particular it is zero for j>m.
[prop:p202-homology-computations, complex projective spaces] For m>=1, H_j(CP^m;Z) ≅ Z for j=0,2,...,2m and is zero for all other nonnegative j.
[prop:p202-homology-computations, real projective spaces] For m>=1, H_j(RP^m;Z) ≅ Z if j=0 or if j=m is odd; it is Z/2 when 0<j<m is odd; it is zero for all other nonnegative j.

[prop:p202-homology-computations, orientable surfaces] The closed oriented genus-g surface in its standard polygon model has integral H_0 ≅ Z, H_1 ≅ Z^{2g}, H_2 ≅ Z, and zero homology above its cell dimension 2 (including g=0).

[prop:p202-homology-computations, nonorientable surfaces] For k>=1 the standard closed nonorientable genus-k polygon model has integral H_0 ≅ Z, H_1 ≅ Z^{k-1} direct_sum Z/2, H_2=0, and zero homology above cell dimension 2.

[cor:p202-euler] For every finite CW complex X and field F, its Euler characteristic, the finite alternating sum of its numbers of q-cells, equals sum_q (-1)^q dim_F H_q(X;F). Consequently the Euler characteristic is independent of the chosen finite CW structure.
[prop:p202-degree, degree definition] For n>=0 and continuous f:S^n -> S^n, define deg(f) to be the integer by which f_* acts on reduced H_n(S^n;Z) ≅ Z.

[prop:p202-degree, degree properties] Degree of a continuous sphere self-map is homotopy invariant and multiplicative under composition. This includes n=0: the degrees of self-maps of S^0 are 1 for the identity, -1 for the interchange, and 0 for a constant map.
[prop:p202-degree, no retraction] For every n>=0, there is no continuous retraction from the closed (n+1)-disk D^{n+1} onto its boundary S^n.
[prop:p202-degree, Brouwer fixed point] For every n>=0, every continuous self-map of D^{n+1} has a fixed point.
[thm:p202-hurewicz-one] For a path-connected space X with chosen basepoint, sending a based loop to its singular integral 1-cycle induces an isomorphism π_1(X)_ab ≅ H_1(X;Z).

For any space pair Y subset X and abelian group A, define C^q(X,Y;A)=Hom_Z(C_q(X;Z)/C_q(Y;Z),A), with coboundary (delta a)(c)=a(boundary c). Equivalently these are cochains on X vanishing on every simplex in Y. Define H^q(X,Y;A) to be this cochain complex's cohomology; absolute cohomology is the case Y=empty.

[lem:p202-free-chain-dual] A quasi-isomorphism between bounded-below chain complexes of free modules over a ring is a chain homotopy equivalence. Consequently its image under Hom(-,A) induces a cohomology isomorphism for every coefficient module A.
[prop:p202-cohomology-pairs, functoriality and invariance] Ordinary cohomology with any abelian coefficient group is contravariant for continuous maps and is homotopy invariant.

[prop:p202-cohomology-pairs, pair sequence] Every pair (X,Y), without an openness assumption, has a natural cohomology long exact sequence ... -> H^q(X,Y;A) -> H^q(X;A) -> H^q(Y;A) -> H^{q+1}(X,Y;A) -> ..., for any abelian coefficient group A.

[prop:p202-cohomology-pairs, excision] For Z subset Y subset X with closure_X(Z) subset interior_X(Y), inclusion (X minus Z,Y minus Z) -> (X,Y) induces an isomorphism H^q(X,Y;A) -> H^q(X minus Z,Y minus Z;A) in every degree, with arbitrary abelian coefficients. This expands the singular-homology excision hypothesis referred to in this passage (stated at paper.tex 1318–1324).

[prop:p202-cohomology-pairs, Mayer–Vietoris] An open cover X=U union V yields the ordinary natural cohomological Mayer–Vietoris long exact sequence ... -> H^q(X;A) -> H^q(U;A) direct_sum H^q(V;A) -> H^q(U intersection V;A) -> H^{q+1}(X;A) -> ..., for any abelian coefficient group A.

For a singular simplex σ, σ[i_0,...,i_j] denotes restriction to the ordered face with those vertices. The tensor complex of chain complexes uses boundary(a tensor b)=boundary a tensor b+(-1)^{deg a} a tensor boundary b.

[thm:p202-ez] For arbitrary spaces X,Y and commutative unital R, there are natural chain homotopy inverse maps AW:C_*(X times Y;R) -> C_*(X;R) tensor_R C_*(Y;R) and sh in the opposite direction. On an n-simplex (x,y), AW(x,y)=sum_{i=0}^n x[0,...,i] tensor y[i,...,n]. For simplices σ,τ of degrees p,q, sh(σ tensor τ) is the oriented shuffle triangulation of σ times τ:Delta^p times Delta^q -> X times Y. Both composites are naturally chain homotopic to the identity; sh induces the homological external product.

[cor:p202-topological-kunneth] For a PID R, arbitrary spaces X,Y, and every n>=0, there is a natural short exact sequence 0 -> direct_sum_{i+j=n}(H_i(X;R) tensor_R H_j(Y;R)) -> H_n(X times Y;R) -> direct_sum_{i+j=n-1} Tor_1^R(H_i(X;R),H_j(Y;R)) -> 0. The first arrow is the external product. The sequence splits noncanonically; no natural splitting is asserted, and its Tor sum is zero in degree zero.

The Alexander–Whitney and shuffle chain constructions restrict to smooth singular simplices: their face and shuffle parametrizations are smooth. For smooth simplices σ,τ, the shuffle chain is the oriented triangulation of their product used for integration.

[thm:p202-cup] For any space X and commutative unital ring R, singular H^*(X;R), with the stated cup product, is a natural unital associative graded ring. If a has degree p and b degree q, then a cup b=(-1)^{pq} b cup a. Naturality means pullbacks of continuous maps are unital graded ring homomorphisms.

The singular cup product over commutative R is defined on cochains a of degree p and b of degree q by (a cup b)(σ)=a(σ[0,...,p]) b(σ[p,...,p+q]); equivalently it is evaluation on the (p,q) component of AW composed with the chain diagonal. The unit cochain is the constant degree-zero cochain 1. This construction induces the cup operation on cohomology.

[prop:p202-relative-cup] For open subspaces U,V subset X and commutative R there is a natural relative cup product H^p(X,U;R) tensor_R H^q(X,V;R) -> H^{p+q}(X,U union V;R). It is compatible with passage to absolute cohomology and natural for maps respecting both subspaces. The long exact sequence for an individual pair has no openness hypothesis.

[thm:p202-topological-uct, homology] For a PID R, R-module A, any space X, and n>=0, there is a natural exact sequence 0 -> H_n(X;R) tensor_R A -> H_n(X;A) -> Tor_1^R(H_{n-1}(X;R),A) -> 0. It splits noncanonically and uses H_{-1}=0 in degree zero.

[thm:p202-topological-uct, cohomology] For a PID R, R-module A, any space X, and n>=0, there is a natural exact sequence 0 -> Ext^1_R(H_{n-1}(X;R),A) -> H^n(X;A) -> Hom_R(H_n(X;R),A) -> 0. The last arrow is evaluation on cycles; the sequence splits noncanonically, with H_{-1}=0 in degree zero.

[Unnumbered relative extension of thm:p202-topological-uct] The same homology and cohomology universal-coefficient exact sequences apply to the relative singular complex of any pair (X,Y): replace every H_*(X;-) and H^*(X;-) in the PID statements by H_*(X,Y;-) and H^*(X,Y;-), with the same naturality, evaluation arrow, noncanonical splitting and H_{-1}=0 convention.

[Unnumbered field evaluation consequence] Over a field F, evaluation on cycles identifies singular cohomology H^n(X;F) with the full F-linear dual Hom_F(H_n(X;F),F), without any finite-dimensionality hypothesis on homology.

Standing scope for Orientation, Duality, and Comparison: topological manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable, and are finite-dimensional in duality theorems. Boundary is included only when explicitly indicated. Homology groups without a support superscript use ordinary finite singular chains, rather than locally finite chains. Each duality map retains its stated coefficient ring/module and support convention.

For a point x in a boundaryless n-manifold M, excision in a coordinate ball identifies H_j(M,M minus {x};R) with H_j(R^n,R^n minus {0};R). These local groups are isomorphic to R when j=n and are zero in other degrees. For n=0 the local pair is a point and the empty space.

An R-orientation of a boundaryless n-manifold M is a choice of generator o_x of H_n(M,M minus {x};R) at every point x, locally given on a coordinate ball by one oriented chart generator multiplied by a locally constant unit of R. Restriction of an oriented closed ball class to each interior point gives the same chart orientation, so this agreement condition is independent of the sufficiently small balls used.

The orientation cover of a boundaryless manifold has as fiber over x the two generators of its integral local top homology group. Signed local chart generators give trivializations with locally constant sign transitions; these glue to a two-sheeted covering. A continuous section is exactly an integral orientation.
Every boundaryless manifold is canonically oriented over F_2, because every local top homology group over F_2 has a unique generator.

[thm:p202-compact-orientation] If M is an R-oriented boundaryless n-manifold and K subset M is compact, there is a unique μ_K in H_n(M,M minus K;R) whose restriction at each x in K is o_x. These classes are compatible under K subset L. Moreover H_j(M,M minus K;R)=0 for j>n, and the map from H_n(M,M minus K;R) to the family of local degree-n groups at points of K is injective. If M is compact and boundaryless, μ_M is its ordinary homology fundamental class.
For a degree-p singular R-cochain a and a singular q-simplex σ, define a cap σ=a(σ[0,...,p]) σ[p,...,q] when q>=p and zero when q<p; extend R-linearly to chains.

[prop:p202-cap, identities] With the front-face cap convention, boundary(a cap c)=(-1)^p(a cap boundary c-(delta a) cap c), and evaluation satisfies <b,a cap c>=<a cup b,c>. For a continuous f:X -> Y, f_#((f^*a) cap c)=a cap f_#c. These include the zero and negative-degree endpoint conventions.
[prop:p202-cap, pair products] For every pair (X,B) the specified cap operation induces H^p(X;R) tensor_R H_q(X,B;R) -> H_{q-p}(X,B;R), and H^p(X,B;R) tensor_R H_q(X,B;R) -> H_{q-p}(X;R).

Compactly supported cohomology is H_c^p(M;R)=colim_{K compact subset M} H^p(M,M minus K;R), with transition maps for increasing K extending allowed supports. An equality in the limit is witnessed on a larger compact set. Equivalently it is the cohomology of the union of these relative cochain complexes.

[thm:p202-poincare] For an R-oriented boundaryless finite-dimensional n-manifold M, cap with the compatible compact orientation classes induces an isomorphism D_M:H_c^p(M;R) -> H_{n-p}(M;R), [a] -> a cap μ_K when a has support in compact K. If M is compact, this is cap with μ_M on ordinary cohomology. In the noncompact case the target still consists of ordinary finite-chain singular homology.

[thm:p202-lefschetz, relative fundamental class] If M is a compact R-oriented n-manifold with collared boundary B=boundary M, there is a relative fundamental class μ in H_n(M,B;R) restricting to the given orientation at every interior point. With B carrying the induced outward-normal-first boundary orientation, its connecting boundary is boundary μ=μ_B.

[thm:p202-lefschetz, both duality isomorphisms] For a compact R-oriented n-manifold M with collared boundary B and the stated relative fundamental class μ, both cap maps H^p(M,B;R) -> H_{n-p}(M;R) and H^p(M;R) -> H_{n-p}(M,B;R) are isomorphisms. The conclusion includes empty boundary, recovering compact Poincaré duality.

[lem:p202-enr] Let K subset R^n be compact. Suppose that for each x in K and each relative neighborhood U of x in K there is a smaller relative neighborhood V of x such that the inclusion V -> U is nullhomotopic. Then some open neighborhood of K in R^n retracts onto K. The assertion includes K=empty and ambient dimension zero, and imposes no local-flatness hypothesis on the embedding.

[thm:p202-alexander] If K is a nonempty proper compact locally contractible subset of S^n with n>=1, then for every i>=0 there is an isomorphism reduced H_i(S^n minus K;Z) ≅ reduced H^{n-i-1}(K;Z). The same conclusion holds with any fixed field in place of Z. Reduced cohomology of nonempty K in negative degrees is zero, so the assertion includes all endpoint and high-degree cases.

[lem:p202-projective-thom, normal orientation class] For a compact embedded smooth submanifold N subset M whose normal bundle has rank d and an R-orientation, there is a unique class in H^d(M,M minus N;R) restricting to the orientation generator on every normal fiber at its origin. No ambient orientation of M is assumed.

[lem:p202-projective-thom, transverse products] For a finite ordered family of compact embedded smooth submanifolds of M with R-oriented normal bundles that meet transversely, the relative cup product of their normal orientation classes restricts, on a normal slice to the intersection, to the product orientation generator, with the product order determining the orientation convention.
[prop:p202-cohomology-rings, real projective spaces] For m>=0, H^*(RP^m;F_2) is isomorphic as a graded F_2-algebra to F_2[u]/(u^{m+1}), with degree(u)=1. This includes m=0, when RP^0 is a point.
[prop:p202-cohomology-rings, complex projective spaces] For m>=0, H^*(CP^m;Z) is isomorphic as a graded Z-algebra to Z[v]/(v^{m+1}), with degree(v)=2. This includes m=0, when CP^0 is a point.

[prop:p202-cohomology-rings, tori] The integral graded cohomology ring of T^m is the exterior algebra over Z on the m degree-one classes pulled back from the circle factors, including their integral square-zero relations.

[prop:p202-cohomology-rings, oriented surfaces] For the closed oriented genus-g surface, the bilinear integral form on H^1 given by (a,b) -> <a cup b,[M]> is unimodular and alternating, and it admits a symplectic basis consisting of g pairs.

A smooth singular simplex in a smooth manifold M is a map from the standard simplex that is smooth as a map from a manifold with corners, with local smooth extensions in charts. Its face restrictions are smooth, giving the subcomplex C_*^sm(M;R) subset C_*(M;R). The comparison here uses R=real numbers.

[lem:p202-smooth-singular] For a finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold M, including the case of a smooth boundary, inclusion C_*^sm(M;R) -> C_*(M;R) induces an isomorphism in homology. Restriction of real singular cochains induces the corresponding cohomology isomorphism. These comparisons are natural for smooth maps; the boundary case is explicitly established at paper.tex 2702–2710.

[thm:p202-de-rham] For a finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold M, including smooth boundary, integration over smooth singular simplices induces a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras H_dR^*(M) ≅ H^*(M;R). Under this isomorphism wedge of forms corresponds to singular cup product. Naturality is for smooth maps; the smooth-boundary case is established at paper.tex 2809–2813.

The integration cochain map is I_M(ω)(σ)=integral_{Delta^q} σ^*ω for a smooth q-form ω and smooth singular q-simplex σ, with the standard ordered orientation. It satisfies I_M(dω)(σ)=I_M(ω)(boundary σ) and is natural under smooth pullback. Together with the smooth/continuous cochain comparison, it is the map inducing thm:p202-de-rham.

[thm:p202-invariance-domain, Jordan–Brouwer] For n>=1, the complement in S^n of any topologically embedded S^{n-1} has exactly two connected components, each with boundary equal to the embedded sphere. No collar or local-flatness assumption on the embedding is imposed.
[thm:p202-invariance-domain, invariance of domain] For n>=1, every continuous injection f:U -> R^n from an open subset U of R^n is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of R^n.

For a continuous self-map f of a finite polyhedron X, define its rational Lefschetz number Λ(f)=sum_j (-1)^j tr(f_*:H_j(X;Q) -> H_j(X;Q)); the finite-polyhedron hypothesis ensures the sum and traces are finite-dimensional.
[thm:p202-fixed-point] If X is a finite polyhedron and f:X -> X is continuous with Λ(f) nonzero, then f has a fixed point.

A Riemannian metric on a smooth manifold M is a smooth section g of Sym²(T*M) whose value on every tangent space is a positive-definite inner product. Its pairing and norm are denoted ⟨ , ⟩ and |·|_g. A local isometry is a local diffeomorphism preserving the metric. The ambient convention is finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifolds, without boundary unless one is specified.

Theorem [Existence, pullback, and length distance], label thm:p202-metric-distance. Every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold admits a Riemannian metric. If F:N→M is a smooth immersion and g is a Riemannian metric on M, then F*g is Riemannian on N. Local isometries preserve the lengths L_g(γ)=∫_a^b |γ̇(t)|_g dt of piecewise C¹ curves on compact intervals. For every connected component of a Riemannian manifold, d_g(p,q)=inf_{γ:p↝q} L_g(γ), over such curves, is a finite metric inducing the original topology; no positive-dimension hypothesis is imposed.

The existence of Riemannian metrics and the length-distance theorem also apply to smooth manifolds with smooth boundary, with their original manifold-with-boundary topology. The distance is defined componentwise using piecewise C¹ curves in the manifold; convex half-balls in boundary charts replace coordinate balls.

For a smooth vector bundle E→M, a connection is a real-bilinear operation (X,s)↦∇_X s on smooth vector fields and smooth sections, C∞(M)-linear in X and satisfying ∇_X(fs)=X(f)s+f∇_X s. In a local frame written as a row e, sections are e v for columns v, and the matrix of connection one-forms Γ is specified by ∇e=eΓ.

Proposition [Local connection calculus], label prop:p202-pullback-connection. For a smooth connection on E→M, the local formula on a section e v is e(dv+Γv). Under a frame change e′=eA the matrix is Γ′=A⁻¹ΓA+A⁻¹dA. Every smooth F:N→M induces a unique pullback connection on F*E satisfying the covariant chain rule on pulled-back sections in direction dF. Along a C¹ curve γ it gives D_t(e(γ(t))v(t))=e(γ(t))(v′(t)+Γ_{γ(t)}(γ̇(t))v(t)). The dual and tensor bundles have induced connections satisfying the product rule and commuting with contraction.
For a connection ∇ on TM, its torsion is T(X,Y)=∇_X Y−∇_Y X−[X,Y]. This expression is tensorial in X and Y (a tangent-valued 2-tensor).

A connection on the tangent bundle of a Riemannian manifold is metric compatible if X⟨Y,Z⟩=⟨∇_X Y,Z⟩+⟨Y,∇_X Z⟩ for all smooth vector fields X,Y,Z. With the induced connection on covariant tensors this is equivalent to ∇g=0. The same product identity holds for fields along a smooth map, using its pullback connection.

For any smooth two-parameter family F(s,t) into a manifold carrying a connection ∇ on TM, put V=F_*∂_s and T=F_*∂_t. Then D_s T−D_t V=Torsion(V,T), where the derivatives use the pullback connection. F may have nonconstant rank. In particular these two mixed derivatives agree for a torsion-free connection.

Theorem [Levi–Civita and the Koszul formula], label thm:p202-levi-civita. Every Riemannian metric has a unique torsion-free metric connection. For all smooth X,Y,Z it satisfies 2⟨∇_X Y,Z⟩=X⟨Y,Z⟩+Y⟨Z,X⟩−Z⟨X,Y⟩−⟨X,[Y,Z]⟩+⟨Y,[Z,X]⟩+⟨Z,[X,Y]⟩. In coordinates, Γ^k_{ij}=(1/2)∑_ℓ g^{kℓ}(∂_i g_{jℓ}+∂_j g_{iℓ}−∂_ℓ g_{ij}). A local isometry intertwines the Levi–Civita connections of source and target.

Theorem [Parallel transport and its inverse], label thm:p202-parallel. For a piecewise C¹ curve γ:[a,b]→M and a smooth connection on E→M, prescribing any vector at any parameter value determines a unique continuous field along γ that is C¹ and parallel on each smooth piece and has that value. Parallel transport P_st:E_{γ(s)}→E_{γ(t)} is linear, satisfies P_tu∘P_st=P_su for all parameter values, and P_ts=P_st⁻¹. If the connection is metric, every P_st preserves the inner product.

Parallel transport at a corner requires agreement of the continuous field and its one-sided values; the directional derivatives on the two pieces use their respective actual path velocities. The cited references and corrections explain this regularity convention, rather than imposing agreement of derivatives across a corner.

Theorem [Geodesic spray and smooth dependence], label thm:p202-geodesic-ivp. For each p∈M and v∈T_pM there exists a unique maximal geodesic γ_v with γ_v(0)=p and γ̇_v(0)=v, where a geodesic has D_tγ̇=0. Both position and velocity depend smoothly on (t,v) on their actual open domain of existence in ℝ×TM. Every affine reparametrization is again a geodesic, with the correspondingly scaled initial velocity (including zero scaling and constant geodesics). A Levi–Civita geodesic has constant speed.

For v∈T_pM whose maximal initial-value geodesic γ_v is defined at time 1, define exp_p(v)=γ_v(1). The total exponential map is defined on the subset of TM consisting of these vectors; exp_p is its restriction to T_pM.

Proposition [The exponential map near the zero section], label prop:p202-exp-local. The exponential map is smooth on its open domain in TM, the domain contains the entire zero section, and its intersection with every tangent fiber is star-shaped about zero. For every p, d(exp_p)_0=id_{T_pM}; thus exp_p is a diffeomorphism from a neighborhood of zero onto a neighborhood of p and defines normal coordinates. Normal coordinates obtained from an orthonormal basis have Euclidean metric at p, and all Christoffel symbols and all first coordinate derivatives of the metric vanish at p.

For a Riemannian metric with coordinate matrix (g_ij), set ρ=√det(g_ij). The local densities dV_g=ρ|dx¹⋯dxⁿ| agree to define the Riemannian density: under coordinate change ρ transforms by the absolute Jacobian. If the manifold is oriented, the signed expressions ρ dx¹∧⋯∧dxⁿ in oriented charts define its Riemannian volume form. These density and form constructions do not impose orientability when only the density is used.

For a smooth function u on a Riemannian manifold with Levi–Civita connection, grad_g u is specified by g(grad_g u,X)=du(X), Hess_g u(X,Y)=g(∇_X grad_g u,Y), and Δ_g u=tr_g Hess_g u=div_g grad_g u (the sign convention of the introduction). For a smooth vector field X, div_g X=tr(Y↦∇_Y X).

The coordinate-formula portion of Theorem [Scalar intrinsic differential and integral formulas], label thm:p202-green. For every smooth vector field X and smooth scalar function u, with ρ=√det(g_ij), div_g X=ρ⁻¹∂_i(ρX^i) and Δ_g u=tr_g Hess_g u=ρ⁻¹∂_i(ρg^{ij}∂_j u), with repeated indices summed.

The divergence-theorem portion of Theorem thm:p202-green. On any compact Riemannian manifold M with smooth boundary, outward unit normal ν, Riemannian volume density dV_g and induced boundary density dS_g, ∫_M div_g X dV_g=∫_{∂M}⟨X,ν⟩dS_g for every smooth vector field X. No orientability or connectedness assumption is made.

The Green-identity and compact-support portions of Theorem thm:p202-green. On a compact Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary and outward unit normal ν, all smooth u,v satisfy ∫_M(⟨grad_g u,grad_g v⟩+vΔ_g u)dV_g=∫_{∂M}v⟨grad_g u,ν⟩dS_g. On a Riemannian manifold without boundary, ∫_M div_g X dV_g=0 for every smooth compactly supported X; accordingly the analogous Green identity has zero right side when the field X=v grad_g u being integrated has compact support. These formulas use densities and apply without orientability or connectedness assumptions.

The explicitly stated second Green identity follows by swapping u,v in the first identity and subtracting: on a compact Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, ∫_M(vΔ_g u−uΔ_g v)dV_g=∫_{∂M}(v⟨grad_g u,ν⟩−u⟨grad_g v,ν⟩)dS_g. The same derivation gives zero boundary flux on a boundaryless manifold under the corresponding compact-support hypotheses for the integrated fields. This is an additional stated consequence, not an intermediate needed to prove the first identity.

The scalar Laplacian sign is compared with the classical Green identity in P201, and Lee is cited for coordinate formulas. These are reference and convention comments, not further independent assertions.

For a smooth variation F(s,t) of a curve on [a,b], define the tangent field T=∂_tF and variation field V=∂_sF. The varied base curve is γ(t)=F(0,t), and V along γ means ∂_sF evaluated at s=0. Energy is E(γ)=(1/2)∫_a^b|γ̇|_g²dt and length is L(γ)=∫_a^b|γ̇|_gdt, with the conventions fixed in the introduction.

The first-variation-formula portion of Theorem [The first variation of energy and length], label thm:p202-first-variation. For any smooth curve segment γ:[a,b]→M and smooth variation with variation field V, E′(0)=[⟨V,γ̇⟩]_a^b−∫_a^b⟨V,D_tγ̇⟩dt. If γ has positive speed throughout the compact segment, L′(0)=[⟨V,γ̇/|γ̇|_g⟩]_a^b−∫_a^b⟨V,D_t(γ̇/|γ̇|_g)⟩dt. The endpoint terms remain when endpoints move; the energy formula does not require nonzero speed.

The criticality portion of Theorem thm:p202-first-variation. With endpoints fixed, a smooth curve is energy critical among all smooth variations if and only if it is a geodesic; constant curves are included. A regular smooth curve is length critical among all smooth fixed-endpoint variations if and only if, after arc-length reparametrization, it is a geodesic.

The no-corner portion of Theorem thm:p202-first-variation. If a concatenation of nonconstant geodesic segments minimizes length between its endpoints, its left and right unit tangent velocities match at each join. Consequently unit-speed reparametrization glues those pieces to smooth geodesic segments.

For a curve γ on a compact interval [a,b], the energy–length estimate is L(γ)²≤2(b−a)E(γ), with equality at constant speed. A regular piecewise smooth length minimizer admits arc-length parametrization and has no corners.
Stationarity in the first variation gives a local candidate for minimization, not a general assertion of minimality; references to Lee, do Carmo and P106 supply comparison context.

The Gauss-lemma portion of Theorem [Gauss lemma and short minimizing geodesics], label thm:p202-gauss-normal. For every p∈M, every v in the fiber domain of exp_p, and every w∈T_pM (identified with a tangent vector to that fiber at v), ⟨d(exp_p)_v(v),d(exp_p)_v(w)⟩_{exp_p(v)}=⟨v,w⟩_p.

The radial-minimization portion of Theorem thm:p202-gauss-normal. For every p, on a sufficiently small normal ball centered at p, the radial geodesic from p to each point minimizes length among all piecewise C¹ competitors in M. Its minimizing image is unique, and every minimizing competitor differs only by increasing reparametrization and pauses.

The convex-neighborhood portion of Theorem thm:p202-gauss-normal. Each point of a Riemannian manifold has arbitrarily small neighborhoods such that every pair of points in the neighborhood is joined by a unique constant-speed minimizing geodesic, when parametrized on a fixed common interval, staying in the neighborhood. The geodesic depends smoothly on its two endpoints, and the squared Riemannian distance is smooth on the product neighborhood (including along the diagonal).

Normal coordinates at one center are distinguished from the stronger convex normal neighborhood property. The passage cites the corrected version of Lee's local-convexity theorem and do Carmo; it adds no extra theorem beyond the preceding normal-neighborhood conclusions.

Theorem [Hopf–Rinow], label thm:p202-hopf-rinow. Let M be a connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary. The following three conditions are equivalent: (1) its length metric d_g is complete; (2) every maximal geodesic is defined on all of ℝ; (3) every closed bounded subset is compact. Under these conditions every pair of points is joined by a geodesic whose length equals their distance. Moreover it already suffices for completeness that exp_p be defined on all of T_pM for one single p∈M; no completeness assumption at every center is required in this sufficient condition.

Hopf–Rinow asserts existence, without asserting uniqueness for arbitrary distant endpoints. The following discussion of conjugate and cut phenomena explains possible failure of the local normal-neighborhood uniqueness conclusion, and cites Lee and do Carmo.

For the Levi–Civita curvature convention R(X,Y)Z=∇_X∇_Y Z−∇_Y∇_X Z−∇_[X,Y]Z, define the covariant curvature tensor r(X,Y,Z,W)=⟨R(X,Y)Z,W⟩. Sectional curvature uses K(X,Y)=r(X,Y,Y,X)/(|X|²|Y|²−⟨X,Y⟩²) for linearly independent X,Y, with the convention fixed in the introduction.

The tensor-and-symmetry portion of Theorem [Curvature symmetries and commutators], label thm:p202-curvature-symmetry. For a Riemannian manifold with Levi–Civita connection, R is tensorial in all three arguments. Its four-tensor satisfies r(X,Y,Z,W)=−r(Y,X,Z,W)=−r(X,Y,W,Z) and r(X,Y,Z,W)=r(Z,W,X,Y). The first Bianchi identity is R(X,Y)Z+R(Y,Z)X+R(Z,X)Y=0; the differential Bianchi identity is (∇_X R)(Y,Z)+(∇_Y R)(Z,X)+(∇_Z R)(X,Y)=0, as endomorphism-valued expressions.

The tensor-commutator portion of Theorem thm:p202-curvature-symmetry. On every bundle of mixed tensors induced from TM and T*M, the induced connection satisfies that ∇_X∇_Y−∇_Y∇_X−∇_[X,Y] acts as the sum of R(X,Y) on each vector factor and its negative transpose on each covector factor. This includes compatibility with all tensor contractions.
Lee and do Carmo are cited for comparison of the algebraic and differential curvature identities; this is bibliographic context.

The recovery portion of Theorem [Recovery and contraction of curvature], label thm:p202-sectional-recovery. At any point of a Riemannian manifold, knowing the sectional curvature of every tangent 2-plane determines the entire covariant curvature tensor r. Equivalently, two tensors satisfying skew symmetry in the first and last pairs, pair interchange, and the first Bianchi identity on the same inner-product tangent space and identical sectional-curvature values are equal. The statement imposes no additional dimension restriction.
For an orthonormal frame (e_i), define Ric(Y,Z)=∑_i r(e_i,Y,Z,e_i), and define scalar curvature Scal=tr_g Ric. These contractions are independent of the choice of orthonormal frame.

The contraction portion of Theorem thm:p202-sectional-recovery. The Ricci tensor of a Riemannian manifold is symmetric, and it satisfies contracted Bianchi: ∇^i Ric_ij=(1/2)∂_j Scal, where the raised derivative index is contracted with the inverse metric.

The Schur portion of Theorem thm:p202-sectional-recovery. On a connected Riemannian manifold of dimension n≥3, assume that at every point p all tangent sectional curvatures have a common value κ(p), allowed initially to depend on p. Then κ is constant on the whole manifold. Connectedness and n≥3 are essential hypotheses of this stated conclusion; no analogous constancy conclusion is asserted in dimension two.

Theorem [Local Euclidean geometry and flatness], label thm:p202-flat. For any open subset U of a Riemannian manifold, the metric has zero curvature on U if and only if every p∈U has a neighborhood contained in U isometric to an open subset of Euclidean space of the same dimension.
The cited theorems in Lee provide reference context for the local-flatness results.

Let F:M→M̄ be an isometric immersion into a Riemannian manifold. In the pullback bundle F*T M̄, identify TM with the image of dF and define the normal bundle NM as its orthogonal complement. Use the pullback of the ambient Levi–Civita connection, denoted ∇̄, to differentiate ambient fields along F. These are constructions over the source M and remain applicable when the immersion has self-intersections in the ambient manifold.

Proposition [Gauss and Weingarten decompositions], label prop:p202-gauss-weingarten. For every isometric immersion F:M→M̄, all tangent fields X,Y and all normal fields ξ, ∇̄_X Y=∇_X Y+B(X,Y), ∇̄_X ξ=−A_ξ X+∇^⊥_X ξ, and ⟨A_ξ X,Y⟩=⟨B(X,Y),ξ⟩. The tangential connection ∇ is the intrinsic Levi–Civita connection; B is a symmetric normal-valued tensor (second fundamental form); ∇^⊥ is a metric connection on NM; and A_ξ is the shape operator defined by this pairing, with the indicated minus sign in the Weingarten formula. The formulas hold in arbitrary codimension and require only an immersion, not an embedding.

Theorem [Curvature equations in arbitrary codimension], label thm:p202-gauss-codazzi-ricci. For an isometric immersion F:M→M̄ with the preceding tangent and normal connections, let R^⊥ be the curvature of ∇^⊥. For all tangent X,Y,Z,W and normal ξ,η: r(X,Y,Z,W)=r̄(X,Y,Z,W)+⟨B(X,W),B(Y,Z)⟩−⟨B(Y,W),B(X,Z)⟩; (R̄(X,Y)Z)^⊥=(∇_X B)(Y,Z)−(∇_Y B)(X,Z); and ⟨R^⊥(X,Y)ξ,η⟩=⟨R̄(X,Y)ξ,η⟩+⟨[A_ξ,A_η]X,Y⟩. Ambient curvature is evaluated on the dF-images of tangent fields; ∇B uses ∇^⊥ on its value and the intrinsic tangent connection on its two inputs. All three equations apply in arbitrary codimension.

Corollary [The intrinsic meaning of Gaussian curvature], label cor:p202-egregium. For any immersed surface in Euclidean three-space and any local unit normal with shape operator A, the intrinsic Gaussian curvature is K=det A. In any parametrization, K is the determinant of the scalar second fundamental form divided by the determinant of the first fundamental form. Consequently this curvature is invariant under local isometries of the induced metrics, and the statement does not require a globally chosen normal.

Proposition [Mean curvature and first variation of volume], label prop:p202-volume-variation. Let F_s:M→M̄ be a smooth variation through immersions of a compact manifold M, with smooth boundary if present, and give M the induced metrics. At s=0 decompose V=∂_sF_s|_0=dF(W)+V^⊥ and set H=tr_g B (the mean-curvature vector is the trace, with no division by dimension). With outward unit normal ν on ∂M, (d/ds)Vol(M,F_s*ḡ)|_{s=0}=−∫_M⟨V^⊥,H⟩dV_g+∫_{∂M}⟨W,ν⟩dS_g. The same formula for the local change in volume applies to a compactly supported smooth variation of a noncompact immersion, using the density difference, with only the original boundary contributing. No orientability or connectedness assumption is imposed.

The source reiterates the trace convention for mean curvature and cites Lee and do Carmo for the immersion and volume-variation formulas. The trace convention is incorporated into the preceding proposition.

The completeness, topology and curvature portion of Theorem [The three simply connected curvature models], label thm:p202-models. For every n≥2 and a>0, Euclidean ℝⁿ, the radius-a sphere S_aⁿ, and the upper hyperboloid H_aⁿ with the specified induced metrics are complete and simply connected. Their sectional curvatures at every point and tangent 2-plane are respectively 0, a⁻² and −a⁻². Completeness is both geodesic and metric completeness by the stated Hopf–Rinow equivalence.

For n≥2 and radius a>0, the model spaces are Euclidean ℝⁿ with its Euclidean metric; the radius-a sphere S_aⁿ with its induced Euclidean metric; and the upper hyperboloid H_aⁿ={(x,τ)∈ℝⁿ×ℝ: |x|²−τ²=−a², τ>0}, with the restriction of the Lorentz bilinear form ⟨(x,τ),(y,σ)⟩_L=x·y−τσ to tangent spaces. That restriction is positive definite, hence defines a Riemannian metric on H_aⁿ. The upper half-space is {(y,z):y∈ℝ^{n−1},z>0} with Riemannian metric a²z⁻²(dy²+dz²).

The explicit-geodesic portion of Theorem thm:p202-models. For each model, every point p and unit tangent vector u at p have the following unit-speed geodesic with initial data (p,u), defined for every real t: γ(t)=p+tu in Euclidean space; γ(t)=cos(t/a)p+a sin(t/a)u on S_aⁿ; γ(t)=cosh(t/a)p+a sinh(t/a)u on H_aⁿ. Here n≥2 and a>0, and p,u are interpreted in the indicated Euclidean or Lorentz ambient space.

The half-space portion of Theorem thm:p202-models. For n≥2 and a>0, the entire upper half-space {(y,z):y∈ℝ^{n−1},z>0} with metric a²z⁻²(dy²+dz²) is globally isometric to the upper hyperboloid H_aⁿ with its induced Lorentz Riemannian metric. The obligation is existence of an isometry of the full spaces, not merely a local coordinate identification or metric sample.

Lee and do Carmo are cited for the three model metrics. Radial Jacobi fields and classification of complete constant-curvature manifolds are explicitly deferred to later sections G20 and G22 rather than asserted as additional results in this passage.

Chapter-wide setting and conventions: the Riemannian metric is smooth and positive definite, and geodesic and completeness results are used on manifolds without boundary. Use R(X,Y)Z = ∇_X∇_Y Z − ∇_Y∇_X Z − ∇_[X,Y] Z, D_t for covariant differentiation along a curve, and T = γ̇ along a geodesic. The energy of a curve γ on [a,b] is E(γ) = (1/2)∫_a^b |γ̇|² dt.

With the stated curvature sign convention, the round sphere has positive sectional curvature. For a unit tangent vector T, the radial curvature operator V ↦ R(V,T)T preserves T⊥ and is self-adjoint there.
A Jacobi field J along an affinely parametrized geodesic γ is a solution of D_t²J + R(J,T)T = 0, where T = γ̇.

Linearized geodesic equation (thm:p202-jacobi-variation): for every geodesic γ, the variation field J of any smooth variation through affinely parametrized geodesics satisfies D_t²J + R(J,T)T = 0. Jacobi fields exist and are uniquely specified by arbitrary initial data J(t₀) and D_tJ(t₀), throughout the interval of γ. Conversely, on every compact parameter segment contained in that interval, each Jacobi field is the variation field of a smooth geodesic variation. If γ is nonconstant, the tangential component of any Jacobi field is (a+bt)T for constants a,b, and its normal component is also a Jacobi field.

Exponential differential (thm:p202-exp-jacobi): let γ(t)=exp_p(tv), and let w∈T_pM. Wherever γ is defined, the Jacobi field with J(0)=0 and D_tJ(0)=w obeys J(t)=d(exp_p)_{tv}(tw). For every t>0, the vector space of Jacobi fields along γ vanishing at both 0 and t has dimension equal to the nullity of d(exp_p)_{tv}. Consequently γ(t) is conjugate to p along this particular γ exactly when this differential is singular; multiplicity is that of the chosen geodesic, not an aggregate over geodesics with the same endpoint.

Conjugacy and multiplicity along a specified geodesic γ from p: a positive-time endpoint γ(t) is conjugate to p when there is a nonzero Jacobi field along γ vanishing at 0 and t; the multiplicity is the dimension of that space of fields. The specification is along the given geodesic, rather than merely a property of the endpoint reached by all possible geodesics.
For vector fields V,W along a geodesic γ:[a,b]→M with tangent T, the index form is I(V,W)=∫_a^b(⟨D_tV,D_tW⟩−⟨R(V,T)T,W⟩)dt.

Second variation of energy (thm:p202-second-variation): for a smooth variation F(s,t) of a geodesic γ:[a,b]→M, let S=∂_sF and V=S|_{s=0}. Then d²/ds² E(F(s,·))|_{s=0}=I(V,V)+[⟨D_sS,T⟩]_{t=a}^{t=b}|_{s=0}. For a fixed-endpoint variation the boundary term is zero. The same formula holds when F is continuous, smooth in s, and piecewise smooth in t, with fixed break parameters and smooth matching traces in s.

Index lemma (thm:p202-index-lemma): let γ:[0,b]→M be a geodesic with b>0 and no point conjugate to γ(0) at any 0<t≤b. For every terminal vector z∈T_{γ(b)}M there is a unique Jacobi field J with J(0)=0 and J(b)=z. Every continuous piecewise C¹ field V with these same endpoint values satisfies I(V,V)≥I(J,J), and equality holds if and only if V=J. In particular, any nonzero continuous piecewise C¹ field vanishing at both endpoints has I(V,V)>0.

A minimizing segment has no interior conjugate point (cor:p202-no-interior-conjugate): if a geodesic segment minimizes length between its endpoints, no point strictly between those endpoints is conjugate to its initial point along that segment.

Terminal conjugacy is compatible with minimality: a great semicircle on a round sphere ending at the antipode minimizes length, while a nonzero Jacobi field obtained by rotating that great circle about the antipodal axis vanishes at both endpoints.

Cut time and cut locus: fix p in a connected complete positive-dimensional Riemannian manifold, and let S_pM be the unit sphere in T_pM. For v∈S_pM define c(v)=sup{t≥0 : d(p,exp_p(tv))=t}, valued in (0,∞]. If c(v)<∞, exp_p(c(v)v) is the cut point in direction v. Cut(p) is the union of these finite-time cut points over v∈S_pM.

Cut-point criterion and polar domain (thm:p202-cut-polar): on a connected complete positive-dimensional Riemannian manifold, fix p and define c and Cut(p) as above. If q=exp_p(c(v)v) is a finite-time cut point, then q is conjugate to p along that minimizing segment, or there are two distinct minimizing geodesics from p to q, or both. For every 0<t<c(v), the minimizing segment from p to exp_p(tv) is unique and nonconjugate. The cut-time function c:S_pM→(0,∞] is continuous for the extended positive half-line topology. The polar exponential (t,v)↦exp_p(tv), with 0<t<c(v), is a diffeomorphism onto M∖({p}∪Cut(p)). This complement is open, and on it the distance to p is smooth with gradient equal to the unit radial vector.

For every unit v based at p in the complete connected setting defining cut time, the set {t≥0 : d(p,exp_p(tv))=t} is an initial interval, is closed as a subset of [0,∞), and has positive length. Thus it equals [0,c(v)] when c(v)<∞, and [0,∞) when c(v)=∞.
For every real k, define s_k(t)=sin(√k t)/√k if k>0, s_0(t)=t, and s_k(t)=sinh(√(−k)t)/√(−k) if k<0.
The model radial function s_k satisfies s_k″+k s_k=0, s_k(0)=0, and s_k′(0)=1 for every real k.

Constant-curvature polar metric (prop:p202-model-polar): on an n-dimensional Riemannian manifold of constant sectional curvature k, along any unit-speed geodesic the normal Jacobi field with J(0)=0 and D_tJ(0)=w⊥T(0) is J(t)=s_k(t)P_t w, where P_t is parallel transport. On any normal ball centered at p the polar-coordinate metric is dt²+s_k(t)²g_{S^{n−1}}, with angular metric the unit-sphere metric in T_pM. The same tensor identity for the pullback by (t,v)↦exp_p(tv) holds away from the origin on the entire exponential domain, including degeneracy where s_k vanishes.

Rauch comparison for fields vanishing initially (thm:p202-rauch): let γ:[0,b]→M and γ̄:[0,b]→M̄ be unit-speed geodesics in Riemannian manifolds of the same dimension n≥2. Suppose that for every t and every unit normals u⊥γ̇(t), ū⊥γ̄̇(t), K(γ̇(t),u)≤K̄(γ̄̇(t),ū). Suppose γ̄ has no point conjugate to γ̄(0) at any 0<t≤b. Then γ has no point conjugate to γ(0) at any 0<t≤b. For all normal Jacobi fields J,J̄ with J(0)=J̄(0)=0 and |D_tJ(0)|=|D̄_tJ̄(0)|, one has |J(t)|≥|J̄(t)| for every 0≤t≤b.
The cut locus has volume zero (lem:p202-cut-null): for every p on any complete connected positive-dimensional Riemannian manifold, Cut(p) has zero Riemannian volume.

Bishop–Gromov volume comparison (thm:p202-bishop-gromov): let Mⁿ be complete and connected with n≥2 and Ric≥(n−1)k g for a real k. For every p∈M, r↦Vol(B(p,r))/V_k^n(r) is nonincreasing on 0<r<π/√k when k>0, and on all r>0 when k≤0. Its limit as r↓0 is 1. If k>0, the comparison also holds at r=π/√k by the one-sided limit.
For n≥2, real k, and r>0, V_k^n(r) is the Riemannian volume of a radius-r ball in the simply connected n-dimensional complete constant-sectional-curvature-k model.

Complete local isometries (thm:p202-complete-cover): let F:X→Y be a local isometry between connected Riemannian manifolds without boundary. If X is complete, then F is a covering map, in particular surjective. Conversely, on every smooth covering of a complete Riemannian manifold, the pullback Riemannian metric is complete on each connected component.

Killing–Hopf classification (thm:p202-killing-hopf): if Mⁿ is complete and connected, without boundary, n≥2, and has constant sectional curvature k, its Riemannian universal cover is isometric to the simply connected constant-curvature model X_kⁿ: Euclidean space for k=0, the round sphere of radius 1/√k for k>0, and hyperbolic space of curvature k for k<0. If M is simply connected, M itself is isometric to that model. In general M is the quotient of the model by its group of covering transformations, whose action is by isometries, is free, and is properly discontinuous.

Cartan–Hadamard (thm:p202-cartan-hadamard): let M be a complete connected Riemannian manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature. For every p∈M, exp_p:T_pM→M is a covering map. If M is simply connected, every such exponential is a diffeomorphism, and any two points of M are joined by a unique minimizing geodesic up to parametrization.

As a consequence of Cartan–Hadamard, the universal cover of a complete connected n-dimensional Riemannian manifold of nonpositive sectional curvature is diffeomorphic to ℝⁿ. Completeness is included in the hypotheses.

Bonnet–Myers (thm:p202-bonnet-myers): let Mⁿ be a complete connected Riemannian manifold without boundary, with n≥2. If Ric≥(n−1)k g for a real k>0, then diam(M)≤π/√k, M is compact, and its fundamental group is finite.
The n≥2 condition in the stated Bonnet–Myers normalization is essential: when n=1, Ric≥(n−1)k g is vacuous, and the complete Euclidean line satisfies it for k>0 while having unbounded diameter.

Signed geodesic curvature and corner conventions: on an oriented Riemannian surface let J be rotation by +π/2 in oriented tangent planes. For a regular oriented curve with unit tangent T define k_g=⟨D_TT,JT⟩. Positive boundary orientation puts the region on the left, so JT is its inward surface unit normal on smooth boundary arcs. At a corner with interior angle 0<α<2π, define the signed exterior angle ε=π−α; a reflex corner contributes a negative angle.

Euler characteristic of a planar region (lem:p202-planar-region): let D be the compact closure of a nonempty connected planar domain, with boundary consisting of b≥1 disjoint simple closed piecewise smooth regular curves having finitely many noncuspidal corners. Suppose locally at every boundary point D occupies one side of its boundary curve. Then χ(D)=2−b. In the induced boundary orientation, exactly one boundary curve has its bounded side on the left, and every other boundary curve has its bounded side on the right.

Turning of a positively oriented simple plane boundary (lem:p202-plane-turning): let a piecewise smooth regular Jordan curve in an oriented plane have its bounded side on the left, finitely many corners, and no cusps. Choose continuous tangent angles on its smooth arcs. The sum of their total angle changes plus the signed exterior angles at corners is 2π. Reversing the orientation makes this total −2π.

Local Gauss–Bonnet (thm:p202-local-gb): let D be a compact disk contained in an oriented coordinate neighborhood of a Riemannian surface, with simple piecewise smooth regular boundary and finitely many noncuspidal corners, endowed with positive boundary orientation. Then ∫_D K dA + ∫_{∂D} k_g ds + Σ_corners ε = 2π, where the boundary integral is over smooth arcs and ε=π−α for the interior angle α. More generally, if D is a connected compact chart region satisfying all hypotheses of lem:p202-planar-region, the same left side equals 2πχ(D), with induced orientation on each boundary component.

Planar regions cut out on a compact surface (lem:p202-surface-regions): for every compact smooth surface S with smooth boundary, possibly empty, construct a finite embedded graph G containing ∂S and having smooth regular open edges, such that the closures D_j of all complementary components lie in individual charts and satisfy the planar-region hypotheses: each is the compact closure of a nonempty connected planar domain, with nonempty boundary a finite disjoint union of simple closed piecewise smooth regular curves with finitely many noncuspidal corners, and locally occupies one side of each boundary curve. Near each graph vertex the regions occupy graph sectors. If G has V vertices and E edges, then χ(S)=V−E+Σ_jχ(D_j).

Gauss–Bonnet for compact Riemannian surfaces (thm:p202-global-gb): let S be a compact smooth Riemannian surface, either closed or with smooth boundary, without any requirement of orientability or connectedness. Along ∂S define k_g=⟨D_TT,N_in⟩, where T is either unit tangent and N_in is the inward surface unit normal to the boundary. Then ∫_S K dA + ∫_{∂S} k_g ds = 2πχ(S), where dA is the Riemannian area density and χ(S) is the topological Euler characteristic. This includes the empty surface, for which both sides vanish.

Throughout the notes, congruence moduli and rational denominators are positive unless explicitly stated otherwise; primes are positive prime integers; gcds are nonnegative; finite prime valuations of integers have nonzero arguments unless a zero convention is specified. Arithmetic functions are defined on positive integers and divisor sums use positive divisors. Rational approximation distinguishes |x−p/q| from |qx−p|.
