Chapter title and explanation that the chapter fixes the arithmetic conventions used throughout the notes.
The natural numbers are N={0,1,2,...}, and N_{>0} denotes the positive integers. Gcds and lcms of integers are taken to be nonnegative.
For integers a,b, a divides b means that there exists an integer c such that b=a*c. Consequently 0 divides b if and only if b=0.
All congruence moduli m are positive integers; for integers a,b, a≡b (mod m) means m divides a-b.
References for the elementary arithmetic conventions and results.
For every integer a and positive integer m there exist unique integers q,r with a=q*m+r and 0≤r<m (division with remainder).
For all integers a,b and d=gcd(a,b), the set aZ+bZ of integer linear combinations equals dZ, and every common divisor of a,b divides d. This includes a=b=0 and d=0.
For any integers a,b, the Euclidean algorithm on |a|,|b|, using successive nonnegative division remainders, terminates and returns d=gcd(a,b), the nonnegative gcd. In particular a=b=0 gives d=0.
For every prime p and integers a,b, if p divides a*b, then p divides a or p divides b.
For all integers a,b and d=gcd(a,b), lcm(a,b)=0 if a*b=0 and lcm(a,b)=|a*b|/d otherwise; in every case the common integer multiples of a and b are exactly the multiples of lcm(a,b).
A prime is an integer p>1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p.
For a nonzero integer n, its sign is +1 when n>0 and -1 when n<0.
The units of the integer ring Z are exactly 1 and -1.
Every positive integer is a product of primes, unique up to the order of the factors; the factorization of 1 is the empty product.
Every nonzero integer is its sign times a prime product, with the prime product unique up to order.
For a prime p and nonzero integer n, v_p(n) is the exponent of p in the prime factorization of n (equivalently of |n|).
For nonzero integers a,b, a divides b if and only if v_p(a)≤v_p(b) for every prime p.
For every prime p and nonzero integers a,b, v_p(a*b)=v_p(a)+v_p(b).
For every prime p and nonzero integers a,b, v_p(gcd(a,b))=min(v_p(a),v_p(b)) and v_p(lcm(a,b))=max(v_p(a),v_p(b)).
For every prime p, v_p(1)=v_p(-1)=0; for every nonzero integer n and natural exponent j, p^j divides n if and only if j≤v_p(n).

With v_p(0)=+∞, for arbitrary integers a,b the product formula v_p(a*b)=v_p(a)+v_p(b), the divisibility equivalence a divides b iff v_p(a)≤v_p(b) for every prime p, and the gcd/lcm minimum/maximum valuation formulas continue to hold, including either or both inputs zero; min(+∞,+∞)=max(+∞,+∞)=+∞.
The prime valuation may be extended to every integer by v_p(0)=+∞, taking values in N∪{+∞}, with +∞+k=+∞. Any statement using a finite valuation assumes its argument is nonzero.
For a prime p and integers U,V, if v_p(U)=j is finite and p^(j+1) divides V, then v_p(U+V)=j.
For integers a,b,c with d=gcd(a,b)>0, if (x0,y0) is one solution of a*x+b*y=c, its full set of integer solutions is {(x0+(b/d)*t, y0-(a/d)*t) : t∈Z}.

For integers a,b,c and d=gcd(a,b), the equation a*x+b*y=c has an integer solution (x,y) if and only if d divides c. Thus when a=b=0 it has every integer pair as a solution if c=0, and no solution otherwise.

For integers a,b and positive integer m, put d′=gcd(a,m). The congruence a*x≡b (mod m) has an integer solution if and only if d′ divides b. Whenever solvable it has exactly d′ distinct solution classes modulo m, including m=1.
For a prime p and n∈N, v_p(n!)=sum_{j≥1} floor(n/p^j).
For a prime p and natural integers 0≤k≤n, v_p(binomial(n,k))=sum_{j≥1}(floor(n/p^j)-floor(k/p^j)-floor((n-k)/p^j)); every summand is either 0 or 1, and every summand with p^j>n is zero.
Explanation that the counting formula is used for later prime-counting bounds, with bibliographic reference.

For any finite list of positive integer moduli m1,...,ms and integer residues a1,...,as, there exists an integer x satisfying x≡ai (mod mi) for every i if and only if ai≡aj (mod gcd(mi,mj)) for every pair i,j. If a solution exists, all solutions form one class modulo L=lcm(m1,...,ms). This includes the empty list, with empty lcm 1, for which every integer is a solution and there is one class modulo 1.

For a finite pairwise coprime family of positive integer moduli mi and M=product_i mi, the map Z/MZ → product_i Z/miZ given by simultaneous reduction is a ring isomorphism. This includes moduli equal to 1 and the empty family, with empty product 1.

For the pairwise coprime finite family of positive moduli mi with M=product_i mi, for every index with mi>1 let Mi=M/mi, choose an integer ui satisfying Mi*ui≡1 (mod mi), and put ei=Mi*ui. Such choices exist, and the inverse of the reduction ring isomorphism sends a tuple of residue classes (ai)i to the class modulo M of sum_{mi>1} ai*ei, independent of representatives. A modulus 1 contributes no term; the empty lcm and product equal 1.
Comparison with Apostol and existing MathGenome counterparts; these are reuse pointers, not additional assertions to formalize.
The set of prime numbers is infinite.
There are infinitely many primes p satisfying p≡3 (mod 4).
Explanation of the elementary factorization proof, forward pointer to Dirichlet prime existence, and references; the later Dirichlet theorem is inventoried at its own statement.

For each positive integer m, U_m=(Z/mZ)^× is the multiplicative group of units. A primitive root modulo m is an integer representative of a generator of U_m. This includes m=1, whose sole class is its multiplicative identity.
Chapter arithmetic conventions and bibliographic references.
For an element g of a finite group, its order is the least positive integer d with g^d=1.

For every element g of a finite group G, there exists a positive power equal to the identity. If d is its order, then for every integer exponent j, g^j=1 iff d divides j; its powers 1,g,...,g^(d-1) form a subgroup of size d, and d divides |G|.
For m≥1, φ(m)=|U_m|, equivalently the number of integers a satisfying 0≤a<m and gcd(a,m)=1.
For positive integers m,n, φ(1)=1; for every prime p and k≥1, φ(p^k)=p^(k-1)*(p-1); φ(m)=m*product_{prime p divides m}(1-1/p); and if gcd(m,n)=1, then φ(m*n)=φ(m)*φ(n).
For an integer a and positive integer m, gcd(a,m)=1 implies a^φ(m)≡1 (mod m), including m=1.
For a prime p and integer a not divisible by p, a^(p-1)≡1 (mod p).
For every integer a and prime p, a^p≡a (mod p).
For every integer m>1, m is prime if and only if (m-1)!≡-1 (mod m).
Bibliographic reference for the totient and classical congruence results.
For every field K and nonzero polynomial F over K of degree d, F has at most d distinct roots in K.

For every field K and nonconstant polynomial F over K, there exists an extension field L generated over K by all roots of F in L such that F splits over L, and any two such splitting fields are isomorphic by a K-isomorphism.
Every finite field has prime characteristic p and cardinality p^f for some integer f≥1.
For every prime p and integer f≥1 there exists a field of cardinality p^f; any two fields of that cardinality are isomorphic by an isomorphism fixing the prime field.
Every finite subgroup of the multiplicative group of any field is cyclic.
For every finite field of cardinality q, its multiplicative group is cyclic of order q-1 and has exactly φ(q-1) generators, including q=2.
Bibliographic references and pointers to existing finite-field counterparts in MathGenome.
For every odd prime p and integer u with u≡1 (mod p) and u≠1, v_p(u^p-1)=v_p(u-1)+1.
For every odd prime p there exists one integer g whose class generates U_(p^k) for every integer k≥1.
For every positive integer m, U_m is cyclic if and only if m is 1, 2, 4, p^k, or 2*p^k for an odd prime p and integer k≥1.
For every positive integer m such that U_m is cyclic, the number of primitive-root classes modulo m is φ(φ(m)), including m=1 and m=2.
For every integer k≥3, every unit class modulo 2^k has a unique representation (-1)^a*5^b with a∈{0,1} and integer 0≤b<2^(k-2).
Bibliographic references and a pointer to Mathlib primitive-root classification.

Let p be prime, F∈Z[X], j≥1, and a∈Z satisfy F(a)≡0 (mod p^j) and p not dividing F′(a). Among the p classes a+p^j*t modulo p^(j+1), for t modulo p, exactly one is a root of F modulo p^(j+1). Its derivative has the same nonzero residue modulo p as F′(a).

For every prime p and polynomial F∈Z[X], every simple root class of F modulo p extends uniquely to a root class modulo each higher prime power p^k (k≥1), with compatible reductions and derivative nonzero modulo p.
Identification of the finite-modulus simple-root scope, warning that derivative-zero roots need separate analysis, and reference.
For an odd prime p and integer a, the Legendre symbol (a/p) is 0 if p divides a, 1 if a is a nonzero square modulo p, and -1 otherwise.
For every odd prime p, h=(p-1)/2, and integer a, a^h≡(a/p) (mod p).
For every odd prime p and integers a,b, (a*b/p)=(a/p)*(b/p).
For every odd prime p and integer a not divisible by p, let h=(p-1)/2 and let N count those least positive residues of a,2a,...,h*a modulo p that exceed p/2. Then (a/p)=(-1)^N.
References for Euler criterion and Gauss lemma.
For distinct odd primes p,q, (q/p)*(p/q)=(-1)^(((p-1)/2)*((q-1)/2)).
For every odd prime p, (-1/p)=(-1)^((p-1)/2).
For every odd prime p, (2/p)=(-1)^((p^2-1)/8).
Bibliographic references for quadratic reciprocity and its supplements.

For every positive odd integer m=product_p p^(e_p) and integer a, the Jacobi symbol (a/m)_J is product_{p:e_p>0}(a/p)^(e_p), using Legendre symbols. For m=1 the empty product is 1, and for an odd prime denominator it equals the Legendre symbol.

For integer numerators and positive odd denominators, the Jacobi symbol depends only on the numerator class modulo the denominator; it is multiplicative in the numerator and in the denominator (no coprimality condition on denominator factors); and (a/m)_J=0 if and only if gcd(a,m)>1.
For every positive odd integer m, (-1/m)_J=(-1)^((m-1)/2), including m=1.
For every positive odd integer m, (2/m)_J=(-1)^((m^2-1)/8), including m=1.
For all positive odd integers a,m, including noncoprime a,m and either equal to 1, (a/m)_J=(-1)^(((a-1)/2)*((m-1)/2))*(m/a)_J.

The Jacobi rules give a terminating Euclidean-reduction algorithm to compute (a/m)_J for every integer a and positive odd m: return 1 at m=1; otherwise reduce a to 0≤r<m, return 0 if r=0, factor r=2^v*c with c odd, apply the supplement for 2, return the remaining symbol 1 if c=1, and otherwise apply reciprocity and repeat with numerator m and strictly smaller odd denominator c. The resulting value equals the defining Jacobi symbol, including zero outputs.

The explicit composite-modulus counterexample: (2/15)_J=(2/3)*(2/5)=1, whereas 2 is not a square modulo 3 and hence is not a square modulo 15. Thus a Jacobi-symbol value +1 does not imply a square residue for composite positive odd moduli.
References for Jacobi symbols and their computation.

For every integer a and positive integer m=product_p p^(k_p) over the positive prime exponents, the number of solution classes x modulo m of x^2≡a (mod m) equals the product of the counts for its prime-power factors. The empty product is 1, so there is exactly one root class when m=1.
For every prime p, integer k≥1, and integer a with a≡0 (mod p^k), the roots of x^2≡a (mod p^k) are precisely the classes divisible by p^ceil(k/2), and their number is p^floor(k/2).

For every prime p, k≥1, and integer a not congruent to 0 modulo p^k, let s=v_p(a)<k. If s is odd, x^2≡a (mod p^k) has no roots. If s=2*t, set j=k-2*t and a′=a/p^(2*t), so p does not divide a′. The number of roots modulo p^k is p^t times the number of roots of y^2≡a′ (mod p^j).
For every odd prime p, integer j≥1, and integer a′ not divisible by p, the number of roots of y^2≡a′ (mod p^j) is 2 if (a′/p)=1 and 0 otherwise.
For every odd integer a′, the number of roots of y^2≡a′ (mod 2^j) is 1 when j=1; when j=2 it is 2 if a′≡1 (mod 4) and 0 otherwise; and when j≥3 it is 4 if a′≡1 (mod 8) and 0 otherwise.
Explanation that the classification separates singular and simple roots, explicitly includes modulus 1, and bibliographic references.

Chapter 3 conventions: ℕ_{>0} denotes the positive integers; every summation index n≤x with real x is a positive integer satisfying that inequality; logarithms are natural. O and asymp refer to x→+∞, and F asymp G means there exist constants c,C>0 for which cG(x)≤F(x)≤CG(x) eventually.
For every commutative ring R with identity, consider arithmetic functions f:ℕ_{>0}→R, with pointwise addition and Dirichlet convolution (f*g)(n)=∑_{d|n} f(d)g(n/d). Define δ(1)=1 and δ(n)=0 for n≠1.

Theorem C01: For every commutative ring R with identity, the arithmetic functions ℕ_{>0}→R form a commutative ring under pointwise addition and Dirichlet convolution, with convolution identity δ. An arithmetic function f is a convolution unit if and only if f(1) is a unit of R.
For arithmetic functions f:ℕ_{>0}→R (R a commutative ring with identity), multiplicative means f(1)=1 and f(ab)=f(a)f(b) whenever a,b are positive coprime integers.

Let R be any commutative ring with identity. Theorem C02, algebraic assertions: A multiplicative f:ℕ_{>0}→R satisfies f(n)=∏_{p|n} f(p^{v_p(n)}) for every positive n, with product over prime divisors. Every assignment of elements of R to positive prime powers extends uniquely to a multiplicative function. Multiplicative functions are closed under Dirichlet convolution and under taking their inverses in the convolution ring.

Theorem C02, analytic assertions: If f:ℕ_{>0}→ℂ is multiplicative and s∈ℝ satisfies ∑_{n≥1}|f(n)|n^{-s}<∞, then ∑_{n≥1} f(n)/n^s=∏_p(∑_{j≥0} f(p^j)/p^{js}), with the prime product defined as the limit of products over p≤y as y→∞. In particular, for real s>1, ζ(s):=∑_{n≥1}n^{-s}=∏_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}.
Bibliographic references for finite convolution and analytic Euler products; this passage adds no mathematical deliverable.

Classical arithmetic functions on positive integers: 1(n)=1; id_k(n)=n^k; log(n)=log n; μ(n)=0 when n has a squared prime factor and μ(n)=(-1)^r when n is a product of r distinct primes (including μ(1)=1 via the empty product); φ(n) counts integers from 1 through n coprime to n; τ(n) is the number of positive divisors of n and σ_k(n) is their kth-power sum, for k≥0 as in the source.
Proposition C03: For k≥0, the divisor-count and divisor-power-sum functions satisfy τ=1*1 and σ_k=1*id_k, with Dirichlet convolution.

Proposition C03: The functions μ, φ, τ, and σ_k (k≥0) are multiplicative. For every prime p and integer j≥1, μ(p^j)=-1 if j=1 and 0 if j≥2; φ(p^j)=p^j-p^{j-1}; τ(p^j)=j+1; and σ_k(p^j)=∑_{i=0}^j p^{ik}. In particular σ_0=τ.
For positive integers n define the real-valued von Mangoldt function Λ(n)=log p if n=p^j for a prime p and integer j≥1, and Λ(n)=0 otherwise.
The von Mangoldt function satisfies 1*Λ=log in the real-valued Dirichlet-convolution ring: for every positive integer n, ∑_{d|n}Λ(d)=log n, with the sum over positive divisors.

Theorem C04: For a commutative ring R with identity and functions f,g:ℕ_{>0}→R, interpreting integer coefficients via the unital map ℤ→R, [g(n)=∑_{d|n}f(d) for every positive n] if and only if [f(n)=∑_{d|n}μ(d)g(n/d) for every positive n].
Theorem C04: In the integer-valued convolution ring μ*1=δ, ∑_{d|n}φ(d)=n for every positive n, and φ=μ*id_1. In the real-valued convolution ring Λ=μ*log.
Bibliographic references for classical arithmetic functions and Möbius inversion; no added mathematical deliverable.

Theorem C05: Let R be a commutative ring with identity and f,g:ℕ_{>0}→R. Set F(t)=∑_{n≤t}f(n) and G(t)=∑_{n≤t}g(n), with positive integer indices. For nonnegative integers U,V and real x with UV≤x<(U+1)(V+1), ∑_{n≤x}(f*g)(n)=∑_{u≤U}f(u)G(x/u)+∑_{v≤V}g(v)F(x/v)-F(U)G(V). Empty sums are permitted when U or V is zero. For any real x≥0 one may take U=V=⌊√x⌋.

Theorem C06, discrete identity: In a commutative ring, let (a_n),(w_n) be sequences indexed by positive integers and A(t)=∑_{n≤t}a_n. For integers 1≤m≤N, ∑_{n=m}^N a_n w_n=A(N)w_N-A(m-1)w_m+∑_{n=m}^{N-1}A(n)(w_n-w_{n+1}).

Theorem C06, Abel identity: For real or complex coefficients a_n indexed by positive integers, A(t)=∑_{n≤t}a_n, arbitrary real a≤b, and a weight w of class C¹ on [a,b], ∑_{a<n≤b} a_n w(n)=A(b)w(b)-A(a)w(a)-∫_a^b A(t)w′(t)dt. When a=b the sum is empty and the integral zero. The lower endpoint is excluded and upper endpoint included.
Bibliographic references for summation identities; no added mathematical deliverable.
Lemma (Harmonic numbers and the Basel sum), second assertion: The reciprocal-square series satisfies ∑_{n≥1}n^{-2}=π²/6.
Lemma (Harmonic numbers and the Basel sum), first assertion: For positive integers m set H_m=∑_{j=1}^m1/j. The real limit γ=lim_{m→∞}(H_m-log m) exists, and H_m=log m+γ+O(1/m).
Theorem C07, first average order: For real x→+∞, ∑_{n≤x}τ(n)=x log x+(2γ-1)x+O(√x), with positive integer summation indices and γ the harmonic limit.
Theorem C07, third average order: For real x→+∞, ∑_{n≤x}μ(n)²=(6/π²)x+O(√x), with positive integer summation indices; this is the squarefree counting function.
Theorem C07, second average order: For real x→+∞, ∑_{n≤x}φ(n)=(3/π²)x²+O(x log x), with positive integer summation indices.
Bibliographic references for the three average orders; no added mathematical deliverable.

For real x≥1 define P(x)=∏_{p≤x}p; θ(x)=∑_{p≤x}log p; ψ(x)=∑_{p^k≤x, k≥1}log p; and π(x)=#{p≤x:p is prime}. Here p always ranges over positive primes, and in ψ the exponent k ranges over positive integers.
Lemma (A bound for the prime product): For every real x≥1, P(x)≤4^x.
Theorem C08: As real x→+∞, θ(x) asymp x and ψ(x) asymp x; each comparison means eventual lower and upper bounds by positive constant multiples of x.
Theorem C08: As real x→+∞, π(x) asymp x/log x, meaning there exist c,C>0 with c x/log x≤π(x)≤C x/log x eventually.
Theorem C08: As real x→+∞, ψ(x)-θ(x)=O(√x).

Theorem C09, second Mertens estimate and consequence: There exists a real constant B such that, for real x→+∞, ∑_{p≤x}1/p=log log x+B+O(1/log x). Consequently the sum of the reciprocals of all positive primes diverges.
Theorem C09, first Mertens estimate: For real x→+∞, ∑_{p≤x}(log p)/p=log x+O(1).
Bibliographic references for Chebyshev and Mertens estimates; no added mathematical deliverable.
Theorem C10 (Bertrand): For every real x>1 there exists a positive prime p satisfying the strict inequalities x<p<2x.
Bibliographic reference and comparison of the proof to Chebyshev’s valuation argument; no added mathematical deliverable.

Theorem D01: Let a,b,c be positive integers satisfying a²+b²=c² and gcd(a,b)=1. After interchanging a and b if necessary so that b is even, there exist unique integers r>s>0 with a=r²-s², b=2rs, c=r²+s², gcd(r,s)=1, and r not congruent to s modulo 2. Conversely any integers r>s>0 with gcd(r,s)=1 and opposite parity give a primitive positive Pythagorean triple by these formulas.
Theorem D02: For all nonzero integers x,y there is no integer z satisfying x⁴+y⁴=z². In particular the equation x⁴+y⁴=z⁴ has no integer solution with xy≠0.
Bibliographic references for the classical parametrization and descent; no added mathematical deliverable.

Theorem D03: The Gaussian integer ring ℤ[i], with norm N(a+bi)=a²+b², is Euclidean for that norm. Its units are exactly 1,-1,i,-i and it has unique factorization up to units and order. The rational prime 2 is a unit times (1+i)². Every odd rational prime p congruent to 3 modulo 4 is prime as an element of ℤ[i]; every rational prime p congruent to 1 modulo 4 is the product of two nonassociate conjugate Gaussian primes of norm p.

For n>0, r₂(n) counts ordered signed pairs (a,b)∈ℤ² with a²+b²=n; different coordinate orders and sign choices are counted separately. Define χ₄(d)=0 for even d, χ₄(d)=1 for d congruent to 1 modulo 4, and χ₄(d)=-1 for d congruent to 3 modulo 4.
Theorem D04, representation count: For every positive integer n, r₂(n)=4∑_{d|n}χ₄(d), summing over positive divisors. At n=0 there is exactly one ordered signed pair of integers with a²+b²=0.

Theorem D04, representability: A positive integer n is a sum of two integer squares if and only if every prime p congruent to 3 modulo 4 occurs to an even exponent in n. In particular an odd positive prime is a sum of two integer squares if and only if it is congruent to 1 modulo 4.

Bibliographic references and explicit clarification that the two-square count treats coordinates as ordered and does not identify sign changes; the counting convention is included in D04’s definition and result.
For A=(a₀,a⃗), B=(b₀,b⃗) with a₀,b₀∈ℤ and a⃗,b⃗∈ℤ³, define C(A,B)=(a₀b₀+a⃗·b⃗, b₀a⃗-a₀b⃗-a⃗×b⃗)∈ℤ⁴, and write ‖A‖²=a₀²+‖a⃗‖².

The unnumbered, separately displayed four-square product identity: For A,B∈ℤ⁴ as in the bilinear construction, ‖C(A,B)‖²=‖A‖²‖B‖²; all four coordinates of C(A,B) are integers. For a positive integer modulus m, if A≡B modulo m coordinatewise, then the last three coordinates of C(A,B) are 0 modulo m and its first coordinate is congruent to ‖B‖² modulo m.
Theorem D05 (Lagrange): Every nonnegative integer is a sum of four squares of nonnegative integers.
Bibliographic reference for the descent argument; no added mathematical deliverable.

Explanation that the following separately stated prime-existence theorem supports D06, with bibliographic references to Taylor expansion and locally uniform holomorphic limits; these comments do not add separate proof-internal deliverables.

Lemma (Characters of a finite abelian group): Let G be a finite abelian group of order h, and let Ĝ be the group of homomorphisms from G to the complex numbers of absolute value 1. Then |Ĝ|=h and (1/h)∑_{χ∈Ĝ}χ(g)=1 if g=1 and 0 otherwise. Every nontrivial character χ satisfies ∑_{g∈G}χ(g)=0. If g has order f, then the values χ(g), as χ ranges through Ĝ, are all fth roots of unity, each with multiplicity h/f.

Lemma (Continuation from nonnegative coefficients): Let b_n≥0 for positive integer n, and let F(s)=∑_{n≥1}b_n n^{-s}, with n^{-s}=exp(-s log n), converge absolutely on the complex half-plane Re(s)>1. If F has a holomorphic continuation throughout Re(s)>0, then the defining series converges at every positive real σ.

Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions: For every integer modulus M≥1 and integer a with gcd(a,M)=1, and every real bound T, there exists a positive prime q>T satisfying q≡a modulo M. The modulus-one case is included.
Bibliographic references for Dirichlet’s theorem and the all-character product proof; no added mathematical deliverable.

Lemma (A three-dimensional lattice bound): Let B be an invertible real 3×3 matrix and L=Bℤ³. Every open Euclidean ball centered at 0 whose volume is strictly greater than 8|det B| contains a nonzero point of L.

Theorem D06 (Legendre): For every positive integer n, n is a sum of three integer squares if and only if there do not exist nonnegative integers a,b such that n=4^a(8b+7). Zero is also a sum of three integer squares.

Bibliographic attribution of the sufficiency proof to Ankeny with Fan’s modular setup, and clarification that the proof also covers even squarefree cases. Its calculations inside the proof are not separate deliverables.
Represent a rational number by p/q with p,q in Z and q>0; it is reduced when gcd(p,q)=1. Distinguish the two approximation-error quantities |x-p/q| and |qx-p|.

Rational-root theorem: Let P(X)=c_d X^d+...+c_0 in Z[X], d>=1 and c_d!=0. If p/q is a nonzero root with p,q in Z, q>0 and gcd(p,q)=1, then p divides c_0 and q divides c_d. If 0 is a root, c_0=0 and its reduced denominator is 1. Every rational root of a monic integer polynomial is an integer.

For every integer k>=2 and nonnegative integer m that is not a kth power in Z_{>=0}, the nonnegative real kth root of m is irrational; in particular sqrt(m) is irrational whenever m is a nonnegative nonsquare integer.
The real number e=exp(1) is irrational.
The real number pi is irrational.
Bibliographic reference for rational roots and classical irrationality; it introduces no further mathematical obligation.

For any real x construct its simple-continued-fraction algorithm: alpha_0=x, a_j=floor(alpha_j); stop exactly when alpha_j=a_j, and otherwise alpha_{j+1}=1/(alpha_j-a_j). The alpha_j are complete quotients and a_j are partial quotients. Every defined alpha_{j+1}>1; hence every defined a_j with j>=1 is >=1, while a_0 is an arbitrary integer.
For a finite simple-continued-fraction digit list with a_0 in Z and a_j>=1 for j>=1, define [a_0;a_1,...,a_n]=a_0+1/(a_1+1/(...+1/a_n)), and [a_0]=a_0.

For a normalized finite expansion of length n+1 with n>=1 and a_n>=2, replacing its final entry a_n by the two entries a_n-1,1 preserves its value. For every integer a_0, its other finite simple-continued-fraction expansion under the stated digit conventions is [a_0-1;1].
Every rational number has a unique finite simple-continued-fraction expansion with a_0 in Z, a_j>=1 for j>=1, and a_n>=2 when n>=1.
For every real x, the simple-continued-fraction algorithm terminates if and only if x is rational.
Bibliographic references for finite continued fractions; no additional mathematical obligation.
For the simple continued fraction of x define integer convergent sequences at every defined index by p_{-2}=0, p_{-1}=1, p_n=a_n p_{n-1}+p_{n-2}, and q_{-2}=1, q_{-1}=0, q_n=a_n q_{n-1}+q_{n-2}.
At every defined index n>=0, p_n/q_n equals [a_0;...;a_n] in lowest terms with q_n>0, and p_n q_{n-1}-p_{n-1} q_n=(-1)^(n+1).
The convergent denominators satisfy q_0=1, q_1=a_1 when index 1 exists, and q_{n+1}>q_n for every n>=1 for which both denominators exist. The possible equality q_0=q_1 is retained.
For every irrational real x and every n>=0, x=(p_n alpha_{n+1}+p_{n-1})/(q_n alpha_{n+1}+q_{n-1}) and q_n x-p_n=(-1)^n/(q_n alpha_{n+1}+q_{n-1}).
For every irrational real x and every n>=0, 1/(q_n(q_{n+1}+q_n)) < |x-p_n/q_n| < 1/(q_n q_{n+1}); in particular, the convergents p_n/q_n tend to x.

An infinite digit string produced by the simple-continued-fraction algorithm determines its real value uniquely: its value is the limit of its convergents. In particular, two reals producing the same infinite digit string are equal.
Bibliographic comparison for recurrences, determinants and tail formulas; no further obligation.

Let x be irrational, let p_n/q_n be its nth convergent (n>=0), and let p,q be integers with 0<q<q_{n+1}. Then |qx-p|>=|q_n x-p_n|. Equality is possible only for (p,q)=(p_n,q_n) under this denominator constraint; no coprimality assumption on p,q is imposed.
If x is irrational and p/q is reduced with p,q in Z, q>0 and |x-p/q|<1/(2q^2), then p/q is a convergent of x.
Bibliographic reference for best approximation and Legendre criterion; no further obligation.
For every real x and every integer N>=1, there exist integers p,q with 1<=q<=N and |qx-p|<=1/(N+1). If x is irrational the inequality can be made strict.
Every irrational real x has infinitely many distinct reduced fractions p/q with q>0 and |x-p/q|<1/q^2.
Bibliographic reference for Dirichlet approximation; no further obligation.
For every integer N>=1, F_N is the increasing list of all reduced fractions in [0,1] having positive denominator at most N, including 0/1 and 1/1.
If a/b<c/d are consecutive members of F_N with N>=1 and the fractions in reduced positive-denominator form, then bc-ad=1 and b+d>N.
For each integer N>=1, obtain F_{N+1} from F_N by inserting (a+c)/(b+d) in exactly those neighboring intervals a/b<c/d of F_N for which b+d=N+1, with all other neighboring intervals unchanged.

For consecutive a/b<c/d in F_N, the unique reduced rational strictly between them whose positive denominator is least is the mediant (a+c)/(b+d); in particular, this mediant is reduced and every reduced p/q in that interval has q>=b+d, with equality only for the mediant.
Bibliographic references for Farey fractions; no additional obligation.
For every irrational real x, infinitely many distinct reduced fractions p/q with q>0 satisfy the strict bound |x-p/q|<1/(sqrt(5) q^2).
For every real C>sqrt(5), the strict infinitely-many assertion |x-p/q|<1/(C q^2) fails for x=(1+sqrt(5))/2: only finitely many distinct reduced fractions p/q with q>0 satisfy that stronger bound.
Identifies the Farey-neighbor proof route and references; the auxiliary gap comparison is proof-only, not an additional required result.
A quadratic irrational is a real number of degree two over Q. Its conjugate y-prime is the other root of its irreducible quadratic polynomial.
A real quadratic irrational y is reduced precisely when y>1 and -1<y-prime<0, with y-prime its quadratic conjugate.

An infinite simple continued fraction is eventually periodic when its digit sequence is periodic after finitely many entries, and purely periodic when its digit sequence is periodic from the first entry. Period lengths are positive.
The map T(y)=1/(y-floor(y)) sends every reduced real quadratic irrational y to a reduced real quadratic irrational.
Every reduced real quadratic irrational z has exactly one reduced predecessor y under T, and it is y=floor(-1/z-prime)+1/z, where z-prime is its conjugate.

Let P,Q,D be integers, D>0 nonsquare, Q!=0 and Q divides D-P^2, and set y=(P+sqrt(D))/Q. Its next continued-fraction quotient has the same D: writing P_plus=floor(y) Q-P and Q_plus=(D-P_plus^2)/Q gives T(y)=(P_plus+sqrt(D))/Q_plus. Here Q_plus is a nonzero integer and Q_plus divides D-P_plus^2. This part imposes no reducedness or positivity assumption on Q.
For every real irrational x, its simple continued fraction is eventually periodic if and only if x is a quadratic irrational.
For every real quadratic irrational x, its simple continued fraction is purely periodic if and only if x is reduced, i.e. x>1 and -1<x-prime<0.

For a positive nonsquare integer D and x=sqrt(D), the quadratic-surd recurrence uses initial coefficients P_0=0 and Q_0=1. This specializes the general surd representation to the square-root expansion subsequently used for Pell equations.
For every real algebraic irrational x of degree d>=2, there exists a real constant c_x>0 such that every reduced p/q with p,q in Z and q>0 satisfies |x-p/q|>=c_x/q^d.
Define the real number L by the convergent series L=sum_{j=1 to infinity} 10^(-j!).
The real number L=sum_{j=1 to infinity} 10^(-j!) is transcendental.
Bibliographic reference for Liouville inequality and the explicit transcendental number; no further obligation.

Throughout Pell equations fix an arbitrary positive nonsquare integer D (hence D>=2), put a_0=floor(sqrt(D)), use the earlier complete-quotient and convergent indexing, and work in Z[sqrt(D)]={x+y sqrt(D): x,y in Z}. No squarefreeness hypothesis and no identification with the quadratic field full ring of integers are imposed.
For every positive nonsquare integer D and every convergent index n>=0 of sqrt(D), p_n^2-D q_n^2=(-1)^(n+1) Q_{n+1}, with Q_j from its complete quotients.

Fix a positive nonsquare integer D and work in ℤ[√D] with the continued-fraction conventions above. Write the complete quotients of sqrt(D) as alpha_j=(P_j+sqrt(D))/Q_j with the square-root surd recurrence. Then Q_0=1, and for every j>=1, Q_j=1 if and only if ell divides j, where ell is the least square-root period length.

For every positive nonsquare integer D with a_0=floor(sqrt(D)), there exists a least integer ell>=1 such that sqrt(D)=[a_0; overline(a_1,...,a_{ell-1},2a_0)]. The case ell=1 means the periodic block is just 2a_0.

Fix a positive nonsquare integer D and work in ℤ[√D] with the continued-fraction conventions above. For either epsilon in {1,-1}, order positive solutions to x^2-D y^2=epsilon by x+y sqrt(D). The least such solution, when one exists, is the convergent indexed by k ell-1 for the least k>=1 with (-1)^(k ell)=epsilon. For epsilon=1, k=1 when ell is even and k=2 when ell is odd. For epsilon=-1 a solution exists exactly when ell is odd, and then the least occurs at k=1.

Fix a positive nonsquare integer D and the least period ell of sqrt(D). For either epsilon in {1,-1}, the positive-integer solutions x,y>0 of x^2-D y^2=epsilon are exactly (x,y)=(p_{k ell-1},q_{k ell-1}) with integer k>=1 and (-1)^(k ell)=epsilon, using the convergents of sqrt(D). Both directions, both signs, and exact numerator/denominator equality are included.

Fix a positive nonsquare integer D and work in ℤ[√D] with the continued-fraction conventions above. For u=x+y sqrt(D) in Z[sqrt(D)], with x,y integers, define its conjugate as u-bar=x-y sqrt(D) and its norm N(u)=u u-bar=x^2-D y^2.

Fix a positive nonsquare integer D and work in ℤ[√D] with the continued-fraction conventions above. For integral-coefficient elements u,v of Z[sqrt(D)], the norm is multiplicative. Such an element u is a unit if and only if N(u) is 1 or -1. More precisely, if N(u)=epsilon in {1,-1}, then u inverse=epsilon u-bar lies in Z[sqrt(D)]; conversely the norm of a unit is an invertible integer.

Fix a positive nonsquare integer D and work in ℤ[√D] with the continued-fraction conventions above. Let u=x+y sqrt(D) be an integral-coefficient unit with N(u)=epsilon in {1,-1}. If u>1 as a real number, then x=(u+epsilon/u)/2>0 and y=(u-epsilon/u)/(2 sqrt(D))>0. Conversely, x,y>0 implies u>1. Thus for these units positivity of both integer coefficients is equivalent to real value greater than 1.

Fix a positive nonsquare integer D and work in ℤ[√D] with the continued-fraction conventions above. With u_plus the least unit >1 of norm 1 in Z[sqrt(D)], all units with positive real value and norm 1 are exactly the integer powers u_plus^j (j in Z), uniquely; exponent 0 yields 1.

For every positive nonsquare integer D, x^2-D y^2=1 has a positive-integer solution. There exists a least unit u_plus=x_plus+y_plus sqrt(D)>1 of norm 1. Every positive-integer solution x,y>0 is obtained uniquely as x+y sqrt(D)=u_plus^j for an integer j>=1, and every such positive power yields a positive-integer solution.

Fix a positive nonsquare integer D and work in ℤ[√D] with the continued-fraction conventions above. If the least period ell of sqrt(D) is odd, let u_minus=x_minus+y_minus sqrt(D)>1 be the least unit of norm -1 greater than 1. Then u_plus=u_minus^2 and {x+y sqrt(D): x,y positive integers and x^2-D y^2=-1}={u_minus u_plus^j: j=0,1,2,...}. If ell is even the set of positive solutions of norm -1 is empty.
Bibliographic reference for square-root expansions and both Pell signs; no further obligation.
For D=2 the simple continued fraction of sqrt(2) has least period length 1, its least norm -1 unit >1 is u_minus=1+sqrt(2), and its least norm 1 unit >1 is u_plus=3+2 sqrt(2).

For D=3 the simple continued fraction of sqrt(3) has least period length 2, its least norm 1 unit >1 is u_plus=2+sqrt(3), and it has no norm -1 solution in Z[sqrt(3)] (in particular no positive-integer pair).

The Möbius reciprocal-square series converges absolutely, its product with the reciprocal-square series is 1, and its value is 6/π².
For real y→+∞, the reciprocal-square tail and the absolute Möbius reciprocal-square tail are O(1/y), and the signed Möbius tail is bounded in absolute value by the same order.

Every Gaussian prime belongs, up to units, to the ramified 1+i family, the inert positive rational primes congruent to 3 modulo 4, or the Gaussian elements of positive rational prime norm congruent to 1 modulo 4; all three families are prime.

Every finite expansion satisfying the digit conventions is either the canonical expansion or its final-digit split: a noncanonical list ends in 1 and merges to the canonical list, including the integer case.
For all integers x,y,z, if gcd(x,y)=1 and x divides y*z, then x divides z.
If a group element g has finite positive order d, then g^j has order d/gcd(d,j); a power of a generator generates a finite cyclic group exactly for exponent coprime to d.

Every Gaussian prime is associate to 1+i, associate to a positive rational prime p≡3 modulo 4, or has prime norm congruent to 1 modulo 4; each listed type is prime. This exhaustion, stated at the end of the Gaussian-arithmetic proof, is explicitly included in the agreed D03Primes goal.
For arbitrary integers x,y,z, if gcd(x,y)=1 and x divides y*z, then x divides z.
If g has finite order d, then g^j has order d/gcd(d,j); in a cyclic group of order d its generators are exactly powers with exponents coprime to d, and there are phi(d) such generators.
Agreed C07b: the positive-index real Möbius reciprocal-square series converges absolutely, its product with the reciprocal-square series equals 1, and it has sum 6/π².

Agreed C07b quantitative shared tail bounds: for every real y≥1, the reciprocal-square tail, the absolute Möbius reciprocal-square tail, and the absolute value of the signed Möbius tail are each at most 2/y, with all tails summable.

Every Gaussian prime divides a positive rational prime; the ramified, inert rational, and split norm-prime cases exhaust all Gaussian primes, including all unit associates. This full classification is also explicitly agreed in goal D03Primes.
For signed integers x,y,z, if gcd(x,y)=1 and x divides y*z, then x divides z.
If g has finite positive order d, then g^j has order d/gcd(d,j); a cyclic group of order d has exactly φ(d) generators.

All admissible finite simple-continued-fraction expansions of a rational are its canonical list or that list with its final digit split; any noncanonical list ends in 1 and merges to the canonical list.
Every purely periodic canonical irrational is quadratic and reduced; every eventually periodic canonical irrational is quadratic.

Every real quadratic irrational has all canonical complete quotients represented by a single positive nonsquare integer discriminant D and integer P_j,Q_j with Q_j nonzero, Q_j∣D−P_j² and the signed surd updates.
Every real quadratic irrational has an index after which all its canonical complete quotients are reduced.
For a fixed positive nonsquare integer D, every reduced integer surd state (P+√D)/Q has −√D<P<√D and 0<Q<2√D, so there are finitely many such states.
For signed integers x,y,z, gcd(x,y)=1 and x∣yz imply x∣z.
If g has finite positive order d, then order(g^j)=d/gcd(d,j), using gcd(d,|j|) for signed j.
A finite cyclic group of order d≥1 has exactly φ(d) generators, corresponding to exponent classes coprime to d.
