Global conventions: empty sums and products have their neutral values; formal series are interpreted coefficientwise, with coefficient-ring and division/composition conditions as stated locally; graph chapters concern finite simple undirected graphs except when an edge-labelled multigraph or directed network is specified; network source and sink are distinct; matroids have finite specified ground sets, and bases maximize cardinality, independently of weights.

Prerequisite and attribution discussion concerning finite-dimensional linear algebra, elementary group theory, cited orbit–stabilizer and arithmetic inversion proofs, and later proof methods; no additional stand-alone theorem is asserted for formalization here.

Chapter 1 uses finite sets; 0! = 1 counts the unique ordering of the empty set; an empty sum is zero and an empty product is one; integer coefficients of counting identities are mapped into the coefficient ring when used there.

For finite sets A and B, every bijection A → B gives |A| = |B|, every injection A → B gives |A| ≤ |B|, and every surjection A → B gives |B| ≤ |A|. If |A| = |B|, a given map A → B is injective if and only if it is surjective, equivalently bijective. Empty sets are included.
For a family (A_i) indexed by a finite set I, with each A_i finite, |⋃_{i∈I} A_i| = Σ_{∅≠J⊆I} (-1)^(|J|+1)|⋂_{j∈J} A_j|. This includes I empty, when both sides are zero.
For finite sets A and B and any relation R ⊆ A × B, |R| = Σ_{a∈A}|{b∈B : (a,b)∈R}| = Σ_{b∈B}|{a∈A : (a,b)∈R}|.

For a finite n-element set and an ordered finite list of nonnegative block sizes k_1,…,k_r with sum n, the number of ordered pairwise disjoint blocks of these sizes whose union is the set equals n!/(k_1!⋯k_r!). Empty blocks and the global empty-family conventions are retained.
For natural numbers n and k, the number of k-element subsets of any n-element set is binom(n,k), with value zero when k > n.

For natural n and finitely many commuting variables/elements x_1,…,x_r, (x_1+⋯+x_r)^n = Σ_{k_1+⋯+k_r=n} [n!/(k_1!⋯k_r!)]x_1^k_1⋯x_r^k_r, where the k_i are nonnegative integers and integer coefficients are interpreted in the coefficient ring. For r = 2 this includes the binomial theorem.
The binomial coefficients satisfy Pascal’s recurrence: for n ≥ 1, binom(n,k) = binom(n−1,k)+binom(n−1,k−1), with entries outside the range 0 ≤ k ≤ n−1 for the row n−1 understood as zero.

Let d_n be the number of permutations of [n]={1,…,n} having no fixed points. Then d_n = Σ_{j=0}^n (-1)^j binom(n,j)(n−j)! = n! Σ_{j=0}^n (-1)^j/j!. This includes n = 0 and its unique empty permutation.

Define the unsigned first-kind Stirling number [n k] as the number of permutations of [n] with k cycles and the second-kind Stirling number {n k} as the number of partitions of [n] into k nonempty blocks. In each array the entry (0,0) is one and out-of-range entries are zero.
For the two combinatorially defined Stirling arrays, [n+1 k] = [n k−1] + n[n k] and {n+1 k} = {n k−1} + k{n k}, with the stated zero conventions for out-of-range entries.
The falling factorial is x^{underlined k} = x(x−1)⋯(x−k+1) for k ≥ 1, and x^{underlined 0} = 1.

For every n ≥ 0, the polynomial identities x^{underlined n} = Σ_{k=0}^n (-1)^(n−k)[n k]x^k and x^n = Σ_{k=0}^n {n k}x^{underlined k} hold. Consequently the lower-triangular integer matrices with entries (-1)^(n−k)[n k] and {n k} are mutual inverses (equivalently their finite truncations give inverse changes between power and falling-factorial bases).

Let L be a finite distributive lattice with bottom 0 and J its nonzero join-irreducible elements, ordered as in L, where j ≠ 0 is join-irreducible when j = u∨v implies j = u or j = v. Then x ↦ {j∈J : j≤x} is a lattice isomorphism from L to the lattice of lower sets of J (subsets S for which j∈S and i≤j in J imply i∈S). The lattice with only its bottom and the empty lower set are included.

For a finite poset P and commutative coefficient ring R, an incidence function assigns an R-value to every comparable pair x≤z. Its convolution is (f*g)(x,z) = Σ_{x≤y≤z} f(x,y)g(y,z). Define δ(x,z)=1 when x=z and 0 when x<z, and ζ(x,z)=1 on every comparable pair.
For a finite poset P and commutative ring R, incidence functions with pointwise addition and the defined convolution form an associative R-algebra with two-sided unit δ.

For every finite poset P, commutative ring R, and functions f,g:P→R, using its incidence Möbius function μ, the identities g(x)=Σ_{y≤x}f(y) for all x hold if and only if f(x)=Σ_{y≤x}μ(y,x)g(y) for all x.
For a finite poset P and commutative ring R as in the incidence-algebra definition, ζ has a two-sided convolution inverse μ. It is specified uniquely by μ(x,x)=1 and μ(x,z)=−Σ_{x≤y<z}μ(x,y) for x<z.

For every finite poset P, commutative ring R, and functions f,g:P→R, using its incidence Möbius function μ, the identities g(x)=Σ_{y≥x}f(y) for all x hold if and only if f(x)=Σ_{y≥x}μ(x,y)g(y) for all x.
On the poset of subsets of a finite set ordered by inclusion, the Möbius value on every interval S⊆T equals (-1)^|T\S|, including S=T with value one.

For every positive integer N, consider the finite poset of its positive divisors ordered by divisibility. For its elements a∣b, its incidence Möbius value at (a,b) equals the arithmetic Möbius function μ_arith(b/a).
For finite posets P and Q, at every comparable pair (x_1,x_2)≤(z_1,z_2) in P×Q, μ_{P×Q}((x_1,x_2),(z_1,z_2)) = μ_P(x_1,z_1)μ_Q(x_2,z_2), interpreted in the commutative coefficient ring.

The usual arithmetic divisor inversion is obtained by this specialization: for functions f,g on positive integers with values in a commutative ring, g(n)=Σ_{d∣n}f(d) for all positive n if and only if f(n)=Σ_{d∣n}μ_arith(n/d)g(d) for all positive n. In particular the displayed conclusion at each positive N follows by applying finite-poset lower inversion on the divisors of N.
References for standard enumeration terminology; no new mathematical assertion.
Over a commutative Q-algebra R (in particular a characteristic-zero field), the exponential generating function of (a_n)_{n≥0} is Σ_{n≥0} a_n z^n/n!.

Over a commutative ring R with identity, a formal power series is a sequence (a_n)_{n≥0}, denoted Σ_{n≥0}a_n z^n, with coefficient notation [z^n]A=a_n. The ordinary generating function of the sequence is that series, and equality is coefficientwise.
For formal series A=Σa_n z^n and B=Σb_n z^n over a commutative ring with identity, [z^n](AB)=Σ_{i=0}^n a_i b_{n−i}, [z^n]A′=(n+1)a_{n+1}, and the formal derivative satisfies (AB)′=A′B+AB′.
Over a commutative Q-algebra, the product of the exponential generating functions of sequences (a_n) and (b_n) is the exponential generating function of c_n=Σ_{i=0}^n binom(n,i)a_i b_{n−i}.
For formal series A and B over a commutative ring R with identity, if B(0)=0 then A(B)=Σ_{j≥0} a_j B^j is a well-defined formal series, with each coefficient determined by finitely many terms.

Among zero-constant formal series B over a commutative ring R with identity, B has a two-sided compositional inverse with zero constant coefficient if and only if its linear coefficient [z]B is a unit. Such an inverse is unique.
A formal series A over a commutative ring R with identity has a multiplicative inverse in R[[z]] if and only if its constant coefficient A(0) is a unit of R.

Over the chapter’s commutative ring R with identity, for any integer r≥1, recurrence coefficients c_0,…,c_{r−1}∈R, and initial values a_0,…,a_{r−1}∈R, there is exactly one sequence a:Nat→R with these initial values and a_{n+r}=Σ_{j=0}^{r−1}c_j a_{n+j} for every n≥0.

For an order-r recurrence sequence from W13, set Q(z)=1−Σ_{j=0}^{r−1}c_j z^{r−j} and A(z)=Σ_{n≥0}a_n z^n. Then Q A=P for a polynomial P∈R[z] of degree less than r determined by the r initial values. In particular Q(0)=1 and A=P/Q as a formal series.

Let K be any field, r≥1, and χ(t)=t^r−Σ_{j=0}^{r−1}c_j t^j have r distinct roots λ_1,…,λ_r in K. Every sequence satisfying a_{n+r}=Σ_{j=0}^{r−1}c_j a_{n+j} for all n≥0 is a unique K-linear combination of the sequences n↦λ_i^n. The convention λ_i^0=1 applies also when λ_i=0; arbitrary initial values are allowed.

Under the split-recurrence hypotheses of W16, if K has characteristic zero and λ≠0, the λ-root space is exactly the space of sequences n↦P(n)λ^n with P∈K[t] and deg P<m_λ (equivalently the span of b_{λ,j} for 0≤j<m_λ).

Over any field K, suppose an order-r homogeneous constant-coefficient recurrence holds from index 0 and its characteristic polynomial splits in K as χ(t)=∏_λ(t−λ)^{m_λ}, over its distinct roots with their multiplicities. A basis of its entire solution space consists of b_{λ,j}(n)=[z^n](z^j/(1−λz)^{j+1}), for each root λ and every 0≤j<m_λ. Explicitly b_{λ,j}(n)=binom(n,j)λ^{n−j} when n≥j and is zero when n<j, with integer binomial coefficients mapped into K. For λ=0 the series is z^j, so b_{0,j} is the unit spike at j.

Over any field K, an ordinary generating series A=Σ_{n≥0}a_n z^n is a quotient P/Q of polynomials with Q(0)=1 if and only if (a_n) eventually satisfies a homogeneous constant-coefficient linear recurrence. This includes polynomial series/eventually zero sequences and does not require a positive-degree denominator.

For every finite square matrix M over a commutative ring, the matrix formal series I−zM has two-sided inverse Σ_{n≥0}M^n z^n. Over a field each entry of this inverse is a rational formal series. The finite index set may be empty.

For a finite directed weighted graph over a commutative ring, let M_uv be the sum of weights of all arcs from u to v. For every n≥0, (M^n)_uv is the sum, over all n-step walks from u to v, of the products of their arc weights. At n=0 the identity matrix represents the weight-one empty walk at each vertex; the empty graph/matrix has no entry assertions.
Let R be a commutative Q-algebra, φ,H∈R[[z]], and φ(0) a unit, and let F be the unique zero-constant solution F=zφ(F). Then for every integer n≥1, [z^n]H(F(z))=(1/n)[u^{n−1}]H′(u)φ(u)^n.
Let R be a commutative Q-algebra and φ∈R[[z]] with unit constant coefficient. There exists a unique zero-constant formal series F∈zR[[z]] satisfying F=zφ(F).
Comparison references for generating functions and recurrences; no new mathematical assertion.

An unlabelled combinatorial class consists of finite sets A_n of objects of each natural size n. A labelled class additionally specifies objects on each finite label set S with consistent transports under bijections, so its count a_n on an n-element label set is independent of the chosen labels. The product of labelled classes uses a disjoint split of the label set.

For locally finite unlabelled classes, the product with additive size has count Σ_{i=0}^n a_i b_{n−i} and its ordinary generating function is the product of the two ordinary generating functions. For locally finite labelled classes the product on a disjoint split of an n-element label set has count Σ_{i=0}^n binom(n,i)a_i b_{n−i}, and its exponential generating function is the product of the two exponential generating functions.
For locally finite unlabelled or labelled classes with respective counting sequences (a_n) and (b_n), their disjoint sum (with the two classes tagged) has count a_n+b_n in size n.

If a labelled locally finite class A has no size-zero objects and exponential generating function A(z), finite sets of A-objects on disjoint nonempty label blocks covering the prescribed finite label set have exponential generating function exp(A(z)). The empty set of components on the empty label set is included.

If an unlabelled locally finite class A has no size-zero objects and ordinary generating function A(z), the class of all finite ordered sequences of A-objects, with total size the sum of component sizes, has ordinary generating function 1/(1−A(z)). The empty sequence is included and contributes one.

A Dyck path of semilength n is a word with n up-steps and n down-steps whose every partial height is nonnegative. Interpreting an up-step as an opening parenthesis and a down-step as a closing parenthesis identifies these words with balanced-parenthesis strings. Write C_n for their common number. The theorem also repeats that k-subsets of an n-element set are counted by binom(n,k).
For every n≥0, the Dyck-path/balanced-parenthesis counts satisfy C_0=1, C_{n+1}=Σ_{i=0}^n C_i C_{n−i}, and C_n=binom(2n,n)/(n+1). The empty word is the sole object at n=0.
Define the Bell number B_n=Σ_{k=0}^n {n k}, the total number of set partitions of an n-element set. Its exponential generating function is Σ_{n≥0}B_n z^n/n! = exp(e^z−1).

For ordinary set partitions of labelled n-element sets, giving each block a factor u yields the exponential-series identity exp(u(e^z−1))=Σ_{n≥0}(Σ_{k=0}^n {n k}u^k)z^n/n!. Thus the u^k coefficient records partitions with k nonempty blocks, including the empty partition for n=k=0.

For a locally finite labelled class A whose objects all have positive size, cycles of components on disjoint label blocks covering the label set have exponential generating function Σ_{k≥1}A(z)^k/k=−log(1−A(z)), where A is the exponential generating function of A. Cycles are nonempty cyclic orders, with components identified under cyclic rotation.

Let a finite acyclic directed graph have edge weights in a commutative ring. Let a_1,…,a_r and b_1,…,b_r be vertices, distinct within each list (cross-list equality is permitted). Let M_ij be the sum of products of edge weights over paths from a_i to b_j, giving an empty path weight one. Then det M equals the sum over σ∈S_r and all pairwise vertex-disjoint path families P_i:a_i→b_{σ(i)} of sgn(σ)∏_{i=1}^r w(P_i). If all disjoint families necessarily have σ=id, this is the unsigned weight sum for that matching. This includes r=0: the empty family contributes the empty determinant one.
Bibliographic attribution for the determinant construction and enumerative use; no new mathematical assertion.

For every n≥0, partitions of n as decreasing positive-part lists are bijective with finitely supported multiplicity sequences (m_i)_{i≥1} of nonnegative integers satisfying Σ_i i m_i=n. The empty list, equivalently the identically zero multiplicity sequence, is the only partition of zero.

For each n≥0, a partition of n is a finite weakly decreasing list λ=(λ_1,…,λ_k) of positive integers with sum n. Its multiplicities are m_i=|{j:λ_j=i}| for positive integers i, giving a finitely supported sequence of nonnegative integers with Σ_{i≥1}i m_i=n.

Let p(n) be the number of partitions of n. In Z[[z]], and consequently in Q[[z]], Σ_{n≥0}p(n)z^n = ∏_{k≥1}(1−z^k)^(−1). The infinite product is defined by stabilization of each coefficient in the finite initial products.

For each n≥0, partitions of n all of whose parts are odd and partitions of n whose parts are pairwise distinct have equal cardinality (equivalently there is a bijection between these finite sets). The empty partitions at n=0 are included.

Transposition of Ferrers-diagram cell coordinates defines an involution on partitions preserving their weight/sum. It interchanges the number of parts and the largest part; both statistics equal zero on the empty partition.
For a partition λ=(λ_1,…,λ_k), its Ferrers diagram is the finite set of cells {(i,j):1≤i≤k and 1≤j≤λ_i}. Conjugation transposes the two cell coordinates.

For nonnegative integers a,b, define F(a,b)∈Z[q] as Σ_λ q^|λ| over partitions with at most a parts and largest part at most b, including the empty partition. For integers 0≤k≤n define the Gaussian coefficient [n k]_q=F(k,n−k), and define it to be zero outside this range.

For every n≥0 and 0≤k≤n, the rectangular-partition Gaussian polynomial satisfies [n k]_q=∏_{j=1}^k (1−q^(n−k+j))/(1−q^j). The equality is in Q(q), identifying the displayed rational function with the polynomial defined from partitions. At k=0 the product is one.
The rectangular partition weight polynomials satisfy F(a,b)=F(a,b−1)+q^b F(a−1,b) for a,b≥1, and F(a,0)=F(0,b)=1 for all nonnegative a,b.
For every n≥0, the polynomial identity ∏_{i=0}^{n−1}(1+tq^i)=Σ_{k=0}^n q^(k(k−1)/2)[n k]_q t^k holds, with Gaussian coefficients defined by rectangular partitions. At n=0 both sides are one.

For the partition numbers extended by p(0)=1 and p(m)=0 for negative integers m, every integer n>0 satisfies p(n)=Σ_{k≥1}(-1)^(k+1)(p(n−k(3k−1)/2)+p(n−k(3k+1)/2)). The sum has only finitely many nonzero summands.

In Z[[z]], the coefficientwise stabilized infinite product satisfies ∏_{i≥1}(1−z^i)=Σ_{j∈Z}(-1)^j z^(j(3j−1)/2). The integer-indexed exponents are nonnegative and only finitely many terms contribute to each coefficient; j=0 contributes one.
Historical comparison references for partition and Gaussian-binomial identities; no new mathematical assertion.

Let G be any finite group acting on a finite set X on the left, with no faithfulness requirement. Define Fix_X(g)={x in X : g·x=x}, the point stabilizer G_x={g in G : g·x=x}, and the orbit set X/G. The action orbits partition X, including the empty partition when X is empty.
For every finite group G acting on a finite set X on the left, |G|·|X/G|=sum_{g in G}|Fix_X(g)|. The action need not be faithful, and X may be empty.

For a finite group G acting on a finite set X, let c_k(g) count the length-k cycles of the permutation x↦g·x. Define its cycle index over Q by Z_{G,X}(s_1,…,s_|X|)=(1/|G|) sum_{g in G} product_{k=1}^{|X|} s_k^{c_k(g)}. Fixed points are length-one cycles. When X is empty, each product monomial is 1.
For any finite color set C and finite G-set X, define the induced left G-action on colorings f:X→C by (g·f)(x)=f(g⁻¹·x). This formula is a left group action, including empty X or C.

For each g in a finite group acting on finite X, and each finite color set C of size q, the number of fixed colorings X→C under the induced action is q^(sum_{k=1}^{|X|} c_k(g)); the empty-position convention gives q^0=1 even at q=0.

For a finite group G acting on finite X and a finite color set C of cardinality q, the number of orbits of colorings under (g·f)(x)=f(g⁻¹·x) equals Z_{G,X}(q,…,q). If C is empty and X is nonempty the count is 0; if X is empty there is exactly one coloring and one orbit, even when C is empty.

For a finite color set C introduce commuting indeterminates w_c. For f:X→C define W(f)=product_{x in X} w_{f(x)}. This weight is invariant under the induced group action on colorings, and W(O) denotes the common weight of a coloring orbit O.

For a finite group G acting on finite X and a finite color set C, with W(f)=product_{x in X}w_{f(x)}, sum_{O in C^X/G} W(O)=Z_{G,X}(sum_{c in C}w_c, sum_{c in C}w_c², …, sum_{c in C}w_c^{|X|}). This polynomial identity includes empty color sets and empty position sets.

The weighted cycle-index substitution Z_{G,X}(sum_c w_c,…,sum_c w_c^{|X|}), initially a polynomial over Q, has nonnegative integer coefficients. Consequently it specializes through that integral polynomial to arbitrary weights in any commutative semiring, without requiring division by |G|. This includes empty color and position sets.

For n≥1 and the rotations of Z/nZ, Z_rot,n=(1/n) sum_{d|n} φ(d) s_d^{n/d}, where φ(d) is the number of residues modulo d coprime to d. The sum includes d=1 and zero exponents follow the empty-product convention.

For n≥1 and the abstract dihedral action on Z/nZ, Z_dih,n=(1/2)Z_rot,n plus (1/2)s_1 s_2^{(n−1)/2} when n is odd, or (1/4)(s_1²s_2^{(n−2)/2}+s_2^{n/2}) when n is even. Omit factors with exponent zero, including s_2^0 at n=1. The formula also covers n=1,2 despite the possible action kernel.

For n≥1, the necklace positions are Z/nZ with rotation action x↦x+a. Bracelet symmetry uses the abstract group of pairs (a,ε), a in Z/nZ and ε in {1,−1}, with product (a,ε)(b,η)=(a+εb,εη) and action x↦a+εx. This abstract action is used even at n=1,2 when different elements can induce the same permutation. At n=0 use an empty-position action.

For the necklace and bracelet actions at n≥1, substitution s_k=|C| gives the number of coloring orbits for any finite color set C, and substitution s_k=sum_{c in C}w_c^k gives their orbit-weight polynomial. At n=0, the empty-position action has exactly one empty object, including for an empty color set.
Bibliographic reference to Pólya for background and applications; this is contextual citation, not an additional theorem obligation.

Graphs in Chapter 6 are finite simple undirected graphs G=(V,E), where E is a set of two-element subsets of the finite set V. The notation uv∈E means {u,v}∈E, and d_G(v) is the number of neighbors of v. Later parallel directed arcs retain their individual indices.

A subgraph of a finite simple graph consists of a vertex subset and an edge subset whose endpoints lie in that vertex subset. The induced subgraph G[S] on S⊆V contains every edge of G with both endpoints in S.

A walk of length k≥0 is a sequence v_0,…,v_k with v_{i−1}v_i∈E for every 1≤i≤k. A path is a walk with all vertices distinct. A cycle is a closed walk v_0,…,v_k=v_0 with k≥3 and v_0,…,v_{k−1} distinct. A graph is acyclic exactly when it has no such cycle.

Connected components are equivalence classes of the relation of being joined by a walk. A graph is connected when it is nonempty and has exactly one component. A forest is an acyclic graph, and a tree is a connected forest. The empty graph has no components and is not connected.
For any finite simple graph, being joined by a walk is a reflexive, symmetric, and transitive relation on vertices.
Every walk in a finite simple graph can be shortened to a path with the same endpoints.
A nonempty finite simple graph is connected if and only if every pair of its vertices is joined by a path.

For a nonempty finite simple graph on n vertices the following three conditions are equivalent: it is a tree; it is connected with n−1 edges; and every pair of vertices is joined by exactly one path. Paths use distinct vertices, so the unique path from a vertex to itself is the length-zero path.
Every finite simple graph, including the empty graph, has a spanning forest whose restriction to each connected component is a spanning tree of that component.
Every connected finite simple graph has a spanning tree, a tree subgraph containing every vertex.
Every finite tree with at least two vertices has at least two distinct leaves, where a leaf has degree exactly one.
For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), sum_{v in V} d_G(v)=2|E|, including the empty graph.
For a finite tree on n vertices, sum_{v in V}d_G(v)=2(n−1).
Every finite simple graph has an even number of vertices of odd degree.

Deleting an edge retains all vertices. A bridge is an edge whose deletion increases the component count. Deleting a vertex deletes all incident edges. In a connected graph a cut vertex is a vertex whose deletion leaves at least two components. A graph is 2-connected when it has at least three vertices, is connected, and remains connected after deletion of any vertex. A block is a maximal 2-connected subgraph, the subgraph consisting of a bridge and its two endpoints, or a singleton at an isolated vertex; cut-vertex terminology for a general graph is applied within its connected component.
Every finite forest with n vertices and c connected components has n−c edges, including n=c=0.
For every edge of a finite simple graph, it is a bridge if and only if it lies on no cycle.
Every edge of a finite simple graph belongs to exactly one block, using maximal 2-connected subgraphs, bridge blocks, and isolated-vertex blocks as defined.
Any two distinct blocks of a finite simple graph share at most one vertex.
A vertex of a finite simple graph belongs to at least two distinct blocks if and only if it is a cut vertex of its connected component.

For each connected component of a finite simple graph, form the bipartite incidence graph with a node for each block and a node for each cut vertex, joining a cut-vertex node to precisely the block nodes containing that vertex. This graph is a tree. A component consisting of an isolated vertex yields a single block node.

A trail is a walk whose edges are all distinct, and an Euler trail uses every edge of the graph. The edge support is the subgraph induced by the vertices of positive degree. A Hamilton cycle is a cycle containing every vertex.
For a finite simple graph with at least one edge and connected edge support, a closed Euler trail exists if and only if every vertex has even degree; isolated vertices are allowed.

For a finite simple graph with at least one edge and connected edge support, an open Euler trail exists if and only if exactly two vertices have odd degree. Those two vertices are necessarily the endpoints of any open Euler trail.
If a finite simple graph has no edges and at least one vertex, every length-zero walk is a closed Euler trail. A graph with empty vertex set has no walk under the sequence-based walk definition.
If a finite simple graph G has n≥3 vertices and d_G(v)≥n/2 for every vertex v (ordinary numerical half, equivalently 2d_G(v)≥n), then G has a Hamilton cycle.
If a finite simple graph G has n≥3 vertices and d_G(u)+d_G(v)≥n for every pair of distinct nonadjacent vertices u,v, then G has a Hamilton cycle.
For any finite linearly ordered label set V of size n≥2 there are n^(n−2) trees on V. There is exactly one tree on a one-element label set.

For any finite linearly ordered label set V of size n≥2, trees with vertex set V are in bijection with sequences of length n−2 over V, such that for each corresponding tree and sequence every v∈V occurs exactly d_G(v)−1 times in the sequence. The n=2 sequence length is zero.

For a finite simple graph G with n≥1 vertices and weights w_e in an arbitrary field K, define its weighted Laplacian L by L_uu=sum_{e incident to u}w_e, L_uv=−w_{ {u,v} } if u≠v and uv∈E, and L_uv=0 if u≠v and uv∉E.

For a finite simple graph with n≥1 vertices, arbitrary edge weights in any field K, and every vertex r, the determinant of the weighted Laplacian with row and column r deleted equals sum_T product_{e in E(T)} w_e over all spanning trees T. No connectivity or weight-positivity hypothesis is imposed.

In the matrix-tree identity, over Q with all edge weights equal to 1 the cofactor determinant is the number of spanning trees. For arbitrary field-valued weights it is 0 for a disconnected graph and 1 for a single-vertex graph, with the determinant and tree products empty in the latter case.

Identify each edge subset with its indicator in the vector space F_2^E, so addition is symmetric difference. For S⊆V define δ(S) as the edges with exactly one endpoint in S. The cut space is the F_2-span of all δ(S); the cycle space is the F_2-span of the edge sets of simple cycles.

For a finite graph and a spanning forest F containing one spanning tree per component, every edge e outside F has a fundamental cycle formed from e and the unique forest path between its endpoints. For e in F, deleting e splits its forest tree; either side defines the fundamental cut δ(S). These objects use cuts in the original graph.

For a finite simple graph with n vertices, m edges, and c connected components, the dimensions over F_2 of its cycle and cut spaces are respectively m−n+c and n−c. This includes graphs with isolated vertices and the empty graph.
For any finite simple graph G and any spanning forest F with one tree per component, the fundamental cuts indexed by edges of F form a basis of the cut space.
For any finite simple graph G and any spanning forest F with one tree per component, the fundamental cycles indexed by edges outside F form a basis of the cycle space.
The cycle and cut spaces of any finite simple graph are orthogonal under the coordinate dot product on F_2^E.
For every finite simple graph, its cycle space consists exactly of the edge subsets in which every vertex has even degree.
Bibliographic comparisons with Bondy–Murty and D05, including reference to the Cauchy–Binet interface, are contextual citations rather than extra mathematical obligations.

A finite capacitated directed network consists of finite vertex set V, finite arc set A, tail and head maps τ,η:A→V, finite real capacities c_a≥0, and distinct vertices s,t∈V. Parallel arcs, opposite arcs, and loops are allowed, retaining individual arc identities.

A feasible real flow on such a network assigns 0≤f_a≤c_a to every arc and satisfies div_f(v)=sum_{τ(a)=v}f_a−sum_{η(a)=v}f_a=0 for every v outside {s,t}. Its value |f| is div_f(s), a signed quantity that can be negative; the notation does not mean absolute value.
An s–t cut is S⊆V with s∈S and t∉S. Define A⁺(S)={a:τ(a)∈S,η(a)∉S}, A⁻(S)={a:τ(a)∉S,η(a)∈S}, and c(S)=sum_{a∈A⁺(S)}c_a.
For every flow on a finite directed network, the sum of its divergences over all vertices is 0, and hence a feasible s–t flow satisfies div_f(t)=−|f|.

Loops contribute to neither divergence nor cut capacity. Removing loops does not change the flow optimization problem: restriction of a feasible flow preserves feasibility and value, and a feasible flow in the loop-deleted network extends to the original network by assigning zero to removed loops. Loops remain allowed in circulation decompositions.

For every feasible real flow f and every s–t cut S, |f|=sum_{a∈A⁺(S)}f_a−sum_{a∈A⁻(S)}f_a≤c(S). Equality holds if and only if every outgoing cut arc is saturated (f_a=c_a) and every incoming cut arc has zero flow.

For a feasible flow f, form tagged residual copies of every original arc a:u→v: the forward copy u→v has capacity c_a−f_a, and the backward copy v→u has capacity f_a. The residual digraph uses exactly the copies with positive capacity. Arc identity and modification direction are retained as tags, even for coincident endpoints.
If the residual digraph of a feasible flow in a finite network has a directed walk from s to t, there exists a feasible flow with strictly larger signed value.
If no directed residual walk from s to t exists for a feasible flow f, the set of vertices residually reachable from s is an s–t cut with capacity exactly |f|.

Every finite directed network with finite nonnegative real capacities and distinct s,t has a maximum-value feasible real flow and a minimum-capacity s–t cut, and their values are equal. Networks with no arcs, parallel or opposite arcs, and loops are included.
A feasible real flow in a finite network is of maximum value if and only if its residual digraph has no directed s-to-t path.

Every nonnegative circulation on a finite directed multigraph is a finite nonnegative weighted sum of directed simple cycles, allowing a loop as a one-arc cycle. The decomposition preserves the load on every original arc. If all loads are integers, the nonzero summands can be chosen with positive integer weights; the zero circulation admits the empty sum.

A nonnegative circulation on a finite directed multigraph is a nonnegative real assignment to the individually indexed arcs whose divergence is zero at every vertex. It need not have designated source or sink; loops are allowed.

Every feasible flow of positive signed value on a finite directed network is a finite nonnegative weighted sum of directed simple cycles (including loops) and simple directed s-to-t paths. The path weights sum to the flow value, and each original arc load is preserved. If all loads are integers, all nonzero summands can have positive integer weights.

Every feasible flow of value zero on a finite directed network decomposes into directed simple cycles alone, allowing loops, with nonnegative weights and preservation of every original arc load. Integral loads permit positive integer weights for all nonzero summands; the empty sum is allowed.

Every feasible flow of negative signed value on a finite directed network decomposes into nonnegative weighted directed simple cycles and simple directed t-to-s paths. The path weights sum to minus the flow value, each original arc load is preserved, and integral loads permit positive integer weights for all nonzero summands.
For a finite directed network whose capacities are nonnegative integers, there exists a maximum-value feasible flow all of whose arc loads are integers.

For distinct vertices s,t in any finite simple undirected graph, the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint s-to-t paths equals the minimum cardinality of an edge set whose deletion separates s and t. The graph need not initially connect s and t; then the empty path family and separator attain 0.

For distinct nonadjacent vertices s,t in any finite simple undirected graph, the maximum number of pairwise internally vertex-disjoint s-to-t paths equals the minimum cardinality of a vertex subset of V\{s,t} whose deletion separates s and t. Initial separation is allowed, yielding 0 on both sides.

For a finite simple graph on n≥2 vertices, define κ as the least number of vertices whose removal disconnects the remaining graph or leaves one vertex, λ as the least number of edges whose removal disconnects the graph, and δ as the minimum vertex degree. Set κ=λ=0 when the graph is initially disconnected.
For every finite simple graph on n≥2 vertices with the stated conventions for vertex connectivity κ, edge connectivity λ, and minimum degree δ, κ≤λ≤δ. For a complete graph, κ=n−1.
References to Bondy–Murty and Schrijver give historical and textbook comparison, with no additional theorem statement.

In a finite simple graph, a matching is an edge subset no two of whose edges share an endpoint. A vertex is saturated by a matching when it is incident to a matching edge. A matching is perfect when every vertex is saturated. A vertex cover is a vertex set meeting every edge. The empty matching is perfect on the empty graph.
For every matching M and every vertex cover C in any finite simple graph, |M|≤|C|.

An augmenting path for a matching M has distinct vertices, starts and ends at unsaturated vertices, and has edges alternating outside and inside M, beginning and ending with edges outside M (hence a positive odd number of edges).
A matching in a finite graph has maximum cardinality if and only if it has no augmenting path.
In a finite bipartite graph the vertex parts L and R are disjoint, and for S⊆L its neighborhood N(S)⊆R consists of right vertices adjacent to at least one element of S.

In a finite bipartite graph with maximum matching M, let U⊆L be the unmatched left vertices. Direct nonmatching edges left-to-right and matching edges right-to-left. Let S⊆L and T⊆R be the vertices reachable from U in this digraph, with roots U included in S. Then T=N(S), and matching partners give a bijection T≃S\U.
A finite bipartite graph with parts L,R has a matching saturating L if and only if |N(X)|≥|X| for every subset X⊆L. Empty parts are allowed.
For every finite bipartite graph, the maximum matching cardinality equals the minimum vertex-cover cardinality. This includes empty parts and the empty graph.
For S⊆V of a finite simple graph, G−S denotes the induced graph on V\S, and o(G−S) is its number of connected components of odd vertex cardinality.
A finite graph G has a perfect matching if and only if o(G−S)≤|S| for every subset S⊆V, with o counting odd-order connected components of the induced deletion graph. The empty graph is included.

For every finite graph G, the minimum number of vertices left unsaturated by any matching is d=max_{S⊆V}(o(G−S)−|S|), where the subtraction is integer subtraction, not truncated natural subtraction. Equivalently its maximum matching cardinality is (|V|−d)/2. Empty graphs are included.

In a poset, a chain is a subset whose elements are pairwise comparable, and an antichain is a subset with no two distinct comparable elements. For a finite poset the width is the maximum size of an antichain and the height the maximum size of a chain, both zero on the empty poset. Chain and antichain decompositions are partitions into nonempty parts.

For every finite poset P, the minimum number of nonempty chains in a partition of P equals its width, the maximum cardinality of an antichain. On the empty poset both quantities are 0, using the empty partition.

For every finite poset P, the minimum number of nonempty antichains in a partition of P equals its height, the maximum cardinality of a chain. On the empty poset both quantities are 0, using the empty partition.
References to Bondy–Murty and Schrijver for classical matching and decomposition statements are contextual bibliography, not extra mathematical obligations.
Chapter 9 uses finite simple undirected graphs unless parallel edges are explicitly permitted; [k]={1,...,k} and [0]=∅. These conventions supply hypotheses for the following obligations.
For a finite simple graph G=(V,E) and k≥0, a proper k-coloring is a function c:V→[k] with c(u)≠c(v) for every edge uv. The chromatic number χ(G) is the least k admitting such a coloring.

For every finite simple G the minimum defining χ(G) exists: assigning distinct colors to all vertices is proper (so χ(G)≤|V|). The graph with no vertices has χ=0; every nonempty edgeless graph has χ=1.

Transporting a coloring along a graph isomorphism, by composition with its inverse, preserves properness; relabeling its colors by a bijection also preserves properness. Thus χ depends only on the graph isomorphism class and the cardinality of the color set.

For a finite simple graph and nonnegative integer d, the condition that each nonempty induced subgraph has a vertex whose degree in that subgraph is at most d is equivalent to existence of a vertex order in which every vertex has at most d later neighbors. Under this condition χ(G)≤d+1. The empty graph/order is included.
Every finite simple graph of maximum degree Δ has χ(G)≤Δ+1, taking Δ=0 for the graph with no vertices.
A finite simple graph is bipartite if and only if it has no cycle of odd length. In particular, a nonempty bipartite graph admits a proper two-coloring.

If a finite simple graph G is two-connected, noncomplete, and has minimum degree at least three, there are a vertex v and distinct nonadjacent neighbors a,b of v for which G−{a,b} is connected. This separately stated lemma is required in its own right.
If a finite connected simple graph is neither a complete graph nor an odd cycle, then χ(G)≤Δ(G).
The degree bounds are independent of a drawing; references are supplied for related graph-coloring material. This paragraph adds no further mathematical deliverable.
For A⊆E in a finite graph G=(V,E), c(A) is the number of connected components of the spanning graph (V,A), counting isolated vertices.
For a simple edge e=uv of G, construct G/e by identifying u and v, removing e, and merging any parallel edges produced by the identification; G/e is a simple graph.

For every finite simple G there is a unique P_G(q)∈ℤ[q] whose evaluation at every nonnegative integer k is the number of proper k-colorings. It is given by P_G(q)=Σ_{A⊆E}(−1)^|A| q^{c(A)}, satisfies P_G=P_{G−e}−P_{G/e} for every e∈E (using the simple contraction above), and equals q^n for an edgeless graph on n vertices. These statements include n=0, k=0, and the empty coloring, with q^0=1.

A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to distinct edges sharing an endpoint; χ′(G) is the least number of colors admitting one. For loopless multigraphs parallel edges remain distinct, and vertex degrees count them with multiplicity.
For a finite loopless graph or multigraph, χ′(G)≥Δ(G), because all edges incident to a maximum-degree vertex must receive distinct colors.
Every finite bipartite multigraph has χ′(G)=Δ(G), including the zero-degree/edgeless case.
Every finite simple graph satisfies χ′(G)≤Δ(G)+1.
References and explanation of the particular fan proof are contextual; the proof route does not add fan-rotation or two-color-component deliverables.

A plane embedding places vertices at distinct points and edges along simple polygonal arcs meeting only at prescribed endpoints. Regard it as an embedding in S² by adding the point at infinity. A face is a connected component of the complement of the embedded graph; the unbounded plane face is the component containing infinity. Planarity means admitting such a drawing.
A finite simple planar graph with v≥3 vertices has e≤3v−6; if it is bipartite, e≤2v−4. Neither bound assumes connectivity. Consequently K₅ and K₃,₃ are nonplanar.

For a finite graph embedded by the stated noncrossing polygonal-arc convention, let v,e,c,f be respectively the numbers of vertices, edges, graph components, and complementary faces in S². There are finitely many faces, and v−e+f=1+c. The graph with no vertices has v=e=c=0 and f=1.
Every finite simple planar graph admits a proper five-coloring, including graphs with no vertices.
References for the drawing conventions and coloring results; no additional theorem is asserted.
All matroid ground sets are finite. A+e denotes A∪{e}, A−e denotes A∖{e}, and complements are relative to the specified ground E unless another ground is given.

An independence system on finite E is a family 𝓘⊆2^E containing ∅ and hereditary under subsets. It is a matroid when, for I,J∈𝓘 with |I|<|J|, some e∈J∖I has I+e∈𝓘. A basis of A⊆E is an inclusion-maximal independent subset of A; a matroid basis is a basis of E. For E=∅ the unique basis is ∅.

On a finite E, a nonempty family 𝓑⊆2^E satisfying basis exchange—whenever B,D∈𝓑 and e∈B∖D, some f∈D∖B has B−e+f∈𝓑—determines a matroid by declaring precisely the subsets of members of 𝓑 independent. Its bases are exactly the original 𝓑. Conversely the bases of every matroid give such a presentation; the transformations recover the original data.

On a finite E, let 𝓒 be a family of nonempty subsets, with no member properly containing another, such that distinct C,D∈𝓒 sharing e have a member of 𝓒 contained in (C∪D)−e. Declare I independent exactly when it contains no member of 𝓒. This determines a matroid whose circuits are the original 𝓒. Conversely every finite matroid yields such circuit data. The family 𝓒 may be empty.

On a finite E, a map cl:2^E→2^E that is extensive, monotone, idempotent, and satisfies y∈cl(A+x)∖cl(A) ⇒ x∈cl(A+y) for all A⊆E and x,y∈E determines a matroid by the rule I independent iff e∉cl(I−e) for all e∈I. Its closure is the original cl. Conversely every finite matroid supplies this closure presentation, and all five presentations in W64 recover one another.

On a finite E, suppose r:2^E→ℤ has r(∅)=0, 0≤r(A+e)−r(A)≤1 for every A⊆E and e∈E, and r(A∪B)+r(A∩B)≤r(A)+r(B) for every A,B⊆E. Then I is independent exactly when r(I)=|I|, defining a matroid whose rank is the original r. Conversely every finite matroid has this rank presentation, compatible with the other presentations in W64.

For a finite matroid, r(A) is the common cardinality of the bases of A (equivalently the maximum size of an independent subset of A); circuits are the inclusion-minimal dependent sets; and cl(A)={e∈E : r(A+e)=r(A)}. These are the canonical objects used by the equivalent presentations, not additional assumed certificates.

For every A⊆E in a finite matroid, all bases of A have the same cardinality. Bases B,D of E satisfy: e∈B∖D ⇒ ∃f∈D∖B with B−e+f again a basis. Rank is monotone, has one-element increments between zero and one, and is submodular. In particular A⊆B and r(A+e)=r(A) imply r(B+e)=r(B).
In a finite matroid the circuits are precisely the inclusion-minimal dependent sets; distinct circuits C,D with e∈C∩D contain a circuit in (C∪D)−e. For every A⊆E and e∈E, e∈cl(A) iff r(A+e)=r(A).

For a finite matroid M on E, the complements E∖B of its bases form the bases of a matroid M* on the same E. Duality is involutive: (M*)*=M. For every A⊆E, r_{M*}(A)=|A|+r_M(E∖A)−r_M(E). Empty grounds and rank-zero cases are included.

For C⊆E, deletion M∖C is the matroid on E∖C whose independent sets are the M-independent sets contained there; contraction is M/C=(M*∖C)* on E∖C, with the second dual relative to that smaller ground. They satisfy (M/C)*=M*∖C and (M∖C)*=M*/C.
Let I be independent in a finite matroid and e∈cl(I)∖I. Exactly one circuit is contained in I+e, called the fundamental circuit. For each f∈I, I−f+e is independent iff f lies in that circuit.
In a finite matroid, an element is a loop when its singleton is a circuit; it is a coloop when it belongs to every basis. A cocircuit of M is a circuit of M*.
The cocircuits of a finite matroid M are exactly the inclusion-minimal sets meeting every basis of M. The coloops of M are exactly the loops of M*.
Among the nonloops of a finite matroid, distinct elements are parallel when their pair has rank one. A matroid is simple when it has no loops and no distinct parallel elements.

Equality or parallelism is an equivalence relation on the nonloops. Choose exactly one representative of each class, let S be the representative set, and restrict M to S (deleting all other elements, including loops). This is a simple matroid. For any A⊆E let q(A)⊆S be the representatives of the nonloops in A. Then r_{M|S}(q(A))=r_M(A) and cl_{M|S}(q(A))=cl_M(A)∩S. These formulas hold with empty A or S and with arbitrary loops or parallel classes.

For a finite matroid M, C⊆E, any basis I of C, and J⊆E∖C, J is independent in M/C iff I∪J is independent in M. No positivity-of-rank assumption is made; empty sets and empty remaining grounds are included.

For a finite matroid M on E, successive deletions and successive contractions combine: for C⊆E and D⊆E∖C, (M∖C)∖D=M∖(C∪D) and (M/C)/D=M/(C∪D), on the common remaining ground. Deletion and contraction on disjoint C,D⊆E commute: (M∖D)/C=(M/C)∖D. These identities include empty operation sets and empty remaining grounds.
For every finite matroid M, C⊆E, and A⊆E∖C, r_{M∖C}(A)=r_M(A) and r_{M/C}(A)=r_M(A∪C)−r_M(C). Empty deleted/contracted sets and an empty remaining ground are included.
References compare standard matroid presentations and conventions; they add no new mathematical obligation.
Representations use indexed vector families: zero, repeated, and distinct proportional columns retain their indices. Fields in this chapter may have any characteristic.

Let K be any field, V a K-vector space (not assumed finite-dimensional), and (v_e)_{e∈E} a finitely indexed family. Declare I⊆E independent iff the indexed subfamily (v_e)_{e∈I} is linearly independent. These independent sets form a matroid; on each A⊆E its rank is dim_K span{v_e:e∈A}. Repeated and zero columns are permitted, and zero columns are loops.

If the K-vector family (v_e)_{e∈E} represents M, deleting C⊆E is represented by omitting the C-columns. Contracting C is represented on E∖C by the images of its remaining columns in V/span{v_e:e∈C}. This applies also to dependent C, zero columns, C=∅, and C=E.

For every field embedding K→L and every finitely indexed K-vector family, extension of scalars to L preserves the rank of every subfamily and therefore preserves its represented matroid. No characteristic-zero or ambient finite-dimensionality assumption is imposed.

For finite undirected graphs allowing loops and parallel edges, components include isolated vertices, a loop counts as a cycle of length one, and two distinct parallel edges form a cycle of length two. A forest has no cycle of any of these kinds. Over any field, orient each nonloop edge u→v and give it incidence column e_v−e_u in the vertex coordinate space; give loops column zero.

A matroid flat is a set F with cl(F)=F. In a lattice x≺y means x<y and no element lies strictly between. A finite lattice is geometric here when every element is a join of atoms (elements covering its bottom 0) and it is upper semimodular in the covering form: if x covers x∧y, then x∨y covers y. The empty join equals 0, so the one-element lattice is permitted.

For every finite undirected graph, permitting loops and parallel edges under the stated cycle convention, incidence columns over every field and with every orientation represent the same matroid, whose independent sets are exactly the forests. Its bases are the unions of one spanning tree of each graph component. Its total rank is v−c, with isolated vertices counted in c; equivalently the rank of any edge subset A is v−c(V,A). Empty and edgeless graphs are included.

The flats of every finite matroid, ordered by inclusion, form a geometric lattice. The meet is intersection, the join of flats F,G is cl(F∪G), and the bottom is cl(∅), so loops need not be absent. These operations specify the asserted flat lattice.

For every finite geometric lattice L, its atom set carries a simple matroid, constructed from L alone, whose lattice of flats is order-isomorphic to L. In this correspondence a lattice element x corresponds to the set of atoms below x, and joining those atoms recovers x. The one-element lattice yields the matroid on the empty atom set.

The uniform matroid U_{2,4} on four elements, with exactly the subsets of size at most two independent, is representable over a field K iff K has at least three elements. More generally, every simple rank-two matroid represented over the finite field 𝔽_q has at most q+1 elements.
Define the Fano matroid by the seven indexed nonzero vectors of 𝔽₂³. It is representable over a field K if and only if char(K)=2.

If a rank-r matroid on n indexed columns is represented over a field by [I_r A], its dual, with exactly the same column indexing and order, is represented by [−Aᵀ I_{n−r}]. The formula includes r=0 and r=n.

For a finite field 𝔽_q and integer r≥1, choose one nonzero vector from each one-dimensional subspace of 𝔽_q^r. The indexed projective points, independent according to these representative columns, form a simple rank-r matroid with (q^r−1)/(q−1) points. For r≥2 every projective line (the points of a two-dimensional linear subspace) has q+1 points.

For a finite field 𝔽_q and integer d≥0, represent each affine point x∈𝔽_q^d by (1,x)∈𝔽_q^{d+1}. These indexed points form a simple rank-(d+1) matroid with q^d points; for d=0 this is a single rank-one point. For d≥1 each affine line {x+ta:t∈𝔽_q}, a≠0, has q points.
For any finite bipartite relation with sides E and R, the subsets I⊆E which can be saturated by a matching into R are the independent sets of a matroid on E. The empty side cases are included.

For a finite matroid M on E define the integer polynomial T_M(x,y)∈ℤ[x,y] by T_M(x,y)=Σ_{A⊆E}(x−1)^{r_M(E)−r_M(A)}(y−1)^{|A|−r_M(A)}. The exponents are nonnegative integers, so this is a polynomial; constant monomials use exponent zero, including the rank-zero and empty-ground cases.
For every e∈E in a finite matroid, T_M=y T_{M∖e} if e is a loop, T_M=x T_{M/e} if e is a coloop, and T_M=T_{M∖e}+T_{M/e} if e is neither. Deletion and contraction remove the singleton {e}.

For finite matroids on disjoint grounds, T_{M₁⊕M₂}=T_{M₁}T_{M₂}. For every finite M, T_M(1,1) equals its number of bases. These conclusions include rank zero and empty grounds, where the appropriate empty sum/product and constant monomial conventions apply.

For finite matroids M₁,M₂ on disjoint grounds, their direct sum is the matroid on the union whose subsets are independent exactly when each intersection with a component ground is independent in that component. This specifies the direct sum used in the polynomial multiplicativity assertion.

For every finite simple graph G, let M(G) be its cycle matroid, c(G) its number of components including isolated vertices, and χ_G(t) its chromatic polynomial. Then χ_G(t)=(−1)^{r_{M(G)}(E)} t^{c(G)} T_{M(G)}(1−t,0) as a polynomial identity, including for the empty graph.
References compare representation/geometry conventions and situate the rank-polynomial bridge. No further mathematical statement is required.
For w:E→ℝ and A⊆E define w(A)=Σ_{e∈A}w(e). In an independence system, maximal independent means maximal by inclusion; without augmentation such a set need not have the largest possible cardinality.

On a finite independence system and real weight function, fix a total tie order and list the ground elements e₁,...,e_n in nonincreasing weight, breaking equal weights by that order. Put I₀=∅; at step i set I_i=I_{i−1}∪{e_i} if this is independent, and otherwise leave I_i=I_{i−1}; return I_n. The basis objective maximizes w over maximal independent sets, whereas the independent-set objective maximizes w over all independent sets.

For the weighted greedy algorithm on any finite independence system, after every step 0≤i≤n, I_i is a maximal independent subset of prefix P_i={e₁,...,e_i}. If the system is a matroid, |I_n∩P_i|=|I_i|=r(P_i). The empty prefix and empty ground are included. This is a separately stated lemma, not merely a proof-route intermediate.

For every real weight function on a finite matroid and every total tie order, weighted greedy returns a maximum-weight basis. Negative weights are allowed, and the empty ground has the empty optimal basis.

If all weights on a finite matroid are nonnegative, weighted greedy also maximizes weight over all independent sets, for any tie order. For arbitrary real weights, delete all elements of negative weight, restrict the matroid to the remaining elements, and apply weighted greedy there; its output is a maximum-weight independent set of the original matroid. Zero weights remain allowed and the resulting restriction may be empty.

In the one-element matroid whose element is a coloop of weight −1, the unique basis must contain that element, while the maximum-weight independent set omits it (the empty set has weight 0). This substantive example explains why the two optimization objectives differ with negative weights.

Let 𝓘 be a nonempty hereditary family on finite E. The following are equivalent: (1) 𝓘 satisfies augmentation; (2) for every nonnegative real weight function, weighted greedy maximizes weight over maximal independent sets; (3) for every nonnegative real weight function, weighted greedy maximizes weight over all independent sets. In (2) and (3) either one may fix any total tie order in advance, or one may require optimality for every tie order; both versions are equivalent to augmentation. The empty ground is included.
The closing paragraph explains the distinction between basis and independent-set conventions for negative weights and provides references; it adds no theorem beyond the stated greedy results.

For a finite group acting on a finite set and every point x, the size of the orbit of x times the size of its stabilizer is the group order, without a faithfulness requirement.
