Unless an infinite ground set is explicitly specified, extremal graphs are finite simple undirected graphs. Directed networks have labelled arcs and divergence means net outflow. Matroids have a specified finite ground set. Finite probability models include outcomes and probabilities; statements on general probability spaces retain their stated measurability and integrability requirements. Empty sums and products are 0 and 1, respectively.

Bibliographic and reuse conventions for separation, Farkas, linear programming, matching, graph, network, matroid, and elementary probability results; no additional statement is imported into the required scope merely by these references.
In Chapter 1 every graph is finite simple undirected. A copy of H in G is a subgraph copy, allowing extra ambient edges; e(G) denotes the number of edges.

For all n≥0 and r≥1, every finite simple undirected K_(r+1)-free graph G on n vertices satisfies e(G)≤e(T_r(n)); equality holds if and only if G is isomorphic to T_r(n). This includes n=0, r=1, and r>n.

For every integer n≥0 and r≥1, construct T_r(n), the complete r-partite graph on n vertices whose part sizes differ by at most one; empty parts are allowed. The graph is determined up to isomorphism by these conditions.
For integers n≥0, r≥1, q≥0 and 0≤b<r satisfying n=qr+b, e(T_r(n))=binom(n,2)−(r−b)binom(q,2)−b binom(q+1,2).
For every n≥0, a triangle-free finite simple undirected graph on n vertices has at most floor(n²/4) edges.

For integers 1≤s≤t and every finite simple undirected graph G with n≥0 vertices and no subgraph copy of K_(s,t), 2e(G)≤(s−1)n+(t−1)^(1/s) n^(2−1/s), with powers interpreted over the nonnegative reals. In particular, for fixed s,t the edge counts of such graphs are uniformly O(n^(2−1/s)) as n→∞. The cases n=0, s=1 and t=1 remain included.
For r,t≥1, K_r(t) is the complete r-partite graph with exactly t vertices in each part.

For every fixed pair of integers r,t≥1 and real 0<c≤1, there exists N such that for every integer n≥N, all finite sets V_1,…,V_r with |V_i|≤n, and every E⊆V_1×⋯×V_r with |E|≥c n^r, there are T_i⊆V_i with |T_i|=t for all i and T_1×⋯×T_r⊆E. The sets V_i need not be disjoint.

For all fixed integers r≥2, t≥1 and real ε>0, there exists N such that for every n≥N, every n-vertex finite simple undirected graph G with e(G)≥(1−1/(r−1)+ε)binom(n,2) contains a subgraph copy of K_r(t). No upper bound on ε is assumed.

For every finite simple graph H with at least one edge, lim_(n→∞) ex(n,H)/binom(n,2)=1−1/(χ(H)−1), where χ(H) is the chromatic number. The limit concerns sufficiently large n, so the initial n=0,1 denominator values do not change it. In particular this limit is zero whenever H is bipartite (still with at least one edge).
For a finite simple graph H having at least one edge and every n≥0, ex(n,H) is the maximum number of edges among n-vertex finite simple undirected graphs with no subgraph copy of H.
References for the clique bounds, general density theorem and classical bipartite estimate; no further required mathematical statement.

For a finite ground set X, binom(X,k) is its family of k-element subsets. A family is an antichain when distinct members are incomparable by inclusion. A family is intersecting when any two members have nonempty intersection. For F⊆binom(X,k) and k≥1, its lower shadow ∂F consists of the (k−1)-element subsets contained in some member of F. The shadow of a family of empty sets (rank k=0) is empty.
For every finite X of size n≥0 and every antichain A⊆P(X), ∑_(S∈A) binom(n,|S|)^(−1)≤1. Equality holds if and only if A is a full layer binom(X,k) for some integer 0≤k≤n.

For every finite X of size n≥0 and every antichain A⊆P(X), |A|≤binom(n,floor(n/2)). Equality holds if and only if A equals a full middle layer: binom(X,floor(n/2)) or binom(X,ceil(n/2)). Both n=0 and n=1 are included.
For every finite X of size n and integer 1≤k≤n, if A⊆binom(X,k) then |∂A|/binom(n,k−1)≥|A|/binom(n,k).
For a family A⊆binom(X,k) on finite X and 0≤k<|X|, its upper shadow ∂⁺A is the family of all (k+1)-sets of X containing a member of A.
For every finite X of size n, every integer 0≤k<n and A⊆binom(X,k), |∂⁺A|/binom(n,k+1)≥|A|/binom(n,k). The k=0 case is included.
For every finite X of size n and integer k with 1≤k and 2k≤n, every intersecting F⊆binom(X,k) satisfies |F|≤binom(n−1,k−1).
For a fixed point x∈X, the full star of k-sets at x is {A∈binom(X,k) : x∈A}.

Under the Erdős–Ko–Rado hypotheses 1≤k and 2k≤n=|X|, each full star is intersecting and attains size binom(n−1,k−1). When n=2k, an intersecting family attains this bound if and only if it contains exactly one member from every complementary pair {A,X∖A} of k-sets.
For every finite X with n=|X| and integer k≥1 satisfying n>2k, the intersecting families F⊆binom(X,k) with |F|=binom(n−1,k−1) are exactly the full stars.

For every finite linearly ordered X, colex is a linear order on each rank. If X is increasingly enumerated as x_1<⋯<x_n, the colex comparison between two same-rank sets agrees with comparison of their binary weights ∑_(x_i∈A)2^(i−1).

On a finite linearly ordered ground set X, for distinct same-size subsets A,B define A<_(colex)B when the largest element of A△B belongs to B. For each rank k and 0≤m≤binom(|X|,k), I_k(m) is the family of the first m k-sets in this order, including I_k(0)=∅.

For a finite linearly ordered X of size n and 1≤k≤n, the lower shadow of any colex initial segment in binom(X,k) is a colex initial segment in binom(X,k−1). If the original segment is nonempty with greatest member S, its shadow has greatest member S∖{min S}. This includes k=1 and the empty initial segment in the first assertion.

For every family F of subsets of finite X and disjoint U,V⊆X with |U|=|V|, C_(U,V) preserves the cardinality of F and the rank of each moved set; in particular it takes k-uniform families to k-uniform families of the same size. The replacement bijection is inverted on moved images by removing U and restoring V.

For disjoint sets U,V⊆X of equal size, a set A is movable when V⊆A and A∩U=∅; its replacement is A*=(A∖V)∪U. C_(U,V)F replaces exactly those movable members of F whose replacements are absent from F, leaving all other members in place. F is C_(U,V)-closed when it contains the replacement of each of its movable members. When U=V=∅ every family is closed and compression is the identity.

Let U,V⊆X be disjoint nonempty equal-size sets. Suppose that for each x∈U there exists y∈V for which F is C_(U∖{x},V∖{y})-closed. Then ∂(C_(U,V)F)⊆C_(U,V)(∂F), and consequently |∂(C_(U,V)F)|≤|∂F|. The shadow is the chapter’s one-point deletion shadow (in particular for every uniform family F⊆binom(X,k), including the declared rank-zero convention).

For every finite linearly ordered X, integer 1≤k≤|X| and F⊆binom(X,k), put m=|F|. For every integer 0≤j≤k, |∂^j I_k(m)|≤|∂^j F|, where ∂^0 is the identity and higher ∂^j are iterated lower shadows. Empty F and the boundary j=k are included.

An order-preserving bijection between finite linearly ordered ground sets sends the greatest point of every nonempty symmetric difference to the greatest point of the image symmetric difference, preserves ranks, and sends one-point deletions bijectively to one-point deletions. Consequently it transports colex initial segments and every iterated shadow. In particular the increasing enumeration identifies an arbitrary n-point linearly ordered ground set with the ordered standard n-point set.

The colex proof route is compared with Mathlib and a reference is given for the binomial-expansion formulation. This citation does not separately state a binomial-expansion version of Kruskal–Katona as a deliverable.

For every finite index set I and pairs (A_i,B_i)_(i∈I) of finite sets, if A_i∩B_i=∅ for every i and A_i∩B_j≠∅ for every ordered pair i≠j, then ∑_(i∈I) binom(|A_i|+|B_i|,|A_i|)^(−1)≤1. Empty index sets and empty sides are not excluded.
References for the classical antichain, intersecting-family and set-pair bounds, with no additional mathematical statement.

For any set X and positive integer k, [X]^k denotes the k-element subsets of X. A subset Y⊆X is homogeneous for a coloring c:[X]^k→C when there exists a color d∈C with c(A)=d for every A∈[Y]^k. If C is nonempty this holds vacuously whenever |Y|<k.

For every pair of integers k,r≥1, every coloring [ℕ]^k→C with |C|=r has an infinite homogeneous subset of ℕ. More generally, for every infinite set X and every coloring [X]^k→C with |C|=r, there exists an infinite homogeneous Y⊆X. The ground set is arbitrary, not assumed countable.

For every integers k,r,m≥1 there exists an integer N≥m such that, for every N-element set X and every coloring [X]^k→C with |C|=r, there is a homogeneous subset Y⊆X of cardinality exactly m. The cases m<k, k=1 and r=1 remain included.

For every integers a,b≥1, R(a,b) is the least positive integer n such that every red–blue edge coloring of K_n contains a red K_a or a blue K_b. The construction includes existence of such a positive n, supplied by finite Ramsey; cliques are subgraph cliques, and a single vertex is a clique in either color.
For every integers a,b≥1, R(1,b)=1 and R(a,1)=1.
For every integers a,b≥2, R(a,b)≤binom(a+b−2,a−1).
For every integers a,b≥2, R(a,b)≤R(a−1,b)+R(a,b−1).
The two-color graph Ramsey number satisfies R(3,3)=6.
References discussing infinite induction, finite compactness, and two-color graph bounds, with no additional mathematical theorem.

Chapter 4 introduces positive-probability existence, avoidance, alteration, and deterministic selection in finite probabilistic experiments; the classical-method citation is background, not an additional theorem obligation.

A finite weighted probability experiment consists of a finite outcome set Ω, all its subsets as measurable events, and weights p_ω≥0 with ∑_{ω∈Ω}p_ω=1. Its event probabilities are P(A)=∑_{ω∈A}p_ω, its positive support is {ω∈Ω:p_ω>0}, and for any real quantity Z:Ω→ℝ its expectation is E Z=∑_{ω∈Ω}p_ω Z(ω).

For an event A in a finite weighted experiment, its indicator 1_A equals 1 on A and 0 off A and satisfies E 1_A=P(A). Expectation of a finite sum of real quantities equals the sum of their expectations, without an independence assumption.

On any probability space (Ω,𝓕,P), every measurable event A with P(A)>0 is nonempty. For a finite weighted experiment such A contains an outcome ω with p_ω>0. Consequently, if a map f sends outcomes to combinatorial objects and every outcome in A maps to an object with a specified property, some object f(ω) has that property.
For a finite set I and measurable events A_i on a probability space, P(⋃_{i∈I}A_i)≤∑_{i∈I}P(A_i), including I=∅ with union empty and sum 0.
For a finite family of measurable events (A_i) on a probability space, if ∑_{i∈I}P(A_i)<1, then P(⋂_{i∈I}A_iᶜ)>0. For I=∅ the avoidance event is Ω and its probability is 1.
For every integer k≥3, the diagonal Ramsey number satisfies R(k,k)>2^(k/2), where the comparison is with the real number 2^(k/2).

For integers n≥0 and k≥2, if (n choose k)·2^(1−(k choose 2))<1, then the diagonal Ramsey number satisfies R(k,k)>n; equivalently, there exists a red–blue edge coloring of K_n with no monochromatic K_k. The assertion includes n<k, where the forbidden k-vertex event family is empty.

For each outcome in a finite weighted experiment let a finite object have size S and nonnegative integer defect count D. Assume a specified deterministic deletion procedure, for every outcome in the positive support, removes at most D items, clears all defects, and returns an object of size at least S−D. Then some repaired object has size at least E(S−D). The subtraction S−D is an integer/real difference before expectation, not truncated natural subtraction; repair is required only on positive-support outcomes.
Let G be a finite simple graph with n vertices and m edges. For every real p∈[0,1], its independence number satisfies α(G)≥pn−p²m. The claim includes p=0, p=1, and an empty vertex set.

For any finite weighted experiment revealed in finitely many stages and any real objective Z, one can select a positive-weight outcome with Z at least its initial expectation by choosing at every stage a positive-probability branch whose conditional expectation is at least the current one. Stages can be represented by successively refining outcome partitions starting with the trivial partition and ending with singleton cells; on a cell C of positive probability the conditional expectation is (∑_{ω∈C}p_ω Z(ω))/P(C). The terminal singleton value is the selected objective value.

Every finite simple graph with m edges has a cut containing at least m/2 edges, obtainable by the conditional-expectation selection rule while revealing successive independent fair vertex colors. This includes an empty graph and an empty sequence of vertex choices.

Chapter 5 states moment inequalities on general probability spaces, under their indicated integrability conditions, while its finite combinatorial applications need only weighted sums. This scope explanation is context.

For a real random variable X, E X denotes integration with respect to the probability measure. For real random variables X,Y with finite second moments, Var(X)=E[(X−E X)²] and Cov(X,Y)=E[(X−E X)(Y−E Y)].
If X,Y are real random variables with finite second moments, their centered product (X−E X)(Y−E Y) is integrable, and Var(X)=E[X²]−(E X)² and Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]−E X·E Y.

Let (A_i)_{i∈I} be a finite family of measurable events on a probability space, let Z=∑_{i∈I}1_{A_i}, and put p_i=P(A_i). Then E Z=∑_i p_i and Var(Z)=∑_{i,j∈I}Cov(1_{A_i},1_{A_j}). For any enumeration of I, the latter also equals ∑_i p_i(1−p_i)+2∑_{i<j}(P(A_i∩A_j)−p_i p_j). Empty-index families are allowed.
For every finite simple graph G with vertex degrees d(v), α(G)≥∑_{v∈V(G)}1/(d(v)+1). This includes isolated vertices (summand 1) and the empty vertex set (sum 0).
If X is an integrable real random variable with X≥0 almost surely and a>0, then P(X≥a)≤E X/a.

If X is a measurable real random variable that is nonnegative integer-valued almost surely and has finite expectation E X<1, then P(X=0)>0. The finite expectation is the usual integrable expectation; nonnegativity and integer-valuedness are required only almost surely.

If X is a real random variable with X≥0 almost surely, 0<E X<∞, and E[X²]<∞, then P(X>0)≥(E X)²/E[X²]. In particular the denominator is positive under these hypotheses; the event uses a strict positive threshold.
Let X≥0 almost surely be a real random variable with 0<E X<∞ and E[X²]<∞, and write μ=E X. For every real θ with 0≤θ<1, P(X>θμ)≥(1−θ)²μ²/E[X²]. The threshold is strict, and θ=0 is included.
For a real random variable X≥0 almost surely with 0<μ=E X<∞ and E[X²]<∞, one has P(X=0)≤Var(X)/μ².

For any sequence (X_n) of nonnegative-almost-surely real random variables, each satisfying 0<E X_n<∞ and E[X_n²]<∞, on possibly different probability spaces, if Var(X_n)/(E X_n)²→0 as n→∞, then P(X_n>0)→1.
For every pair of integers g≥3 and k≥1, there exists a finite simple graph with no cycle of length at most g and with chromatic number greater than k.
For a bounded real random variable X, define its moment-generating function for real λ by M_X(λ)=E[e^(λX)].

For a finite family of independent bounded real random variables X_i and bounded measurable functions f_i on their essential ranges, E[∏_i f_i(X_i)]=∏_i E[f_i(X_i)]. In particular, for every real λ, M_{∑_i X_i}(λ)=∏_i M_{X_i}(λ). The functions need not be indicators, and finite empty products are included.
For any bounded real random variable Y, any real threshold t, and any λ>0, P(Y≥t)≤e^(−λt)E[e^(λY)]. No positivity restriction on t is imposed.

Let X_1,…,X_m be independent real random variables with a_i≤X_i≤b_i almost surely, where a_i≤b_i are finite real endpoints. Put S=∑_{i=1}^m(X_i−E X_i) and V=∑_{i=1}^m(b_i−a_i)². If t>0 and V>0, both P(S≥t) and P(S≤−t) are at most exp(−2t²/V). If V=0, then S=0 almost surely, and both tail probabilities are zero for every t>0. An empty sum is permitted through the V=0 case.
For a finite family of independent Bernoulli random variables X_i with success probabilities p_i∈[0,1], put S=∑_i X_i and μ=∑_i p_i. For every real δ≥0, P(S≥(1+δ)μ)≤(e^δ/(1+δ)^(1+δ))^μ.

For a finite family of independent Bernoulli random variables X_i with success probabilities p_i∈[0,1], put S=∑_i X_i and μ=∑_i p_i. For every real δ with 0≤δ<1, P(S≤(1−δ)μ)≤(e^(−δ)/(1−δ)^(1−δ))^μ. At δ=1 the lower-tail assertion is instead P(S=0)≤e^(−μ).
Under the independent Bernoulli-sum hypotheses, if μ=∑_i p_i=0, then S=∑_i X_i=0 almost surely, and all the stated Chernoff inequalities hold with right-hand side 1. This includes an empty family.

Chapter 6 motivates the Lovász local lemma as an alternative to the union-bound criterion, and announces its exact independence assumption and product lower bound. The accompanying classical references are context.

For a finite family (A_i)_{i∈I} of measurable events on a probability space, a simple graph D on I with neighbor sets N(i) is a dependency graph if, for each i, A_i is independent of the sigma-algebra generated by all A_j with j∉N(i)∪{i}. Explicitly, for every B in that generated sigma-algebra, P(A_i∩B)=P(A_i)P(B). Pairwise independence alone is not this definition.

In a finite product of finite weighted sample spaces with independent coordinates, let each event A_i in a finite family be determined by a coordinate set S_i. The simple graph joining distinct i,j exactly when S_i∩S_j≠∅ is a dependency graph in the full sigma-algebra sense of W27. Thus A_i is independent of every event in the sigma-algebra generated by its non-neighbor events, including when its own coordinate block or the union of non-neighbor coordinate blocks is empty.

For independent fair bits U,V, the events A={U=0}, B={V=0}, C={U=V} each have probability 1/2 and each distinct pair has intersection probability 1/4, so they are pairwise independent. Nevertheless A∩B lies in the sigma-algebra generated by A,B, P(C∩(A∩B))=1/4, and P(C)P(A∩B)=1/8. Hence the edgeless graph on these three events is not a dependency graph as defined in W27.

Let D be a dependency graph for a finite family of measurable events (A_i)_{i∈I}. If real numbers x_i∈[0,1) satisfy P(A_i)≤x_i∏_{j∈N(i)}(1−x_j) for every i∈I, then P(⋂_{i∈I}A_iᶜ)≥∏_{i∈I}(1−x_i)>0. Values x_i=0 are allowed, and for an empty event family both probability and product equal 1.

Suppose a dependency graph for a finite family of measurable events has maximum degree at most an integer d≥0, and P(A_i)≤p for a real p≥0 and every i. If e·p·(d+1)≤1, then P(⋂_i A_iᶜ)>0. The equality case in the numerical hypothesis, d=0, and an empty event family are included.

Let a finite hypergraph have all edges of size at least k≥1, and suppose every edge intersects at most d≥0 other edges. If e·2^(1−k)·(d+1)≤1, there exists a red–blue vertex coloring with no monochromatic edge. Here k,d are the edge-size and intersection-count parameters; edges are nonempty because k≥1, and an edgeless hypergraph is allowed.

Chapter and section headings and bibliographic context for finite-dimensional linear programming, Farkas and total unimodularity. The citations identify background; they do not add all results of those references to this source scope.
In Chapter 7 vectors and matrices are finite and real unless integrality is specified; vector inequalities are coordinatewise.

For any finite real matrix A and compatible real vectors b,c, use primal feasibility Ax=b, x≥0 and dual feasibility Aᵀy≤c. For every such feasible pair x,y, cᵀx=bᵀy if and only if x_i(c−Aᵀy)_i=0 for every coordinate i. Either condition makes x a minimizer of cᵀx over the primal feasible set and y a maximizer of bᵀy over the dual feasible set.

For the finite real standard-form primal inf{cᵀx : Ax=b, x≥0} and dual sup{bᵀy : Aᵀy≤c}, if the primal is feasible and its infimum is finite, there exist primal- and dual-feasible vectors x,y with cᵀx=bᵀy. In particular both optima are attained and equal.
For any finite real A,b,c in the stated standard-form LP, the system Ax=b, x≥0 is infeasible if and only if there is a real vector u satisfying Aᵀu≥0 and bᵀu<0.
For a feasible finite real standard-form primal inf{cᵀx : Ax=b, x≥0}, its infimum is −∞ if and only if there exists a vector d≥0 with Ad=0 and cᵀd<0.

Transform a finite real linear program with free coordinates, mixed equalities and inequalities, and either objective direction to standard equality form with nonnegative variables: split each free coordinate as a difference of two nonnegative coordinates, introduce one slack for each upper inequality, and negate the objective for maximization. Splitting and introducing slacks preserve the set of attainable objective values; objective negation negates that set and exchanges minimization with maximization. In the corresponding maximization dual, a row used as an upper inequality has a nonnegative multiplier, whereas an equality row has a free real multiplier.
The source announces that standard-form correspondence will be applied to the two matching models in Chapter 8 and introduces the vertices/active-rows section.

For a point x of a convex set P in a finite-dimensional real coordinate space, the midpoint extreme-point condition says there do not exist distinct x₊,x₋∈P with x=(x₊+x₋)/2. Membership x∈P is part of being an extreme point.

For every convex set P in a finite-dimensional real coordinate space and x∈P, the midpoint extreme-point condition is equivalent to exclusion of every nontrivial two-point convex decomposition: whenever y,z∈P and 0<t<1 satisfy x=t y+(1−t)z, necessarily y=z=x. This is a statement for arbitrary convex P, without a polyhedron, closedness, boundedness, or pointedness assumption.
A polyhedron is pointed if it contains no affine line {x+t d : t∈ℝ} with d≠0. A vertex of a polyhedron means an extreme point of that polyhedron.
For any finite real A,b and P={x∈ℝⁿ : Ax≤b}, and every x∈P, x is a vertex if and only if the active row functionals {a_iᵀ : a_iᵀx=b_i} span the full dual coordinate space.

For P={x∈ℝⁿ : Ax≤b} nonempty and pointed, any linear functional with finite optimum over P attains that optimum at a vertex. This applies to either minimization or maximization by objective negation; no boundedness assumption on P is required.
Every nonempty bounded finite real polyhedron P={x∈ℝⁿ : Ax≤b} equals the convex hull of its vertices.
An integer matrix is totally unimodular if each square submatrix has determinant in {0,1,−1}; the size-zero determinant 1 is included.
If A is a totally unimodular integer matrix and b is an integer vector, every vertex of the real polyhedron P={x : Ax≤b} has integer coordinates.

For every totally unimodular integer A and integral b, the real polyhedron P={x : Ax≤b} equals conv(P∩ℤⁿ). This holds even when P contains affine lines or is empty; the convex hull of the empty set is interpreted as empty.

If A is totally unimodular, b is integral, and P={x : Ax≤b} is nonempty and pointed, every finite linear optimum on P has an integral optimizer. In particular this applies to a nonempty bounded P, with either objective direction.
An integer matrix A is totally unimodular if and only if, for every integral right-hand-side vector b, every vertex of the real polyhedron {x : x≥0, Ax≤b} is integral.

If B is a finite network incidence matrix with the net-outflow sign and b,ℓ,u are integral vectors with finite coordinate bounds, every vertex of {f : Bf=b, ℓ≤f≤u} is integral. Whenever this set is nonempty, every real linear objective has an integral optimizer on it. No independent zero-sum hypothesis on b is added; feasibility enforces all necessary compatibility conditions.

For every finite bipartite graph (V,E), conv{1_M : M is a matching} equals {x∈ℝᴱ : x≥0 and ∑_{e incident to v}x_e≤1 for every v∈V}. Replacing all degree inequalities by equalities gives exactly conv{1_M : M is a perfect matching}, including the case of no perfect matching, when both sets are empty.

The net-outflow node–arc incidence matrix of every finite directed network is totally unimodular: a nonloop arc has +1 at its tail and −1 at its head, and a loop has zero column. Labelled parallel and oppositely oriented arcs are allowed. The unsigned vertex–edge incidence matrix of every finite bipartite graph is also totally unimodular.

For a finite graph with edge set E, its matching polytope is the convex hull in ℝᴱ of the zero-one incidence vectors of its matchings. The perfect-matching polytope means the convex hull of the incidence vectors of perfect matchings, with an empty hull if no such matching exists.

In the degree relaxation {x∈ℝ³ : x≥0, x₁+x₂≤1, x₂+x₃≤1, x₃+x₁≤1} for a triangle, x=(1/2,1/2,1/2) is feasible and all three degree constraints are active. Their equality system has that unique solution, so x is a fractional vertex. Every actual triangle matching has at most one edge.

A finite directed network consists of a finite vertex set V and finite labelled arc set E with specified tail/head; different labels permit parallel and opposite arcs. A flow is f∈ℝᴱ; net outflow at v is the sum over outgoing arcs minus the sum over incoming arcs, so loops contribute zero. For S⊆V, δ⁺(S) and δ⁻(S) are the arcs respectively leaving and entering S. For an arc vector a and arc set F, a(F)=∑_{e∈F}a_e.

Given ℓ≤f≤u, create a labelled forward residual copy of e with capacity u_e−f_e whenever positive, and a labelled backward copy with capacity f_e−ℓ_e whenever positive, retaining the original arc label and a direction sign. Augment by adding a chosen amount on forward copies and subtracting it on backward copies. A simple residual path or simple residual cycle may be augmented by any nonnegative amount at most its minimum residual capacity; bounds remain feasible, internal path vertices preserve divergence, and cycles preserve all divergences. If both copies of an arc occur on a cycle their signed increments cancel.

For a finite directed labelled network, distinct vertices s,t, and finite real capacities u_e≥0, consider flows 0≤f≤u conserving at every vertex other than s,t, with val(f) equal to net outflow at s. If a feasible flow f and a cut S with s∈S and t∉S satisfy val(f)=u(δ⁺(S)), then f is a maximum flow and S is a minimum-capacity cut. There always exist such a flow and cut with equal value. If u is integral, an equal-value pair exists with f integral.

Under the finite real-capacity network hypotheses of W36, initialize the flow at zero and, while a residual s–t path exists, choose a shortest such path by number of residual arcs and augment by its full residual bottleneck. This is the shortest augmenting path / Edmonds–Karp rule, allowing arbitrary choices among shortest paths.

For the shortest augmenting path rule from zero in W36, arbitrary finite nonnegative real capacities are permitted. The algorithm terminates with a maximum flow after O(|V||E|) augmentations. Using breadth-first search and updates, each iteration uses O(|V|+|E|) arc inspections and elementary operations, with one final unsuccessful search when no path remains. These are exact residual-operation counts independent of the numerical capacity values.

The source identifies the shortest-path rule as Edmonds–Karp and cites Schrijver. Its exact-operation/capacity-independence interpretation belongs to the algorithmic complexity obligation rather than an additional theorem from the reference.

For every finite directed network, finite real bounds ℓ_e≤u_e, and real vertex vector b with ∑_v b_v=0, a flow f with ℓ≤f≤u and net outflow b exists if and only if b(S)≤u(δ⁺(S))−ℓ(δ⁻(S)) for every S⊆V, where b(S)=∑_{v∈S}b_v. If b,ℓ,u are integral and these conditions hold, an integral such f exists. The b=0 specialization is the circulation criterion; empty subsets and zero demand remain included.

For an arc cost vector w∈ℝᴱ and residual network of a feasible bounded flow f, the forward residual copy of e has cost w_e and its backward copy has cost −w_e. Given a real potential π on vertices, the reduced cost of a residual arc v→z of cost w is w+π(v)−π(z). Residual loops are allowed and count as directed cycles.

Let ℓ≤u be finite real arc bounds and b a zero-sum real vertex divergence, and let f be feasible for ℓ≤f≤u with that divergence. For arbitrary real arc costs w, the following are equivalent: (i) f minimizes ∑_e w_e f_e among all flows feasible for the same bounds and divergence; (ii) its positive-capacity residual graph, with forward costs w_e and backward costs −w_e, has no directed cycle of strictly negative total cost, including loops as cycles; (iii) there is a real vertex potential π with w+π(v)−π(z)≥0 for every residual arc v→z of residual cost w.

In a finite directed network with finite integral bounds ℓ≤u and integral zero-sum prescribed divergence b, every nonempty feasible flow set admits an integral minimum-cost flow for any real arc cost vector. Costs need not be integral.
Bibliographic context for feasible-flow and reduced-cost constructions; this does not incorporate all flow results of the cited book.

Take a finite bipartite graph with sides L,R and an allowed edge ij only between i∈L and j∈R, bearing arbitrary real weight w_ij. Its allowed-edge incidence matrix A has rows indexed by L⊔R. A feasible potential pair satisfies u_i+v_j≥w_ij on every allowed edge; an edge is tight when equality holds. The perfect and unrestricted matching duals impose different sign conditions on potentials.

For every finite real-weighted bipartite graph with at least one perfect matching, the maximum weight of a perfect matching equals min{∑_{i∈L}u_i+∑_{j∈R}v_j : u_i+v_j≥w_ij for each allowed ij}, over free real potentials u,v. This minimum is attained, including the empty graph with empty sides.

Under W40, for every perfect matching and every feasible free real potential pair, they are jointly optimal if and only if every edge of that matching is tight, equivalently u_i+v_j=w_ij on each of its edges.

For every finite bipartite graph with arbitrary real allowed-edge weights, the maximum matching weight (including the empty matching) equals the attained minimum of ∑_{i∈L}u_i+∑_{j∈R}v_j subject to u_i,v_j≥0 and u_i+v_j≥w_ij for every allowed edge. A matching and such feasible potentials are jointly optimal if and only if all matching edges are tight and every unmatched vertex has potential zero. No perfect matching hypothesis is imposed.

For every finite square size, including zero, each real matrix with nonnegative entries and all row and column sums equal to one is a finite convex combination of permutation matrices of that size. The extreme points of the set of all such matrices are exactly those permutation matrices.

For any prescribed forbidden positions in a finite square matrix, every nonnegative real matrix with all row and column sums one and zeros at those positions is a convex combination of permutation matrices supported on the complementary allowed positions. Exactly these supported permutation matrices are the extreme points of the restricted set. Arbitrary allowed-position patterns and size zero are included; existence of a compatible permutation is not assumed.

For every finite bipartite graph admitting a perfect matching and every real weight assignment, the tight-edge Hungarian method terminates after finitely many potential updates and matching augmentations. It returns a maximum-weight perfect matching together with a feasible optimal pair of free real potentials for W40. The empty graph with empty sides is included.

On a finite real-weighted bipartite graph admitting a perfect matching, the tight-edge Hungarian method starts with an empty matching, v_j=0 and u_i=max{w_ij : ij allowed}, treating empty sides separately. For an unmatched left root, search on tight unmatched edges left-to-right and matched edges right-to-left; reaching an unmatched right vertex gives alternating augmentation. Otherwise, for reached left/right sets S,T, subtract the minimum slack over allowed edges from S to R\T from potentials on S and add it to potentials on T, then continue the search.
Historical/reference context for Kuhn and Schrijver, followed by the matroid-polytopes chapter heading.
For every finite matroid and every S⊆E, all maximal independent subsets of S have cardinality r(S), the maximum independent cardinality in S.

A finite matroid on finite E is a family of independent subsets containing ∅, hereditary under subsets, and satisfying augmentation: independent I,J with |I|<|J| admit e∈J\I with I∪{e} independent. For S⊆E, r(S) is the maximum cardinality of an independent subset of S, and a basis of S is a maximal independent subset of S. Bases of the matroid mean bases of E.
For x∈ℝᴱ and S⊆E put x(S)=∑_{e∈S}x_e; 1_S is the indicator vector of S; w·x=∑_{e∈E}w_e x_e.

Assign arbitrary real weights, including negative weights, to a finite matroid on E. Starting with the empty independent set, scan every element in nonincreasing weight order and add an element precisely when independence is preserved. For every ordering within ties, the output is a basis with maximum total weight among all bases. Empty E is included.
References for the wider greedy characterization and the weight/polytope arguments; the wider characterization is cited for background, not asserted here as an additional source theorem.

For any nonempty finite subset F of a Euclidean space and any point x in that space, if w·x≤max_{z∈F}w·z for every vector w, then x∈conv(F). The nonempty hypothesis on F is required; the ambient Euclidean space is not restricted to a matroid coordinate space.

For every finite matroid M on E with rank r, conv{1_B : B is a basis of M} equals {x∈ℝᴱ : x≥0, x(S)≤r(S) for every S⊆E, x(E)=r(E)}. Its vertices are exactly the basis indicators, hence all are integral. The empty ground set is included.
For every finite matroid M on E with rank r, conv{1_I : I is independent in M} equals {x∈ℝᴱ : x≥0 and x(S)≤r(S) for every S⊆E}, including the empty ground set.

For every finite undirected graph G=(V,E), the convex hull of incidence vectors of its forests equals {x∈ℝᴱ : x≥0 and x(E(S))≤|S|−1 for every nonempty S⊆V}, where E(S) is the set of edges with both endpoints in S. The quantification over S excludes the empty set; the graph itself may be empty.

For a finite undirected graph G=(V,E), its spanning-forest polytope, the hull of forests spanning each original component, is the forest polytope of W46 with the extra equation x(E)=|V|−c(G), where c(G) counts every component including isolated vertices. For a connected G with at least one vertex this is the spanning-tree polytope and the extra equation is x(E)=|V|−1.

For every finite undirected graph with arbitrary real edge weights, start with no edges, process all edges in nondecreasing weight order, and include an edge whenever it creates no cycle. For every tie order the resulting forest spans each graph component and has minimum total weight among spanning forests. If the graph is connected with at least one vertex, it is a minimum spanning tree; the empty graph gives the empty forest.

Let G be a finite connected undirected graph with at least one vertex and arbitrary real weights; parallel edges are distinguished and loops may be discarded. If F is a forest contained in some minimum spanning tree and a nontrivial vertex cut has no edge of F crossing it, then for every minimum-weight edge e crossing that cut, F∪{e} is contained in a minimum spanning tree.

For a finite connected undirected graph with at least one vertex and arbitrary real edge weights, Prim’s algorithm, beginning from any starting vertex and repeatedly adding any minimum-weight edge from the visited vertex set to its complement, produces a minimum spanning tree for arbitrary tie choices. Parallel edges remain distinguished; loops can be discarded.

Under the finite connected nonempty graph and real-weight hypotheses of W48, a spanning tree T is minimum if and only if, for every non-tree edge e with distinct endpoints, w_e≥max{w_f : f∈P_T(e)}, where P_T(e) is the unique T-path between those endpoints. Loops impose no condition, parallel edges are distinguished, and the statement includes the case of no qualifying non-tree edges.

Under the same hypotheses, a spanning tree T is the unique minimum spanning tree if and only if w_e>max{w_f : f∈P_T(e)} for every e∉T with distinct endpoints. Thus all the non-tree path inequalities are strict; the family may be empty.
References for spanning-tree algorithms, graphic polytopes and certificates, and the intersection/union section heading.
For every finite matroid M on E and U⊆E, restriction M|U is a matroid on U whose independent sets are exactly the M-independent subsets of U. Its rank at every S⊆U is r_M(S).

For every finite matroid M on E and C⊆E, contraction M/C is a matroid on E\C, with rank r_{M/C}(S)=r_M(S∪C)−r_M(C) for all S⊆E\C. For every basis I of C and every J⊆E\C, J is independent in M/C if and only if I∪J is independent in M. In particular the construction and independence relation do not depend on a chosen basis of C.
The source identifies its restriction/contraction lemma as the part of the cited minor calculus needed for the next argument; this does not add all minor calculus from the cited source.

For every two finite matroids M₁,M₂ on the same finite ground set E, with respective ranks r₁,r₂, max{|I| : I independent in both M₁ and M₂} equals min_{U⊆E}(r₁(U)+r₂(E\U)). Both extrema are attained because the families are finite and nonempty; E may be empty.

For the same finite matroids and every S⊆E, there exists a disjoint partition S=⊔_{i=1}^k S_i with each S_i independent in its respective M_i if and only if |T|≤∑_{i=1}^k r_i(T) for every T⊆S. Empty parts are allowed. For k=0 the partition exists exactly for S=∅.

For any k≥0 finite matroids M₁,…,M_k on the same finite ground set E, with ranks r_i, the sets that are unions of one independent set of each M_i are exactly the independent sets of a matroid on E. Its rank at each S⊆E is ρ(S)=min_{T⊆S}(|S\T|+∑_{i=1}^k r_i(T)). For k=0 its only independent set is ∅ and its rank is identically zero.
