Scope: rounding, conditioning, backward error and finite-time stability; matrix factorizations, least squares, eigenvalues and low-rank approximation; interpolation, differentiation, quadrature, root enclosures, fixed points and Newton convergence. Computed values in rounding analyses mean the exact real values stored by the specified model, each primitive has its own safe-domain assumption, exact-arithmetic algorithms use the indicated field operations, and certificates require hypotheses making residuals/enclosures valid. References and the writing-group/contract map describe prerequisites and organization rather than additional assertions to formalize.

Stored floating-point numbers are identified with their exact real values; ordinary arithmetic symbols denote exact arithmetic and fl denotes a rounding operation. This is the interpretive convention for the finite model and all following error statements.

For integers beta>=2, p>=1 and emin<=emax, define positive normal numbers m*beta^e for integer beta^(p-1)<=m<beta^p and integer emin<=e<=emax; adjoin negatives and zero. The gradual-underflow variant also includes signed m*beta^emin for integers 1<=m<beta^(p-1). F is the resulting finite set. Define nearest rounding on all real x by choosing a distance-minimizing element of F with a fixed deterministic tie rule, e.g. the smaller tied point. Define u=(1/2)*beta^(1-p), amin=beta^(p-1+emin), amax=(beta^p-1)*beta^emax, and the normal safe domain {0} union {x: amin<=abs(x)<=amax}.

For every real x in the finite radix model normal safe domain, nearest rounding satisfies fl(x)=x*(1+delta) for some real delta with abs(delta)<=u. This includes x=0 and is independent of the deterministic nearest-rounding tie rule.

The mathematical nearest map is defined on all reals; the normal safe domain limits applicability of its relative-error theorem. Other formats may use another proved domain or an absolute underflow bound.

For representable a,b (and c for fused multiply-add), rounded addition/subtraction/multiplication/division are fl(a+b), fl(a-b), fl(a*b), fl(a/b), with b nonzero for division. Fused multiply-add is fl(a*b+c) with exact product and addition before its single rounding. Rounded square root is one rounding applied to the real square root of a nonnegative exact argument.

Relative-error estimates apply to each primitive exact result: separately rounded multiplication followed by addition needs separate range checks, while fused multiply-add needs the check only on exact a*b+c. The later analyses also permit an abstract relative model on a specified domain with these same bounds.

If real z=x*(1+delta) and abs(delta)<=u<1, then x lies in the closed interval whose endpoints are z/(1-u) and z/(1+u), ordered by size; in particular z=0 implies x=0. If instead abs(z-x)<=eta, then x is in [z-eta,z+eta]. Available directed values z_down<=x<=z_up themselves constitute an enclosure.
In the finite radix model with gradual underflow, every real x with abs(x)<=amin has nearest-rounding absolute error abs(fl(x)-x)<=beta^emin/2.

In the finite radix model with gradual underflow, if a,b are positive representable numbers and a/2<=b<=2*a, then a-b is representable. The reflected assertion holds for like-signed negative representable inputs (equivalently, their magnitudes satisfy the same factor-two relation).

For stored real inputs a,b with a-b nonzero and epsilon>=0, perturbations Delta a, Delta b satisfying abs(Delta a)<=epsilon*abs(a) and abs(Delta b)<=epsilon*abs(b) change their exact difference by at most epsilon*(abs(a)+abs(b)); the bound is attained by choosing perturbations of opposite signs. Thus the maximum relative change, compared to input relative scale epsilon, is (abs(a)+abs(b))/abs(a-b), which may be large even when stored-input subtraction is exact.

For real intervals X=[a,b], Y=[c,d] (a<=b and c<=d), all exact sums are enclosed by outward rounding of [a+c,b+d], all differences by outward rounding of [a-d,b-c], and all products by outward rounding of [min(ac,ad,bc,bd),max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]. If 0 is not in Y, reciprocals of its members are enclosed by outward rounding of [1/d,1/c], and all quotients are enclosed by multiplying X with that reciprocal enclosure using the preceding outward product operation. Every outward endpoint used must exist.

Let n be a nonnegative integer, 0<=u<1, n*u<1, abs(delta_i)<=u for 1<=i<=n, and rho_i in {-1,1}. Then product_i (1+delta_i)^rho_i = 1+theta for some real theta with abs(theta)<=gamma_n, where gamma_n=n*u/(1-n*u). For the empty product n=0, theta=0.

For exact stored real inputs x_i,y_i, if every primitive satisfies the relative model and n*u<1, both specified sequential algorithms produce s_hat=sum_i x_i*y_i*(1+theta_i) with abs(theta_i)<=gamma_n=n*u/(1-n*u), hence abs(s_hat-sum_i x_i*y_i)<=gamma_n*sum_i abs(x_i*y_i). The first algorithm forms p_i=fl(x_i*y_i), initializes s_hat_1=p_1, and for j>=2 forms s_hat_j=fl(s_hat_(j-1)+p_j); the second initializes s_hat_0=0 and forms s_hat_i=fl(x_i*y_i+s_hat_(i-1)) using one fused multiply-add per term. The empty dot product is zero.

Changing evaluation order changes the relevant proved rounding-path length N and requires N*u<1 for a gamma_N argument. In particular invoking N=2*n requires 2*n*u<1 even when a sharper analysis of the same algorithm only requires n*u<1. This is an applicability clarification of the rounding-factor estimates.
For every integer n>=1, a balanced binary summation tree with n leaves can be chosen so that every input-to-output addition path has length at most ceil(log_2(n)).

For real summands x_i with nonzero exact sum s=sum_i x_i, the componentwise relative condition number of summation (individual perturbations bounded by epsilon*abs(x_i) and output scale abs(s)) equals sum_i abs(x_i)/abs(s).

For a binary rounded sum of real leaves x_i, if d bounds the number of additions on every input-to-output path, every addition satisfies the relative model, and d*u<1, then the absolute error from the exact sum is at most gamma_d*sum_i abs(x_i), where gamma_d=d*u/(1-d*u).

For compatible real matrices A,B with inner dimension k, if each output entry is computed by either sequential dot-product form above and each primitive satisfies the relative model with k*u<1, then abs(AB_hat-A*B)<=gamma_k*abs(A)*abs(B), entrywise. Include k=0, for which each exact and computed entry is the zero dot product.

Condition numbers belong to a mathematical problem together with chosen input/output scales. Throughout chapter 2 a matrix norm accompanying a vector norm is subordinate; input and output vector spaces may use different norms.

Let U be open in a finite-dimensional normed space X, let Y be normed, and let f:U->Y be Frechet differentiable at x in U. Define kappa_abs(f,x)=norm(Df(x)) and, only when x!=0 and f(x)!=0, kappa_rel(f,x)=norm(Df(x))*norm(x)/norm(f(x)). Absolute conditioning remains defined at zero input/output scales; singular problems that do not define a differentiable solution map are outside this derivative formula.

Under the derivative-condition-number hypotheses, for sufficiently small r>0 with x+v in U for norm(v)<=r, define K(r)=sup_{norm(v)<=r} norm(f(x+v)-f(x))/r. Then K(r) tends to norm(Df(x)) as r decreases to zero. In zero-dimensional X, K(r)=0. When x and f(x) are nonzero, define K_rel(r)=sup_{norm(v)<=r*norm(x)} norm(f(x+v)-f(x))/(r*norm(f(x))); this tends to norm(Df(x))*norm(x)/norm(f(x)).

Let X,Y be Banach spaces, let A:X->Y be bounded invertible linear with bounded inverse, and let Delta A:X->Y be bounded linear. Set E=A^(-1)*Delta A and assume norm(E)<1. Then A+Delta A is invertible, norm((A+Delta A)^(-1))<=norm(A^(-1))/(1-norm(E)), (I+E)^(-1)=sum_{j>=0}(-E)^j with convergence in operator norm, and (A+Delta A)^(-1)-A^(-1)=-(A+Delta A)^(-1)*Delta A*A^(-1). The same conclusions also hold in a unital Banach algebra with norm(1)<=1: for an invertible element A and any Delta A with E=A^(-1)*Delta A of norm less than one, A+Delta A is invertible, the same inverse-norm estimate and inverse-difference identity hold, and the operator-norm series is replaced by the norm-convergent algebra series sum_{j>=0}(-E)^j=(1+E)^(-1).

Let A be invertible in the chapter subordinate-norm setting, Ax=b, and norm(A^(-1))*norm(Delta A)<1. Let (A+Delta A)*x_tilde=b+Delta b. For every b, norm(x_tilde-x)<=norm(A^(-1))/(1-norm(A^(-1))*norm(Delta A))*(norm(Delta b)+norm(Delta A)*norm(x)). If b!=0, define a=norm(Delta A)/norm(A), c=norm(Delta b)/norm(b), and kappa(A)=norm(A)*norm(A^(-1)); then norm(x_tilde-x)/norm(x)<=kappa(A)*(a+c)/(1-kappa(A)*a). Include b=0 through the absolute bound.

For exact data x and observed output y_hat, absolute forward error is norm(y_hat-f(x)); relative forward error divides it by a chosen nonzero output scale. Given admissible perturbations D_x and nonnegative size s on D_x, backward error is inf{s(v):v in D_x, x+v in U, f(x+v)=y_hat}, interpreted as +infinity if no feasible perturbation exists. A backward certificate is a particular feasible perturbation with a bound on its size.
Examples of permitted perturbation sizes are a norm, a relative norm, or componentwise bounds scaled by selected input data.

For the backward-error feasible-size set, a finite infimum guarantees feasible perturbations whose sizes approach it arbitrarily closely from above (for every positive tolerance there is a feasible size within that tolerance of the infimum).

In finite dimension, if the feasible perturbations form a nonempty closed subset of the perturbation space and the size function is a norm, then the backward-error infimum is attained by a feasible minimizing perturbation. The source warns that restricting admissible inputs to an open region need not supply this closedness hypothesis.

If f is Frechet differentiable at x with x!=0 and f(x)!=0, then for actual feasible perturbations v with y_hat=f(x+v), epsilon=norm(v)/norm(x) tending to zero, norm(y_hat-f(x))/norm(f(x)) <= kappa_rel(f,x)*epsilon+o(epsilon). The Frechet remainder bound applies uniformly to sufficiently small perturbations. For the relative norm size s(v)=norm(v)/norm(x), the same first-order conclusion applies to the backward-error infimum b_* as b_* tends to zero, using feasible perturbations with size at most b_*+tau and letting tau decrease to zero; a minimum need not be attained. In particular b_*=0 forces y_hat=f(x) by continuity.

For a fixed segment [x,x+v], if f is continuous on that segment, Frechet differentiable along its interior, and its derivative operator norm there is uniformly bounded by L, then norm(f(x+v)-f(x))<=L*norm(v). The statement applies in the normed-space setting, including complex spaces through realification and the coincident-endpoint case.

Let A be invertible, Ax=b, and r=b-A*x_hat. Then norm(x_hat-x)<=norm(A^(-1))*norm(r). If b!=0 then norm(x_hat-x)/norm(x)<=kappa(A)*norm(r)/norm(b), where kappa(A)=norm(A)*norm(A^(-1)). When only the right-hand side may change, the absolute normwise backward error is exactly norm(r); the feasible right-hand-side perturbation is Delta b=-r.

Given A,b,x_hat and r=b-A*x_hat, let E and f be entrywise nonnegative matrix/vector scales. The least nonnegative epsilon for which abs(Delta A)<=epsilon*E and abs(Delta b)<=epsilon*f entrywise permit (A+Delta A)*x_hat=b+Delta b equals max_i abs(r_i)/(E*abs(x_hat)+f)_i. Interpret 0/0 as 0, a nonzero numerator over 0 as +infinity, and a maximum over no rows as 0. Every finite value is attained; no invertibility hypothesis is required. The source phase construction covers real or complex scalar entries.

Given A,b,x_hat and r=b-A*x_hat, let alpha,beta>=0 and use a subordinate matrix norm. The least nonnegative epsilon allowing norm(Delta A)<=epsilon*alpha, norm(Delta b)<=epsilon*beta and (A+Delta A)*x_hat=b+Delta b equals norm(r)/(alpha*norm(x_hat)+beta). Interpret 0/0 as 0 and a nonzero numerator over 0 as +infinity. Every finite value is attained, including zero-denominator feasible cases; no invertibility hypothesis on A is required.

Let X be a Banach space, C_h:X->X a bounded linear operator for every h>0, and T(t):X->X a strongly continuous semigroup of bounded linear operators for t>=0: T(0)=I, T(s+t)=T(s)*T(t), and t->T(t)x is continuous for every x. Both C_h^n and T(n*h) act on X. Fix a horizon T0>0.

For the Banach-space/semigroup/time-step setup and fixed T0>0, finite-horizon small-step stability means there exist h0>0 and finite M such that norm(C_h^n)<=M for every 0<h<=h0 and integer n>=0 with n*h<=T0. Pointwise local consistency at x means norm((C_h-T(h))*x)/h->0 as h decreases to zero. Uniform orbit consistency at x means tau_h(x)=max over integers j>=0 with (j+1)*h<=T0 of norm((C_h-T(h))*T(j*h)*x)/h tends to zero, with empty maximum 0. Strong convergence uniform in mesh times means E_h(x)=max over integers n>=0 with n*h<=T0 of norm(C_h^n*x-T(n*h)*x) tends to zero for every x. For statements on every finite horizon, bounds may depend on T0.

If x belongs to the domain of the strongly continuous semigroup generator A, pointwise local consistency norm((C_h-T(h))*x)/h->0 is equivalent to (C_h-I)*x/h -> A*x as h decreases to zero. This is pointwise in x.

The positive convergence result below requires stronger defect control along the exact trajectory, or verification of that orbit control on a dense class; pointwise generator consistency alone is not substituted for it.

Let L>=0, tau_h>=0, h>0, T0>0, and nonnegative errors e_j satisfy e_(j+1)<=(1+L*h)*e_j+h*tau_h whenever (j+1)*h<=T0. For every n>=0 with n*h<=T0, e_n<=exp(L*T0)*e_0+T0*exp(L*T0)*tau_h. If e_0 and tau_h tend to zero as h decreases to zero, the maximum of e_n over n*h<=T0 tends to zero. Include L=0 and n=0.

More generally, if nonnegative errors satisfy e_(j+1)<=(1+L*h)*e_j+h*tau_(h,j) with L>=0, h>0 and tau_(h,j)>=0, then for n*h<=T0, e_n<=(1+L*h)^n*e_0+sum_{j=0}^{n-1} h*(1+L*h)^(n-1-j)*tau_(h,j). In particular n=0 has the empty sum.

For a family of bounded linear maps on a Banach space, if for every x the family of values is bounded in norm, then the operator norms of the family have a common finite bound. The following Baire-category argument supplies a proof rather than additional obligations.
For the strongly continuous semigroup T on the Banach space X and every finite horizon T0>0, K_T0=sup_{0<=t<=T0} norm(T(t)) is finite.

In the Banach-space/semigroup/time-step setup, strong convergence uniform in mesh times on [0,T0] for every initial vector x implies finite-horizon small-step stability on that same horizon: some h0>0 and finite M bound norm(C_h^n) for all 0<h<=h0 and n*h<=T0.

On X=R with T(t)=I and T0=1, define C_h=I for 0<h<=1/2, scalar multiplication by 1/abs(h-3/4) for h>1/2 with h!=3/4, and C_(3/4)=I. Every C_h is individually bounded and small-step convergence is exact, but there is no common bound on norm(C_h^n) over all h>0 and integers n>=0 with n*h<=1, because n=1 and h->3/4 give unbounded norms. This shows why convergence yields stability only on a sufficiently small step range.

In the Banach-space/semigroup/time-step setup, if finite-horizon small-step stability holds and tau_h(x)->0 as h decreases to zero on a dense class of initial vectors x, then E_h(x)->0 for every x in X. No commutation between C_h and T(h) is required.

Under finite-horizon small-step stability with constants h0,M, for every x and 0<h<=h0, E_h(x)<=M*T0*tau_h(x), where E_h is maximum mesh-time error and tau_h the uniform exact-orbit one-step defect defined above. The estimate includes a step range with no nontrivial mesh times or no defect steps through the specified zero-maximum conventions.

Chapter 4 conventions: ^* is conjugate transpose (transpose over R); entrywise |A| inequalities and ordinary products of nonnegative matrices are intended; ||.||_2 is the Euclidean operator norm. Exact arguments permit real or complex data where specified. Rounded bounds use Chapter 1's real relative scalar model, safe operations with no exceptional range events, and stored input entries; gamma_k=ku/(1-ku) and the signed-product bound are inherited from W06.

For every n-by-n matrix A over any field, including the empty matrix, there exist a permutation matrix P, unit lower-triangular L, and an upper-triangular row-echelon U such that PA=LU. Row-pivoted elimination constructs this factorization by scanning columns and allowing a column to be skipped if all its remaining entries vanish; previous multiplier columns are exchanged consistently with rows.

For unexchanged elimination that takes a pivot in each column through n-1, the ability to take all nonzero division pivots is equivalent to nonvanishing of every leading principal minor of orders 1,...,n-1. Once these preceding pivots exist, the terminal diagonal entry is nonzero iff det A is nonzero. This is a criterion for the specified no-skip division algorithm, not merely for existence of some unpivoted LU factorization; empty/singleton pivot lists are interpreted vacuously.

An invertible matrix may have a zero leading principal minor: the matrix exchanging two coordinates does. Conversely, the singular real matrix diag(0,1) has the bare factorization I·diag(0,1), although its first Doolittle division pivot is zero. Thus invertibility does not justify unpivoted elimination, and existence of an unpivoted LU does not certify the no-skip division run.

The sequential kernel s_t=fl(s_{t-1}-fl(a_t b_t)) and its unrolled exact identities (4.1) specify the common operation trace used to prove W21, W22, and W26; they impose no separate proof-route deliverable. The required theorem entries retain sequential multiply-subtract evaluation and their terminal division/square-root conventions.

Let T be a real n-by-n upper- or lower-triangular matrix with nonzero diagonal. Compute forward/backward substitution using sequential rounded multiply-subtracts and one final rounded division per row. If all operations are safe and n u<1, the computed xhat has a componentwise backward error: there exists DeltaT with (T+DeltaT)xhat=b and |DeltaT|<=gamma_n |T|. DeltaT preserves the triangular pattern and every structural zero. The n=0 case is included.

For a real square row-pivoted Doolittle run using the W20 row-exchange convention, suppose columns 1,...,n-1 are processed in order without skips, every pivot used as a divisor is nonzero, and each rounded multiplier division and sequential trailing-entry multiply-subtract obeys the safe relative error model. If 3n u<1, the stored unit lower-triangular Lhat and upper-triangular Uhat satisfy PA+DeltaA=Lhat Uhat for a correction with |DeltaA|<=gamma_{3n}|Lhat||Uhat|. The certificate is conditional on the actual stated run, including its pivots, and includes the empty factorization.

For exact elimination of a nonzero real n-by-n matrix, choosing a largest-magnitude available entry in each current pivot column bounds the largest magnitude in every successive trailing submatrix and every computed U row by 2^(n-1) max_{i,j}|a_ij|. The bound is attainable when the first available row is chosen on ties (n>=1 is forced by a nonzero square matrix).

For a rounded factorization satisfying W22 and forward/backward solves Lhat y=Pb and Uhat x=y satisfying W21, the final computed xhat satisfies (PA+DeltaA_solve)xhat=Pb for a correction with |DeltaA_solve|<=(gamma_{3n}+2 gamma_n+gamma_n^2)|Lhat||Uhat|. The hypotheses include the nonzero diagonal required by the two solves and safe rounding. The certificate uses the actual stored factors. Multiplication by P^(-1) gives the corresponding original-system correction.
Bibliographical comparison of the stated elimination/triangular-solve conventions with Higham Chapters 8–9 and Golub–Van Loan Sections 3.2–3.4; no additional mathematical assertion.

Every real symmetric or complex Hermitian positive-definite square matrix A, including the empty matrix, has a unique upper-triangular R with positive real diagonal such that A=R^* R. Equivalently A=L L^* with L=R^* lower triangular and positive real diagonal, uniquely with this convention.

Every Hermitian positive-semidefinite square matrix A has a unique upper-triangular factor R satisfying A=R^* R, real nonnegative diagonal, and the normalization that the entire row i of R vanishes whenever R_ii=0. Zero and empty matrices are allowed; no positive-definiteness or rank condition is imposed.

Without the zero-row normalization, a nonnegative-diagonal upper-triangular Cholesky factor need not be unique: A=diag(0,1) admits the ordinary factor diag(0,1) and also R=[[0,1],[0,0]], since R^* R=A. The example explains the extra normalization in W25.

For real symmetric stored input A, run lower-triangular columnwise Cholesky as follows: for i>=j start from a_ij and sequentially subtract rounded products lhat_it lhat_jt for t<j; take a rounded square root for the diagonal residual and divide off-diagonal residuals by that stored diagonal. Suppose all square-root arguments are positive, all divisors are nonzero, and every operation, including square roots, follows the safe relative model. If (3n+3)u<1, there exists DeltaA with A+DeltaA=Lhat Lhat^* and |DeltaA|<=gamma_{3n+3}|Lhat||Lhat^*|. This is conditional on successful execution rather than a claim that every positive-definite input has such a rounded execution.

In binary arithmetic of precision 4 with round to nearest, the real symmetric matrix A=[[9/32,1/4],[1/4,1/4]] is positive definite (a_11>0 and det A=1/128>0). Its first exact square root lies between 1/2 and 17/32, the midpoint between 1/2 and successor 9/16, so the stored root is 1/2. The first multiplier is exactly 1/2 and its computed square is exactly 1/4; the computed second diagonal residual is zero, although the exact Schur complement is positive. Hence exact positive definiteness alone does not ensure the positive residual hypothesis in W26.
References for exact Cholesky and conditional rounded Cholesky bounds; no new assertion beyond W24–W26.

For K=R or C and every full-column-rank A in K^(m-by-n), including n=0, there exist unique Q in K^(m-by-n) and upper-triangular R in K^(n-by-n) with A=QR, Q^* Q=I_n, and positive real diagonal in R. Full column rank supplies m>=n; no square or surjective assumption is made.

For every linear map A between finite-dimensional real or complex inner-product spaces and every target vector b, x minimizes ||Ax-b||_2 iff A^* (Ax-b)=0. Such minimizers always exist. If A is injective, there is a unique minimizer and it is (A^* A)^(-1) A^* b.
For the full-column-rank reduced factorization A=QR of W27, the unique least-squares minimizer for any target b is x=R^(-1) Q^* b.

For nonzero x in R^d (hence d>=1), define sign_+(t)=1 at t=0 and the usual sign otherwise, alpha=-sign_+(x_1)||x||_2, v=x-alpha e_1, and H(v)=I-2v v^*/(v^* v). Then |v_1|=|x_1|+||x||_2, v is nonzero, H(v) is orthogonal, and H(v)x=alpha e_1. For a zero tail one may instead take the identity reflector and leave the tail fixed.

For every real m-by-n A with m>=n, successive exact Householder reflections on the current column tails, extended by the identity on earlier rows and leaving a zero tail unchanged, construct A=QR with Q in R^(m-by-n), Q^* Q=I_n, and R upper triangular. If A has full column rank, corresponding sign changes in Q columns and R rows give positive R diagonal. Empty columns are permitted; full rank is required only for the positivity conclusion.

For real m-by-n A of full column rank with n>0, the least singular value on its domain is positive, kappa_2(A)=sigma_max(A)/sigma_min(A), and kappa_2(A^* A)=kappa_2(A)^2, using Euclidean operator norms (and the full-column-rank/least-squares condition number for rectangular A).
References to projection, least-squares, normal-equation, exact QR, and Householder interfaces; these are bibliographic context for the preceding results.

Let m>=n and use the following real Householder trace on stored A. At step j, d=m-j+1 and x is the stored pivot-column tail. Skip if x=0. Otherwise compute the sequential rounded self-dot-product, its rounded square root nuhat, alphahat=-sign_+(x_1)nuhat, and w=(fl(x_1-alphahat),x_2,...,x_d), and replace the pivot tail by alphahat e_1. For each trailing tail y compute sequential rounded p_hat for w^* y and q_hat for w^* w, t_hat=fl(fl(2 p_hat)/q_hat), and y_hat_i=fl(y_i-fl(t_hat w_i)). Assume all listed operations are safe, signs/copying are exact, and du<1 and gamma_d<1 at every nontrivial step. Then a product of exact orthogonal reflectors has first n columns Q with Q^* Q=I_n, and for the stored upper-triangular Rhat there is E with A+E=Q Rhat and, for every column i, ||E_:i||_2 <= (product_{j=1}^n(1+c_j)-1)||A_:i||_2. The constants are c_j=0 on skipped steps and otherwise, writing gamma=gamma_d, a=max{1-(1-u)sqrt(1-gamma),(1+u)sqrt(1+gamma)-1}, b_0=a+u(2+a), R_0=(1+u)^2/(1-gamma), D_0=max{R_0-1,1-(1-u)^2/(1+gamma)}, c_tail=2(D_0+R_0 gamma)+u+2(2u+u^2)R_0(1+gamma), and c_j=max{a+8b_0,c_tail}. The n=0 product gives zero error. Q is the exact implicit orthogonal factor.

For m>=n, m-by-n real or complex matrices A,Qhat and n-by-n Rhat, suppose ||A-Qhat Rhat||_2<=rho and ||Qhat^* Qhat-I_n||_2<=eta with 0<=eta<1. There exists an m-by-n Qtilde with Qtilde^* Qtilde=I_n and ||A-Qtilde Rhat||_2 <= rho + [eta/(1+sqrt(1-eta))]||Rhat||_2. No triangularity/rank hypothesis on Rhat is required; the empty-column case is allowed. The supplied residual and orthogonality bounds are hypotheses, not conclusions about every numerical QR run.

For real full-column-rank A and real b, put x=(A^* A)^(-1) A^* b, r=b-Ax, and A_dagger=(A^* A)^(-1) A^*. The least-squares solution map (A,b)↦x is Frechet differentiable on the full-column-rank domain, and its derivative in every matrix/vector direction (E,f) is A_dagger(f-Ex)+(A^* A)^(-1) E^* r. This includes the residual term for inconsistent systems; that term vanishes when r=0.

For an arbitrary real or complex matrix with an exact SVD, define its pseudoinverse action by A_dagger b=sum_{sigma_i>0} sigma_i^(-1) v_i(u_i^* b), where v_i and u_i are the orthonormal right and left singular vectors for positive sigma_i. The empty sum in rank zero is zero. This is the pseudoinverse intended in W35; in full column rank it agrees with the formula in W34.

For every real or complex matrix A and target vector b, with no rank assumption, the full set of Euclidean least-squares minimizers is A_dagger b+ker A. Among all such minimizers A_dagger b is the unique vector of minimum Euclidean norm, including the rank-zero case.
Bibliographical context for Householder error analysis, least-squares sensitivity, and the exact rank-deficient formula; no additional assertion.

Chapter 5 works over C, with real versions when data and asserted decompositions are real, and uses Euclidean operator/Frobenius norms. It cites the established orthonormal spectral theorems for Hermitian/normal matrices and finite SVD as inputs, rather than requiring their particular prior proofs.

For A:K^n→K^m, right singular vectors form an orthonormal basis obtained from A^* A; the singular values are listed in nonincreasing order and padded with zeros beyond the positive rank (including all right-kernel directions and additional zero indices). Eigenvalues of an n-by-n Hermitian matrix are listed in nondecreasing order. These are the ordering/padding conventions used by W36–W45.

For an n-by-n Hermitian matrix A with eigenvalues lambda_1<=...<=lambda_n, set R_A(x)=x^* A x for ||x||_2=1. For each 1<=i<=n, lambda_i(A)=min_{dim S=i} max_{x∈S,||x||_2=1} R_A(x)=max_{dim S=n-i+1} min_{x∈S,||x||_2=1} R_A(x). The extrema over unit vectors in each subspace and the outer extrema are attained; repeated eigenvalues do not require simple spectrum. For n=0 there are no indices.
For same-size Hermitian matrices A and E and every eigenvalue index i, using their nondecreasing order, |lambda_i(A+E)-lambda_i(A)|<=||E||_2. No eigenvalue simplicity or gap is assumed.

Every eigenvalue lambda of every complex square matrix A belongs to at least one row Gershgorin disk: |lambda-a_ii|<=sum_{j≠i}|a_ij| for some i. It also belongs to at least one column disk with center a_jj and radius sum_{i≠j}|a_ij|. No Hermitian, diagonalizable, or irreducibility hypothesis is needed.

If A is Hermitian, v is any unit vector, and mu is real, then dist(mu,spectrum A)<=||(A-mu I)v||_2. Thus a nonzero-dimensional test vector supplies a spectral-distance certificate without assuming that v is an approximate vector for a simple eigenvalue.

Let A be Hermitian, ||v||_2=1, mu∈R, and P be the orthogonal projection onto the joint eigenspaces of any selected group of eigenvalues. If every eigenvalue outside that group has distance at least delta>0 from mu, then ||(I-P)v||_2<=||(A-mu I)v||_2/delta. Multiplicities are included through whole eigenspaces, and no gap inside the selected group is required.
References for the variational, perturbation, Gershgorin, and residual comparisons and the existing row-disk implementation; no additional theorem.

Under the same diagonalization and perturbed-eigenvalue hypotheses, if the chosen subordinate norm satisfies ||diag(d_i)||=max_i|d_i|, then min_i|mu-lambda_i|<=||V|| ||V^(-1)|| ||E||. This includes mu already in spectrum A, where the left side is zero. The diagonal-norm hypothesis holds for every subordinate l_p norm, 1<=p<=infinity.

Let a complex square A have a diagonalization A=V Lambda V^(-1) with V invertible and Lambda diagonal, and let mu be an eigenvalue of A+E. For any subordinate matrix norm, if mu is not in spectrum A, then 1<=||(mu I-Lambda)^(-1)|| · ||V^(-1) E V||. This assertion requires no special norm property for diagonal matrices.

The diagonal-norm hypothesis in W39 cannot be omitted. For M>2, set A=diag(0,1), S=[[1,M],[0,1]], and choose E by SES^(-1)=[[0,0],[1/M,0]]. Use the vector norm ||x||=||Sx||_infinity and its subordinate matrix norm. Then ||E||=1/M and A can be diagonalized with V=I of norm condition number one, but S(A+E)S^(-1)=[[0,M],[1/M,1]] has eigenvalues (1±sqrt(5))/2, each at distance (sqrt(5)-1)/2>1/M from {0,1}. Thus the usual spectral-distance Bauer–Fike bound fails for this arbitrary subordinate norm, while W39's resolvent inequality remains valid.

For same-size real or complex rectangular matrices A and A+E and every singular-value index i, with singular values in nonincreasing order and padded by zeros as specified, |sigma_i(A+E)-sigma_i(A)|<=||E||_2. This includes rank deficiency, zero right dimension, and indices beyond the right-space dimension (both values then zero).

For every real or complex rectangular A and every integer k>=0, its SVD truncated after its first k singular terms has rank at most k and minimizes ||A-B||_2 over all B of rank at most k. The minimum equals sigma_{k+1}(A), with zero padding; when k>=rank A the truncation is A and the minimum is zero. Empty and rank-zero matrices are included.

For the same real or complex rectangular A and every integer k>=0, the same first-k-term SVD truncation minimizes ||A-B||_F over matrices of rank at most k, and the squared minimum equals sum_{i>k}sigma_i(A)^2. This includes k=0, k>=rank A, rank zero, and empty dimensions under the zero-padding convention.
References to SVD constructions and norm identities supporting W40–W42; no extra proof-route obligations.

For arbitrary normal complex n-by-n matrices A,B with eigenvalue lists lambda_i,mu_i (including algebraic multiplicities), there exists a permutation pi with sum_i|lambda_i-mu_{pi(i)}|^2<=||A-B||_F^2. No common eigenbasis or normality of A-B is required. The empty case uses the empty permutation/sum.

For same-size Hermitian A,B the Hoffman–Wielandt inequality can use the increasing eigenvalue pairing directly: sum_i|lambda_i(A)-lambda_i(B)|^2<=||A-B||_F^2. Repeated eigenvalues and ties are included.

For all same-size real or complex rectangular A,B, singular values in the prescribed nonincreasing order and padded by zero satisfy sum_i(sigma_i(A)-sigma_i(B))^2<=||A-B||_F^2. No rank equality is assumed; empty dimensions are allowed.
Classical references for the Hoffman–Wielandt and Mirsky inequalities; no new mathematical result.

Let A be diagonalizable over the chapter's scalar field, and let lambda_1≠0 be a distinct eigenvalue whose modulus is strictly larger than the modulus of every other distinct eigenvalue. Let p_1 be the spectral component of x_0 in its entire eigenspace and assume p_1≠0. Then A^j x_0≠0 for every j>=0, and z_j=A^j x_0/||A^j x_0||_2 has phase-corrected directions (|lambda_1|/lambda_1)^j z_j converging to p_1/||p_1||_2 with error O(r^j), where r=max_{lambda≠lambda_1}|lambda/lambda_1|<1 and max(empty)=0. The estimate can be read for j>=1; if all other eigenvalues are zero the first and later corrected iterates are exact. A multiple-dimensional dominant eigenspace is allowed; over R the correction is a sign.

Let A be diagonalizable and mu not in spectrum A. Suppose one distinct eigenvalue lambda_1 uniquely minimizes |lambda-mu| and x_0 has nonzero spectral component p_1 in its eigenspace. Exact iterations solving (A-mu I)y=x followed by normalization are defined and converge in direction to p_1. With beta_1=(lambda_1-mu)^(-1), multiply the j-th unit direction by (|beta_1|/beta_1)^j to obtain convergence to p_1/||p_1||_2 at error O(r^j), r=max_{lambda≠lambda_1}|lambda_1-mu|/|lambda-mu|<1, with empty maximum zero. If A has a single distinct eigenvalue the directions are already exact up to phase. The iteration uses exact solves.

For a field K and n>=0, P_n(K) is the vector space of polynomials over K of degree at most n, including the zero polynomial. Over R, on a specified interval these are also viewed as polynomial functions restricted to that interval. Ordinary interpolation uses distinct nodes; repeated nodes are used for higher-order data.

For pairwise distinct x_0,...,x_n in any field K and arbitrary y_0,...,y_n in K, define ell_i(X)=product_{j≠i}(X-x_j)/(x_i-x_j) and p(X)=sum_{i=0}^n y_i ell_i(X). All denominators are nonzero, ell_i∈P_n(K), ell_i(x_j)=delta_ij, and p∈P_n(K) satisfies p(x_i)=y_i. For singleton data ell_0=1; for empty data the empty interpolation sum is the zero polynomial.

Over any field K, arbitrary data at n+1 distinct nodes have exactly one interpolating polynomial in P_n(K); their Lagrange cardinal polynomials ell_i form the basis dual to evaluation at the nodes. The n=0 singleton case is included. Empty data alone do not give uniqueness in P_n(K) for n>=0.
References to ordinary distinct-node interpolation and the fixed Mathlib Lagrange construction, evaluation, and degree lemmas; no additional assertion.

For field-valued data at pairwise distinct nodes, define a divided difference for every nonempty ordered sublist by f[x_i]=y_i and f[x_i,...,x_j]=(f[x_{i+1},...,x_j]-f[x_i,...,x_{j-1}])/(x_j-x_i). The divided difference on a list of r nodes equals the coefficient of X^(r-1) in its degree-<=r-1 interpolation polynomial, even when the actual degree is smaller, and is invariant under permutations of the node-value pairs.

For the original ordered n+1 pairwise distinct field nodes, let c_k=f[x_0,...,x_k]. The unique interpolant is p(X)=sum_{k=0}^n c_k product_{j=0}^{k-1}(X-x_j), with the empty product for k=0 equal to 1. This is valid for n=0 as well as higher degrees.

The Newton interpolant can be evaluated at any field element x by starting r=c_n and, for k=n-1,...,0, replacing r with c_k+(x-x_k)r. The resulting r equals p(x); for singleton data no replacements are needed.

For n+1 pairwise distinct field nodes and their data, define omega(X)=product_j(X-x_j) and nonzero weights w_i=1/product_{j≠i}(x_i-x_j). At any non-node x the exact interpolant satisfies p(x)=omega(x) sum_i w_i y_i/(x-x_i)=[sum_i w_i y_i/(x-x_i)]/[sum_i w_i/(x-x_i)], and the second denominator is nonzero. At node x_i the prescribed value is y_i. The identities include singleton data.

The source notes that floating-point barycentric analysis additionally requires error bounds on computed nodes and weights, and gives a bibliographic reference. No such rounded-error theorem is stated here.

The C^r[a,b] convention means continuous derivatives through order r on the closed interval, with the usual one-sided interpretation at its endpoints. Interval Rolle's theorem is cited as an established real-analysis input.

Let g∈C^(N-1)[a,b]. Let t_1<...<t_s be distinct marked points in [a,b], with s>=1 and positive integer multiplicities m_i having sum N. If g^(j)(t_i)=0 for every i and every 0<=j<m_i, then some xi∈[t_1,t_s] satisfies g^(N-1)(xi)=0. This includes N=1 and a single marked point, for which the closed hull may be a singleton.

For distinct nodes x_0,...,x_n in a real interval I, any other point x∈I (possibly a node), f∈C^(n+1)(I), and the degree-<=n interpolant p of f(x_i), there is xi in the closed convex hull of x,x_0,...,x_n such that f(x)-p(x)=f^(n+1)(xi)/(n+1)! · product_{i=0}^n(x-x_i). Endpoint smoothness uses the stated one-sided convention. Node evaluation and singleton data are included; the interval need not be enlarged beyond the closed hull.

Let s>=1, x_1,...,x_s be pairwise distinct nodes of any field K, and m_i>=1 integers, with N=sum_i m_i. For each i prescribe an arbitrary polynomial residue class modulo (X-x_i)^(m_i). There exists exactly one representative p of degree <N satisfying all those residues. The algebraic statement is valid in arbitrary characteristic: its data are residue classes, not ordinary derivatives divided by factorials.

For real nodes x_1,...,x_s in an interval I, positive multiplicities m_i and N=sum_i m_i, and f∈C^N(I), prescribe at x_i the Taylor-polynomial residue through degree m_i-1. The unique degree-<N Hermite interpolant p then satisfies p^(j)(x_i)=f^(j)(x_i) for 0<=j<m_i. At every x∈I there exists xi in the closed hull of the nodes and x with f(x)-p(x)=f^(N)(xi)/N! · product_{i=1}^s(x-x_i)^(m_i). The equation includes x equal to a node and arbitrary repeated-data multiplicities, with closed-interval/one-sided endpoint smoothness as specified.

For a<b and n+1 distinct nodes in [a,b], define I_n:C[a,b]→P_n(R) by interpolation, with uniform norms, and define the Lebesgue constant Lambda_n=max_{x∈[a,b]}sum_{i=0}^n|ell_i(x)|. The maximum exists and the bounded linear interpolation operator has exact norm ||I_n||=Lambda_n.

With the same nondegenerate compact interval, distinct-node interpolation I_n, and Lebesgue constant Lambda_n, every continuous real f satisfies ||f-I_n f||_infinity <= (1+Lambda_n) inf_{p∈P_n(R)}||f-p||_infinity. The infimum is over all polynomials of degree at most n, not only over interpolants.

At the m=n+1 roots cos((j+1/2)pi/m) of T_m, the interpolation Lebesgue constants obey Lambda_n=O(1+log(n+1)) with an absolute constant, uniformly for all n>=0. Affine images of these nodes on every fixed nondegenerate compact interval have the same Lebesgue constant and hence the same bound.

For each integer m>=1, let T_m be the Chebyshev polynomial defined by T_m(cos theta)=cos(m theta). The unique monic polynomial of degree m minimizing uniform norm on [-1,1] is 2^(1-m) T_m, with minimum norm 2^(1-m); its m distinct roots are cos(theta_j), theta_j=(j+1/2)pi/m for 0<=j<m. This includes m=1 and asserts uniqueness, not merely existence of a minimizer.

For every a<b and m>=1, the affine Chebyshev-root nodes x_j=(a+b)/2+(b-a)cos((j+1/2)pi/m)/2 have the unique minimax monic nodal polynomial on [a,b]. Explicitly it is ((b-a)/2)^m · 2^(1-m) T_m((2X-a-b)/(b-a)), of degree m and uniform norm ((b-a)/2)^m · 2^(1-m). The affine change preserves cardinal values and the Lebesgue constant.

On any fixed compact nondegenerate real interval, Chebyshev-root interpolants (and the affine images just specified) converge uniformly to every Holder-continuous real function f as n→infinity. In the proof's smoothness convention, f satisfies |f(t)-f(s)|<=L|t-s|^alpha for some L>=0 and 0<alpha<=1.

For n>=2 and the n+1 equally spaced nodes including both endpoints of any fixed nondegenerate compact interval [a,b], a<b, the Lebesgue constant satisfies Lambda_n>=2^n/[2n(n+1)^2]. The bound is independent of the affine interval scaling.

On every fixed nondegenerate compact real interval there exists a single continuous real function f whose interpolation polynomials at the equally spaced n+1 nodes including both endpoints have unbounded uniform norms as n varies. Equivalently sup_n||I_n f||_infinity=infinity. The function is common to the entire sequence, rather than a separately chosen worst-case datum for each n.

For a quadrature rule Q the error is the integral of f minus Q(f). For f on a compact interval, ‖f‖∞ is its uniform norm on that interval. Numerical differentiation distinguishes analytic stencil error from error in the sample values.

Peano kernel representation, including its kernel construction: Let a<b, integer r≥2, and E:C[a,b]→ℝ be a bounded linear functional that annihilates every polynomial of degree <r. Define u₊=max(u,0) and K(t)=E(x↦(x−t)₊^(r−1)/(r−1)!) for a≤t≤b. Then K is continuous. For every f∈C^r[a,b], E(f)=∫_a^b f^(r)(t)K(t)dt and |E(f)|≤‖f^(r)‖∞∫_a^b|K(t)|dt. If K has a constant sign, ∫_a^b|K(t)|dt=|E(x↦x^r/r!)|.

For a<b, the functional f↦∫_a^b f(x)dx−∑_{i=1}^m w_i f(x_i), for any finite collection of real weights and nodes x_i∈[a,b], is bounded linear on C[a,b]. Thus, when it annihilates the requisite low-degree polynomials, the Peano representation applies.

Composite midpoint and trapezoidal constructions and errors: Let a<b, f∈C²[a,b], integer n≥1 and h=(b−a)/n. Add the ordinary midpoint and trapezoidal rules on the n equal subintervals to obtain M_n(f)=h∑_{j=0}^{n−1}f(a+(j+1/2)h) and T_n(f)=h(f(a)/2+∑_{j=1}^{n−1}f(a+jh)+f(b)/2), with the interior sum empty if n=1. Then |∫_a^b f−M_n(f)|≤(b−a)h²‖f″‖∞/24 and |∫_a^b f−T_n(f)|≤(b−a)h²‖f″‖∞/12.

Composite Simpson construction and error: Let a<b, f∈C⁴[a,b], n≥2 even and h=(b−a)/n. Define S_n by summing the three-node rule with weights h(1,4,1)/3 on successive disjoint panels [a+2jh,a+(2j+2)h] of length 2h. Then |∫_a^b f−S_n(f)|≤(b−a)h⁴‖f^(4)‖∞/180.
For a finite positive Borel measure μ on ℝ and integer n≥1, if ∫|x|^(2n)dμ<∞, then all moments of orders 0 through 2n exist absolutely.

In Gaussian quadrature μ is a finite positive Borel measure on ℝ concentrated on an interval. A finite moment of order 2n means ∫|x|^(2n)dμ<∞. Its closed support is the set of x such that every open neighborhood of x has positive μ-measure.
For the closed support of a finite positive Borel measure μ on ℝ, defined by positive measure of every open neighborhood, its complement has μ-measure zero.

For a finite positive Borel measure μ on ℝ concentrated on an interval, integer n≥1 and finite moment ∫|x|^(2n)dμ<∞, define G_n=(∫x^(i+j)dμ)_{0≤i,j≤n}. Then G_n is positive definite if and only if the closed support of μ contains at least n+1 distinct points. The equivalence includes measures of finite support and the zero measure.

For a finite positive Borel measure μ on ℝ concentrated on an interval, integer n≥1, finite 2n-th absolute moment, and positive definite Gram matrix G_n=(∫x^(i+j)dμ)_{0≤i,j≤n} (equivalently support with at least n+1 points), there exists a unique monic polynomial π_n of degree n such that ∫π_n p dμ=0 for every real polynomial p of degree <n. It has n distinct real roots x₁,…,x_n strictly between the infimum and supremum of the support, allowing unbounded support and interpreting the extremes in the extended real sense.

Under the W58 hypotheses (μ finite positive Borel on ℝ concentrated on an interval, n≥1, finite 2n-th absolute moment and G_n positive definite), the n distinct roots x_i of the unique degree-n monic orthogonal polynomial π_n admit weights w_i>0 such that ∫p dμ=∑_{i=1}^n w_i p(x_i) for every real polynomial of degree ≤2n−1.

Under the W58 hypotheses (μ finite positive Borel on ℝ concentrated on an interval, n≥1, finite 2n-th absolute moment and G_n positive definite), no deterministic point-evaluation rule using at most n queried values of its input can be exact for the μ-integral of every real polynomial of degree ≤2n. This includes rules that choose their query points adaptively from earlier returned values, as clarified by the zero-data-path argument at lines 2267–2273.

References identify the construction as general orthogonal-polynomial Gaussian quadrature and explain that degree-n nondegeneracy is what supports the stated exactness limit; no additional mathematical conclusion beyond W58 is imposed here.

Under the W58 hypotheses (μ finite positive Borel on ℝ, n≥1, finite 2n-th absolute moment, positive definite G_n and its Gaussian nodes x_i, weights w_i and monic polynomial π_n), additionally assume supp μ⊆[a,b] and f∈C^(2n)[a,b]. For Q_n(f)=∑_{i=1}^n w_i f(x_i), |∫f dμ−Q_n(f)|≤‖f^(2n)‖∞∫π_n²dμ/(2n)!. In fact there exists ξ∈[a,b] such that ∫f dμ−Q_n(f)=f^(2n)(ξ)∫π_n²dμ/(2n)!.

Under the W58 moment and Gram hypotheses alone (μ finite positive Borel on ℝ concentrated on an interval, n≥1, finite 2n-th absolute moment, positive definite G_n), let p₀,…,p_n be the orthonormal real polynomials of degrees 0,…,n with positive leading coefficients. Define the order-n Jacobi matrix in the basis p₀,…,p_{n−1} to represent multiplication by x followed by orthogonal projection onto their span. This real matrix is symmetric and tridiagonal, with positive subdiagonal entries wherever present (none when n=1). Its eigenvalues are precisely the Gaussian nodes x_i. For any unit eigenvector v_i for x_i, indexing coordinates from zero, w_i=μ(ℝ)|(v_i)₀|². Compact support and smoothness of a function f are not hypotheses of these matrix conclusions.

Fix x∈ℝ and h>0. Let sample values y(x−h),y(x+h) satisfy |y(t)−f(t)|≤η at the two stencil points. If f∈C³[x−h,x+h] and M₃=sup_{[x−h,x+h]}|f‴|, then |(y(x+h)−y(x−h))/(2h)−f′(x)|≤M₃h²/6+η/h. Subtraction and division of the sample values are exact.

Fix x∈ℝ and h>0. Let sample values y(x),y(x+h) satisfy |y(t)−f(t)|≤η at both stencil points. If f∈C²[x,x+h] and M₂=sup_{[x,x+h]}|f″|, then |(y(x+h)−y(x))/h−f′(x)|≤M₂h/2+2η/h. Subtraction and division of the sample values are exact.

Take an allowed upper step H>0 and bounds M₂,M₃,η≥0 independent of h on 0<h≤H, using derivative bounds over the entire allowed neighborhood and a uniform sample-error bound. If M₃,η>0, the central error bound B_c(h)=M₃h²/6+η/h has its unconstrained minimum at (3η/M₃)^(1/3), and its minimum over 0<h≤H occurs at min(H,(3η/M₃)^(1/3)). If M₂,η>0, the forward bound B_f(h)=M₂h/2+2η/h similarly minimizes at min(H,(4η/M₂)^(1/2)). For either bound, if η>0 and its derivative coefficient is zero, it decreases up to H; if η=0 and its derivative coefficient is positive, it tends to zero as h↓0; and if both coefficients vanish, the bound is identically zero.

If forming a stencil includes rounded subtraction or division, Chapter 1 supplies an additional arithmetic error beyond the sample-value error budget; this is an applicability caveat, not a new quantified rounding estimate here.

One-step Richardson construction and bounds: Suppose A(h)=A+c h^p+O(h^(p+q)) as h↓0, with p,q>0 and fixed λ>1. Define R(h)=(λ^p A(h/λ)−A(h))/(λ^p−1). Then R(h)=A+O(h^(p+q)). If the two values used at h/λ and h have absolute data errors bounded by δ_{h/λ} and δ_h, the exact-arithmetic extrapolated combination has an additional absolute error at most (λ^p δ_{h/λ}+δ_h)/(λ^p−1).

For the central derivative stencil A(h)=(f(x+h)−f(x−h))/(2h) on exact data with f∈C⁵ on a neighborhood of the stencil point, Richardson extrapolation with p=2 and λ=2 gives the derivative formula (4A(h/2)−A(h))/3 with error O(h⁴) as h decreases to zero.
Motivation and references distinguish residual and root error, geometric brackets and contraction-based certificates, and exact versus approximate evaluation.
Let a<b and f:[a,b]→ℝ be continuous. If f(a)f(b)≤0, then ∃x∈[a,b], f(x)=0. If both endpoint values are nonzero and of opposite signs, ∃x∈(a,b), f(x)=0.
The polynomial f(x)=x(x²−1) has opposite signs at −2 and 2, while its three roots −1,0,1 all lie in the bracket [−2,2]. Thus a sign bracket need not isolate a unique root.

Let a<b, f continuous on [a,b], and f(a)f(b)≤0. Set I₀=[a₀,b₀]=[a,b]. At each current bracket form its exact midpoint m_n=(a_n+b_n)/2; either return a known endpoint/midpoint root or keep a half interval with endpoint product ≤0. At every completed update I_{n+1}⊆I_n, the bracket condition f(a_n)f(b_n)≤0 holds, and b_n−a_n=2^(−n)(b−a). Every current midpoint lies within 2^(−n−1)(b−a) of some root in its own bracket. If updates continue indefinitely, both endpoint sequences and the midpoint sequence converge to one root x_*, and |m_n−x_*|≤2^(−n−1)(b−a) for every n. Endpoint zeros and midpoint zeros are allowed, including retained root endpoints.

For exact bisection on a<b with f continuous and f(a)f(b)≤0, and ε>0, at most N_ε=max(0,ceil(log₂((b−a)/(2ε)))) completed half-interval updates suffice for the current midpoint to certify absolute error ≤ε relative to a root in its bracket. The initial midpoint suffices when (b−a)/2≤ε. The final midpoint need not be evaluated when the bracket and midpoint constitute the desired certificate.

If an evaluation gives a certified enclosure [l,u] containing f(x), then l>0 implies f(x)>0, u<0 implies f(x)<0, and [l,u]=[0,0] implies f(x)=0. Strict-sign updates require a certified sign. If the enclosure contains zero and is not [0,0], that enclosure alone certifies neither a strict sign nor a root; retain the existing bracket while seeking a sharper enclosure. A fixed-format implementation also needs an interior representable update point.

For a verified root bracket [a′,b′] and a stored output z∈[a′,b′], every certified upper bound R on max(z−a′,b′−z) is a valid absolute root-error radius for z (relative to any root certified to lie in that bracket). The existing bracket remains a certificate if the exact midpoint is unrepresentable or a new sign cannot be certified. The exact bisection step count concerns completed exact halvings; directed rounding can establish the enclosure hypotheses using Chapter 1.

Let f be continuous on an initial strict sign bracket [a,b], a<b, and fix 0<α≤1/2. For [a_n,b_n] of width w_n, accept a proposed point from another method only when it belongs to [a_n+αw_n,b_n−αw_n], otherwise use the exact midpoint. Given a certified nonzero value sign, replace the endpoint of the same sign; return a certified root. Every successful update preserves the sign bracket and has w_{n+1}≤(1−α)w_n. An infinite run of successful updates converges to a root x_*, and its nth bracket midpoint obeys |m_n−x_*|≤(b−a)(1−α)^n/2. Undefined proposals may fall back to the midpoint. If sign certification or representation of an admissible point fails, retain the old bracket; the geometric count includes only successful updates.

Let (X,d) be a nonempty complete metric space and T:X→X satisfy d(Tx,Ty)≤q d(x,y) for all x,y∈X, with 0≤q<1. Then T has a unique fixed point p, and for every x₀∈X the exact iterates x_n=T^n(x₀) converge to p, including q=0.

Let D be a nonempty closed subset of a complete metric space. If T(D)⊆D and d(Tx,Ty)≤q d(x,y) for all x,y∈D, for some 0≤q<1, then T has a unique fixed point in D and its iterates from every point of D converge to that fixed point.

In one metric space, suppose T has fixed point p and satisfies d(Tx,Ty)≤q d(x,y) with 0≤q<1, and T̃ has fixed point p̃. If d(Tx,T̃x)≤δ for all x, then d(p,p̃)≤δ/(1−q). The weaker hypothesis d(Tp̃,T̃p̃)≤δ at p̃ alone suffices; no contraction or completeness assumption on T̃ is required once its fixed point exists.

Under Banach fixed-point hypotheses (nonempty complete metric X, T:X→X, 0≤q<1, and d(Tx,Ty)≤q d(x,y)), let p be the unique fixed point and x_n=T^n(x₀). For every n≥0, d(x_n,p)≤q^n d(x₁,x₀)/(1−q) and d(x_n,p)≤d(x_{n+1},x_n)/(1−q). These include q=0, using q⁰=1, and the case x₀=p.

For any x in a domain on which T is a contraction with factor 0≤q<1 and fixed point p in that domain, d(x,p)≤d(x,Tx)/(1−q). Any certified upper bound on d(x,Tx) may replace the exact residual. In particular, an upper bound ≤(1−q)ε certifies d(x,p)≤ε.

In the setting of Banach fixed-point iteration on a nonempty complete metric space, or its nonempty closed invariant contraction domain, let p be the fixed point and 0≤q<1 the contraction factor. Suppose x_j stays in that contraction domain and d(x_{j+1},Tx_j)≤δ_j for every j≥0. For every n≥0, d(x_n,p)≤q^n d(x₀,p)+∑_{j=0}^{n−1}q^(n−1−j)δ_j, with the sum empty at n=0 and exponent-zero value 1 also for q=0. If δ_j≤δ for all j, limsup_n d(x_n,p)≤δ/(1−q). If δ_j→0, then x_n→p, including q=0.

In a contraction domain, if y approximates Tx with certified d(y,Tx)≤δ_x, then d(x,Tx)≤d(x,y)+δ_x. Therefore an upper bound on d(x,y) plus δ_x is a valid residual bound for the fixed-point stopping certificate d(x,p)≤(d(x,y)+δ_x)/(1−q). Membership of computed iterates in the contraction domain remains a separate hypothesis.

Let x,x_* lie in a real interval, f(x_*)=0, f continuous on the closed segment between x and x_*, differentiable in its interior, and |f′(t)|≥m>0 there. Then |x−x_*|≤|f(x)|/m, including x=x_*. A verified lower slope bound on a whole certified bracket containing x and a root suffices even if the root location is unknown.
For f(x)=x² with root x_*=0, the residual |f(x)| equals the square of the root error |x|. Consequently no constant C gives |x|≤C|f(x)| throughout a neighborhood of zero.

For σ>0, f_σ(x)=σx has a simple root at zero, residual |f_σ(1)|=σ and root error 1 at x=1. Thus no function-independent linear inverse-residual bound, or inference of small root error from residual size alone, is possible even for simple roots.
Local Newton results presuppose an existing root; semilocal results instead use starting-point data and bounds on a specified ball to certify both existence and convergence.

Let f be real and C² on a neighborhood of [x_*−R,x_*+R], with R>0 and f(x_*)=0. On this interval assume |f′|≥m>0 and |f″|≤M. Choose 0<r≤R with Mr/(2m)<1. For every |x₀−x_*|≤r, the exact Newton sequence x_{n+1}=x_n−f(x_n)/f′(x_n) is well defined, stays in [x_*−r,x_*+r], converges to x_*, and, with e_n=x_n−x_*, satisfies |e_{n+1}|≤M|e_n|²/(2m). When M=0 one step reaches the root; a reached root remains fixed.

Near x_*, assume f(x)=(x−x_*)^m g(x), where integer m≥2, g∈C² and g(x_*)≠0. For e=x−x_*, ordinary Newton is defined away from the root in some sufficiently small neighborhood and has e_new=(1−1/m)e+O(e²). The multiplicity-corrected step x−m f(x)/f′(x) has e_new=O(e²). Both iterations converge to x_* from a sufficiently small neighborhood, with an iterate at the root treated as a successful stop. In a nonterminating ordinary Newton run, |e_{n+1}|/|e_n|→1−1/m.

Let f be real C² near a simple root x_* (f(x_*)=0 and f′(x_*)≠0). For every pair of distinct starting points x₀,x₁ sufficiently close to x_*, stop when any root is encountered; otherwise the exact secant iterates x_{n+1}=x_n−f(x_n)/f[x_{n−1},x_n] for n≥1 are well defined and converge to x_*. Here f[u,v]=(f(v)−f(u))/(v−u). If the run does not terminate and f″(x_*)≠0, write e_n=x_n−x_*, φ=(1+√5)/2 and C=|f″(x_*)/(2f′(x_*))|. Then lim_n |e_{n+1}|/|e_n|^φ=C^(1/φ)>0.

Banach-space Newton derivatives are Fréchet derivatives; for complex spaces the line-segment parameter used in the estimates is real. Every ball on which derivative estimates are assumed is contained in an open domain of differentiability.

Let X,Y be Banach spaces (real or complex, with real line segments), U⊆X open and F:U→Y differentiable. If D⊆U is convex and F′ is Lipschitz with constant L on D, then for all x,y∈D, ‖F(y)−F(x)−F′(x)(y−x)‖≤(L/2)‖y−x‖².

Let X,Y be Banach spaces, U⊆X open and F:U→Y differentiable. Assume F(x_*)=0, F′(x_*):X→Y is a bounded isomorphism, and F′ is Lipschitz with constant L on the closed ball B̄(x_*,R)⊆U. Put b=‖F′(x_*)⁻¹‖. For every 0<r≤R satisfying bLr<1 and bLr/[2(1−bLr)]<1, Newton iteration x_{n+1}=x_n−F′(x_n)⁻¹F(x_n) from every x₀∈B̄(x_*,r) is well defined, remains in that ball, converges to x_*, and obeys ‖x_{n+1}−x_*‖≤bL‖x_n−x_*‖²/[2(1−bLr)]. In particular L=0 yields one-step convergence. Derivatives are Fréchet derivatives, with real segment parameters also for complex Banach spaces.

Newton–Kantorovich, including scalar majorant construction and critical case: Let X,Y be Banach spaces, U⊆X open, F:U→Y differentiable, x₀∈U and F′(x₀) a bounded isomorphism. Put B=F′(x₀)⁻¹. Suppose η,L>0 and 2ηL≤1. Set D=√(1−2ηL), t_*=(1−D)/L, t_**=(1+D)/L, and assume B̄(x₀,t_*)⊆U, ‖BF(x₀)‖≤η, and ‖B(F′(x)−F′(y))‖≤L‖x−y‖ for all x,y in that closed ball. Define m(t)=η−t+(L/2)t², t₀=0 and t_{n+1}=t_n−m(t_n)/m′(t_n). Then the Newton sequence x_{n+1}=x_n−F′(x_n)⁻¹F(x_n) is well defined for every n, ‖x_n−x₀‖≤t_n<t_*, and it converges to the unique zero x_* of F in B̄(x₀,t_*). For every n≥0, ‖x_{n+1}−x_n‖≤t_{n+1}−t_n, ‖x_*−x_n‖≤t_*−t_n, and ‖x_*−x_{n+1}‖≤(1/2)‖x_*−x_n‖. All these conclusions include the critical equality 2ηL=1, without requiring invertibility of F′ at the limiting root.

In the full semilocal setting of W77 (Banach X,Y; open U; differentiable F; invertible F′(x₀), B=F′(x₀)⁻¹; η,L>0; ‖BF(x₀)‖≤η; normalized derivative Lipschitz bound ‖B(F′(x)−F′(y))‖≤L‖x−y‖ on B̄(x₀,t_*)⊆U), assume strictly 2ηL<1 and put D=√(1−2ηL), t_*=(1−D)/L, t_**=(1+D)/L. Then the Newton limit x_* obeys ‖x_*−x_{n+1}‖≤L‖x_*−x_n‖²/(2D) for every n. If the domain inclusion and normalized derivative bound extend to B̄(x₀,ρ) for t_*≤ρ<t_**, the same zero x_* is unique in that larger closed ball.

For η,L>0 with 2ηL=1, the scalar quadratic F(t)=η−t+(L/2)t² has a double zero at t_*=(1−√(1−2ηL))/L=1/L. Starting Newton at t₀=0, the error to t_* halves at each step. Thus the critical W77 conclusions apply even though the derivative vanishes at the limiting root.

For η,L>0 with 2ηL<1, the scalar quadratic F(t)=η−t+(L/2)t² has distinct zeros t_*=(1−√(1−2ηL))/L and t_**=(1+√(1−2ηL))/L. Hence W77 cannot in general assert uniqueness on a closed ball of radius t_**; the strict upper radius bound ρ<t_** is necessary.

In the semilocal setting (differentiable F on open U in Banach X with values in Banach Y, x₀∈U, bounded isomorphism F′(x₀) and B=F′(x₀)⁻¹), if the residual bound is η=0, i.e. ‖BF(x₀)‖≤0, then F(x₀)=0 and its certified existence radius is zero. This is the degenerate residual case, not an application assuming η>0.

In the semilocal setting with η≥0, F differentiable on open U⊆X between Banach spaces, x₀∈U, bounded isomorphism F′(x₀), B=F′(x₀)⁻¹, and ‖BF(x₀)‖≤η, assume the closed ball B̄(x₀,η) lies in U and the normalized derivative bound ‖B(F′(x)−F′(y))‖≤0 holds for all x,y in that ball (L=0). A single Newton step from x₀ gives a zero in that ball, and this zero is unique there, including η=0.

For L>0, η≥0 and 0≤2ηL≤1, the semilocal radius t_*=(1−√(1−2ηL))/L equals 2η/[1+√(1−2ηL)]. The latter expression has continuous extension to L=0 with value η, and avoids subtracting nearly equal numbers. Computed numerical data and radii still require certified bounds.
