The agreed domain-space singular-value minmax formula sigma_i=min_{dim S=n-i+1} max_{x in S,||x||=1}||Ax|| for 1<=i<=n, with attained extrema and all right-kernel directions.
For n>=1 and alpha-Holder real f on [0,1], ||B_n f-f||_infinity<=L*(4n)^(-alpha/2); affine transport to [a,b] multiplies L by (b-a)^alpha.
For n>=1, Holder data on [a,b] have Chebyshev interpolation error <=(1+Lambda_n)*L*(b-a)^alpha*(4n)^(-alpha/2), hence O((1+log(n+1))*n^(-alpha/2)).

Document setup, title, table of contents, scope and global conventions. The required scope is discrete time starting at 0; countable discrete-state chains; and real martingales/submartingales, with Bochner Banach values only for UI/Vitali. All conditional statements are almost sure. The terminal sigma-algebra is generated by the increasing filtration union, stopping times may be infinite only with the stopped-value conventions specified in the applicable results, transition laws act as row vectors, and total variation is the supremum over events. Continuous time, general-state Harris recurrence, scaling limits and martingale CLTs are outside scope. Cited measure/integration, conditional-expectation, path-extension, strong-law and spectral-theorem foundations are prerequisites, not new independent results of this manuscript.

Time is N₀={0,1,...}. For an increasing filtration, its terminal sigma-algebra is generated by its union. Stopping times may equal infinity, and any process value there must be specified separately. Conditional equalities and inequalities are almost sure. Countable state spaces have their full discrete sigma-algebra; stochastic matrices use the current state as row index and laws act as row vectors. Total variation is sup_A |mu(A)-nu(A)|; Lᵖ norms use the probability measure in the statement.

On a probability space (Omega,F,P), a filtration (F_n) indexed by n∈N₀ is an increasing sequence of sub-sigma-algebras of F. A process X is adapted when X_n is F_n-measurable for every n. Its natural filtration at n is sigma(X_0,...,X_n), and F_infinity=sigma(union_n F_n).

Conditional expectation E[Y|G] for integrable Y, its test-event identity, linearity, positivity, tower property, and bounded G-measurable pullout rule are explicitly imported prerequisite interfaces from P1-05; the footnote gives provenance rather than a new independent theorem.

For a countable family of almost-sure conditional equalities or inequalities, there is one event of probability one on which all those relations hold simultaneously (remove the countable union of exceptional null sets).
A real adapted process X with E|X_n|<infinity for every n is a martingale if E[X_{n+1}|F_n]=X_n almost surely for every n, and is a submartingale if E[X_{n+1}|F_n]≥X_n almost surely for every n.

For a real adapted process integrable at every time, the one-step martingale equality is equivalent to E[X_j|F_i]=X_i almost surely for every i≤j. The one-step submartingale inequality is equivalent to E[X_j|F_i]≥X_i almost surely for every i≤j, including i=j.

If for every k≥1 the real xi_k is integrable and F_k-measurable, has E xi_k=0, and is independent of F_{k-1}, then M_n=sum_{k=1}^n xi_k (empty sum M_0=0) is a martingale relative to (F_n). Mutual independence of all increments is not an extra assumption.
For every real Y∈L¹ on the probability space, M_n=E[Y|F_n] is a martingale relative to the filtration (F_n).
Textbook terminology, provenance or comparison for filtrations and martingales; no additional mathematical statement is introduced.

A stopping time is tau:Omega→N₀∪{infinity} with {tau≤n}∈F_n for every finite n. Its stopped sigma-algebra is F_tau={A∈F_infinity : A∩{tau≤n}∈F_n for every finite n}. The stopped process is X^tau_n=X_{min(n,tau)}. X_tau equals X_n on {tau=n}; its value on {tau=infinity} is prescribed separately whenever a random variable on all Omega is needed.

For every stopping time tau, F_tau as defined using ambient F_infinity is a sigma-algebra. For A∈F_infinity, A∈F_tau iff A∩{tau=n}∈F_n for every finite n. For pointwise ordered stopping times sigma≤tau, F_sigma⊆F_tau.
If X is adapted and tau is any possibly infinite stopping time, X^tau is adapted. If each X_n is integrable, each finite-time stopped value X^tau_n is integrable.

For an adapted process X, a stopping time tau, and an F_infinity-measurable random variable Y of the same state type, the full-space value equal to X_n on each {tau=n} and equal to Y on {tau=infinity} is F_tau-measurable. In the manuscript proof state measurability is expressed by Borel inverse images.
For every stopping time tau, {tau<infinity} belongs to F_tau. For the constant stopping time tau=n with n finite, the stopped sigma-algebra F_tau is exactly F_n.
Textbook terminology, provenance or comparison for stopping-time sigma-algebras; no additional mathematical statement is introduced.

For a real process X put Delta X_k=X_{k+1}-X_k. A coefficient H_k used on this increment is predictable when H_k is F_k-measurable. For a predictable real sequence H, its time-n gain is (H·X)_n=sum_{k=0}^{n-1} H_k Delta X_k, with value zero at n=0.

For a real martingale X and predictable real H, the transform H·X is a martingale if every H_k is bounded (a separate bound may depend on k). The same conclusion holds for finite real H_k without boundedness when each individual product H_k Delta X_k is integrable.

For a real submartingale X and predictable nonnegative H_k, the transform H·X is a submartingale if every H_k is bounded. The same conclusion holds for nonnegative finite real H_k without boundedness when each product H_k Delta X_k is integrable.

Every integrable real adapted process X admits X_n=M_n+A_n for all n, where M is a martingale, A_0=0, every A_n is integrable, and A_{n+1} is F_n-measurable for every n. Such a decomposition is unique up to almost-sure equality at every time. Moreover X is a submartingale iff A is almost surely nondecreasing. The proof-specific formula for A is a witness, not a separately required result.
Textbook terminology, provenance or comparison for predictable transforms and Doob decomposition; no additional mathematical statement is introduced.

For any possibly infinite stopping time tau, if X is a martingale then X^tau is a martingale, and if X is a submartingale then X^tau is a submartingale. The evaluation min(n,tau) is finite at each process time n; no terminal-value assumption or bound on tau is required.

Let S be any nonempty countable set with its full sigma-algebra. Delta_ij is 1_{i=j}. A stochastic matrix P has nonnegative entries P_ij and sum_j P_ij=1 for every i. For A⊆S set P(i,A)=sum_{j∈A}P_ij; for nonnegative f set (Pf)(i)=sum_j P_ij f(j), using 0·infinity=0 in extended nonnegative sums. Matrix multiplication is (PQ)_ij=sum_x P_ix Q_xj.
For stochastic matrices on a nonempty countable set, the countably summed product PQ is again stochastic, and this matrix multiplication is associative.
Define P⁰=I=(Delta_ij), P^{m+1}=P^m P for m≥0. For a probability law lambda on S, lambda P^m is a probability law with masses (lambda P^m)_j=sum_i lambda_i (P^m)_ij. These constructions include m=0.

A time-homogeneous P-Markov chain with initial law lambda relative to a specified filtration (F_n) is an S-valued adapted process (X_n)_{n≥0} such that P(X_0=i)=lambda_i and E[1_{X_{n+1}=j}|F_n]=P_{X_n,j} almost surely for every n≥0,j∈S. Its natural filtration is sigma(X_0,...,X_n). A larger filtration is permitted only when this one-step identity holds for that filtration; all subsequent conditional identities refer to a filtration with respect to which the chain is Markov.

For a P-Markov chain with initial law lambda relative to (F_n), every m,n≥0 and every A⊆S satisfy E[1_{X_{n+m}∈A}|F_n]=P^m(X_n,A) almost surely. In particular X_n has probability law lambda P^n for every n≥0.
Textbook terminology, provenance or comparison for countable chain conventions; no additional mathematical statement is introduced.

The canonical path space S^{N₀} has its product sigma-algebra. P_lambda denotes the Markov path law with initial distribution lambda and transition matrix P; P_i and E_i denote its probability and expectation when lambda is point mass at i.

For every stochastic P on nonempty countable S and every probability lambda on S, there exists a unique probability P_lambda on S^{N₀} with atomic prefix-cylinder probabilities P_lambda(X_0=i_0,...,X_n=i_n)=lambda_{i_0} product_{k=0}^{n-1}P_{i_k,i_{k+1}} for every n≥0 and every word i_0,...,i_n (empty product one at n=0). The coordinate process is P-Markov relative to its natural filtration. Every P-Markov chain with initial law lambda, on any probability space and any filtration satisfying the Markov assumption, has this same joint path law.
For all m,n≥0 and i,j∈S, (P^{m+n})_ij=sum_x (P^m)_ix (P^n)_xj, with the same countable stochastic-matrix powers including P⁰=I.
Textbook terminology, provenance or comparison for canonical Markov path laws; no additional mathematical statement is introduced.
For bounded product-measurable g:S^{N₀}→R, define G(i)=E_i[g(X_0,X_1,...)]. The function G:S→R is bounded and measurable.

Let X be a P-Markov chain relative to (F_n), let tau:Omega→N₀∪{infinity} be a stopping time, let g:S^{N₀}→R be bounded and measurable, and put G(i)=E_i g. For every A∈F_tau, integral_{A∩{tau<infinity}} g(X_tau,X_{tau+1},...) dP = integral_{A∩{tau<infinity}} G(X_tau) dP. In particular, if tau is finite almost surely, the conditional law of the shifted full path given F_tau is P_{X_tau}. For possibly infinite tau the identity is restricted to {tau<infinity}; it does not assume a future path at infinity.
Textbook terminology, provenance or comparison for finite stopping-time strong Markov property; no additional mathematical statement is introduced.

Let X be a P-Markov chain on nonempty countable S relative to (F_n), let tau:Omega→N₀∪{infinity} be a stopping time, let g:S^{N₀}→[0,infinity] be product-measurable, and set G(i)=E_i[g(X_0,X_1,...)]. For every A∈F_tau, integral_{A∩{tau<infinity}} g(X_tau,X_{tau+1},...) dP = integral_{A∩{tau<infinity}} G(X_tau) dP, with both integrals in the extended nonnegative reals. No value of the shifted path at an infinite stop is required.

For any subset A⊆S define T_A=inf{n≥0:X_n∈A}, with infimum infinity when the set is empty, h(i)=P_i(T_A<infinity), and u(i)=E_i T_A as an extended nonnegative expectation. First hits include time zero.

For every subset A⊆S of a nonempty countable Markov state space, h(i)=P_i(T_A<infinity) satisfies h=1 on A and h=Ph on S\A, and is the smallest nonnegative solution of these equations: every nonnegative function satisfying both boundary and harmonic equations dominates h pointwise. No boundedness assumption on competing nonnegative solutions is imposed in the source.

For every subset A⊆S, u(i)=E_i T_A is the smallest [0,infinity]-valued solution of u=0 on A and u=1+Pu on S\A. Thus u itself satisfies both equations in extended nonnegative arithmetic and is pointwise bounded above by every competing nonnegative extended solution.
The first-hit minimal-solution statements include A=emptyset. In this boundary case h(i)=0 and u(i)=infinity for every i∈S.
Communication defined by mutual accessibility is an equivalence relation on S, using accessibility at length zero and composition of positive finite-step transitions.

State j is accessible from i when (P^n)_ij>0 for some n≥0. States communicate when each is accessible from the other; their equivalence classes are communicating classes. The chain is irreducible when S is one communicating class. A class is closed when every one-step transition from a state in the class to a state outside it has probability zero.
For every i∈S, tau_i^+=inf{n≥1:X_n=i} is a stopping time relative to a filtration to which X is adapted; its finite cutoff at n is the union of the state events at times 1,...,n.

The first positive return to i is tau_i^+=inf{n≥1:X_n=i}, with value infinity if no positive return occurs. Put r_i=P_i(tau_i^+<infinity). State i is recurrent when r_i=1 and transient when r_i<1; it is positive recurrent when E_i tau_i^+<infinity, and is null recurrent when it is recurrent with E_i tau_i^+=infinity.
If E_i tau_i^+ is finite as an extended expectation, then P_i(tau_i^+<infinity)=1. Hence every positive recurrent state is recurrent; any positive mass at infinity forces infinite mean return time.
For a chain started at i, the number of visits including time zero is N_i=sum_{n≥0}1_{X_n=i}∈N∪{infinity}. For every integer k≥1, P_i(N_i≥k)=r_i^{k-1}, with r_i⁰=1, including r_i=0 and k=1.

For a chain started at i, sum_{n≥0}(P^n)_ii=E_i N_i, which equals 1/(1-r_i) when r_i<1 and infinity when r_i=1. In particular recurrence is equivalent to divergence of the diagonal Green series, and a recurrent state is visited infinitely often almost surely when the chain starts there.
Textbook terminology, provenance or comparison for Green criterion; no additional mathematical statement is introduced.
Fix i∈S and define p_n=(P^n)_ii for n≥0 and f_n=P_i(tau_i^+=n) for n≥1. Then p_0=1 and p_n=sum_{k=1}^n f_k p_{n-k} for every n≥1.

With p_n=(P^n)_ii and f_n=P_i(tau_i^+=n), define G(z)=sum_{n≥0}p_n z^n and F(z)=sum_{n≥1}f_n z^n for 0≤z<1. They satisfy G(z)=1/(1-F(z)), lim_{z↑1}F(z)=r_i, and lim_{z↑1}G(z)=sum_{n≥0}p_n, where the last limit and series may equal infinity.
Textbook terminology, provenance or comparison for first-return decomposition; no additional mathematical statement is introduced.
The period of i is d(i)=gcd{n≥1:(P^n)_ii>0}, with d(i)=0 when this return-length set is empty. A state or communicating class of period one is aperiodic.
Any two communicating states have the same recurrent/transient classification and the same period, including the convention d=0 when there are no positive return lengths.

A communicating class containing a recurrent state is closed. Within any recurrent communicating class, starting from any state in that class, the first hit T_{j}=inf{n≥0:X_n=j} of each specified state j in the class is finite almost surely (including the time-zero case when the start is j).
Every finite nonempty irreducible Markov chain is positive recurrent: E_i tau_i^+<infinity for every state i. Aperiodicity is not assumed.
Textbook terminology, provenance or comparison for classes, periods and recurrence; no additional mathematical statement is introduced.

A probability pi on S is stationary for P when pi P=pi. It satisfies detailed balance when pi_i P_ij=pi_j P_ji for all i,j. A stationary chain is reversible when every finite path segment has the same law as the same segment read in reverse order.

A P-Markov chain with initial law pi has shift-invariant finite-dimensional distributions iff pi P=pi. For every probability pi satisfying detailed balance with P, pi is stationary. No irreducibility is required for either statement.
If P is irreducible on a nonempty countable state space and pi is a stationary probability, then pi_i>0 for every i∈S.

For any stationary probability pi, on its support S_pi={i:pi_i>0} define P*_ij=pi_j P_ji/pi_i. This is a stochastic kernel on S_pi, and the reversal of every finite segment of the stationary P-chain has the segment law of the P*-Markov chain started from pi on S_pi. A stationary P-chain is reversible iff pi satisfies detailed balance; no irreducibility is assumed.
Textbook terminology, provenance or comparison for stationarity and reversal; no additional mathematical statement is introduced.

For a countable nonempty irreducible chain P, a stationary probability exists iff at least one state is positive recurrent. In that event every state is positive recurrent, the stationary probability pi is unique, and pi_i=1/E_i tau_i^+ for every state i. Aperiodicity is not assumed.

For the countable irreducible positive recurrent chain with its unique stationary probability pi, for every reference state i and every j∈S, E_i[sum_{0≤n<tau_i^+}1_{X_n=j}]=pi_j/pi_i. The excursion includes time zero and excludes the returning endpoint.

A closed communicating class can be treated as a countable irreducible chain by restricting P to that class. Consequently within a recurrent communicating class, positive recurrence and null recurrence are class properties: if one state is positive recurrent then all are; if one state is null recurrent then all are.
For probability measures μ,ν on a countable state set S with all subsets measurable, define d_TV(μ,ν)=sup_{A⊆S}|μ(A)−ν(A)|.
For probabilities μ,ν on a countable state set S, d_TV(μ,ν)=(1/2)∑_{i∈S}|μ_i−ν_i|=1−∑_{i∈S}min(μ_i,ν_i).
For every stochastic matrix P on the countable state set S and every pair of probabilities μ,ν on S, d_TV(μP,νP)≤d_TV(μ,ν).
For every coupling (U,V) of probabilities μ,ν on a countable state set S, d_TV(μ,ν)≤P(U≠V); there exists a coupling with equality.
If μ_n and μ are probabilities on a countable state set S and μ_n(i)→μ_i for every i∈S, then d_TV(μ_n,μ)→0.
Bibliographic reference to textbook treatments of total variation and coupling; context only.

For a countable irreducible positive recurrent aperiodic stochastic matrix P with stationary probability π, d_TV(P^n(i,·),π)→0 for every i∈S. For every initial probability λ on S, d_TV(λP^n,π)→0 as well.
Bibliographic comparison for the aperiodic-convergence theorem; context only.

If a countable stochastic matrix P is irreducible and positive recurrent with period d, there is a partition S=D_0⊔⋯⊔D_{d−1} into nonempty classes, with every one-step law from D_ℓ supported on D_{ℓ+1 mod d}; its stationary probability π assigns each D_ℓ mass 1/d. Here positive recurrence ensures d≥1.

For a countable irreducible positive recurrent P of period d and a cyclic partition S=⊔_{ℓ=0}^{d−1}D_ℓ as in this theorem, every i∈D_ℓ and integer 0≤r<d satisfy P^{md+r}(i,·)→d·π(·∩D_{ℓ+r mod d}) in total variation as m→∞.

For a countable irreducible positive recurrent stochastic matrix P with stationary probability π, without assuming aperiodicity, every initial probability λ satisfies (1/n)∑_{k=0}^{n−1}λP^k→π in total variation as n→∞.
Under the cyclic-class theorem hypotheses, if the period d>1, every point-start time-n law is supported on a single cyclic class and d_TV(P^n(i,·),π)≥1−1/d for every i and n≥0.

The two-state stochastic chain that deterministically alternates between its states has period 2, stationary law assigning each state mass 1/2, and point-start laws that alternate the single states and stay at total variation distance 1/2 from stationarity.
A periodic chain initialized with a stationary probability retains that stationary probability as every time marginal.
Bibliographic references for periodic and Cesàro convergence; context only.

For a finite irreducible aperiodic stochastic matrix P, there exists an integer m≥1 for which every entry of P^m is positive. Define c_j=min_i(P^m)_{ij} and ε=∑_j c_j. Then 0<ε≤1, and for all initial probabilities μ,ν and every n≥0, d_TV(μP^n,νP^n)≤(1−ε)^{floor(n/m)}d_TV(μ,ν), with a power of exponent zero equal to 1, including when ε=1.

Let P be finite, irreducible and aperiodic with stationary law π, and choose m≥1 with all entries of P^m positive. Put ε=∑_j min_i(P^m)_{ij}∈(0,1]. For every initial law μ and every real 0<δ<1, if ε<1 then at every integer n≥m·ceil(log(1/δ)/(−log(1−ε))) one has d_TV(μP^n,π)≤δ. If ε=1 then μP^m=π (and stationarity persists thereafter).
Description of the common-mass proof method and its textbook provenance; context only.

For a countable irreducible positive recurrent P with stationary probability π, every real function f:S→ℝ satisfying ∑_jπ_j|f(j)|<∞ and every initial law λ satisfy (1/n)∑_{k=0}^{n−1}f(X_k)→∑_jπ_j f(j) almost surely under P_λ. No aperiodicity is assumed.

Description of the regenerative proof and its textbook provenance. The L¹(π) scope and absence of an aperiodicity assumption are already retained in the trajectory ergodic theorem; no additional independent result is introduced.

For a random walk, P_i and E_i denote probability and expectation with initial point i. For A in the state space, T_A=inf{n≥0:X_n∈A}, with inf∅=∞; T_a=T_{\{a\}}, and T_i^+=inf{n≥1:X_n=i} is the first positive return to the initial point.

For an integer N≥1 and real 0<p<1, put q=1−p and define the nearest-neighbor chain on {0,…,N} that moves from an interior i to i+1 with probability p and to i−1 with probability q, with 0 and N absorbing; let T=T_{\{0,N\}}.

For the absorbing ruin walk with integer N≥1 and 0<p<1, the boundary hitting time T=T_{\{0,N\}} is almost surely finite and has finite expectation from every i∈{0,…,N}, including the endpoints and the case N=1.
For the absorbing ruin walk with integer N≥1, 0<p<1, q=1−p, and every i∈{0,…,N}, h_i=P_i(T_N<T_0) equals i/N if p=q and (1−(q/p)^i)/(1−(q/p)^N) if p≠q. The formula includes i=0, i=N, and N=1.
Bibliographic references for first-step equations and gambler’s ruin; context only.
For the absorbing ruin walk of W20 with integer N≥1, 0<p<1, q=1−p, T=T_{\{0,N\}}, and h_i=P_i(T_N<T_0), every i∈{0,…,N} satisfies E_i T=i(N−i) if p=q and E_i T=(N h_i−i)/(p−q) if p≠q.

For the nearest-neighbor walk on all of ℤ with independent increments +1 of probability 0<p<1 and −1 of probability q=1−p, for every integer i>0, P_i(T_0<∞)=(q/p)^i if p>q and 1 if p≤q. For every integer i<0, P_i(T_0<∞)=(p/q)^{−i} if p<q and 1 if p≥q.
For the nearest-neighbor walk on ℤ with independent +1/−1 increments of probabilities 0<p<1 and q=1−p, the probability from 0 of a positive return to 0 is P_0(T_0^+<∞)=2 min(p,q).
For the symmetric independent nearest-neighbor walk on ℤ (p=q=1/2), E_1 T_0=E_{−1} T_0=E_0 T_0^+=∞, with expectations in the extended nonnegative sense.
For every integer d≥1, define the simple symmetric walk on ℤ^d by X_n=X_0+ξ_1+⋯+ξ_n, where ξ_i are independent and each point ±e_j, 1≤j≤d, has probability 1/(2d).
For d≥1 define the torus T^d=(ℝ/(2πℤ))^d, with its Lebesgue probability measure m, namely Lebesgue measure on a fundamental cube divided by (2π)^d.
Bibliographic provenance for the lattice-walk Fourier argument; context only.
For integer d≥1 and t∈T^d, define φ(t)=(1/d)∑_{j=1}^d cos(t_j).

For the simple symmetric walk on ℤ^d, d≥1, with φ(t)=(1/d)∑ cos(t_j) and normalized Lebesgue measure m on T^d, its origin return probabilities satisfy P^n_{00}=∫_{T^d}φ(t)^n dm(t) for every n≥0, and P^n_{00}=0 for odd n.

For d≥1 and φ(t)=(1/d)∑ cos(t_j) on T^d, the set {|φ|=1} consists exactly of 0 and boldπ=(π,…,π). For each t_* in this pair there exist a local Euclidean coordinate u centered at t_*, positive constants a,b,η, and a coordinate ball of radius η such that whenever ||u||≤η, a||u||²≤1−|φ(t_*+u)|≤b||u||².
The simple symmetric walk on ℤ^d is recurrent for d=1 or d=2 and transient for each integer d≥3 (the standing dimension domain is d≥1).
For every integer d≥1, the simple symmetric walk on ℤ^d admits finite constants 0<c_d≤C_d such that c_d n^{−d/2}≤P^{2n}_{00}≤C_d n^{−d/2} for every integer n≥1.

For a finite connected undirected simple graph G=(V,E) with at least two vertices, define the uniform-neighbor transition kernel P_{uv}=1/deg(u) if {u,v}∈E and 0 otherwise. All degrees are positive, so this defines a stochastic kernel.
For a finite connected undirected simple graph with at least two vertices, the uniform-neighbor random walk is reversible and has unique stationary probability π(u)=deg(u)/(2·#E).

For the uniform-neighbor random walk on a finite connected undirected simple graph with at least two vertices, the period is 2 when the graph is bipartite and 1 when it is nonbipartite. In the nonbipartite case its laws converge in total variation to π(u)=deg(u)/(2·#E) from every initial probability.

For the uniform-neighbor kernel P of a finite connected undirected simple graph with at least two vertices and every real 0<α<1, the kernel αI+(1−α)P has the same stationary probability π(u)=deg(u)/(2·#E), is aperiodic, and converges in total variation to π from every initial probability.
Bibliographic provenance for the detailed-balance and graph-period arguments; context only.

For an irreducible reversible stochastic matrix P on a finite nonempty state space S, let π be its strictly positive stationary probability. Define the real ℓ²(π) inner product ⟨f,g⟩_π=∑_{x∈S}π(x)f(x)g(x), the norm by ||f||²_{2,π}=⟨f,f⟩_π, and the function operator Pf(x)=∑_yP_{xy}f(y).

For an irreducible reversible stochastic matrix P on a finite nonempty S with stationary π, P is self-adjoint on real ℓ²(π) and has operator norm at most 1. For every real f,g:S→ℝ, E(f,g)=⟨f,(I−P)g⟩_π=(1/2)∑_{x,y∈S}π(x)P_{xy}(f(x)−f(y))(g(x)−g(y)). The nullspace of I−P consists exactly of constant functions.

For an irreducible reversible stochastic matrix P on a finite state space with at least two states and stationary π, all eigenvalues of the half-lazy kernel (I+P)/2 are nonnegative, and its spectral radius on H_0={f:∑_xπ(x)f(x)=0} is strictly less than 1.

For an irreducible reversible stochastic matrix P on a finite state space S with at least two states, stationary π, and r the maximum absolute eigenvalue on H_0={f:∑_xπ(x)f(x)=0}, every i∈S and every integer n≥0 satisfy d_TV(P^n(i,·),π)≤(1/2)√(π(i)^{−1}−1)·r^n, with r^0=1.
For a finite irreducible reversible P with stationary probability π, define its Dirichlet form on real functions by E(f,g)=⟨f,(I−P)g⟩_π.

For finite irreducible reversible P with strictly positive stationary π and at least two states, let H_0={f:S→ℝ:∑_xπ(x)f(x)=0}; let r be the maximum of the absolute values of the eigenvalues of the restriction of P to H_0.

For an irreducible reversible stochastic matrix P on a finite nonempty state set S with stationary π, a nonempty boundary B⊆S and arbitrary prescribed real values g:B→ℝ, there exists a unique h:S→ℝ equal to g on B and satisfying Ph=h on S∖B. It is h(x)=E_x[g(X_{T_B})], and it is the unique minimizer of E(f,f) among real functions f:S→ℝ equal to g on B. This includes B=S and the singleton-state case; T_B is almost surely finite, making the displayed boundary expectation defined.
Bibliographic reference for boundary hitting equations; context only.

For every finite horizon n≥0, real submartingale X_0,…,X_n relative to its filtration on a probability space, Z=max_{0≤k≤n}X_k, and λ>0, λP(Z≥λ)≤E[X_n·1_{Z≥λ}]≤E[X_n^+]. If X is nonnegative, the last term is E X_n.
Bibliographic references for Doob’s weak maximal inequality; context only.

For a nonnegative real submartingale X_0,…,X_n on a probability space, real exponent 1<p<∞, and X_n∈L^p, the finite maximum Z=max_{0≤k≤n}X_k satisfies ||Z||_p≤p/(p−1)||X_n||_p. In particular, for every real martingale M with M_n∈L^p, ||max_{0≤k≤n}|M_k|||_p≤p/(p−1)||M_n||_p.
Textbook comparisons for the strong Lᵖ maximal inequality; no additional mathematical assertion.

Fix real a<b and n≥0. For a finite real sequence x₀,…,xₙ, an upcrossing of [a,b] is a buy time s with x_s≤a followed by a strictly later sale time t with x_t≥b. Define the greedy completed upcrossing count Uₙ(a,b) by buying at the first available time with value≤a, selling at the first later time with value≥b, and restarting the next search at the time after that sale. Only completed upcrossings count; a sale at n counts.

For every finite real sequence x₀,…,xₙ and real a<b, its greedy completed upcrossing count Uₙ(a,b) equals the largest natural m for which there are ordered crossing pairs 0≤s₁<t₁<s₂<t₂<⋯<s_m<t_m≤n with x_(s_j)≤a and x_(t_j)≥b for every j. The empty list gives m=0.

For an integrable real submartingale X on a filtered probability space, every finite n≥0 and real a<b, let Uₙ(a,b) count greedy completed upcrossings along X₀,…,Xₙ with the inclusive endpoint and final-time conventions above. Then (b−a) E Uₙ(a,b) ≤ E[(Xₙ−a)⁺]−E[(X₀−a)⁺] ≤ E[(Xₙ−a)⁺]+E[(X₀−a)⁻].
Textbook provenance and comparison of the source’s inclusive endpoint convention with the strict cutoff of a fixed Mathlib implementation; no additional mathematical conclusion.

Let M₀,…,Mₙ be a real martingale and suppose deterministic finite real bounds a_k,b_k satisfy a_k≤M_(k+1)−M_k≤b_k almost surely for each 0≤k<n. Put V=∑_(k<n)(b_k−a_k)². For V>0 and every t>0, max{P(Mₙ−M₀≥t), P(Mₙ−M₀≤−t)}≤exp(−2t²/V), and consequently P(|Mₙ−M₀|≥t)≤2 exp(−2t²/V). If V=0, both one-sided probabilities are zero for every t>0. Independence of increments is not a hypothesis.
Citation to Azuma for the classical martingale bound; mathematical scope is the stated theorem.

For the uniform-integrability and convergence chapter, the ambient measure is a probability measure. Integrability of Banach-valued random variables means Bochner integrability; a strongly measurable representative means a representative that is an almost-everywhere limit of measurable simple functions. All martingales and submartingales in the chapter’s convergence theorems are real-valued.

Every Bochner-integrable Banach-valued random variable has a strongly measurable representative, meaning an almost-everywhere limit of measurable simple functions. Such a representative can be obtained by taking the limit on the measurable set where the approximating simple functions converge and setting its value to zero elsewhere.

For an arbitrary index set I and a family (X_i)_(i∈I) of integrable random variables in a real or complex Banach space, define uniform integrability by lim_(R→∞) sup_(i∈I) E[‖X_i‖ 1_{‖X_i‖>R}]=0. For real values use absolute value. The supremum of an empty family of nonnegative bounds is defined to be zero.

For every integrable family of random variables in a real or complex Banach space on a probability space, the uniform-integrability condition lim_(R→∞) sup_i E[‖X_i‖ 1_{‖X_i‖>R}]=0 is equivalent to the same condition with ‖X_i‖≥R in the indicator. The empty-family supremum is zero.

Every uniformly integrable family (X_i) of integrable random variables with values in a real or complex Banach space on a probability space is bounded in L¹: sup_i E‖X_i‖<∞, with the empty-family supremum equal to zero.

On a sequence of independent fair coin tosses, let Fₙ reveal the first n tosses, let Aₙ be the event that those n tosses are all heads, take A₀=Ω, and define Mₙ=2ⁿ1_(Aₙ). This is a real martingale and E|Mₙ|=1 for every n≥0. The probability of heads forever is limₙ2^(−n)=0, and Mₙ→0 almost surely. For every real threshold R one can choose n with 2ⁿ>R and E[Mₙ1_{Mₙ>R}]=1. Thus (Mₙ) is neither uniformly integrable nor convergent in L¹, despite being L¹-bounded and converging almost surely.

For any integrable family (X_i)_(i∈I) in a real or complex Banach space on a probability space, the following are equivalent (empty-family suprema of nonnegative quantities are zero): (1) the family is uniformly integrable; (2) sup_i E‖X_i‖<∞ and for every ε>0 there is δ>0 such that E[‖X_i‖1_A]<ε for every i and every measurable event A with P(A)<δ; (3) there exists a finite nonnegative nondecreasing convex function Φ:[0,∞)→[0,∞) such that Φ(t)/t→∞ as t→∞ and sup_i E Φ(‖X_i‖)<∞. This includes the existence of such a Φ under uniform integrability, not a prescribed Φ as an extra assumption.
Textbook provenance for uniform-integrability criteria and the scalar case; no additional result.

Let Xₙ be Bochner-integrable random variables in a Banach space on a probability space and let X be a random variable in that same space. If Xₙ→X in probability and (Xₙ) is uniformly integrable, then X has a Bochner-integrable representative and E‖Xₙ−X‖→0. A strong-measurability hypothesis on the limit is not silently added; the representative is part of the conclusion. The Banach space may be real or complex.

For a sequence of Bochner-integrable random variables in a real or complex Banach space on a probability space, convergence in L¹ to a Banach-valued limit implies convergence in probability to that limit and uniform integrability of the sequence.
Comparison with Kallenberg and scalar Vitali versions in prerequisite sources; no additional result.

If a real submartingale (Xₙ,Fₙ) satisfies supₙE|Xₙ|<∞, then there exists an integrable real random variable X∞ measurable for F∞=σ(⋃ₙFₙ) such that Xₙ→X∞ almost surely. The theorem does not assert L¹ convergence under this first-moment bound alone.
For a real submartingale (Xₙ,Fₙ) on a probability space, supₙE|Xₙ|<∞ if and only if supₙ E Xₙ⁺<∞.
The remark repeats that the already-required doubling example shows the first-moment bound alone does not imply L¹ convergence, and supplies references for the upcrossing proof.

For a uniformly integrable real martingale (Mₙ,Fₙ), there is an integrable F∞-measurable real variable M∞, with F∞=σ(⋃ₙFₙ), such that Mₙ→M∞ almost surely and in L¹, and Mₙ=E[M∞|Fₙ] almost surely for every n≥0.
For any integrable real random variable Y and increasing filtration (Fₙ) of sub-sigma-algebras of the ambient probability space, the process (E[Y|Fₙ])_(n≥0) is a uniformly integrable martingale.
Every uniformly integrable real submartingale (Xₙ,Fₙ) has an integrable F∞-measurable real limit X∞, where F∞=σ(⋃ₙFₙ), with Xₙ→X∞ almost surely and in L¹; for every n≥0, Xₙ≤E[X∞|Fₙ] almost surely.
Conditional-expectation prerequisite provenance and textbook comparison; no additional result.

Let M be a real martingale, let real p satisfy 1<p<∞, and assume C=supₙ E|Mₙ|ᵖ<∞. Then Mₙ→M∞ almost surely and in Lᵖ for an integrable terminal limit M∞ (with the F∞-measurable representative supplied by terminal closure), and Mₙ=E[M∞|Fₙ] almost surely for each n.
Textbook comparisons for higher-moment martingale convergence; no additional result.

For increasing sub-sigma-algebras Fₙ on a probability space and any integrable real Y, put F∞=σ(⋃ₙFₙ). Then E[Y|Fₙ]→E[Y|F∞] almost surely and in L¹. If additionally Y∈Lᵖ for a real p with 1<p<∞, the same convergence also holds in Lᵖ.
Textbook comparison for Lévy’s upward theorem; no additional result.
For decreasing sub-sigma-algebras Gₙ on a probability space, put G∞=⋂ₙGₙ. For any integrable real random variable Y, E[Y|Gₙ]→E[Y|G∞] almost surely and in L¹.
Textbook comparisons for Lévy’s downward theorem; no additional result.

For a real martingale M with Mₙ∈L² at every n≥0, put D_k=M_(k+1)−M_k. The increments D_k are pairwise orthogonal in L²: E[D_iD_j]=0 for every distinct i,j; and each D_k is orthogonal to M₀: E[M₀D_k]=0.
For a real martingale M with Mₙ∈L² for every n, and D_k=M_(k+1)−M_k, E[Mₙ²]=E[M₀²]+∑_(k<n)E[D_k²] for every n≥0.
For a real martingale M with Mₙ∈L² for every n and D_k=M_(k+1)−M_k, M is L²-bounded if and only if the nonnegative series ∑_(k≥0)E[D_k²] is finite.

For a real martingale M with Mₙ∈L² for every n, if M is L²-bounded (equivalently, ∑_(k≥0)E[(M_(k+1)−M_k)²]<∞), then it converges almost surely and in L² to M∞. With D_k=M_(k+1)−M_k, E[M∞²]=E[M₀²]+∑_(k≥0)E[D_k²] and, for every n≥0, E[(M∞−Mₙ)²]=∑_(k≥n)E[D_k²].
Textbook comparison for orthogonal martingale increments; no additional result.

Let X be a real integrable submartingale on a filtered probability space. If σ and τ are stopping times with σ≤τ≤N pointwise, where N is a finite deterministic nonnegative integer, then the stopped variables are integrable and E[X_τ|F_σ]≥X_σ almost surely, and E X_σ≤E X_τ. The stopped sigma-algebra uses the source definition inside F∞=σ(⋃ₙFₙ).
Textbook comparisons for bounded optional sampling; no additional result.

Let M be a real integrable martingale and let stopping times σ,τ satisfy σ≤τ≤N pointwise for a finite deterministic nonnegative integer N. Then E[M_τ|F_σ]=M_σ almost surely and E M_τ=E M_σ; the stopped variables are integrable.

Let M be a uniformly integrable real martingale and let stopping times σ≤τ be pointwise ordered and possibly infinite. Use the integrable F∞-measurable terminal representative M∞ from terminal closure as the value M_ρ on {ρ=∞}, for ρ=σ,τ, with M_ρ=M_n on {ρ=n}. Then M_σ and M_τ are integrable, E[M_τ|F_σ]=M_σ almost surely, and E M_τ=E M_σ=E M₀. The specified terminal value on the infinite layer is essential to the statement.
Textbook comparisons for sampling closed martingales; no additional result.

Let M be a real martingale and tau a stopping time with E tau<infinity. Suppose there exists a finite deterministic C≥0 such that E[ |M_{k+1}−M_k| | F_k ]≤C almost surely for every k≥0. Then M_tau is integrable and E M_tau=E M_0. The stop is finite almost surely, so the value on its null infinite layer may be assigned zero.
In particular, if M is a real martingale, τ is a stopping time with Eτ<∞, and a finite deterministic C≥0 satisfies |M_(k+1)−M_k|≤C almost surely for every k≥0, then M_τ is integrable and E M_τ=E M₀.

For simple symmetric random walk on Z starting at zero, the first hitting time τ of +1 is finite almost surely but Eτ=∞. Its stopped walk value is 1 almost surely, whereas its initial value is 0. Thus almost-sure finiteness of a stopping time together with bounded increments does not suffice to preserve a martingale’s expectation.

For the independent fair-coin doubling martingale Mₙ=2ⁿ1_(Aₙ), with Aₙ the event of n initial heads and M₀=1, take τ to be the first tail numbered from one. Then τ is a stopping time, P(τ>k)=2^(−k) for every k≥0, and Eτ=2. The stopped value M_τ is zero almost surely although M₀=1. On A_k, which has positive probability, E[ |M_(k+1)−M_k| | F_k ]=2ᵏ. Therefore there is no deterministic uniform bound on these conditional expected absolute increments, and an integrable stop alone does not suffice to preserve expectation.

Let (Y_k)_(k≥1) be identically distributed integrable real variables such that Y_k is F_k-measurable and independent of F_(k−1) for every k≥1. Put μ=E Y₁, S₀=0 and Sₙ=∑_(k=1)^n Y_k. If τ is a stopping time for this filtration with Eτ<∞, then S_τ is integrable and E S_τ=μ Eτ. Stopped values are taken on finite layers, and the a.s.-finite stop permits arbitrary null-layer representatives.

Under the hypotheses of Wald’s first identity—identically distributed integrable real Y_k, each F_k-measurable and independent of F_(k−1), μ=E Y₁, S₀=0, Sₙ=∑_(k=1)^nY_k, and stopping time τ with Eτ<∞—assume additionally v=E[(Y₁−μ)²]<∞. Then E[(S_τ−μτ)²]=v Eτ. This asserts a finite second moment for the centered stopped sum, without requiring Eτ²<∞ or asserting S_τ∈L² when μ≠0.
