For a commutative ring R with identity and any R-module M, form the tensor algebra T_R(M) = ⨁_{n≥0} M^{⊗_R n}, with M^{⊗_R 0} = R and tensor concatenation as multiplication. Define Sym_R(M) as the quotient by the two-sided ideal J generated by x⊗y − y⊗x for x,y ∈ M. The degree-n piece of this quotient is Sym_R^n(M). Write x₁⋯xₙ for the image of the pure tensor, with empty product 1 (lines 175–176). The chapter uses identity-preserving algebra maps.
For any commutative ring R with identity and any R-module M, the defining ideal J is homogeneous for the tensor grading, so Sym_R(M) inherits the quotient grading.

For any commutative ring R with identity and any R-module M, J has zero components in degrees 0 and 1. The canonical maps from scalars and from M identify Sym_R^0(M) with R and Sym_R^1(M) with M, respectively.
For any commutative ring R with identity and any R-module M, Sym_R(M) is a commutative R-algebra generated by the image of M in degree one.

For every commutative ring R with identity, R-modules M and N, and n≥0, sending an R-linear g : Sym_R^n(M) → N to (x₁,…,xₙ) ↦ g(x₁⋯xₙ) is a bijection onto the R-multilinear maps M^n → N invariant under every permutation of the n inputs. In degree zero this is evaluation at 1 and the target is the set of elements of N. In degree one it identifies the maps with all R-linear maps M → N.

For every commutative ring R with identity and n≥0, the symmetric multilinear bijection commutes with postcomposition along every R-linear map N → N′ and with precomposition along every R-linear map f : M → M′, using the induced Sym_R^n(f) on the linear-map side and applying f to each input on the multilinear side.

For any commutative ring R with identity, any R-module M, and any commutative R-algebra A, each R-linear map f : M → A extends uniquely along the canonical degree-one map M → Sym_R(M) to a unital R-algebra map Sym_R(M) → A.

Over a commutative ring R with identity, for a free module M with a specified finite basis e₁,…,eᵣ, including r=0, the assignment eᵢ ↦ Xᵢ induces a graded R-algebra isomorphism Sym_R(M) ≅ R[X₁,…,Xᵣ] with each Xᵢ of degree one.

For a finite free R-module with specified basis e₁,…,eᵣ over a commutative ring R with identity, in every degree n≥0 the monomials e₁^{a₁}⋯eᵣ^{aᵣ} indexed by nonnegative exponents of total degree n are an R-basis of Sym_R^n(M). If r=0 the basis is the singleton consisting of 1 in degree zero and is empty in positive degrees.
For a finite free module of basis size r≥1 over a commutative ring with identity, the degree-n monomial basis has binomial(n+r−1,n) indices for every n≥0.
Citation to Conrad for an alternative treatment of the already stated monomial basis.

For every unital homomorphism R → S of commutative rings and any R-module M, write M_S = S⊗_R M. The graded S-algebra map β_M : S⊗_R Sym_R(M) → Sym_S(M_S) given by s⊗(x₁⋯xₙ) ↦ s(1⊗x₁)⋯(1⊗xₙ) is an isomorphism. In degree zero the product is empty.

For every unital homomorphism R → S of commutative rings, any R-module M, and every n≥0, the degree-n restriction of the canonical symmetric-algebra comparison induces an S-linear isomorphism S⊗_R Sym_R^n(M) ≅ Sym_S^n(S⊗_R M), with the same formula on pure tensors.
For every unital homomorphism R → S of commutative rings and every R-linear map f : M → M′, the canonical symmetric-algebra comparisons satisfy β_{M′} ∘ (S⊗_R Sym_R(f)) = Sym_S(S⊗_R f) ∘ β_M.

For every pair of composable unital maps R → S → U of commutative rings and every R-module M, the direct canonical comparison from R to U agrees with first extending the R-to-S comparison to U and then applying the S-to-U comparison for S⊗_R M. The identifications on both sides are the usual associativity isomorphisms for scalar extension.
Citation to the Stacks Project for the corresponding pullback formula.

For a commutative ring R with identity, an R-module M, and q≥0, the exterior power is the quotient of M^{⊗_R q} imposing the vanishing of pure tensors with repeated inputs. The pure tensor class is the wedge x₁∧⋯∧x_q. The alternating condition applies in characteristic two as well.

For every unital homomorphism R → S of commutative rings, any R-module M, and each n≥0, the canonical exterior-power comparison S⊗_R ∧_R^n M → ∧_S^n(S⊗_R M) is an S-linear isomorphism. The paper gives its action on wedges at lines 305–312.

For every unital homomorphism R → S of commutative rings, any R-module M, and each q≥0, the degree-q exterior-power comparison sends s⊗(x₁∧⋯∧x_q) to s(1⊗x₁)∧⋯∧(1⊗x_q), with s acting on the resulting wedge. The comparison is the isomorphism displayed at lines 133–135. In a Koszul complex this gives the termwise comparison for every ring map, by taking the exterior powers of its defining free module.
The flatness remark refers to RK-04's external Koszul homology statement.
For M = (ℤ/2ℤ)e, the symmetric ℤ-algebra has the graded presentation Sym_ℤ(M) ≅ ℤ[X]/(2X) with e corresponding to the class of X in degree one.

For M = (ℤ/2ℤ)e with the presentation sending e to X in Sym_ℤ(M) ≅ ℤ[X]/(2X), the degree-zero part is ℤ. For every n>0 the degree-n part is the cyclic ℤ-module ℤ/2ℤ with generator e^n corresponding to X^n.

Along the reduction map ℤ → 𝔽₂, scalar extension of the graded presentation of Sym_ℤ((ℤ/2ℤ)e) yields 𝔽₂[X]. The base-changed module 𝔽₂⊗_ℤ(ℤ/2ℤ)e has rank one over 𝔽₂ with generator 1⊗e, and the canonical symmetric comparison identifies its symmetric algebra with that polynomial algebra, with 1⊗e corresponding to X.
The scalar extension ℤ → 𝔽₂ in this example is nonflat.
For M = 𝔽₂e₁ ⊕ 𝔽₂e₂ and τ the swap of the two factors of M⊗_{𝔽₂}M, the fixed subspace has basis e₁⊗e₁, e₂⊗e₂, and e₁⊗e₂ + e₂⊗e₁.

For that two-dimensional 𝔽₂-module the quotient map M⊗_{𝔽₂}M → Sym^2_{𝔽₂}(M) restricted to the τ-fixed subspace is neither injective nor surjective. It takes the nonzero fixed vector e₁⊗e₂ + e₂⊗e₁ to 2e₁e₂ = 0, while the nonzero symmetric basis monomial e₁e₂ is outside the restricted image.
The archived D05 averaging construction uses invertible factorials in its field setting. The quotient construction and basis results stated here apply in every characteristic.

Let k be a field of characteristic different from 2. For a quadratic form q on a finite-dimensional k-space use the normalized symmetric bilinear form B(x,y) = (q(x+y) − q(x) − q(y))/2. It satisfies q(x) = B(x,x).

Over a field k of characteristic different from 2, a quadratic space is nondegenerate when its normalized polar form has zero radical. An isometry of quadratic spaces is a k-linear isomorphism preserving q, equivalently preserving the normalized polar forms. The ambient spaces in this chapter are finite dimensional and nondegenerate.
The notation U ⊥ W means the direct sum with quadratic form equal to the sum of the two forms on their respective coordinates. For a ∈ k, ⟨a⟩ is the line k with form x ↦ ax².
Pointers to archived polarization and diagonalization.
For a subspace U of a quadratic space V with the stated normalized polar form B, define U^⊥ = {x ∈ V | B(x,u)=0 for every u ∈ U}.

Let V be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic space over a field of characteristic different from 2. For every subspace U with nondegenerate restricted form, the sum of the inclusions U and U^⊥ gives the orthogonal direct sum decomposition V = U ⊥ U^⊥, with the restriction to U^⊥ nondegenerate.
Over the chapter's field k, a vector e is isotropic when e≠0 and q(e)=0. A space is anisotropic when the only vector with value zero is the zero vector. In particular, the zero space is anisotropic.
A subspace T of a quadratic space over a field of characteristic different from 2 is totally isotropic when q restricts to zero on T. Equivalently, the normalized polar form is zero on T×T.
Over a field k of characteristic different from 2, the hyperbolic plane H is k² equipped with q_H(x,y)=xy.
Over a field of characteristic different from 2, H is isometric to ⟨1⟩ ⊥ ⟨−1⟩. The coordinates (s,t) ↦ (s+t,s−t) exhibit the equivalence with q_H.

Let V be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic space over a field of characteristic different from 2. For each e∈V with e≠0 and q(e)=0, there exists f∈V with f≠0, q(f)=0, and 2B(e,f)=1. For P=ke+kf, the map (s,t) ↦ se+tf identifies H isometrically with P, and V = P ⊥ P^⊥ with P^⊥ nondegenerate.

Let V be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic space over a field of characteristic different from 2. For every w∈V with q(w)≠0 the reflection s_w given by s_w(x)=x−(2B(x,w)/q(w))w is a linear isometry of V.

Let V be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic space over a field of characteristic different from 2. For every u,v∈V with q(u)=q(v)=a≠0, some composition of at most two reflections of the displayed form s_w with q(w)≠0 sends u to v. This includes equal u and v.

For finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic spaces U,V,W over a field of characteristic different from 2, an isometry U ⊥ W ≅ V ⊥ W implies an isometry U ≅ V. The common summand W may have dimension zero.
For finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic spaces U,V,W₁,W₂ over a field of characteristic different from 2, isometries W₁ ≅ W₂ and U ⊥ W₁ ≅ V ⊥ W₂ imply U ≅ V.

Every finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic space V over a field of characteristic different from 2 has a decomposition up to isometry V ≅ H^{⊥r} ⊥ A for an integer r≥0 and a finite-dimensional nondegenerate anisotropic quadratic space A, which may be zero. Here H^{⊥r} is the orthogonal sum of r hyperbolic planes, with H^{⊥0}=0.

For any two decompositions of a finite-dimensional nondegenerate space V over a field of characteristic different from 2 as H^{⊥r} ⊥ A and H^{⊥s} ⊥ A′ with A,A′ anisotropic and r,s≥0, one has r=s and A ≅ A′. The count and the isometry class of the remainder thus depend only on the isometry class of V.
The Witt index of V is the uniquely determined number r of hyperbolic planes in the Witt decomposition. The anisotropic part is its remainder A, determined up to isometry.

Let V be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic space over a field k of characteristic different from 2. For every totally isotropic subspace T⊆V of dimension m, there are m hyperbolic planes inside V in orthogonal direct sum whose chosen first isotropic basis vectors span T. For m=0 the sum is empty.

Let V be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic space over a field of characteristic different from 2, with Witt index r. Every totally isotropic subspace of dimension m satisfies m≤r, and there exists a totally isotropic subspace of dimension r.

Let V be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic space over a field of characteristic different from 2, with Witt index r. Every totally isotropic subspace maximal by inclusion among all totally isotropic subspaces of V has dimension r.
Citation to Elman, Karpenko, and Merkurjev for the general theory.
Over ℚ, the form q(x,y,u,v)=xy+u²−2v² on ℚ⁴ is the orthogonal sum of H and the nondegenerate anisotropic binary form u²−2v². Its Witt index is 1.

After extending scalars of the same form q(x,y,u,v)=xy+u²−2v² from ℚ to ℚ(√2), the last-coordinate binary form is hyperbolic and the extended form is isometric to H ⊥ H. Its Witt index over ℚ(√2) is 2.

The degreewise kernel of the tensor quotient is spanned by differences of pure tensors related by an adjacent exchange. These span the same relation module as all permutation differences.
Cancel a common quadratic line of value a ≠ 0 from the orthogonal sums of the finite-dimensional nondegenerate spaces in Witt cancellation.

The degree-n relation submodule of the symmetric quotient for n at least two is the R-linear span of differences of pure tensors related by adjacent swaps, equivalently by arbitrary permutations. The quotient by that span is canonically the actual symmetric degree, with the canonical quotient map on tensors.
For finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic spaces U,V over a field of characteristic different from two and a≠0, an isometry U⊥⟨a⟩≃V⊥⟨a⟩ implies U≃V.
The kernel in each tensor degree n ≥ 2 is the span of adjacent-swap differences, equivalently of all permutation differences. The quotient by this span is canonically the nth symmetric degree.
The algebra extension sends the class of each pure product to the product of the linear images and acts on scalars by the structure map.
Over a field of characteristic different from two, the common nondegenerate line of value a can be cancelled from an isometry U ⊥ ⟨a⟩ ≅ V ⊥ ⟨a⟩ for finite-dimensional nondegenerate U and V and a ≠ 0.
The intersection of the commutator ideal with the nth tensor degree for n≥2 is the span of adjacent-swap differences of pure tensors; permutation invariance is equivalent to adjacent-swap invariance.
Cancelling a common nondegenerate line with coefficient a ≠ 0 from two orthogonal sums U ⊥ ⟨a⟩ and V ⊥ ⟨a⟩ leaves isometric U and V.

For a finite group G, a chief series is a strictly increasing chain 1 = N₀ < N₁ < ⋯ < Nᵣ = G of subgroups normal in G such that no subgroup normal in G lies strictly between any consecutive Nᵢ₋₁ and Nᵢ. Its length is r and its chief factors are Nᵢ/Nᵢ₋₁ for 1 ≤ i ≤ r. For G = 1 the length-zero chain is allowed and the factor list is empty.
A G-group is a group equipped with an action of the ambient group G by group automorphisms.
For K ≤ L with both K and L normal in the same ambient group G, equip L/K with the well-defined conjugation action by automorphisms given by g · (xK) = (gxg⁻¹)K for g ∈ G and x ∈ L.
A G-isomorphism between two factors with actions of the same ambient G is a group isomorphism intertwining those actions.

For K ≤ L normal in G, the action of L on L/K obtained by restricting the ambient G-action induces every inner automorphism of L/K. Consequently every subgroup of L/K invariant under the G-action is normal in L/K.
Every finite group has a chief series.

For a finite group G, a strictly increasing chain from 1 to G of subgroups normal in G is a chief series if and only if for each consecutive pair Nᵢ₋₁ < Nᵢ the factor Nᵢ/Nᵢ₋₁ is a minimal nontrivial normal subgroup of G/Nᵢ₋₁.

Any two chief series of the same finite group G have equal lengths and the same multiset of G-isomorphism classes of factors. In particular their factors can be matched by a bijection of indices with a group isomorphism on each matched pair intertwining the two conjugation actions of the same G.
Proof comparison with D07 and reference to the ordinary group-isomorphism version of chief-factor uniqueness, which also follows by forgetting the action in GR02-C02.03.
A finite group G is solvable if and only if it has a chief series with elementary abelian factors. This includes the trivial group with the length-zero series.

If a finite group G is solvable, each factor of every chief series is the additive group of a nonzero finite-dimensional 𝔽ₚ-vector space for some prime p that may depend on the factor, and the ambient G-action on that factor is 𝔽ₚ-linear.

In A₄ let V = {1, (12)(34), (13)(24), (14)(23)}. The subgroup V is elementary abelian of order 4 and is minimal nontrivial normal in A₄. Conjugation by (123) cycles its three nonidentity elements. The quotient A₄/V has order 3. The chain 1 < V < A₄ is chief with factors isomorphic to V and C₃, respectively. The conjugation action on V factors through A₄/V and permutes the three nonzero vectors of V, while the action on A₄/V is trivial.

For the specified V of double transpositions and the identity in A₄ and U = ⟨(12)(34)⟩, the chain 1 < U < V < A₄ is a composition series with adjacent normality and factors of orders 2, 2 and 3. Conjugation by (123) sends U to a different subgroup, so U fails ambient normality and the chain fails to be chief.

An extension of Q by N is an exact sequence of discrete groups 1 → N → E → Q → 1 with the inclusion and quotient homomorphism p specified, and N identified with its image. A splitting is a homomorphism s:Q → E with p ∘ s = id_Q. A complement is a subgroup H ≤ E with NH = E and N ∩ H = {1}. Abelian coefficient kernels are written additively, and integral group homology uses trivial coefficients unless otherwise specified.

For every specified extension, taking the image sends a splitting to a complement and taking the inverse of the isomorphism p|_H:H → Q sends a complement H to its splitting. These operations are inverse.

For a specified extension of Q by an arbitrary group N, choose a set-theoretic section s:Q → E with s(1) = 1. Put α_q = conj_{s(q)}|_N ∈ Aut(N) and f(q,r) = s(q)s(r)s(qr)⁻¹ ∈ N. These are normalized by α₁ = id_N and f(q,1) = f(1,q) = 1. They satisfy α_q ∘ α_r = Inn(f(q,r)) ∘ α_{qr} and f(q,r)f(qr,t) = α_q(f(r,t))f(q,rt) for all q,r,t ∈ Q, where Inn(n)(x) = nxn⁻¹.

For the normalized section s of an extension of Q by N, any normalized change s′(q) = b(q)s(q) with b:Q → N and b(1) = 1 changes the data to α′_q = Inn(b(q)) ∘ α_q and f′(q,r) = b(q)α_q(b(r))f(q,r)b(qr)⁻¹.

For each specified extension of Q by N, q ↦ [α_q] defines a homomorphism Q → Out(N) = Aut(N)/Inn(N), the quotient by the normal subgroup of inner automorphisms. It is independent of the normalized section used to compute α_q.

Conversely, for groups N and Q and any α:Q → Aut(N), f:Q × Q → N satisfying the two factor-system identities and α₁ = id_N, f(q,1) = f(1,q) = 1, the product (n,q)(m,r) = (nα_q(m)f(q,r), qr) makes N × Q an extension with inclusion n ↦ (n,1) and quotient (n,q) ↦ q. For data extracted from a normalized s of an original extension, (n,q) ↦ ns(q) identifies the constructed extension with the original, preserving N and Q.
For an extension of Q by an abelian group A, conjugation on A by any lift of q ∈ Q is independent of the lift and defines the induced left Q-action on A by automorphisms.
For extensions with specified common abelian kernel A and quotient Q, an equivalence is a homomorphism of the middle groups inducing the identity on A and on Q.
Every homomorphism between the middle groups of such extensions that induces the identity on the abelian kernel A and quotient Q is an isomorphism.

For a left Q-module A and a one-cochain a:Q → A, the inhomogeneous two-coboundary is (δa)(q,r) = a(q) + q·a(r) − a(qr). A two-cochain c:Q × Q → A is a two-cocycle if c(q,r) + c(qr,t) = q·c(r,t) + c(q,rt) for all q,r,t. It is normalized if c(1,q) = c(q,1) = 0 for all q.

Every ordinary inhomogeneous H²(Q,A) class has a normalized two-cocycle representative. If two normalized cocycles differ by δa, then a(1) = 0. Thus inclusion identifies normalized cocycles modulo coboundaries from normalized one-cochains with ordinary H²(Q,A).

For a fixed left Q-action on an abelian group A, the equivalence classes of specified extensions of Q by A inducing that action correspond bijectively to ordinary H²(Q,A). The correspondence sends an extension to the class of its factor cocycle, and the class of a normalized c corresponds to the extension with product (x,q)(y,r) = (x + q·y + c(q,r), qr).

In the correspondence for the fixed left Q-action on A, an extension represents zero in H²(Q,A) if and only if it admits a splitting. The split class is represented by the semidirect product for that action.

Given a split extension of Q by an abelian A and a chosen reference splitting s₀, the A-conjugacy classes of complements to A in E are in bijection with H¹(Q,A) for the induced left action. The complement with splitting s(q) = z(q)s₀(q) corresponds to the class of z, and the class of s₀(Q) corresponds to zero.
Further reading for the extension correspondences and for the cohomological Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre sequence, with a transition to the homological sequence developed here.

For A = C₂ and Q = C₂ = {1,t} with trivial action, evaluation at (t,t) determines a normalized two-cocycle uniquely and takes both values in A. Normalized two-coboundaries are zero. There are exactly two H² classes and corresponding extension classes. The class c(t,t) = 0 has middle group C₂ × C₂. The class c(t,t) equal to the nonzero element of A has middle group C₄, in which the specified lift (0,t) generates the group and has square (1,1_Q), with 1 in A denoting its nonzero element.
For subgroups U,V of an ambient group E, [U,V] is the subgroup generated by uvu⁻¹v⁻¹ for u ∈ U and v ∈ V. In particular [E,E] is the commutator subgroup.
For any group K, integral group homology in degree one with trivial coefficients identifies naturally with K/[K,K], taking the class of the bar cycle [k] to the class of k in the abelianization.

For each extension 1 → N → E → Q → 1 of discrete groups there is a natural exact sequence H₂(E;ℤ) → H₂(Q;ℤ) → N/[E,N] → H₁(E;ℤ) → H₁(Q;ℤ) → 0 for trivial integral coefficients. The maps on homology between E and Q are induced by the quotient p:E → Q. The map out of N/[E,N] is induced by inclusion into E and the identification with H₁(E;ℤ) after abelianization. The map from H₂(Q;ℤ) is the homological transgression d²₂,₀ into the stated quotient. Its sign in the bar convention d[a|b] = [b] − [ab] + [a] is specified at lines 578–585. For a lifted normalized bar two-cycle with boundary written as a sum of differences [nx] − [x], the transgression gives the same sum of classes of n in N/[E,N], using additive notation in that quotient. Naturality is with respect to compatible maps of extensions.

For any free presentation 1 → R → F → G → 1, the Schur multiplier H₂(G;ℤ) identifies naturally with (R ∩ [F,F])/[F,R]. The isomorphisms commute with maps of free presentations. The induced map of the displayed subquotients for a group homomorphism G → G′ is independent of the choice of lift between free presentations, giving the canonical comparison for different presentations of a fixed G (lines 618–627).
For every finite cyclic group C_m of positive order m, H₂(C_m;ℤ) = 0.
For all m,n ≥ 1, H₂(C_m × C_n;ℤ) is isomorphic to C_{gcd(m,n)}, with the trivial group in the case gcd(m,n) = 1.

A central extension of G is an extension whose kernel lies in the center of the middle group. It is universal if for every central extension of G there is a unique homomorphism from its middle group to the other middle group commuting with the two maps to G. A group is perfect if it equals its commutator subgroup.
A group G admits a universal central extension if and only if G is perfect.

For a perfect group G and any free presentation F/R ≅ G, the homomorphism [F,F]/[F,R] → G induced by the presentation is a universal central extension. Its source is perfect and its central kernel is isomorphic to H₂(G;ℤ).
Downstream reference to the Algebraic K-Theory B12 application, which identifies K₂(R) with H₂(E(R);ℤ) for the stable elementary group E(R) in that application.
Chapter motivation and reference to the companion Krull-topology construction, introducing the use of all finite-index normal subgroups of an arbitrary abstract group.

For any abstract group G let 𝒩(G) be all normal subgroups of finite index, including G itself. For M ⊆ N in 𝒩(G), the transition homomorphism q_{M,N}:G/M → G/N sends gM to gN. Define Ĝ as the compatible tuples (x_N)_N in the product of these finite quotients, satisfying q_{M,N}(x_M) = x_N for every M ⊆ N. Give it coordinatewise group operations and the subspace topology from the product of finite discrete groups. The projection p_N evaluates at N, and the canonical group homomorphism η_G is g ↦ (gN)_N.

The intersection of any finite collection from 𝒩(G) belongs to 𝒩(G), including the empty intersection G. It is a common refinement of the collection under inclusion. The transition homomorphisms obey identity and composition, so these quotients constitute a cofiltered inverse system.
For every abstract group G, the specified completion Ĝ is a compact, Hausdorff and totally disconnected topological group.
For every N ∈ 𝒩(G), p_N:Ĝ → G/N is a continuous surjective homomorphism. The kernels ker(p_N) are clopen normal subgroups and form a neighborhood basis at the identity of Ĝ.
For every abstract group G, η_G has dense image in Ĝ and ker(η_G) is the intersection of all N ∈ 𝒩(G).

For every finite group G with the discrete topology, η_G:G → Ĝ is a topological group isomorphism. Its inverse is the coordinate at the trivial subgroup, under the canonical identification G/{1} ≅ G.

For any abstract group G, any profinite group P regarded as a topological inverse limit of finite discrete groups, and any abstract group homomorphism f:G → P, there is a unique continuous group homomorphism f̂:Ĝ → P with f̂ ∘ η_G = f.

Every abstract group homomorphism f:G → H induces a continuous group homomorphism f̂:Ĝ → Ĥ with f̂ ∘ η_G = η_H ∘ f. The induced map of the identity is the identity, and the induced map of a composite is the composite of the induced maps.

Let G be any abstract group and 𝒟 ⊆ 𝒩(G) satisfy that for every N ∈ 𝒩(G) there is a D ∈ 𝒟 with D ⊆ N. Restriction of compatible tuples to 𝒟 induces a topological group isomorphism Ĝ → lim_{D ∈ 𝒟} G/D, using the induced transition maps and the inverse-limit topology.

The finite-index subgroups of the additive integers are precisely nℤ with n > 0. The completion ℤ̂ identifies as a topological group with the compatible residue classes in lim_{n>0} ℤ/nℤ, with transition from m to n whenever n divides m. The canonical map sends k to its residue class at each coordinate.

The family of subgroups j!ℤ is cofinal among the finite-index subgroups of ℤ, since every positive integer divides some factorial. Restriction identifies ℤ̂ with the inverse limit of the quotients ℤ/j!ℤ by a topological group isomorphism.

For every finite field 𝔽_q, the absolute Galois group Gal(𝔽̄_q/𝔽_q) with its Krull topology is topologically isomorphic to the profinite completion of the additive integers. The q-power Frobenius x ↦ x^q corresponds to η_ℤ(1). This is the finite-field residue comparison cited in the example.
An abstract group G is residually finite if, for each g ≠ 1 in G, there exists a homomorphism from G to a finite group with nonidentity value on g.
For any abstract group G, residual finiteness is equivalent to injectivity of its canonical map η_G:G → Ĝ.
In a residually finite group G, every finite subset S of G, including the empty set and singletons, admits an N ∈ 𝒩(G) such that the single quotient map G → G/N is injective on S.
Every finitely generated abelian group is residually finite.
For every set of generators, with no finiteness restriction, the free group on that set is residually finite.
Reference explaining the relationship between the proof's partial permutations and completing a labelled path to a finite covering graph.
Every homomorphism from the additive rationals ℚ to any finite group is trivial. Hence every finite quotient of ℚ is trivial, its profinite completion is trivial, and η_ℚ has dense image.

For a nonempty reduced free word of length ℓ on any set of generators, the right-to-left signed steps prescribe injective domain and range assignments for each generator and extend to permutations on {0,…,ℓ}. Each signed permutation moves vertex i−1 to vertex i in action order, and generators absent from the word act by the identity.

Agreed low-degree bar model. The identity-containing tuples span a subcomplex of the standard integral bar complex. Projection to its quotient computes integral homology naturally through degree two, with the signed bar boundaries and the entrywise group maps.

For every group extension the induced normalized chain projection is degreewise surjective, its kernel complex J has J₀=0, and H₁(J) is naturally N/[E,N], sending the class of [i(n)x]−[x] to the class of n. The homology map from J into the middle-group bars is induced by the inclusion of N under this identification.

The specified stable Steinberg map is a universal central extension, with perfect middle and base groups.

Scope and notation for the supplement. Rings and algebra maps are unital, the algebra structure map is central, density and quivers use left modules, and full corners use right modules. Endomorphisms multiply by composition and the rightmost path acts first. The passage also explains the result keys.

Coverage and cross-references to companion work. The current mathematical scope is the supplement for C03 through C06. The C01 and C02 foundations and the foundations and companion results cited under C03 through C06 are existing work referred to for context and reuse.
Chapter orientation and references to Schur’s lemma, semisimple splitting and a field version of density. These references supply background for the chapter’s interpolation theorem.

Let R be a unital ring and M a nonzero simple left R-module, with right D-vector-space structure m · f^op = f(m) for D = End_R(M)^op. For every finite right D-linearly independent list x₁,…,xₙ in M, including the empty list, and every list y₁,…,yₙ of the same length in M, there is a single r ∈ R such that rxᵢ = yᵢ for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n.

For a unital ring R and nonzero simple left R-module M, set D = End_R(M)^op, with the endomorphism ring multiplied by composition. D is a division ring, and m · f^op = f(m) gives the right D-vector-space structure on M. Left multiplication by R on M gives the unital ring homomorphism ρ: R → End_D(M), where End_D(M) consists of right D-linear endomorphisms.

For every unital ring R and nonzero simple left R-module M with D = End_R(M)^op acting by evaluation on the right, the image of ρ: R → End_D(M) is dense in the topology of agreement on finite subsets. Equivalently, for each T ∈ End_D(M) and each finite subset S of M, there exists r ∈ R such that rs = T(s) for all s ∈ S.

For a unital ring R and a nonzero simple left R-module M, put D = End_R(M)^op with its right evaluation action. If M is finite-dimensional over D on the right, the action ρ: R → End_D(M) induces an isomorphism of unital rings R/Ann_R(M) → End_D(M), sending r + Ann_R(M) to the operator m ↦ rm. Here Ann_R(M) is the two-sided ideal {r ∈ R | rm = 0 for every m ∈ M}.
On End_D(M) for the density setting, the finite topology has a neighborhood basis at each T consisting of {U ∈ End_D(M) : U(s) = T(s) for all s ∈ S}, for finite subsets S of M.

Let k be a field and V a k-vector space with countably infinite basis v₀,v₁,…. Let F(V) be the ideal of finite-rank k-linear endomorphisms of V and R = k·1_V + F(V) ⊆ End_k(V). Under the natural evaluation action V is a faithful simple left R-module, and its commutant End_R(V) is exactly the scalar endomorphisms k·1_V. The action image in End_k(V), identified with the density theorem’s target through the scalar commutant, is proper and dense for agreement on finite subsets.

Throughout the central simple algebra chapter, k is a field and algebras and algebra maps are unital, with the given scalar structure central. A simple algebra is nonzero and has no nonzero proper two-sided ideal. For a field extension L/k use A_L = A ⊗_k L as an L-algebra.

The cited Artin–Wedderburn theorem and finite and real division-ring results are established inputs. The text also points to its finite-dimensional density corollary and to the Stacks Project for comparison.

A central simple k-algebra is a finite-dimensional simple k-algebra A with Z(A) = k1_A. A central division k-algebra is a finite-dimensional division k-algebra with the same center condition. Such a central simple algebra is split if it is k-algebra isomorphic to M_n(k) for some integer n ≥ 1. A field extension L/k splits A if A_L is split over L.

Every central simple k-algebra A has a k-algebra presentation A ≅ M_r(D) for r ≥ 1 and D a central division k-algebra. In any two such presentations, the matrix sizes are equal and the division factors are k-algebra isomorphic.

Let T be a finite-dimensional simple k-algebra, with arbitrary center, and write its simple-Artinian presentation as T ≅ M_s(E) with E a division algebra. Every finite-dimensional nonzero left T-module V is a direct sum of m ≥ 1 copies of the unique simple column module E^s, with m determined by dim_k V. As a k-algebra End_T(V) ≅ M_m(E^op), so it is simple and (dim_k T)(dim_k End_T(V)) = (dim_k V)^2.
For every central simple k-algebra A, the left/right multiplication map A ⊗_k A^op → End_k(A) is a k-algebra isomorphism, sending a ⊗ b^op to the endomorphism x ↦ axb.

Over a field k, if A is central simple and B is any simple k-algebra, A ⊗_k B is simple and its center is exactly the image 1 ⊗ Z(B) under z ↦ 1 ⊗ z. In particular the tensor product of two central simple k-algebras is central simple.
For every central simple k-algebra A and every field extension L/k, the L-algebra A_L is central simple.

For every central simple k-algebra A the dimension dim_k A is a square. Define deg A as the positive integer n with n² = dim_k A. There exists a finite Galois extension K/k with a K-algebra isomorphism A_K ≅ M_n(K).
If a central simple k-algebra A has division presentation A ≅ M_r(D) and d = deg D, then D contains a separable k-subfield E of degree [E:k] = d for which D_E is split. The degree of A is rd.

For a central simple k-algebra A with division presentation A ≅ M_r(D), define its index ind(A) = deg D. For every finite field extension L/k splitting A, ind(A) divides [L:k]. There exists a separable splitting field of A of degree exactly ind(A).

For a central simple k-algebra A and a simple k-algebra B, any two unital k-algebra embeddings f,g:B ↪ A are conjugate by a single unit of A. Equivalently, there exists u ∈ A^× such that f(b)u = ug(b) for every b ∈ B. In particular every k-algebra automorphism of A is inner.

For a unital simple k-subalgebra B of a central simple k-algebra A, put C = C_A(B) = {x ∈ A | ∀ b ∈ B, xb = bx}. Then C is simple, (dim_k B)(dim_k C) = dim_k A, C_A(C) = B, and Z(C) = Z(B) as subalgebras of A.

If B is a unital central simple k-subalgebra of the central simple k-algebra A and C is its centralizer in A, C is central over k and multiplication B ⊗_k C → A, b ⊗ c ↦ bc, is a k-algebra isomorphism.

For a central division k-algebra D, every maximal k-subfield E has [E:k] = deg D and splits D, including when E/k is inseparable. The separable subfield of degree deg D that splits D in RM03-C04.05 is a maximal subfield.

For a central simple k-algebra A of degree n and any a ∈ A, there is a unique reduced characteristic polynomial χ_a^red(t) ∈ k[t] whose coefficientwise image over every splitting field L/k is the matrix characteristic polynomial of φ(a ⊗ 1) for every L-algebra isomorphism φ:A_L ≅ M_n(L). This specifies descent to k and independence of the splitting field and splitting isomorphism.

For a central simple k-algebra A of degree n, define Nrd(a) = (−1)^n χ_a^red(0). The reduced norm is a homogeneous polynomial of degree n on the k-vector space A, commutes as a polynomial with scalar extension along any field extension of k, is multiplicative, and satisfies Nrd(a) ≠ 0 exactly when a is a unit of A.
Over a splitting field K of a central simple k-algebra A of degree n, the reduced norm-one equation is identified by a K-algebra splitting with the determinant-one equation defining SL_n over K.
The text identifies the descended norm-one group as SL_1(A) and refers to companion Result F05 for that descent and the corresponding PGL_1(A) inner form.

For central simple k-algebras A and B define Brauer equivalence by the existence of p,q ≥ 1 with a k-algebra isomorphism M_p(A) ≅ M_q(B). This is an equivalence relation and each class has a unique central division k-algebra representative up to k-algebra isomorphism.

The Brauer-equivalence classes of central simple k-algebras form an abelian group Br(k) with well-defined sum [A]+[B] = [A ⊗_k B], identity 0 = [k], and additive inverse −[A] = [A^op]. The class [A] equals zero exactly when A is split.
Every field extension L/k induces a group homomorphism Br(k) → Br(L), [A] ↦ [A_L]. For a tower k ⊆ L ⊆ F of fields the composite Br(k) → Br(L) → Br(F) is the homomorphism for F/k.

There are exactly two real Brauer classes, represented by ℝ and Hamilton's quaternion algebra ℍ. The class [ℍ] is nonzero and has order two, with quaternion conjugation giving an ℝ-algebra isomorphism ℍ^op ≅ ℍ. Thus Br(ℝ) ≅ ℤ/2ℤ.

In Hamilton's quaternion algebra ℍ, the subfield ℝ[i] ≅ ℂ has degree two over ℝ and splits ℍ. In the Hamilton basis 1,i,j,k with i²=j²=−1 and k=ij=−ji, there is a complex-algebra splitting ℍ_ℂ ≅ M_2(ℂ) sending i to diag(𝑖,−𝑖), where 𝑖 is the complex imaginary unit, and j to the matrix with rows (0,1) and (−1,0). For all a,b,c,d ∈ ℝ, the determinant of the image of a+bi+cj+dk is a²+b²+c²+d², which is the reduced norm of the quaternion.

For every finite Galois extension K/k, define the relative Brauer group Br(K/k) as the kernel of Br(k) → Br(K). It consists exactly of the Brauer classes represented by central simple k-algebras split by K.

Let K/k be finite Galois, let G = Gal(K/k), and fix n ≥ 1. Degree-n central simple k-algebras split by K up to k-algebra isomorphism correspond bijectively to the pointed nonabelian cohomology set H¹(G,PGL_n(K)) for the coefficientwise G-action. A splitting transports the coefficient action to a semilinear action on M_n(K) of the form X ↦ g_σ σ(X) g_σ⁻¹ with projective cocycle (g_σ). Conversely a projective cocycle acts by that semilinear conjugation and its fixed algebra is the corresponding split-by-K central simple k-algebra of degree n. Changes of splitting correspond to projective coboundary equivalence. Here a projective cocycle satisfies g_(στ) = g_σ σ(g_τ) in PGL_n(K), and the equivalence on cocycles identifies g with g′ when g′_σ = h⁻¹g_σ σ(h) for a single h ∈ PGL_n(K) and all σ.

Let K/k be finite Galois with group G and let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space with a semilinear G-action for the given action on K. The fixed vectors span V over K, and the canonical map K ⊗_k V^G → V, λ⊗v ↦ λv, is a K-linear isomorphism. If V is a K-algebra and the action respects multiplication, this is a K-algebra isomorphism. G-equivariant K-algebra maps descend by restriction to the fixed k-subalgebras.

For each finite Galois K/k with group G, the relative Brauer group is isomorphic to H²(G,K^×) with the usual Galois action on K^×. For the transported semilinear action X ↦ g_σ σ(X) g_σ⁻¹ and invertible lifts G_σ of the projective cocycle g_σ, the map sends [A] to the class of the scalar 2-cocycle c_(σ,τ) = G_σ σ(G_τ) G_(στ)⁻¹. Its scalar class is independent of lifts, splitting, and matrix enlargement, and it multiplies under tensor products. This is the convention inverse to Stacks Equation (59.61.5.1) with the same lifts.

For any field k and separable closure k^s, the Brauer group Br(k) is isomorphic to H²_cts(G_k,(k^s)^×), where G_k = Gal(k^s/k) has its profinite topology and the coefficient group (k^s)^× is discrete with its natural Galois action. The isomorphism uses the same scalar cocycle convention as the relative isomorphism and restricts at each finite Galois splitting stage to the relative class map followed by inflation and coefficient inclusion, compatibly with extension between finite Galois stages. The target continuous cohomology is canonically the filtered colimit of H²(Gal(K/k),K^×) over finite Galois subextensions K/k of k^s, with the same inflation and coefficient-inclusion transitions.
The full-corner chapter uses right modules and cites the existing right-progenerator theorem and its converse as background for identifying the corner functors.
For every unital ring R and e ∈ R with e² = e, the right R-module eR is finitely generated and projective.

For every unital ring R and full idempotent e ∈ R, the category of right R-modules and the category of right eRe-modules are equivalent by the specified inverse functors. The forward functor sends M to Me with its induced right eRe-action and restricts morphisms. The inverse sends N to N ⊗_{eRe} eR with its right R-action, using the usual (eRe,R)-bimodule eR and tensoring morphisms with its identity.

For every unital ring R and e ∈ R with e² = e, the map eRe → End_R(eR) given by a ↦ (x ↦ ax) is an isomorphism of unital rings, with identity e in eRe and composition in the right-module endomorphism ring.

For a unital ring R and an idempotent e ∈ R, use the right ideal eR, the corner ring eRe with multiplication inherited from R and identity e, and fullness ReR = R, where ReR denotes the two-sided ideal of finite sums of products res with r,s ∈ R.

For every unital ring R and e ∈ R with e² = e, the right R-module eR generates the category of right R-modules, so that every right R-module is a quotient of a direct sum of copies of eR, if and only if e is full, i.e. ReR = R.

For the stated full-corner equivalence of right-module categories, the counit at each right R-module M is the multiplication isomorphism Me ⊗_{eRe} eR → M, m' ⊗ x ↦ m'x. For any finite expression 1 = Σᵢ rᵢ e sᵢ witnessing fullness, its inverse is m ↦ Σᵢ (m rᵢ e) ⊗ (e sᵢ).

For each unital ring R and n ≥ 1, the diagonal matrix unit e₁₁ is a full idempotent in Mₙ(R). Its corner e₁₁Mₙ(R)e₁₁ is isomorphic as a unital ring to R by taking the (1,1) entry. Thus the stated full-corner functors give the equivalence of right-module categories for Mₙ(R) and R.

For two nonzero unital rings A and B, e = (1,0) is an idempotent in A × B. Its corner is isomorphic as a unital ring to A, and e is non-full. The corner functor M ↦ Me sends the nonzero right (A × B)-module B, obtained by restriction along the second projection A × B → B, to the zero module.

The chapter works over a field k with unital k-algebras and left module actions. End_k(V) uses composition, and an arrow acts from its source summand to its target summand. These conventions govern the chapter's obligations.

For every k-algebra A and k-vector space V, unital k-algebra homomorphisms ρ:A→End_k(V) correspond bijectively to left A-module structures on V extending its given k-vector-space structure. In the correspondence a acts by ρ(a). For any two such representations on k-vector spaces, a k-linear map is an intertwiner if and only if it is A-linear for the corresponding actions.

For every two-sided ideal I of a k-algebra A, restricting along A→A/I identifies the category of unital left A/I-modules with the full subcategory of left A-modules V for which IV=0, preserving all module maps. The inverse action is (a+I)v=av.

The group representation G→GL_k(V) and its linear extension to k[G] illustrate the algebra representation setup. The text refers the group-algebra correspondence, Schur's lemma and Maschke's theorem with its characteristic hypothesis to Algebra Core, and introduces the quiver case.

A finite quiver Q=(Q₀,Q₁,s,t) has a finite nonempty vertex set Q₀, a finite arrow set Q₁, and source and target maps s,t:Q₁→Q₀. Loops and parallel arrows are allowed. There is a length-zero path eᵢ:i→i at each vertex. A positive-length path p=a_ℓ⋯a₁ traverses a₁ first with t(a_b)=s(a_{b+1}) for 1≤b<ℓ, has length ℓ, source s(a₁) and target t(a_ℓ).

For a finite quiver Q as defined above, kQ is the k-vector space freely based on all its paths, allowing finite linear combinations. For basis paths p,q define pq by concatenating with q first when s(p)=t(q), and by zero otherwise. Concatenating with a matching length-zero path leaves the other path unchanged. Extend multiplication k-bilinearly.
For every finite quiver Q, the stated multiplication makes kQ an associative unital k-algebra. The length-zero paths eᵢ are pairwise orthogonal idempotents and their sum over the vertices equals 1.
For every pair of vertices i,j of a finite quiver Q, the paths from i to j form a k-basis of the corner eⱼ(kQ)eᵢ.
For every finite quiver Q, kQ is finite-dimensional over k if and only if Q has no oriented cycle.

A representation V of Q assigns a k-vector space Vᵢ to each vertex and a k-linear map Vₐ:V_{s(a)}→V_{t(a)} to each arrow. Its path map on p=a_ℓ⋯a₁ is V_{a_ℓ}∘⋯∘V_{a₁}, with V_{eᵢ}=id_{Vᵢ}. A morphism f:V→W is a family of k-linear maps fᵢ:Vᵢ→Wᵢ with f_{t(a)}∘Vₐ=Wₐ∘f_{s(a)} for every arrow. Identities and composition are at each vertex.

For every finite quiver Q there is a k-linear equivalence between all unital left kQ-modules and representations of Q. It takes M to vertex spaces eᵢM and to arrow maps m↦am:eᵢM→eⱼM for a:i→j, and restricts module maps to the vertex spaces. Its inverse takes V to ⊕ᵢVᵢ, with p:i→j acting by projection to Vᵢ, V_p, then inclusion of Vⱼ, extended k-linearly, and takes morphisms to the direct sums of component maps. The natural identifications on recovery of the original object give the inverse equivalence.

The stated k-linear module–representation equivalence for a finite Q restricts to an equivalence between kQ-modules finite-dimensional over k and representations with each vertex space finite-dimensional over k.

Under the stated module–representation equivalence for a finite Q, a sequence is exact as a sequence of kQ-modules if and only if its corresponding sequence of k-vector spaces and maps is exact at every vertex.

A relation from i to j is a finite k-linear combination r=∑ₚcₚp of paths from i to j. A representation satisfies r=0 when ∑ₚcₚV_p:Vᵢ→Vⱼ is the zero map. A set of relations defines the two-sided ideal of kQ that they generate.

Every two-sided ideal I of kQ is generated by relations with common source and target within each relation. Specifically the elements eⱼ r eᵢ with r∈I and vertices i,j are such relations in I and generate it, using r=∑_{i,j} eⱼ r eᵢ.
The arrow ideal J of kQ is the two-sided ideal generated by all arrows. A two-sided ideal I of kQ is admissible when some integer m≥2 satisfies J^m⊆I⊆J².

For any two-sided ideal I of kQ generated by a set of relations, the stated path-algebra equivalence via restriction along kQ→kQ/I identifies the category of unital left kQ/I-modules with the full subcategory of quiver representations satisfying every generating relation. On that subcategory the morphisms are the original quiver morphisms, and the direct-sum path action factors through kQ/I.

For any two-sided ideal I of kQ generated by a set of relations, exactness for the corresponding category of left kQ/I-modules, equivalently of representations satisfying those relations, is equivalent to exactness of the induced sequence at every vertex.
For every integer m≥1, the power J^m of the arrow ideal is the k-linear span of all paths of length at least m.
For every integer m≥1 and every two-sided ideal I of kQ with J^m⊆I, kQ/I is finite-dimensional over k and is spanned by the images of the paths of length strictly less than m.
If m≥1 and J^m⊆I⊆J², the images in kQ/I of the entire family of length-zero and length-one paths are k-linearly independent.
Reference to Crawley-Boevey for the path convention, module equivalence and admissible ideals, followed by a lead-in to the two examples.

Let Q have exactly vertices 1,2 and one arrow a:1→2. The path basis is (e₁,e₂,a). The assignments e₁↦E₁₁, e₂↦E₂₂, a↦E₂₁ give a unital k-algebra isomorphism from kQ to the 2×2 lower triangular matrices. Its arrow ideal satisfies J²=0, so the zero ideal is admissible.

For the same one-arrow quiver, the representation given by any k-linear T:V₁→V₂ yields the left lower triangular matrix action on V₁⊕V₂ through the specified isomorphism: the matrix with rows (x,0) and (u,y) sends (v₁,v₂) to (xv₁,uT(v₁)+yv₂).

For the quiver with exactly one vertex and one loop a, the paths are aⁿ for n≥0, with a⁰=e the vertex. The assignment xⁿ↦aⁿ induces k[x]≅kQ as k-algebras. The relation a²=0 generates I=J², which is admissible, and the induced isomorphism k[x]/(x²)≅kQ/I gives the basis of classes of 1 and x.

A left module for the one-loop algebra kQ/I with I generated by a² is a k-vector space V with a k-linear endomorphism T=Vₐ satisfying T²=0. A morphism to another such pair (W,U) is precisely a k-linear f:V→W with fT=Uf. In the polynomial quotient the explicit action is (λ+μx)v=λv+μT(v).
Bibliography and source locators for Algebra Core, Abstract Algebra, Linear Algebraic Groups, Algebraic K-Theory, the MIT lecture notes, the Stacks Project and Crawley-Boevey.

The center of the positive-size matrix algebra over a division algebra consists of the scalar matrices with entries in that division algebra’s center, and the commuting endomorphisms of its simple left column are right multiplication by division coefficients.
For any central simple k-algebra A and field extension L/k, dim_L A_L = dim_k A.
Over an algebraic closure the scalar extension of every central simple k-algebra A is a matrix algebra of size deg A. The same holds for the central division factor.
For any subfield E of degree deg D in a central division algebra D, D has right E-dimension deg D and the map a ⊗ e ↦ (z ↦ aze) is an E-algebra equivalence D ⊗ E ≃ End_E(D).
For a unital simple k-subalgebra B of a central simple k-algebra A, the A ⊗_k B^op-linear endomorphism algebra of A is k-algebra isomorphic to C_A(B)^op by right multiplication.
Reduced characteristic polynomials commute with any field extension, also when the extension does not split the algebra.

For every finite arity, a continuous scalar cochain on the absolute Galois group of a separable closure, with discrete unit coefficients, has finite range and factors through restriction to a finite Galois subextension with values in the units of that subextension. A finite family admits a common stage above any given finite Galois stage.

For an idempotent e of a unital ring R, evaluation at e identifies Hom_R(eR,R) with Re as (R,eRe)-bimodules, and multiplication gives the natural right eRe-linear isomorphism M ⊗_R Re ≅ Me with inverse u ↦ u ⊗ e.
Representation kernels, images and cokernels are computed at the vertices with the induced arrow maps and canonical inclusions, corestrictions and quotient projections.
For each natural bound m and finite vertex and arrow sets, the subtype of paths of length less than m is finite.
Every k-subfield E of a central division k-algebra D with [E:k] = deg D is maximal.

Evaluation at e identifies Hom_R(eR,R) with Re as an (R,eRe)-bimodule, with inverse b ↦ (x ↦ bx). Balanced multiplication gives the natural right eRe-linear isomorphism M ⊗_R Re ≃ Me with inverse u ↦ u ⊗ e.
For a quiver with finitely many vertices and arrows, there are finitely many paths of length strictly below any natural bound.
Kernels, cokernels and images of representation morphisms are computed at vertices, with induced arrow maps and canonical inclusions or projections satisfying the corresponding universal properties.
Every k-subfield of a central division algebra D whose degree over k equals deg D is maximal.
The reduced characteristic polynomial commutes with every field extension, including an extension that does not split the algebra.

For any field k and separable closure S and each nonnegative integer r, a continuous cochain Gal(S/k)^r → Sˣ, with the Krull topology on the Galois group and discrete coefficients, has finite image. It factors through restriction to a finite Galois intermediate field E with coefficients in Eˣ.

For an idempotent e in a unital ring R, evaluation at e identifies Hom_R(eR,R) with Re as an (R,eRe)-bimodule, with inverse b ↦ (x ↦ bx) and with the corner action on Hom by precomposition. The natural right eRe-linear isomorphism M ⊗_R Re ≃ Me sends m⊗b to mb, with inverse u ↦ u⊗e.

For each natural bound, the paths of length strictly below that bound in a quiver with finite vertex and arrow sets form a finite type. The same fact is used in the truncation argument on lines 1085–1087.

The kernel and image of a quiver morphism are given by the vertexwise kernels and ranges with induced restrictions, and the cokernel by the vertexwise quotients by the ranges with descended arrow maps, with their universal properties.
Conversely, every k-subfield E of a central division algebra D with [E:k] = deg D is maximal.
The reduced characteristic polynomial and its generic polynomial commute coefficientwise with arbitrary extension of the base field, including a field that does not split A.

For every separable closure S/k and every nonnegative arity r, a continuous cochain on Gal(S/k)^r with values in discrete Sˣ has finite image and is induced from a cochain on a finite Galois quotient with coefficients in that finite Galois field.

Evaluation at e identifies Hom_R(eR,R) with Re as an (R,eRe)-bimodule. Multiplication M ⊗_R Re → Me is natural in right R-modules with inverse u ↦ u ⊗ e, giving the stated identification of the first corner functor.

For a morphism of quiver representations, the kernel and image are computed on the vertex kernels and ranges, and the cokernel on the vertex quotients by the ranges, with the induced arrow maps and canonical inclusions or quotient maps. The kernel, cokernel and image have their categorical universal properties.

For any field k and separable closure S/k, each continuous cochain Gal(S/k)^r → S^× for any r ≥ 0, with the Krull topology on the Galois group and discrete coefficients, has finite image and factors through the restriction to Gal(E/k)^r and the coefficient inclusion E^× → S^× for a finite Galois intermediate field E/k.

For every idempotent e, evaluation at e identifies Hom_R(eR,R) with Re as an (R,eRe)-bimodule. Balanced multiplication gives the natural right eRe-linear isomorphism M ⊗_R Re ≃ Me, with inverse u ↦ u ⊗ e, and thus identifies the dual tensor functor with the corner functor.
The linear extension of a group representation to the group algebra gives the action in the algebra-representation correspondence.
Vertex kernels and cokernels of maps of quiver representations give the corresponding categorical kernels and cokernels with the induced arrow maps.
For each natural m, a quiver with finite vertex and arrow sets has finitely many paths of length strictly less than m.

TeX preamble, title pages, notation and reading guide for the six ALG-09 chapters. The references to general bases, pseudo-reductive structure, buildings, parahoric models and modular representation theory describe extensions or proof inputs.

Work over an arbitrary field k unless otherwise stated. An affine algebraic group is an affine group scheme of finite type over k, with coordinate algebra k[G] and G(R) its points on a commutative k-algebra R. A closed subgroup is a closed subgroup scheme and may be nonreduced. The trivial group scheme is Spec k. Write k_s and k̄ for a separable and an algebraic closure.

For a finite-type affine k-scheme G, group-scheme structures on G are equivalent to natural group structures on R ↦ G(R) over all commutative k-algebras. Group-scheme homomorphisms correspond bijectively to natural transformations of the resulting group functors.

Taking R-points preserves fiber products, so (G ×_H L)(R) = G(R) ×_{H(R)} L(R) naturally. For any field extension K/k and K-algebra R, (G_K)(R) is naturally G(R), viewing R as a k-algebra. In coordinates A=k[G] this is Hom_K(A ⊗_k K,R) ≅ Hom_k(A,R).

The coordinate algebra functor is a contravariant equivalence between finite-type affine k-group schemes and finitely generated commutative Hopf k-algebras. The multiplication, identity and inverse correspond to the coproduct, counit and antipode and morphisms correspond to homomorphisms respecting these maps. The group is commutative if and only if its coproduct is cocommutative.

The additive group G_a and multiplicative group G_m represent R ↦ (R,+) and R ↦ R^× for every commutative k-algebra R. Their coordinate rings are k[x] and k[t,t⁻¹], with x primitive (counit zero and antipode −x) and t group-like (counit one and antipode t⁻¹).

For every matrix size n, GL_n and SL_n represent invertible matrices and determinant-one matrices over every commutative k-algebra R. Their coordinate rings are k[x_ij, det(X)⁻¹] and its quotient by det(X)−1, with matrix-product coproduct Δ(x_ij)=∑_ℓ x_iℓ⊗x_ℓj, identity-matrix counit and inverse-matrix antipode. The determinant is group-like. The coordinate rings of G_a^r and G_m^r are k[x_1,…,x_r] and k[t_1^±1,…,t_r^±1] with the respective Hopf rules on each variable.

A closed subgroup scheme H of an affine algebraic group G with A=k[G] corresponds to an ideal I for which ΔI⊆I⊗A+A⊗I, εI=0 and SI⊆I, with quotient Hopf algebra A/I. These descriptions commute with field extension.

A group homomorphism f:G→L has normal scheme kernel G×_L Spec k along the identity of L, whose defining ideal is the ideal f*(ker ε_L)k[G]. A closed subgroup is normal when conjugation G×H→G factors through H. The intersection of closed subgroups is cut out by the sum of their ideals, and the kernel and intersection descriptions commute with field extension.

Finite-dimensional rational representations, meaning group homomorphisms G→GL(V) on finite-dimensional k-spaces, correspond to right k[G]-coactions ρ:V→V⊗_k k[G]. Equivariant maps and stable subspaces correspond to comodule maps and subcomodules. This correspondence is compatible with tensor products, duals and change of field.
For a finite-dimensional rational representation with coaction ρ, the invariants are the kernel of v↦ρ(v)−v⊗1. Formation of this invariant subspace commutes with field extension.

For smooth G, a subspace of a finite-dimensional rational G-module is a G-submodule if its scalar extension to k̄ is stable under all G(k̄), using schematic density of the geometric points of smooth G.
Every vector of a k[G]-comodule is in a finite-dimensional subcomodule. Equivalently the comodule is the directed union of its finite-dimensional subcomodules.
Every affine algebraic group over k admits a closed immersion over k into GL(V) for some finite-dimensional k-vector space V.

For an action of an affine algebraic group H on a separated finite-type k-scheme X, the functor of points of X fixed by H after every further base change is represented by a closed subscheme X^H, compatible with field extension. For an action of G on such an X and x∈X(k), its stabilizer is the equalizer of the orbit map and the constant map G→X with value x, hence a closed subgroup of G compatible with field extension.

For any closed subgroup scheme H⊆G, the functor normalizing its base-changed subgroup scheme (conjugation by g carries H_R onto H_R) and the functor centralizing it (conjugation by g on H_R is the identity) are represented by closed subgroup schemes N_G(H) and C_G(H). Both commute with scalar extension.

For an affine algebraic group G, smoothness over k, geometric reducedness and smoothness at the identity are equivalent. Every affine algebraic group is smooth in characteristic zero. Over a perfect field reducedness suffices for smoothness.
If A↪B is an inclusion of finitely generated commutative Hopf k-algebras, B is faithfully flat as an A-algebra.

Every homomorphism f:G→H of affine algebraic groups factors uniquely as a faithfully flat morphism onto its scheme-theoretic image followed by a closed immersion. If N=ker f, this image represents the fppf sheaf quotient by the right action of N.

For every n>0 the power homomorphism [n]:G_m→G_m is faithfully flat, with coordinate algebra free on 1,t,…,t^{n−1} over k[t^n,t^{−n}]. Faithful flatness need not imply surjectivity on k-points, as the squaring map on R^× over k=ℝ shows.
In characteristic p>0 the identity inclusion 1→α_p is surjective on underlying topological spaces and is not flat.
For an affine k-group G in characteristic p>0, the Frobenius twist G^(p) has coordinate algebra k[G]⊗_{k,F_k}k, and the relative Frobenius group morphism F_{G/k}:G→G^(p) is induced by a⊗c↦ca^p.

In characteristic p>0 the relative Frobenius kernels on G_a and G_m are α_p=Spec k[z]/(z^p) and μ_p=Spec k[t,t⁻¹]/(t^p−1) as group schemes with the inherited Hopf structures. Each has length p, exactly one geometric point, and a one-dimensional tangent space at the identity.

Over a nonperfect field k of characteristic p>0, for c∈k∖k^p the equation Y^p−cX^p=0 defines a closed subgroup scheme of G_a² whose k-coordinate ring is a domain, but over k(c^(1/p)) the nonzero class of Y−c^(1/p)X is nilpotent. Thus reducedness over a nonperfect field does not imply geometric reducedness even for a group.

For any affine algebraic group G write m_e for the augmentation ideal of k[G]. The kernel of G(k[ε]/(ε²))→G(k) is the additive group of (m_e/m_e²)^∨. The Lie algebra structure on this tangent space is natural, with bracket extracted as the st coefficient of the commutator of tangent lifts over k[s,t]/(s²,t²). In a faithful matrix embedding this is XY−YX. The Lie algebra construction commutes with extensions of k and the differential of a group homomorphism is a Lie algebra homomorphism.
The differential at the identity of conjugation, after arbitrary base change, gives the rational adjoint representation Ad:G→GL(Lie G). Its differential is ad(X)=[X,−].

The Lie functor preserves finite fiber products. In particular Lie(ker f)=ker(df) for a group homomorphism f, and Lie of an intersection of closed subgroups is the intersection of their Lie algebras in Lie G.
The Lie algebras of GL_n and SL_n are all n×n matrices and trace-zero n×n matrices respectively, with commutator bracket. The Lie algebras of G_a and G_m are one-dimensional and abelian.
For a faithfully flat homomorphism f:G→H of smooth affine algebraic groups, its scheme kernel is smooth if and only if its differential at the identity is surjective.
In characteristic p>0 relative Frobenius G_a→G_a^(p) is faithfully flat with nonsmooth kernel α_p and zero differential. In coordinates k[x] is free of rank p over k[x^p].

The identity component G° of any affine algebraic group is open and closed, normal and geometrically connected. Its component group π₀(G) is finite étale, with a faithfully flat quotient G→π₀(G) whose kernel is G°, universal for homomorphisms from G to étale group schemes. The construction commutes with field extension. Over k̄ the component group is the finite group of connected components under multiplication.

For k perfect and every g∈G(k), there are unique commuting g_s,g_u∈G(k) with g=g_sg_u whose images in every finite-dimensional rational representation are the semisimple and unipotent parts of the operator induced by g, respectively. Both parts are functorial for homomorphisms of affine algebraic groups.

For a nonperfect field k of characteristic p>0 and a∈k∖k^p, multiplication by a^(1/p) on k(a^(1/p)) is an invertible k-linear operator with characteristic polynomial X^p−a. Over k̄ its semisimple part is a^(1/p) times the identity, which does not descend to k.

For every closed subgroup scheme H⊆G of affine algebraic groups there exist a finite-dimensional rational G-module V and a k-line L⊆V with scheme-theoretic stabilizer H. For every commutative k-algebra R, including nonreduced ones, H(R) equals the subgroup of G(R) preserving L⊗_k R.

Splitness is relative to the displayed ground field. Splitness for multiplicative-type groups means trivial Galois action on the character module, and for smooth connected unipotent groups means existence of a series with additive quotients.

For a finitely generated abelian group M set D(M)=Spec(k[M]). Its group-algebra basis has e^m e^n=e^{m+n}, Δ(e^m)=e^m⊗e^m, ε(e^m)=1 and S(e^m)=e^{−m}. For every commutative k-algebra R there is a natural identification D(M)(R)=Hom(M,R^×).

The functor D is an antiequivalence of finitely generated abelian groups with diagonalizable k-group schemes, with inverse the character group Hom_{k-gp}(−,G_m). Closed subgroups and fppf quotient groups correspond to quotient groups and subgroups of M respectively. For N⊆M the quotient D(M)→D(N) is faithfully flat with kernel D(M/N).
D(ℤ^r)=G_m^r and D(ℤ/nℤ)=μ_n. By the finitely generated abelian group decomposition, a diagonalizable group is a product of a split torus and finitely many groups μ_n.

A group of multiplicative type is an affine algebraic group that becomes diagonalizable over a separable extension of k. A torus is a group that becomes G_m^r over a separable extension, for some finite r. Their geometric character modules are the characters over k_s, with the natural action of Γ_k=Gal(k_s/k) and the discrete topology on the module.

Geometric characters give an antiequivalence of multiplicative-type k-groups with finitely generated discrete abelian groups with continuous Γ_k-action. The tori correspond to free abelian groups of finite rank, and trivial Γ_k-action corresponds exactly to the group being diagonalizable over k. The group for a module M can be obtained by descent of K[M] with σ(ae^m)=σ(a)e^{σm} for any finite Galois splitting extension through which the action factors. With compatible separable closures under L/k, the character module of the base change is the restriction along the induced map Γ_L→Γ_k.

In characteristic p>0 a group of multiplicative type is smooth exactly when its geometric character group has no p-torsion. In characteristic zero all such groups are smooth. A smooth connected group of multiplicative type is a torus, and a torus has these two properties.

For all n>0 there is an fppf-exact sequence 1→μ_n→G_m→[n] G_m→1. In characteristic p>0 the kernel is nonreduced if p|n, although the two copies of G_m are smooth. More generally isogenies of k-tori correspond in the opposite direction to Galois-equivariant inclusions of finite index of character lattices, and the character module of the kernel is the finite cokernel.

For a finite field extension K/k and affine finite-type K-scheme X, the affine finite-type Weil restriction Res_{K/k}X represents R↦X(R⊗_k K), and base change is compatible when the restriction after base change is taken for the resulting finite free algebra. It carries the natural group structure when X is a group. For X=G_m its norm morphism to G_m is the determinant of multiplication on R⊗_k K by the element of (R⊗_k K)^×.

For a separable quadratic extension K/k the norm-one kernel of Res_{K/k}G_m→G_m is a torus with geometric character lattice ℤ carrying negation by the nontrivial automorphism of K/k. After extension to K the split norm is (u,v)↦uv and the kernel is parameterized by (u,u⁻¹).
For ℂ/ℝ the norm-one torus as a real affine group is the circle a²+b²=1, with rational action on the real plane ℂ by multiplication by a+ib.

Every finite-dimensional rational D(M)-module has the canonical direct sum decomposition into V_m={v : ρ(v)=v⊗e^m} over m∈M. Tensor-product weights add, dual weights negate, and the invariant summand is V_0.
For every group of multiplicative type over k, the functor of invariants on finite-dimensional rational modules is exact, with no exclusion of torsion characters in the characteristic of k.

The following four conditions on an affine algebraic group U are equivalent. (1) Every nonzero finite-dimensional rational representation has a nonzero invariant vector. (2) Every such representation has a full invariant flag with trivial action on each one-dimensional quotient. (3) There exists a closed embedding U↪U_n. (4) A=k[U] admits an exhaustive increasing filtration by k-subspaces with C_0=k and Δ(C_r)⊆∑_{i=0}^r C_i⊗C_{r−i} for every r≥0.

The upper unitriangular matrix group U_n has all diagonal entries equal to 1. An affine algebraic group is called unipotent when it satisfies the equivalent representation, matrix-embedding or coalgebra conditions of B06.

For a smooth affine algebraic group, unipotence can equivalently be tested by the unipotence of every geometric point as a matrix in a faithful representation. The smoothness assumption is essential. In characteristic p>0 the matrices of μ_p(k̄) are trivial although the group scheme μ_p is not unipotent.

Unipotent affine algebraic groups are closed under closed subgroup schemes, faithfully flat quotients, and extensions with unipotent kernel and quotient. Unipotence is preserved and detected by any field extension.

A group that is both unipotent and of multiplicative type is trivial. Every homomorphism from either of these two types to the other is trivial. In particular the scheme intersection of a unipotent subgroup with a multiplicative-type subgroup is trivial.
A unipotent group is split over k if it admits a subnormal series with every successive fppf quotient isomorphic over k to G_a.

Every smooth connected unipotent group over a perfect field is split. Over any field, every smooth connected unipotent group splits over a finite purely inseparable extension, and if it splits over any separable extension then it was already split.

Every unipotent affine algebraic group is nilpotent. The filtration by vanishing superdiagonals on U_n has [U_n^(i),U_n^(j)]⊆U_n^(i+j) and additive vector-group quotients. For an arbitrary closed subgroup of U_n, the induced filtration refines to a central series with quotients closed subgroup schemes of G_a.

If char(k)=p>0 and c∉k^p, the equation y^p=x−cx^p defines a closed subgroup W of G_a² that is smooth, geometrically connected and unipotent. It is isomorphic to G_a after extension to k(c^(1/p)), but every k-morphism A¹→W is constant. In particular W contains no k-subgroup isomorphic to G_a.

For every smooth connected unipotent group U, there is a unique smooth connected split subgroup U_spl containing every split connected subgroup. It is normal in U, U/U_spl is wound, and formation of U_spl commutes with separable field extensions.

For a smooth connected unipotent k-group, being wound means that every k-morphism A¹→U is constant, equivalently that U contains no k-subgroup isomorphic to G_a. Woundness persists under separable field extension.

D(G) is the smallest normal closed subgroup scheme of G through which the commutator map G×G→G factors, equivalently the kernel of the universal commutative fppf quotient of G. Iteration gives the scheme-theoretic derived series, and G is solvable if that series terminates at 1.

The following four conditions on an affine algebraic k-group G are equivalent. (1) Every simple finite-dimensional rational representation is one-dimensional. (2) Every finite-dimensional rational representation has a full invariant flag. (3) G embeds as a closed subgroup of the group T_n of invertible upper triangular matrices for some n. (4) G has a normal unipotent subgroup U with fppf quotient G/U diagonalizable over k.
The invertible upper triangular group T_n is split solvable over k.

For a smooth connected algebraic group over an algebraically closed field, the scheme-theoretic derived subgroup is smooth and connected, and its geometric points are the ordinary abstract derived subgroup of the geometric points of G.
A split solvable group has a subnormal series over k with successive fppf quotients G_a or G_m.
Over an algebraically closed field, every nonzero finite-dimensional rational representation of a smooth connected solvable group has an invariant line, and hence a full invariant flag.

For a smooth connected solvable group G over a perfect field there is a smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup R_u(G) containing every unipotent closed subgroup scheme, including nonsmooth ones. Its fppf quotient is a torus and formation of this subgroup commutes with arbitrary field extension.

Over an arbitrary field a maximal-dimensional smooth connected normal unipotent k-subgroup is the largest smooth connected normal unipotent k-subgroup, but it need not equal the geometric unipotent radical after base change.

For a smooth connected solvable group over an algebraically closed field, multiplication realizes G as the semidirect product R_u(G)⋊T for a maximal torus T. Any two maximal tori are conjugate by an element of R_u(G)(k).
For a split solvable group over any field k, there exists a split torus T with G=R_u(G)⋊T. Any two maximal split tori of G are conjugate by R_u(G)(k).

If a split torus acts by group automorphisms on a smooth connected unipotent group over a perfect field, that group has a torus-stable central series with one-dimensional additive successive quotients.
For a split solvable group over any field, its smooth connected unipotent radical is split unipotent, and its quotient is a split torus.

If a split solvable k-group acts on a proper finite-type k-scheme X and X(k) is nonempty, the scheme-theoretic fixed-point locus has a k-point. In particular over an algebraically closed field, a smooth connected solvable group fixes a point in every nonempty proper k-scheme on which it acts.
The real norm-one torus for ℂ/ℝ has a two-dimensional rational real representation with no invariant real line, given by multiplication on ℂ viewed as a real plane.

Over ℂ the constant finite group scheme S_3 is solvable and disconnected. The plane x_1+x_2+x_3=0 in the three-dimensional permutation representation is a two-dimensional simple rational representation.

In characteristic p>0 the infinitesimal α_p and μ_p each have trivial geometric points and length p as group schemes. The character μ_p→G_m is nontrivial on the μ_p-valued dual-number point 1+ε, illustrating that geometric points do not detect nontrivial maps on infinitesimal group schemes.
Over a field k a split torus is a k-group isomorphic to a finite product of copies of G_m. A split reductive group contains such a k-torus that becomes a maximal torus over an algebraic closure.
For a smooth geometrically connected affine finite-type k-group, reductivity and semisimplicity are each preserved and reflected by every extension of the field k.

For every smooth geometrically connected affine finite-type k-group G, over an algebraic closure there are unique largest smooth connected normal unipotent and solvable subgroups, respectively R_u(G_bar k) and R(G_bar k). Over perfect k they are the base changes of the respective largest smooth connected normal unipotent and solvable k-subgroups.

A smooth geometrically connected affine finite-type k-group G is reductive when its geometric unipotent radical R_u(G_bar k) is trivial and semisimple when its geometric solvable radical R(G_bar k) is trivial.

For a nontrivial finite purely inseparable K/k, G=Res_{K/k} G_m is a smooth geometrically connected affine k-group with no nontrivial smooth connected unipotent k-subgroup, but has nontrivial geometric unipotent radical. The algebra K⊗_k bar k is local with residue field bar k and nonzero nilpotent maximal ideal J. Its unit group scheme sits in a split exact sequence with quotient G_m and kernel 1+J, whose filtration by 1+J^i has additive vector-group successive quotients J^i/J^{i+1}. Thus 1+J is the geometric unipotent radical.
Every affine connected smooth algebraic k-group has a maximal k-torus that remains maximal over bar k. All maximal tori of its base change to bar k are conjugate by geometric points.

For reductive G and maximal k-torus T the scheme-theoretic centralizer Z_G(T) equals T, and the quotient group scheme W(G,T)=N_G(T)/T is finite étale. For split G all split maximal tori are G(k)-conjugate. For any such T its Weyl group scheme is constant, and every Weyl element lifts to N_G(T)(k).

For a k-cocharacter λ:G_m→G of a smooth affine group, and each k-algebra R, define P_G(λ)(R) by the elements g∈G(R) for which t↦λ(t)gλ(t)^{-1} extends to A¹_R, and U_G(λ)(R) by those whose extension takes 0 to the identity. The subgroup giving a constant conjugation map is the scheme centralizer Z_G(λ). In a faithful λ-weight basis these functors are block triangular, unipotent block triangular and block diagonal respectively intersected with G. Evaluation at 0 gives a homomorphism P_G(λ)→Z_G(λ) split by the inclusion and with kernel U_G(λ).

For a cocharacter λ of a smooth affine k-group G, the limit subgroups P_G(λ), U_G(λ) and the scheme centralizer Z_G(λ) are smooth, with Lie algebras the nonnegative, strictly positive and zero weight subspaces for λ respectively. The limit map exhibits P_G(λ)=U_G(λ)⋊Z_G(λ), and multiplication U_G(−λ)×Z_G(λ)×U_G(λ)→G is an open immersion. If G is geometrically connected, these subgroups are geometrically connected.
The scheme centralizer of any k-torus in a smooth geometrically connected affine algebraic k-group is smooth and geometrically connected.

For a connected reductive k-group and a k-subtorus S, the scheme centralizer Z_G(S) is connected reductive. Geometrically, for any maximal torus T containing S and any Borel B containing T, the scheme intersection Z_G(S)∩B is a Borel of Z_G(S).

Over R the diagonal torus of SL₂ is split, whereas the rotation matrices with rows (a,−b),(b,a) and a²+b²=1 form a nonsplit torus, with its complex eigencharacters exchanged by complex conjugation. Both are one-dimensional maximal tori and are not SL₂(R)-conjugate.

For connected reductive G the scheme centre has a maximal torus Z_tor whose formation commutes with field extension. Multiplication Z_tor×G^der→G is a central isogeny with scheme kernel the intersection Z_tor∩G^der embedded by z↦(z,z^{-1}). A reductive group is semisimple exactly when its scheme centre is finite.
For every connected reductive G its scheme-theoretic derived group G^der is connected semisimple and G/G^der is a torus.

For a connected reductive group G, the scheme-theoretic derived group G^der is the smallest normal closed subgroup with commutative quotient, equivalently the closed subgroup generated schematically by the commutator morphism.

For n≥1 the central isogeny for GL_n is G_m×SL_n→GL_n, (z,A)↦zA, of scheme kernel μ_n embedded as z↦(z,z^{-1}I). For any k-algebra R and M∈GL_n(R), adjoining an n-th root z of det M gives a finite faithfully flat extension over which (z,z^{-1}M) lifts M. The kernel is non-étale in characteristic dividing n.

For a split connected reductive pair (G,T) set X=X*(T)=Hom(T,G_m) and Y=X_*(T)=Hom(G_m,T), with pairing fixed by χ(λ(t))=t^{⟨χ,λ⟩}. The absolute roots Φ(G,T) are the nonzero T-characters occurring in the adjoint representation on Lie(G).
For a split connected reductive pair (G,T), the zero-weight space in Lie(G) is Lie(T) and each absolute root space is one-dimensional. Thus dim G=dim T+|Φ(G,T)|.

For each absolute root α of a split connected reductive pair (G,T) there is a unique root subgroup U_α≃G_a normalized by T with conjugation weight α. There is a coroot α∨∈Y with ⟨α,α∨⟩=2 and a rational normalizer representative n_α∈N_G(T)(k) acting on X by s_α(x)=x−⟨x,α∨⟩α.

For the split connected reductive pair (G,T), the tuple (X,Φ,Y,Φ∨), with the perfect integer character–cocharacter pairing and root-to-coroot correspondence, is a reduced root datum. Its Weyl group generated by s_α identifies naturally with the group scheme W(G,T) viewed as a constant group.

For a split connected reductive pair (G,T), the scheme centre is the intersection in T of the scheme kernels of the roots α:T→G_m, equivalently the diagonalizable group D(X/ℤΦ). The formula holds as group schemes, including on nonreduced test algebras.

For a positive system given by a Weyl chamber, a simple root is a positive root that is not the sum of two positive roots. The base Δ consists of these simple roots, which are the inward root normals of the chamber walls. It is a linearly independent basis of the root lattice, and every root has integer coordinates in the base all of one sign.

For a split connected reductive pair and any cocharacter λ of the split maximal torus, the root groups U_α for ⟨α,λ⟩>0 multiply in any chosen order to give a scheme isomorphism from their product onto U_G(λ). This includes cocharacters on walls, keeping just the strictly positive weights.
The root lattice for SL₂ has index two in the torus character lattice. Its scheme centre is μ₂, including in characteristic two when the centre is not smooth.

The geometric Borel subgroups of a connected reductive k-group are the maximal smooth connected solvable subgroups over bar k. A Borel pair is such a Borel with a maximal torus in it. A k-Borel is a k-subgroup whose base change is a geometric Borel.
For a connected reductive k-group the geometric Borel subgroups are conjugate under G(bar k), as are the geometric pairs consisting of a Borel and a maximal torus in it.
